admah.d: earth, one of the five cities of the vale of Siddim (<reflink>Gen. 10:19</reflink>). It was destroyed along with Sodom and Gomorrah (19:24; Deut. 29:23). It is supposed by some to be the same as the Adam of Josh. 3:16, the name of which still lingers in Damieh, the ford of Jordan. (<see target="x-self">See ZEBOIM.</see>)

adjuration.d: a solemn appeal whereby one person imposes on another the obligation of speaking or acting as if under an oath (<reflink>1 Sam. 14:24; Josh. 6:26; 1 Kings 22:16</reflink>).

addi.d: ornament, (<reflink>Luke 3:28</reflink>), the son of Cosam, and father of Melchi, one of the progenitors of Christ.

addon.d: low, one of the persons named in Neh. 7:61 who could not "shew their father's house" on the return from captivity. This, with similar instances (ver. 63), indicates the importance the Jews attached to their genealogies.

adiel.d: ornament of God. (1.) The father of Azmaveth, who was treasurer under David and Solomon (<reflink>1 Chr. 27:25</reflink>). (2.) A family head of the tribe of Simeon (<reflink>1 Chr. 4:36</reflink>). (3.) A priest (<reflink>1 Chr. 9:12</reflink>).

adina.d: slender, one of David's warriors (<reflink>1 Chr. 11:42</reflink>), a Reubenite.

adino.d: the Eznite, one of David's mighty men (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:8</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See JASHOBEAM.</see>)

adbeel.d: miracle of God, the third of the twelve sons of Ishmael, and head of an Arabian tribe (<reflink>Gen. 25:13; 1 Chr. 1:29</reflink>).

addar.d: ample, splendid, son of Bela (<reflink>1 Chr. 8:3</reflink>); called also "Ard" (<reflink>Gen. 46:21</reflink>)

adder.d: (<reflink>Ps. 140:3; Rom. 3:13, "asp"</reflink>) is the rendering of, (1.) Akshub ("coiling" or "lying in wait"), properly an asp or viper, found only in this passage. (2.) Pethen ("twisting"), a viper or venomous serpent identified with the cobra (Naja haje) (<reflink>Ps. 58:4; 91:13</reflink>); elsewhere "asp." (3.) Tziphoni ("hissing") (<reflink>Prov. 23:32</reflink>); elsewhere rendered "cockatrice," Isa. 11:8; 14:29; 59:5; Jer. 8:17, as it is here in the margin of the Authorized Version. The Revised Version has "basilisk." This may have been the yellow viper, the Daboia xanthina, the largest and most dangerous of the vipers of Palestine. (4.) Shephiphon ("creeping"), occurring only in Gen. 49:17, the small speckled venomous snake, the "horned snake," or cerastes. Dan is compared to this serpent, which springs from its hiding-place on the passer-by.

adar.d: large, the sixth month of the civil and the twelfth of the ecclesiastical year of the Jews (<reflink>Esther 3:7, 13; 8:12; 9:1, 15, 17, 19, 21</reflink>). It included the days extending from the new moon of our March to the new moon of April. The name was first used after the Captivity. When the season was backward, and the lambs not yet of a paschal size, or the barley not forward enough for abib, then a month called Veadar, i.e., a second Adar, was intercalated.

adam, a type.d: The apostle Paul speaks of Adam as "the figure of him who was to come." On this account our Lord is sometimes called the second Adam. This typical relation is described in Rom. 5:14-19.

adam, the city of.d: is referred to in Josh. 3:16. It stood "beside Zarethan," on the west bank of Jordan (<reflink>1 Kings 4:12</reflink>). At this city the flow of the water was arrested and rose up "upon an heap" at the time of the Israelites' passing over (<reflink>Josh. 3:16</reflink>).

adamah.d: red earth, a fortified city of Naphtali, probably the modern Damieh, on the west side of the sea of Tiberias (<reflink>Josh. 19:33, 36</reflink>).

adamant.d: (Heb. shamir), Ezek. 3:9. The Greek word adamas means diamond. This stone is not referred to, but corundum or some kind of hard steel. It is an emblem of firmness in resisting adversaries of the truth (<reflink>Zech. 7:12</reflink>), and of hard-heartedness against the truth (<reflink>Jer. 17:1</reflink>).

adah.d: ornament. (1.) The first of Lamech's two wives, and the mother of Jabal and Jubal (<reflink>Gen. 4:19, 20, 23</reflink>).

adam.d: red, a Babylonian word, the generic name for man, having the same meaning in the Hebrew and the Assyrian languages. It was the name given to the first man, whose creation, fall, and subsequent history and that of his descendants are detailed in the first book of Moses (<reflink>Gen. 1:27-ch. 5</reflink>). "God created man [Heb., Adam] in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them."

acts of the apostles.d: the title now given to the fifth and last of the historical books of the New Testament. The author styles it a "treatise" (1:1). It was early called "The Acts," "The Gospel of the Holy Ghost," and "The Gospel of the Resurrection." It contains properly no account of any of the apostles except Peter and Paul. John is noticed only three times; and all that is recorded of James, the son of Zebedee, is his execution by Herod. It is properly therefore not the history of the "Acts of the Apostles," a title which was given to the book at a later date, but of "Acts of Apostles," or more correctly, of "Some Acts of Certain Apostles."

achzib.d: falsehood. (1.) A town in the Shephelah, or plain country of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:44</reflink>); probably the same as Chezib of Gen. 38:5 = Ain Kezbeh.

acre.d: is the translation of a word (tse'med), which properly means a yoke, and denotes a space of ground that may be ploughed by a yoke of oxen in a day. It is about an acre of our measure (<reflink>Isa. 5:10; 1 Sam. 14:14</reflink>).

achsah.d: anklet, Caleb's only daughter (<reflink>1 Chr. 2:49</reflink>). She was offered in marriage to the man who would lead an attack on the city of Debir, or Kirjath-sepher. This was done by Othniel (q.v.), who accordingly obtained her as his wife (<reflink>Josh. 15:16-19; Judg. 1:9-15</reflink>).

achshaph.d: fascination, a royal city of the Canaanites, in the north of Palestine (<reflink>Josh. 11:1; 12:20; 19:25</reflink>). It was in the eastern boundary of the tribe of Asher, and is identified with the modern ruined village of Kesaf or Yasif, N.E. of Accho.

achor.d: trouble, a valley near Jericho, so called in consequence of the trouble which the sin of Achan caused Israel (<reflink>Josh. 7:24,26</reflink>). The expression "valley of Achor" probably became proverbial for that which caused trouble, and when Isaiah (<reflink>Isa. 65:10</reflink>) refers to it he uses it in this sense: "The valley of Achor, a place for herds to lie down in;" i.e., that which had been a source of calamity would become a source of blessing. Hosea also (<reflink>Hos. 2:15</reflink>) uses the expression in the same sense: "The valley of Achor for a door of hope;" i.e., trouble would be turned into joy, despair into hope. This valley has been identified with the Wady Kelt.

achmetha.d: (<reflink>Ezra 6:2</reflink>), called Ecbatana by classical writers, the capital of northern Media. Here was the palace which was the residence of the old Median monarchs, and of Cyrus and Cambyses. In the time of Ezra, the Persian kings resided usually at Susa of Babylon. But Cyrus held his court at Achmetha; and Ezra, writing a century after, correctly mentions the place where the decree of Cyrus was found.

achbor.d: gnawing = mouse. (1.) An Edomitish king (<reflink>Gen. 36:38; 1 Chr. 1:49</reflink>).

achish.d: angry, perhaps only a general title of royalty applicable to the Philistine kings. (1.) The king with whom David sought refuge when he fled from Saul (<reflink>1 Sam. 21:10-15</reflink>). He is called Abimelech in the superscription of Ps. 34. It was probably this same king to whom David a second time repaired at the head of a band of 600 warriors, and who assigned him Ziklag, whence he carried on war against the surrounding tribes (<reflink>1 Sam. 27:5-12</reflink>). Achish had great confidence in the valour and fidelity of David (<reflink>1 Sam. 28:1,2</reflink>), but at the instigation of his courtiers did not permit him to go up to battle along with the Philistine hosts (<reflink>1 Sam. 29:2-11</reflink>). David remained with Achish a year and four months. (2.) Another king of Gath, probably grandson of the foregoing, to whom the two servants of Shimei fled. …

achan.d: called also Achar, i.e., one who troubles (<reflink>1 Chr. 2:7</reflink>), in commemoration of his crime, which brought upon him an awful destruction (<reflink>Josh. 7:1</reflink>). On the occasion of the fall of Jericho, he seized, contrary to the divine command, an ingot of gold, a quantity of silver, and a costly Babylonish garment, which he hid in his tent. Joshua was convinced that the defeat which the Israelites afterwards sustained before Ai was a proof of the divine displeasure on account of some crime, and he at once adopted means by the use of the lot for discovering the criminal. It was then found that Achan was guilty, and he was stoned to death in the valley of Achor. He and all that belonged to him were then consumed by fire, and a heap of stones was raised over the ashes.

achaichus.d: (<reflink>1 Cor. 16:17</reflink>), one of the members of the church of Corinth who, with Fortunatus and Stephanas, visited Paul while he was at Ephesus, for the purpose of consulting him on the affairs of the church. These three probably were the bearers of the letter from Corinth to the apostle to which he alludes in 1 Cor. 7:1.

achaia.d: the name originally of a narrow strip of territory in Greece, on the north-west of the Peloponnesus. Subsequently it was applied by the Romans to the whole Peloponnesus, now called the Morea, and the south of Greece. It was then one of the two provinces (Macedonia being the other) into which they divided the country when it fell under their dominion. It is in this latter enlarged meaning that the name is always used in the New Testament (<reflink>Acts 18:12, 27; 19:21; Rom. 15: 26; 16:5, etc.</reflink>). It was at the time when Luke wrote the Acts of the Apostles under the proconsular form of government; hence the appropriate title given to Gallio as the "deputy," i.e., proconsul, of Achaia (<reflink>Acts 18:12</reflink>).

aceldama.d: the name which the Jews gave in their proper tongue, i.e., in Aramaic, to the field which was purchased with the money which had been given to the betrayer of our Lord. The word means "field of blood." It was previously called "the potter's field" (<reflink>Matt. 27:7, 8; Acts 1:19</reflink>), and was appropriated as the burial-place for strangers. It lies on a narrow level terrace on the south face of the valley of Hinnom. Its modern name is Hak ed-damm.

accuser.d: Satan is styled the "accuser of the brethren" (<reflink>Rev. 12:10. Comp. Job 1:6; Zech. 3:1</reflink>), as seeking to uphold his influence among men by bringing false charges against Christians, with the view of weakening their influence and injuring the cause with which they are identified. He was regarded by the Jews as the accuser of men before God, laying to their charge the violations of the law of which they were guilty, and demanding their punishment. The same Greek word, rendered "accuser," is found in John 8:10 (but omitted in the Revised Version); Acts 23:30, 35; 24:8; 25:16, 18, in all of which places it is used of one who brings a charge against another.

accho.d: sultry or sandy, a town and harbour of Phoenicia, in the tribe of Asher, but never acquired by them (<reflink>Judg. 1:31</reflink>). It was known to the ancient Greeks and Romans by the name of Ptolemais, from Ptolemy the king of Egypt, who rebuilt it about B.C. 100. Here Paul landed on his last journey to Jerusalem (<reflink>Acts 21:7</reflink>). During the crusades of the Middle Ages it was called Acra; and subsequently, on account of its being occupied by the Knights Hospitallers of Jerusalem, it was called St. Jean d'Acre, or simply Acre.

accad.d: the high land or mountains, a city in the land of Shinar. It has been identified with the mounds of Akker Kuf, some 50 miles to the north of Babylon; but this is doubtful. It was one of the cities of Nimrod's kingdom (<reflink>Ge 10:10</reflink>). It stood close to the Euphrates, opposite Sippara. (<see target="x-self">See SEPHARVAIM.</see>)

acacia.d: (Heb. shittim) Ex. 25:5, R.V. probably the Acacia seyal (the gum-arabic tree); called the "shittah" tree (<reflink>Isa. 41:19</reflink>). Its wood is called shittim wood (<reflink>Ex. 26:15,26; 25:10,13,23,28, etc.</reflink>). This species (A. seyal) is like the hawthorn, a gnarled and thorny tree. It yields the gum-arabic of commerce. It is found in abundance in the Sinaitic peninsula.

absalom.d: father of peace; i.e., "peaceful" David's son by Maacah (<reflink>2 Sam. 3:3; comp. 1 Kings 1:6</reflink>). He was noted for his personal beauty and for the extra-ordinary profusion of the hair of his head (<reflink>2 Sam. 14:25,26</reflink>). The first public act of his life was the blood-revenge he executed against Amnon, David's eldest son, who had basely wronged Absalom's sister Tamar. This revenge was executed at the time of the festivities connected with a great sheep-shearing at Baal-hazor. David's other sons fled from the place in horror, and brought the tidings of the death of Amnon to Jerusalem. Alarmed for the consequences of the act, Absalom fled to his grandfather at Geshur, and there abode for three years (<reflink>2 Sam. 3:3; 13:23-38</reflink>).

abronah.d: R.V., one of Israel's halting-places in the desert (<reflink>Num.33:34,35</reflink>), just before Ezion-gaber. In A.V., "Ebronah."

abraham's bosom.d: (<reflink>Luke 16:22,23</reflink>) refers to the custom of reclining on couches at table, which was prevalent among the Jews, an arrangement which brought the head of one person almost into the bosom of the one who sat or reclined above him. To "be in Abraham's bosom" thus meant to enjoy happiness and rest (<reflink>Matt. 8:11; Luke 16:23</reflink>) at the banquet in Paradise. (See BANQUET; MEALS

abraham.d: father of a multitude, son of Terah, named (<reflink>Gen. 11:27</reflink>) before his older brothers Nahor and Haran, because he was the heir of the promises. Till the age of seventy, Abram sojourned among his kindred in his native country of Chaldea. He then, with his father and his family and household, quitted the city of Ur, in which he had hitherto dwelt, and went some 300 miles north to Haran, where he abode fifteen years. The cause of his migration was a call from God (<reflink>Acts 7:2-4</reflink>). There is no mention of this first call in the Old Testament; it is implied, however, in Gen. 12. While they tarried at Haran, Terah died at the age of 205 years. Abram now received a second and more definite call, accompanied by a promise from God (<reflink>Gen. 12:1,2</reflink>); whereupon he took his departure, taking his nephew Lot with him, "not knowing whither he went" (<reflink>Heb. 11:8</reflink>). He trusted implicitly to the guidance of Him who had called him.

abomination.d: This word is used, (1.) To express the idea that the Egyptians considered themselves as defiled when they ate with strangers (<reflink>Gen. 43:32</reflink>). The Jews subsequently followed the same practice, holding it unlawful to eat or drink with foreigners (<reflink>John 18:28; Acts 10:28; 11:3</reflink>).

abital.d: father of dew; i.e., "fresh", David's fifth wife (<reflink>2 Sam. 3:4</reflink>).

abitub.d: father of goodness, a Benjamite (<reflink>1 Chr. 8:11</reflink>).

abjects.d: (<reflink>Ps. 35:15</reflink>), the translation of a Hebrew word meaning smiters; probably, in allusion to the tongue, slanderers. (<reflink>Comp. Jer. 18:18.</reflink>)

ablution.d: or washing, was practised, (1.) When a person was initiated into a higher state: e.g., when Aaron and his sons were set apart to the priest's office, they were washed with water previous to their investiture with the priestly robes (<reflink>Lev. 8:6</reflink>).

abner.d: father of light; i.e., "enlightening", the son of Ner and uncle of Saul. He was commander-in-chief of Saul's army (<reflink>1 Sam. 14:50; 17:55; 20:25</reflink>). He first introduced David to the court of Saul after the victory over Goliath (<reflink>1 Sam. 17:57</reflink>). After the death of Saul, David was made king over Judah, and reigned in Hebron. Among the other tribes there was a feeling of hostility to Judah; and Abner, at the head of Ephraim, fostered this hostility in the interest of the house of Saul, whose son Ish-bosheth he caused to be proclaimed king (<reflink>2 Sam. 2:8</reflink>). A state of war existed between these two kings. A battle fatal to Abner, who was the leader of Ish-boseth's army, was fought with David's army under Joab at Gibeon (<reflink>2 Sam. 2:12</reflink>). …

adnah.d: delight. (1.) A chief of the tribe of Manasseh who joined David at Ziklag (<reflink>1 Chr. 12:20</reflink>). (2.) A general under Jehoshaphat, chief over 300,000 men (<reflink>2 Chr. 17:14</reflink>).

adoni-zedec.d: lord of justice or righteousness, was king in Jerusalem at the time when the Israelites invaded Palestine (<reflink>Josh. 10:1,3</reflink>). He formed a confederacy with the other Canaanitish kings against the Israelites, but was utterly routed by Joshua when he was engaged in besieging the Gibeonites. The history of this victory and of the treatment of the five confederated kings is recorded in Josh. 10:1-27. (<reflink>Comp. Deut. 21:23</reflink>). Among the Tell Amarna tablets (<see target="x-self">see EGYPT</see>) are some very interesting letters from Adoni-zedec to the King of Egypt. These illustrate in a very remarkable manner the history recorded in Josh. 10, and indeed throw light on the wars of conquest generally, so that they may be read as a kind of commentary on the book of Joshua. …

adonibezek.d: lord of Bezek, a Canaanitish king who, having subdued seventy of the chiefs that were around him, made an attack against the armies of Judah and Simeon, but was defeated and brought as a captive to Jerusalem, where his thumbs and great toes were cut off. He confessed that God had requited him for his like cruelty to the seventy kings whom he had subdued (<reflink>Judg. 1:4-7; comp. 1 Sam. 15:33</reflink>).

adonijah.d: my Lord is Jehovah. (1.) The fourth son of David (<reflink>2 Sam. 3:4</reflink>). After the death of his elder brothers, Amnon and Absalom, he became heir-apparent to the throne. But Solomon, a younger brother, was preferred to him. Adonijah, however, when his father was dying, caused himself to be proclaimed king. But Nathan and Bathsheba induced David to give orders that Solomon should at once be proclaimed and admitted to the throne. Adonijah fled and took refuge at the altar, and received pardon for his conduct from Solomon on the condition that he showed himself "a worthy man" (<reflink>1 Kings 1:5-53</reflink>). He afterwards made a second attempt to gain the throne, but was seized and put to death (<reflink>1 Kings 2:13-25</reflink>).

adonikam.d: whom the Lord sets up, one of those "which came with Zerubbabel" (<reflink>Ezra 2:13</reflink>). His "children," or retainers, to the number of 666, came up to Jerusalem (8:13).

adoniram.d: (Adoram, 1 Kings 12:18), the son of Abda, was "over the tribute," i.e., the levy or forced labour. He was stoned to death by the people of Israel (<reflink>1 Kings 4:6; 5:14</reflink>)

adoption.d: the giving to any one the name and place and privileges of a son who is not a son by birth.

a.d: Alpha, the first letter of the Greek alphabet, as Omega is the last. These letters occur in the text of Rev. 1:8,11; 21:6; 22:13, and are represented by "Alpha" and "Omega" respectively (omitted in R.V., 1:11). They mean "the first and last." (<reflink>Comp. Heb. 12:2; Isa. 41:4; 44:6; Rev. 1:11,17; 2:8.</reflink>) In the symbols of the early Christian Church these two letters are frequently combined with the cross or with Christ's monogram to denote his divinity.

aaron.d: the eldest son of Amram and Jochebed, a daughter of Levi (<reflink>Ex. 6:20</reflink>). Some explain the name as meaning mountaineer, others mountain of strength, illuminator. He was born in Egypt three years before his brother Moses, and a number of years after his sister Miriam (2:1,4; 7:7). He married Elisheba, the daughter of Amminadab of the house of Judah (6:23; 1 Chr. 2:10), by whom he had four sons, Nadab and Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar. When the time for the deliverance of Isarael out of Egypt drew nigh, he was sent by God (<reflink>Ex. 4:14,27-30</reflink>) to meet his long-absent brother, that he might co-operate with him in all that they were required to do in bringing about the Exodus. He was to be the "mouth" or "prophet" of Moses, i.e., was to speak for him, because he was a man of a ready utterance (7:1,2,9,10,19). He was faithful to his trust, and stood by Moses in all his interviews with Pharaoh.

aaronites.d: the descendants of Aaron, and therefore priests. Jehoiada, the father of Benaiah, led 3,700 Aaronites as "fighting men" to the support of David at Hebron (<reflink>1 Chr. 12:27</reflink>). Eleazar (<reflink>Num. 3:32</reflink>), and at a later period Zadok (<reflink>1 Chr. 27:17</reflink>), was their chief.

abaddon.d: destruction, the Hebrew name (equivalent to the Greek Apollyon, i.e., destroyer) of "the angel of the bottomless pit" (<reflink>Rev. 9:11</reflink>). It is rendered "destruction" in Job 28:22; 31:12; 26:6; Prov. 15:11; 27:20. In the last three of these passages the Revised Version retains the word "Abaddon." We may regard this word as a personification of the idea of destruction, or as sheol, the realm of the dead.

abagtha.d: one of the seven eunuchs in Ahasuerus's court (<reflink>Esther 1:10; 2:21</reflink>).

abana.d: stony (Heb. marg. "Amanah," perennial), the chief river of Damascus (<reflink>2 Kings 5:12</reflink>). Its modern name is Barada, the Chrysorrhoas, or "golden stream," of the Greeks. It rises in a cleft of the Anti-Lebanon range, about 23 miles north-west of Damascus, and after flowing southward for a little way parts into three smaller streams, the central one flowing through Damascus, and the other two on each side of the city, diffusing beauty and fertility where otherwise there would be barrenness.

abarim.d: regions beyond; i.e., on the east of Jordan, a mountain, or rather a mountain-chain, over against Jericho, to the east and south-east of the Dead Sea, in the land of Moab. From "the top of Pisgah", i.e., Mount Nebo (q.v.), one of its summits, Moses surveyed the Promised Land (<reflink>Deut. 3:27; 32:49</reflink>), and there he died (34:1,5). The Israelites had one of their encampments in the mountains of Abarim (<reflink>Num. 33:47,48</reflink>) after crossing the Arnon.

abba.d: This Syriac or Chaldee word is found three times in the New Testament (<reflink>Mark 14:36; Rom. 8:15; Gal. 4:6</reflink>), and in each case is followed by its Greek equivalent, which is translated "father." It is a term expressing warm affection and filial confidence. It has no perfect equivalent in our language. It has passed into European languages as an ecclesiastical term, "abbot."

abda.d: servant. (1.) The father of Adoniram, whom Solomon set over the tribute (<reflink>1 Kings 4:6</reflink>); i.e., the forced labour (R.V., "levy").

abdeel.d: servant of God, (<reflink>Jer. 36:26</reflink>), the father of Shelemiah.

abdiel.d: servant of God, (<reflink>1 Chr. 5:15</reflink>), a Gadite chief.

abdon.d: servile. (1.) The son of Hillel, a Pirathonite, the tenth judge of Israel (<reflink>Judg. 12:13-15</reflink>). He is probably the Bedan of 1 Sam. 12:11.

abednego.d: servant of Nego=Nebo, the Chaldee name given to Azariah, one of Daniel's three companions (<reflink>Dan. 2:49</reflink>). With Shadrach and Meshach, he was delivered from the burning fiery furnace (3:12-30).

abel.d: (Heb. Hebhel), a breath, or vanity, the second son of Adam and Eve. He was put to death by his brother Cain (<reflink>Gen. 4:1-16</reflink>). Guided by the instruction of their father, the two brothers were trained in the duty of worshipping God. "And in process of time" (marg. "at the end of days", i.e., on the Sabbath) each of them offered up to God of the first-fruits of his labours. Cain, as a husbandman, offered the fruits of the field; Abel, as a shepherd, of the firstlings of his flock. "The Lord had respect unto Abel and his offering; but unto Cain and his offering he had not respect" (<reflink>Gen. 4:3-5</reflink>). On this account Cain was angry with his brother, and formed the design of putting him to death; a design which he at length found an opportunity of carrying into effect (<reflink>Gen. 4:8,9. Comp. 1 John 3:12</reflink>). There are several references to Abel in the New Testament. Our Saviour speaks of him as "righteous" (<reflink>Matt. 23:35</reflink>). …

abel-beth-maachah.d: meadow of the house of Maachah, a city in the north of Palestine, in the neighbourhood of Dan and Ijon, in the tribe of Naphtali. It was a place of considerable strength and importance. It is called a "mother in Israel", i.e., a metropolis (<reflink>2 Sam. 20:19</reflink>). It was besieged by Joab (<reflink>2 Sam. 20:14</reflink>), by Benhadad (<reflink>1 Kings 15:20</reflink>), and by Tiglath-pileser (<reflink>2 Kings 15:29</reflink>) about B.C. 734. It is elsewhere called Abel-maim, meadow of the waters, (<reflink>2 Chr. 16:4</reflink>). Its site is occupied by the modern Abil or Abil-el-kamh, on a rising ground to the east of the brook Derdarah, which flows through the plain of Huleh into the Jordan, about 6 miles to the west-north-west of Dan.

abel-cheramim.d: (<reflink>Judg. 11:33, R.V.; A. V., "plain of the vineyards"</reflink>), a village of the Ammonites, whither Jephthah pursued their forces.

abel-meholah.d: meadow of dancing, or the dancing-meadow, the birth-place and residence of the prophet Elisha, not far from Beth-shean (<reflink>1 Kings 4:12</reflink>), in the tribe of Issachar, near where the Wady el-Maleh emerges into the valley of the Jordan, "the rich meadow-land which extends about 4 miles south of Beth-shean; moist and luxuriant." Here Elisha was found at his plough by Elijah on his return up the Jordan valley from Horeb (<reflink>1 Kings 19:16</reflink>). It is now called 'Ain Helweh.

abel-mizraim.d: meadow of Egypt, or mourning of Egypt, a place "beyond," i.e., on the west of Jordan, at the "threshing-floor of Atad." Here the Egyptians mourned seventy days for Jacob (<reflink>Gen. 50:4-11</reflink>). Its site is unknown.

abel-shittim.d: meadow of the acacias, frequently called simply "Shittim" (<reflink>Num. 25:1; Josh. 2:1; Micah 6:5</reflink>), a place on the east of Jordan, in the plain of Moab, nearly opposite Jericho. It was the forty-second encampment of the Israelites, their last resting-place before they crossed the Jordan (<reflink>Num. 33:49; 22:1; 26:3; 31:12; comp. 25:1; 31:16</reflink>).

abez.d: tin, or white, a town in the tribe of Issachar (<reflink>Josh. 19:20</reflink>), at the north of the plain of Esdraelon. It is probably identified with the ruins of el-Beida.

abi-albon.d: father of strength; i.e., "valiant", one of David's body-guard of thirty mighty men (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:31</reflink>); called also Abiel (<reflink>1 Chr. 11:32</reflink>).

abia.d: my father is the Lord, the Greek form of Abijah, or Abijam (<reflink>Matt. 1:7</reflink>), instead of Abiah (<reflink>1 Chr. 7:8</reflink>). In Luke 1:5, the name refers to the head of the eighth of the twenty-four courses into which David divided the priests (<reflink>1 Chr. 24:10</reflink>).

abiasaph.d: father of gathering; the gatherer, the youngest of the three sons of Korah the Levite, head of a family of Korhites (<reflink>Ex. 6:24</reflink>); called Ebisaph (<reflink>1 Chr. 6:37</reflink>).

abiathar.d: father of abundance, or my father excels, the son of Ahimelech the high priest. He was the tenth high priest, and the fourth in descent from Eli. When his father was slain with the priests of Nob, he escaped, and bearing with him the ephod, he joined David, who was then in the cave of Adullam (<reflink>1 Sam. 22:20-23; 23:6</reflink>). He remained with David, and became priest of the party of which he was the leader (<reflink>1 Sam. 30:7</reflink>). When David ascended the throne of Judah, Abiathar was appointed high priest (<reflink>1 Chr. 15:11; 1 Kings 2:26</reflink>) and the "king's companion" (<reflink>1 Chr. 27:34</reflink>). Meanwhile Zadok, of the house of Eleazar, had been made high priest. These appointments continued in force till the end of David's reign (<reflink>1 Kings 4:4</reflink>). …

abib.d: an ear of corn, the month of newly-ripened grain (<reflink>Ex. 13:4; 23:15</reflink>); the first of the Jewish ecclesiastical year, and the seventh of the civil year. It began about the time of the vernal equinox, on 21st March. It was called Nisan, after the Captivity (<reflink>Neh. 2:1</reflink>). On the fifteenth day of the month, harvest was begun by gathering a sheaf of barley, which was offered unto the Lord on the sixteenth (<reflink>Lev. 23:4-11</reflink>).

abida.d: or Abi'dah, father of knowledge; knowing, one of the five sons of Midian, who was the son of Abraham by Keturah (<reflink>1 Chr. 1:33</reflink>), and apparently the chief of an Arab tribe.

abidan.d: father of judgment; judge, head of the tribe of Benjamin at the Exodus (<reflink>Num. 1:11; 2:22</reflink>).

abieezer.d: father of help; i.e., "helpful." (1.) The second of the three sons of Hammoleketh, the sister of Gilead. He was the grandson of Manasseh (<reflink>1 Chr. 7:18</reflink>). From his family Gideon sprang (<reflink>Josh. 17:2; comp. Judg. 6:34; 8:2</reflink>). He was also called Jeezer (<reflink>Num. 26:30</reflink>).

abiel.d: father (i.e., "possessor") of God = "pious." (1.) The son of Zeror and father of Ner, who was the grandfather of Saul (<reflink>1 Sam. 14:51; 1 Chr. 8:33; 9:39</reflink>). In 1 Sam. 9:1, he is called the "father," probably meaning the grandfather, of Kish. (2.) An Arbathite, one of David's warriors (<reflink>1 Chr. 11:32</reflink>); called also Abi-albon (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:31</reflink>).

abiezrite.d: father of help, a descendant of Abiezer (<reflink>Judg. 6:11,24; 8:32</reflink>).

abigail.d: father (i.e., "leader") of the dance, or "of joy." (1.) The sister of David, and wife of Jether an Ishmaelite (<reflink>1 Chr. 2:16,17</reflink>). She was the mother of Amasa (<reflink>2 Sam. 17:25</reflink>).

abihail.d: father of might. (1.) Num. 3:35. (2.) 1 Chr. 2:29. (3.) 1 Chr. 5:14.

abihu.d: father of Him; i.e., "worshipper of God", the second of the sons of Aaron (<reflink>Ex. 6:23; Num. 3:2; 26:60; 1 Chr. 6:3</reflink>). Along with his three brothers he was consecrated to the priest's office (<reflink>Ex. 28:1</reflink>). With his father and elder brother he accompanied the seventy elders part of the way up the mount with Moses (<reflink>Ex. 24:1,9</reflink>). On one occasion he and Nadab his brother offered incense in their censers filled with "strange" (i.e., common) fire, i.e., not with fire taken from the great brazen altar (<reflink>Lev. 6:9, etc.</reflink>), and for this offence they were struck dead, and were taken out and buried without the camp (<reflink>Lev. 10:1-11; comp. Num. 3:4; 26:61; 1 Chr. 24:2</reflink>). It is probable that when they committed this offence they were intoxicated, for immediately after is given the law prohibiting the use of wine or strong drink to the priests.

abihud.d: father (i.e., "possessor") of renown. (1.) One of the sons of Bela, the son of Benjamin (<reflink>1 Chr. 8:3</reflink>); called also Ahihud (ver. 7).

abijah.d: father (i.e., "possessor or worshipper") of Jehovah. (1.) 1 Chr. 7:8. (2.) 1 Chr. 2:24.

abijam.d: father of the sea; i.e., "seaman" the name always used in Kings of the king of Judah, the son of Rehoboam, elsewhere called Abijah (<reflink>1 Kings 15:1,7,8</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See ABIJAH, 5.</see>)

abilene.d: a plain, a district lying on the east slope of the Anti-Lebanon range; so called from its chief town, Abila (<reflink>Luke 3:1</reflink>), which stood in the Suk Wady Barada, between Heliopolis (Baalbec) and Damascus, 38 miles from the former and 18 from the latter. Lysanias was governor or tetrarch of this province.

abimael.d: father of Mael, one of the sons or descendants of Joktan, in Northern Arabia (<reflink>Gen. 10:28; 1 Chr. 1:22</reflink>).

abimelech.d: my father a king, or father of a king, a common name of the Philistine kings, as "Pharaoh" was of the Egyptian kings. (1.) The Philistine king of Gerar in the time of Abraham (<reflink>Gen. 20:1-18</reflink>). By an interposition of Providence, Sarah was delivered from his harem, and was restored to her husband Abraham. As a mark of respect he gave to Abraham valuable gifts, and offered him a settlement in any part of his country; while at the same time he delicately and yet severely rebuked him for having practised a deception upon him in pretending that Sarah was only his sister. Among the gifts presented by the king were a thousand pieces of silver as a "covering of the eyes" for Sarah; i.e., either as an atoning gift and a testimony of her innocence in the sight of all, or rather for the purpose of procuring a veil for Sarah to conceal her beauty, and thus as a reproof to her for not having worn a veil which, as a married woman, she ought to have done. …

abinadab.d: father of nobleness; i.e., "noble." (1.) A Levite of Kirjath-jearim, in whose house the ark of the covenant was deposited after having been brought back from the land of the Philistines (<reflink>1 Sam. 7:1</reflink>). It remained there twenty years, till it was at length removed by David (<reflink>1 Sam. 7:1,2; 1 Chr. 13:7</reflink>).

abinoam.d: father of kindness, the father of Barak (<reflink>Judg. 4:6; 5:1</reflink>).

abiram.d: father of height; i.e., "proud." (1.) One of the sons of Eliab, who joined Korah in the conspiracy against Moses and Aaron. He and all the conspirators, with their families and possessions (except the children of Korah), were swallowed up by an earthquake (<reflink>Num. 16:1-27; 26:9; Ps. 106:17</reflink>).

abishag.d: father of (i.e., "given to") error, a young woman of Shunem, distinguished for her beauty. She was chosen to minister to David in his old age. She became his wife (<reflink>1 Kings 1:3,4,15</reflink>). After David's death Adonijah persuaded Bathsheba, Solomon's mother, to entreat the king to permit him to marry Abishag. Solomon suspected in this request an aspiration to the throne, and therefore caused him to be put to death (<reflink>1 Kings 2:17-25</reflink>).

abishai.d: father of (i.e., "desirous of") a gift, the eldest son of Zeruiah, David's sister. He was the brother of Joab and Asahel (<reflink>2 Sam. 2:18; 1 Chr. 2:16</reflink>). Abishai was the only one who accompanied David when he went to the camp of Saul and took the spear and the cruse of water from Saul's bolster (<reflink>1 Sam. 26:5-12</reflink>). He had the command of one of the three divisions of David's army at the battle with Absalom (<reflink>2 Sam. 18:2,5,12</reflink>). He slew the Philistine giant Ishbi-benob, who threatened David's life (<reflink>2 Sam. 21:15-17</reflink>). He was the chief of the second rank of the three "mighties" (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:18, 19; 1 Chr. 11:20,21</reflink>); and on one occasion withstood 300 men, and slew them with his own spear (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:18</reflink>). Abishai is the name of the Semitic chief who offers gifts to the lord of Beni-Hassan. See illustration facing page 10.

abishua.d: father of welfare; i.e., "fortunate." (1.) The grandson of Benjamin (<reflink>1 Chr. 8:4</reflink>).

abishur.d: father of the wall; i.e., "mason", one of the two sons of Shammai of the tribe of Judah (<reflink>1 Chr. 2:28,29</reflink>).

adore.d: to worship; to express reverence and homage. The forms of adoration among the Jews were putting off the shoes (<reflink>Ex. 3:5; Josh. 5:15</reflink>), and prostration (<reflink>Gen. 17:3; Ps. 95:6; Isa. 44:15, 17, 19; 46:6</reflink>). To "kiss the Son" in Ps. 2:12 is to adore and worship him. (<reflink>See Dan. 3:5, 6.</reflink>) The word itself does not occur in Scripture.

adrammelech.d: Adar the king. (1.) An idol; a form of the sun-god worshipped by the inhabitants of Sepharvaim (<reflink>2 Kings 17:31</reflink>), and brought by the Sepharvite colonists into Samaria. (2.) A son of Sennacherib, king of Assyria (<reflink>2 Kings 19:37; Isa. 37:38</reflink>).

adramyttium.d: a city of Asia Minor on the coast of Mysia, which in early times was called AEolis. The ship in which Paul embarked at Caesarea belonged to this city (<reflink>Acts 27:2</reflink>). He was conveyed in it only to Myra, in Lycia, whence he sailed in an Alexandrian ship to Italy. It was a rare thing for a ship to sail from any port of Palestine direct for Italy. It still bears the name Adramyti, and is a place of some traffic.

adria.d: (<reflink>Acts 27:27; R.V., "the sea of Adria"</reflink>), the Adriatic Sea, including in Paul's time the whole of the Mediterranean lying between Crete and Sicily. It is the modern Gulf of Venice, the _Mare Superum_ of the Romans, as distinguished from the _Mare Inferum_ or Tyrrhenian Sea.

adriel.d: flock of God, the son of Barzillai, the Meholathite, to whom Saul gave in marriage his daughter Merab (<reflink>1 Sam. 18:19</reflink>). The five sons that sprang from this union were put to death by the Gibeonites (<reflink>2 Sam. 21:8, 9. Here it is said that Michal "brought up" [R.V., "bare"] these five sons, either that she treated them as if she had been their own mother, or that for "Michal" we should read "Merab," as in 1 Sam. 18:19</reflink>).

adullam.d: one of the royal cities of the Canaanites, now 'Aid-el-ma (<reflink>Josh. 12:15; 15:35</reflink>). It stood on the old Roman road in the valley of Elah (q.v.), which was the scene of David's memorable victory over Goliath (<reflink>1 Sam. 17:2</reflink>), and not far from Gath. It was one of the towns which Rehoboam fortified against Egypt (<reflink>2 Chr. 11:7</reflink>). It was called "the glory of Israel" (<reflink>Micah 1:15</reflink>).

adullamite.d: an inhabitant of the city of Adullam (<reflink>Gen. 38:1, 12, 20</reflink>).

adultery.d: conjugal infidelity. An adulterer was a man who had illicit intercourse with a married or a betrothed woman, and such a woman was an adulteress. Intercourse between a married man and an unmarried woman was fornication. Adultery was regarded as a great social wrong, as well as a great sin.

adummim.d: the red ones, a place apparently on the road between Jericho and Jerusalem, "on the south side of the torrent" Wady Kelt, looking toward Gilgal, mentioned Josh. 15:7; 18:17. It was nearly half-way between Jerusalem and Jericho, and now bears the name of Tal-at-ed-Dumm. It is supposed to have been the place referred to in the parable of the Good Samaritan (<reflink>Luke 10:30-37</reflink>). Recently a new carriage-road has been completed, and carriages for the first time have come along this road from Jerusalem.

adversary.d: (Heb. satan), an opponent or foe (<reflink>1 Kings 5:4; 11:14, 23, 25; Luke 13:17</reflink>); one that speaks against another, a complainant (<reflink>Matt. 5:25; Luke 12:58</reflink>); an enemy (<reflink>Luke 18:3</reflink>), and specially the devil (<reflink>1 Pet. 5:8</reflink>).

advocate.d: (Gr. parakletos), one who pleads another's cause, who helps another by defending or comforting him. It is a name given by Christ three times to the Holy Ghost (<reflink>John 14:16; 15:26; 16:7, where the Greek word is rendered "Comforter," q.v.</reflink>). It is applied to Christ in 1 John 2:1, where the same Greek word is rendered "Advocate," the rendering which it should have in all the places where it occurs. Tertullus "the orator" (<reflink>Acts 24:1</reflink>) was a Roman advocate whom the Jews employed to accuse Paul before Felix.

aenon.d: springs, a place near Salim where John baptized (<reflink>John 3:23</reflink>).  It was probably near the upper source of the Wady Far'ah, an open valley extending from Mount Ebal to the Jordan.  It is full of springs.  A place has been found called 'Ainun, four miles north of the springs.

affection.d: feeling or emotion. Mention is made of "vile affections" (<reflink>Rom. 1:26</reflink>) and "inordinate affection" (<reflink>Col. 3:5</reflink>). Christians are exhorted to set their affections on things above (<reflink>Col. 3:2</reflink>). There is a distinction between natural and spiritual or gracious affections (<reflink>Ezek. 33:32</reflink>).

affinity.d: relationship by alliance (<reflink>2 Chr. 18:1</reflink>) or by marriage (<reflink>1 Kings 3:1</reflink>). Marriages are prohibited within certain degrees of affinity, enumerated Lev. 18:6-17. Consanguinity is relationship by blood.

afflictions.d: common to all (<reflink>Job 5:7; 14:1; Ps. 34:19</reflink>); are for the good of men (<reflink>James 1:2, 3, 12; 2 Cor. 12:7</reflink>) and the glory of God (<reflink>2 Cor. 12:7-10; 1 Pet. 4:14</reflink>), and are to be borne with patience by the Lord's people (<reflink>Ps. 94:12; Prov. 3:12</reflink>). They are all directed by God (<reflink>Lam. 3:33</reflink>), and will result in the everlasting good of his people (<reflink>2 Cor. 4:16-18</reflink>) in Christ Jesus (<reflink>Rom. 8:35-39</reflink>).

agabus.d: a "prophet," probably one of the seventy disciples of Christ. He prophesied at Antioch of an approaching famine (<reflink>Acts 11:27, 28</reflink>). Many years afterwards he met Paul at Caesarea, and warned him of the bonds and affliction that awaited him at Jerusalem should he persist in going thither (<reflink>Acts 21:10-12</reflink>).

agag.d: flame, the usual title of the Amalekite kings, as "Pharaoh" was of the Egyptian. (1.) A king of the Amalekites referred to by Balaam (<reflink>Num. 24:7</reflink>). He lived at the time of the Exodus.

agagite.d: a name applied to Haman and also to his father (<reflink>Esther 3:1, 10; 8:3, 5</reflink>). Probably it was equivalent to Amalekite.

agate.d: (Heb. shebo), a precious stone in the breast-plate of the high priest (<reflink>Ex. 28:19; 39:12</reflink>), the second in the third row. This may be the agate properly so called, a semi-transparent crystallized quartz, probably brought from Sheba, whence its name. In Isa. 54:12 and Ezek. 27:16, this word is the rendering of the Hebrew cadcod, which means "ruddy," and denotes a variety of minutely crystalline silica more or less in bands of different tints.

age.d: used to denote the period of a man's life (<reflink>Gen. 47:28</reflink>), the maturity of life (<reflink>John 9:21</reflink>), the latter end of life (<reflink>Job 11:17</reflink>), a generation of the human race (<reflink>Job 8:8</reflink>), and an indefinite period (<reflink>Eph. 2:7; 3:5, 21; Col. 1:26</reflink>). Respect to be shown to the aged (<reflink>Lev. 19:32</reflink>). It is a blessing to communities when they have old men among them (<reflink>Isa. 65:20; Zech. 8:4</reflink>). The aged supposed to excel in understanding (<reflink>Job 12:20; 15:10; 32:4, 9; 1 Kings 12:6, 8</reflink>). A full age the reward of piety (<reflink>Job 5:26; Gen. 15:15</reflink>).

agee.d: fugitive, the father of Shammah, who was one of David's mighty men (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:11</reflink>)

agony.d: contest; wrestling; severe struggling with pain and suffering. Anguish is the reflection on evil that is already past, while agony is a struggle with evil at the time present. It is only used in the New Testament by Luke (22:44) to describe our Lord's fearful struggle in Gethsemane.

agriculture.d: Tilling the ground (<reflink>Gen. 2:15; 4:2, 3, 12</reflink>) and rearing cattle were the chief employments in ancient times. The Egyptians excelled in agriculture. And after the Israelites entered into the possession of the Promised Land, their circumstances favoured in the highest degree a remarkable development of this art. Agriculture became indeed the basis of the Mosaic commonwealth.

agrippa i.d: the grandson of Herod the Great, and son of Aristobulus and Bernice. The Roman emperor Caligula made him governor first of the territories of Philip, then of the tetrarchy of Lysanias, with the title of king ("king Herod"), and finally of that of Antipas, who was banished, and of Samaria and Judea. Thus he became ruler over the whole of Palestine. He was a persecutor of the early Christians. He slew James, and imprisoned Peter (<reflink>Acts 12:1-4</reflink>). He died at Caesarea, being "eaten of worms" (<reflink>Acts 12:23</reflink>), A.D. 44. (Comp. Josephus, Ant. xix. 8.)

agrippa ii.d: son of the foregoing, was born at Rome, A.D. 27. He was the brother of Bernice and Drusilla. The Emperor Claudius (A.D. 48) invested him with the office of superintendent of the Temple of Jerusalem, and made him governor (A.D. 50) of Chalcis. He was afterwards raised to the rank of king, and made governor over the tetrarchy of Philip and Lysanias (<reflink>Acts 25:13; 26:2, 7</reflink>). It was before him that Paul delivered (A.D. 59) his speech recorded in Acts 26. His private life was very profligate. He died (the last of his race) at Rome, at the age of about seventy years, A.D. 100.

ague.d: the translation in Lev. 26:16 (R.V., "fever") of the Hebrew word kaddah'ath, meaning "kindling", i.e., an inflammatory or burning fever. In Deut. 28:22 the word is rendered "fever."

agur.d: gatherer; the collector, mentioned as author of the sayings in Prov. 30. Nothing is known of him beyond what is there recorded.

ah!.d: an exclamation of sorrow or regret (<reflink>Ps. 35:25; Isa. 1:4, 24; Jer. 1:6; 22:18; Mark 15:29</reflink>).

aha!.d: an exclamation of ridicule (<reflink>Ps. 35:21; 40:15; 70:3</reflink>). In Isa. 44:16 it signifies joyful surprise, as also in Job 39:25, R.V.

ahab.d: father's brother. (1.) The son of Omri, whom he succeeded as the seventh king of Israel. His history is recorded in 1 Kings 16-22. His wife was Jezebel (q.v.), who exercised a very evil influence over him. To the calf-worship introduced by Jeroboam he added the worship of Baal. He was severely admonished by Elijah (q.v.) for his wickedness. His anger was on this account kindled against the prophet, and he sought to kill him. He undertook three campaigns against Ben-hadad II., king of Damascus. In the first two, which were defensive, he gained a complete victory over Ben-hadad, who fell into his hands, and was afterwards released on the condition of his restoring all the cities of Israel he then held, and granting certain other concessions to Ahab. …

ahasuerus.d: There are three kings designated by this name in Scripture. (1.) The father of Darius the Mede, mentioned in Dan. 9:1. This was probably the Cyaxares I. known by this name in profane history, the king of Media and the conqueror of Nineveh.

ahava.d: water, the river (<reflink>Ezra 8:21</reflink>) by the banks of which the Jewish exiles assembled under Ezra when about to return to Jerusalem from Babylon. In all probability this was one of the streams of Mesopotamia which flowed into the Euphrates somewhere in the north-west of Babylonia. It has, however, been supposed to be the name of a place (<reflink>Ezra 8:15</reflink>) now called Hit, on the Euphrates, east of Damascus.

ahaz.d: possessor. (1.) A grandson of Jonathan (<reflink>1 Chr. 8:35; 9:42</reflink>).

ahaziah.d: held by Jehovah. (1.) The son and successor of Ahab. He followed the counsels of his mother Jezebel, and imitated in wickedness the ways of his father. In his reign the Moabites revolted from under his authority (<reflink>2 Kings 3:5-7</reflink>). He united with Jehoshaphat in an attempt to revive maritime trade by the Red Sea, which proved a failure (<reflink>2 Chr. 20:35-37</reflink>). His messengers, sent to consult the god of Ekron regarding his recovery from the effects of a fall from the roof-gallery of his palace, were met on the way by Elijah, who sent them back to tell the king that he would never rise from his bed (<reflink>1 Kings 22:51; 2 Kings 1:18</reflink>).

ahiam.d: mother's brother, one of David's thirty heroes (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:33; 1 Chr. 11:35</reflink>).

ahiezer.d: brother of help; i.e., "helpful." (1.) The chief of the tribe of Dan at the time of the Exodus (<reflink>Num. 1:12; 2:25; 10:25</reflink>).

ahihud.d: brother (i.e., "friend") of union. (1.) A son of Bela, the son of Benjamin (<reflink>1 Chr. 8:7</reflink>).

ahijah.d: brother (i.e., "friend") of Jehovah. (1.) One of the sons of Bela (<reflink>1 Chr. 8:7, R.V.</reflink>). In A.V. called "Ahiah."

ahikam.d: brother of support = helper, one of the five whom Josiah sent to consult the prophetess Huldah in connection with the discovery of the book of the law (<reflink>2 Kings 22:12-14; 2 Chr. 34:20</reflink>). He was the son of Shaphan, the royal secretary, and the father of Gedaliah, governor of Judea after the destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonians (<reflink>2 Kings 25:22; Jer. 40:5-16; 43:6</reflink>). On one occasion he protected Jeremiah against the fury of Jehoiakim (<reflink>Jer. 26:24</reflink>). It was in the chamber of another son (Germariah) of Shaphan that Baruch read in the ears of all the people Jeremiah's roll.

ahimaaz.d: brother of anger = irascible. (1.) The father Ahinoam, the wife of Saul (<reflink>1 Sam. 14:50</reflink>).

ahiman.d: brother of a gift = liberal. (1.) One of the three giant Anakim brothers whom Caleb and the spies saw in Mount Hebron (<reflink>Num. 13:22</reflink>) when they went in to explore the land. They were afterwards driven out and slain (<reflink>Josh. 15:14; Judg. 1:10</reflink>).

ahimelech.d: brother of the king, the son of Ahitub and father of Abiathar (<reflink>1 Sam. 22:20-23</reflink>). He descended from Eli in the line of Ithamar. In 1 Chr. 18:16 he is called Abimelech, and is probably the same as Ahiah (<reflink>1 Sam. 14:3, 18</reflink>). He was the twelfth high priest, and officiated at Nob, where he was visited by David (to whom and his companions he gave five loaves of the showbread) when he fled from Saul (<reflink>1 Sam. 21:1-9</reflink>). He was summoned into Saul's presence, and accused, on the information of Doeg the Edomite, of disloyalty because of his kindness to David; whereupon the king commanded that he, with the other priests who stood beside him (86 in all), should be put to death. This sentence was carried into execution by Doeg in the most cruel manner (<reflink>1 Sam. 22:9-23</reflink>). Possibly Abiathar had a son also called Ahimelech, or the two names, as some think, may have been accidentally transposed in 2 Sam. 8:17; 1 Chr. …

ahinadab.d: brother of liberality = liberal, one of the twelve commissariat officers appointed by Solomon in so many districts of his kingdom to raise supplies by monthly rotation for his household. He was appointed to the district of Mahanaim (<reflink>1 Kings 4:14</reflink>), east of Jordan.

ahinoam.d: brother of pleasantness = pleasant. (1.) The daughter of Ahimaaz, and wife of Saul (<reflink>1 Sam. 14:50</reflink>).

ahio.d: brotherly. (1.) One of the sons of Beriah (<reflink>1 Chr. 8:14</reflink>).

ahira.d: brother of evil = unlucky, or my brother is friend, chief of the tribe of Naphtali at the Exodus (<reflink>Num. 1:15; 2:29</reflink>).

ahishar.d: brother of song = singer, the officer who was "over the household" of Solomon (<reflink>1 Kings 4:6</reflink>).

ahithophel.d: brother of insipidity or impiety, a man greatly renowned for his sagacity among the Jews. At the time of Absalom's revolt he deserted David (<reflink>Ps. 41:9; 55:12-14</reflink>) and espoused the cause of Absalom (<reflink>2 Sam. 15:12</reflink>). David sent his old friend Hushai back to Absalom, in order that he might counteract the counsel of Ahithophel (<reflink>2 Sam. 15:31-37</reflink>). This end was so far gained that Ahithophel saw he had no longer any influence, and accordingly he at once left the camp of Absalom and returned to Giloh, his native place, where, after arranging his wordly affairs, he hanged himself, and was buried in the sepulchre of his fathers (<reflink>2 Sam. 17:1-23</reflink>). He was the type of Judas (<reflink>Ps. 41:9</reflink>).

ahitub.d: brother of goodness = good. (1.) The son of Phinehas. On the death of his grandfather Eli he succeeded to the office of high priest, and was himself succeeded by his son Ahijah (<reflink>1 Sam. 14:3; 22:9, 11, 12, 20</reflink>).

ahlab.d: fatness, a town of Asher lying within the unconquered Phoenician border (<reflink>Judg. 1:31</reflink>), north-west of the Sea of Galilee; commonly identified with Giscala, now el-Jish.

ahoah.d: brotherly, one of the sons of Bela, the son of Benjamin (<reflink>1 Chr. 8:4</reflink>). He is also called Ahiah (ver. 7) and Iri (<reflink>1 Chr. 7:7</reflink>). His descendants were called Ahohites (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:9, 28</reflink>).

ahohite.d: an epithet applied to Dodo, one of Solomon's captains (<reflink>1 Chr. 27:4</reflink>); to his son Eleazar, one of David's three mightiest heroes (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:9; 1 Chr. 11:12</reflink>); and to Zalmon, one of the thirty (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:28; 1 Chr. 11:29</reflink>), from their descent from Ahoah.

aholah.d: she has her own tent, a name used by Ezekiel (23:4, 5, 36, 44) as a symbol of the idolatry of the kingdom of Israel. This kingdom is described as a lewdwoman, an adulteress, given up to the abominations and idolatries of the Egyptians and Assyrians. Because of her crimes, she was carried away captive, and ceased to be a kingdom. (<reflink>Comp. Ps. 78:67-69; 1 Kings 12:25-33; 2 Chr. 11:13-16.</reflink>)

aholiab.d: tent of the father, an artist of the tribe of Dan, appointed to the work of preparing materials for the tabernacle (<reflink>Ex. 31:6; 35:34; 36:1, 2; 38:23</reflink>).

aholibah.d: my tent is in her, the name of an imaginary harlot, applied symbolically to Jerusalem, because she had abandoned the worship of the true God and given herself up to the idolatries of foreign nations. (<reflink>Ezek. 23:4, 11, 22, 36, 44</reflink>).

aholibamah.d: tent of the height, the name given to Judith, the daughter of Beeri = Anah (<reflink>Gen. 26:34; 36:2</reflink>), when she became the wife of Esau. A district among the mountains of Edom, probably near Mount Hor, was called after her name, or it may be that she received her name from the district. From her descended three tribes of Edomites, founded by her three sons.

ai.d: ruins. (1.) One of the royal cities of the Canaanites (<reflink>Josh. 10:1; Gen. 12:8; 13:3</reflink>). It was the scene of Joshua's defeat, and afterwards of his victory. It was the second Canaanite city taken by Israel (<reflink>Josh. 7:2-5; 8:1-29</reflink>). It lay rebuilt and inhibited by the Benjamites (<reflink>Ezra 2:28; Neh. 7:32; 11:31</reflink>). It lay to the east of Bethel, "beside Beth-aven." The spot which is most probably the site of this ancient city is Haiyan, 2 miles east from Bethel. It lay up the Wady Suweinit, a steep, rugged valley, extending from the Jordan valley to Bethel.

aijeleth shahar.d: hind of the dawn, a name found in the title of Ps. 22. It is probably the name of some song or tune to the measure of which the psalm was to be chanted. Some, however, understand by the name some instrument of music, or an allegorical allusion to the subject of the psalm.

air.d: the atmosphere, as opposed to the higher regions of the sky (<reflink>1 Thess. 4:17; Rev. 9:2; 16:17</reflink>). This word occurs once as the rendering of the Hebrew _ruah_ (<reflink>Job 41:16</reflink>); elsewhere it is the rendering of _shamaiyim_, usually translated "heavens."

ajalon.d: and Aij'alon, place of deer. (1.) A town and valley originally assigned to the tribe of Dan, from which, however, they could not drive the Amorites (<reflink>Judg. 1:35</reflink>). It was one of the Levitical cities given to the Kohathites (<reflink>1 Chr. 6:69</reflink>). It was not far from Beth-shemesh (<reflink>2 Chr. 28:18</reflink>). It was the boundary between the kingdoms of Judah and Israel, and is frequently mentioned in Jewish history (<reflink>2 Chr. 11:10; 1 Sam. 14:31; 1 Chr. 8:13</reflink>). With reference to the valley named after the town, Joshua uttered the celebrated command, "Sun, stand thou still on Gibeon; and thou, Moon, in the valley of Ajalon" (<reflink>Josh. 10:12</reflink>). It has been identified as the modern Yalo, at the foot of the Beth-horon pass (q.v.). …

akkub.d: (another form of Jacob). (1.) The head of one of the families of Nethinim (<reflink>Ezra 2:45</reflink>).

akrabbim.d: scorpions, probably the general name given to the ridge containing the pass between the south of the Dead Sea and Zin, es-Sufah, by which there is an ascent to the level of the land of Palestine. Scorpions are said to abound in this whole district, and hence the name (<reflink>Num. 34:4</reflink>). It is called "Maaleh-acrabbim" in Josh. 15:3, and "the ascent of Akrabbim" in Num. 34:4.

alabaster.d: occurs only in the New Testament in connection with the box of "ointment of spikenard very precious," with the contents of which a woman anointed the head of Jesus as he sat at supper in the house of Simon the leper (<reflink>Matt. 26:7; Mark 14:3; Luke 7:37</reflink>). These boxes were made from a stone found near Alabastron in Egypt, and from this circumstance the Greeks gave them the name of the city where they were made. The name was then given to the stone of which they were made; and finally to all perfume vessels, of whatever material they were formed. The woman "broke" the vessel; i.e., she broke off, as was usually done, the long and narrow neck so as to reach the contents. This stone resembles marble, but is softer in its texture, and hence very easily wrought into boxes. Mark says (14:5) that this box of ointment was worth more than 300 pence, i.e., denarii, each of the value of sevenpence halfpenny of our money, and therefore worth about 10 pounds. …

alamoth.d: virgins, a musical term (<reflink>1 Chr. 15:20</reflink>), denoting that the psalm which bears this inscription (Ps. 46) was to be sung by soprano or female voices.

alarm.d: a particular quivering sound of the silver trumpets to give warning to the Hebrews on their journey through the wilderness (<reflink>Num. 10:5, 6</reflink>), a call to arms, or a war-note (<reflink>Jer. 4:19; 49:2; Zeph. 1:16</reflink>).

alemeth.d: covering. (1.) One of the nine sons of Becher, the son of Benjamin (<reflink>1 Chr. 7:8</reflink>).

alexander.d: man-defender. (1.) A relative of Annas the high priest, present when Peter and John were examined before the Sanhedrim (<reflink>Acts 4:6</reflink>).

alexander the great.d: the king of Macedonia, the great conqueror; probably represented in Daniel by the "belly of brass" (<reflink>Dan. 2:32</reflink>), and the leopard and the he-goat (7:6; 11:3,4). He succeeded his father Philip, and died at the age of thirty-two from the effects of intemperance, B.C. 323. His empire was divided among his four generals.

alexandria.d: the ancient metropolis of Lower Egypt, so called from its founder, Alexander the Great (about B.C. 333). It was for a long period the greatest of existing cities, for both Nineveh and Babylon had been destroyed, and Rome had not yet risen to greatness. It was the residence of the kings of Egypt for 200 years. It is not mentioned in the Old Testament, and only incidentally in the New. Apollos, eloquent and mighty in the Scriptures, was a native of this city (<reflink>Acts 18:24</reflink>). Many Jews from Alexandria were in Jerusalem, where they had a synagogue (<reflink>Acts 6:9</reflink>), at the time of Stephen's martyrdom. At one time it is said that as many as 10,000 Jews resided in this city. It possessed a famous library of 700,000 volumes, which was burned by the Saracens (A.D. 642). It was here that the Hebrew Bible was translated into Greek. This is called the Septuagint version, from the tradition that seventy learned men were engaged in executing it. …

algum.d: (<reflink>2 Chr. 2:8; 9:10,11</reflink>), the same as almug (<reflink>1 Kings 10:11</reflink>).

alien.d: a foreigner, or person born in another country, and therefore not entitled to the rights and privileges of the country where he resides. Among the Hebrews there were two classes of aliens.

allegory.d: used only in Gal. 4:24, where the apostle refers to the history of Isaac the free-born, and Ishmael the slave-born, and makes use of it allegorically.

alleluia.d: the Greek form (<reflink>Rev. 19:1, 3, 4, 6</reflink>) of the Hebrew Hallelujah = Praise ye Jehovah, which begins or ends several of the psalms (106, 111, 112, 113, etc.).

alliance.d: a treaty between nations, or between individuals, for their mutual advantage.

allon.d: oak. (1.) The expression in the Authorized Version of Josh. 19:33, "from Allon to Zaanannim," is more correctly rendered in the Revised Version, "from the oak in Zaanannim." The word denotes some remarkable tree which stood near Zaanannim, and which served as a landmark.

allon-bachuth.d: oak of weeping, a tree near Bethel, at the spot where Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, was buried (<reflink>Gen. 35:8</reflink>). Large trees, from their rarity in the plains of Palestine, were frequently designated as landmarks. This particular tree was probably the same as the "palm tree of Deborah" (<reflink>Judg. 4:5</reflink>).

almodad.d: immeasurable, the first named of the sons of Joktan (<reflink>Gen. 10:26</reflink>), the founder of an Arabian tribe.

almon.d: hidden, one of the sacerdotal cities of Benjamin (<reflink>Josh. 21:18</reflink>), called also Alemeth (<reflink>1 Chr. 6:60</reflink>).

almond.d: a native of Syria and Palestine. In form, blossoms, and fruit it resembles the peach tree. Its blossoms are of a very pale pink colour, and appear before its leaves. Its Hebrew name, _shaked_, signifying "wakeful, hastening," is given to it on account of its putting forth its blossoms so early, generally in February, and sometimes even in January. In Eccl. 12:5, it is referred to as illustrative, probably, of the haste with which old age comes. There are others, however, who still contend for the old interpretation here. "The almond tree bears its blossoms in the midst of winter, on a naked, leafless stem, and these blossoms (reddish or flesh-coloured in the beginning) seem at the time of their fall exactly like white snow-flakes. In this way the almond blossom is a very fitting symbol of old age, with its silvery hair and its wintry, dry, barren, unfruitful condition." In Jer. …

alms.d: Not found in the Old Testament, but repeatedly in the New. The Mosaic legislation (<reflink>Lev. 25:35; Deut. 15:7</reflink>) tended to promote a spirit of charity, and to prevent the occurrence of destitution among the people. Such passages as these, Ps. 41:1; 112:9; Prov. 14:31; Isa. 10:2; Amos 2:7; Jer. 5:28; Ezek. 22:29, would also naturally foster the same benevolent spirit.

almug.d: (<reflink>1 Kings 10:11, 12</reflink>) = algum (<reflink>2 Chr. 2:8; 9:10, 11</reflink>), in the Hebrew occurring only in the plural _almuggim_ (indicating that the wood was brought in planks), the name of a wood brought from Ophir to be used in the building of the temple, and for other purposes. Some suppose it to have been the white sandal-wood of India, the Santalum album of botanists, a native of the mountainous parts of the Malabar coasts. It is a fragrant wood, and is used in China for incense in idol-worship. Others, with some probability, think that it was the Indian red sandal-wood, the pterocarpus santalinus, a heavy, fine-grained wood, the Sanscrit name of which is valguka. It is found on the Coromandel coast and in Ceylon.

aloes.d: (Heb. 'ahalim), a fragrant wood (<reflink>Num. 24:6; Ps. 45:8; Prov. 7:17; Cant. 4:14</reflink>), the Aquilaria agallochum of botanists, or, as some suppose, the costly gum or perfume extracted from the wood. It is found in China, Siam, and Northern India, and grows to the height sometimes of 120 feet. This species is of great rarity even in India. There is another and more common species, called by Indians aghil, whence Europeans have given it the name of Lignum aquile, or eagle-wood. Aloewood was used by the Egyptians for embalming dead bodies. Nicodemus brought it (pounded aloe-wood) to embalm the body of Christ (<reflink>John 19:39</reflink>); but whether this was the same as that mentioned elsewhere is uncertain.

alphaeus.d: (1.) The father of James the Less, the apostle and writer of the epistle (<reflink>Matt. 10:3; Mark 3:18; Luke 6:15; Acts 1:13</reflink>), and the husband of Mary (<reflink>John 19:25</reflink>). The Hebrew form of this name is Cleopas, or Clopas (q.v.).

altar.d: (Heb. mizbe'ah, from a word meaning "to slay"), any structure of earth (<reflink>Ex. 20:24</reflink>) or unwrought stone (20:25) on which sacrifices were offered. Altars were generally erected in conspicuous places (<reflink>Gen. 22:9; Ezek. 6:3; 2 Kings 23:12; 16:4; 23:8; Acts 14:13</reflink>). The word is used in Heb. 13:10 for the sacrifice offered upon it--the sacrifice Christ offered.

altaschith.d: destroy not, the title of Ps. 57, 58, 59, and 75. It was probably the name of some song to the melody of which these psalms were to be chanted.

alush.d: one of the places, the last before Rephidim, at which the Hebrews rested on their way to Sinai (<reflink>Num. 33:13, 14</reflink>). It was probably situated on the shore of the Red Sea.

amalek.d: dweller in a valley, the son of Eliphaz and grandson of Esau (<reflink>Gen. 36:12; 1 Chr. 1:36</reflink>); the chief of an Idumean tribe (<reflink>Gen. 36:16</reflink>). His mother was a Horite, a tribe whose territory the descendants of Esau had seized.

amalekite.d: a tribe that dwelt in Arabia Petraea, between the Dead Sea and the Red Sea. They were not the descendants of Amalek, the son of Eliphaz, for they existed in the days of Abraham (<reflink>Gen. 14:7</reflink>). They were probably a tribe that migrated from the shores of the Persian Gulf and settled in Arabia. "They dwelt in the land of the south...from Havilah until thou comest to Shur" (<reflink>Num. 13:29; 1 Sam. 15:7</reflink>). They were a pastoral, and hence a nomadic race. Their kings bore the hereditary name of Agag (<reflink>Num. 24:7; 1 Sam. 15:8</reflink>). They attempted to stop the Israelites when they marched through their territory (<reflink>Deut. 25:18</reflink>), attacking them at Rephidim (<reflink>Ex. 17:8-13; comp. Deut. 25:17; 1 Sam. 15:2</reflink>). They afterwards attacked the Israelites at Hormah (<reflink>Num. 14:45</reflink>). We read of them subsequently as in league with the Moabites (<reflink>Judg. 3:13</reflink>) and the Midianites (<reflink>Judg. …

amana.d: perennial. (1.) The Hebrew margin of 2 Kings 5:12 gives this as another reading of Abana (q.v.), a stream near Damascus.

amariah.d: said by Jehovah. (1.) One of the descendants of Aaron by Eleazar (<reflink>1 Chr. 6:7,52</reflink>). He was probably the last of the high priests of Eleazar's line prior to the transfer of that office to Eli, of the line of Ithamar.

amasa.d: burden. (1.) The son of Abigail, a sister of king David (<reflink>1 Chr. 2:17; 2 Sam. 17:25</reflink>). He was appointed by David to command the army in room of his cousin Joab (<reflink>2 Sam. 19:13</reflink>), who afterwards treacherously put him to death as a dangerous rival (<reflink>2 Sam. 20:4-12</reflink>).

amasai.d: burdensome. (1.) A Levite, son of Elkanah, of the ancestry of Samuel (<reflink>1 Chr. 6:25, 35</reflink>).

amashai.d: the son of Azareel, appointed by Nehemiah to reside at Jerusalem and do the work of the temple (<reflink>Neh. 11:13</reflink>).

amasiah.d: burden of (i.e., "sustained by") Jehovah, the "son of Zichri, who willingly offered himself unto the Lord," a captain over thousands under Jehoshaphat (<reflink>2 Chr. 17:16; comp. Judg. 5:9</reflink>).

amaziah.d: strengthened by Jehovah. (1.) A Levite, son of Hilkiah, of the descendants of Ethan the Merarite (<reflink>1 Chr. 6:45</reflink>).

ambassador.d: In the Old Testament the Hebrew word _tsir_, meaning "one who goes on an errand," is rendered thus (<reflink>Josh. 9:4; Prov. 13:17; Isa. 18:2; Jer. 49:14; Obad. 1:1</reflink>). This is also the rendering of _melits_, meaning "an interpreter," in 2 Chr. 32:31; and of _malak_, a "messenger," in 2 Chr. 35:21; Isa. 30:4; 33:7; Ezek. 17:15. This is the name used by the apostle as designating those who are appointed by God to declare his will (<reflink>2 Cor. 5:20; Eph. 6:20</reflink>).

amber.d: (<reflink>Ezek. 1:4, 27; 8:2. Heb., hashmal, rendered by the LXX. elektron, and by the Vulgate electrum</reflink>), a metal compounded of silver and gold. Some translate the word by "polished brass," others "fine brass," as in Rev. 1:15; 2:18. It was probably the mixture now called electrum. The word has no connection, however, with what is now called amber, which is a gummy substance, reckoned as belonging to the mineral kingdom though of vegetable origin, a fossil resin.

ambush.d: Joshua at the capture of Ai lay in ambush, and so deceived the inhabitants that he gained an easy victory (<reflink>Josh. 8:4-26</reflink>). Shechem was taken in this manner (<reflink>Judg. 9:30-45. Comp. Jer. 51:12</reflink>).

amen.d: This Hebrew word means firm, and hence also faithful (<reflink>Rev. 3:14</reflink>). In Isa. 65:16, the Authorized Version has "the God of truth," which in Hebrew is "the God of Amen." It is frequently used by our Saviour to give emphasis to his words, where it is translated "verily." Sometimes, only, however, in John's Gospel, it is repeated, "Verily, verily." It is used as an epithet of the Lord Jesus Christ (<reflink>Rev. 3:14</reflink>).

amethyst.d: one of the precious stones in the breastplate of the high priest (<reflink>Ex. 28:19; 39:12</reflink>), and in the foundation of the New Jerusalem (<reflink>Rev. 21:20</reflink>). The ancients thought that this stone had the power of dispelling drunkenness in all who wore or touched it, and hence its Greek name formed from _a_, "privative," and _methuo_, "to get drunk." Its Jewish name, _ahlamah'_, was derived by the rabbins from the Hebrew word _halam_, "to dream," from its supposed power of causing the wearer to dream.

amittai.d: true, the father of Jonah the prophet, a native of Gath-hepher (<reflink>2 Kings 14:25; Jonah 1:1</reflink>).

apharsites.d: another of the tribes removed to Samaria (<reflink>Ezra 4:9</reflink>), or perhaps the same as the preceding.

aphik.d: (<reflink>Judg. 1:31</reflink>); Aphek (<reflink>Josh. 13:4; 19:30</reflink>), stronghold. (1.) A city of the tribe of Asher. It was the scene of the licentious worship of the Syrian Aphrodite. The ruins of the temple, "magnificent ruins" in a "spot of strange wildness and beauty", are still seen at Afka, on the north-west slopes of Lebanon, near the source of the river Adonis (now Nahr Ibrahim), 12 miles east of Gebal.

apocalypse.d: the Greek name of the Book of Revelation (q.v.).

apocrypha.d: hidden, spurious, the name given to certain ancient books which found a place in the LXX. and Latin Vulgate versions of the Old Testament, and were appended to all the great translations made from them in the sixteenth century, but which have no claim to be regarded as in any sense parts of the inspired Word.

apollonia.d: a city of Macedonia between Amphipolis and Thessalonica, from which it was distant about 36 miles. Paul and Silas passed through it on their way to Thessalonica (<reflink>Acts 17:1</reflink>).

apollos.d: a Jew "born at Alexandria," a man well versed in the Scriptures and eloquent (<reflink>Acts 18:24; R.V., "learned"</reflink>). He came to Ephesus (about A.D. 49), where he spake "boldly" in the synagogue (18:26), although he did not know as yet that Jesus of Nazareth was the Messiah. Aquila and Priscilla instructed him more perfectly in "the way of God", i.e., in the knowledge of Christ. He then proceeded to Corinth, where he met Paul (<reflink>Acts 18:27; 19:1</reflink>). He was there very useful in watering the good seed Paul had sown (<reflink>1 Cor. 1:12</reflink>), and in gaining many to Christ. His disciples were much attached to him (<reflink>1 Cor. 3:4-7, 22</reflink>). He was with Paul at Ephesus when he wrote the First Epistle to the Corinthians; and Paul makes kindly reference to him in his letter to Titus (3:13). Some have supposed, although without sufficient ground, that he was the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews.

apollyon.d: destroyer, the name given to the king of the hosts represented by the locusts (<reflink>Rev. 9:11</reflink>). It is the Greek translation of the Hebrew Abaddon (q.v.).

apostle.d: a person sent by another; a messenger; envoy. This word is once used as a descriptive designation of Jesus Christ, the Sent of the Father (<reflink>Heb. 3:1; John 20:21</reflink>). It is, however, generally used as designating the body of disciples to whom he intrusted the organization of his church and the dissemination of his gospel, "the twelve," as they are called (<reflink>Matt. 10:1-5; Mark 3:14; 6:7; Luke 6:13; 9:1</reflink>). We have four lists of the apostles, one by each of the synoptic evangelists (<reflink>Matt. 10:2-4; Mark 3:16; Luke 6:14</reflink>), and one in the Acts (1:13). No two of these lists, however, perfectly coincide.

apothecary.d: rendered in the margin and the Revised Version "perfumer," in Ex. 30:25; 37:29; Eccl. 10:1. The holy oils and ointments were prepared by priests properly qualified for this office. The feminine plural form of the Hebrew word is rendered "confectionaries" in 1 Sam. 8:13.

apparel.d: In Old Testament times the distinction between male and female attire was not very marked. The statute forbidding men to wear female apparel (<reflink>Deut. 22:5</reflink>) referred especially to ornaments and head-dresses. Both men and women wore (1) an under garment or tunic, which was bound by a girdle. One who had only this tunic on was spoken of as "naked" (<reflink>1 Sam. 19:24; Job 24:10; Isa. 20:2</reflink>). Those in high stations sometimes wore two tunics, the outer being called the "upper garment" (<reflink>1 Sam. 15:27; 18:4; 24:5; Job 1:20</reflink>). (2.) They wore in common an over-garment ("mantle," Isa. 3:22; 1 Kings 19:13; 2 Kings 2:13), a loose and flowing robe. The folds of this upper garment could be formed into a lap (<reflink>Ruth 3:15; Ps. 79:12; Prov. 17:23; Luke 6:38</reflink>). Generals of armies usually wore scarlet robes (<reflink>Judg. 8:26; Nah. 2:3</reflink>). A form of conspicuous raiment is mentioned in Luke 20:46; comp. Matt. 23:5.

appeal.d: a reference of any case from an inferior to a superior court. Moses established in the wilderness a series of judicatories such that appeals could be made from a lower to a higher (<reflink>Ex. 18:13-26.</reflink>)

apphia.d: increasing, a female Christian at Colosse (<reflink>Philemon 1:2</reflink>), supposed by some to have been the wife of Philemon.

appii forum.d: i.e., "the market of Appius" (<reflink>Acts 28:15, R.V.</reflink>), a town on the road, the "Appian Way," from Rome to Brundusium. It was 43 miles from Rome. Here Paul was met by some Roman Christians on his way to the capital. It was natural that they should halt here and wait for him, because from this place there were two ways by which travellers might journey to Rome.

apple.d: (Heb. tappuah, meaning "fragrance"). Probably the apricot or quince is intended by the word, as Palestine was too hot for the growth of apples proper. It is enumerated among the most valuable trees of Palestine (<reflink>Joel 1:12</reflink>), and frequently referred to in Canticles, and noted for its beauty (2:3, 5; 8:5). There is nothing to show that it was the "tree of the knowledge of good and evil." Dr. Tristram has suggested that the apricot has better claims than any other fruit-tree to be the apple of Scripture. It grows to a height of 30 feet, has a roundish mass of glossy leaves, and bears an orange coloured fruit that gives out a delicious perfume. The "apple of the eye" is the Heb. _ishon_, meaning manikin, i.e., the pupil of the eye (<reflink>Prov. 7:2</reflink>). (Comp. the promise, Zech. 2:8; the prayer, Ps. 17:8; and its fulfilment, Deut. 32:10.)

apron.d: found in the Authorized Version in Gen. 3:7, of the bands of fig-leaves made by our first parents. In Acts 19:12, it denotes the belt or half-girdle worn by artisans and servants round the waist for the purpose of preserving the clothing from injury. In marg. of Authorized Version, Ruth 3:15, correctly rendered instead of "vail." (R.V., "mantle.")

aquila.d: eagle, a native of Pontus, by occupation a tent-maker, whom Paul met on his first visit to Corinth (<reflink>Acts 18:2</reflink>). Along with his wife Priscilla he had fled from Rome in consequence of a decree (A.D. 50) by Claudius commanding all Jews to leave the city. Paul sojourned with him at Corinth, and they wrought together at their common trade, making Cilician hair-cloth for tents. On Paul's departure from Corinth after eighteen months, Aquila and his wife accompanied him to Ephesus, where they remained, while he proceeded to Syria (<reflink>Acts 18:18, 26</reflink>). When they became Christians we are not informed, but in Ephesus they were (<reflink>1 Cor. 16:19</reflink>) Paul's "helpers in Christ Jesus." We find them afterwards at Rome (<reflink>Rom. 16:3</reflink>), interesting themselves still in the cause of Christ. They are referred to some years after this as being at Ephesus (<reflink>2 Tim. 4:19</reflink>). This is the last notice we have of them.

arab.d: ambush, a city in the mountains of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:52</reflink>), now Er-Rabiyeh.

arabah.d: plain, in the Revised Version of 2 Kings 14:25; Josh. 3:16; 8:14; 2 Sam. 2:29; 4:7 (in all these passages the A.V. has "plain"); Amos 6:14 (A.V. "wilderness"). This word is found in the Authorized Version only in Josh. 18:18. It denotes the hollow depression through which the Jordan flows from the Lake of Galilee to the Dead Sea. It is now called by the Arabs el-Ghor. But the Ghor is sometimes spoken of as extending 10 miles south of the Dead Sea, and thence to the Gulf of Akabah on the Red Sea is called the Wady el-Arabah.

arabia.d: arid, an extensive region in the south-west of Asia. It is bounded on the west by the Isthmus of Suez and the Red Sea, on the south by the Indian Ocean, and on the east by the Persian Gulf and the Euphrates. It extends far into the north in barren deserts, meeting those of Syria and Mesopotamia. It is one of the few countries of the world from which the original inhabitants have never been expelled.

arad.d: (1.) Now Tell Arad, a Canaanite city, about 20 miles south of Hebron. The king of Arad "fought against Israel and took of them prisoners" when they were retreating from the confines of Edom (<reflink>Num. 21:1; 33:40; Judg. 1:16</reflink>). It was finally subdued by Joshua (12:14).

aram.d: the son of Shem (<reflink>Gen. 10:22</reflink>); according to Gen. 22:21, a grandson of Nahor. In Matt. 1:3, 4, and Luke 3:33, this word is the Greek form of Ram, the father of Amminadab (<reflink>1 Chr. 2:10</reflink>).

aram-naharaim.d: Aram of the two rivers, is Mesopotamia (<reflink>as it is rendered in Gen. 24:10</reflink>), the country enclosed between the Tigris on the east and the Euphrates on the west (Ps. 60, title); called also the "field of Aram" (<reflink>Hos. 12:12, R.V.</reflink>) i.e., the open country of Aram; in the Authorized Version, "country of Syria." Padan-aram (q.v.) was a portion of this country.

aram-zobah.d: (Ps. 60, title), probably the region between the Euphrates and the Orontes.

aran.d: wild goat, a descendant of Seir the Horite (<reflink>Gen. 36:28</reflink>).
