ararat.d: sacred land or high land, the name of a country on one of the mountains of which the ark rested after the Flood subsided (<reflink>Gen. 8:4</reflink>). The "mountains" mentioned were probably the Kurdish range of South Armenia. In 2 Kings 19:37, Isa. 37:38, the word is rendered "Armenia" in the Authorized Version, but in the Revised Version, "Land of Ararat." In Jer. 51:27, the name denotes the central or southern portion of Armenia. It is, however, generally applied to a high and almost inaccessible mountain which rises majestically from the plain of the Araxes. It has two conical peaks, about 7 miles apart, the one 14,300 feet and the other 10,300 feet above the level of the plain. Three thousand feet of the summit of the higher of these peaks is covered with perpetual snow. It is called Kuh-i-nuh, i.e., "Noah's mountain", by the Persians. …

araunah.d: agile; also called Ornan 1 Chr. 21:15, a Jebusite who dwelt in Jerusalem before it was taken by the Israelites. The destroying angel, sent to punish David for his vanity in taking a census of the people, was stayed in his work of destruction near a threshing-floor belonging to Araunah which was situated on Mount Moriah. Araunah offered it to David as a free gift, together with the oxen and the threshing instruments; but the king insisted on purchasing it at its full price (<reflink>2 Sam. 24:24; 1 Chr. 21:24, 25</reflink>), for, according to the law of sacrifices, he could not offer to God what cost him nothing. On the same place Solomon afterwards erected the temple (<reflink>2 Sam. 24:16; 2 Chr. 3:1</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See ALTAR.</see>)

arba.d: four, a giant, father of Anak. From him the city of Hebron derived its name of Kirjath-arba, i.e., the city of Araba (<reflink>Josh. 14:15; 15:13; 21:11; Gen. 13:18; 23:2</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See HEBRON.</see>)

arbathite.d: a name given to Abi-albon, or, as elsewhere called, Abiel, one of David's warriors (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:31; 1 Chr. 11:32</reflink>), probably as being an inhabitant of Arabah (<reflink>Josh. 15:61</reflink>), a town in the wilderness of Judah.

arch.d: an architectural term found only in Ezek. 40:16, 21, 22, 26, 29. There is no absolute proof that the Israelites employed arches in their buildings. The arch was employed in the building of the pyramids of Egypt. The oldest existing arch is at Thebes, and bears the date B.C. 1350. There are also still found the remains of an arch, known as Robinson's Arch, of the bridge connecting Zion and Moriah. (<see target="x-self">See TYROPOEON VALLEY.</see>)

archangel.d: (<reflink>1Thess. 4:16; Jude 1:9</reflink>), the prince of the angels.

archelaus.d: ruler of the people, son of Herod the Great, by Malthace, a Samaritan woman. He was educated along with his brother Antipas at Rome. He inherited from his father a third part of his kingdom viz., Idumea, Judea, and Samaria, and hence is called "king" (<reflink>Matt. 2:22</reflink>). It was for fear of him that Joseph and Mary turned aside on their way back from Egypt. Till a few days before his death Herod had named Antipas as his successor, but in his last moments he named Archelaus.

archer.d: a shooter with the bow (<reflink>1 Chr. 10:3</reflink>). This art was of high antiquity (<reflink>Gen. 21:20; 27:3</reflink>). Saul was wounded by the Philistine archers (<reflink>1 Sam. 31:3</reflink>). The phrase "breaking the bow" (<reflink>Hos. 1:5; Jer. 49:35</reflink>) is equivalent to taking away one's power, while "strengthening the bow" is a symbol of its increase (<reflink>Gen. 49:24</reflink>). The Persian archers were famous among the ancients (<reflink>Isa. 13:18; Jer. 49:35; 50:9, 14, 29, 42.</reflink>) (<see target="x-self">See BOW</see>).

archevite.d: one of the nations planted by the Assyrians in Samaria (<reflink>Ezra 4:9</reflink>); the men of Erech.

archi.d: a city on the boundary of Ephraim and Benjamin (<reflink>Josh. 16:2</reflink>), between Bethel and Beth-horon the nether.

archippus.d: master of the horse, a "fellow-soldier" of Paul's (<reflink>Philemon 1:2</reflink>), whom he exhorts to renewed activity (<reflink>Col. 4:17</reflink>). He was a member of Philemon's family, probably his son.

archite.d: the usual designation of Hushai (<reflink>2 Sam. 15:32; 17:5, 14; 1 Chr. 27:33</reflink>), who was a native of Archi. He was "the king's friend", i.e., he held office under David similar to that of our modern privy councillor.

arcturus.d: bear-keeper, the name given by the ancients to the brightest star in the constellation Bootes. In the Authorized Version (<reflink>Job 9:9; 38:32</reflink>) it is the rendering of the Hebrew word _'ash_, which probably designates the constellation the Great Bear. This word ('ash) is supposed to be derived from an Arabic word meaning night-watcher, because the Great Bear always revolves about the pole, and to our nothern hemisphere never sets.

ard.d: descent, a grandson of Benjamin (<reflink>Num. 26:38-40</reflink>). In 1 Chr. 8:3 he is called Addar. His descendants are mentioned in Num. 26:40.

ardon.d: descendant, the last of the three sons of Caleb by his first wife Azubah (<reflink>1 Chr. 2:18</reflink>).

areopagite.d: a member of the court of Areopagus (<reflink>Acts 17:34</reflink>).

areopagus.d: the Latin form of the Greek word rendered "Mars' hill." But it denotes also the council or court of justice which met in the open air on the hill. It was a rocky height to the west of the Acropolis at Athens, on the south-east summit of which the council was held which was constituted by Solon, and consisted of nine archons or chief magistrates who were then in office, and the ex-archons of blameless life.

aretas.d: the father-in-law of Herod Antipas, and king of Arabia Petraea. His daughter returned to him on the occasion of her husband's entering into an adulterous alliance with Herodias, the wife of Herod-Philip, his half-brother (<reflink>Luke 3:19, 20; Mark 6:17; Matt. 14:3</reflink>). This led to a war between Aretas and Herod Antipas. Herod's army was wholly destroyed (A.D. 36). Aretas, taking advantage of the complications of the times on account of the death of the Emperor Tiberius (A.D. 37), took possession of Damascus (<reflink>2 Cor. 11:32; comp. Acts 9:25</reflink>). At this time Paul returned to Damascus from Arabia.

argob.d: stony heap, an "island," as it has been called, of rock about 30 miles by 20, rising 20 or 30 feet above the table-land of Bashan; a region of crags and chasms wild and rugged in the extreme. On this "island" stood sixty walled cities, ruled over by Og. It is called Trachonitis ("the rugged region") in the New Testament (<reflink>Luke 3:1</reflink>). These cities were conquered by the Israelites (<reflink>Deut. 3:4; 1 Kings 4:13</reflink>). It is now called the Lejah. Here "sixty walled cities are still traceable in a space of 308 square miles. The architecture is ponderous and massive. Solid walls 4 feet thick, and stones on one another without cement; the roofs enormous slabs of basaltic rock, like iron; the doors and gates are of stone 18 inches thick, secured by ponderous bars. …

arieh.d: the lion, the name of one of the body-guard slain with Pekahiah at Samaria (<reflink>2 Kings 15:25</reflink>) by the conspirator Pekah.

ariel.d: the lion of God. (1.) One of the chief men sent by Ezra to procure Levites for the sanctuary (<reflink>Ezra 8:16</reflink>).

arimathea.d: a "city of the Jews" (<reflink>Luke 23:51</reflink>), the birth-place of Joseph in whose sepulchre our Lord was laid (<reflink>Matt. 27:57, 60; John 19:38</reflink>). It is probably the same place as Ramathaim in Ephraim, and the birth-place of Samuel (<reflink>1 Sam. 1:1, 19</reflink>). Others identify it with Ramleh in Dan, or Rama (q.v.) in Benjamin (<reflink>Matt. 2:18</reflink>).

ammah.d: a cubit, the name of a hill which Joab and Abishai reached as the sun went down, when they were in pursuit of Abner (<reflink>2 Sam. 2:24</reflink>). It lay to the east of Gibeon.

ammi.d: my people, a name given by Jehovah to the people of Israel (<reflink>Hos. 2:1, 23. Comp. 1:9; Ezek. 16:8; Rom. 9:25, 26; 1 Pet. 2:10</reflink>).

ammiel.d: people of God. (1.) One of the twelve spies sent by Moses to search the land of Canaan (<reflink>Num. 13:12</reflink>). He was one of the ten who perished by the plague for their unfavourable report (<reflink>Num. 14:37</reflink>).

ammihud.d: people of glory; i.e., "renowned." (1.) The father of the Ephraimite chief Elishama, at the time of the Exodus (<reflink>Num. 1:10; 2:18; 7:48, 53</reflink>).

amminadab.d: kindred of the prince. (1.) The father of Nahshon, who was chief of the tribe of Judah (<reflink>Num. 1:7; 2:3; 7:12, 17; 10:14</reflink>). His daughter Elisheba was married to Aaron (<reflink>Ex. 6:23</reflink>).

amminadib.d: a person mentioned in Cant. 6:12, whose chariots were famed for their swiftness. It is rendered in the margin "my willing people," and in the Revised Version "my princely people."

ammishaddai.d: people of the Almighty, the father of Ahiezer, who was chief of the Danites at the time of the Exodus (<reflink>Num. 1:12; 2:25</reflink>). This is one of the few names compounded with the name of God, Shaddai, "Almighty."

ammizabad.d: people of the giver, the son of Benaiah, who was the third and chief captain of the host under David (<reflink>1 Chr. 27:6</reflink>).

ammon.d: another form of the name Ben-ammi, the son of Lot (<reflink>Gen. 19:38</reflink>). This name is also used for his posterity (<reflink>Ps. 83:7</reflink>).

ammonite.d: the usual name of the descendants of Ammon, the son of Lot (<reflink>Gen. 19:38</reflink>). From the very beginning (<reflink>Deut. 2:16-20</reflink>) of their history till they are lost sight of (<reflink>Judg. 5:2</reflink>), this tribe is closely associated with the Moabites (<reflink>Judg. 10:11; 2 Chr. 20:1; Zeph. 2:8</reflink>). Both of these tribes hired Balaam to curse Israel (<reflink>Deut. 23:4</reflink>). The Ammonites were probably more of a predatory tribe, moving from place to place, while the Moabites were more settled. They inhabited the country east of the Jordan and north of Moab and the Dead Sea, from which they had expelled the Zamzummims or Zuzims (<reflink>Deut. 2:20; Gen. 14:5</reflink>). They are known as the Beni-ammi (<reflink>Gen. 19:38</reflink>), Ammi or Ammon being worshipped as their chief god. They were of Semitic origin, and closely related to the Hebrews in blood and language. …

amnon.d: faithful. (1.) One of the sons of Shammai, of the children of Ezra (<reflink>1 Chr. 4:20; comp. 17</reflink>).

amon.d: builder. (1.) The governor of Samaria in the time of Ahab. The prophet Micaiah was committed to his custody (<reflink>1 Kings 22:26; 2 Chr. 18:25</reflink>).

amorites.d: highlanders, or hillmen, the name given to the descendants of one of the sons of Canaan (<reflink>Gen. 14:7</reflink>), called Amurra or Amurri in the Assyrian and Egyptian inscriptions. On the early Babylonian monuments all Syria, including Palestine, is known as "the land of the Amorites." The southern slopes of the mountains of Judea are called the "mount of the Amorites" (<reflink>Deut. 1:7, 19, 20</reflink>). They seem to have originally occupied the land stretching from the heights west of the Dead Sea (<reflink>Gen. 14:7</reflink>) to Hebron (<reflink>13. Comp. 13:8; Deut. 3:8; 4:46-48</reflink>), embracing "all Gilead and all Bashan" (<reflink>Deut. 3:10</reflink>), with the Jordan valley on the east of the river (4:49), the land of the "two kings of the Amorites," Sihon and Og (<reflink>Deut. 31:4; Josh. 2:10; 9:10</reflink>). The five kings of the Amorites were defeated with great slaughter by Joshua (10:10). …

amos.d: borne; a burden, one of the twelve minor prophets. He was a native of Tekota, the modern Tekua, a town about 12 miles south-east of Bethlehem. He was a man of humble birth, neither a "prophet nor a prophet's son," but "an herdman and a dresser of sycomore trees," R.V. He prophesied in the days of Uzziah, king of Judah, and was contemporary with Isaiah and Hosea (<reflink>Amos 1:1; 7:14, 15; Zech. 14:5</reflink>), who survived him a few years. Under Jeroboam II. the kingdom of Israel rose to the zenith of its prosperity; but that was followed by the prevalence of luxury and vice and idolatry. At this period Amos was called from his obscurity to remind the people of the law of God's retributive justice, and to call them to repentance.

amoz.d: strong, the father of the prophet Isaiah (<reflink>2 Kings 19:2, 20; 20:1; Isa. 1:1; 2:1</reflink>). As to his personal history little is positively known. He is supposed by some to have been the "man of God" spoken of in 2 Chr. 25:7, 8.

amphipolis.d: city on both sides, a Macedonian city, a great Roman military station, through which Paul and Silas passed on their way from Philippi to Thessalonica, a distance of 33 Roman miles from Philippi (<reflink>Acts 17:1</reflink>).

amplias.d: a Roman Christian saluted by Paul (<reflink>Rom. 16:8</reflink>).

amram.d: kindred of the High; i.e., "friend of Jehovah." (1.) The son of Kohath, the son of Levi. He married Jochebed, "his father's sister," and was the father of Aaron, Miriam, and Moses (<reflink>Ex. 6:18, 20; Num. 3:19</reflink>). He died in Egypt at the age of 137 years (<reflink>Ex. 6:20</reflink>). His descendants were called Amramites (<reflink>Num. 3:27; 1 Chr. 26:23</reflink>). (2.) Ezra 10:34.

amraphel.d: king of Shinar, southern Chaldea, one of the confederates of Chedorlaomer, king of Elam, in a war against Sodom and cities of the plain (<reflink>Gen. 14:1, 4</reflink>). It is now found that Amraphel (or Ammirapaltu) is the Khammu-rabi whose name appears on recently-discovered monuments. (<see target="x-self">See CHEDORLAOMER</see>). After defeating Arioch (q.v.) he united Babylonia under one rule, and made Babylon his capital.

anab.d: grape-town, one of the cities in the mountains of Judah, from which Joshua expelled the Anakim (<reflink>Josh. 11:21; 15:50</reflink>). It still retains its ancient name. It lies among the hills, 10 miles south-south-west of Hebron.

anah.d: speech. (1.) One of the sons of Seir, and head of an Idumean tribe, called a Horite, as in course of time all the branches of this tribe were called from their dwelling in caves in Mount Seir (<reflink>Gen. 36:20, 29; 1 Chr. 1:38</reflink>).

anak.d: long-necked, the son of Arba, father of the Anakim (<reflink>Josh. 15:13; 21:11, Heb. _Anok_</reflink>).

anakim.d: the descendants of Anak (<reflink>Josh. 11:21; Num. 13:33; Deut. 9:2</reflink>). They dwelt in the south of Palestine, in the neighbourhood of Hebron (<reflink>Gen. 23:2; Josh. 15:13</reflink>). In the days of Abraham (<reflink>Gen. 14:5, 6</reflink>) they inhabited the region afterwards known as Edom and Moab, east of the Jordan. They were probably a remnant of the original inhabitants of Palestine before the Canaanites, a Cushite tribe from Babel, and of the same race as the Phoenicians and the Egyptian shepherd kings. Their formidable warlike appearance, as described by the spies sent to search the land, filled the Israelites with terror. They seem to have identified them with the Nephilim, the "giants" (<reflink>Gen. 6:4; Num. 13:33</reflink>) of the antediluvian age. There were various tribes of Anakim (<reflink>Josh. 15:14</reflink>). Joshua finally expelled them from the land, except a remnant that found a refuge in the cities of Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod (<reflink>Josh. …

anamim.d: the name of an Egyptian tribe descended from Mizraim (<reflink>Gen. 10:13; 1 Chr. 1:11</reflink>).

anammelech.d: one of the gods worshipped by the people of Sepharvaim, who colonized Samaria (<reflink>2 Kings 17:31</reflink>). The name means "Anu is king." It was a female deity representing the moon, as Adrammelech (q.v.) was the male representing the sun.

anan.d: cloud, one of the Israelites who sealed the covenant after the return from Babylon (<reflink>Neh. 10:26</reflink>).

ananiah.d: protected by Jehovah, the name of a town in the tribe of Benjamin between Nob and Hazor (<reflink>Neh. 11:32</reflink>). It is probably the modern Beit Hanina, a small village 3 miles north of Jerusalem.

ananias.d: a common Jewish name, the same as Hananiah. (1.) One of the members of the church at Jerusalem, who conspired with his wife Sapphira to deceive the brethren, and who fell down and immediately expired after he had uttered the falsehood (<reflink>Acts 5:5</reflink>). By common agreement the members of the early Christian community devoted their property to the work of furthering the gospel and of assisting the poor and needy. The proceeds of the possessions they sold were placed at the disposal of the apostles (<reflink>Acts 4:36, 37</reflink>). Ananias might have kept his property had he so chosen; but he professed agreement with the brethren in the common purpose, and had of his own accord devoted it all, as he said, to these sacred ends. Yet he retained a part of it for his own ends, and thus lied in declaring that he had given it all. …

anath.d: an answer; i.e., to "prayer", the father of Shamgar, who was one of the judges of Israel (<reflink>Judg. 3:31</reflink>).

anathema.d: anything laid up or suspended; hence anything laid up in a temple or set apart as sacred. In this sense the form of the word is _anath(ee)ma_, once in plural used in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 21:5, where it is rendered "gifts." In the LXX. the form _anathema_ is generally used as the rendering of the Hebrew word _herem_, derived from a verb which means (1) to consecrate or devote; and (2) to exterminate. Any object so devoted to the Lord could not be redeemed (<reflink>Num. 18:14; Lev. 27:28, 29</reflink>); and hence the idea of exterminating connected with the word. The Hebrew verb (haram) is frequently used of the extermination of idolatrous nations. It had a wide range of application. The _anathema_ or _herem_ was a person or thing irrevocably devoted to God (<reflink>Lev. 27:21, 28</reflink>); and "none devoted shall be ransomed. He shall surely be put to death" (27:29). The word therefore carried the idea of devoted to destruction (<reflink>Num. 21:2, 3; Josh. …

anathoth.d: the name of one of the cities of refuge, in the tribe of Benjamin (<reflink>Josh. 21:18</reflink>). The Jews, as a rule, did not change the names of the towns they found in Palestine; hence this town may be regarded as deriving its name from the goddess Anat. It was the native place of Abiezer, one of David's "thirty" (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:27</reflink>), and of Jehu, another of his mighty men (<reflink>1 Chr. 12:3</reflink>). It is chiefly notable, however, as the birth-place and usual residence of Jeremiah (<reflink>Jer. 1:1; 11:21-23; 29:27; 32:7-9</reflink>). It suffered greatly from the army of Sennacherib, and only 128 men returned to it from the Exile (<reflink>Neh. 7:27; Ezra 2:23</reflink>). It lay about 3 miles north of Jerusalem. It has been identified with the small and poor village of 'Anata, containing about 100 inhabitants.

anchor.d: From Acts 27:29, 30, 40, it would appear that the Roman vessels carried several anchors, which were attached to the stern as well as to the prow. The Roman anchor, like the modern one, had two teeth or flukes. In Heb. 6:19 the word is used metaphorically for that which supports or keeps one steadfast in the time of trial or of doubt. It is an emblem of hope.

ancient of days.d: an expression applied to Jehovah three times in the vision of Daniel (7:9, 13, 22) in the sense of eternal. In contrast with all earthly kings, his days are past reckoning.

andrew.d: manliness, a Greek name; one of the apostles of our Lord. He was of Bethsaida in Galilee (<reflink>John 1:44</reflink>), and was the brother of Simon Peter (<reflink>Matt. 4:18; 10:2</reflink>). On one occasion John the Baptist, whose disciple he then was, pointing to Jesus, said, "Behold the Lamb of God" (<reflink>John 1:40</reflink>); and Andrew, hearing him, immediately became a follower of Jesus, the first of his disciples. After he had been led to recognize Jesus as the Messiah, his first care was to bring also his brother Simon to Jesus. The two brothers seem to have after this pursued for a while their usual calling as fishermen, and did not become the stated attendants of the Lord till after John's imprisonment (<reflink>Matt. 4:18, 19; Mark 1:16, 17</reflink>). Very little is related of Andrew. …

andronicus.d: man-conquering, a Jewish Christian, the kinsman and fellowprisoner of Paul (<reflink>Rom. 16:7</reflink>); "of note among the apostles."

anem.d: two fountains, a Levitical city in the tribe of Issachar (<reflink>1 Chr. 6:73</reflink>). It is also called En-gannim (q.v.) in Josh. 19:21; the modern Jenin.

aner.d: a boy. (1.) A Canaanitish chief who joined his forces with those of Abraham in pursuit of Chedorlaomer (<reflink>Gen. 14:13,24</reflink>).

angel.d: a word signifying, both in the Hebrew and Greek, a "messenger," and hence employed to denote any agent God sends forth to execute his purposes. It is used of an ordinary messenger (<reflink>Job 1:14: 1 Sam. 11:3; Luke 7:24; 9:52</reflink>), of prophets (<reflink>Isa. 42:19; Hag. 1:13</reflink>), of priests (<reflink>Mal. 2:7</reflink>), and ministers of the New Testament (<reflink>Rev. 1:20</reflink>).

anger.d: the emotion of instant displeasure on account of something evil that presents itself to our view. In itself it is an original susceptibility of our nature, just as love is, and is not necessarily sinful. It may, however, become sinful when causeless, or excessive, or protracted (<reflink>Matt. 5:22; Eph. 4:26; Col. 3:8</reflink>). As ascribed to God, it merely denotes his displeasure with sin and with sinners (<reflink>Ps. 7:11</reflink>).

anim.d: fountains, a city in the mountains of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:50</reflink>), now el-Ghuwein, near Eshtemoh, about 10 miles south-west of Hebron.

animal.d: an organized living creature endowed with sensation. The Levitical law divided animals into clean and unclean, although the distinction seems to have existed before the Flood (<reflink>Gen. 7:2</reflink>). The clean could be offered in sacrifice and eaten. All animals that had not cloven hoofs and did not chew the cud were unclean. The list of clean and unclean quadrupeds is set forth in the Levitical law (<reflink>Deut. 14:3-20; Lev. 11</reflink>).

anise.d: This word is found only in Matt. 23:23. It is the plant commonly known by the name of dill, the Peucedanum graveolens of the botanist. This name dill is derived from a Norse word which means to soothe, the plant having the carminative property of allaying pain. The common dill, the Anethum graveolens, is an annual growing wild in the cornfields of Spain and Portugal and the south of Europe generally. There is also a species of dill cultivated in Eastern countries known by the name of shubit. It was this species of garden plant of which the Pharisees were in the habit of paying tithes. The Talmud requires that the seeds, leaves, and stem of dill shall pay tithes. It is an umbelliferous plant, very like the caraway, its leaves, which are aromatic, being used in soups and pickles. The proper anise is the Pimpinella anisum.

anna.d: grace, an aged widow, the daughter of Phanuel. She was a "prophetess," like Miriam, Deborah, and Huldah (<reflink>2 Chr. 34:22</reflink>). After seven years of married life her husband died, and during her long widowhood she daily attended the temple services. When she was eighty-four years old, she entered the temple at the moment when the aged Simeon uttered his memorable words of praise and thanks to God that he had fulfilled his ancient promise in sending his Son into the world (<reflink>Luke 2:36, 37</reflink>).

annas.d: was high priest A.D. 7-14. In A.D. 25 Caiaphas, who had married the daughter of Annas (<reflink>John 18:13</reflink>), was raised to that office, and probably Annas was now made president of the Sanhedrim, or deputy or coadjutor of the high priest, and thus was also called high priest along with Caiaphas (<reflink>Luke 3:2</reflink>). By the Mosaic law the high-priesthood was held for life (<reflink>Num. 3:10</reflink>); and although Annas had been deposed by the Roman procurator, the Jews may still have regarded him as legally the high priest. Our Lord was first brought before Annas, and after a brief questioning of him (<reflink>John 18:19-23</reflink>) was sent to Caiaphas, when some members of the Sanhedrim had met, and the first trial of Jesus took place (<reflink>Matt. 26:57-68</reflink>). This examination of our Lord before Annas is recorded only by John. Annas was president of the Sanhedrim before which Peter and John were brought (<reflink>Acts 4:6</reflink>).

anoint.d: The practice of anointing with perfumed oil was common among the Hebrews. (1.) The act of anointing was significant of consecration to a holy or sacred use; hence the anointing of the high priest (<reflink>Ex. 29:29; Lev. 4:3</reflink>) and of the sacred vessels (<reflink>Ex. 30:26</reflink>). The high priest and the king are thus called "the anointed" (<reflink>Lev. 4:3, 5, 16; 6:20; Ps. 132:10</reflink>). Anointing a king was equivalent to crowning him (<reflink>1 Sam. 16:13; 2 Sam. 2:4, etc.</reflink>). Prophets were also anointed (<reflink>1 Kings 19:16; 1 Chr. 16:22; Ps. 105:15</reflink>). The expression, "anoint the shield" (<reflink>Isa. 21:5</reflink>), refers to the custom of rubbing oil on the leather of the shield so as to make it supple and fit for use in war.

ant.d: (Heb. nemalah, from a word meaning to creep, cut off, destroy), referred to in Prov. 6:6; 30:25, as distinguished for its prudent habits. Many ants in Palestine feed on animal substances, but others draw their nourishment partly or exclusively from vegetables. To the latter class belongs the ant to which Solomon refers. This ant gathers the seeds in the season of ripening, and stores them for future use; a habit that has been observed in ants in Texas, India, and Italy.

antichrist.d: against Christ, or an opposition Christ, a rival Christ. The word is used only by the apostle John. Referring to false teachers, he says (<reflink>1 John 2:18, 22; 4:3; 2 John 1:7</reflink>), "Even now are there many antichrists."

antioch.d: (1.) In Syria, on the river Orontes, about 16 miles from the Mediterranean, and some 300 miles north of Jerusalem. It was the metropolis of Syria, and afterwards became the capital of the Roman province in Asia. It ranked third, after Rome and Alexandria, in point of importance, of the cities of the Roman empire. It was called the "first city of the East." Christianity was early introduced into it (<reflink>Acts 11:19, 21, 24</reflink>), and the name "Christian" was first applied here to its professors (<reflink>Acts 11:26</reflink>). It is intimately connected with the early history of the gospel (<reflink>Acts 6:5; 11:19, 27, 28, 30; 12:25; 15:22-35; Gal. 2:11, 12</reflink>). It was the great central point whence missionaries to the Gentiles were sent forth. It was the birth-place of the famous Christian father Chrysostom, who died A.D. 407. It bears the modern name of Antakia, and is now a miserable, decaying Turkish town. Like Philippi, it was raised to the rank of a Roman colony.

antiochus.d: the name of several Syrian kings from B.C. 280 to B.C. 65. The most notable of these were, (1.) Antiochus the Great, who ascended the throne B.C. 223. He is regarded as the "king of the north" referred to in Dan. 11:13-19. He was succeeded (B.C. 187) by his son, Seleucus Philopater, spoken of by Daniel (11:20) as "a raiser of taxes", in the Revised Version, "one that shall cause an exactor to pass through the glory of the kingdom."

antipas.d: (1.) Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great by his Samaritan wife Malthace. He was tetrarch of Galilee and Peraea during the whole period of our Lord's life on earth (<reflink>Luke 23:7</reflink>). He was a frivolous and vain prince, and was chargeable with many infamous crimes (<reflink>Mark 8:15; Luke 3:19; 13:31, 32</reflink>). He beheaded John the Baptist (<reflink>Matt. 14:1-12</reflink>) at the instigation of Herodias, the wife of his half-brother Herod-Philip, whom he had married. Pilate sent Christ to him when he was at Jerusalem at the Passover (<reflink>Luke 23:7</reflink>). He asked some idle questions of him, and after causing him to be mocked, sent him back again to Pilate. The wife of Chuza, his house-steward, was one of our Lord's disciples (<reflink>Luke 8:3</reflink>).

antipatris.d: a city built by Herod the Great, and called by this name in honour of his father, Antipater. It lay between Caesarea and Lydda, two miles inland, on the great Roman road from Caesarea to Jerusalem. To this place Paul was brought by night (<reflink>Acts 23:31</reflink>) on his way to Caesarea, from which it was distant 28 miles. It is identified with the modern, Ras-el-Ain, where rise the springs of Aujeh, the largest springs in Palestine.

antonia.d: a fortress in Jerusalem, at the north-west corner of the temple area. It is called "the castle" (<reflink>Acts 21:34, 37</reflink>). From the stairs of this castle Paul delivered his famous speech to the multitude in the area below (<reflink>Acts 22:1-21</reflink>). It was originally a place in which were kept the vestments of the high priest. Herod fortified it, and called it Antonia in honour of his friend Mark Antony. It was of great size, and commanded the temple. It was built on a plateau of rock, separated on the north from the hill Bezetha by a ditch about 30 feet deep and 165 feet wide.

antothite.d: an inhabitant of Anathoth, found only in 1 Chr. 11:28; 12:3. In 2 Sam. 23:27 it is Anethothite; in 1 Chr. 27:12, Anetothite. (R.V., "Anathothite.")

anvil.d: the rendering of the Hebrew word , "beaten," found only in Isa. 41:7.

ape.d: an animal of the monkey tribe (<reflink>1 Kings 10:22; 2 Chr. 9:21</reflink>). It was brought from India by the fleets of Solomon and Hiram, and was called by the Hebrews _koph_, and by the Greeks _kepos_, both words being just the Indian Tamil name of the monkey, kapi, i.e., swift, nimble, active. No species of ape has ever been found in Palestine or the adjacent regions.

apelles.d: a Christian at Rome whom Paul salutes (<reflink>Rom. 16:10</reflink>), and styles "approved in Christ."

apharsachites.d: a company of the colonists whom the Assyrian king planted in Samaria (<reflink>Ezra 5:6; 6:6</reflink>).

azazel.d: (<reflink>Lev. 16:8, 10, 26, Revised Version only here; rendered "scape-goat" in the Authorized Version</reflink>). This word has given rise to many different views. Some Jewish interpreters regard it as the name of a place some 12 miles east of Jerusalem, in the wilderness. Others take it to be the name of an evil spirit, or even of Satan. But when we remember that the two goats together form a type of Christ, on whom the Lord "laid the iniquity of us all," and examine into the root meaning of this word (viz., "separation"), the interpretation of those who regard the one goat as representing the atonement made, and the other, that "for Azazel," as representing the effect of the great work of atonement (viz., the complete removal of sin), is certainly to be preferred. The one goat which was "for Jehovah" was offered as a sin-offering, by which atonement was made. …

azaziah.d: whom Jehovah strengthened. (1.) One of the Levitical harpers in the temple (<reflink>1 Chr. 15:21</reflink>).

azekah.d: dug over, a town in the Shephelah or low hills of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:35</reflink>), where the five confederated Amoritish kings were defeated by Joshua and their army destroyed by a hailstrom (10:10, 11). It was one of the places re-occupied by the Jews on their return from the Captivity (<reflink>Neh. 11:30</reflink>).

azel.d: noble, a descendant of king Saul (<reflink>1 Chr. 8:37; 9:43, 44</reflink>).

azmaveth.d: strong as death. (1.) One of David's thirty warriors (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:31</reflink>).

azotus.d: the Grecized form (<reflink>Acts 8:40, etc.</reflink>) of Ashdod (q.v.).

azubah.d: deserted. (1.) The wife of Caleb (<reflink>1 Chr. 2:18, 19</reflink>).

azur and azzur.d: helper. (1.) The father of Hananiah, a false prophet (<reflink>Jer. 28:1</reflink>).

baal.d: lord. (1.) The name appropriated to the principal male god of the Phoenicians. It is found in several places in the plural BAALIM (<reflink>Judg. 2:11; 10:10; 1 Kings 18:18; Jer. 2:23; Hos. 2:17</reflink>). Baal is identified with Molech (<reflink>Jer. 19:5</reflink>). It was known to the Israelites as Baal-peor (<reflink>Num. 25:3; Deut. 4:3</reflink>), was worshipped till the time of Samuel (<reflink>1 Sam 7:4</reflink>), and was afterwards the religion of the ten tribes in the time of Ahab (<reflink>1 Kings 16:31-33; 18:19, 22</reflink>). It prevailed also for a time in the kingdom of Judah (<reflink>2 Kings 8:27; comp. 11:18; 16:3; 2 Chr. 28:2</reflink>), till finally put an end to by the severe discipline of the Captivity (<reflink>Zeph. 1:4-6</reflink>). The priests of Baal were in great numbers (<reflink>1 Kings 18:19</reflink>), and of various classes (<reflink>2 Kings 10:19</reflink>). Their mode of offering sacrifices is described in 1 Kings 18:25-29. …

baal-berith.d: covenant lord, the name of the god worshipped in Shechem after the death of Gideon (<reflink>Judg. 8:33; 9:4</reflink>). In 9:46 he is called simply "the god Berith." The name denotes the god of the covenant into which the Israelites entered with the Canaanites, contrary to the command of Jehovah (<reflink>Ex. 34:12</reflink>), when they began to fall away to the worship of idols.

baal-gad.d: lord of fortune, or troop of Baal, a Canaanite city in the valley of Lebanon at the foot of Hermon, hence called Baal-hermon (<reflink>Judge. 3:3; 1 Chr. 5:23</reflink>), near the source of the Jordan (<reflink>Josh. 13:5; 11:17; 12:7</reflink>). It was the most northern point to which Joshua's conquests extended. It probably derived its name from the worship of Baal. Its modern representative is Banias. Some have supposed it to be the same as Baalbec.

baal-hamon.d: place of a multitude, a place where Solomon had an extensive vineyard (<reflink>Cant. 8:11</reflink>). It has been supposed to be identical with Baal-gad, and also with Hammon in the tribe of Asher (<reflink>Josh. 19:28</reflink>). Others identify it with Belamon, in Central Palestine, near Dothaim.

baal-hanan.d: lord of grace. (1.) A king of Edom, son of Achbor (<reflink>Gen. 36:38, 39; 1 Chr. 1:49, 50</reflink>).

baal-hazor.d: having a courtyard, or Baal's village, the place on the borders of Ephraim and Benjamin where Absalom held the feast of sheep-shearing when Amnon was assassinated (<reflink>2 Sam. 13:23</reflink>). Probably it is the same with Hazor (<reflink>Neh. 11:33</reflink>), now Tell' Asur, 5 miles north-east of Bethel.

baal-hermon.d: lord of Hermon. (1.) A city near Mount Hermon inhabited by the Ephraimites (<reflink>1 Chr. 5:23</reflink>). Probably identical with Baal-gad (<reflink>Josh. 11:17</reflink>).

baal-meon.d: lord of dwelling, a town of Reuben (<reflink>Num. 32:38</reflink>), called also Beth-meon (<reflink>Jer. 48:23</reflink>) and Beth-baal-meon (<reflink>Josh. 13:17</reflink>). It is supposed to have been the birth-place of Elisha. It is identified with the modern M'ain, about 3 miles south-east of Heshbon.

baal-peor.d: lord of the opening, a god of the Moabites (<reflink>Num. 25:3; 31:16; Josh. 22:17</reflink>), worshipped by obscene rites. So called from Mount Peor, where this worship was celebrated, the Baal of Peor. The Israelites fell into the worship of this idol (<reflink>Num. 25:3, 5, 18; Deut. 4:3; Ps. 106:28; Hos. 9:10</reflink>).

baal-perazim.d: Baal having rents, bursts, or destructions, the scene of a victory gained by David over the Philistines (<reflink>2 Sam. 5:20; 1 Chr. 14:11</reflink>). Called Mount Perazim (<reflink>Isa. 28:21</reflink>). It was near the valley of Rephaim, west of Jerusalem. Identified with the modern Jebel Aly.

baal-shalisha.d: lord of Shalisha, a place from which a man came with provisions for Elisha, apparently not far from Gilgal (<reflink>2 Kings 4:42</reflink>). It has been identified with Sirisia, 13 miles north of Lydda.

baal-tamar.d: lord of palm trees, a place in the tribe of Benjamin near Gibeah of Saul (<reflink>Judg. 20:33</reflink>). It was one of the sanctuaries or groves of Baal. Probably the palm tree of Deborah (<reflink>Judg. 4:5</reflink>) is alluded to in the name.

baal-zebub.d: fly-lord, the god of the Philistines at Ekron (<reflink>2 Kings 1:2, 3, 16</reflink>). This name was given to the god because he was supposed to be able to avert the plague of flies which in that region was to be feared. He was consulted by Ahaziah as to his recovery.

baal-zephon.d: Baal of the north, an Egyptian town on the shores of the Gulf of Suez (<reflink>Ex. 14:2; Num. 33:7</reflink>), over against which the children of Israel encamped before they crossed the Red Sea. It is probably to be identified with the modern Jebel Deraj or Kulalah, on the western shore of the Gulf of Suez. Baal-zapuna of the Egyptians was a place of worship.

baalah.d: mistress; city. (1.) A city in the south of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:29</reflink>), elsewhere called Balah (<reflink>Josh. 19:3</reflink>) and Bilhah (<reflink>1 Chr. 4:29</reflink>). Now Khurbet Zebalah.

baalath.d: a town of the tribe of Dan (<reflink>Josh. 19:44</reflink>). It was fortified by Solomon (<reflink>1 Kings 9:18; 2 Chr. 8:6</reflink>). Some have identified it with Bel'ain, in Wady Deir Balut.

baalath-beer.d: Baalah of the well, (Josh. 19:8, probably the same as Baal, mentioned in 1 Chr. 4:33, a city of Simeon.

baalbec.d: called by the Greeks Heliopolis i.e., "the city of the sun", because of its famous Temple of the Sun, has by some been supposed to be Solomon's "house of the forest of Lebanon" (<reflink>1 Kings 7:2; 10:17; 2 Chr. 9:16</reflink>); by others it is identified with Baal-gad (q.v.). It was a city of Coele-Syria, on the lowest declivity of Anti-Libanus, about 42 miles north-west of Damascus. It was one of the most splendid of Syrian cities, existing from a remote antiquity. After sustaining several sieges under the Moslems and others, it was finally destroyed by an earthquake in 1759. Its ruins are of great extent.

baale of judah.d: lords of Judah, a city in the tribe of Judah from which David brought the ark into Jerusalem (<reflink>2 Sam. 6:2</reflink>). Elsewhere (<reflink>1 Chr. 13:6</reflink>) called Kirjath-jearim. (<see target="x-self">See BAALAH.</see>)

baali.d: my lord, a title the prophet (<reflink>Hos. 2:16</reflink>) reproaches the Jewish church for applying to Jehovah, instead of the more endearing title Ishi, meaning "my husband."

baalim.d: plural of Baal; images of the god Baal (<reflink>Judg. 2:11; 1 Sam. 7:4</reflink>).

baalis.d: king of the Ammonites at the time of the Babylonian captivity (<reflink>Jer. 40:14</reflink>). He hired Ishmael to slay Gedaliah who had been appointed governor over the cities of Judah.

baana.d: son of affliction. (1.) One of Solomon's purveyors (<reflink>1 Kings 4:12</reflink>).

baanah.d: son of affliction. (1.) One of the two sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, a captain in Saul's army. He and his brother Rechab assassinated Ishbosheth (<reflink>2 Sam. 4:2</reflink>), and were on this account slain by David, and their mutilated bodies suspended over the pool at Hebron (5, 6, 12).

baasha.d: bravery, the third king of the separate kingdom of Israel, and founder of its second dynasty (1 Kings 15; 16; 2 Chr. 16:1-6). He was the son of Ahijah of the tribe of Issachar. The city of Tirzah he made the capital of his kingdom, and there he was buried, after an eventful reign of twenty-four years (<reflink>1 Kings 15:33</reflink>). On account of his idolatries his family was exterminated, according to the word of the prophet Jehu (<reflink>1 Kings 16:3, 4, 10-13</reflink>).

babe.d: used of children generally (<reflink>Matt. 11:25; 21:16; Luke 10:21; Rom. 2:20</reflink>). It is used also of those who are weak in Christian faith and knowledge (<reflink>1 Cor. 3:1; Heb. 5:13; 1 Pet. 2:2</reflink>). In Isa. 3:4 the word "babes" refers to a succession of weak and wicked princes who reigned over Judah from the death of Josiah downward to the destruction of Jerusalem.

babel, tower of.d: the name given to the tower which the primitive fathers of our race built in the land of Shinar after the Deluge (<reflink>Gen. 11:1-9</reflink>). Their object in building this tower was probably that it might be seen as a rallying-point in the extensive plain of Shinar, to which they had emigrated from the uplands of Armenia, and so prevent their being scattered abroad. But God interposed and defeated their design by condounding their language, and hence the name Babel, meaning "confusion." In the Babylonian tablets there is an account of this event, and also of the creation and the deluge. (<see target="x-self">See CHALDEA.</see>)

babylon.d: the Greek form of BABEL; Semitic form Babilu, meaning "The Gate of God." In the Assyrian tablets it means "The city of the dispersion of the tribes." The monumental list of its kings reaches back to B.C. 2300, and includes Khammurabi, or Amraphel (q.v.), the contemporary of Abraham. It stood on the Euphrates, about 200 miles above its junction with the Tigris, which flowed through its midst and divided it into two almost equal parts. The Elamites invaded Chaldea (i.e., Lower Mesopotamia, or Shinar, and Upper Mesopotamia, or Accad, now combined into one) and held it in subjection. At length Khammu-rabi delivered it from the foreign yoke, and founded the new empire of Chaldea (q.v.), making Babylon the capital of the united kingdom. This city gradually grew in extent and grandeur, but in process of time it became subject to Assyria. On the fall of Nineveh (B.C. 606) it threw off the Assyrian yoke, and became the capital of the growing Babylonian empire. …

babylon, kingdom of.d: called "the land of the Chaldeans" (<reflink>Jer. 24:5; Ezek, 12:13</reflink>), was an extensive province in Central Asia along the valley of the Tigris from the Persian Gulf northward for some 300 miles. It was famed for its fertility and its riches. Its capital was the city of Babylon, a great commercial centre (<reflink>Ezek. 17:4; Isa. 43:14</reflink>). Babylonia was divided into the two districts of Accad in the north, and Summer (probably the Shinar of the Old Testament) in the south. Among its chief cities may be mentioned Ur (now Mugheir or Mugayyar), on the western bank of the Euphrates; Uruk, or Erech (<reflink>Gen. 10:10</reflink>) (now Warka), between Ur and Babylon; Larsa (now Senkereh), the Ellasar of Gen. …

babylonish garment.d: a robe of rich colours fabricated at Babylon, and hence of great value (<reflink>Josh.7:21</reflink>).

baca, valley of.d: (<reflink>Ps. 84:6; R.V., "valley of weeping," marg., "or balsam trees"</reflink>), probably a valley in some part of Palestine, or generally some one of the valleys through which pilgrims had to pass on their way to the sanctuary of Jehovah on Zion; or it may be figuratively "a valley of weeping."

backbite.d: In Ps. 15:3, the rendering of a word which means to run about tattling, calumniating; in Prov. 25:23, secret talebearing or slandering; in Rom. 1:30 and 2 Cor. 12:20, evil-speaking, maliciously defaming the absent.

backslide.d: to draw back or apostatize in matters of religion (<reflink>Acts 21:21; 2 Thess. 2:3; 1 Tim. 4:1</reflink>). This may be either partial (<reflink>Prov. 14:14</reflink>) or complete (<reflink>Heb. 6:4-6; 10:38, 39</reflink>). The apostasy may be both doctrinal and moral.

badger.d: this word is found in Ex. 25:5; 26:14; 35:7, 23; 36:19; 39:34; Num. 4:6, etc. The tabernacle was covered with badgers' skins; the shoes of women were also made of them (<reflink>Ezek. 16:10</reflink>). Our translators seem to have been misled by the similarity in sound of the Hebrew _tachash_ and the Latin _taxus_, "a badger." The revisers have correctly substituted "seal skins." The Arabs of the Sinaitic peninsula apply the name _tucash_ to the seals and dugongs which are common in the Red Sea, and the skins of which are largely used as leather and for sandals. Though the badger is common in Palestine, and might occur in the wilderness, its small hide would have been useless as a tent covering. The dugong, very plentiful in the shallow waters on the shores of the Red Sea, is a marine animal from 12 to 30 feet long, something between a whale and a seal, never leaving the water, but very easily caught. It grazes on seaweed, and is known by naturalists as Halicore tabernaculi.

bag.d: (1.) A pocket of a cone-like shape in which Naaman bound two pieces of silver for Gehazi (<reflink>2 Kings 5:23</reflink>). The same Hebrew word occurs elsewhere only in Isa. 3:22, where it is rendered "crisping-pins," but denotes the reticules (or as R.V., "satchels") carried by Hebrew women.

bahurim.d: young men, a place east of Jerusalem (<reflink>2 Sam. 3:16; 19:16</reflink>), on the road to the Jordan valley. Here Shimei resided, who poured forth vile abuse against David, and flung dust and stones at him and his party when they were making their way down the eastern slopes of Olivet toward Jordan (16:5); and here Jonathan and Ahimaaz hid themselves (17:18).

bajith.d: house, probably a city of Moab, which had a celebrated idol-temple (<reflink>Isa. 15:2</reflink>). It has also been regarded as denoting simply the temple of the idol of Moab as opposed to the "high place."

arioch.d: lion-like, venerable. (1.) A king of Ellasar who was confederate with Chedorlamer (<reflink>Gen. 14:1,9</reflink>). The tablets recently discovered by Mr. Pinches (<see target="x-self">see CHALDEA</see>) show the true reading is Eri-Aku of Larsa. This Elamite name meant "servant of the moon-god." It was afterwards changed into Rimsin, "Have mercy, O moon-god." (2.) Dan. 2:14.

aristarchus.d: best ruler, native of Thessalonica (<reflink>Acts 20:4</reflink>), a companion of Paul (<reflink>Acts 19:29; 27:2</reflink>). He was Paul's "fellow-prisoner" at Rome (<reflink>Col. 4:10; Philemon 1:24</reflink>).

aristobulus.d: a Roman mentioned in Paul's Epistle to the Romans (16:10), whose "household" is saluated.

ark.d: Noah's ark, a building of gopher-wood, and covered with pitch, 300 cubits long, 50 cubits broad, and 30 cubits high (<reflink>Gen. 6:14-16</reflink>); an oblong floating house of three stories, with a door in the side and a window in the roof. It was 100 years in building (<reflink>Gen. 5:32; 7:6</reflink>). It was intended to preserve certain persons and animals from the deluge which God was about to bring over the earth. It contained eight persons (<reflink>Gen. 7:13; 2 Pet. 2:5</reflink>), and of all "clean" animals seven pairs, and of "unclean" one pair, and of birds seven pairs of each sort (<reflink>Gen. 7:2, 3</reflink>). It was in the form of an oblong square, with flat bottom and sloping roof. Traditions of the Deluge, by which the race of man was swept from the earth, and of the ark of Noah have been found existing among all nations.

arkite.d: (<reflink>Gen. 10:17; 1 Chr. 1:15</reflink>), a designation of certain descendants from the Phoenicians or Sidonians, the inhabitants of Arka, 12 miles north of Tripoli, opposite the northern extremity of Lebanon.

arm.d: used to denote power (<reflink>Ps. 10:15; Ezek. 30:21; Jer. 48:25</reflink>). It is also used of the omnipotence of God (<reflink>Ex. 15:16; Ps. 89:13; 98:1; 77:15; Isa. 53:1; John 12:38; Acts 13:17</reflink>)

armageddon.d: occurs only in Rev. 16:16 (R.V., "Har-Magedon"), as symbolically designating the place where the "battle of that great day of God Almighty" (ver. 14) shall be fought. The word properly means the "mount of Megiddo." It is the scene of the final conflict between Christ and Antichrist. The idea of such a scene was suggested by the Old Testament great battle-field, the plain of Esdraelon (q.v.).

armenia.d: high land, occurs only in Authorized Version, 2 Kings 19:37; in Revised Version, "Ararat," which is the Hebrew word. A country in western Asia lying between the Caspian and the Black Sea. Here the ark of Noah rested after the Deluge (<reflink>Gen. 8:4</reflink>). It is for the most part high table-land, and is watered by the Aras, the Kur, the Euphrates, and the Tigris. Ararat was properly the name of a part of ancient Armenia. Three provinces of Armenia are mentioned in Jer. 51:27, Ararat, Minni, and Ashchenaz. Some, however, think Minni a contraction for Armenia. (See ARARAT

armoni.d: inhabitant of a fortress, the first-named of the two sons of Saul and Rizpah. He was delivered up to the Gibeonites by David, and hanged by them (<reflink>2 Sam. 21:8, 9</reflink>).

armour.d: is employed in the English Bible to denote military equipment, both offensive and defensive.

armour-bearer.d: an officer selected by kings and generals because of his bravery, not only to bear their armour, but also to stand by them in the time of danger. They were the adjutants of our modern armies (<reflink>Judg. 9:54; 1 Sam. 14:7; 16:21; 31:6</reflink>).

armoury.d: the place in which armour was deposited when not used (<reflink>Neh. 3:19; Jer. 50:25</reflink>). At first each man of the Hebrews had his own arms, because all went to war. There were no arsenals or magazines for arms till the time of David, who had a large collection of arms, which he consecrated to the Lord in his tabernacle (1 Sa,. 21:9; 2 Sam. 8:7-12; 1 Chr. 26:26, 27).

army.d: The Israelites marched out of Egypt in military order (<reflink>Ex. 13:18, "harnessed;" marg., "five in a rank"</reflink>). Each tribe formed a battalion, with its own banner and leader (<reflink>Num. 2:2; 10:14</reflink>). In war the army was divided into thousands and hundreds under their several captains (<reflink>Num. 31:14</reflink>), and also into families (<reflink>Num. 2:34; 2 Chr. 25:5; 26:12</reflink>). From the time of their entering the land of Canaan to the time of the kings, the Israelites made little progress in military affairs, although often engaged in warfare. The kings introduced the custom of maintaining a bodyguard (the Gibborim; i.e., "heroes"), and thus the nucleus of a standing army was formed. Saul had an army of 3,000 select warriors (<reflink>1 Sam. 13:2; 14:52; 24:2</reflink>). David also had a band of soldiers around him (<reflink>1 Sam. 23:13; 25:13</reflink>). To this band he afterwards added the Cherethites and the Pelethites (<reflink>2 Sam. …

arnon.d: swift, the southern boundary of the territory of Israel beyond Jordan, separating it from the land of Moab (<reflink>Deut. 3:8, 16</reflink>). This river (referred to twenty-four times in the Bible) rises in the mountains of Gilead, and after a circuitous course of about 80 miles through a deep ravine it falls into the Dead Sea nearly opposite Engedi. The stream is almost dry in summer. It is now called el-Mujeb. The territory of the Amorites extended from the Arnon to the Jabbok.

aroer.d: ruins. (1.) A town on the north bank of the Arnon (<reflink>Deut. 4:48; Judg. 11:26; 2 Kings 10:33</reflink>), the southern boundary of the kingdom of Sihon (<reflink>Josh. 12:2</reflink>). It is now called Arair, 13 miles west of the Dead Sea.

arpad.d: (<reflink>Isa. 10:9; 36:19; 37:13</reflink>), also Arphad, support, a Syrian city near Hamath, along with which it is invariably mentioned (<reflink>2 Kings 19:13; 18:34; Isa. 10:9</reflink>), and Damascus (<reflink>Jer. 49:23</reflink>). After a siege of three years it fell (B.C. 742) before the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser II. Now Tell Erfud.

arphaxad.d: son of Shem, born the year after the Deluge. He died at the age of 438 years (<reflink>Gen. 11:10-13; 1 Chr. 1:17, 18; Luke 3:36</reflink>). He dwelt in Mesopotamia, and became, according to the Jewish historian Josephus, the progenitor of the Chaldeans. The tendency is to recognize in the word the name of the country nearest the ancient domain of the Chaldeans. Some regard the word as an Egypticized form of the territorial name of Ur Kasdim, or Ur of the Chaldees.

arrows.d: At first made of reeds, and then of wood tipped with iron. Arrows are sometimes figuratively put for lightning (<reflink>Deut. 32:23, 42; Ps. 7:13; 18:14; 144:6; Zech. 9:14</reflink>). They were used in war as well as in the chase (<reflink>Gen. 27:3; 49:23</reflink>). They were also used in divination (<reflink>Ezek. 21:21</reflink>).

artaxerxes.d: the Greek form of the name of several Persian kings. (1.) The king who obstructed the rebuilding of the temple (<reflink>Ezra 4:7</reflink>). He was probably the Smerdis of profane history.

artificer.d: a person engaged in any kind of manual occupation (<reflink>Gen. 4:22; Isa. 3:3</reflink>).

artillery.d: 1 Sam. 20:40, (Heb. keli, meaning "apparatus;" here meaning collectively any missile weapons, as arrows and lances. In Revised Version, "weapons"). This word is derived from the Latin artillaria = equipment of war.

arvad.d: wandering, (<reflink>Ezek. 27:8</reflink>), a small island and city on the coast of Syria, mentioned as furnishing mariners and soldiers for Tyre. The inhabitants were called Arvadites. The name is written Aruada or Arada in the Tell-el-Amarna tablets.

asa.d: physician, son of Abijah and grandson of Rehoboam, was the third king of Judah. He was zealous in maintaining the true worship of God, and in rooting all idolatry, with its accompanying immoralities, out of the land (<reflink>1 Kings 15:8-14</reflink>). The Lord gave him and his land rest and prosperity. It is recorded of him, however, that in his old age, when afflicted, he "sought not to the Lord, but to the physicians" (<reflink>comp. Jer. 17:5</reflink>). He died in the forty-first year of his reign, greatly honoured by his people (<reflink>2 Chr. 16:1-13</reflink>), and was succeeded by his son Jehoshaphat.

asahel.d: made by God, the youngest son of Zeruiah, David's sister. He was celebrated for his swiftness of foot. When fighting against Ish-bosheth at Gibeon, in the army of his brother Joab, he was put to death by Abner, whom he pursued from the field of battle (<reflink>2 Sam. 2:18, 19</reflink>). He is mentioned among David's thirty mighty men (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:24; 1 Chr. 11:26</reflink>). Others of the same name are mentioned (<reflink>2 Chr. 17:8; 31:13; Ezra 10:15</reflink>).

asaph.d: convener, or collector. (1.) A Levite; one of the leaders of David's choir (<reflink>1 Chr. 6:39</reflink>). Psalms 50 and 73-83 inclusive are attributed to him. He is mentioned along with David as skilled in music, and a "seer" (<reflink>2 Chr. 29:30</reflink>). The "sons of Asaph," mentioned in 1 Chr. 25:1, 2 Chr. 20:14, and Ezra 2:41, were his descendants, or more probably a class of poets or singers who recognized him as their master.

asenath.d: an Egyptian name, meaning "gift of the sun-god", daughter of Potipherah, priest of On or Heliopolis, wife of Joseph (<reflink>Gen. 41:45</reflink>). She was the mother of Manasseh and Ephraim (50-52; 46:20).

ash.d: (Heb. o'ren, "tremulous"), mentioned only Isa. 44:14 (R.V., "fir tree"). It is rendered "pine tree" both in the LXX. and Vulgate versions. There is a tree called by the Arabs _aran_, found still in the valleys of Arabia Petraea, whose leaf resembles that of the mountain ash. This may be the tree meant. Our ash tree is not known in Syria.

ashdod.d: stronghold, a Philistine city (<reflink>Josh. 15:47</reflink>), about midway between Gaza and Joppa, and 3 miles from the Mediterranean. It was one of the chief seats of the worship of Dagon (<reflink>1 Sam. 5:5</reflink>). It belonged to the tribe of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:47</reflink>), but it never came into their actual possession. It was an important city, as it stood on the highroad from Egypt to Palestine, and hence was strongly fortified (<reflink>2 Chr. 26:6; Isa. 20:1</reflink>). Uzziah took it, but fifty years after his death it was taken by the Assyrians (B.C. 758). According to Sargon's record, it was captured by him in B.C. 711. The only reference to it in the New Testament, where it is called Azotus, is in the account of Philip's return from Gaza (<reflink>Acts 8:40</reflink>). It is now called Eshdud.

ashdoth-pisgah.d: (<reflink>Deut. 3:17; Josh. 12:3; 13:20</reflink>) in Authorized Version, but in Revised Version translated "slopes of Pisgah." In Deut. 4:49 it is translated in the Authorized Version "springs of Pisgah." The name Ashdoth is translated "springs" in the Authorized Version, but "slopes" in the Revised Version, of Josh. 10:40 and 12:8. It has been identified with the springs under Mount Nebo, now called 'Ayun Musa.

asher.d: happy, Jacob's eigth son; his mother was Zilpah, Leah's handmaid (<reflink>Gen. 30:13</reflink>). Of the tribe founded by him nothing is recorded beyond its holding a place in the list of the tribes (35:26; 46:17; Ex. 1:4, etc.) It increased in numbers twenty-nine percent, during the thirty-eight years' wanderings. The place of this tribe during the march through the desert was between Dan and Naphtali (<reflink>Num. 2:27</reflink>). The boundaries of the inheritance given to it, which contained some of the richest soil in Palestine, and the names of its towns, are recorded in Josh. 19:24-31; Judg. 1:31, 32. Asher and Simeon were the only tribes west of the Jordan which furnished no hero or judge for the nation. Anna the prophetess was of this tribe (<reflink>Luke 2:36</reflink>).

asherah.d: and pl. Asherim in Revised Version, instead of "grove" and "groves" of the Authorized Version. This was the name of a sensual Canaanitish goddess Astarte, the feminine of the Assyrian Ishtar. Its symbol was the stem of a tree deprived of its boughs, and rudely shaped into an image, and planted in the ground. Such religious symbols ("groves") are frequently alluded to in Scripture (<reflink>Ex. 34:13; Judg. 6:25; 2 Kings 23:6; 1 Kings 16:33, etc.</reflink>). These images were also sometimes made of silver or of carved stone (<reflink>2 Kings 21:7; "the graven image of Asherah," R.V.</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See GROVE [1].</see>).

ashes.d: The ashes of a red heifer burned entire (<reflink>Num. 19:5</reflink>) when sprinkled on the unclean made them ceremonially clean (<reflink>Heb. 9:13</reflink>).

ashkelon.d: =Askelon=Ascalon, was one of the five cities of the Philistines (<reflink>Josh. 13:3; 1 Sam. 6:17</reflink>). It stood on the shore of the Mediterranean, 12 miles north of Gaza. It is mentioned on an inscription at Karnak in Egypt as having been taken by king Rameses II., the oppressor of the Hebrews. In the time of the judges (<reflink>Judg. 1:18</reflink>) it fell into the possession of the tribe of Judah; but it was soon after retaken by the Philistines (<reflink>2 Sam. 1:20</reflink>), who were not finally dispossessed till the time of Alexander the Great. Samson went down to this place from Timnath, and slew thirty men and took their spoil. The prophets foretold its destruction (<reflink>Jer. 25:20; 47:5, 7</reflink>). It became a noted place in the Middle Ages, having been the scene of many a bloody battle between the Saracens and the Crusaders. …

ashkenaz.d: one of the three sons of Gomer (<reflink>Gen. 10:3</reflink>), and founder of one of the tribes of the Japhetic race. They are mentioned in connection with Minni and Ararat, and hence their original seat must have been in Armenia (<reflink>Jer. 51:27</reflink>), probably near the Black Sea, which, from their founder, was first called Axenus, and afterwards the Euxine.

ashpenaz.d: the master of the eunuchs of Nebuchadnezzar (<reflink>Dan. 1:3</reflink>), the "Rabsaris" of the court. His position was similar to that of the Kislar-aga of the modern Turkish sultans.

ashtaroth.d: a city of Bashan, in the kingdom of Og (<reflink>Deut. 1:4; Josh. 12:4; 13:12; 9:10</reflink>). It was in the half-tribe of Manasseh (<reflink>Josh. 13:12</reflink>), and as a Levitical city was given to the Gershonites (<reflink>1 Chr. 6:71</reflink>). Uzzia, one of David's valiant men (<reflink>1 Chr. 11:44</reflink>), is named as of this city. It is identified with Tell Ashterah, in the Hauran, and is noticed on monuments B.C. 1700-1500. The name Beesh-terah (<reflink>Josh. 21:27</reflink>) is a contraction for Beth-eshterah, i.e., "the house of Ashtaroth."

ashteroth karnaim.d: Ashteroth of the two horns, the abode of the Rephaim (<reflink>Gen. 14:5</reflink>). It may be identified with Ashtaroth preceding; called "Karnaim", i.e., the "two-horned" (the crescent moon). The Samaritan version renders the word by "Sunamein," the present es-Sunamein, 28 miles south of Damascus.

ashtoreth.d: the moon goddess of the Phoenicians, representing the passive principle in nature, their principal female deity; frequently associated with the name of Baal, the sun-god, their chief male deity (<reflink>Judg. 10:6; 1 Sam. 7:4; 12:10</reflink>). These names often occur in the plural (Ashtaroth, Baalim), probably as indicating either different statues or different modifications of the deities. This deity is spoken of as Ashtoreth of the Zidonians. She was the Ishtar of the Accadians and the Astarte of the Greeks (<reflink>Jer. 44:17; 1 Kings 11:5, 33; 2 Kings 23:13</reflink>). There was a temple of this goddess among the Philistines in the time of Saul (<reflink>1 Sam. 31:10</reflink>). Under the name of Ishtar, she was one of the great deities of the Assyrians. The Phoenicians called her Astarte. Solomon introduced the worship of this idol (<reflink>1 Kings 11:33</reflink>). Jezebel's 400 priests were probably employed in its service (<reflink>1 Kings 18:19</reflink>). …

ashurites.d: mentioned among those over whom Ish-bosheth was made king (<reflink>2 Sam. 2:9</reflink>).

asia.d: is used to denote Proconsular Asia, a Roman province which embraced the western parts of Asia Minor, and of which Ephesus was the capital, in Acts 2:9; 6:9; 16:6; 19:10,22; 20:4, 16, 18, etc., and probably Asia Minor in Acts 19:26, 27; 21:27; 24:18; 27:2. Proconsular Asia contained the seven churches of the Apocalypse (<reflink>Rev. 1:11</reflink>). The "chiefs of Asia" (<reflink>Acts 19:31</reflink>) were certain wealthy citizens who were annually elected to preside over the games and religious festivals of the several cities to which they belonged. Some of these "Asiarchs" were Paul's friends.

asnapper.d: probably the same as Assur-bani-pal (Sardanapalos of the Greeks), styled the "great and noble" (<reflink>Ezra 4:10</reflink>), was the son and successor (B.C. 668) of Esar-haddon (q.v.). He was "luxurious, ambitious, and cruel, but a magnificent patron of literature." He formed at Nineveh a library of clay tablets, numbering about 10,000. These are now mostly in the British Museum. They throw much light on the history and antiquities of Assyria.

asp.d: (Heb. pethen), Deut. 32:33; Job 20:14, 16; Isa. 11:8. It was probably the Egyptian cobra (Naja haje), which was very poisonous (<reflink>Rom. 3:13; Gr. aspis</reflink>). The Egyptians worshipped it as the _uraeus_, and it was found in the desert and in the fields. The peace and security of Messiah's reign is represented by the figure of a child playing on the hole of the asp. (See ADDER

ass.d: frequently mentioned throughout Scripture. Of the domesticated species we read of, (1.) The she ass (Heb. 'athon), so named from its slowness (<reflink>Gen. 12:16; 45:23; Num. 22:23; 1 Sam. 9:3</reflink>). (2.) The male ass (Heb. hamor), the common working ass of Western Asia, so called from its red colour. Issachar is compared to a strong ass (<reflink>Gen. 49:14</reflink>). It was forbidden to yoke together an ass and an ox in the plough (<reflink>Deut. 22:10</reflink>). (3.) The ass's colt (Heb. 'air), mentioned Judg. 10:4; 12:14. It is rendered "foal" in Gen. 32:15; 49:11. (<reflink>Comp. Job 11:12; Isa. 30:6.</reflink>) The ass is an unclean animal, because it does not chew the cud (<reflink>Lev. 11:26. Comp. 2 Kings 6:25</reflink>). Asses constituted a considerable portion of wealth in ancient times (<reflink>Gen. 12:16; 30:43; 1 Chr. 27:30; Job 1:3; 42:12</reflink>). They were noted for their spirit and their attachment to their master (<reflink>Isa. 1:3</reflink>). …

asshur.d: second son of Shem (<reflink>Gen. 10:22; 1 Chr. 1:17</reflink>). He went from the land of Shinar and built Nineveh, etc. (<reflink>Gen. 10:11,12</reflink>). He probably gave his name to Assyria, which is the usual translation of the word, although the form Asshur is sometimes retained (<reflink>Num. 24:22, 24; Ezek. 27:23, etc.</reflink>). In Gen. 2:14 "Assyria" ought to be "Asshur," which was the original capital of Assyria, a city represented by the mounds of Kalah Sherghat, on the west bank of the Tigris. This city was founded by Bel-kap-kapu about B.C. 1700. At a later date the capital was shifted to Ninua, or Nineveh, now Koyunjik, on the eastern bank of the river. (<see target="x-self">See CALAH; NINEVEH.</see>)

assos.d: a sea-port town of Proconsular Asia, in the district of Mysia, on the north shore of the Gulf of Adramyttium. Paul came hither on foot along the Roman road from Troas (<reflink>Acts 20:13, 14</reflink>), a distance of 20 miles. It was about 30 miles distant from Troas by sea. The island of Lesbos lay opposite it, about 7 miles distant.

assurance.d: The resurrection of Jesus (<reflink>Acts 17:31</reflink>) is the "assurance" (Gr. pistis, generally rendered "faith") or pledge God has given that his revelation is true and worthy of acceptance. The "full assurance [Gr. plerophoria, 'full bearing'] of faith" (<reflink>Heb. 10:22</reflink>) is a fulness of faith in God which leaves no room for doubt. The "full assurance of understanding" (<reflink>Col. 2:2</reflink>) is an entire unwavering conviction of the truth of the declarations of Scripture, a joyful steadfastness on the part of any one of conviction that he has grasped the very truth. The "full assurance of hope" (<reflink>Heb. 6:11</reflink>) is a sure and well-grounded expectation of eternal glory (<reflink>2 Tim. 4:7, 8</reflink>). This assurance of hope is the assurance of a man's own particular salvation.

assyria.d: the name derived from the city Asshur on the Tigris, the original capital of the country, was originally a colony from Babylonia, and was ruled by viceroys from that kingdom. It was a mountainous region lying to the north of Babylonia, extending along the Tigris as far as to the high mountain range of Armenia, the Gordiaean or Carduchian mountains. It was founded in B.C. 1700 under Bel-kap-kapu, and became an independent and a conquering power, and shook off the yoke of its Babylonian masters. It subdued the whole of Northern Asia. The Assyrians were Semites (<reflink>Gen. 10:22</reflink>), but in process of time non-Semite tribes mingled with the inhabitants. They were a military people, the "Romans of the East."

astrologer.d: (<reflink>Dan. 1:20; 2:2, 10, 27, etc.</reflink>) Heb. 'ashshaph', an enchanter, one who professes to divine future events by the appearance of the stars. This science flourished among the Chaldeans. It was positively forbidden to the Jews (<reflink>Deut. 4:19; 18:10; Isa. 47:13</reflink>).

astronomy.d: The Hebrews were devout students of the wonders of the starry firmanent (<reflink>Amos 5:8; Ps. 19</reflink>). In the Book of Job, which is the oldest book of the Bible in all probability, the constellations are distinguished and named. Mention is made of the "morning star" (<reflink>Rev. 2:28; comp. Isa. 14:12</reflink>), the "seven stars" and "Pleiades," "Orion," "Arcturus," the "Great Bear" (<reflink>Amos 5:8; Job 9:9; 38:31</reflink>), "the crooked serpent," Draco (<reflink>Job 26:13</reflink>), the Dioscuri, or Gemini, "Castor and Pollux" (<reflink>Acts 28:11</reflink>). The stars were called "the host of heaven" (<reflink>Isa. 40:26; Jer. 33:22</reflink>).

asuppim.d: (<reflink>1 Chr. 26:15, 17, Authorized Version; but in Revised Version, "storehouse"</reflink>), properly the house of stores for the priests. In Neh. 12:25 the Authorized Version has "thresholds," marg. "treasuries" or "assemblies;" Revised Version, "storehouses."

atad.d: buckthorn, a place where Joseph and his brethren, when on their way from Egypt to Hebron with the remains of their father Jacob, made for seven days a "great and very sore lamentation." On this account the Canaanites called it "Abel-mizraim" (<reflink>Gen. 50:10, 11</reflink>). It was probably near Hebron. The word is rendered "bramble" in Judg. 9:14, 15, and "thorns" in Ps. 58:9.

ataroth.d: crowns. (1.) A city east of Jordan, not far from Gilead (<reflink>Num. 32:3</reflink>).

athaliah.d: whom God afflicts. (1.) The daughter of Ahab and Jezebel, and the wife of Jehoram, king of Judah (<reflink>2 Kings 8:18</reflink>), who "walked in the ways of the house of Ahab" (<reflink>2 Chr. 21:6</reflink>), called "daughter" of Omri (<reflink>2 Kings 8:26</reflink>). On the death of her husband and of her son Ahaziah, she resolved to seat herself on the vacant throne. She slew all Ahaziah's children except Joash, the youngest (<reflink>2 Kings 11:1,2</reflink>). After a reign of six years she was put to death in an insurrection (<reflink>2 Kings 11:20; 2 Chr. 21:6; 22:10-12; 23:15</reflink>), stirred up among the people in connection with Josiah's being crowned as king.

athens.d: the capital of Attica, the most celebrated city of the ancient world, the seat of Greek literature and art during the golden period of Grecian history. Its inhabitants were fond of novelty (<reflink>Acts 17:21</reflink>), and were remarkable for their zeal in the worship of the gods. It was a sarcastic saying of the Roman satirist that it was "easier to find a god at Athens than a man."

atonement.d: This word does not occur in the Authorized Version of the New Testament except in Rom. 5:11, where in the Revised Version the word "reconciliation" is used. In the Old Testament it is of frequent occurrence.

atonement, day of.d: the great annual day of humiliation and expiation for the sins of the nation, "the fast" (<reflink>Acts 27:9</reflink>), and the only one commanded in the law of Moses. The mode of its observance is described in Lev. 16:3-10; 23:26-32; and Num. 29:7-11.

augustus.d: the cognomen of the first Roman emperor, C. Julius Caesar Octavianus, during whose reign Christ was born (<reflink>Luke 2:1</reflink>). His decree that "all the world should be taxed" was the divinely ordered occasion of Jesus' being born, according to prophecy (<reflink>Micah 5:2</reflink>), in Bethlehem. This name being simply a title meaning "majesty" or "venerable," first given to him by the senate (B.C. 27), was borne by succeeding emperors. Before his death (A.D. 14) he associated Tiberius with him in the empire (<reflink>Luke 3:1</reflink>), by whom he was succeeded.

augustus band.d: (<reflink>Acts 27:1.: literally, of Sebaste, the Greek form of Augusta, the name given to Caesarea in honour of Augustus Caesar</reflink>). Probably this "band" or cohort consisted of Samaritan soldiers belonging to Caesarea.

ava.d: a place in Assyria from which colonies were brought to Samaria (<reflink>2 Kings 17:24</reflink>). It is probably the same with Ivah (18:34; 19:13; Isa. 37:13). It has been identified with Hit on the Euphrates.

aven.d: nothingness; vanity. (1.) Hosea speaks of the "high places of Aven" (10:8), by which he means Bethel. He also calls it Beth-aven, i.e., "the house of vanity" (4:15), on account of the golden calves Jeroboam had set up there (<reflink>1 Kings 12:28</reflink>).

avenger of blood.d: (Heb. goel, from verb gaal, "to be near of kin," "to redeem"), the nearest relative of a murdered person. It was his right and duty to slay the murderer (<reflink>2 Sam. 14:7, 11</reflink>) if he found him outside of a city of refuge. In order that this law might be guarded against abuse, Moses appointed six cities of refuge (<reflink>Ex. 21:13; Num. 35:13; Deut. 19:1,9</reflink>). These were in different parts of the country, and every facility was afforded the manslayer that he might flee to the city that lay nearest him for safety. Into the city of refuge the avenger durst not follow him. This arrangement applied only to cases where the death was not premeditated. The case had to be investigated by the authorities of the city, and the wilful murderer was on no account to be spared. He was regarded as an impure and polluted person, and was delivered up to the _goel_ (<reflink>Deut. 19:11-13</reflink>). …

avim.d: a people dwelling in Hazerim, or "the villages" or "encampments" on the south-west corner of the sea-coast (<reflink>Deut. 2:23</reflink>). They were subdued and driven northward by the Caphtorim. A trace of them is afterwards found in Josh. 13:3, where they are called Avites.

awl.d: an instrument only referred to in connection with the custom of boring the ear of a slave (<reflink>Ex. 21:6; Deut. 15:17</reflink>), in token of his volunteering perpetual service when he might be free. (<reflink>Comp. Ps. 40:6; Isa. 50:5</reflink>).

axe.d: used in the Authorized Version of Deut. 19:5; 20:19; 1 Kings 6:7, as the translation of a Hebrew word which means "chopping." It was used for felling trees (<reflink>Isa. 10:34</reflink>) and hewing timber for building. It is the rendering of a different word in Judg. 9:48, 1 Sam. 13:20, 21, Ps. 74:5, which refers to its sharpness. In 2 Kings 6:5 it is the translation of a word used with reference to its being made of iron. In Isa. 44:12 the Revised Version renders by "axe" the Hebrew _maatsad_, which means a "hewing" instrument. In the Authorized Version it is rendered "tongs." It is also used in Jer. 10:3, and rendered "axe." The "battle-axe" (army of Medes and Persians) mentioned in Jer. 51:20 was probably, as noted in the margin of the Revised Version, a "maul" or heavy mace. In Ps. 74:6 the word so rendered means "feller." (<reflink>See the figurative expression in Matt. 3:10; Luke 3:9.</reflink>)

azal.d: (<reflink>Zech. 14:5</reflink>) should perhaps be rendered "very near" = "the way of escape shall be made easy." If a proper name, it may denote some place near the western extremity of the valley here spoken of near Jerusalem.

azariah.d: whom Jehovah helps. (1.) Son of Ethan, of the tribe of Judah (<reflink>1 Chr. 2:8</reflink>).

benjamin.d: son of my right hand. (1.) The younger son of Jacob by Rachel (<reflink>Gen. 35:18</reflink>). His birth took place at Ephrath, on the road between Bethel and Bethlehem, at a short distance from the latter place. His mother died in giving him birth, and with her last breath named him Ben-oni, son of my pain, a name which was changed by his father into Benjamin. His posterity are called Benjamites (<reflink>Gen. 49:27; Deut. 33:12; Josh. 18:21</reflink>).

beor.d: a torch. (1.) The father of Bela, one of the kings of Edom (<reflink>Gen. 36:32</reflink>).

bera.d: gift, or son of evil, king of Sodom at the time of the invasion of the four kings under Chedorlaomer (<reflink>Gen. 14:2, 8, 17, 21</reflink>).

berachah.d: blessing. (1.) A valley not far from Engedi, where Jehoshaphat overthrew the Moabites and Ammonites (<reflink>2 Chr. 20:26</reflink>). It has been identified with the valley of Bereikut. (R.V., "Beracah.")

berea.d: a city of Macedonia to which Paul with Silas and Timotheus went when persecuted at Thessalonica (<reflink>Acts 17:10, 13</reflink>), and from which also he was compelled to withdraw, when he fled to the sea-coast and thence sailed to Athens (14, 15). Sopater, one of Paul's companions belonged to this city, and his conversion probably took place at this time (<reflink>Acts 20:4</reflink>). It is now called Verria.

berechiah.d: blessed by Jehovah. (1.) Son of Shimea, and father of Asaph the musician (<reflink>1 Chr. 6:39; 15:17</reflink>).

bered.d: hail. (1.) A town in the south of Palestine (<reflink>Gen. 16:14</reflink>), in the desert of Shur, near Lahai-roi.

beriah.d: a gift, or in evil. (1.) One of Asher's four sons, and father of Heber (<reflink>Gen. 46:17</reflink>).

bernice.d: bearer of victory, the eldest daughter of Agrippa I., the Herod Agrippa of Acts 12:20. After the early death of her first husband she was married to her uncle Herod, king of Chalcis. After his death (A.D. 40) she lived in incestuous connection with her brother Agrippa II. (<reflink>Acts 25:13, 23; 26:30</reflink>). They joined the Romans at the outbreak of the final war between them and the Jews, and lived afterwards at Rome.

berodach-baladan.d: the king of Babylon who sent a friendly deputation to Hezekiah (<reflink>2 Kings 20:12</reflink>). In Isa. 39:1 he is called Merodach-baladan (q.v.).

beryl.d: the rendering in the Authorized Version of the Hebrew word _tarshish_, a precious stone; probably so called as being brought from Tarshish. It was one of the stones on the breastplate of the high priest (<reflink>Ex. 28:20; R.V. marg., "chalcedony;" 39:13</reflink>). The colour of the wheels in Ezekiel's vision was as the colour of a beryl stone (1:16; 10:9; R.V., "stone of Tarshish"). It is mentioned in Cant. 5:14; Dan. 10:6; Rev. 21:20. In Ezek. 28:13 the LXX. render the word by "chrysolite," which the Jewish historian Josephus regards as its proper translation. This also is the rendering given in the Authorized Version in the margin. That was a gold-coloured gem, the topaz of ancient authors.

besom.d: the rendering of a Hebrew word meaning sweeper, occurs only in Isa. 14:23, of the sweeping away, the utter ruin, of Babylon.

besor.d: cold, a ravine or brook in the extreme south-west of Judah, where 200 of David's men stayed behind because they were faint, while the other 400 pursued the Amalekites (<reflink>1 Sam. 30:9, 10, 21</reflink>). Probably the Wadyes Sheriah, south of Gaza.

bestead.d: the rendering in Isa. 8:21, where alone it occurs, of a Hebrew word meaning to oppress, or be in circumstances of hardship.

betah.d: confidence, a city belonging to Hadadezer, king of Zobah, which yielded much spoil of brass to David (<reflink>2 Sam. 8:8</reflink>). In 1 Chr. 18:8 it is called Tibhath.

beth.d: occurs frequently as the appellation for a house, or dwelling-place, in such compounds as the words immediately following:

beth-anath.d: house of response, one of the fenced cities of Naphtali (<reflink>Josh. 19:38</reflink>). It is perhaps identical with the modern village 'Ainata, 6 miles west of Kedesh.

beth-anoth.d: house of answers, a city in the mountainous district of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:59</reflink>). It has been identified with the modern Beit-'Anun, about 3 miles northeast of Hebron.

beth-arabah.d: house of the desert, one of the six cities of Judah, situated in the sunk valley of the Jordan and Dead Sea (<reflink>Josh. 18:22</reflink>). In Josh. 15:61 it is said to have been "in the wilderness." It was afterwards included in the towns of Benjamin. It is called Arabah (<reflink>Josh. 18:18</reflink>).

beth-aram.d: house of the height; i.e., "mountain-house", one of the towns of Gad, 3 miles east of Jordan, opposite Jericho (<reflink>Josh. 13:27</reflink>). Probably the same as Beth-haran in Num. 32:36. It was called by king Herod, Julias, or Livias, after Livia, the wife of Augustus. It is now called Beit-haran.

beth-arbel.d: house of God's court, a place alluded to by Hosea (10:14) as the scene of some great military exploit, but not otherwise mentioned in Scripture. The Shalman here named was probably Shalmaneser, the king of Assyria (<reflink>2 Kings 17:3</reflink>).

beth-aven.d: house of nothingness; i.e., "of idols", a place in the mountains of Benjamin, east of Bethel (<reflink>Josh. 7:2; 18:12; 1 Sam. 13:5</reflink>).
