In Hos. 4:15; 5:8; 10:5 it stands for "Bethel" (q.v.), and it is so called because it was no longer the "house of God," but "the house of idols," referring to the calves there worshipped.

beth-barah.d: house of crossing, a place south of the scene of Gideon's victory (<reflink>Judg. 7:24</reflink>). It was probably the chief ford of the Jordan in that district, and may have been that by which Jacob crossed when he returned from Mesopotamia, near the Jabbok (<reflink>Gen. 32:22</reflink>), and at which Jephthah slew the Ephraimites (<reflink>Judg. 12:4</reflink>). Nothing, however, is certainly known of it. (See BETHABARA

beth-car.d: sheep-house, a place to which the Israelites pursued the Philistines west from Mizpeh (<reflink>1 Sam. 7:11</reflink>).

beth-dagon.d: house of Dagon. (1.) A city in the low country or plain of Judah, near Philistia (<reflink>Josh. 15:41</reflink>); the modern Beit Degan, about 5 miles from Lydda.

beth-diblathaim.d: house of two cakes of figs, a city of Moab, upon which Jeremiah (48:22) denounced destruction. It is called also Almon-diblathaim (<reflink>Num. 33:46</reflink>) and Diblath (<reflink>Ezek. 6:14</reflink>). (R.V., "Diblah.")

beth-gamul.d: camel-house, a city in the "plain country" of Moab denounced by the prophet (<reflink>Jer. 48:23</reflink>); probably the modern Um-el-Jemal, near Bozrah, one of the deserted cities of the Hauran.

beth-gilgal.d: house of Gilgal, a place from which the inhabitants gathered for the purpose of celebrating the rebuilding of the walls on the return exile (<reflink>Neh. 12:29</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See GILGAL.</see>)

beth-haccerem.d: house of a vineyard, a place in the tribe of Judah (<reflink>Neh. 3:14</reflink>) where the Benjamites were to set up a beacon when they heard the trumpet against the invading army of the Babylonians (<reflink>Jer. 6:1</reflink>). It is probable that this place is the modern 'Ain Karim, or "well of the vineyards," near which there is a ridge on which are cairns which may have served as beacons of old, one of which is 40 feet high and 130 in diameter.

beth-horon.d: house of the hollow, or of the cavern, the name of two towns or villages (<reflink>2 Chr. 8:5; 1 Chr. 7:24</reflink>) in the territory of Ephraim, on the way from Jerusalem to Joppa. They are distinguished as Beth-horon "the upper" and Beth-horon "the nether." They are about 2 miles apart, the former being about 10 miles north-west of Jerusalem. Between the two places was the ascent and descent of Beth-horon, leading from Gibeon down to the western plain (<reflink>Josh. 10:10, 11; 18:13, 14</reflink>), down which the five kings of the Amorites were driven by Joshua in that great battle, the most important in which the Hebrews had been as yet engaged, being their first conflict with their enemies in the open field. Jehovah interposed in behalf of Israel by a terrific hailstorm, which caused more deaths among the Canaanites than did the swords of the Israelites. Beth-horon is mentioned as having been taken by Shishak, B.C. …

beth-jeshimoth.d: house of wastes, or deserts, a town near Abel-shittim, east of Jordan, in the desert of Moab, where the Israelites encamped not long before crossing the Jordan (<reflink>Num. 33:49; A.V., "Bethjesimoth"</reflink>). It was within the territory of Sihon, king of the Amorites (<reflink>Josh. 12:3</reflink>).

beth-le-aphrah.d: (<reflink>R.V. Micah 1:10</reflink>), house of dust. The Authorized Version reads "in the house of Aphrah." This is probably the name of a town in the Shephelah, or "low country," between Joppa and Gaza.

beth-peor.d: house of Peor; i.e., "temple of Baal-peor", a place in Moab, on the east of Jordan, opposite Jericho. It was in the tribe of Reuben (<reflink>Josh. 13:20; Deut. 3:29; 4:46</reflink>). In the "ravine" or valley over against Beth-peor Moses was probably buried (<reflink>Deut. 34:6</reflink>).

beth-phage.d: house of the unripe fig, a village on the Mount of Olives, on the road from Jerusalem to Jericho (<reflink>Matt. 21:1; Mark 11:1; Luke 19:29</reflink>), and very close to Bethany. It was the limit of a Sabbath-day's journey from Jerusalem, i.e., 2,000 cubits. It has been identified with the modern Kefr-et-Tur.

beth-shean.d: house of security or rest, a city which belonged to Manasseh (<reflink>1 Chr. 7:29</reflink>), on the west of Jordan. The bodies of Saul and his sons were fastened to its walls. In Solomon's time it gave its name to a district (<reflink>1 Kings 4:12</reflink>). The name is found in an abridged form, Bethshan, in 1 Sam. 31:10, 12 and 2 Sam. 21:12. It is on the road from Jerusalem to Damascus, about 5 miles from the Jordan, and 14 from the south end of the Lake of Gennesaret. After the Captivity it was called Scythopolis, i.e., "the city of the Scythians," who about B.C. 640 came down from the steppes of Southern Russia and settled in different places in Syria. It is now called Beisan.

beth-shemesh.d: house of the sun. (1.) A sacerdotal city in the tribe of Dan (<reflink>Josh. 21:16; 1 Sam. 6:15</reflink>), on the north border of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:10</reflink>). It was the scene of an encounter between Jehoash, king of Israel, and Amaziah, king of Judah, in which the latter was made prisoner (<reflink>2 Kings 14:11, 13</reflink>). It was afterwards taken by the Philistines (<reflink>2 Chr. 28:18</reflink>). It is the modern ruined Arabic village 'Ain-shems, on the north-west slopes of the mountains of Judah, 14 miles west of Jerusalem.

beth-tappuah.d: house of apples, a town of Judah, now Tuffuh, 5 miles west of Hebron (<reflink>Josh. 15:53</reflink>).

bethabara.d: house of the ford, a place on the east bank of the Jordan, where John was baptizing (<reflink>John 1:28</reflink>). It may be identical with Bethbarah, the ancient ford of Jordan of which the men of Ephraim took possession (<reflink>Judg. 7:24</reflink>). The Revised Version reads "Bethany beyond Jordan." It was the great ford, and still bears the name of "the ford," Makhadhet 'Abarah, "the ford of crossing over," about 25 miles from Nazareth. (<see target="x-self">See BETHBARAH.</see>)

bethany.d: house of dates. (1.) The Revised Version in John 1:28 has this word instead of Bethabara, on the authority of the oldest manuscripts. It appears to have been the name of a place on the east of Jordan.

bethel.d: house of God. (1.) A place in Central Palestine, about 10 miles north of Jerusalem, at the head of the pass of Michmash and Ai. It was originally the royal Canaanite city of Luz (<reflink>Gen. 28:19</reflink>). The name Bethel was at first apparently given to the sanctuary in the neighbourhood of Luz, and was not given to the city itself till after its conquest by the tribe of Ephraim. When Abram entered Canaan he formed his second encampment between Bethel and Hai (<reflink>Gen. 12:8</reflink>); and on his return from Egypt he came back to it, and again "called upon the name of the Lord" (13:4). Here Jacob, on his way from Beersheba to Haran, had a vision of the angels of God ascending and descending on the ladder whose top reached unto heaven (28:10, 19); and on his return he again visited this place, "where God talked with him" (35:1-15), and there he "built an altar, and called the place El-beth-el" (q.v.). …

bethelite.d: a designation of Hiel (q.v.), who rebuilt Jericho and experienced the curse pronounced long before (<reflink>1 Kings 16:34</reflink>).

bether.d: dissection or separation, certain mountains mentioned in Cant. 2:17; probably near Lebanon.

bake.d: The duty of preparing bread was usually, in ancient times, committed to the females or the slaves of the family (<reflink>Gen. 18:6; Lev. 26:26; 1 Sam. 8:13</reflink>); but at a later period we find a class of public bakers mentioned (<reflink>Hos. 7:4, 6; Jer. 37:21</reflink>).

bake-meats.d: baked provisions (<reflink>Gen. 40:17</reflink>), literally "works of the baker," such as biscuits and cakes.

balaam.d: lord of the people; foreigner or glutton, as interpreted by others, the son of Beor, was a man of some rank among the Midianites (<reflink>Num. 31:8; comp. 16</reflink>). He resided at Pethor (<reflink>Deut. 23:4</reflink>), in Mesopotamia (<reflink>Num. 23:7</reflink>). It is evident that though dwelling among idolaters he had some knowledge of the true God; and was held in such reputation that it was supposed that he whom he blessed was blessed, and he whom he cursed was cursed. When the Israelites were encamped on the plains of Moab, on the east of Jordan, by Jericho, Balak sent for Balaam "from Aram, out of the mountains of the east," to curse them; but by the remarkable interposition of God he was utterly unable to fulfil Balak's wish, however desirous he was to do so. The apostle Peter refers (<reflink>2 Pet. 2:15, 16</reflink>) to this as an historical event. In Micah 6:5 reference also is made to the relations between Balaam and Balak. …

baladan.d: he has given a son, the father of the Babylonian king (<reflink>2 Kings 20:12; Isa. 39:1</reflink>) Merodach-baladan (q.v.).

balah.d: a city in the tribe of Simeon (<reflink>Josh. 19:3</reflink>), elsewhere called Bilhah (<reflink>1 Chr. 4:29</reflink>) and Baalah (<reflink>Josh. 15:29</reflink>).

balak.d: empty; spoiler, a son of Zippor, and king of the Moabites (<reflink>Num. 22:2, 4</reflink>). From fear of the Israelites, who were encamped near the confines of his territory, he applied to Balaam (q.v.) to curse them; but in vain (<reflink>Josh. 24:9</reflink>).

balance.d: occurs in Lev. 19:36 and Isa. 46:6, as the rendering of the Hebrew _kanch'_, which properly means "a reed" or "a cane," then a rod or beam of a balance. This same word is translated "measuring reed" in Ezek. 40:3,5; 42:16-18. There is another Hebrew word, _mozena'yim_, i.e., "two poisers", also so rendered (<reflink>Dan. 5:27</reflink>). The balances as represented on the most ancient Egyptian monuments resemble those now in use. A "pair of balances" is a symbol of justice and fair dealing (<reflink>Job 31:6; Ps. 62:9; Prov. 11:1</reflink>). The expression denotes great want and scarcity in Rev. 6:5.

baldness.d: from natural causes was uncommon (<reflink>2 Kings 2:23; Isa. 3:24</reflink>). It was included apparently under "scab" and "scurf," which disqualified for the priesthood (<reflink>Lev. 21:20</reflink>). The Egyptians were rarely subject to it. This probably arose from their custom of constantly shaving the head, only allowing the hair to grow as a sign of mourning. With the Jews artificial baldness was a sign of mourning (<reflink>Isa. 22:12; Jer. 7:29; 16:6</reflink>); it also marked the conclusion of a Nazarite's vow (<reflink>Acts 18:18; 21:24; Num. 6:9</reflink>). It is often alluded to (<reflink>Micah 1:16; Amos 8:10; Jer. 47:5</reflink>). The Jews were forbidden to follow the customs of surrounding nations in making themselves bald (<reflink>Deut. 14:1</reflink>).

balm.d: contracted from Bal'sam, a general name for many oily or resinous substances which flow or trickle from certain trees or plants when an incision is made through the bark.

bamah.d: a height, a name used simply to denote a high place where the Jews worshipped idols (<reflink>Ezek. 20:29</reflink>). The plural is translated "high places" in Num. 22:41 and Ezek. 36:2.

bamoth.d: heights, the forty-seventh station of the Israelites (<reflink>Num. 21:19,20</reflink>) in the territory of the Moabites.

bamoth-baal.d: heights of Baal, a place on the river Arnon, or in the plains through which it flows, east of Jordan (<reflink>Josh. 13:17; comp. Num. 21:28</reflink>). It has been supposed to be the same place as Bamoth.

bands.d: (1) of love (<reflink>Hos. 11:4</reflink>); (2) of Christ (<reflink>Ps. 2:3</reflink>); (3) uniting together Christ's body the church (<reflink>Col. 2:19; 3:14; Eph. 4:3</reflink>); (4) the emblem of the captivity of Israel (<reflink>Ezek. 34:27; Isa. 28:22; 52:2</reflink>); (5) of brotherhood (<reflink>Ezek. 37:15-28</reflink>); (6) no bands to the wicked in their death (<reflink>Ps. 73:4; Job 21:7; Ps. 10:6</reflink>). Also denotes chains (<reflink>Luke 8:29</reflink>); companies of soldiers (<reflink>Acts 21:31</reflink>); a shepherd's staff, indicating the union between Judah and Israel (<reflink>Zech. 11:7</reflink>).

bani.d: built. (1.) 1 Chr. 6:46. (2.) One of David's thirty-seven warriors, a Gadite (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:36</reflink>). (3.) Ezra 2:10; 10:29,34,38. (4.) A Levite who was prominent in the reforms on the return from Babylon (<reflink>Neh. 8:7; 9:4,5</reflink>). His son Rehum took part in rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem (<reflink>Neh. 3:17</reflink>).

banner.d: (1.) The flag or banner of the larger kind, serving for three tribes marching together. These standards, of which there were four, were worked with embroidery and beautifully ornamented (<reflink>Num. 1:52; 2:2, 3, 10, 18, 25; Cant. 2:4; 6:4, 10</reflink>).

banquet.d: a feast provided for the entertainment of a company of guests (Esther 5; 7; 1 Pet. 4:3); such as was provided for our Lord by his friends in Bethany (<reflink>Matt. 26:6; Mark 14:3; comp. John 12:2</reflink>). These meals were in the days of Christ usually called "suppers," after the custom of the Romans, and were partaken of toward the close of the day. It was usual to send a second invitation (<reflink>Matt. 22:3; Luke 14:17</reflink>) to those who had been already invited. When the whole company was assembled, the master of the house shut the door with his own hands (<reflink>Luke 13:25; Matt. 25:10</reflink>).

baptism for the dead.d: only mentioned in 1 Cor. 15:29. This expression as used by the apostle may be equivalent to saying, "He who goes through a baptism of blood in order to join a glorified church which has no existence [i.e., if the dead rise not] is a fool." Some also regard the statement here as an allusion to the strange practice which began, it is said, to prevail at Corinth, in which a person was baptized in the stead of others who had died before being baptized, to whom it was hoped some of the benefits of that rite would be extended. This they think may have been one of the erroneous customs which Paul went to Corinth to "set in order."

baptism of christ.d: Christ had to be formally inaugurated into the public discharge of his offices. For this purpose he came to John, who was the representative of the law and the prophets, that by him he might be introduced into his offices, and thus be publicly recognized as the Messiah of whose coming the prophecies and types had for many ages borne witness.

baptism, christian.d: an ordinance immediately instituted by Christ (<reflink>Matt. 28:19, 20</reflink>), and designed to be observed in the church, like that of the Supper, "till he come." The words "baptize" and "baptism" are simply Greek words transferred into English. This was necessarily done by the translators of the Scriptures, for no literal translation could properly express all that is implied in them.

baptism, john's.d: was not Christian baptism, nor was that which was practised by the disciples previous to our Lord's crucifixion. Till then the New Testament economy did not exist. John's baptism bound its subjects to repentance, and not to the faith of Christ. It was not administered in the name of the Trinity, and those whom John baptized were rebaptized by Paul (<reflink>Acts 18:24; 19:7</reflink>).

bar.d: used to denote the means by which a door is bolted (<reflink>Neh. 3:3</reflink>); a rock in the sea (<reflink>Jonah 2:6</reflink>); the shore of the sea (<reflink>Job 38:10</reflink>); strong fortifications and powerful impediments, etc. (<reflink>Isa. 45:2; Amos 1:5</reflink>); defences of a city (<reflink>1 Kings 4:13</reflink>). A bar for a door was of iron (<reflink>Isa. 45:2</reflink>), brass (<reflink>Ps. 107:16</reflink>), or wood (<reflink>Nah. 3:13</reflink>).

bar-jesus.d: son of Joshua, the patronymic of Elymas the sorcerer (<reflink>Acts 13:6</reflink>), who met Paul and Barnabas at Paphos. Elymas is a word of Arabic origin meaning "wise."

bar-jona.d: son of Jonah, the patronymic of Peter (<reflink>Matt. 16:17; John 1:42</reflink>), because his father's name was Jonas. (<see target="x-self">See PETER.</see>)

barabbas.d: i.e., son of Abba or of a father, a notorious robber whom Pilate proposed to condemn to death instead of Jesus, whom he wished to release, in accordance with the Roman custom (<reflink>John 18:40; Mark 15:7; Luke 23:19</reflink>). But the Jews were so bent on the death of Jesus that they demanded that Barabbas should be pardoned (<reflink>Matt. 27:16-26; Acts 3:14</reflink>). This Pilate did.

barachel.d: whom God has blessed, a Buzite, the father of Elihu, one of Job's friends (<reflink>Job 32:2, 6</reflink>).

barachias, berechiah.d: 4 (q.v.), whom Jehovah hath blessed, father of the prophet Zechariah (<reflink>Zech. 1:1,7; Matt. 23:35</reflink>).

barak.d: lightning, the son of Abinoam (<reflink>Judg. 4:6</reflink>). At the summons of Deborah he made war against Jabin. She accompanied him into the battle, and gave the signal for the little army to make the attack; in which the host of Jabin was completely routed. The battle was fought (<reflink>Judg. 4:16</reflink>) in the plain of Jezreel (q.v.). This deliverance of Israel is commemorated in Judg. 5. Barak's faith is commended (<reflink>Heb. 11:32</reflink>). "The character of Barak, though pious, does not seem to have been heroic. Like Gideon, and in a sense Samson, he is an illustration of the words in Heb. 11:34, 'Out of weakness were made strong.'" (<see target="x-self">See DEBORAH.</see>)

barbarian.d: a Greek word used in the New Testament (<reflink>Rom. 1:14</reflink>) to denote one of another nation. In Col. 3:11, the word more definitely designates those nations of the Roman empire that did not speak Greek. In 1 Cor. 14:11, it simply refers to one speaking a different language. The inhabitants of Malta are so called (<reflink>Acts 28:1,2, 4</reflink>). They were originally a Carthaginian colony. This word nowhere in Scripture bears the meaning it does in modern times.

barber.d: Found only once, in Ezek. 5:1, where reference is made to the Jewish custom of shaving the head as a sign of mourning. The Nazarites were untouched by the razor from their birth (<reflink>Num. 6:5</reflink>). Comp. Judg. 16:19.

barefoot.d: To go barefoot was a sign of great distress (<reflink>Isa. 20:2, 3, 4</reflink>), or of some great calamity having fallen on a person (<reflink>2 Sam. 15:30</reflink>).

bariah.d: fugitive, one of Shemaiah's five sons. Their father is counted along with them in 1 Chr. 3:22.

barkos.d: painter, (<reflink>Ezra 2:53; Neh. 7:55</reflink>). The father of some of the Nethinim.

barley.d: a grain much cultivated in Egypt (<reflink>Ex. 9:31</reflink>) and in Palestine (<reflink>Lev. 27:16; Deut. 8:8</reflink>). It was usually the food of horses (<reflink>1 Kings 4:28</reflink>). Barley bread was used by the poorer people (<reflink>Judg. 7:13; 2 Kings 4:42</reflink>). Barley of the first crop was ready for the harvest by the time of the Passover, in the middle of April (<reflink>Ruth 1:22; 2 Sam. 21:9</reflink>). Mention is made of barley-meal (<reflink>Num. 5:15</reflink>). Our Lord fed five thousand with "five barley loaves and two small fishes" (<reflink>John 6:9</reflink>).

barn.d: a storehouse (<reflink>Deut. 28:8; Job 39:12; Hag. 2:19</reflink>) for grain, which was usually under ground, although also sometimes above ground (<reflink>Luke 12:18</reflink>).

barnabas.d: son of consolation, the surname of Joses, a Levite (<reflink>Acts 4:36</reflink>). His name stands first on the list of prophets and teachers of the church at Antioch (13:1). Luke speaks of him as a "good man" (11:24). He was born of Jewish parents of the tribe of Levi. He was a native of Cyprus, where he had a possession of land (<reflink>Acts 4:36, 37</reflink>), which he sold. His personal appearance is supposed to have been dignified and commanding (<reflink>Acts 14:11, 12</reflink>). When Paul returned to Jerusalem after his conversion, Barnabas took him and introduced him to the apostles (9:27). They had probably been companions as students in the school of Gamaliel.

barrel.d: a vessel used for keeping flour (<reflink>1 Kings 17:12, 14, 16</reflink>). The same word (cad) so rendered is also translated "pitcher," a vessel for carrying water (<reflink>Gen. 24:14; Judg. 7:16</reflink>).

barren.d: For a woman to be barren was accounted a severe punishment among the Jews (<reflink>Gen. 16:2; 30:1-23; 1 Sam. 1:6, 27; Isa. 47:9; 49:21; Luke 1:25</reflink>). Instances of barrenness are noticed (<reflink>Gen. 11:30; 25:21; 29:31; Judg. 13:2, 3; Luke 1:7, 36</reflink>).

barsabas.d: son of Saba, the surname (1) of Joseph, also called Justus (<reflink>Acts 1:23</reflink>), some identify him with Barnabas; (2) of Judas, who was a "prophet." Nothing more is known of him than what is mentioned in Acts 15:32.

bartholomew.d: son of Tolmai, one of the twelve apostles (<reflink>Matt. 10:3; Acts 1:13</reflink>); generally supposed to have been the same as Nathanael. In the synoptic gospels Philip and Bartholomew are always mentioned together, while Nathanael is never mentioned; in the fourth gospel, on the other hand, Philip and Nathanael are similarly mentioned together, but nothing is said of Bartholomew. He was one of the disciples to whom our Lord appeared at the Sea of Tiberias after his resurrection (<reflink>John 21:2</reflink>). He was also a witness of the Ascension (<reflink>Acts 1:4, 12, 13</reflink>). He was an "Israelite indeed" (<reflink>John 1:47</reflink>).

bartimaeus.d: son of Timaeus, one of the two blind beggars of Jericho (<reflink>Mark 10:46; Matt. 20:30</reflink>). His blindness was miraculously cured on the ground of his faith.

baruch.d: blessed. (1.) The secretary of the prophet Jeremiah (32:12; 36:4). He was of the tribe of Judah (51:59). To him Jeremiah dictated his prophecies regarding the invasion of the Babylonians and the Captivity. These he read to the people from a window in the temple in the fourth year of the reign of Jehoiakim, king of Judah (Jer. 36). He afterwards read them before the counsellors of the king at a private interview; and then to the king himself, who, after hearing a part of the roll, cut it with a penknife, and threw it into the fire of his winter parlour, where he was sitting.

barzillai.d: of iron. (1.) A Meholathite, the father of Adriel (<reflink>2 Sam. 21:8</reflink>).

bashan.d: light soil, first mentioned in Gen. 14:5, where it is said that Chedorlaomer and his confederates "smote the Rephaim in Ashteroth," where Og the king of Bashan had his residence. At the time of Israel's entrance into the Promised Land, Og came out against them, but was utterly routed (<reflink>Num. 21:33-35; Deut. 3:1-7</reflink>). This country extended from Gilead in the south to Hermon in the north, and from the Jordan on the west to Salcah on the east. Along with the half of Gilead it was given to the half-tribe of Manasseh (<reflink>Josh. 13:29-31</reflink>). Golan, one of its cities, became a "city of refuge" (<reflink>Josh. 21:27</reflink>). Argob, in Bashan, was one of Solomon's commissariat districts (<reflink>1 Kings 4:13</reflink>). The cities of Bashan were taken by Hazael (<reflink>2 Kings 10:33</reflink>), but were soon after reconquered by Jehoash (<reflink>2 Kings 13:25</reflink>), who overcame the Syrians in three battles, according to the word of Elisha (19). …

bashan, hill of.d: (<reflink>Ps. 68:15</reflink>), probably another name for Hermon, which lies to the north of Bashan.

bashan-havoth-jair.d: the Bashan of the villages of Jair, the general name given to Argob by Jair, the son of Manasseh (<reflink>Deut. 3:14</reflink>), containing sixty cities with walls and brazen gates (<reflink>Josh. 13:30; 1 Kings 4:13</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See ARGOB.</see>)

bashemath.d: sweet-smelling. (1.) The daughter of Ishmael, the last of Esau's three wives (<reflink>Gen. 36:3, 4, 13</reflink>), from whose son Reuel four tribes of the Edomites sprung. She is also called Mahalath (<reflink>Gen. 28:9</reflink>). It is noticeable that Esau's three wives receive different names in the genealogical table of the Edomites (Gen. 36) from those given to them in the history (<reflink>Gen. 26:34; 28:9</reflink>).

basilisk.d: (in R.V., Isa. 11:8; 14:29; 59:5; Jer. 8:17), the "king serpent," as the name imports; a fabulous serpent said to be three spans long, with a spot on its head like a crown. Probably the yellow snake is intended. (<see target="x-self">See COCKATRICE.</see>)

basin.d: or Bason. (1.) A trough or laver (Heb. aggan') for washing (<reflink>Ex. 24:6</reflink>); rendered also "goblet" (<reflink>Cant. 7:2</reflink>) and "cups" (<reflink>Isa. 22:24</reflink>).

basket.d: There are five different Hebrew words so rendered in the Authorized Version: (1.) A basket (Heb. sal, a twig or osier) for holding bread (<reflink>Gen. 40:16; Ex. 29:3, 23; Lev. 8:2, 26, 31; Num. 6:15, 17, 19</reflink>). Sometimes baskets were made of twigs peeled; their manufacture was a recognized trade among the Hebrews.

bastard.d: In the Old Testament the rendering of the Hebrew word _mamzer'_, which means "polluted." In Deut. 23:2, it occurs in the ordinary sense of illegitimate offspring. In Zech. 9:6, the word is used in the sense of foreigner. From the history of Jephthah we learn that there were bastard offspring among the Jews (<reflink>Judg. 11:1-7</reflink>). In Heb. 12:8, the word (Gr. nothoi) is used in its ordinary sense, and denotes those who do not share the privileges of God's children.

bastinado.d: beating, a mode of punishment common in the East. It is referred to by "the rod of correction" (<reflink>Prov. 22:15</reflink>), "scourging" (<reflink>Lev. 19:20</reflink>), "chastising" (<reflink>Deut. 22:18</reflink>). The number of blows could not exceed forty (<reflink>Deut. 25:2, 3</reflink>).

bat.d: The Hebrew word (atalleph') so rendered (<reflink>Lev. 11:19; Deut. 14:18</reflink>) implies "flying in the dark." The bat is reckoned among the birds in the list of unclean animals. To cast idols to the "moles and to the bats" means to carry them into dark caverns or desolate places to which these animals resort (<reflink>Isa. 2:20</reflink>), i.e., to consign them to desolation or ruin.

bath.d: a Hebrew liquid measure, the tenth part of an homer (<reflink>1 Kings 7:26, 38; Ezek. 45:10, 14</reflink>). It contained 8 gallons 3 quarts of our measure. "Ten acres of vineyard shall yield one bath" (<reflink>Isa. 5:10</reflink>) denotes great unproductiveness.

bath-rabbim.d: daughter of many, the name of one of the gates of the city of Heshbon, near which were pools (<reflink>Cant.7:4</reflink>).

bath-sheba.d: daughter of the oath, or of seven, called also Bath-shu'a (<reflink>1 Chr. 3:5</reflink>), was the daughter of Eliam (<reflink>2 Sam. 11:3</reflink>) or Ammiel (<reflink>1 Chr. 3:5</reflink>), and wife of Uriah the Hittite. David committed adultery with her (<reflink>2 Sam. 11:4, 5; Ps. 51:1</reflink>). The child born in adultery died (<reflink>2 Sam. 12:15-19</reflink>). After her husband was slain (11:15) she was married to David (11:27), and became the mother of Solomon (12:24; 1 Kings 1:11; 2:13). She took a prominent part in securing the succession of Solomon to the throne (<reflink>1 Kings 1:11, 16-21</reflink>).

baths.d: The use of the bath was very frequent among the Hebrews (<reflink>Lev. 14:8; Num. 19:19, ect.</reflink>). The high priest at his inauguration (<reflink>Lev. 8:6</reflink>), and on the day of atonement, was required to bathe himself (16:4, 24). The "pools" mentioned in Neh. 3:15, 16, 2 Kings 20:20, Isa. 22:11, John 9:7, were public bathing-places.

battering-ram.d: (<reflink>Ezek. 4:2; 21:22</reflink>), a military engine, consisting of a long beam of wood hung upon a frame, for making breaches in walls. The end of it which was brought against the wall was shaped like a ram's head.

battle-axe.d: a mallet or heavy war-club. Applied metaphorically (<reflink>Jer. 51:20</reflink>) to Cyrus, God's instrument in destroying Babylon.

battle-bow.d: the war-bow used in fighting (<reflink>Zech. 9:10; 10:4</reflink>). "Thy bow was made quite naked" (<reflink>Hab. 3:9</reflink>) means that it was made ready for use. By David's order (<reflink>2 Sam. 1:18</reflink>) the young men were taught the use, or rather the song of the bow. (<see target="x-self">See ARMOUR, BOW.</see>)

battlement.d: a parapet wall or balustrade surrounding the flat roofs of the houses, required to be built by a special law (<reflink>Deut. 22:8</reflink>). In Jer. 5:10, it denotes the parapet of a city wall.

bay.d: denotes the estuary of the Dead Sea at the mouth of the Jordan (<reflink>Josh. 15:5; 18:19</reflink>), also the southern extremity of the same sea (15:2). The same Hebrew word is rendered "tongue" in Isa. 11:15, where it is used with reference to the forked mouths of the Nile.

bay tree.d: named only in Ps. 37:35, Authorized Version. The Hebrew word so rendered is _ereh_, which simply means "native born", i.e., a tree not transplanted, but growing on its native soil, and therefore luxuriantly. If the psalmist intended by this word to denote any particular tree, it may have been the evergreen bay laurel (Laurus nobilis), which is a native of Palestine. Instead of "like a green bay tree" in the Authorized Version, the Revised Version has, "like a green tree in its native soil."

bdellium.d: occurs only in Gen. 2:12, where it designates a product of the land of Havilah; and in Num. 11:7, where the manna is likened to it in colour. It was probably an aromatic gum like balsam which exuded from a particular tree (Borassus flabelliformis) still found in Arabia, Media, and India. It bears a resemblance in colour to myrrh. Others think the word denotes "pearls," or some precious stone.

beacon.d: a pole (Heb. to'ren) used as a standard or ensign set on the tops of mountains as a call to the people to assemble themselves for some great national purpose (<reflink>Isa. 30:17</reflink>). In Isa. 33:23 and Ezek. 27:5, the same word is rendered "mast." (See Banner

bealiah.d: whose Lord is Jehovah, a Benjamite, one of David's thirty heroes of the sling and bow (<reflink>1 Chr. 12:5</reflink>).

bealoth.d: citizens, a town in the extreme south of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:24</reflink>); probably the same as Baalath-beer (19:8). In 1 Kings 4:16, the Authorized Version has "in Aloth," the Revised Version "Bealoth."

beam.d: occurs in the Authorized Version as the rendering of various Hebrew words. In 1 Sam. 17:7, it means a weaver's frame or principal beam; in Hab. 2:11, a crossbeam or girder; 2 Kings 6:2, 5, a cross-piece or rafter of a house; 1 Kings 7:6, an architectural ornament as a projecting step or moulding; Ezek. 41:25, a thick plank. In the New Testament the word occurs only in Matt. 7:3, 4, 5, and Luke 6:41, 42, where it means (Gr. dokos) a large piece of wood used for building purposes, as contrasted with "mote" (Gr. karphos), a small piece or mere splinter. "Mote" and "beam" became proverbial for little and great faults.

beans.d: mentioned in 2 Sam. 17:28 as having been brought to David when flying from Absalom. They formed a constituent in the bread Ezekiel (4:9) was commanded to make, as they were in general much used as an article of diet. They are extensively cultivated in Egypt and Arabia and Syria.

bear.d: a native of the mountain regions of Western Asia, frequently mentioned in Scripture. David defended his flocks against the attacks of a bear (<reflink>1 Sam. 17:34-37</reflink>). Bears came out of the wood and destroyed the children who mocked the prophet Elisha (<reflink>2 Kings 2:24</reflink>). Their habits are referred to in Isa. 59:11; Prov. 28:15; Lam. 3:10. The fury of the female bear when robbed of her young is spoken of (<reflink>2 Sam. 17:8; Prov. 17:12; Hos. 13:8</reflink>). In Daniel's vision of the four great monarchies, the Medo-Persian empire is represented by a bear (7:5).

beard.d: The mode of wearing it was definitely prescribed to the Jews (<reflink>Lev. 19:27; 21:5</reflink>). Hence the import of Ezekiel's (5:1-4) description of the "razor" i.e., the agents of an angry providence being used against the guilty nation of the Jews. It was a part of a Jew's daily toilet to anoint his beard with oil and perfume (<reflink>Ps. 133:2</reflink>). Beards were trimmed with the most fastidious care (<reflink>2 Sam. 19:24</reflink>), and their neglet was an indication of deep sorrow (<reflink>Isa. 15:2; Jer. 41:5</reflink>). The custom was to shave or pluck off the hair as a sign of mourning (<reflink>Isa. 50:6; Jer. 48:37; Ezra 9:3</reflink>). The beards of David's ambassadors were cut off by hanun (<reflink>2 Sam. 10:4</reflink>) as a mark of indignity.

beast.d: This word is used of flocks or herds of grazing animals (<reflink>Ex. 22:5; Num. 20:4, 8, 11; Ps. 78:48</reflink>); of beasts of burden (<reflink>Gen. 45:17</reflink>); of eatable beasts (<reflink>Prov. 9:2</reflink>); and of swift beasts or dromedaries (<reflink>Isa. 60:6</reflink>). In the New Testament it is used of a domestic animal as property (<reflink>Rev. 18:13</reflink>); as used for food (<reflink>1 Cor. 15:39</reflink>), for service (<reflink>Luke 10:34; Acts 23:24</reflink>), and for sacrifice (<reflink>Acts 7:42</reflink>).

beaten gold.d: in Num. 8:4, means "turned" or rounded work in gold. The Greek Version, however, renders the word "solid gold;" the Revised Version, "beaten work of gold." In 1 Kings 10:16, 17, it probably means "mixed" gold, as the word ought to be rendered, i.e., not pure gold. Others render the word in these places "thin plates of gold."

beaten oil.d: (<reflink>Ex. 27:20; 29:40</reflink>), obtained by pounding olives in a mortar, not by crushing them in a mill. It was reckoned the best. (See OLIVE

beautiful gate.d: the name of one of the gates of the temple (<reflink>Acts 3:2</reflink>). It is supposed to have been the door which led from the court of the Gentiles to the court of the women. It was of massive structure, and covered with plates of Corinthian brass.

becher.d: first-born; a youth, the second son of Benjamin (<reflink>Gen. 46:21</reflink>), who came down to Egypt with Jacob. It is probable that he married an Ephraimitish heiress, and that his descendants were consequently reckoned among the tribe of Ephraim (<reflink>Num. 26:35; 1 Chr. 7:20, 21</reflink>). They are not reckoned among the descendants of Benjamin (<reflink>Num. 26:38</reflink>).

bed.d: (Heb. mittah), for rest at night (<reflink>Ex. 8:3; 1 Sam. 19:13, 15, 16, etc.</reflink>); during sickness (<reflink>Gen. 47:31; 48:2; 49:33, etc.</reflink>); as a sofa for rest (<reflink>1 Sam. 28:23; Amos 3:12</reflink>). Another Hebrew word (er'es) so rendered denotes a canopied bed, or a bed with curtains (<reflink>Deut. 3:11; Ps. 132:3</reflink>), for sickness (<reflink>Ps. 6:6; 41:3</reflink>).

bed-chamber.d: an apartment in Eastern houses, furnished with a slightly elevated platform at the upper end and sometimes along the sides, on which were laid mattresses. This was the general arrangement of the public sleeping-room for the males of the family and for guests, but there were usually besides distinct bed-chambers of a more private character (<reflink>2 Kings 4:10; Ex. 8:3; 2 Kings 6:12</reflink>). In 2 Kings 11:2 this word denotes, as in the margin of the Revised Version, a store-room in which mattresses were kept.

bedan.d: one of the judges of Israel (<reflink>1 Sam. 12:11</reflink>). It is uncertain who he was. Some suppose that Barak is meant, others Samson, but most probably this is a contracted form of Abdon (<reflink>Judg. 12:13</reflink>).

bedstead.d: used in Deut. 3:11, but elsewhere rendered "couch," "bed." In 2 Kings 1:4; 16:2; Ps. 132:3; Amos 3:12, the divan is meant by this word.

bee.d: First mentioned in Deut. 1:44. Swarms of bees, and the danger of their attacks, are mentioned in Ps. 118:12. Samson found a "swarm of bees" in the carcass of a lion he had slain (<reflink>Judg. 14:8</reflink>). Wild bees are described as laying up honey in woods and in clefts of rocks (<reflink>Deut. 32:13; Ps. 81:16</reflink>). In Isa. 7:18 the "fly" and the "bee" are personifications of the Egyptians and Assyrians, the inveterate enemies of Israel.

beelzebub.d: (Gr. form Beel'zebul), the name given to Satan, and found only in the New Testament (<reflink>Matt. 10:25; 12:24, 27; Mark 3:22</reflink>). It is probably the same as Baalzebub (q.v.), the god of Ekron, meaning "the lord of flies," or, as others think, "the lord of dung," or "the dung-god."

beer.d: well. (1.) A place where a well was dug by the direction of Moses, at the forty-fourth station of the Hebrews in their wanderings (<reflink>Num. 21:16-18</reflink>) in the wilderness of Moab. (See WELL

beer-elim.d: well of heroes, probably the name given to Beer, the place where the chiefs of Israel dug a well (<reflink>Num. 21:16; Isa. 15:8</reflink>).

beer-lahai-roi.d: i.e., "the well of him that liveth and seeth me," or, as some render it, "the well of the vision of life", the well where the Lord met with Hagar (<reflink>Gen. 16:7-14</reflink>). Isaac dwelt beside this well (24:62; 25:11). It has been identified with 'Ain Muweileh, or Moilahhi, south-west of Beersheba, and about 12 miles W. from Kadesh-barnea.

beeri.d: illustrious, or the well-man. (1.) The father of Judith, one of the wives of Esau (<reflink>Gen. 26:34</reflink>), the same as Adah (<reflink>Gen. 36:2</reflink>). (2.) The father of the prophet Hosea (1:1).

beeroth.d: wells, one of the four cities of the Hivites which entered by fraud into a league with Joshua. It belonged to Benjamin (<reflink>Josh. 18:25</reflink>). It has by some been identified with el-Bireh on the way to Nablus, 10 miles north of Jerusalem.

beeroth of the children of jaakan.w: Beeroth of the children of Jaakan

beersheba.d: well of the oath, or well of seven, a well dug by Abraham, and so named because he and Abimelech here entered into a compact (<reflink>Gen. 21:31</reflink>). On re-opening it, Isaac gave it the same name (<reflink>Gen. 26:31-33</reflink>). It was a favourite place of abode of both of these patriarchs (21:33-22:1, 19; 26:33; 28:10). It is mentioned among the "cities" given to the tribe of Simeon (<reflink>Josh. 19:2; 1 Chr. 4:28</reflink>). From Dan to Beersheba, a distance of about 144 miles (<reflink>Judg. 20:1; 1 Chr. 21:2; 2 Sam. 24:2</reflink>), became the usual way of designating the whole Promised Land, and passed into a proverb. After the return from the Captivity the phrase is narrowed into "from Beersheba unto the valley of Hinnom" (<reflink>Neh. 11:30</reflink>). The kingdom of the ten tribes extended from Beersheba to Mount Ephraim (<reflink>2 Chr. 19:4</reflink>). The name is not found in the New Testament. …

beetle.d: (Heb. hargol, meaning "leaper"). Mention of it is made only in Lev. 11:22, where it is obvious the word cannot mean properly the beetle. It denotes some winged creeper with at least four feet, "which has legs above its feet, to leap withal." The description plainly points to the locust (q.v.). This has been an article of food from the earliest times in the East to the present day. The word is rendered "cricket" in the Revised Version.

beeves.d: (an old English plural of the word beef), a name applicable to all ruminating animals except camels, and especially to the Bovidce, or horned cattle (<reflink>Lev. 22:19, 21; Num. 31:28, 30, 33, 38, 44</reflink>).

beg.d: That the poor existed among the Hebrews we have abundant evidence (<reflink>Ex. 23:11; Deut. 15:11</reflink>), but there is no mention of beggars properly so called in the Old Testament. The poor were provided for by the law of Moses (<reflink>Lev. 19:10; Deut. 12:12; 14:29</reflink>). It is predicted of the seed of the wicked that they shall be beggars (<reflink>Ps. 37:25; 109:10</reflink>).

behead.d: a method of taking away life practised among the Egyptians (<reflink>Gen. 40:17-19</reflink>). There are instances of this mode of punishment also among the Hebrews (<reflink>2 Sam. 4:8; 20:21,22; 2 Kings 10:6-8</reflink>). It is also mentioned in the New Testament (<reflink>Matt. 14:8-12; Acts 12:2</reflink>).

behemoth.d: (<reflink>Job 40:15-24</reflink>). Some have supposed this to be an Egyptian word meaning a "water-ox." The Revised Version has here in the margin "hippopotamus," which is probably the correct rendering of the word. The word occurs frequently in Scripture, but, except here, always as a common name, and translated "beast" or "cattle."

bekah.d: Both the name and its explanation, "a half shekel," are given in Ex. 38:26. The word properly means a "division," a "part." (R.V., "beka.")

bel.d: the Aramaic form of Baal, the national god of the Babylonians (<reflink>Isa. 46:1; Jer. 50:2; 51:44</reflink>). It signifies "lord." (See BAAL

bela.d: a thing swallowed. (1.) A city on the shore of the Dead Sea, not far from Sodom, called also Zoar. It was the only one of the five cities that was spared at Lot's intercession (<reflink>Gen. 19:20,23</reflink>). It is first mentioned in Gen. 14:2,8.

belial.d: worthlessness, frequently used in the Old Testament as a proper name. It is first used in Deut. 13:13. In the New Testament it is found only in 2 Cor. 6:15, where it is used as a name of Satan, the personification of all that is evil. It is translated "wicked" in Deut. 15:9; Ps. 41:8 (R.V. marg.); 101:3; Prov. 6:12, etc. The expression "son" or "man of Belial" means simply a worthless, lawless person (<reflink>Judg. 19:22; 20:13; 1 Sam. 1:16; 2:12</reflink>).

bell.d: The bells first mentioned in Scripture are the small golden bells attached to the hem of the high priest's ephod (<reflink>Ex. 28:33, 34, 35</reflink>). The "bells of the horses" mentioned by Zechariah (14:20) were attached to the bridles or belts round the necks of horses trained for war, so as to accustom them to noise and tumult.

bellows.d: occurs only in Jer. 6:29, in relation to the casting of metal. Probably they consisted of leather bags similar to those common in Egypt.

belly.d: the seat of the carnal affections (<reflink>Titus 1:12; Phil. 3:19; Rom. 16:18</reflink>). The word is used symbolically for the heart (<reflink>Prov. 18:8; 20:27; 22:18, marg.</reflink>). The "belly of hell" signifies the grave or underworld (<reflink>Jonah 2:2</reflink>).

belshazzar.d: Bel protect the king!, the last of the kings of Babylon (<reflink>Dan. 5:1</reflink>). He was the son of Nabonidus by Nitocris, who was the daughter of Nebuchadnezzar and the widow of Nergal-sharezer. When still young he made a great feast to a thousand of his lords, and when heated with wine sent for the sacred vessels his "father" (<reflink>Dan. 5:2</reflink>), or grandfather, Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from the temple in Jerusalem, and he and his princes drank out of them. In the midst of their mad revelry a hand was seen by the king tracing on the wall the announcement of God's judgment, which that night fell upon him. At the instance of the queen (i.e., his mother) Daniel was brought in, and he interpreted the writing. That night the kingdom of the Chaldeans came to an end, and the king was slain (<reflink>Dan. 5:30</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See NERGAL-SHAREZER.</see>)

belteshazzar.d: Beltis protect the king!, the Chaldee name given to Daniel by Nebuchadnezzar (<reflink>Dan. 1:7</reflink>).

ben-ammi.d: son of my kindred; i.e., "born of incest", the son of Lot by his youngest daughter (<reflink>Gen. 19:38</reflink>).

ben-hadad.d: the standing title of the Syrian kings, meaning "the son of Hadad." (<see target="x-self">See HADADEZER.</see>)

benaiah.d: built up by Jehovah. (1.) The son of Jehoiada, chief priest (<reflink>1 Chr. 27:5</reflink>). He was set by David over his body-guard of Cherethites and Pelethites (<reflink>2 Sam. 8:18; 1 Kings 1:32; 1 Chr. 18:17</reflink>). His exploits are enumerated in 2 Sam. 23:20, 21, 22; 1 Chr. 11:22. He remained faithful to Solomon (<reflink>1 Kings 1:8, 10, 26</reflink>), by whom he was raised to the rank of commander-in-chief (<reflink>1 Kings 2:25, 29, 30, 34, 35; 4:4</reflink>).

bench.d: deck of a Tyrian ship, described by Ezekiel (27:6) as overlaid with box-wood.

bene-jaakan.d: children of Jaakan (<reflink>Num. 33:31, 32</reflink>), the same as Beeroth.

bethesda.d: house of mercy, a reservoir (Gr. kolumbethra, "a swimming bath") with five porches, close to the sheep-gate or market (<reflink>Neh. 3:1; John 5:2</reflink>). Eusebius the historian (A.D. 330) calls it "the sheep-pool." It is also called "Bethsaida" and "Beth-zatha" (<reflink>John 5:2, R.V. marg.</reflink>). Under these "porches" or colonnades were usually a large number of infirm people waiting for the "troubling of the water." It is usually identified with the modern so-called Fountain of the Virgin, in the valley of the Kidron, and not far from the Pool of Siloam (q.v.); and also with the Birket Israel, a pool near the mouth of the valley which runs into the Kidron south of "St. Stephen's Gate." Others again identify it with the twin pools called the "Souterrains," under the convent of the Sisters of Zion, situated in what must have been the rock-hewn ditch between Bezetha and the fortress of Antonia. …

bethlehem.d: house of bread. (1.) A city in the "hill country" of Judah. It was originally called Ephrath (<reflink>Gen. 35:16, 19; 48:7; Ruth 4:11</reflink>). It was also called Beth-lehem Ephratah (<reflink>Micah 5:2</reflink>), Beth-lehem-judah (<reflink>1 Sam. 17:12</reflink>), and "the city of David" (<reflink>Luke 2:4</reflink>). It is first noticed in Scripture as the place where Rachel died and was buried "by the wayside," directly to the north of the city (<reflink>Gen. 48:7</reflink>). The valley to the east was the scene of the story of Ruth the Moabitess. There are the fields in which she gleaned, and the path by which she and Naomi returned to the town. Here was David's birth-place, and here also, in after years, he was anointed as king by Samuel (<reflink>1 Sam. 16:4-13</reflink>); and it was from the well of Bethlehem that three of his heroes brought water for him at the risk of their lives when he was in the cave of Adullam (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:13-17</reflink>). …

bethsaida.d: house of fish. (1.) A town in Galilee, on the west side of the sea of Tiberias, in the "land of Gennesaret." It was the native place of Peter, Andrew, and Philip, and was frequently resorted to by Jesus (<reflink>Mark 6:45; John 1:44; 12:21</reflink>). It is supposed to have been at the modern 'Ain Tabighah, a bay to the north of Gennesaret.

bethuel.d: man of God, or virgin of God, or house of God. (1.) The son of Nahor by Milcah; nephew of Abraham, and father of Rebekah (<reflink>Gen. 22:22, 23; 24:15, 24, 47</reflink>). He appears in person only once (24:50).

bethzur.d: house of rock, a town in the mountains of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:58</reflink>), about 4 miles to the north of Hebron. It was built by Rehoboam for the defence of his kingdom (<reflink>2 Chr. 11:7</reflink>). It stood near the modern ed-Dirweh. Its ruins are still seen on a hill which bears the name of Beit-Sur, and which commands the road from Beer-sheba and Hebron to Jerusalem from the south.

betroth.d: to promise "by one's truth." Men and women were betrothed when they were engaged to be married. This usually took place a year or more before marriage. From the time of betrothal the woman was regarded as the lawful wife of the man to whom she was betrothed (<reflink>Deut. 28:30; Judg. 14:2, 8; Matt. 1:18-21</reflink>). The term is figuratively employed of the spiritual connection between God and his people (<reflink>Hos. 2:19, 20</reflink>).

beulah.d: married, is used in Isa. 62:4 metaphorically as the name of Judea: "Thy land shall be married," i.e., favoured and blessed of the Lord.

bewray.d: to reveal or disclose; an old English word equivalent to "betray" (<reflink>Prov. 27:16; 29:24, R.V., "uttereth;" Isa. 16:3; Matt. 26:73</reflink>).

beyond.d: when used with reference to Jordan, signifies in the writings of Moses the west side of the river, as he wrote on the east bank (<reflink>Gen. 50:10, 11; Deut. 1:1, 5; 3:8, 20; 4:46</reflink>); but in the writings of Joshua, after he had crossed the river, it means the east side (<reflink>Josh. 5:1; 12:7; 22:7</reflink>).

bezaleel.d: in the shadow of God; i.e., "under his protection", the artificer who executed the work of art in connection with the tabernacle in the wilderness (<reflink>Ex. 31:2; 35:30</reflink>). He was engaged principally in works of metal, wood, and stone; while Aholiab, who was associated with him and subordinate to him, had the charge of the textile fabrics (36:1, 2; 38:22). He was of the tribe of Judah, the son of Uri, and grandson of Hur (31:2). Mention is made in Ezra 10:30 of another of the same name.

bezek.d: lightning. (1.) The residence of Adoni-bezek, in the lot of Judah (<reflink>Judg. 1:5</reflink>). It was in the mountains, not far from Jerusalem. Probably the modern Bezkah, 6 miles south-east of Lydda.

bezer.d: ore of gold or silver. (1.) A city of the Reubenites; one of the three cities of refuge on the east of Jordan (<reflink>Deut. 4: 43; Josh. 20:8</reflink>). It has been identified with the modern ruined village of Burazin, some 12 miles north of Heshbon; also with Kasur-el-Besheir, 2 miles south-west of Dibon.

bible.d: Bible, the English form of the Greek name _Biblia_, meaning "books," the name which in the fifth century began to be given to the entire collection of sacred books, the "Library of Divine Revelation." The name Bible was adopted by Wickliffe, and came gradually into use in our English language. The Bible consists of sixty-six different books, composed by many different writers, in three different languages, under different circumstances; writers of almost every social rank, statesmen and peasants, kings, herdsmen, fishermen, priests, tax-gatherers, tentmakers; educated and uneducated, Jews and Gentiles; most of them unknown to each other, and writing at various periods during the space of about 1600 years: and yet, after all, it is only one book dealing with only one subject in its numberless aspects and relations, the subject of man's redemption.

bier.d: the frame on which dead bodies were conveyed to the grave (<reflink>Luke 7:14</reflink>).

bigtha.d: garden, or gift of fortune, one of the seven eunuchs or chamberlains who had charge of the harem of Ahasuerus (<reflink>Esther 1:10</reflink>).

bigthan.d: one of the eunuchs who "kept the door" in the court of Ahasuerus. With Teresh he conspired against the king's life. Mordecai detected the conspiracy, and the culprits were hanged (<reflink>Esther 2:21-23; 6:1-3</reflink>).

bildad.d: son of contention, one of Job's friends. He is called "the Shuhite," probably as belonging to Shuah, a district in Arabia, in which Shuah, the sixth son of Abraham by Keturah, settled (<reflink>Gen. 25:2</reflink>). He took part in each of the three controversies into which Job's friends entered with him (<reflink>Job 8:1; 18:1; 25:1</reflink>), and delivered three speeches, very severe and stern in their tone, although less violent than those of Zophar, but more so than those of Eliphaz.

bilgah.d: cheerful. (1.) The head of the fifteenth sacerdotal course for the temple service (<reflink>1 Chr. 24:14</reflink>). (2.) A priest who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel (<reflink>Neh. 12:5, 18</reflink>).

bilhah.d: faltering; bashful, Rachel's handmaid, whom she gave to Jacob (<reflink>Gen. 29:29</reflink>). She was the mother of Dan and Naphtali (<reflink>Gen. 30:3-8</reflink>). Reuben was cursed by his father for committing adultry with her (35:22; 49:4). He was deprived of the birth-right, which was given to the sons of Joseph.

bilshan.d: son of the tongue; i.e., "eloquent", a man of some note who returned from the Captivity with Zerubbabel (<reflink>Ezra 2:2; Neh. 7:7</reflink>).

bird.d: Birds are divided in the Mosaic law into two classes, (1) the clean (<reflink>Lev. 1:14-17; 5:7-10; 14:4-7</reflink>), which were offered in sacrifice; and (2) the unclean (<reflink>Lev. 11:13-20</reflink>). When offered in sacrifice, they were not divided as other victims were (<reflink>Gen. 15:10</reflink>). They are mentioned also as an article of food (<reflink>Deut. 14:11</reflink>). The art of snaring wild birds is referred to (<reflink>Ps. 124:7; Prov. 1:17; 7:23; Jer. 5:27</reflink>). Singing birds are mentioned in Ps. 104:12; Eccl. 12:4. Their timidity is alluded to (<reflink>Hos. 11:11</reflink>). The reference in Ps. 84:3 to the swallow and the sparrow may be only a comparison equivalent to, "What her house is to the sparrow, and her nest to the swallow, that thine altars are to my soul."

birsha.d: son of wickedness, a king of Gomorrah whom Abraham succoured in the invasion of Chedorlaomer (<reflink>Gen. 14:2</reflink>).

birth.d: As soon as a child was born it was washed, and rubbed with salt (<reflink>Ezek. 16:4</reflink>), and then swathed with bandages (<reflink>Job 38:9; Luke 2:7, 12</reflink>). A Hebrew mother remained forty days in seclusion after the birth of a son, and after the birth of a daughter double that number of days. At the close of that period she entered into the tabernacle or temple and offered up a sacrifice of purification (<reflink>Lev. 12:1-8; Luke 2:22</reflink>). A son was circumcised on the eighth day after his birth, being thereby consecrated to God (<reflink>Gen. 17:10-12; comp. Rom. 4:11</reflink>). Seasons of misfortune are likened to the pains of a woman in travail, and seasons of prosperity to the joy that succeeds child-birth (<reflink>Isa. 13:8; Jer. 4:31; John 16:21, 22</reflink>). The natural birth is referred to as the emblem of the new birth (<reflink>John 3:3-8; Gal. 6:15; Titus 3:5, etc.</reflink>).

birth-day.d: The observance of birth-days was common in early times (<reflink>Job 1:4, 13, 18</reflink>). They were specially celebrated in the land of Egypt (<reflink>Gen. 40:20</reflink>). There is no recorded instance in Scripture of the celebration of birth-days among the Jews. On the occasion of Herod's birth-day John the Baptist was beheaded (<reflink>Matt. 14:6</reflink>).

birthright.d: (1.) This word denotes the special privileges and advantages belonging to the first-born son among the Jews. He became the priest of the family. Thus Reuben was the first-born of the patriarchs, and so the priesthood of the tribes belonged to him. That honour was, however, transferred by God from Reuben to Levi (<reflink>Num. 3:12, 13; 8:18</reflink>).

bishop.d: an overseer. In apostolic times, it is quite manifest that there was no difference as to order between bishops and elders or presbyters (<reflink>Acts 20:17-28; 1 Pet. 5:1, 2; Phil. 1:1; 1 Tim. 3</reflink>). The term bishop is never once used to denote a different office from that of elder or presbyter. These different names are simply titles of the same office, "bishop" designating the function, namely, that of oversight, and "presbyter" the dignity appertaining to the office. Christ is figuratively called "the bishop [episcopos] of souls" (<reflink>1 Pet. 2:25</reflink>).

bit.d: the curb put into the mouths of horses to restrain them. The Hebrew word (metheg) so rendered in Ps. 32:9 is elsewhere translated "bridle" (<reflink>2 Kings 19:28; Prov. 26:3; Isa. 37:29</reflink>). Bits were generally made of bronze or iron, but sometimes also of gold or silver. In James 3:3 the Authorized Version translates the Greek word by "bits," but the Revised Version by "bridles."

bith-ron.d: the broken or divided place, a district in the Arabah or Jordan valley, on the east of the river (<reflink>2 Sam. 2:29</reflink>). It was probably the designation of the region in general, which is broken and intersected by ravines.

bithynia.d: a province in Asia Minor, to the south of the Euxine and Propontis. Christian congregations were here formed at an early time (<reflink>1 Pet. 1:1</reflink>). Paul was prevented by the Spirit from entering this province (<reflink>Acts 16:7</reflink>). It is noted in church history as the province ruled over by Pliny as Roman proconsul, who was perplexed as to the course he should take with the numerous Christians brought before his tribunal on account of their profession of Christianity and their conduct, and wrote to Trajan, the emperor, for instructions (A.D. 107).

bitter.d: Bitterness is symbolical of affliction, misery, and servitude (<reflink>Ex. 1:14; Ruth 1:20; Jer. 9:15</reflink>). The Chaldeans are called the "bitter and hasty nation" (<reflink>Hab. 1:6</reflink>). The "gall of bitterness" expresses a state of great wickedness (<reflink>Acts 8:23</reflink>). A "root of bitterness" is a wicked person or a dangerous sin (<reflink>Heb. 12:15</reflink>).

bittern.d: is found three times in connection with the desolations to come upon Babylon, Idumea, and Nineveh (<reflink>Isa. 14:23; 34:11; Zeph. 2:14</reflink>). This bird belongs to the class of cranes. Its scientific name is Botaurus stellaris. It is a solitary bird, frequenting marshy ground. The Hebrew word (kippod) thus rendered in the Authorized Version is rendered "porcupine" in the Revised Version. But in the passages noted the kippod is associated with birds, with pools of water, and with solitude and desolation. This favours the idea that not the "porcupine" but the "bittern" is really intended by the word.

bitumen.d: Gen. 11:3, R.V., margin, rendered in the A.V. "slime"), a mineral pitch. With this the ark was pitched (6:14. See also Ex. 2:3.) (<see target="x-self">See SLIME.</see>)

black.d: properly the absence of all colour. In Prov. 7:9 the Hebrew word means, as in the margin of the Revised Version, "the pupil of the eye." It is translated "apple" of the eye in Deut. 32:10; Ps. 17:8; Prov. 7:2. It is a different word which is rendered "black" in Lev. 13:31,37; Cant. 1:5; 5:11; and Zech. 6:2, 6. It is uncertain what the "black marble" of Esther 1:6 was which formed a part of the mosaic pavement.

blade.d: applied to the glittering point of a spear (<reflink>Job 39:23</reflink>) or sword (<reflink>Nah. 3:3</reflink>), the blade of a dagger (<reflink>Judg. 3:22</reflink>); the "shoulder blade" (<reflink>Job 31:22</reflink>); the "blade" of cereals (<reflink>Matt. 13:26</reflink>).

blains.d: occurs only in connection with the sixth plague of Egypt (<reflink>Ex. 9:9, 10</reflink>). In Deut. 28:27, 35, it is called "the botch of Egypt." It seems to have been the fearful disease of black leprosy, a kind of elephantiasis, producing burning ulcers.

blasphemy.d: In the sense of speaking evil of God this word is found in Ps. 74:18; Isa. 52:5; Rom. 2:24; Rev. 13:1, 6; 16:9, 11, 21. It denotes also any kind of calumny, or evil-speaking, or abuse (<reflink>1 Kings 21:10; Acts 13:45; 18:6, etc.</reflink>). Our Lord was accused of blasphemy when he claimed to be the Son of God (<reflink>Matt. 26:65; comp. Matt. 9:3; Mark 2:7</reflink>). They who deny his Messiahship blaspheme Jesus (<reflink>Luke 22:65; John 10:36</reflink>).

blastus.d: chamberlain to king Herod Agrippa I. (<reflink>Acts 12:20</reflink>). Such persons generally had great influence with their masters.

blemish.d: imperfection or bodily deformity excluding men from the priesthood, and rendering animals unfit to be offered in sacrifice (<reflink>Lev. 21:17-23; 22:19-25</reflink>). The Christian church, as justified in Christ, is "without blemish" (<reflink>Eph. 5:27</reflink>). Christ offered himself a sacrifice "without blemish," acceptable to God (<reflink>1 Pet. 1:19</reflink>).

bless.d: (1.) God blesses his people when he bestows on them some gift temporal or spiritual (<reflink>Gen. 1:22; 24:35; Job 42:12; Ps. 45:2; 104:24, 35</reflink>).

blind.d: Blind beggars are frequently mentioned (<reflink>Matt. 9:27; 12:22; 20:30; John 5:3</reflink>). The blind are to be treated with compassion (<reflink>Lev. 19:14; Deut. 27:18</reflink>). Blindness was sometimes a punishment for disobedience (<reflink>1 Sam. 11:2; Jer. 39:7</reflink>), sometimes the effect of old age (<reflink>Gen. 27:1; 1 Kings 14:4; 1 Sam. 4:15</reflink>). Conquerors sometimes blinded their captives (<reflink>2 Kings 25:7; 1 Sam. 11:2</reflink>). Blindness denotes ignorance as to spiritual things (<reflink>Isa. 6:10; 42:18, 19; Matt. 15:14; Eph. 4:18</reflink>). The opening of the eyes of the blind is peculiar to the Messiah (<reflink>Isa. 29:18</reflink>). Elymas was smitten with blindness at Paul's word (<reflink>Acts 13:11</reflink>).

blood.d: (1.) As food, prohibited in Gen. 9:4, where the use of animal food is first allowed. Comp. Deut. 12:23; Lev. 3:17; 7:26; 17:10-14. The injunction to abstain from blood is renewed in the decree of the council of Jerusalem (<reflink>Acts 15:29</reflink>). It has been held by some, and we think correctly, that this law of prohibition was only ceremonial and temporary; while others regard it as still binding on all. Blood was eaten by the Israelites after the battle of Gilboa (<reflink>1 Sam. 14:32-34</reflink>).

bloody sweat.d: the sign and token of our Lord's great agony (<reflink>Luke 22:44</reflink>).

blot.d: a stain or reproach (<reflink>Job 31:7; Prov. 9:7</reflink>). To blot out sin is to forgive it (<reflink>Ps. 51:1, 9; Isa. 44:22; Acts 3:19</reflink>). Christ's blotting out the handwriting of ordinances was his fulfilling the law in our behalf (<reflink>Col. 2:14</reflink>).

blue.d: generally associated with purple (<reflink>Ex. 25:4; 26:1, 31, 36, etc.</reflink>). It is supposed to have been obtained from a shellfish of the Mediterranean, the Helix ianthina of Linnaeus. The robe of the high priest's ephod was to be all of this colour (<reflink>Ex. 28:31</reflink>), also the loops of the curtains (26:4) and the ribbon of the breastplate (28:28). Blue cloths were also made for various sacred purposes (<reflink>Num. 4:6, 7, 9, 11, 12</reflink>). (See COLOUR

boanerges.d: sons of thunder, a surname given by our Lord to James and John (<reflink>Mark 3:17</reflink>) on account of their fervid and impetuous temper (<reflink>Luke 9:54</reflink>).

boar.d: occurs only in Ps. 80:13. The same Hebrew word is elsewhere rendered "swine" (<reflink>Lev. 11:7; Deut. 14:8; Prov. 11:22; Isa. 65:4; 66:3, 17</reflink>). The Hebrews abhorred swine's flesh, and accordingly none of these animals were reared, except in the district beyond the Sea of Galilee. In the psalm quoted above the powers that destroyed the Jewish nation are compared to wild boars and wild beasts of the field.

boaz.d: alacrity. (1.) The husband of Ruth, a wealthy Bethlehemite. By the "levirate law" the duty devolved on him of marrying Ruth the Moabitess (<reflink>Ruth 4:1-13</reflink>). He was a kinsman of Mahlon, her first husband.

bochim.d: weepers, a place where the angel of the Lord reproved the Israelites for entering into a league with the people of the land. This caused them bitterly to weep, and hence the name of the place (<reflink>Judg. 2:1, 5</reflink>). It lay probably at the head of one of the valleys between Gilgal and Shiloh.

boil.d: (rendered "botch" in Deut. 28:27, 35), an aggravated ulcer, as in the case of Hezekiah (<reflink>2 Kings 20:7; Isa. 38:21</reflink>) or of the Egyptians (<reflink>Ex. 9:9, 10, 11; Deut. 28:27, 35</reflink>). It designates the disease of Job (2:7), which was probably the black leprosy.

bolled.d: (<reflink>Ex. 9:31</reflink>), meaning "swollen or podded for seed," was adopted in the Authorized Version from the version of Coverdale (1535). The Revised Version has in the margin "was in bloom," which is the more probable rendering of the Hebrew word. It is the fact that in Egypt when barley is in ear (about February) flax is blossoming.

bolster.d: The Hebrew word _kebir_, rendered "pillow" in 1 Sam. 19:13, 16, but in Revised Version marg. "quilt" or "network," probably means some counterpane or veil intended to protect the head of the sleeper. A different Hebrew word (meraashoth') is used for "bolster" (<reflink>1 Sam. 26:7, 11, 16</reflink>). It is rightly rendered in Revised Version "at his head." In Gen. 28:11, 18 the Authorized Version renders it "for his pillows," and the Revised Version "under his head." In Ezek. 13:18, 20 another Hebrew word (kesathoth) is used, properly denoting "cushions" or "pillows," as so rendered both in the Authorized and the Revised Version.

bond.d: an obligation of any kind (<reflink>Num. 30:2, 4, 12</reflink>). The word means also oppression or affliction (<reflink>Ps. 116:16; Phil. 1:7</reflink>). Christian love is the "bond of perfectness" (<reflink>Col. 3:14</reflink>), and the influences of the Spirit are the "bond of peace" (<reflink>Eph. 4:3</reflink>).

bondage.d: of Israel in Egypt (<reflink>Ex. 2:23, 25; 5</reflink>), which is called the "house of bondage" (13:3; 20:2). This word is used also with reference to the captivity in Babylon (<reflink>Isa. 14:3</reflink>), and the oppression of the Persian king (<reflink>Ezra 9:8, 9</reflink>).

bonnet.d: (Heb. peer), Ex. 39:28 (R.V., "head-tires"); Ezek. 44:18 (R.V., "tires"), denotes properly a turban worn by priests, and in Isa. 3:20 (R.V., "head-tires") a head-dress or tiara worn by females. The Hebrew word so rendered literally means an ornament, as in Isa. 61:10 (R.V., "garland"), and in Ezek. 24:17, 23 "tire" (R.V., "head-tire"). It consisted of a piece of cloth twisted about the head. In Ex. 28:40; 29:9 it is the translation of a different Hebrew word (migba'ah), which denotes the turban (R.V., "head-tire") of the common priest as distinguished from the mitre of the high priest. (<see target="x-self">See MITRE.</see>)

book.d: This word has a comprehensive meaning in Scripture. In the Old Testament it is the rendering of the Hebrew word _sepher_, which properly means a "writing," and then a "volume" (<reflink>Ex. 17:14; Deut. 28:58; 29:20; Job 19:23</reflink>) or "roll of a book" (<reflink>Jer. 36:2, 4</reflink>).

booth.d: a hut made of the branches of a tree. In such tabernacles Jacob sojourned for a season at a place named from this circumstance Succoth (<reflink>Gen. 33:17</reflink>). Booths were erected also at the feast of Tabernacles (q.v.), Lev. 23:42, 43, which commemorated the abode of the Israelites in the wilderness.

booty.d: captives or cattle or objects of value taken in war. In Canaan all that breathed were to be destroyed (<reflink>Deut. 20: 16</reflink>). The "pictures and images" of the Canaanites were to be destroyed also (<reflink>Num. 33:52</reflink>). The law of booty as to its division is laid down in Num. 31:26-47. David afterwards introduced a regulation that the baggage-guard should share the booty equally with the soldiers engaged in battle. He also devoted of the spoils of war for the temple (<reflink>1 Sam. 30:24-26; 2 Sam. 8:11; 1 Chr. 26:27</reflink>).

borrow.d: The Israelites "borrowed" from the Egyptians (<reflink>Ex. 12:35, R.V., "asked"</reflink>) in accordance with a divine command (3:22; 11:2). But the word (sha'al) so rendered here means simply and always to "request" or "demand." The Hebrew had another word which is properly translated "borrow" in Deut. 28:12; Ps. 37:21. It was well known that the parting was final. The Egyptians were so anxious to get the Israelites away out of their land that "they let them have what they asked" (<reflink>Ex. 12:36, R.V.</reflink>), or literally "made them to ask," urged them to take whatever they desired and depart. (<see target="x-self">See LOAN.</see>)

bosom.d: In the East objects are carried in the bosom which Europeans carry in the pocket. To have in one's bosom indicates kindness, secrecy, or intimacy (<reflink>Gen. 16:5; 2 Sam. 12:8</reflink>). Christ is said to have been in "the bosom of the Father," i.e., he had the most perfect knowledge of the Father, had the closest intimacy with him (<reflink>John 1:18</reflink>). John (13:23) was "leaning on Jesus' bosom" at the last supper. Our Lord carries his lambs in his bosom, i.e., has a tender, watchful care over them (<reflink>Isa. 40:11</reflink>).

bosor.d: the Chaldee or Aramaic form of the name Beor, the father of Balaam (<reflink>2 Pet. 2:15</reflink>).

bosses.d: the projecting parts of a shield (<reflink>Job 15:26</reflink>). The Hebrew word thus rendered means anything convex or arched, and hence the back, as of animals.

botch.d: the name given in Deut. 28:27, 35 to one of the Egyptian plagues (<reflink>Ex. 9:9</reflink>). The word so translated is usually rendered "boil" (q.v.).

bottle.d: a vessel made of skins for holding wine (<reflink>Josh. 9:4. 13; 1 Sam. 16:20; Matt. 9:17; Mark 2:22; Luke 5:37, 38</reflink>), or milk (<reflink>Judg. 4:19</reflink>), or water (<reflink>Gen. 21:14, 15, 19</reflink>), or strong drink (<reflink>Hab. 2:15</reflink>).

bow.d: The bow was in use in early times both in war and in the chase (<reflink>Gen. 21:20; 27:3; 48:22</reflink>). The tribe of Benjamin were famous for the use of the bow (<reflink>1 Chr. 8:40; 12:2; 2 Chr. 14:8; 17:17</reflink>); so also were the Elamites (<reflink>Isa. 22:6</reflink>) and the Lydians (<reflink>Jer. 46:9</reflink>). The Hebrew word commonly used for bow means properly to tread (<reflink>1 Chr. 5:18; 8:40</reflink>), and hence it is concluded that the foot was employed in bending the bow. Bows of steel (correctly "copper") are mentioned (<reflink>2 Sam. 22:35; Ps. 18:34</reflink>).

bowing.d: a mode of showing respect. Abraham "bowed himself to the people of the land" (<reflink>Gen. 23:7</reflink>); so Jacob to Esau (<reflink>Gen. 33:3</reflink>); and the brethren of Joseph before him as the governor of the land (<reflink>Gen. 43:28</reflink>). Bowing is also frequently mentioned as an act of adoration to idols (<reflink>Josh. 23:7; 2 Kings 5:18; Judg. 2:19; Isa. 44:15</reflink>), and to God (<reflink>Josh. 5:14; Ps. 22:29; 72:9; Micah 6:6; Ps. 95:6; Eph. 3:14</reflink>).

bowl.d: The sockets of the lamps of the golden candlestick of the tabernacle are called bowls (<reflink>Ex. 25:31, 33, 34; 37:17, 19, 20</reflink>); the same word so rendered being elsewhere rendered "cup" (<reflink>Gen. 44:2, 12, 16</reflink>), and wine "pot" (<reflink>Jer. 35:5</reflink>). The reservoir for oil, from which pipes led to each lamp in Zechariah's vision of the candlestick, is called also by this name (<reflink>Zech. 4:2, 3</reflink>); so also are the vessels used for libations (<reflink>Ex. 25:29; 37:16</reflink>).

box.d: for holding oil or perfumery (<reflink>Mark 14:3</reflink>). It was of the form of a flask or bottle. The Hebrew word (pak) used for it is more appropriately rendered "vial" in 1 Sam. 10:1, and should also be so rendered in 2 Kings 9:1, where alone else it occurs.

box-tree.d: (Heb. teashshur), mentioned in Isa. 60:13; 41:19, was, according to some, a species of cedar growing in Lebanon. The words of Ezek. 27:6 literally translated are, "Thy benches they have made of ivory, the daughter of the ashur tree," i.e., inlaid with ashur wood. The ashur is the box-tree, and accordingly the Revised Version rightly reads "inlaid in box wood." This is the Buxus sempervirens of botanists. It is remarkable for the beauty of its evergreen foliage and for the utility of its hard and durable wood.

bozrah.d: enclosure; fortress. (1.) The city of Jobab, one of the early Edomite kings (<reflink>Gen. 36:33</reflink>). This place is mentioned by the prophets in later times (<reflink>Isa. 34:6; Jer. 49:13; Amos 1:12; Micah 2:12</reflink>). Its modern representative is el-Busseireh. It lies in the mountain district of Petra, 20 miles to the south-east of the Dead Sea.

bracelet.d: (1.) Anklets (<reflink>Num. 31:50; 2 Sam. 1:10</reflink>), and with reference to men.

bramble.d: (1.) Hebrew _atad_, Judg. 9:14; rendered "thorn," Ps. 58:9. The LXX. and Vulgate render by rhamnus, a thorny shrub common in Palestine, resembling the hawthorn.

branch.d: a symbol of kings descended from royal ancestors (<reflink>Ezek. 17:3, 10; Dan. 11:7</reflink>); of prosperity (<reflink>Job 8:16</reflink>); of the Messiah, a branch out of the root of the stem of Jesse (<reflink>Isa. 11:1</reflink>), the "beautiful branch" (4:2), a "righteous branch" (<reflink>Jer. 23:5</reflink>), "the Branch" (<reflink>Zech. 3:8; 6:12</reflink>).

brass.d: which is an alloy of copper and zinc, was not known till the thirteenth century. What is designated by this word in Scripture is properly copper (<reflink>Deut. 8:9</reflink>). It was used for fetters (<reflink>Judg. 16:21; 2 Kings 25:7</reflink>), for pieces of armour (<reflink>1 Sam. 17:5, 6</reflink>), for musical instruments (<reflink>1 Chr. 15:19; 1 Cor. 13:1</reflink>), and for money (<reflink>Matt. 10:9</reflink>).

bravery.d: (<reflink>Isa. 3:18</reflink>), an old English word meaning comeliness or beauty.

breach.d: an opening in a wall (<reflink>1 Kings 11:27; 2 Kings 12:5</reflink>); the fracture of a limb (<reflink>Lev. 24:20</reflink>), and hence the expression, "Heal, etc." (<reflink>Ps. 60:2</reflink>). Judg. 5:17, a bay or harbour; R.V., "by his creeks."

bread.d: among the Jews was generally made of wheat (<reflink>Ex. 29:2; Judg. 6:19</reflink>), though also sometimes of other grains (<reflink>Gen. 14:18; Judg. 7:13</reflink>). Parched grain was sometimes used for food without any other preparation (<reflink>Ruth 2:14</reflink>).

breastplate.d: (1.) That piece of ancient armour that protected the breast. This word is used figuratively in Eph. 6:14 and Isa. 59:17. (<see target="x-self">See ARMOUR.</see>)

breeches.d: (<reflink>Ex. 28:42</reflink>), rather linen drawers, reaching from the waist to a little above the knee, worn by the priests (<reflink>Ezek. 44:17, 18</reflink>).

bribe.d: None to be taken; "for the gift maketh open eyes blind, and perverteth the cause of the righteous" (<reflink>Ex. 23:8, literally rendered</reflink>).

bricks.d: the making of, formed the chief labour of the Israelites in Egypt (<reflink>Ex. 1:13, 14</reflink>). Those found among the ruins of Babylon and Nineveh are about a foot square and four inches thick. They were usually dried in the sun, though also sometimes in kilns (<reflink>2 Sam. 12:31; Jer. 43:9; Nah. 3:14</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See NEBUCHADNEZZAR.</see>)

bride.d: frequently used in the ordinary sense (<reflink>Isa. 49:18; 61:10, etc.</reflink>). The relation between Christ and his church is set forth under the figure of that between a bridegroom and bride (<reflink>John 3:29</reflink>). The church is called "the bride" (<reflink>Rev. 21:9; 22:17</reflink>). Compare parable of the Ten Virgins (<reflink>Matt. 25:1-13</reflink>).

bridle.d: Three Hebrew words are thus rendered in the Authorized Version. (1.) Heb. _mahsom'_ signifies a muzzle or halter or bridle, by which the rider governs his horse (<reflink>Ps.39:1</reflink>).

brier.d: This word occurs frequently, and is the translation of several different terms. (1.) Micah 7:4, it denotes a species of thorn shrub used for hedges. In Prov. 15:19 the word is rendered "thorn" (Heb. _hedek_, "stinging"), supposed by some to be what is called the "apple of Sodom" (q.v.).

brigandine.d: (<reflink>Jer. 46:4; 51:3</reflink>), an obsolete English word denoting a scale coat of armour, or habergeon, worn by light-armed "brigands." The Revised Version has "coat of mail."

brimstone.d: an inflammable mineral substance found in quantities on the shores of the Dead Sea. The cities of the plain were destroyed by a rain of fire and brimstone (<reflink>Gen. 19:24, 25</reflink>). In Isa. 34:9 allusion is made to the destruction of these cities. This word figuratively denotes destruction or punishment (<reflink>Job 18:15; Isa. 30:33; 34:9; Ps. 11:6; Ezek. 38:22</reflink>). It is used to express the idea of excruciating torment in Rev. 14:10; 19:20; 20:10.

brook.d: a torrent. (1.) Applied to small streams, as the Arnon, Jabbok, etc. Isaiah (15:7) speaks of the "book of the willows," probably the Wady-el-Asha. (2.) It is also applied to winter torrents (<reflink>Job 6:15; Num. 34:5; Josh. 15:4, 47</reflink>), and to the torrent-bed or wady as well as to the torrent itself (<reflink>Num. 13:23; 1 Kings 17:3</reflink>). (3.) In Isa. 19:7 the river Nile is meant, as rendered in the Revised Version.

brother.d: (1.) In the natural and common sense (<reflink>Matt. 1:2; Luke 3:1, 19</reflink>).

bruit.d: a rumour or report (<reflink>Jer. 10:22, R.V. "rumour;" Nah. 3:19</reflink>).

bucket.d: a vessel to draw water with (<reflink>Isa. 40:15</reflink>); used figuratively, probably, of a numerous issue (<reflink>Num. 24:7</reflink>).

building.d: among the Jews was suited to the climate and conditions of the country. They probably adopted the kind of architecture for their dwellings which they found already existing when they entered Canaan (<reflink>Deut. 6:10; Num. 13:19</reflink>). Phoenician artists (<reflink>2 Sam. 5:11; 1 Kings 5:6, 18</reflink>) assisted at the erection of the royal palace and the temple at Jerusalem. Foreigners also assisted at the restoration of the temple after the Exile (<reflink>Ezra 3:7</reflink>).

bul.d: rainy, the eighth ecclesiastical month of the year (<reflink>1 Kings 6:38</reflink>), and the second month of the civil year; later called Marchesvan (q.v.). (<see target="x-self">See MONTH.</see>)

bullock.d: (1.) The translation of a word which is a generic name for horned cattle (<reflink>Isa. 65:25</reflink>). It is also rendered "cow" (<reflink>Ezek. 4:15</reflink>), "ox" (<reflink>Gen. 12:16</reflink>).

bulrush.d: (1.) In Isa. 58:5 the rendering of a word which denotes "belonging to a marsh," from the nature of the soil in which it grows (<reflink>Isa. 18:2</reflink>). It was sometimes platted into ropes (<reflink>Job. 41:2; A.V., "hook," R.V., "rope," lit. "cord of rushes"</reflink>).

bulwarks.d: mural towers, bastions, were introduced by king Uzziah (<reflink>2 Chr. 26:15; Zeph. 1:16; Ps. 48:13; Isa. 26:1</reflink>). There are five Hebrew words so rendered in the Authorized Version, but the same word is also variously rendered.

bunch.d: (1.) A bundle of twigs (<reflink>Ex. 12:22</reflink>). (2.) Bunch or cake of raisins (<reflink>2 Sam. 16:1</reflink>). (3.) The "bunch of a camel" (<reflink>Isa. 30:6</reflink>).

burden.d: (1.) A load of any kind (<reflink>Ex. 23:5</reflink>). (2.) A severe task (<reflink>Ex. 2:11</reflink>). (3.) A difficult duty, requiring effort (<reflink>Ex. 18:22</reflink>). (4.) A prophecy of a calamitous or disastrous nature (<reflink>Isa. 13:1; 17:1; Hab. 1:1, etc.</reflink>).

burial.d: The first burial we have an account of is that of Sarah (Gen. 23). The first commercial transaction recorded is that of the purchase of a burial-place, for which Abraham weighed to Ephron "four hundred shekels of silver current money with the merchants." Thus the patriarch became the owner of a part of the land of Canaan, the only part he ever possessed. When he himself died, "his sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the cave of Machpelah," beside Sarah his wife (<reflink>Gen. 25:9</reflink>).

burnt offering.d: Hebrew _olah_; i.e., "ascending," the whole being consumed by fire, and regarded as ascending to God while being consumed. Part of every offering was burnt in the sacred fire, but this was wholly burnt, a "whole burnt offering." It was the most frequent form of sacrifice, and apparently the only one mentioned in the book of Genesis. Such were the sacrifices offered by Abel (<reflink>Gen. 4:3, 4, here called _minhah_; i.e., "a gift"</reflink>), Noah (<reflink>Gen. 8:20</reflink>), Abraham (<reflink>Gen. 22:2, 7, 8, 13</reflink>), and by the Hebrews in Egypt (<reflink>Ex. 10:25</reflink>).
