bush.d: in which Jehovah appeared to Moses in the wilderness (<reflink>Ex. 3:2; Acts 7:30</reflink>). It is difficult to say what particular kind of plant or bush is here meant. Probably it was the mimosa or acacia. The words "in the bush" in Mark 12:26; Luke 20:37, mean "in the passage or paragraph on the bush;" i.e., in Ex. 3.

butler.d: properly a servant in charge of the wine (<reflink>Gen. 40:1-13; 41:9</reflink>). The Hebrew word, _mashkeh_, thus translated is rendered also (plural) "cup-bearers" (<reflink>1 Kings 10:5; 2 Chr. 9:4</reflink>). Nehemiah (1:11) was cup-bearer to king Artaxerxes. It was a position of great responsibility and honour in royal households.

butter.d: (Heb. hemah), curdled milk (<reflink>Gen. 18:8; Judg. 5:25; 2 Sam. 17:29</reflink>), or butter in the form of the skim of hot milk or cream, called by the Arabs kaimak, a semi-fluid (<reflink>Job 20:17; 29:6; Deut. 32:14</reflink>). The words of Prov. 30:33 have been rendered by some "the pressure [not churning] of milk bringeth forth cheese."

buz.d: contempt. (1.) The second son of Nahor and Milcah, and brother of Huz (<reflink>Gen. 22:21</reflink>). Elihu was one of his descendants (<reflink>Job 32:2</reflink>).

buzi.d: the father of the prophet Ezekiel (1:3).

by.d: in the expression "by myself" (A.V., 1 Cor. 4:4), means, as rendered in the Revised Version, "against myself."

by-ways.d: only in Judg. 5:6 and Ps. 125:5; literally "winding or twisted roads." The margin has "crooked ways."

by-word.d: Hebrew _millah_ (<reflink>Job 30:9</reflink>), a word or speech, and hence object of talk; Hebrew _mashal_ (<reflink>Ps. 44:14</reflink>), a proverb or parable. When it denotes a sharp word of derision, as in Deut. 28:37, 1 Kings 9:7, 2 Chr. 7:20, the Hebrew _sheninah_ is used. In Jer. 24:9 it is rendered "taunt."

cab.d: hollow (R.V., "kab"), occurs only in 2 Kings 6:25; a dry measure, the sixth part of a seah, and the eighteenth part of an ephah, equal to about two English quarts.

cabins.d: only in Jer. 37:16 (R.V., "cells"), arched vaults or recesses off a passage or room; cells for the closer confinement of prisoners.

cabul.d: how little! as nothing. (1.) A town on the eastern border of Asher (<reflink>Josh. 19:27</reflink>), probably one of the towns given by Solomon to Hiram; the modern Kabul, some 8 miles east of Accho, on the very borders of Galilee.

caesar.d: the title assumed by the Roman emperors after Julius Caesar. In the New Testament this title is given to various emperors as sovereigns of Judaea without their accompanying distinctive proper names (<reflink>John 19:15; Acts 17:7</reflink>). The Jews paid tribute to Caesar (<reflink>Matt. 22:17</reflink>), and all Roman citizens had the right of appeal to him (<reflink>Acts 25:11</reflink>). The Caesars referred to in the New Testament are Augustus (<reflink>Luke 2:1</reflink>), Tiberius (3:1; 20:22), Claudius (<reflink>Acts 11:28</reflink>), and Nero (<reflink>Acts 25:8; Phil. 4:22</reflink>).

caesara philippi.d: a city on the northeast of the marshy plain of el-Huleh, 120 miles north of Jerusalem, and 20 miles north of the Sea of Galilee, at the "upper source" of the Jordan, and near the base of Mount Hermon. It is mentioned in Matt. 16:13 and Mark 8:27 as the northern limit of our Lord's public ministry. According to some its original name was Baal-Gad (<reflink>Josh. 11:17</reflink>), or Baal-Hermon (<reflink>Judg. 3:3; 1 Chr. 5:23</reflink>), when it was a Canaanite sanctuary of Baal. It was afterwards called Panium or Paneas, from a deep cavern full of water near the town. This name was given to the cavern by the Greeks of the Macedonian kingdom of Antioch because of its likeness to the grottos of Greece, which were always associated with the worship of their god Pan. Its modern name is Banias. Here Herod built a temple, which he dedicated to Augustus Caesar. …

caesarea.d: (Palestinae), a city on the shore of the Mediterranean, on the great road from Tyre to Egypt, about 70 miles northwest of Jerusalem, at the northern extremity of the plain of Sharon. It was built by Herod the Great (B.C. 10), who named it after Caesar Augustus, hence called Caesarea Sebaste (Gr. Sebastos = "Augustus"), on the site of an old town called "Strato's Tower." It was the capital of the Roman province of Judaea, the seat of the governors or procurators, and the headquarters of the Roman troops. It was the great Gentile city of Palestine, with a spacious artificial harbour. It was adorned with many buildings of great splendour, after the manner of the Roman cities of the West. Here Cornelius the centurion was converted through the instrumentality of Peter (<reflink>Acts 10:1, 24</reflink>), and thus for the first time the door of faith was opened to the Gentiles. Philip the evangelist resided here with his four daughters (21:8). …

cage.d: (Heb. kelub', Jer. 5:27, marg. "coop;" rendered "basket" in Amos 8:1), a basket of wicker-work in which birds were placed after being caught. In Rev. 18:2 it is the rendering of the Greek _phulake_, properly a prison or place of confinement.

caiaphas.d: the Jewish high priest (A.D. 27-36) at the beginning of our Lord's public ministry, in the reign of Tiberius (<reflink>Luke 3:2</reflink>), and also at the time of his condemnation and crucifixion (<reflink>Matt. 26:3,57; John 11:49; 18:13, 14</reflink>). He held this office during the whole of Pilate's administration. His wife was the daughter of Annas, who had formerly been high priest, and was probably the vicar or deputy (Heb. sagan) of Caiaphas. He was of the sect of the Sadducees (<reflink>Acts 5:17</reflink>), and was a member of the council when he gave his opinion that Jesus should be put to death "for the people, and that the whole nation perish not" (<reflink>John 11:50</reflink>). In these words he unconsciously uttered a prophecy. "Like Saul, he was a prophet in spite of himself." Caiaphas had no power to inflict the punishment of death, and therefore Jesus was sent to Pilate, the Roman governor, that he might duly pronounce the sentence against him (<reflink>Matt. …

cain.d: a possession; a spear. (1.) The first-born son of Adam and Eve (Gen. 4). He became a tiller of the ground, as his brother Abel followed the pursuits of pastoral life. He was "a sullen, self-willed, haughty, vindictive man; wanting the religious element in his character, and defiant even in his attitude towards God." It came to pass "in process of time" (marg. "at the end of days"), i.e., probably on the Sabbath, that the two brothers presented their offerings to the Lord. Abel's offering was of the "firstlings of his flock and of the fat," while Cain's was "of the fruit of the ground." Abel's sacrifice was "more excellent" (<reflink>Heb. 11:4</reflink>) than Cain's, and was accepted by God. On this account Cain was "very wroth," and cherished feelings of murderous hatred against his brother, and was at length guilty of the desperate outrage of putting him to death (<reflink>1 John 3:12</reflink>). …

cainan.d: possession; smith. (1.) The fourth antediluvian patriarch, the eldest son of Enos. He was 70 years old at the birth of his eldest son Mahalaleel, after which he lived 840 years (<reflink>Gen. 5:9-14</reflink>), and was 910 years old when he died. He is also called Kenan (<reflink>1 Chr. 1:2</reflink>).

cake.d: Cakes made of wheat or barley were offered in the temple. They were salted, but unleavened (<reflink>Ex. 29:2; Lev. 2:4</reflink>). In idolatrous worship thin cakes or wafers were offered "to the queen of heaven" (<reflink>Jer. 7:18; 44:19</reflink>).

calah.d: one of the most ancient cities of Assyria. "Out of that land he [i.e., Nimrod] went forth into Assyria, and built Nineveh, Rehoboth-Ir, and Calah, and Resen" (<reflink>Gen. 10:11, R.V.</reflink>). Its site is now marked probably by the Nimrud ruins on the left bank of the Tigris. These cover an area of about 1,000 acres, and are second only in size and importance to the mass of ruins opposite Mosul. This city was at one time the capital of the empire, and was the residence of Sardanapalus and his successors down to the time of Sargon, who built a new capital, the modern Khorsabad. It has been conjectured that these four cities mentioned in Gen. 10:11 were afterwards all united into one and called Nineveh (q.v.).

calamus.d: the Latin for cane, Hebrew _Kaneh_, mentioned (<reflink>Ex. 30:23</reflink>) as one of the ingredients in the holy anointing oil, one of the sweet scents (<reflink>Cant. 4:14</reflink>), and among the articles sold in the markets of Tyre (<reflink>Ezek. 27:19</reflink>). The word designates an Oriental plant called the "sweet flag," the Acorus calamus of Linnaeus. It is elsewhere called "sweet cane" (<reflink>Isa. 43:24; Jer. 6:20</reflink>). It has an aromatic smell, and when its knotted stalk is cut and dried and reduced to powder, it forms an ingredient in the most precious perfumes. It was not a native of Palestine, but was imported from Arabia Felix or from India. It was probably that which is now known in India by the name of "lemon grass" or "ginger grass," the Andropogon schoenanthus. (<see target="x-self">See CANE.</see>)

calcol.d: (<reflink>1 Chr. 2:6</reflink>), sustenance, the same probably as Chalcol (<reflink>1 Kings 4:31</reflink>), one of the four sages whom Solomon excelled in wisdom; for "he was wiser than all men."

caleb.d: a dog. (1.) One of the three sons of Hezron of the tribe of Judah. He is also called Chelubai (<reflink>1 Chr. 2:9</reflink>). His descendants are enumerated (18-20, 42-49).

calf.d: Calves were commonly made use of in sacrifices, and are therefore frequently mentioned in Scripture. The "fatted calf" was regarded as the choicest of animal food; it was frequently also offered as a special sacrifice (<reflink>1 Sam. 28:24; Amos 6:4; Luke 15:23</reflink>). The words used in Jer. 34:18, 19, "cut the calf in twain," allude to the custom of dividing a sacrifice into two parts, between which the parties ratifying a covenant passed (<reflink>Gen. 15:9, 10, 17, 18</reflink>). The sacrifice of the lips, i.e., priase, is called "the calves of our lips" (<reflink>Hos. 14:2, R.V., "as bullocks the offering of our lips." Comp. Heb. 13:15; Ps. 116:7; Jer. 33:11</reflink>).

calkers.d: workmen skilled in stopping the seams of the deck or sides of vessels. The inhabitants of Gebel were employed in such work on Tyrian vessels (<reflink>Ezek. 27:9, 27; marg., "strengtheners" or "stoppers of chinks"</reflink>).

call.d: (1.) To cry for help, hence to pray (<reflink>Gen. 4:26</reflink>). Thus men are said to "call upon the name of the Lord" (<reflink>Acts 2:21; 7:59; 9:14; Rom. 10:12; 1 Cor. 1:2</reflink>).

calling.d: a profession, or as we usually say, a vocation (<reflink>1 Cor. 7:20</reflink>). The "hope of your calling" in Eph. 4:4 is the hope resulting from your being called into the kingdom of God.

calneh.d: fort, one of the four cities founded by Nimrod (<reflink>Gen. 10:10</reflink>). It is the modern Niffer, a lofty mound of earth and rubbish situated in the marshes on the left, i.e., the east, bank of the Euphrates, but 30 miles distant from its present course, and about 60 miles south-south-east from Babylon. It is mentioned as one of the towns with which Tyre carried on trade. It was finally taken and probably destroyed by one of the Assyrian kings (<reflink>Amos 6:2</reflink>). It is called Calno (<reflink>Isa. 10:9</reflink>) and Canneh (<reflink>Ezek. 27:23</reflink>).

calvary.d: only in Luke 23:33, the Latin name Calvaria, which was used as a translation of the Greek word _Kranion_, by which the Hebrew word _Gulgoleth_ was interpreted, "the place of a skull." It probably took this name from its shape, being a hillock or low, rounded, bare elevation somewhat in the form of a human skull. It is nowhere in Scripture called a "hill." The crucifixion of our Lord took place outside the city walls (<reflink>Heb. 13:11-13</reflink>) and near the public thoroughfare. "This thing was not done in a corner." (<see target="x-self">See GOLGOTHA.</see>)

camel.d: from the Hebrew _gamal_, "to repay" or "requite," as the camel does the care of its master. There are two distinct species of camels, having, however, the common characteristics of being "ruminants without horns, without muzzle, with nostrils forming oblique slits, the upper lip divided and separately movable and extensile, the soles of the feet horny, with two toes covered by claws, the limbs long, the abdomen drawn up, while the neck, long and slender, is bent up and down, the reverse of that of a horse, which is arched."

channel.d: (1.) The bed of the sea or of a river (<reflink>Ps. 18:15; Isa. 8:7</reflink>).

chapel.d: a holy place or sanctuary, occurs only in Amos 7:13, where one of the idol priests calls Bethel "the king's chapel."

chapiter.d: the ornamental head or capital of a pillar. Three Hebrew words are so rendered. (1.) _Cothereth_ (<reflink>1 Kings 7:16; 2 Kings 25:17; 2 Chr. 4:12</reflink>), meaning a "diadem" or "crown." (2.) _Tzepheth_ (<reflink>2 Chr. 3:15</reflink>). (3.) _Rosh_ (<reflink>Ex. 36:38; 38:17, 19, 28</reflink>), properly a "head" or "top."

chapter.d: The several books of the Old and New Testaments were from an early time divided into chapters. The Pentateuch was divided by the ancient Hebrews into 54 _parshioth_ or sections, one of which was read in the synagogue every Sabbath day (<reflink>Acts. 13:15</reflink>). These sections were afterwards divided into 669 _sidrim_ or orders of unequal length. The Prophets were divided in somewhat the same manner into _haphtaroth_ or passages.

charashim.d: craftsmen, a valley named in 1 Chr. 4:14. In Neh. 11:35 the Hebrew word is rendered "valley of craftsmen" (R.V. marg., Geha-rashim). Nothing is known of it.

charger.d: a bowl or deep dish. The silver vessels given by the heads of the tribes for the services of the tabernacle are so named (<reflink>Num. 7:13, etc.</reflink>). The "charger" in which the Baptist's head was presented was a platter or flat wooden trencher (<reflink>Matt. 14:8, 11; Mark 6:25, 28</reflink>). The chargers of gold and silver of Ezra 1:9 were probably basins for receiving the blood of sacrifices.

chariot.d: a vehicle generally used for warlike purposes. Sometimes, though but rarely, it is spoken of as used for peaceful purposes.

charity.d: (1 Cor. 13), the rendering in the Authorized Version of the word which properly denotes love, and is frequently so rendered (always so in the Revised Version). It is spoken of as the greatest of the three Christian graces (<reflink>1 Cor. 12:31-13:13</reflink>).

charmer.d: one who practises serpent-charming (<reflink>Ps. 58:5; Jer. 8:17; Eccl. 10:11</reflink>). It was an early and universal opinion that the most venomous reptiles could be made harmless by certain charms or by sweet sounds. It is well known that there are jugglers in India and in other Eastern lands who practise this art at the present day.

chebar.d: length, a river in the "land of the Chaldeans" (<reflink>Ezek. 1:3</reflink>), on the banks of which were located some of the Jews of the Captivity (<reflink>Ezek. 1:1; 3:15, 23; 10:15, 20, 22</reflink>). It has been supposed to be identical with the river Habor, the Chaboras, or modern Khabour, which falls into the Euphrates at Circesium. To the banks of this river some of the Israelites were removed by the Assyrians (<reflink>2 Kings 17:6</reflink>). An opinion that has much to support it is that the "Chebar" was the royal canal of Nebuchadnezzar, the Nahr Malcha, the greatest in Mesopotamia, which connected the Tigris with the Euphrates, in the excavation of which the Jewish captives were probably employed.

chedorlaomer.d: (= Khudur-Lagamar of the inscriptions), king of Elam. Many centuries before the age of Abraham, Canaan and even the Sinaitic peninsula had been conquered by Babylonian kings, and in the time of Abraham himself Babylonia was ruled by a dynasty which claimed sovereignity over Syria and Palestine. The kings of the dynasty bore names which were not Babylonian, but at once South Arabic and Hebrew. The most famous king of the dynasty was Khammu-rabi, who united Babylonia under one rule, and made Babylon its capital. When he ascended the throne, the country was under the suzerainty of the Elamites, and was divided into two kingdoms, that of Babylon (the Biblical Shinar) and that of Larsa (the Biblical Ellasar). …

cheek.d: Smiting on the cheek was accounted a grievous injury and insult (<reflink>Job 16:10; Lam. 3:30; Micah 5:1</reflink>). The admonition (<reflink>Luke 6:29</reflink>), "Unto him that smiteth thee on the one cheek offer also the other," means simply, "Resist not evil" (<reflink>Matt. 5:39; 1 Pet. 2:19-23</reflink>). Ps. 3:7 = that God had deprived his enemies of the power of doing him injury.

cheese.d: (A.S. cese). This word occurs three times in the Authorized Version as the translation of three different Hebrew words: (1.) 1 Sam. 17:18, "ten cheeses;" i.e., ten sections of curd. (2.) 2 Sam. 17:29, "cheese of kine" = perhaps curdled milk of kine. The Vulgate version reads "fat calves." (3.) Job 10:10, curdled milk is meant by the word.

chemarim.d: black, (<reflink>Zeph. 1:4; rendered "idolatrous priests" in 2 Kings 23:5, and "priests" in Hos. 10:5</reflink>). Some derive this word from the Assyrian Kamaru, meaning "to throw down," and interpret it as describing the idolatrous priests who prostrate themselves before the idols. Others regard it as meaning "those who go about in black," or "ascetics."

chemosh.d: the destroyer, subduer, or fish-god, the god of the Moabites (<reflink>Num. 21:29; Jer. 48:7, 13, 46</reflink>). The worship of this god, "the abomination of Moab," was introduced at Jerusalem by Solomon (<reflink>1 Kings 11:7</reflink>), but was abolished by Josiah (<reflink>2 Kings 23:13</reflink>). On the "Moabite Stone" (q.v.), Mesha (<reflink>2 Kings 3:5</reflink>) ascribes his victories over the king of Israel to this god, "And Chemosh drove him before my sight."

chenaanah.d: merchant. (1.) A Benjamite (<reflink>1 Chr. 7:10</reflink>). (2.) The father of Zedekiah (<reflink>1 Kings 22:11, 24</reflink>).

chenaiah.d: whom Jehovah hath made. "Chief of the Levites," probably a Kohathite (<reflink>1 Chr. 15:22</reflink>), and therefore not the same as mentioned in 26:29.

chephirah.d: village, one of the four cities of the Gibeonitish Hivites with whom Joshua made a league (9:17). It belonged to Benjamin. It has been identified with the modern Kefireh, on the west confines of Benjamin, about 2 miles west of Ajalon and 11 from Jerusalem.

cherethim.d: (<reflink>Ezek. 25:16</reflink>), more frequently Cherethites, the inhabitants of Southern Philistia, the Philistines (<reflink>Zeph. 2:5</reflink>). The Cherethites and the Pelethites were David's life-guards (<reflink>1 Sam. 30:14; 2 Sam. 8:18; 20:7, 23; 23:23</reflink>). This name is by some interpreted as meaning "Cretans," and by others "executioners," who were ready to execute the king's sentence of death (<reflink>Gen. 37:36, marg.; 1 Kings 2:25</reflink>).

cherith.d: a cutting; separation; a gorge, a torrent-bed or winter-stream, a "brook," in whose banks the prophet Elijah hid himself during the early part of the three years' drought (<reflink>1 Kings 17:3, 5</reflink>). It has by some been identified as the Wady el-Kelt behind Jericho, which is formed by the junction of many streams flowing from the mountains west of Jericho. It is dry in summer. Travellers have described it as one of the wildest ravines of this wild region, and peculiarly fitted to afford a secure asylum to the persecuted. But if the prophet's interview with Ahab was in Samaria, and he thence journeyed toward the east, it is probable that he crossed Jordan and found refuge in some of the ravines of Gilead. The "brook" is said to have been "before Jordan," which probably means that it opened toward that river, into which it flowed. This description would apply to the east as well as to the west of Jordan. …

cherub.d: plural cherubim, the name of certain symbolical figures frequently mentioned in Scripture. They are first mentioned in connection with the expulsion of our first parents from Eden (<reflink>Gen. 3:24</reflink>). There is no intimation given of their shape or form. They are next mentioned when Moses was commanded to provide furniture for the tabernacle (<reflink>Ex. 25:17-20; 26:1, 31</reflink>). God promised to commune with Moses "from between the cherubim" (25:22). This expression was afterwards used to denote the Divine abode and presence (<reflink>Num. 7:89; 1 Sam. 4:4; Isa. 37:16; Ps. 80:1; 99:1</reflink>). In Ezekiel's vision (10:1-20) they appear as living creatures supporting the throne of God. From Ezekiel's description of them (1;10; 41:18, 19), they appear to have been compound figures, unlike any real object in nature; artificial images possessing the features and properties of several animals. …

chesalon.d: strength; confidence, a place on the border of Judah, on the side of Mount Jearim (<reflink>Josh. 15:10</reflink>); probably identified with the modern village of Kesla, on the western mountains of Judah.

chesil.d: ungodly, a town in the south of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:30</reflink>); probably the same as Bethul (19:4) and Bethuel (<reflink>1 Chr. 4:30</reflink>); now Khelasa.

chest.d: (Heb. _'aron_, generally rendered "ark"), the coffer into which the contributions for the repair of the temple were put (<reflink>2 Kings 12:9, 10; 2 Chr. 24:8, 10, 11</reflink>). In Gen. 50:26 it is rendered "coffin." In Ezek. 27:24 a different Hebrew word, _genazim_ (plur.), is used. It there means "treasure-chests."

chestnut tree.d: (Heb. _'armon_; i.e., "naked"), mentioned in connection with Jacob's artifice regarding the cattle (<reflink>Gen. 30:37</reflink>). It is one of the trees of which, because of its strength and beauty, the Assyrian empire is likened (<reflink>Ezek. 31:8; R.V., "plane trees"</reflink>). It is probably the Oriental plane tree (Platanus orientalis) that is intended. It is a characteristic of this tree that it annually sheds its outer bark, becomes "naked." The chestnut tree proper is not a native of Palestine.

chesulloth.d: fertile places; the loins, a town of Issachar, on the slopes of some mountain between Jezreel and Shunem (<reflink>Josh. 19:18</reflink>). It has been identified with Chisloth-tabor, 2 1/2 miles to the west of Mount Tabor, and north of Jezreel; now Iksal.

chezib.d: deceitful, a town where Shelah, the son of Judah, was born (<reflink>Gen. 38:5</reflink>). Probably the same as Achzib (q.v.).

chidon.d: dart, the name of the threshing-floor at which the death of Uzzah took place (<reflink>1 Chr. 13:9</reflink>). In the parallel passage in Samuel (<reflink>2 Sam. 6:6</reflink>) it is called "Nachon's threshing-floor." It was a place not far north-west from Jerusalem.

chief of the three.d: a title given to Adino the Eznite, one of David's greatest heroes (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:8</reflink>); also called Jashobeam (<reflink>1 Chr. 11:11</reflink>).

chiefs of asia.d: "Asiarchs," the title given to certain wealthy persons annually appointed to preside over the religious festivals and games in the various cities of proconsular Asia (<reflink>Acts 19:31</reflink>). Some of these officials appear to have been Paul's friends.

child.d: This word has considerable latitude of meaning in Scripture. Thus Joseph is called a child at the time when he was probably about sixteen years of age (<reflink>Gen. 37:3</reflink>); and Benjamin is so called when he was above thirty years (44:20). Solomon called himself a little child when he came to the kingdom (<reflink>1 Kings 3:7</reflink>).

chileab.d: protected by the father, David's second son by Abigail (<reflink>2 Sam. 3:3</reflink>); called also Daniel (<reflink>1 Chr. 3:1</reflink>). He seems to have died when young.

chilion.d: the pining one, the younger son of Elimelech and Naomi, and husband of Orpah, Ruth's sister (<reflink>Ruth 1:2; 4:9</reflink>).

chilmad.d: a place or country unknown which, along with Sheba and Asshur, traded with Tyre (<reflink>Ezek. 27:23</reflink>).

chimham.d: pining, probably the youngest son of Barzillai the Gileadite (<reflink>2 Sam. 19:37-40</reflink>). The "habitation of Chimham" (<reflink>Jer. 41:17</reflink>) was probably an inn or khan, which is the proper meaning of the Hebrew _geruth_, rendered "habitation", established in later times in his possession at Bethlehem, which David gave to him as a reward for his loyalty in accompanying him to Jerusalem after the defeat of Absalom (<reflink>1 Kings 2:7</reflink>). It has been supposed that, considering the stationary character of Eastern institutions, it was in the stable of this inn or caravanserai that our Saviour was born (<reflink>Luke 2:7</reflink>).

chinnereth.d: lyre, the singular form of the word (<reflink>Deut. 3:17; Josh. 19:35</reflink>), which is also used in the plural form, Chinneroth, the name of a fenced city which stood near the shore of the lake of Galilee, a little to the south of Tiberias. The town seems to have given its name to a district, as appears from 1 Kings 15:20, where the plural form of the word is used.

chios.d: mentioned in Acts 20:15, an island in the Aegean Sea, about 5 miles distant from the mainland, having a roadstead, in the shelter of which Paul and his companions anchored for a night when on his third missionary return journey. It is now called Scio.

chisleu.d: the name adopted from the Babylonians by the Jews after the Captivity for the third civil, or ninth ecclesiastical, month (<reflink>Neh. 1:1; Zech. 7:1</reflink>). It corresponds nearly with the moon in November.

chittim.d: or Kittim, a plural form (<reflink>Gen. 10:4</reflink>), the name of a branch of the descendants of Javan, the "son" of Japheth. Balaam foretold (<reflink>Num. 24:24</reflink>) "that ships shall come from the coast of Chittim, and afflict Eber." Daniel prophesied (11:30) that the ships of Chittim would come against the king of the north. It probably denotes Cyprus, whose ancient capital was called Kition by the Greeks.

chiun.d: occurs only in Amos 5:26 (R.V. marg., "shrine"). The LXX. translated the word by Rhephan, which became corrupted into Remphan, as used by Stephen (<reflink>Acts 7:43; but R.V., "Rephan"</reflink>). Probably the planet Saturn is intended by the name. Astrologers represented this planet as baleful in its influences, and hence the Phoenicians offered to it human sacrifices, especially children.

chloe.d: verdure, a female Christian (<reflink>1 Cor. 1:11</reflink>), some of whose household had informed Paul of the divided state of the Corinthian church. Nothing is known of her.

chor-ashan.d: smoking furnace, one of the places where "David himself and his men were wont to haunt" (<reflink>1 Sam. 30:30, 31</reflink>). It is probably identical with Ashan (<reflink>Josh. 15:42; 19:7</reflink>), a Simeonite city in the Negeb, i.e., the south, belonging to Judah. The word ought, according to another reading, to be "Bor-ashan."

chorazin.d: named along with Bethsaida and Capernaum as one of the cities in which our Lord's "mighty works" were done, and which was doomed to woe because of signal privileges neglected (<reflink>Matt. 11:21; Luke 10:13</reflink>). It has been identified by general consent with the modern Kerazeh, about 2 1/2 miles up the Wady Kerazeh from Capernaum; i.e., Tell Hum.

chosen.d: spoken of warriors (<reflink>Ex. 15:4; Judg. 20:16</reflink>), of the Hebrew nation (<reflink>Ps. 105:43; Deut. 7:7</reflink>), of Jerusalem as the seat of the temple (<reflink>1 Kings 11:13</reflink>). Christ is the "chosen" of God (<reflink>Isa. 42:1</reflink>); and the apostles are "chosen" for their work (<reflink>Acts 10:41</reflink>). It is said with regard to those who do not profit by their opportunities that "many are called, but few are chosen" (<reflink>Matt. 20:16</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See ELECTION.</see>)

chozeba.d: (<reflink>1 Chr. 4:22</reflink>), the same as Chezib and Achzib, a place in the lowlands of Judah (<reflink>Gen. 38:5; Josh. 15:44</reflink>).

christ.d: anointed, the Greek translation of the Hebrew word rendered "Messiah" (q.v.), the official title of our Lord, occurring five hundred and fourteen times in the New Testament. It denotes that he was anointed or consecrated to his great redemptive work as Prophet, Priest, and King of his people. He is Jesus the Christ (<reflink>Acts 17:3; 18:5; Matt. 22:42</reflink>), the Anointed One. He is thus spoken of by Isaiah (61:1), and by Daniel (9:24-26), who styles him "Messiah the Prince."

christian.d: the name given by the Greeks or Romans, probably in reproach, to the followers of Jesus. It was first used at Antioch. The names by which the disciples were known among themselves were "brethren," "the faithful," "elect," "saints," "believers." But as distinguishing them from the multitude without, the name "Christian" came into use, and was universally accepted. This name occurs but three times in the New Testament (<reflink>Acts 11:26; 26:28; 1 Pet. 4:16</reflink>).

christs, false.d: Our Lord warned his disciples that they would arise (<reflink>Matt. 24:24</reflink>). It is said that no fewer than twenty-four persons have at different times appeared (the last in 1682) pretending to be the Messiah of the prophets.

chronicles.d: the words of the days, (<reflink>1 Kings 14:19; 1 Chr. 27:24</reflink>), the daily or yearly records of the transactions of the kingdom; events recorded in the order of time.

chronicles of king david.d: (<reflink>1 Chr. 27:24</reflink>) were statistical state records; one of the public sources from which the compiler of the Books of Chronicles derived information on various public matters.

chronicles, books of.d: The two books were originally one. They bore the title in the Massoretic Hebrew _Dibre hayyamim_, i.e., "Acts of the Days." This title was rendered by Jerome in his Latin version "Chronicon," and hence "Chronicles." In the Septuagint version the book is divided into two, and bears the title Paraleipomena, i.e., "things omitted," or "supplements", because containing many things omitted in the Books of Kings.

chronology.d: is the arrangement of facts and events in the order of time. The writers of the Bible themselves do not adopt any standard era according to which they date events. Sometimes the years are reckoned, e.g., from the time of the Exodus (<reflink>Num. 1:1; 33:38; 1 Kings 6:1</reflink>), and sometimes from the accession of kings (<reflink>1 Kings 15:1, 9, 25, 33, etc.</reflink>), and sometimes again from the return from Exile (<reflink>Ezra 3:8</reflink>).

chrysoprasus.d: golden leek, a precious stone of the colour of leek's juice, a greenish-golden colour (<reflink>Rev. 21:20</reflink>).

chub.d: the name of a people in alliance with Egypt in the time of Nebuchadnezzar. The word is found only in Ezek. 30:5. They were probably a people of Northern Africa, or of the lands near Egypt in the south.

chun.d: one of the cities of Hadarezer, king of Syria. David procured brass (i.e., bronze or copper) from it for the temple (<reflink>1 Chr. 18:8</reflink>). It is called Berothai in 2 Sam. 8:8; probably the same as Berothah in Ezek. 47:16.

church.d: Derived probably from the Greek kuriakon (i.e., "the Lord's house"), which was used by ancient authors for the place of worship.

churl.d: in Isa. 32:5 (R.V. marg., "crafty"), means a deceiver. In 1 Sam. 25:3, the word churlish denotes a man that is coarse and ill-natured, or, as the word literally means, "hard." The same Greek word as used by the LXX. here is found in Matt. 25:24, and there is rendered "hard."

chushan-rishathaim.d: Cush of double wickedness, or governor of two presidencies, the king of Mesopotamia who oppressed Israel in the generation immediately following Joshua (<reflink>Judg. 3:8</reflink>). We learn from the Tell-el-Amarna tablets that Palestine had been invaded by the forces of Aram-naharaim (A.V., "Mesopotamia") more than once, long before the Exodus, and that at the time they were written the king of Aram-naharaim was still intriguing in Canaan. It is mentioned among the countries which took part in the attack upon Egypt in the reign of Rameses III. (of the Twentieth Dynasty), but as its king is not one of the princes stated to have been conquered by the Pharaoh, it would seem that he did not actually enter Egypt. As the reign of Rameses III. corresponds with the Israelitish occupation of Canaan, it is probable that the Egyptian monuments refer to the oppression of the Israelites by Chushan-rishathaim. …

camon.d: full of stalks, a place (<reflink>Judg. 10:5</reflink>) where Jair was buried. It has usually been supposed to have been a city of Gilead, on the east of Jordan. It is probably, however, the modern Tell-el-Kaimun, on the southern slopes of Carmel, the Jokneam of Carmel (<reflink>Josh. 12:22; 1 Kings 4:12</reflink>), since it is not at all unlikely that after he became judge, Jair might find it more convenient to live on the west side of Jordan; and that he was buried where he had lived.

camp.d: During their journeys across the wilderness, the twelve tribes formed encampments at the different places where they halted (<reflink>Ex. 16:13; Num. 2:3</reflink>). The diagram here given shows the position of the different tribes and the form of the encampment during the wanderings, according to Num. 1:53; 2:2-31; 3:29, 35, 38; 10:13-28.

camphire.d: (Heb. copher), mentioned in Cant. 1:14 (R.V., "henna-flowers"); 4:13 (R.V., "henna"), is the al-henna of the Arabs, a native of Egypt, producing clusters of small white and yellow odoriferous flowers, whence is made the Oleum Cyprineum. From its leaves is made the peculiar auburn dye with which Eastern women stain their nails and the palms of their hands. It is found only at Engedi, on the shore of the Dead Sea. It is known to botanists by the name Lawsonia alba or inermis, a kind of privet, which grows 6 or 8 feet high. The margin of the Authorized Version of the passages above referred to has "or cypress," not with reference to the conifer so called, but to the circumstance that one of the most highly appreciated species of this plant grew in the island of Cyprus.

cana.d: reedy, a town of Galilee, near Capernaum. Here our Lord wrought his first miracle, the turning of water into wine (<reflink>John 2:1-11; 4:46</reflink>). It is also mentioned as the birth-place of Nathanael (21:2). It is not mentioned in the Old Testament. It has been identified with the modern Kana el-Jelil, also called Khurbet Kana, a place 8 or 9 miles north of Nazareth. Others have identified it with Kefr Kenna, which lies on the direct road to the Sea of Galilee, about 5 miles north-east of Nazareth, and 12 in a direct course from Tiberias. It is called "Cana of Galilee," to distinguish it from Cana of Asher (<reflink>Josh. 19:28</reflink>).

canaan.d: (1.) The fourth son of Ham (<reflink>Gen. 10:6</reflink>). His descendants were under a curse in consequence of the transgression of his father (9:22-27). His eldest son, Zidon, was the father of the Sidonians and Phoenicians. He had eleven sons, who were the founders of as many tribes (10:15-18).

canaan, the language of.d: mentioned in Isa. 19:18, denotes the language spoken by the Jews resident in Palestine. The language of the Canaanites and of the Hebrews was substantially the same. This is seen from the fragments of the Phoenician language which still survive, which show the closest analogy to the Hebrew. Yet the subject of the language of the "Canaanites" is very obscure. The cuneiform writing of Babylon, as well as the Babylonian language, was taught in the Canaanitish schools, and the clay tablets of Babylonian literature were stored in the Canaanitish libraries. Even the Babylonian divinities were borrowed by the Canaanites.

canaanite.d: a name given to the apostle Simon (<reflink>Matt. 10:4; Mark 3:18</reflink>). The word here does not, however, mean a descendant of Canaan, but is a translation, or rather almost a transliteration, of the Syriac word Kanenyeh (R.V. rendered "Cananaen"), which designates the Jewish sect of the Zealots. Hence he is called elsewhere (<reflink>Luke 6:15</reflink>) "Simon Zelotes;" i.e., Simon of the sect of the Zealots. (<see target="x-self">See SIMON.</see>)

canaanites.d: the descendants of Canaan, the son of Ham. Migrating from their original home, they seem to have reached the Persian Gulf, and to have there sojourned for some time. They thence "spread to the west, across the mountain chain of Lebanon to the very edge of the Mediterranean Sea, occupying all the land which later became Palestine, also to the north-west as far as the mountain chain of Taurus. This group was very numerous, and broken up into a great many peoples, as we can judge from the list of nations (Gen. 10), the 'sons of Canaan.'" Six different tribes are mentioned in Ex. 3:8, 17; 23:23; 33:2; 34:11. In Ex. 13:5 the "Perizzites" are omitted. The "Girgashites" are mentioned in addition to the foregoing in Deut. 7:1; Josh. 3:10.

candace.d: the queen of the Ethiopians whose "eunuch" or chamberlain was converted to Christianity by the instrumentality of Philip the evangelist (<reflink>Acts 8:27</reflink>). The country which she ruled was called by the Greeks Meroe, in Upper Nubia. It was long the centre of commercial intercourse between Africa and the south of Asia, and hence became famous for its wealth (<reflink>Isa. 45:14</reflink>).

candle.d: Heb. ner, Job 18:6; 29:3; Ps. 18:28; Prov. 24:20, in all which places the Revised Version and margin of Authorized Version have "lamp," by which the word is elsewhere frequently rendered. The Hebrew word denotes properly any kind of candle or lamp or torch. It is used as a figure of conscience (<reflink>Prov. 20:27</reflink>), of a Christian example (<reflink>Matt. 5:14, 15</reflink>), and of prosperity (<reflink>Job 21:17; Prov. 13:9</reflink>).

candlestick.d: the lamp-stand, "candelabrum," which Moses was commanded to make for the tabernacle, according to the pattern shown him. Its form is described in Ex. 25:31-40; 37:17-24, and may be seen represented on the Arch of Titus at Rome. It was among the spoils taken by the Romans from the temple of Jerusalem (A.D. 70). It was made of fine gold, and with the utensils belonging to it was a talent in weight.

cane.d: a tall sedgy plant with a hollow stem, growing in moist places. In Isa. 43:24; Jer. 6:20, the Hebrew word _kaneh_ is thus rendered, giving its name to the plant. It is rendered "reed" in 1 Kings 14:15; Job 40:21; Isa. 19:6; 35:7. In Ps. 68:30 the expression "company of spearmen" is in the margin and the Revised Version "beasts of the reeds," referring probably to the crocodile or the hippopotamus as a symbol of Egypt. In 2 Kings 18:21; Isa. 36:6; Ezek. 29:6, 7, the reference is to the weak, fragile nature of the reed. (<see target="x-self">See CALAMUS.</see>)

canker.d: a gangrene or mortification which gradually spreads over the whole body (<reflink>2 Tim. 2:17</reflink>). In James 5:3 "cankered" means "rusted" (R.V.) or tarnished.

cankerworm.d: (Heb. yelek), "the licking locust," which licks up the grass of the field; probably the locust at a certain stage of its growth, just as it emerges from the caterpillar state (<reflink>Joel 1:4; 2:25</reflink>). The word is rendered "caterpillar" in Ps. 105:34; Jer. 51:14, 17 (but R.V. "canker-worm"). "It spoileth and fleeth away" (<reflink>Nah. 3:16</reflink>), or as some read the passage, "The cankerworm putteth off [i.e., the envelope of its wings], and fleeth away."

canneh.d: Mentioned only in Ezek. 27:23. (<see target="x-self">See CALNEH.</see>)

canon.d: This word is derived from a Hebrew and Greek word denoting a reed or cane. Hence it means something straight, or something to keep straight; and hence also a rule, or something ruled or measured. It came to be applied to the Scriptures, to denote that they contained the authoritative rule of faith and practice, the standard of doctrine and duty. A book is said to be of canonical authority when it has a right to take a place with the other books which contain a revelation of the Divine will. Such a right does not arise from any ecclesiastical authority, but from the evidence of the inspired authorship of the book. The canonical (i.e., the inspired) books of the Old and New Testaments, are a complete rule, and the only rule, of faith and practice. They contain the whole supernatural revelation of God to men. The New Testament Canon was formed gradually under divine guidance. …

capernaum.d: Nahum's town, a Galilean city frequently mentioned in the history of our Lord. It is not mentioned in the Old Testament. After our Lord's expulsion from Nazareth (<reflink>Matt. 4:13-16; Luke 4:16-31</reflink>), Capernaum became his "own city." It was the scene of many acts and incidents of his life (<reflink>Matt. 8:5, 14, 15; 9:2-6, 10-17; 15:1-20; Mark 1:32-34, etc.</reflink>). The impenitence and unbelief of its inhabitants after the many evidences our Lord gave among them of the truth of his mission, brought down upon them a heavy denunciation of judgement (<reflink>Matt. 11:23</reflink>).

caphtor.d: a chaplet, the original seat of the Philistines (<reflink>Deut. 2:23; Jer. 47:4; Amos 9:7</reflink>). The name is found written in hieroglyphics in the temple of Kom Ombos in Upper Egypt. But the exact situation of Caphtor is unknown, though it is supposed to be Crete, since the Philistines seem to be meant by the "Cherethites" in 1 Sam. 30:14 (<see target="x-self">see also 2 Sam. 8:18</see>). It may, however, have been a part of Egypt, the Caphtur in the north Delta, since the Caphtorim were of the same race as the Mizraite people (<reflink>Gen. 10:14; 1 Chr. 1:12</reflink>).

cappadocia.d: the easternmost and the largest province of Asia Minor. Christianity very early penetrated into this country (<reflink>1 Pet. 1:1</reflink>). On the day of Pentecost there were Cappadocians at Jerusalem (<reflink>Acts 2:9</reflink>).

captain.d: (1.) Heb. sar (<reflink>1 Sam. 22:2; 2 Sam. 23:19</reflink>). Rendered "chief," Gen. 40:2; 41:9; rendered also "prince," Dan. 1:7; "ruler," Judg. 9:30; "governor,' 1 Kings 22:26. This same Hebrew word denotes a military captain (<reflink>Ex. 18:21; 2 Kings 1:9; Deut. 1:15; 1 Sam. 18:13, etc.</reflink>), the "captain of the body-guard" (<reflink>Gen. 37:36; 39:1; 41:10; Jer. 40:1</reflink>), or, as the word may be rendered, "chief of the executioners" (marg.). The officers of the king's body-guard frequently acted as executioners. Nebuzar-adan (<reflink>Jer. 39:13</reflink>) and Arioch (<reflink>Dan. 2:14</reflink>) held this office in Babylon.

captive.d: one taken in war. Captives were often treated with great cruelty and indignity (<reflink>1 Kings 20:32; Josh. 10:24; Judg. 1:7; 2 Sam. 4:12; Judg. 8:7; 2 Sam. 12:31; 1 Chr. 20:3</reflink>). When a city was taken by assault, all the men were slain, and the women and children carried away captive and sold as slaves (Isa. 20; 47:3; 2 Chr. 28:9-15; Ps. 44:12; Joel 3:3), and exposed to the most cruel treatment (<reflink>Nah. 3:10; Zech. 14:2; Esther 3:13; 2 Kings 8:12; Isa. 13:16, 18</reflink>). Captives were sometimes carried away into foreign countries, as was the case with the Jews (<reflink>Jer. 20:5; 39:9, 10; 40:7</reflink>).

captivity.d: (1.) Of Israel. The kingdom of the ten tribes was successively invaded by several Assyrian kings. Pul (q.v.) imposed a tribute on Menahem of a thousand talents of silver (<reflink>2 Kings 15:19, 20; 1 Chr. 5:26</reflink>) (B.C. 762), and Tiglath-pileser, in the days of Pekah (B.C. 738), carried away the trans-Jordanic tribes and the inhabitants of Galilee into Assyria (<reflink>2 Kings 15:29; Isa. 9:1</reflink>). Subsequently Shalmaneser invaded Israel and laid siege to Samaria, the capital of the kingdom. During the siege he died, and was succeeded by Sargon, who took the city, and transported the great mass of the people into Assyria (B.C. 721), placing them in Halah and in Habor, and in the cities of the Medes (<reflink>2 Kings 17:3, 5</reflink>). Samaria was never again inhabited by the Israelites. The families thus removed were carried to distant cities, many of them not far from the Caspian Sea, and their place was supplied by colonists from Babylon and Cuthah, etc. …

carbuncle.d: (<reflink>Ex. 28:17; 39:10; Ezek. 28:13</reflink>). Heb. barkath; LXX. smaragdos; Vulgate, smaragdus; Revised Version, marg., "emerald." The Hebrew word is from a root meaning "to glitter," "lighten," "flash." When held up to the sun, this gem shines like a burning coal, a dark-red glowing coal, and hence is called "carbunculus", i.e., a little coal. It was one of the jewels in the first row of the high priest's breastplate. It has been conjectured by some that the garnet is meant. In Isa. 54:12 the Hebrew word is _'ekdah_, used in the prophetic description of the glory and beauty of the mansions above. Next to the diamond it is the hardest and most costly of all precious stones.

carcase.d: contact with a, made an Israelite ceremonially unclean, and made whatever he touched also unclean, according to the Mosaic law (<reflink>Hag. 2:13; comp. Num. 19:16, 22; Lev. 11:39</reflink>).

carchemish.d: fortress of Chemosh, a city on the west bank of the Euphrates (<reflink>Jer. 46:2; 2 Chr. 35:20</reflink>), not, as was once supposed, the Circesium at the confluence of the Chebar and the Euphrates, but a city considerably higher up the river, and commanding the ordinary passage of the Euphrates; probably identical with Hierapolis. It was the capital of the kingdom of the northern Hittites. The Babylonian army, under Nebuchadnezzar, the son of Nabopolassar, here met and conquered the army of Pharaoh-necho, king of Egypt (B.C. 607). It is mentioned in monuments in B.C. 1600 and down to B.C. 717.

carmel.d: a park; generally with the article, "the park." (1.) A prominent headland of Central Palestine, consisting of several connected hills extending from the plain of Esdraelon to the sea, a distance of some 12 miles or more. At the east end, in its highest part, it is 1,728 feet high, and at the west end it forms a promontory to the bay of Acre about 600 feet above the sea. It lay within the tribe of Asher. It was here, at the east end of the ridge, at a place called el-Mukhrakah (i.e., the place of burning), that Elijah brought back the people to their allegiance to God, and slew the prophets of Baal (1 Kings 18). Here were consumed the "fifties" of the royal guard; and here also Elisha received the visit of the bereaved mother whose son was restored by him to life (<reflink>2 Kings 4:25-37</reflink>). "No mountain in or around Palestine retains its ancient beauty so much as Carmel. …

carmi.d: vine-dresser. (1.) The last named of the four sons of Reuben (<reflink>Gen. 46:9</reflink>).

carnal.d: Unconverted men are so called (<reflink>1 Cor. 3:3</reflink>). They are represented as of a "carnal mind, which is enmity against God" (<reflink>Rom. 8:6, 7</reflink>). Enjoyments that minister to the wants and desires of man's animal nature are so called (<reflink>Rom. 15:27; 1 Cor. 9:11</reflink>). The ceremonial of the Mosaic law is spoken of as "carnal," because it related to things outward, the bodies of men and of animals, and the purification of the flesh (<reflink>Heb. 7:16; 9:10</reflink>). The weapons of Christian warfare are "not carnal", that is, they are not of man's device, nor are wielded by human power (<reflink>2 Cor. 10:4</reflink>).

carpenter.d: an artificer in stone, iron, and copper, as well as in wood (<reflink>2 Sam. 5:11; 1 Chr. 14:1; Mark 6:3</reflink>). The tools used by carpenters are mentioned in 1 Sam. 13:19, 20; Judg. 4:21; Isa. 10:15; 44:13. It was said of our Lord, "Is not this the carpenter's son?" (<reflink>Matt. 13:55</reflink>); also, "Is not this the carpenter?" (<reflink>Mark 6:3</reflink>). Every Jew, even the rabbis, learned some handicraft: Paul was a tentmaker. "In the cities the carpenters would be Greeks, and skilled workmen; the carpenter of a provincial village could only have held a very humble position, and secured a very moderate competence."

carriage.d: In the Authorized Version this word is found as the rendering of many different words. In Judg. 18:21 it means valuables, wealth, or booty. In Isa. 46:1 (R.V., "the things that ye carried about") the word means a load for a beast of burden. In 1 Sam. 17:22 and Isa. 10:28 it is the rendering of a word ("stuff" in 1 Sam. 10:22) meaning implements, equipments, baggage. The phrase in Acts 21:15, "We took up our carriages," means properly, "We packed up our baggage," as in the Revised Version.

cart.d: a vehicle moving on wheels, and usually drawn by oxen (<reflink>2 Sam. 6:3</reflink>). The Hebrew word thus rendered, _'agalah_ (<reflink>1 Sam. 6:7, 8</reflink>), is also rendered "wagon" (<reflink>Gen. 45:19</reflink>). It is used also to denote a war-chariot (<reflink>Ps. 46:9</reflink>). Carts were used for the removal of the ark and its sacred utensils (<reflink>Num. 7:3, 6</reflink>). After retaining the ark amongst them for seven months, the Philistines sent it back to the Israelites. On this occasion they set it in a new cart, probably a rude construction, with solid wooden wheels like that still used in Western Asia, which was drawn by two milch cows, which conveyed it straight to Beth-shemesh.

carve.d: The arts of engraving and carving were much practised among the Jews. They were practised in connection with the construction of the tabernacle and the temple (<reflink>Ex. 31:2, 5; 35:33; 1 Kings 6:18, 35; Ps. 74:6</reflink>), as well as in the ornamentation of the priestly dresses (<reflink>Ex. 28:9-36; Zech. 3:9; 2 Chr. 2:7, 14</reflink>). Isaiah (44:13-17) gives a minute description of the process of carving idols of wood.

casement.d: a barrier of open-work placed before windows (<reflink>Prov. 7:6</reflink>). In Judg. 5:28 the Hebrew word is rendered "lattice," in the LXX. "network," an opening through which cool air is admitted.

casiphia.d: silver, a place between Babylon and Jerusalem, where Iddo resided (<reflink>Ezra 8:17</reflink>); otherwise unknown.

casluhim.d: fortified, a people descended from Mizraim (<reflink>Gen. 10:14; 1 Chr. 1:12</reflink>). Their original seat was probably somewhere in Lower Egypt, along the sea-coast to the south border of Palestine.

cassia.d: (1.) Hebrew _kiddah'_, i.e., "split." One of the principal spices of the holy anointing oil (<reflink>Ex. 30:24</reflink>), and an article of commerce (<reflink>Ezek. 27:19</reflink>). It is the inner bark of a tree resembling the cinnamon (q.v.), the Cinnamomum cassia of botanists, and was probably imported from India.

castaway.d: Gr. adokimos, (<reflink>1 Cor. 9:27</reflink>), one regarded as unworthy (R.V., "rejected"); elsewhere rendered "reprobate" (<reflink>2 Tim. 3:8, etc.</reflink>); "rejected" (<reflink>Heb. 6:8, etc.</reflink>).

castle.d: a military fortress (<reflink>1 Chr. 11:7</reflink>), also probably a kind of tower used by the priests for making known anything discovered at a distance (<reflink>1 Chr. 6:54</reflink>). Castles are also mentioned (<reflink>Gen. 25:16</reflink>) as a kind of watch-tower, from which shepherds kept watch over their flocks by night. The "castle" into which the chief captain commanded Paul to be brought was the quarters of the Roman soldiers in the fortress of Antonia (so called by Herod after his patron Mark Antony), which was close to the north-west corner of the temple (<reflink>Acts 21:34</reflink>), which it commanded.

castor and pollux.d: the "Dioscuri", two heroes of Greek and Roman mythology. Their figures were probably painted or sculptured on the prow of the ship which Luke refers to (<reflink>Acts 28:11</reflink>). They were regarded as the tutelary divinities of sailors. They appeared in the heavens as the constellation Gemini.

caterpillar.d: the consumer. Used in the Old Testament (<reflink>1 Kings 8:37; 2 Chr. 6:28; Ps. 78:46; Isa. 33:4</reflink>) as the translation of a word (hasil) the root of which means "to devour" or "consume," and which is used also with reference to the locust in Deut. 28:38. It may have been a species of locust, or the name of one of the transformations through which the locust passes, locust-grub. It is also found (<reflink>Ps. 105:34; Jer. 51:14, 27; R.V., "cankerworm"</reflink>) as the rendering of a different Hebrew word, _yelek_, a word elsewhere rendered "cankerworm" (q.v.), Joel 1:4; 2:25. (<see target="x-self">See LOCUST.</see>)

catholic epistles.d: the epistles of James, Peter, John, and Jude; so called because they are addressed to Christians in general, and not to any church or person in particular.

cattle.d: abounded in the Holy Land. To the rearing and management of them the inhabitants chiefly devoted themselves (<reflink>Deut. 8:13; 12:21; 1 Sam. 11:5; 12:3; Ps. 144:14; Jer. 3:24</reflink>). They may be classified as,

caul.d: (Heb. yothe'reth; i.e., "something redundant"), the membrane which covers the upper part of the liver (<reflink>Ex. 29:13, 22; Lev. 3:4, 10, 15; 4:9; 7:4; marg., "midriff"</reflink>). In Hos. 13:8 (Heb. seghor; i.e., "an enclosure") the pericardium, or parts about the heart, is meant.

cauls.d: In Isa. 3:18 this word (Heb. shebisim), in the marg. "networks," denotes network caps to contain the hair, worn by females. Others explain it as meaning "wreaths worn round the forehead, reaching from one ear to the other."

causeway.d: a raised way, an ascent by steps, or a raised slope between Zion and the temple (<reflink>1 Chr. 26:16, 18</reflink>). In 2 Chr. 9:11 the same word is translated "terrace."

cave.d: There are numerous natural caves among the limestone rocks of Syria, many of which have been artificially enlarged for various purposes.

cedar.d: (Heb. e'rez, Gr. kedros, Lat. cedrus), a tree very frequently mentioned in Scripture. It was stately (<reflink>Ezek. 31:3-5</reflink>), long-branched (<reflink>Ps. 80:10; 92:12; Ezek. 31:6-9</reflink>), odoriferous (<reflink>Cant. 4:11; Hos. 14:6</reflink>), durable, and therefore much used for boards, pillars, and ceilings (<reflink>1 Kings 6:9, 10; 7:2; Jer. 22:14</reflink>), for masts (<reflink>Ezek. 27:5</reflink>), and for carved images (<reflink>Isa. 44:14</reflink>).

cedron.d: the black torrent, the brook flowing through the ravine below the eastern wall of Jerusalem (<reflink>John 18:1</reflink>). (See KIDRON

ceiling.d: the covering (<reflink>1 Kings 7:3,7</reflink>) of the inside roof and walls of a house with planks of wood (<reflink>2 Chr. 3:5; Jer. 22:14</reflink>). Ceilings were sometimes adorned with various ornaments in stucco, gold, silver, gems, and ivory. The ceilings of the temple and of Solomon's palace are described 1 Kings 6:9, 15; 7:3; 2 Chr. 3:5,9.

cellar.d: a subterranean vault (<reflink>1 Chr. 27:28</reflink>), a storehouse. The word is also used to denote the treasury of the temple (<reflink>1 Kings 7:51</reflink>) and of the king (14:26). The Hebrew word is rendered "garner" in Joel 1:17, and "armoury" in Jer. 50:25.

cenchrea.d: millet, the eastern harbour of Corinth, from which it was distant about 9 miles east, and the outlet for its trade with the Asiatic shores of the Mediterranean. When Paul returned from his second missionary journey to Syria, he sailed from this port (<reflink>Acts 18:18</reflink>). In Rom. 16:1 he speaks as if there were at the time of his writing that epistle an organized church there. The western harbour of Corinth was Lechaeum, about a mile and a half from the city. It was the channel of its trade with Italy and the west.

censer.d: the vessel in which incense was presented on "the golden altar" before the Lord in the temple (<reflink>Ex. 30:1-9</reflink>). The priest filled the censer with live coal from the sacred fire on the altar of burnt-offering, and having carried it into the sanctuary, there threw upon the burning coals the sweet incense (<reflink>Lev. 16:12, 13</reflink>), which sent up a cloud of smoke, filling the apartment with fragrance. The censers in daily use were of brass (<reflink>Num. 16:39</reflink>), and were designated by a different Hebrew name, _miktereth_ (<reflink>2 Chr. 26:19; Ezek. 8:11</reflink>): while those used on the day of Atonement were of gold, and were denoted by a word (mahtah) meaning "something to take fire with;" LXX. pureion = a fire-pan. Solomon prepared for the temple censers of pure gold (<reflink>1 Kings 7:50; 2 Chr. 4:22</reflink>). The angel in the Apocalypse is represented with a golden censer (<reflink>Rev. 8:3, 5</reflink>). …

census.d: There are five instances of a census of the Jewish people having been taken. (1.) In the fourth month after the Exodus, when the people were encamped at Sinai. The number of men from twenty years old and upward was then 603,550 (<reflink>Ex. 38:26</reflink>). (2.) Another census was made just before the entrance into Canaan, when the number was found to be 601,730, showing thus a small decrease (<reflink>Num. 26:51</reflink>). (3.) The next census was in the time of David, when the number, exclusive of the tribes of Levi and Benjamin, was found to be 1,300,000 (<reflink>2 Sam. 24:9; 1 Chr. 21:5</reflink>). (4.) Solomon made a census of the foreigners in the land, and found 153,600 able-bodied workmen (<reflink>2 Chr. 2:17, 18</reflink>). (5.) After the return from Exile the whole congregation of Israel was numbered, and found to amount to 42,360 (<reflink>Ezra 2:64</reflink>). A census was made by the Roman government in the time of our Lord (<reflink>Luke 2:1</reflink>). …

centurion.d: a Roman officer in command of a hundred men (<reflink>Mark 15:39, 44, 45</reflink>). Cornelius, the first Gentile convert, was a centurion (<reflink>Acts 10:1, 22</reflink>). Other centurions are mentioned in Matt. 8:5, 8, 13; Luke 7:2, 6; Acts 21:32; 22:25, 26; 23:17, 23; 24:23; 27:1, 6, 11, 31, 43; 28:16. A centurion watched the crucifixion of our Lord (<reflink>Matt. 27:54; Luke 23:47</reflink>), and when he saw the wonders attending it, exclaimed, "Truly this man was the Son of God." "The centurions mentioned in the New Testament are uniformly spoken of in terms of praise, whether in the Gospels or in the Acts. It is interesting to compare this with the statement of Polybius (vi. 24), that the centurions were chosen by merit, and so were men remarkable not so much for their daring courage as for their deliberation, constancy, and strength of mind.", Dr. Maclear's N. T. Hist.

cephas.d: a Syriac surname given by Christ to Simon (<reflink>John 1:42</reflink>), meaning "rock." The Greeks translated it by Petros, and the Latins by Petrus.

chaff.d: the refuse of winnowed corn. It was usually burned (<reflink>Ex. 15:7; Isa. 5:24; Matt. 3:12</reflink>). This word sometimes, however, means dried grass or hay (<reflink>Isa. 5:24; 33:11</reflink>). Chaff is used as a figure of abortive wickedness (<reflink>Ps. 1:4; Matt. 3:12</reflink>). False doctrines are also called chaff (<reflink>Jer. 23:28</reflink>), or more correctly rendered "chopped straw." The destruction of the wicked, and their powerlessness, are likened to the carrying away of chaff by the wind (<reflink>Isa. 17:13; Hos. 13:3; Zeph. 2:2</reflink>).

chain.d: (1.) A part of the insignia of office. A chain of gold was placed about Joseph's neck (<reflink>Gen. 41:42</reflink>); and one was promised to Daniel (5:7). It is used as a symbol of sovereignty (<reflink>Ezek. 16:11</reflink>). The breast-plate of the high-priest was fastened to the ephod by golden chains (<reflink>Ex. 39:17, 21</reflink>).

chalcedony.d: Mentioned only in Rev. 21:19, as one of the precious stones in the foundation of the New Jerusalem. The name of this stone is derived from Chalcedon, where it is said to have been first discovered. In modern mineralogy this is the name of an agate-like quartz of a bluish colour. Pliny so names the Indian ruby. The mineral intended in Revelation is probably the Hebrew _nophekh_, translated "emerald" (<reflink>Ex. 28:18; 39:11; Ezek. 27:16; 28:13</reflink>). It is rendered "anthrax" in the LXX., and "carbunculus" in the Vulgate. (<see target="x-self">See CARBUNCLE.</see>)

chaldea.d: The southern portion of Babylonia, Lower Mesopotamia, lying chiefly on the right bank of the Euphrates, but commonly used of the whole of the Mesopotamian plain. The Hebrew name is Kasdim, which is usually rendered "Chaldeans" (<reflink>Jer. 50:10; 51:24,35</reflink>).

chaldee language.d: employed by the sacred writers in certain portions of the Old Testament, viz., Dan. 2:4-7, 28; Ezra 4:8-6:18; 7:12-26; Gen. 31:46; Jer. 10:11. It is the Aramaic dialect, as it is sometimes called, as distinguished from the Hebrew dialect. It was the language of commerce and of social intercourse in Western Asia, and after the Exile gradually came to be the popular language of Palestine. It is called "Syrian" in 2 Kings 18:26. Some isolated words in this language are preserved in the New Testament (<reflink>Matt. 5:22; 6:24; 16:17; 27:46; Mark 3:17; 5:41; 7:34; 14:36; Acts 1:19; 1 Cor. 16:22</reflink>). These are specimens of the vernacular language of Palestine at that period. The term "Hebrew" was also sometimes applied to the Chaldee because it had become the language of the Hebrews (<reflink>John 5:2; 19:20</reflink>).

chaldees.d: or Chaldeans, the inhabitants of the country of which Babylon was the capital. They were so called till the time of the Captivity (2 Kings 25; Isa. 13:19; 23:13), when, particularly in the Book of Daniel (5:30; 9:1), the name began to be used with special reference to a class of learned men ranked with the magicians and astronomers. These men cultivated the ancient Cushite language of the original inhabitants of the land, for they had a "learning" and a "tongue" (1:4) of their own. The common language of the country at that time had become assimilated to the Semitic dialect, especially through the influence of the Assyrians, and was the language that was used for all civil purposes. The Chaldeans were the learned class, interesting themselves in science and religion, which consisted, like that of the ancient Arabians and Syrians, in the worship of the heavenly bodies. There are representations of this priestly class, of magi and diviners, on the walls of the Assyrian palaces.

chamber.d: "on the wall," which the Shunammite prepared for the prophet Elisha (<reflink>2 Kings 4:10</reflink>), was an upper chamber over the porch through the hall toward the street. This was the "guest chamber" where entertainments were prepared (<reflink>Mark 14:14</reflink>). There were also "chambers within chambers" (<reflink>1 Kings 22:25; 2 Kings 9:2</reflink>). To enter into a chamber is used metaphorically of prayer and communion with God (<reflink>Isa. 26:20</reflink>). The "chambers of the south" (<reflink>Job 9:9</reflink>) are probably the constelations of the southern hemisphere. The "chambers of imagery", i.e., chambers painted with images, as used by Ezekiel (8:12), is an expression denoting the vision the prophet had of the abominations practised by the Jews in Jerusalem.

chamberlain.d: a confidential servant of the king (<reflink>Gen. 37:36; 39:1</reflink>). In Rom. 16:23 mention is made of "Erastus the chamberlain." Here the word denotes the treasurer of the city, or the quaestor, as the Romans styled him. He is almost the only convert from the higher ranks of whom mention is made (<reflink>comp. Acts 17:34</reflink>). Blastus, Herod's "chamberlain" (<reflink>Acts 12:20</reflink>), was his personal attendant or valet-de-chambre. The Hebrew word _saris_, thus translated in Esther 1:10, 15; 2:3, 14, 21, etc., properly means an eunuch (as in the marg.), as it is rendered in Isa. 39:7; 56:3.

chameleon.d: a species of lizard which has the faculty of changing the colour of its skin. It is ranked among the unclean animals in Lev. 11:30, where the Hebrew word so translated is _coah_ (R.V., "land crocodile"). In the same verse the Hebrew _tanshemeth_, rendered in Authorized Version "mole," is in Revised Version "chameleon," which is the correct rendering. This animal is very common in Egypt and in the Holy Land, especially in the Jordan valley.

chamois.d: only in Deut. 14:5 (Heb. zemer), an animal of the deer or gazelle species. It bears this Hebrew name from its leaping or springing. The animal intended is probably the wild sheep (Ovis tragelephus), which is still found in Sinai and in the broken ridges of Stony Arabia. The LXX. and Vulgate render the word by camelopardus, i.e., the giraffe; but this is an animal of Central Africa, and is not at all known in Syria.

champion.d: (<reflink>1 Sam. 17:4, 23</reflink>), properly "the man between the two," denoting the position of Goliath between the two camps. Single combats of this kind at the head of armies were common in ancient times. In ver. 51 this word is the rendering of a different Hebrew word, and properly denotes "a mighty man."

chance.d: (<reflink>Luke 10:31</reflink>). "It was not by chance that the priest came down by that road at that time, but by a specific arrangement and in exact fulfilment of a plan; not the plan of the priest, nor the plan of the wounded traveller, but the plan of God. By coincidence (Gr. sungkuria) the priest came down, that is, by the conjunction of two things, in fact, which were previously constituted a pair in the providence of God. In the result they fell together according to the omniscient Designer's plan. This is the true theory of the divine government." Compare the meeting of Philip with the Ethiopian (<reflink>Acts 8:26, 27</reflink>). There is no "chance" in God's empire. "Chance" is only another word for our want of knowledge as to the way in which one event falls in with another (<reflink>1 Sam. 6:9; Eccl. 9:11</reflink>).

chancellor.d: one who has judicial authority, literally, a "lord of judgement;" a title given to the Persian governor of Samaria (<reflink>Ezra 4:8, 9, 17</reflink>).

changes of raiment.d: were reckoned among the treasures of rich men (<reflink>Gen. 45:22; Judg. 14:12, 13; 2 Kings 5:22, 23</reflink>).

darda.d: pearl of wisdom, one of the four who were noted for their wisdom, but whom Solomon excelled (<reflink>1 Kings 4:31</reflink>).

daric.d: in the Revised Version of 1 Chr. 29:7; Ezra 2:69; 8:27; Neh. 7:70-72, where the Authorized Version has "dram." It is the rendering of the Hebrew darkemon and the Greek dareikos. It was a gold coin, bearing the figure of a Persian King with his crown and armed with bow and arrow. It was current among the Jews after their return from Babylon, i.e., while under the Persian domination. It weighed about 128 grains troy, and was of the value of about one guinea or rather more of our money. It is the first coin mentioned in Scripture, and is the oldest that history makes known to us.

darius.d: the holder or supporter, the name of several Persian kings. (1.) Darius the Mede (<reflink>Dan. 11:1</reflink>), "the son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes" (9:1). On the death of Belshazzar the Chaldean he "received the kingdom" of Babylon as viceroy from Cyrus. During his brief reign (B.C. 538-536) Daniel was promoted to the highest dignity (<reflink>Dan. 6:1, 2</reflink>); but on account of the malice of his enemies he was cast into the den of lions. After his miraculous escape, a decree was issued by Darius enjoining "reverence for the God of Daniel" (6:26). This king was probably the "Astyages" of the Greek historians. Nothing can, however, be with certainty affirmed regarding him. Some are of opinion that the name "Darius" is simply a name of office, equivalent to "governor," and that the "Gobryas" of the inscriptions was the person intended by the name.

darkness.d: The plague (the ninth) of darkness in Egypt (<reflink>Ex. 10:21</reflink>) is described as darkness "which may be felt." It covered "all the land of Egypt," so that "they saw not one another." It did not extend to the land of Goshen (ver. 23).

dart.d: an instrument of war; a light spear. "Fiery darts" (<reflink>Eph. 6:16</reflink>) are so called in allusion to the habit of discharging darts from the bow while they are on fire or armed with some combustible material. Arrows are compared to lightning (<reflink>Deut. 32:23, 42; Ps. 7:13; 120:4</reflink>).

date.d: the fruit of a species of palm (q.v.), the Phoenix dactilifera. This was a common tree in Palestine (<reflink>Joel 1:12; Neh. 8:15</reflink>). Palm branches were carried by the Jews on festive occasions, and especially at the feast of Tabernacles (<reflink>Lev. 23:40; Neh. 8:15</reflink>).

dathan.d: welled; belonging to a fountain, a son of Eliab, a Reubenite, who joined Korah (q.v.) in his conspiracy, and with his accomplices was swallowed up by an earthquake (<reflink>Num. 16:1; 26:9; Deut. 11:6; Ps. 106:17</reflink>).

daughter.d: This word, besides its natural and proper sense, is used to designate, (1.) A niece or any female descendant (<reflink>Gen. 20:12; 24:48; 28:6</reflink>). (2.) Women as natives of a place, or as professing the religion of a place; as, "the daughters of Zion" (<reflink>Isa. 3:16</reflink>), "daughters of the Philistines" (<reflink>2 Sam. 1:20</reflink>). (3.) Small towns and villages lying around a city are its "daughters," as related to the metropolis or mother city. Tyre is in this sense called the daughter of Sidon (<reflink>Isa. 23:12</reflink>). (4.) The people of Jerusalem are spoken of as "the daughters of Zion" (<reflink>Isa. 37:22</reflink>). (5.) The daughters of a tree are its boughs (<reflink>Gen. 49:22</reflink>). (6.) The "daughters of music" (<reflink>Eccl. 12:4</reflink>) are singing women.

david.d: beloved, the eighth and youngest son of Jesse, a citizen of Bethlehem. His father seems to have been a man in humble life. His mother's name is not recorded. Some think she was the Nahash of 2 Sam. 17:25. As to his personal appearance, we only know that he was red-haired, with beautiful eyes and a fair face (<reflink>1 Sam. 16:12; 17:42</reflink>).

david, city of.d: (1.) David took from the Jebusites the fortress of Mount Zion. He "dwelt in the fort, and called it the city of David" (<reflink>1 Chr. 11:7</reflink>). This was the name afterwards given to the castle and royal palace on Mount Zion, as distinguished from Jerusalem generally (<reflink>1 Kings 3:1; 8:1</reflink>), It was on the south-west side of Jerusalem, opposite the temple mount, with which it was connected by a bridge over the Tyropoeon valley.

day.d: The Jews reckoned the day from sunset to sunset (<reflink>Lev. 23:32</reflink>). It was originally divided into three parts (<reflink>Ps. 55:17</reflink>). "The heat of the day" (<reflink>1 Sam. 11:11; Neh. 7:3</reflink>) was at our nine o'clock, and "the cool of the day" just before sunset (<reflink>Gen. 3:8</reflink>). Before the Captivity the Jews divided the night into three watches, (1) from sunset to midnight (<reflink>Lam. 2:19</reflink>); (2) from midnight till the cock-crowing (<reflink>Judg. 7:19</reflink>); and (3) from the cock-crowing till sunrise (<reflink>Ex. 14:24</reflink>). In the New Testament the division of the Greeks and Romans into four watches was adopted (<reflink>Mark 13:35</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See WATCHES.</see>)

day's journey.d: The usual length of a day's journey in the East, on camel or horseback, in six or eight hours, is about 25 or 30 miles. The "three days' journey" mentioned in Ex. 3:18 is simply a journey which would occupy three days in going and returning.

daysman.d: an umpire or arbiter or judge (<reflink>Job 9:33</reflink>). This word is formed from the Latin diem dicere, i.e., to fix a day for hearing a cause. Such an one is empowered by mutual consent to decide the cause, and to "lay his hand", i.e., to impose his authority, on both, and enforce his sentence.

dayspring.d: (<reflink>Job 38:12; Luke 1:78</reflink>), the dawn of the morning; daybreak. (<reflink>Comp. Isa. 60:1, 2; Mal. 4:2; Rev. 22:16.</reflink>)

daystar.d: which precedes and accompanies the sun-rising. It is found only in 2 Pet. 1:19, where it denotes the manifestation of Christ to the soul, imparting spiritual light and comfort. He is the "bright and morning star" of Rev. 2:28; 22:16. (<reflink>Comp. Num. 24:17.</reflink>)

deacon.d: Anglicized form of the Greek word diaconos, meaning a "runner," "messenger," "servant." For a long period a feeling of mutual jealousy had existed between the "Hebrews," or Jews proper, who spoke the sacred language of palestine, and the "Hellenists," or Jews of the Grecian speech, who had adopted the Grecian language, and read the Septuagint version of the Bible instead of the Hebrew. This jealousy early appeared in the Christian community. It was alleged by the Hellenists that their widows were overlooked in the daily distribution of alms. This spirit must be checked. The apostles accordingly advised the disciples to look out for seven men of good report, full of the Holy Ghost, and men of practical wisdom, who should take entire charge of this distribution, leaving them free to devote themselves entirely to the spiritual functions of their office (<reflink>Acts 6:1-6</reflink>). This was accordingly done. Seven men were chosen, who appear from their names to have been Hellenists. …

deaconess.d: Rom. 16:1, 3, 12; Phil. 4:2, 3; 1 Tim. 3:11; 5:9, 10; Titus 2:3, 4). In these passages it is evident that females were then engaged in various Christian ministrations. Pliny makes mention of them also in his letter to Trajan (A.D. 110).

dead sea.d: the name given by Greek writers of the second century to that inland sea called in Scripture the "salt sea" (<reflink>Gen. 14:3; Num. 34:12</reflink>), the "sea of the plain" (<reflink>Deut. 3:17</reflink>), the "east sea" (<reflink>Ezek. 47:18; Joel 2:20</reflink>), and simply "the sea" (<reflink>Ezek. 47:8</reflink>). The Arabs call it Bahr Lut, i.e., the Sea of Lot. It lies about 16 miles in a straight line to the east of Jerusalem. Its surface is 1,292 feet below the surface of the Mediterranean Sea. It covers an area of about 300 square miles. Its depth varies from 1,310 to 11 feet. From various phenomena that have been observed, its bottom appears to be still subsiding. It is about 53 miles long, and of an average breadth of 10 miles. It has no outlet, the great heat of that region causing such rapid evaporation that its average depth, notwithstanding the rivers that run into it (<see target="x-self">see JORDAN</see>), is maintained with little variation. …

dearth.d: a scarcity of provisions (1 Kings 17). There were frequent dearths in Palestine. In the days of Abram there was a "famine in the land" (<reflink>Gen. 12:10</reflink>), so also in the days of Jacob (47:4, 13). We read also of dearths in the time of the judges (<reflink>Ruth 1:1</reflink>), and of the kings (<reflink>2 Sam. 21:1; 1 Kings 18:2; 2 Kings 4:38; 8:1</reflink>).

death.d: may be simply defined as the termination of life. It is represented under a variety of aspects in Scripture: (1.) "The dust shall return to the earth as it was" (<reflink>Eccl. 12:7</reflink>).

debir.d: oracle town; sanctuary. (1.) One of the eleven cities to the west of Hebron, in the highlands of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:49; Judg. 1:11-15</reflink>). It was originally one of the towns of the Anakim (<reflink>Josh. 15:15</reflink>), and was also called Kirjath-sepher (q.v.) and Kirjath-sannah (49). Caleb, who had conquered and taken possession of the town and district of Hebron (<reflink>Josh. 14:6-15</reflink>), offered the hand of his daughter to any one who would successfully lead a party against Debir. Othniel, his younger brother (<reflink>Judg. 1:13; 3:9</reflink>), achieved the conquest, and gained Achsah as his wife. She was not satisfied with the portion her father gave her, and as she was proceeding toward her new home, she "lighted from off her ass" and said to him, "Give me a blessing [i.e., a dowry]: for thou hast given me a south land" (<reflink>Josh. …

deborah.d: a bee. (1.) Rebekah's nurse. She accompanied her mistress when she left her father's house in Padan-aram to become the wife of Isaac (<reflink>Gen. 24:59</reflink>). Many years afterwards she died at Bethel, and was buried under the "oak of weeping", Allon-bachuth (35:8).

debt.d: The Mosaic law encouraged the practice of lending (<reflink>Deut. 15:7; Ps. 37:26; Matt. 5:42</reflink>); but it forbade the exaction of interest except from foreigners. Usury was strongly condemned (<reflink>Prov. 28:8; Ezek. 18:8, 13, 17; 22:12; Ps. 15:5</reflink>). On the Sabbatical year all pecuniary obligations were cancelled (<reflink>Deut. 15:1-11</reflink>). These regulations prevented the accumulation of debt.

debtor.d: Various regulations as to the relation between debtor and creditor are laid down in the Scriptures.

decalogue.d: the name given by the Greek fathers to the ten commandments; "the ten words," as the original is more literally rendered (<reflink>Ex. 20:3-17</reflink>). These commandments were at first written on two stone slabs (31:18), which were broken by Moses throwing them down on the ground (32:19). They were written by God a second time (34:1). The decalogue is alluded to in the New Testament five times (<reflink>Matt. 5:17, 18, 19; Mark 10:19; Luke 18:20; Rom. 7:7, 8; 13:9; 1 Tim. 1:9, 10</reflink>).

decapoils.d: ten cities=deka, ten, and polis, a city, a district on the east and south-east of the Sea of Galilee containing "ten cities," which were chiefly inhabited by Greeks. It included a portion of Bashan and Gilead, and is mentioned three times in the New Testament (<reflink>Matt. 4:25; Mark 5:20; 7:31</reflink>). These cities were Scythopolis, i.e., "city of the Scythians", (ancient Bethshean, the only one of the ten cities on the west of Jordan), Hippos, Gadara, Pella (to which the Christians fled just before the destruction of Jerusalem), Philadelphia (ancient Rabbath-ammon), Gerasa, Dion, Canatha, Raphana, and Damascus. When the Romans conquered Syria (B.C. 65) they rebuilt, and endowed with certain privileges, these "ten cities," and the province connected with them they called "Decapolis."

decision, valley of.d: a name given to the valley of Jehoshaphat (q.v.) as the vale of the sentence. The scene of Jehovah's signal inflictions on Zion's enemies (<reflink>Joel 3:14; marg., "valley of concision or threshing"</reflink>).

decrees of god.d: "The decrees of God are his eternal, unchangeable, holy, wise, and sovereign purpose, comprehending at once all things that ever were or will be in their causes, conditions, successions, and relations, and determining their certain futurition. The several contents of this one eternal purpose are, because of the limitation of our faculties, necessarily conceived of by us in partial aspects, and in logical relations, and are therefore styled Decrees." The decree being the act of an infinite, absolute, eternal, unchangeable, and sovereign Person, comprehending a plan including all his works of all kinds, great and small, from the beginning of creation to an unending eternity; ends as well as means, causes as well as effects, conditions and instrumentalities as well as the events which depend upon them, must be incomprehensible by the finite intellect of man. The decrees are eternal (<reflink>Acts 15:18; Eph. 1:4; 2 Thess. 2:13</reflink>), unchangeable (<reflink>Ps. 33:11; Isa. …

dedan.d: low ground. (1.) A son of Raamah (<reflink>Gen. 10:7</reflink>). His descendants are mentioned in Isa. 21:13, and Ezek. 27:15. They probably settled among the sons of Cush, on the north-west coast of the Persian Gulf.
