dedanim.d: the descendants of Dedan, the son of Raamah. They are mentioned in Isa. 21:13 as sending out "travelling companies" which lodged "in the forest of Arabia." They are enumerated also by Ezekiel (27:20) among the merchants who supplied Tyre with precious things.

dedication, feast of the.d: (<reflink>John 10:22, 42</reflink>), i.e., the feast of the renewing. It was instituted B.C. 164 to commemorate the purging of the temple after its pollution by Antiochus Epiphanes (B.C. 167), and the rebuilding of the altar after the Syrian invaders had been driven out by Judas Maccabaeus. It lasted for eight days, beginning on the 25th of the month Chisleu (December), which was often a period of heavy rains (<reflink>Ezra 10:9, 13</reflink>). It was an occasion of much rejoicing and festivity.

deep.d: used to denote (1) the grave or the abyss (<reflink>Rom. 10:7; Luke 8:31</reflink>); (2) the deepest part of the sea (<reflink>Ps. 69:15</reflink>); (3) the chaos mentioned in Gen. 1:2; (4) the bottomless pit, hell (<reflink>Rev. 9:1, 2; 11:7; 20:13</reflink>).

degrees, song of.d: song of steps, a title given to each of these fifteen psalms, 120-134 inclusive. The probable origin of this name is the circumstance that these psalms came to be sung by the people on the ascents or goings up to Jerusalem to attend the three great festivals (<reflink>Deut. 16:16</reflink>). They were well fitted for being sung by the way from their peculiar form, and from the sentiments they express. "They are characterized by brevity, by a key-word, by epanaphora [i.e, repetition], and by their epigrammatic style...More than half of them are cheerful, and all of them hopeful." They are sometimes called "Pilgrim Songs." Four of them were written by David, one (127) by Solomon, and the rest are anonymous.

dehavites.d: villagers, one of the Assyrian tribes which Asnapper sent to repopulate Samaria (<reflink>Ezra 4:9</reflink>). They were probably a nomad Persian tribe on the east of the Caspian Sea, and near the Sea of Azof.

delaiah.d: freed by Jehovah. (1.) The head of the twenty-third division of the priestly order (<reflink>1 Chr. 24:18</reflink>).

delilah.d: languishing, a Philistine woman who dwelt in the valley of Sorek (<reflink>Judg. 16:4-20</reflink>). She was bribed by the "lords of the Philistines" to obtain from Samson the secret of his strength and the means of overcoming it (<reflink>Judg. 16:4-18</reflink>). She tried on three occasions to obtain from him this secret in vain. On the fourth occasion she wrung it from him. She made him sleep upon her knees, and then called the man who was waiting to help her; who "cut off the seven locks of his head," and so his "strength went from him." (<see target="x-self">See SAMSON.</see>)

deluge.d: the name given to Noah's flood, the history of which is recorded in Gen. 7 and 8.

demas.d: a companion and fellow-labourer of Paul during his first imprisonment at Rome (<reflink>Philemon 1:24; Col. 4:14</reflink>). It appears, however, that the love of the world afterwards mastered him, and he deserted the apostle (<reflink>2 Tim. 4:10</reflink>).

demetrius.d: (1.) A silversmith at Ephesus, whose chief occupation was to make "silver shrines for Diana" (q.v.), Acts 19:24,i.e., models either of the temple of Diana or of the statue of the goddess. This trade brought to him and his fellow-craftsmen "no small gain," for these shrines found a ready sale among the countless thousands who came to this temple from all parts of Asia Minor. This traffic was greatly endangered by the progress of the gospel, and hence Demetrius excited the tradesmen employed in the manufacture of these shrines, and caused so great a tumult that "the whole city was filled with confusion."

den.d: a lair of wild beasts (<reflink>Ps. 10:9; 104:22; Job 37:8</reflink>); the hole of a venomous reptile (<reflink>Isa. 11:8</reflink>); a recess for secrecy "in dens and caves of the earth" (<reflink>Heb. 11:38</reflink>); a resort of thieves (<reflink>Matt. 21:13; Mark 11:17</reflink>). Daniel was cast into "the den of lions" (<reflink>Dan. 6:16, 17</reflink>). Some recent discoveries among the ruins of Babylon have brought to light the fact that the practice of punishing offenders against the law by throwing them into a den of lions was common.

deputy.d: in 1 Kings 22:47, means a prefect; one set over others. The same Hebrew word is rendered "officer;" i.e., chief of the commissariat appointed by Solomon (<reflink>1 Kings 4:5, etc.</reflink>).

derbe.d: a small town on the eastern part of the upland plain of Lycaonia, about 20 miles from Lystra. Paul passed through Derbe on his route from Cilicia to Iconium, on his second missionary journey (<reflink>Acts 16:1</reflink>), and probably also on his third journey (18:23; 19:1). On his first journey (14:20, 21) he came to Derbe from the other side; i.e., from Iconium. It was the native place of Gaius, one of Paul's companions (20:4). He did not here suffer persecution (<reflink>2 Tim. 3:11</reflink>).

desert.d: (1.) Heb. midbar, "pasture-ground;" an open tract for pasturage; a common (<reflink>Joel 2:22</reflink>). The "backside of the desert" (<reflink>Ex. 3:1</reflink>) is the west of the desert, the region behind a man, as the east is the region in front. The same Hebrew word is rendered "wildernes," and is used of the country lying between Egypt and Palestine (<reflink>Gen. 21:14, 21; Ex. 4:27; 19:2; Josh. 1:4</reflink>), the wilderness of the wanderings. It was a grazing tract, where the flocks and herds of the Israelites found pasturage during the whole of their journey to the Promised Land.

desire of all nations.d: (<reflink>Hag. 2:7</reflink>), usually interpreted as a title of the Messiah. The Revised Version, however, more correctly renders "the desirable things of all nations;" i.e., the choicest treasures of the Gentiles shall be consecrated to the Lord.

desolation, abomination of.d: (<reflink>Matt. 24:15; Mark 13:14; comp. Luke 21:20</reflink>), is interpreted of the eagles, the standards of the Roman army, which were an abomination to the Jews. These standards, rising over the site of the temple, were a sign that the holy place had fallen under the idolatrous Romans. The references are to Dan. 9:27. (<see target="x-self">See ABOMINATION.</see>)

destroyer.d: (<reflink>Ex. 12:23</reflink>), the agent employed in the killing of the first-born; the destroying angel or messenger of God. (Comp. 2 Kings 19:35; 2 Sam. 24:15, 16; Ps. 78:49; Acts 12:23.)

destruction.d: in Job 26:6, 28:22 (Heb. abaddon) is sheol, the realm of the dead.

destruction, city of.d: (<reflink>Isa. 19:18; Heb. Ir-ha-Heres, "city of overthrow," because of the evidence it would present of the overthrow of heathenism</reflink>), the ideal title of On or Heliopolis (q.v.).

deuteronomy.d: In all the Hebrew manuscripts the Pentateuch (q.v.) forms one roll or volume divided into larger and smaller sections called _parshioth_ and _sedarim_. It is not easy to say when it was divided into five books. This was probably first done by the Greek translators of the book, whom the Vulgate follows. The fifth of these books was called by the Greeks Deuteronomion, i.e., the second law, hence our name Deuteronomy, or a second statement of the laws already promulgated. The Jews designated the book by the two first Hebrew words that occur, _'Elle haddabharim_, i.e., "These are the words." They divided it into eleven _parshioth_. In the English Bible it contains thirty-four chapters.

devil.d: (Gr. diabolos), a slanderer, the arch-enemy of man's spiritual interest (<reflink>Job 1:6; Rev. 2:10; Zech. 3:1</reflink>). He is called also "the accuser of the brethen" (<reflink>Rev. 12:10</reflink>).

dew.d: "There is no dew properly so called in Palestine, for there is no moisture in the hot summer air to be chilled into dew-drops by the coldness of the night. From May till October rain is unknown, the sun shining with unclouded brightness day after day. The heat becomes intense, the ground hard, and vegetation would perish but for the moist west winds that come each night from the sea. The bright skies cause the heat of the day to radiate very quickly into space, so that the nights are as cold as the day is the reverse, a peculiarity of climate from which poor Jacob suffered thousands of years ago (<reflink>Gen. 31:40</reflink>). To this coldness of the night air the indispensable watering of all plant-life is due. The winds, loaded with moisture, are robbed of it as they pass over the land, the cold air condensing it into drops of water, which fall in a gracious rain of mist on every thirsty blade. …

diadem.d: the tiara of a king (<reflink>Ezek. 21:26; Isa. 28:5; 62:3</reflink>); the turban (<reflink>Job 29:14</reflink>). In the New Testament a careful distinction is drawn between the diadem as a badge of royalty (<reflink>Rev. 12:3; 13:1; 19:12</reflink>) and the crown as a mark of distinction in private life. It is not known what the ancient Jewish "diadem" was. It was the mark of Oriental sovereigns. (<see target="x-self">See CROWN.</see>)

dial.d: for the measurement of time, only once mentioned in the Bible, erected by Ahaz (<reflink>2 Kings 20:11; Isa. 38:8</reflink>). The Hebrew word (ma'aloth) is rendered "steps" in Ex. 20:26, 1 Kings 10:19, and "degrees" in 2 Kings 20:9, 10, 11. The _ma'aloth_ was probably stairs on which the shadow of a column or obelisk placed on the top fell. The shadow would cover a greater or smaller number of steps, according as the sun was low or high.

diamond.d: (1.) A precious gem (Heb. yahalom', in allusion to its hardness), otherwise unknown, the sixth, i.e., the third in the second row, in the breastplate of the high priest, with the name of Naphtali engraven on it (<reflink>Ex. 28:18; 39:11; R.V. marg., "sardonyx."</reflink>)

diana.d: so called by the Romans; called Artemis by the Greeks, the "great" goddess worshipped among heathen nations under various modifications. Her most noted temple was that at Ephesus. It was built outside the city walls, and was one of the seven wonders of the ancient world. "First and last it was the work of 220 years; built of shining marble; 342 feet long by 164 feet broad; supported by a forest of columns, each 56 feet high; a sacred museum of masterpieces of sculpture and painting. At the centre, hidden by curtains, within a gorgeous shrine, stood the very ancient image of the goddess, on wood or ebony reputed to have fallen from the sky. Behind the shrine was a treasury, where, as in 'the safest bank in Asia,' nations and kings stored their most precious things. The temple as St. Paul saw it subsisted till A.D. 262, when it was ruined by the Goths" (<reflink>Acts 19:23-41</reflink>)., Moule on Ephesians: Introd.

diblaim.d: doubled cakes, the mother of Gomer, who was Hosea's wife (<reflink>Hos. 1:3</reflink>).

diblathaim.d: two cakes, a city of Moab, on the east of the Dead Sea (<reflink>Num. 33:46; Jer. 48:22</reflink>).

dibon.d: pining; wasting. (1.) A city in Moab (<reflink>Num. 21:30</reflink>); called also Dibon-gad (33:45), because it was built by Gad and Dimon (<reflink>Isa. 15:9</reflink>). It has been identified with the modern Diban, about 3 miles north of the Arnon and 12 miles east of the Dead Sea. (<see target="x-self">See Moabite Stone.</see>)

cilicia.d: a maritime province in the south-east of Asia Minor. Tarsus, the birth-place of Paul, was one of its chief towns, and the seat of a celebrated school of philosophy. Its luxurious climate attracted to it many Greek residents after its incorporation with the Macedonian empire. It was formed into a Roman province, B.C. 67. The Jews of Cilicia had a synagogue at Jerusalem (<reflink>Acts 6:9</reflink>). Paul visited it soon after his conversion (<reflink>Gal. 1:21; Acts 9:30</reflink>), and again, on his second missionary journey (15:41), "he went through Syria and Cilicia, confirming the churches." It was famous for its goat's-hair cloth, called cilicium. Paul learned in his youth the trade of making tents of this cloth.

cinnamon.d: Heb. kinamon, the Cinnamomum zeylanicum of botanists, a tree of the Laurel family, which grows only in India on the Malabar coast, in Ceylon, and China. There is no trace of it in Egypt, and it was unknown in Syria. The inner rind when dried and rolled into cylinders forms the cinnamon of commerce. The fruit and coarser pieces of bark when boiled yield a fragrant oil. It was one of the principal ingredients in the holy anointing oil (<reflink>Ex. 30:23</reflink>). It is mentioned elsewhere only in Prov. 7:17; Cant. 4:14; Rev. 18:13. The mention of it indicates a very early and extensive commerce carried on between Palestine and the East.

cinnereth.d: a harp, one of the "fenced cities" of Naphtali (<reflink>Josh. 19:35; comp. Deut. 3:17</reflink>). It also denotes, apparently, a district which may have taken its name from the adjacent city or lake of Gennesaret, anciently called "the sea of Chinnereth" (q.v.), and was probably that enclosed district north of Tiberias afterwards called "the plain of Gennesaret." Called Chinneroth (R.V., Chinnereth) Josh. 11:2. The phrase "all Cinneroth, with all the land of Naphtali" in 1 Kings 15:20 is parallel to "the store-houses of the cities of Naphtali" (R.V. marg.) in 2 Chr. 16:4.

circuit.d: the apparent diurnal revolution of the sun round the earth (<reflink>Ps. 19:6</reflink>), and the changes of the wind (<reflink>Eccl. 1:6</reflink>). In Job 22:14, "in the circuit of heaven" (R.V. marg., "on the vault of heaven") means the "arch of heaven," which seems to be bent over our heads.

circumcision.d: cutting around. This rite, practised before, as some think, by divers races, was appointed by God to be the special badge of his chosen people, an abiding sign of their consecration to him. It was established as a national ordinance (<reflink>Gen. 17:10, 11</reflink>). In compliance with the divine command, Abraham, though ninety-nine years of age, was circumcised on the same day with Ishmael, who was thirteen years old (17:24-27). Slaves, whether home-born or purchased, were circumcised (17:12, 13); and all foreigners must have their males circumcised before they could enjoy the privileges of Jewish citizenship (<reflink>Ex. 12:48</reflink>). During the journey through the wilderness, the practice of circumcision fell into disuse, but was resumed by the command of Joshua before they entered the Promised Land (<reflink>Josh. 5:2-9</reflink>). …

cistern.d: the rendering of a Hebrew word _bor_, which means a receptacle for water conveyed to it; distinguished from _beer_, which denotes a place where water rises on the spot (<reflink>Jer. 2:13; Prov. 5:15; Isa. 36:16</reflink>), a fountain. Cisterns are frequently mentioned in Scripture. The scarcity of springs in Palestine made it necessary to collect rain-water in reservoirs and cisterns (<reflink>Num. 21:22</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See WELL.</see>)

citizenship.d: the rights and privileges of a citizen in distinction from a foreigner (<reflink>Luke 15:15; 19:14; Acts 21:39</reflink>). Under the Mosaic law non-Israelites, with the exception of the Moabites and the Ammonites and others mentioned in Deut. 23:1-3, were admitted to the general privileges of citizenship among the Jews (<reflink>Ex. 12:19; Lev. 24:22; Num. 15:15; 35:15; Deut. 10:18; 14:29; 16:10, 14</reflink>).

city.d: The earliest mention of city-building is that of Enoch, which was built by Cain (<reflink>Gen. 4:17</reflink>). After the confusion of tongues, the descendants of Nimrod founded several cities (10:10-12). Next, we have a record of the cities of the Canaanites, Sidon, Gaza, Sodom, etc. (10:12, 19; 11:3, 9; 36:31-39). The earliest description of a city is that of Sodom (19:1-22). Damascus is said to be the oldest existing city in the world. Before the time of Abraham there were cities in Egypt (<reflink>Num. 13:22</reflink>). The Israelites in Egypt were employed in building the "treasure cities" of Pithom and Raamses (<reflink>Ex. 1:11</reflink>); but it does not seem that they had any cities of their own in Goshen (<reflink>Gen. 46:34; 47:1-11</reflink>). In the kingdom of Og in Bashan there were sixty "great cities with walls," and twenty-three cities in Gilead partly rebuilt by the tribes on the east of Jordan (<reflink>Num. 21:21, 32, 33, 35; 32:1-3, 34-42; Deut. …

clauda.d: a small island off the southwest coast of Crete, passed by Paul on his voyage to Rome (<reflink>Acts 27:16</reflink>). It is about 7 miles long and 3 broad. It is now called Gozzo (R.V., "Cauda").

claudia.d: a female Christian mentioned in 2 Tim. 4:21. It is a conjecture having some probability that she was a British maiden, the daughter of king Cogidunus, who was an ally of Rome, and assumed the name of the emperor, his patron, Tiberius Claudius, and that she was the wife of Pudens.

claudius.d: lame. (1.) The fourth Roman emperor. He succeeded Caligula (A.D. 41). Though in general he treated the Jews, especially those in Asia and Egypt, with great indulgence, yet about the middle of his reign (A.D. 49) he banished them all from Rome (<reflink>Acts 18:2</reflink>). In this edict the Christians were included, as being, as was supposed, a sect of Jews. The Jews, however soon again returned to Rome.

clay.d: This word is used of sediment found in pits or in streets (<reflink>Isa. 57:20; Jer. 38:60</reflink>), of dust mixed with spittle (<reflink>John 9:6</reflink>), and of potter's clay (<reflink>Isa. 41:25; Nah. 3:14; Jer. 18:1-6; Rom. 9:21</reflink>). Clay was used for sealing (<reflink>Job 38:14; Jer. 32:14</reflink>). Our Lord's tomb may have been thus sealed (<reflink>Matt. 27:66</reflink>). The practice of sealing doors with clay is still common in the East. Clay was also in primitive times used for mortar (<reflink>Gen. 11:3</reflink>). The "clay ground" in which the large vessels of the temple were cast (<reflink>1 Kings 7:46; 2 Chr. 4:17</reflink>) was a compact loam fitted for the purpose. The expression literally rendered is, "in the thickness of the ground,", meaning, "in stiff ground" or in clay.

clean.d: The various forms of uncleanness according to the Mosaic law are enumerated in Lev. 11-15; Num. 19. The division of animals into clean and unclean was probably founded on the practice of sacrifice. It existed before the Flood (<reflink>Gen. 7:2</reflink>). The regulations regarding such animals are recorded in Lev. 11 and Deut. 14:1-21.

clement.d: mild, a Christian of Philippi, Paul's "fellow-labourer," whose name he mentions as "in the book of life" (<reflink>Phil. 4:3</reflink>). It was an opinion of ancient writers that he was the Clement of Rome whose name is well known in church history, and that he was the author of an Epistle to the Corinthians, the only known manuscript of which is appended to the Alexandrian Codex, now in the British Museum. It is of some historical interest, and has given rise to much discussion among critics. It makes distinct reference to Paul's First Epistle to the Corinthians.

cleopas.d: (abbreviation of Cleopatros), one of the two disciples with whom Jesus conversed on the way to Emmaus on the day of the resurrection (<reflink>Luke 24:18</reflink>). We know nothing definitely regarding him. It is not certain that he was the Clopas of John 19:25, or the Alphaeus of Matt. 10:3, although he may have been so.

cleophas.d: (in the spelling of this word _h_ is inserted by mistake from Latin MSS.), rather Cleopas, which is the Greek form of the word, while Clopas is the Aramaic form. In John 19:25 the Authorized Version reads, "Mary, the wife of Clopas." The word "wife" is conjecturally inserted here. If "wife" is rightly inserted, then Mary was the mother of James the Less, and Clopas is the same as Alphaeus (<reflink>Matt. 10:3; 27:56</reflink>).

cloak.d: an upper garment, "an exterior tunic, wide and long, reaching to the ankles, but without sleeves" (<reflink>Isa. 59:17</reflink>). The word so rendered is elsewhere rendered "robe" or "mantle." It was worn by the high priest under the ephod (<reflink>Ex. 28:31</reflink>), by kings and others of rank (<reflink>1 Sam. 15:27; Job 1:20; 2:12</reflink>), and by women (<reflink>2 Sam. 13:18</reflink>).

closet.d: as used in the New Testament, signifies properly a storehouse (<reflink>Luke 12: 24</reflink>), and hence a place of privacy and retirement (<reflink>Matt. 6:6; Luke 12:3</reflink>).

cloud.d: The Hebrew so rendered means "a covering," because clouds cover the sky. The word is used as a symbol of the Divine presence, as indicating the splendour of that glory which it conceals (<reflink>Ex. 16:10; 33:9; Num. 11:25; 12:5; Job 22:14; Ps. 18:11</reflink>). A "cloud without rain" is a proverbial saying, denoting a man who does not keep his promise (<reflink>Prov. 16:15; Isa. 18:4; 25:5; Jude 1:12</reflink>). A cloud is the figure of that which is transitory (<reflink>Job 30:15; Hos. 6:4</reflink>). A bright cloud is the symbolical seat of the Divine presence (<reflink>Ex.29:42, 43; 1 Kings 8:10; 2 Chr. 5:14; Ezek. 43:4</reflink>), and was called the Shechinah (q.v.). Jehovah came down upon Sinai in a cloud (<reflink>Ex. 19:9</reflink>); and the cloud filled the court around the tabernacle in the wilderness so that Moses could not enter it (<reflink>Ex. 40:34, 35</reflink>). …

cnidus.d: a town and harbour on the extreme south-west of the peninsula of Doris in Asia Minor. Paul sailed past it on his voyage to Rome after leaving Myra (<reflink>Acts 27:7</reflink>).

coal.d: It is by no means certain that the Hebrews were acquainted with mineral coal, although it is found in Syria. Their common fuel was dried dung of animals and wood charcoal. Two different words are found in Hebrew to denote coal, both occurring in Prov. 26:21, "As coal [Heb. peham; i.e., "black coal"] is to burning coal [Heb. gehalim]." The latter of these words is used in Job 41:21; Prov. 6:28; Isa. 44:19. The words "live coal" in Isa. 6:6 are more correctly "glowing stone." In Lam. 4:8 the expression "blacker than a coal" is literally rendered in the margin of the Revised Version "darker than blackness." "Coals of fire" (<reflink>2 Sam. 22:9, 13; Ps. 18:8, 12, 13, etc.</reflink>) is an expression used metaphorically for lightnings proceeding from God. A false tongue is compared to "coals of juniper" (<reflink>Ps. 120:4; James 3:6</reflink>). "Heaping coals of fire on the head" symbolizes overcoming evil with good. The words of Paul (<reflink>Rom. …

coat.d: the tunic worn like the shirt next the skin (<reflink>Lev. 16:4; Cant. 5:3; 2 Sam. 15:32; Ex. 28:4; 29:5</reflink>). The "coats of skins" prepared by God for Adam and Eve were probably nothing more than aprons (<reflink>Gen. 3:21</reflink>). This tunic was sometimes woven entire without a seam (<reflink>John 19:23</reflink>); it was also sometimes of "many colours" (<reflink>Gen. 37:3; R.V. marg., "a long garment with sleeves"</reflink>). The "fisher's coat" of John 21:7 was obviously an outer garment or cloak, as was also the "coat" made by Hannah for Samuel (<reflink>1 Sam. 2:19</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See DRESS.</see>)

coat of mail.d: the rendering of a Hebrew word meaning "glittering" (<reflink>1 Sam. 17:5, 38</reflink>). The same word in the plural form is translated "habergeons" in 2 Chr. 26:14 and Neh. 4:16. The "harness" (<reflink>1 Kings 22:34</reflink>), "breastplate" (<reflink>Isa. 59:17</reflink>), and "brigandine" (<reflink>Jer. 46:4</reflink>), were probably also corselets or coats of mail. (<see target="x-self">See ARMOUR.</see>)

cock-crowing.d: In our Lord's time the Jews had adopted the Greek and Roman division of the night into four watches, each consisting of three hours, the first beginning at six o'clock in the evening (<reflink>Luke 12:38; Matt. 14:25; Mark 6:48</reflink>). But the ancient division, known as the first and second cock-crowing, was still retained. The cock usually crows several times soon after midnight (this is the first crowing), and again at the dawn of day (and this is the second crowing). Mark mentions (14:30) the two cock-crowings. Matthew (26:34) alludes to that only which was emphatically the cock-crowing, viz, the second.

cockatrice.d: the mediaeval name (a corruption of "crocodile") of a fabulous serpent supposed to be produced from a cock's egg. It is generally supposed to denote the cerastes, or "horned viper," a very poisonous serpent about a foot long. Others think it to be the yellow viper (Daboia xanthina), one of the most dangerous vipers, from its size and its nocturnal habits (<reflink>Isa. 11:8; 14:29; 59:5; Jer. 8:17; in all which the Revised Version renders the Hebrew _tziph'oni_ by "basilisk"</reflink>). In Prov. 23:32 the Hebrew _tzeph'a_ is rendered both in the Authorized Version and the Revised Version by "adder;" margin of Revised Version "basilisk," and of Authorized Version "cockatrice."

cockle.d: occurs only in Job 31:40 (marg., "noisome weeds"), where it is the rendering of a Hebrew word (b'oshah) which means "offensive," "having a bad smell," referring to some weed perhaps which has an unpleasant odour. Or it may be regarded as simply any noisome weed, such as the "tares" or darnel of Matt. 13:30. In Isa. 5:2, 4 the plural form is rendered "wild grapes."

coele-syria.d: hollow Syria, the name (not found in Scripture) given by the Greeks to the extensive valley, about 100 miles long, between the Lebanon and the Anti-Lebanon range of mountains.

coffer.d: the receptacle or small box placed beside the ark by the Philistines, in which they deposited the golden mice and the emerods as their trespass-offering (<reflink>1 Sam. 6:8, 11, 15</reflink>).

coffin.d: used in Gen. 50:26 with reference to the burial of Joseph. Here, it means a mummy-chest. The same Hebrew word is rendered "chest" in 2 Kings 12:9, 10.

cogitations.d: (or "thoughts," as the Chaldee word in Dan. 7:28 literally means), earnest meditation.

coin.d: Before the Exile the Jews had no regularly stamped money. They made use of uncoined shekels or talents of silver, which they weighed out (<reflink>Gen. 23:16; Ex. 38:24; 2 Sam. 18:12</reflink>). Probably the silver ingots used in the time of Abraham may have been of a fixed weight, which was in some way indicated on them. The "pieces of silver" paid by Abimelech to Abraham (<reflink>Gen. 20:16</reflink>), and those also for which Joseph was sold (37:28), were proably in the form of rings. The shekel was the common standard of weight and value among the Hebrews down to the time of the Captivity. Only once is a shekel of gold mentioned (<reflink>1 Chr. 21:25</reflink>). The "six thousand of gold" mentioned in the transaction between Naaman and Gehazi (<reflink>2 Kings 5:5</reflink>) were probably so many shekels of gold. The "piece of money" mentioned in Job 42:11; Gen. …

collar.d: (Heb. peh), means in Job 30:18 the mouth or opening of the garment that closes round the neck in the same way as a tunic (<reflink>Ex. 39:23</reflink>). The "collars" (Heb. netiphoth) among the spoils of the Midianites (<reflink>Judg. 8:26; R.V., "pendants"</reflink>) were ear-drops. The same Hebrew word is rendered "chains" in Isa. 3:19.

collection.d: The Christians in Palestine, from various causes, suffered from poverty. Paul awakened an interest in them among the Gentile churches, and made pecuniary collections in their behalf (<reflink>Acts 24:17; Rom. 15:25, 26; 1 Cor. 16:1-3; 2 Cor. 8:9; Gal. 2:10</reflink>).

college.d: Heb. mishneh (<reflink>2 Kings 22:14; 2 Chr. 34:22</reflink>), rendered in Revised Version "second quarter", the residence of the prophetess Huldah. The Authorized Version followed the Jewish commentators, who, following the Targum, gave the Hebrew word its post-Biblical sense, as if it meant a place of instruction. It properly means the "second," and may therefore denote the lower city (Acra), which was built after the portion of the city on Mount Zion, and was enclosed by a second wall.

colony.d: The city of Philippi was a Roman colony (<reflink>Acts 16:12</reflink>), i.e., a military settlement of Roman soldiers and citizens, planted there to keep in subjection a newly-conquered district. A colony was Rome in miniature, under Roman municipal law, but governed by military officers (praetors and lictors), not by proconsuls. It had an independent internal government, the jus Italicum; i.e., the privileges of Italian citizens.

colossae.d: or Colosse, a city of Phrygia, on the Lycus, which is a tributary of the Maeander. It was about 12 miles above Laodicea, and near the great road from Ephesus to the Euphrates, and was consequently of some mercantile importance. It does not appear that Paul had visited this city when he wrote his letter to the church there (<reflink>Col. 1:2</reflink>). He expresses in his letter to Philemon (<reflink>ver. 1:22</reflink>) his hope to visit it on being delivered from his imprisonment. From Col. 1:7; 4:12 it has been concluded that Epaphras was the founder of the Colossian church. This town afterwards fell into decay, and the modern town of Chonas or Chonum occupies a site near its ruins.

colossians, epistle to the.d: was written by Paul at Rome during his first imprisonment there (<reflink>Acts 28:16, 30</reflink>), probably in the spring of A.D. 57, or, as some think, 62, and soon after he had written his Epistle to the Ephesians. Like some of his other epistles (e.g., those to Corinth), this seems to have been written in consequence of information which had somehow been conveyed to him of the internal state of the church there (<reflink>Col. 1:4-8</reflink>). Its object was to counteract false teaching. A large part of it is directed against certain speculatists who attempted to combine the doctrines of Oriental mysticism and asceticism with Christianity, thereby promising the disciples the enjoyment of a higher spiritual life and a deeper insight into the world of spirits. Paul argues against such teaching, showing that in Christ Jesus they had all things. He sets forth the majesty of his redemption. …

colour.d: The subject of colours holds an important place in the Scriptures.

comforter.d: the designation of the Holy Ghost (<reflink>John 14:16, 26; 15:26; 16:7; R.V. marg., "or Advocate, or Helper; Gr. paracletos"</reflink>). The same Greek word thus rendered is translated "Advocate" in 1 John 2:1 as applicable to Christ. It means properly "one who is summoned to the side of another" to help him in a court of justice by defending him, "one who is summoned to plead a cause." "Advocate" is the proper rendering of the word in every case where it occurs.

coming of christ.d: (1) with reference to his first advent "in the fulness of the time" (<reflink>1 John 5:20; 2 John 1:7</reflink>), or (2) with reference to his coming again the second time at the last day (<reflink>Acts 1:11; 3:20, 21; 1 Thess. 4:15; 2 Tim. 4:1; Heb. 9:28</reflink>).

commandments, the ten.d: (<reflink>Ex. 34:28; Deut. 10:4, marg. "ten words"</reflink>) i.e., the Decalogue (q.v.), is a summary of the immutable moral law. These commandments were first given in their written form to the people of Israel when they were encamped at Sinai, about fifty days after they came out of Egypt (<reflink>Ex. 19:10-25</reflink>). They were written by the finger of God on two tables of stone. The first tables were broken by Moses when he brought them down from the mount (32:19), being thrown by him on the ground. At the command of God he took up into the mount two other tables, and God wrote on them "the words that were on the first tables" (34:1). These tables were afterwards placed in the ark of the covenant (<reflink>Deut. 10:5; 1 Kings 8:9</reflink>). Their subsequent history is unknown. They are as a whole called "the covenant" (<reflink>Deut. 4:13</reflink>), and "the tables of the covenant" (9:9, 11; Heb. 9:4), and "the testimony."

communion.d: fellowship with God (<reflink>Gen. 18:17-33; Ex. 33:9-11; Num. 12:7, 8</reflink>), between Christ and his people (<reflink>John 14:23</reflink>), by the Spirit (<reflink>2 Cor. 13:14; Phil. 2:1</reflink>), of believers with one another (<reflink>Eph. 4:1-6</reflink>). The Lord's Supper is so called (<reflink>1 Cor. 10:16, 17</reflink>), because in it there is fellowship between Christ and his disciples, and of the disciples with one another.

conaniah.d: whom Jehovah hath set, a Levite placed over the tithes brought into the temple (<reflink>2 Chr. 35:9</reflink>).

concision.d: (Gr. katatome; i.e., "mutilation"), a term used by Paul contemptuously of those who were zealots for circumcision (<reflink>Phil. 3:2</reflink>). Instead of the warning, "Beware of the circumcision" (peritome) i.e., of the party who pressed on Gentile converts the necessity of still observing that ordinance, he says, "Beware of the concision;" as much as to say, "This circumcision which they vaunt of is in Christ only as the gashings and mutilations of idolatrous heathen."

concubine.d: in the Bible denotes a female conjugally united to a man, but in a relation inferior to that of a wife. Among the early Jews, from various causes, the difference between a wife and a concubine was less marked than it would be amongst us. The concubine was a wife of secondary rank. There are various laws recorded providing for their protection (<reflink>Ex. 21:7; Deut. 21:10-14</reflink>), and setting limits to the relation they sustained to the household to which they belonged (<reflink>Gen. 21:14; 25:6</reflink>). They had no authority in the family, nor could they share in the household government.

concupiscence.d: desire, Rom. 7:8 (R.V., "coveting"); Col. 3:5 (R.V., "desire"). The "lust of concupiscence" (<reflink>1 Thess. 4:5; R.V., "passion of lust"</reflink>) denotes evil desire, indwelling sin.

conduit.d: a water-course or channel (<reflink>Job 38:25</reflink>). The "conduit of the upper pool" (<reflink>Isa. 7:3</reflink>) was formed by Hezekiah for the purpose of conveying the waters from the upper pool in the valley of Gihon to the west side of the city of David (<reflink>2 Kings 18:17; 20:20; 2 Chr. 32:30</reflink>). In carrying out this work he stopped "the waters of the fountains which were without the city" i.e., "the upper water-course of Gihon", and conveyed it down from the west through a canal into the city, so that in case of a siege the inhabitants of the city might have a supply of water, which would thus be withdrawn from the enemy. (<see target="x-self">See SILOAM.</see>)

coney.d: (Heb. shaphan; i.e., "the hider"), an animal which inhabits the mountain gorges and the rocky districts of Arabia Petraea and the Holy Land. "The conies are but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks" (<reflink>Prov. 30:26; Ps. 104:18</reflink>). They are gregarious, and "exceeding wise" (<reflink>Prov. 30:24</reflink>), and are described as chewing the cud (<reflink>Lev. 11:5; Deut. 14:7</reflink>).

confection.d: (<reflink>Ex. 30:35, "ointment" in ver. 25; R.V., "perfume"</reflink>). The Hebrew word so rendered is derived from a root meaning to compound oil and perfume.

confectionaries.d: only in 1 Sam. 8:13, those who make confections, i.e., perfumers, who compound species and perfumes.

confession.d: (1) An open profession of faith (<reflink>Luke 12:8</reflink>). (2.) An acknowledment of sins to God (<reflink>Lev. 16:21; Ezra 9:5-15; Dan. 9:3-12</reflink>), and to a neighbour whom we have wronged (<reflink>James 5:16; Matt. 18:15</reflink>).

congregation.d: (Heb. kahal), the Hebrew people collectively as a holy community (<reflink>Num. 15:15</reflink>). Every circumcised Hebrew from twenty years old and upward was a member of the congregation. Strangers resident in the land, if circumcised, were, with certain exceptions (<reflink>Ex. 12:19; Num. 9:14; Deut. 23:1-3</reflink>), admitted to the privileges of citizenship, and spoken of as members of the congregation (<reflink>Ex. 12:19; Num. 9:14; 15:15</reflink>). The congregation were summonded together by the sound of two silver trumpets, and they met at the door of the tabernacle (<reflink>Num. 10:3</reflink>). These assemblies were convened for the purpose of engaging in solemn religious services (<reflink>Ex. 12:27; Num. 25:6; Joel 2:15</reflink>), or of receiving new commandments (<reflink>Ex. 19:7, 8</reflink>). The elders, who were summonded by the sound of one trumpet (<reflink>Num. 10:4</reflink>), represented on various occasions the whole congregation (<reflink>Ex. …

congregation, mount of the.d: (<reflink>Isa. 14:13</reflink>), has been supposed to refer to the place where God promised to meet with his people (<reflink>Ex. 25:22; 29:42, 43</reflink>) i.e., the mount of the Divine presence, Mount Zion. But here the king of Babylon must be taken as expressing himself according to his own heathen notions, and not according to those of the Jews. The "mount of the congregation" will therefore in this case mean the northern mountain, supposed by the Babylonians to be the meeting-place of their gods. In the Babylonian inscriptions mention is made of a mountain which is described as "the mighty mountain of Bel, whose head rivals heaven, whose root is the holy deep." This mountain was regarded in their mythology as the place where the gods had their seat.

conscience.d: that faculty of the mind, or inborn sense of right and wrong, by which we judge of the moral character of human conduct. It is common to all men. Like all our other faculties, it has been perverted by the Fall (<reflink>John 16:2; Acts 26:9; Rom. 2:15</reflink>). It is spoken of as "defiled" (<reflink>Titus 1:15</reflink>), and "seared" (<reflink>1 Tim. 4:2</reflink>). A "conscience void of offence" is to be sought and cultivated (<reflink>Acts 24:16; Rom. 9:1; 2 Cor. 1:12; 1 Tim. 1:5, 19; 1 Pet. 3:21</reflink>).

consecration.d: the devoting or setting apart of anything to the worship or service of God. The race of Abraham and the tribe of Levi were thus consecrated (<reflink>Ex. 13:2, 12, 15; Num. 3:12</reflink>). The Hebrews devoted their fields and cattle, and sometimes the spoils of war, to the Lord (<reflink>Lev. 27:28, 29</reflink>). According to the Mosaic law the first-born both of man and beast were consecrated to God.

consolation of israel.d: a name for the Messiah in common use among the Jews, probably suggested by Isa. 12:1; 49:13. The Greek word thus rendered (<reflink>Luke 2:25, paraklesis</reflink>) is kindred to that translated "Comforter" in John 14:16, etc., parakletos.

constellation.d: a cluster of stars, or stars which appear to be near each other in the heavens, and which astronomers have reduced to certain figures (as the "Great Bear," the "Bull," etc.) for the sake of classification and of memory. In Isa. 13:10, where this word only occurs, it is the rendering of the Hebrew _kesil_, i.e., "fool." This was the Hebrew name of the constellation Orion (<reflink>Job 9:9; 38:31</reflink>), a constellation which represented Nimrod, the symbol of folly and impiety. The word some interpret by "the giant" in this place, "some heaven-daring rebel who was chained to the sky for his impiety."

contentment.d: a state of mind in which one's desires are confined to his lot whatever it may be (<reflink>1 Tim. 6:6; 2 Cor. 9:8</reflink>). It is opposed to envy (<reflink>James 3:16</reflink>), avarice (<reflink>Heb. 13:5</reflink>), ambition (<reflink>Prov. 13:10</reflink>), anxiety (<reflink>Matt. 6:25, 34</reflink>), and repining (<reflink>1 Cor. 10:10</reflink>). It arises from the inward disposition, and is the offspring of humility, and of an intelligent consideration of the rectitude and benignity of divine providence (<reflink>Ps. 96:1, 2; 145</reflink>), the greatness of the divine promises (<reflink>2 Pet. 1:4</reflink>), and our own unworthiness (<reflink>Gen. 32:10</reflink>); as well as from the view the gospel opens up to us of rest and peace hereafter (<reflink>Rom. 5:2</reflink>).

conversation.d: generally the goings out and in of social intercourse (<reflink>Eph. 2:3; 4:22; R.V., "manner of life"</reflink>); one's deportment or course of life. This word is never used in Scripture in the sense of verbal communication from one to another (<reflink>Ps. 50:23; Heb. 13:5</reflink>). In Phil. 1:27 and 3:20, a different Greek word is used. It there means one's relations to a community as a citizen, i.e., citizenship.

conversion.d: the turning of a sinner to God (<reflink>Acts 15:3</reflink>). In a general sense the heathen are said to be "converted" when they abandon heathenism and embrace the Christian faith; and in a more special sense men are converted when, by the influence of divine grace in their souls, their whole life is changed, old things pass away, and all things become new (<reflink>Acts 26:18</reflink>). Thus we speak of the conversion of the Philippian jailer (16:19-34), of Paul (9:1-22), of the Ethiopian treasurer (8:26-40), of Cornelius (10), of Lydia (16:13-15), and others. (See REGENERATION

convocation.d: a meeting of a religious character as distinguished from congregation, which was more general, dealing with political and legal matters. Hence it is called an "holy convocation." Such convocations were the Sabbaths (<reflink>Lev. 23:2, 3</reflink>), the Passover (<reflink>Ex. 12:16; Lev. 23:7, 8; Num. 28:25</reflink>), Pentecost (<reflink>Lev. 23:21</reflink>), the feast of Trumpets (<reflink>Lev. 23:24; Num. 29:1</reflink>), the feast of Weeks (<reflink>Num. 28:26</reflink>), and the feast of Tabernacles (<reflink>Lev. 23:35, 36</reflink>). The great fast, the annual day of atonement, was "the holy convocation" (<reflink>Lev. 23:27; Num. 29:7</reflink>).

cook.d: a person employed to perform culinary service. In early times among the Hebrews cooking was performed by the mistress of the household (<reflink>Gen. 18:2-6; Judg. 6:19</reflink>), and the process was very expeditiously performed (<reflink>Gen. 27:3, 4, 9, 10</reflink>). Professional cooks were afterwards employed (<reflink>1 Sam. 8:13; 9:23</reflink>). Few animals, as a rule, were slaughtered (other than sacrifices), except for purposes of hospitality (<reflink>Gen. 18:7; Luke 15:23</reflink>). The paschal lamb was roasted over a fire (<reflink>Ex. 12:8, 9; 2Chr. 35:13</reflink>). Cooking by boiling was the usual method adopted (<reflink>Lev. 8:31; Ex. 16:23</reflink>). No cooking took place on the Sabbath day (<reflink>Ex. 35:3</reflink>).

coos.d: (written Cos in the R.V.), a small island, one of the Sporades in the Aegean Sea, in the north-west of Rhodes, off the coast of Caria. Paul on his return from his third missionary journey, passed the night here after sailing from Miletus (<reflink>Acts 21:1</reflink>). It is now called Stanchio.

copper.d: derived from the Greek kupros (the island of Cyprus), called "Cyprian brass," occurs only in the Authorized Version in Ezra 8:27. Elsewhere the Hebrew word (nehosheth) is improperly rendered "brass," and sometimes "steel" (<reflink>2 Sam. 22:35; Jer. 15:12</reflink>). The "bow of steel" (<reflink>Job 20:24; Ps. 18:34</reflink>) should have been "bow of copper" (or "brass," as in the R.V.). The vessels of "fine copper" of Ezra 8:27 were probably similar to those of "bright brass" mentioned in 1 Kings 7:45; Dan. 10:6.

cor.d: This Hebrew word, untranslated, denotes a round vessel used as a measure both for liquids and solids. It was equal to one homer, and contained ten ephahs in dry and ten baths in liquid measure (<reflink>Ezek. 45:14</reflink>). The Rabbins estimated the cor at forty-five gallons, while Josephus estimated it at about eighty-seven. In 1 Kings 4:22; 5:11; 2 Chr. 2:10; 27:5, the original word is rendered "measure."

coral.d: Heb. ramoth, meaning "heights;" i.e., "high-priced" or valuable things, or, as some suppose, "that which grows high," like a tree (<reflink>Job 28:18; Ezek. 27:16</reflink>), according to the Rabbins, red coral, which was in use for ornaments.

corban.d: a Hebrew word adopted into the Greek of the New Testament and left untranslated. It occurs only once (<reflink>Mark 7:11</reflink>). It means a gift or offering consecrated to God. Anything over which this word was once pronounced was irrevocably dedicated to the temple. Land, however, so dedicated might be redeemed before the year of jubilee (<reflink>Lev. 27:16-24</reflink>). Our Lord condemns the Pharisees for their false doctrine, inasmuch as by their traditions they had destroyed the commandment which requires children to honour their father and mother, teaching them to find excuse from helping their parents by the device of pronouncing "Corban" over their goods, thus reserving them to their own selfish use.

cord.d: frequently used in its proper sense, for fastening a tent (<reflink>Ex. 35:18; 39:40</reflink>), yoking animals to a cart (<reflink>Isa. 5:18</reflink>), binding prisoners (<reflink>Judg. 15:13; Ps. 2:3; 129:4</reflink>), and measuring ground (2 Sam. 8;2; Ps. 78:55). Figuratively, death is spoken of as the giving way of the tent-cord (<reflink>Job 4:21. "Is not their tent-cord plucked up?" R.V.</reflink>). To gird one's self with a cord was a token of sorrow and humiliation. To stretch a line over a city meant to level it with the ground (<reflink>Lam. 2:8</reflink>). The "cords of sin" are the consequences or fruits of sin (<reflink>Prov. 5:22</reflink>). A "threefold cord" is a symbol of union (<reflink>Eccl. 4:12</reflink>). The "cords of a man" (<reflink>Hos. 11:4</reflink>) means that men employ, in inducing each other, methods such as are suitable to men, and not "cords" such as oxen are led by. …

coriander.d: Heb. gad, (<reflink>Ex. 16:31; Num. 11:7</reflink>), seed to which the manna is likened in its form and colour. It is the Coriandrum sativum of botanists, an umbelliferous annual plant with a round stalk, about two feet high. It is widely cultivated in Eastern countries and in the south of Europe for the sake of its seeds, which are in the form of a little ball of the size of a peppercorn. They are used medicinally and as a spice. The Greek name of this plant is korion or koriannon, whence the name "coriander."

corinth.d: a Grecian city, on the isthmus which joins the Peloponnesus to the mainland of Greece. It is about 48 miles west of Athens. The ancient city was destroyed by the Romans (B.C. 146), and that mentioned in the New Testament was quite a new city, having been rebuilt about a century afterwards and peopled by a colony of freedmen from Rome. It became under the Romans the seat of government for Southern Greece or Achaia (<reflink>Acts 18:12-16</reflink>). It was noted for its wealth, and for the luxurious and immoral and vicious habits of the people. It had a large mixed population of Romans, Greeks, and Jews. When Paul first visited the city (A.D. 51 or 52), Gallio, the brother of Seneca, was proconsul. Here Paul resided for eighteen months (18:1-18). Here he first became aquainted with Aquila and Priscilla, and soon after his departure Apollos came to it from Ephesus. After an interval he visited it a second time, and remained for three months (20:3). …

corinthians, first epistle to the.d: was written from Ephesus (<reflink>1 Cor. 16:8</reflink>) about the time of the Passover in the third year of the apostle's sojourn there (<reflink>Acts 19:10; 20:31</reflink>), and when he had formed the purpose to visit Macedonia, and then return to Corinth (probably A.D. 57).

corinthians, second epistle to the.d: Shortly after writing his first letter to the Corinthians, Paul left Ephesus, where intense excitement had been aroused against him, the evidence of his great success, and proceeded to Macedonia. Pursuing the usual route, he reached Troas, the port of departure for Europe. Here he expected to meet with Titus, whom he had sent from Ephesus to Corinth, with tidings of the effects produced on the church there by the first epistle; but was disappointed (<reflink>1 Cor. 16:9; 2 Cor. 1:8; 2:12, 13</reflink>). He then left Troas and proceeded to Macedonia; and at Philippi, where he tarried, he was soon joined by Titus (<reflink>2 Cor. 7:6, 7</reflink>), who brought him good news from Corinth, and also by Timothy. Under the influence of the feelings awakened in his mind by the favourable report which Titus brought back from Corinth, this second epistle was written. It was probably written at Philippi, or, as some think, Thessalonica, early in the year A.D. 58, and was sent to Corinth by Titus.

cormorant.d: (<reflink>Lev. 11:17; Deut. 14:17</reflink>), Heb. shalak, "plunging," or "darting down," (the Phalacrocorax carbo), ranked among the "unclean" birds; of the same family group as the pelican. It is a "plunging" bird, and is common on the coasts and the island seas of Palestine. Some think the Hebrew word should be rendered "gannet" (Sula bassana, "the solan goose"); others that it is the "tern" or "sea swallow," which also frequents the coasts of Palestine as well as the Sea of Galilee and the Jordan valley during several months of the year. But there is no reason to depart from the ordinary rendering.

corn.d: The word so rendered (dagan) in Gen. 27:28, 37, Num. 18:27, Deut. 28:51, Lam. 2:12, is a general term representing all the commodities we usually describe by the words corn, grain, seeds, peas, beans. With this corresponds the use of the word in John 12:24.

cornelius.d: a centurion whose history is narrated in Acts 10. He was a "devout man," and like the centurion of Capernaum, believed in the God of Israel. His residence at Caesrea probably brought him into contact with Jews who communicated to him their expectations regarding the Messiah; and thus he was prepared to welcome the message Peter brought him. He became the first fruit of the Gentile world to Christ. He and his family were baptized and admitted into the Christian church (<reflink>Acts 10:1, 44-48</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See CENTURION.</see>)

corner.d: The angle of a house (<reflink>Job 1:19</reflink>) or a street (<reflink>Prov. 7:8</reflink>). "Corners" in Neh. 9:22 denotes the various districts of the promised land allotted to the Israelites. In Num. 24:17, the "corners of Moab" denotes the whole land of Moab. The "corner of a field" (<reflink>Lev. 19:9; 23:22</reflink>) is its extreme part, which was not to be reaped. The Jews were prohibited from cutting the "corners," i.e., the extremities, of the hair and whiskers running round the ears (<reflink>Lev. 19:27; 21:5</reflink>). The "four corners of the earth" in Isa. 11:12 and Ezek. 7:2 denotes the whole land. The "corners of the streets" mentioned in Matt. 6:5 means the angles where streets meet so as to form a square or place of public resort.

cornet.d: Heb. shophar, "brightness," with reference to the clearness of its sound (<reflink>1 Chr. 15:28; 2 Chr. 15:14; Ps. 98:6; Hos. 5:8</reflink>). It is usually rendered in the Authorized Version "trumpet." It denotes the long and straight horn, about eighteen inches long. The words of Joel, "Blow the trumpet," literally, "Sound the cornet," refer to the festival which was the preparation for the day of Atonement. In Dan. 3:5, 7, 10, 15, the word (keren) so rendered is a curved horn. The word "cornet" in 2 Sam. 6:5 (Heb. mena'an'im, occurring only here) was some kind of instrument played by being shaken like the Egyptian sistrum, consisting of rings or bells hung loosely on iron rods.

cotes.d: pens or enclosures for flocks (<reflink>2 Chr. 32:28, "cotes for flocks;" R.V., "flocks in folds"</reflink>).

cottage.d: (1.) A booth in a vineyard (<reflink>Isa. 1:8</reflink>); a temporary shed covered with leaves or straw to shelter the watchman that kept the garden. These were slight fabrics, and were removed when no longer needed, or were left to be blown down in winter (<reflink>Job 27:18</reflink>).

couch.d: (<reflink>Gen. 49:4; 1 Chr. 5:1; Job 7:13; Ps. 6:6, etc.</reflink>), a seat for repose or rest. (<see target="x-self">See BED.</see>)

coulter.d: (<reflink>1 Sam. 13:20, 21</reflink>), an agricultural instrument, elsewhere called "ploughshare" (<reflink>Isa. 2:4; Micah 4:3; Joel 3:10</reflink>). It was the facing-piece of a plough, analogous to the modern coulter.

council.d: spoken of counsellors who sat in public trials with the governor of a province (<reflink>Acts 25:12</reflink>).

counsellor.d: an adviser (<reflink>Prov. 11:14; 15:22</reflink>), a king's state counsellor (<reflink>2 Sam. 15:12</reflink>). Used once of the Messiah (<reflink>Isa. 9:6</reflink>). In Mark 15:43, Luke 23:50, the word probably means a member of the Jewish Sanhedrim.

courses.d: When David was not permitted to build the temple, he proceeded, among the last acts of his life, with the assistance of Zadok and Ahimelech, to organize the priestly and musical services to be conducted in the house of God. (1.) He divided the priests into twenty-four courses (<reflink>1 Chr. 24:1-19</reflink>), sixteen being of the house of Eleazar and eight of that of Ithamar. Each course was under a head or chief, and ministered for a week, the order being determined by lot. (2.) The rest of the 38,000 Levites (23:4) were divided also into twenty-four courses, each to render some allotted service in public worship: 4,000 in twenty-four courses were set apart as singers and musicians under separate leaders (25); 4,000 as porters or keepers of the doors and gates of the sanctuary (26:1-19); and 6,000 as officers and judges to see to the administration of the law in all civil and ecclesiastical matters (20-32).

court.d: the enclosure of the tabernacle (<reflink>Ex. 27:9-19; 40:8</reflink>), of the temple (<reflink>1 Kings 6:36</reflink>), of a prison (<reflink>Neh. 3:25</reflink>), of a private house (<reflink>2 Sam. 17:18</reflink>), and of a king's palace (<reflink>2 Kings 20:4</reflink>).

covenant.d: a contract or agreement between two parties. In the Old Testament the Hebrew word _berith_ is always thus translated. _Berith_ is derived from a root which means "to cut," and hence a covenant is a "cutting," with reference to the cutting or dividing of animals into two parts, and the contracting parties passing between them, in making a covenant (Gen. 15; Jer. 34:18, 19).

covering of the eyes.d: occurs only in Gen. 20:16. In the Revised Version the rendering is "it (i.e., Abimelech's present of 1,000 pieces of silver to Abraham) is for thee a covering of the eyes." This has been regarded as an implied advice to Sarah to conform to the custom of married women, and wear a complete veil, covering the eyes as well as the rest of the face.

covetousness.d: a strong desire after the possession of worldly things (<reflink>Col. 3:5; Eph. 5:5; Heb. 13:5; 1 Tim. 6:9, 10; Matt. 6:20</reflink>). It assumes sometimes the more aggravated form of avarice, which is the mark of cold-hearted worldliness.

cow.d: A cow and her calf were not to be killed on the same day (<reflink>Lev. 22:28; Ex. 23:19; Deut. 22:6, 7</reflink>). The reason for this enactment is not given. A state of great poverty is described in the words of Isa. 7:21-25, where, instead of possessing great resources, a man shall depend for the subsistence of himself and his family on what a single cow and two sheep could yield.

crane.d: (<reflink>Isa. 38:14; Jer. 8:7</reflink>). In both of these passages the Authorized Version has reversed the Hebrew order of the words. "Crane or swallow" should be "swallow or crane," as in the Revised Version. The rendering is there correct. The Hebrew for crane is _'agur_, the Grus cincerea, a bird well known in Palestine. It is migratory, and is distinguished by its loud voice, its cry being hoarse and melancholy.

creation.d: "In the beginning" God created, i.e., called into being, all things out of nothing. This creative act on the part of God was absolutely free, and for infinitely wise reasons. The cause of all things exists only in the will of God. The work of creation is attributed (1) to the Godhead (<reflink>Gen. 1:1, 26</reflink>); (2) to the Father (<reflink>1 Cor. 8:6</reflink>); (3) to the Son (<reflink>John 1:3; Col. 1:16, 17</reflink>); (4) to the Holy Spirit (<reflink>Gen. 1:2; Job 26:13; Ps. 104:30</reflink>). The fact that he is the Creator distinguishes Jehovah as the true God (<reflink>Isa. 37:16; 40:12, 13; 54:5; Ps. 96:5; Jer. 10:11, 12</reflink>). The one great end in the work of creation is the manifestation of the glory of the Creator (<reflink>Col. 1:16; Rev. 4:11; Rom. 11:36</reflink>). God's works, equally with God's word, are a revelation from him; and between the teachings of the one and those of the other, when rightly understood, there can be no contradiction.

creature.d: denotes the whole creation in Rom. 8:39; Col. 1:15; Rev. 5:13; the whole human race in Mark 16:15; Rom. 8:19-22.

crescens.d: increasing, probably one of the seventy disciples of Christ. He was one of Paul's assistants (<reflink>2 Tim. 4:10</reflink>), probably a Christian of Rome.

crete.d: now called Candia, one of the largest islands in the Meditterranean, about 140 miles long and 35 broad. It was at one time a very prosperous and populous island, having a "hundred cities." The character of the people is described in Paul's quotation from "one of their own poets" (Epimenides) in his epistle to Titus: "The Cretans are alway liars, evil beasts, slow bellies" (<reflink>Titus 1:12</reflink>). Jews from Crete were in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost (<reflink>Acts 2:11</reflink>). The island was visited by Paul on his voyage to Rome (Acts 27). Here Paul subsequently left Titus (1:5) "to ordain elders." Some have supposed that it was the original home of the Caphtorim (q.v.) or Philistines.

crisping-pin.d: (<reflink>Isa. 3:22; R.V., "satchel"</reflink>), some kind of female ornament, probably like the modern reticule. The Hebrew word _harit_ properly signifies pouch or casket or purse. It is rendered "bag" in 2 Kings 5:23.

crispus.d: curled, the chief of the synagogue at Corinth (<reflink>Acts 18:8</reflink>). He was converted and, with his family, baptized by Paul (<reflink>1 Cor. 1:14</reflink>).

cross.d: in the New Testament the instrument of crucifixion, and hence used for the crucifixion of Christ itself (<reflink>Eph. 2:16; Heb. 12:2; 1 Cor. 1:17, 18; Gal. 5:11; 6:12, 14; Phil. 3:18</reflink>). The word is also used to denote any severe affliction or trial (<reflink>Matt. 10:38; 16:24; Mark 8:34; 10:21</reflink>).

crown.d: (1.) Denotes the plate of gold in the front of the high priest's mitre (<reflink>Ex. 29:6; 39:30</reflink>). The same Hebrew word so rendered (ne'zer) denotes the diadem worn by Saul in battle (<reflink>2 Sam. 1:10</reflink>), and also that which was used at the coronation of Joash (<reflink>2 Kings 11:12</reflink>).

crown of thorns.d: our Lord was crowned with a, in mockery by the Romans (<reflink>Matt. 27:29</reflink>). The object of Pilate's guard in doing this was probably to insult, and not specially to inflict pain. There is nothing to show that the shrub thus used was, as has been supposed, the spina Christi, which could have been easily woven into a wreath. It was probably the thorny nabk, which grew abundantly round about Jerusalem, and whose flexible, pliant, and round branches could easily be platted into the form of a crown. (<see target="x-self">See THORN , 3.</see>)

crucifixion.d: a common mode of punishment among heathen nations in early times. It is not certain whether it was known among the ancient Jews; probably it was not. The modes of capital punishment according to the Mosaic law were, by the sword (Ex. 21), strangling, fire (Lev. 20), and stoning (Deut. 21).

cruse.d: a utensil; a flask or cup for holding water (<reflink>1 Sam. 26:11, 12, 16; 1 Kings 19:6</reflink>) or oil (<reflink>1 Kings 17:12, 14, 16</reflink>). In 1 Kings 14:3 the word there so rendered means properly a bottle, as in Jer. 19:1, 10, or pitcher. In 2 Kings 2:20, a platter or flat metal saucer is intended. The Hebrew word here used is translated "dish" in 21:13; "pans," in 2 Chr. 35:13; and "bosom," in Prov. 19:24; 26:15 (R.V., "dish").

crystal.d: (<reflink>Ezek. 1:22, with the epithet "terrible," as dazzling the spectators with its brightness</reflink>). The word occurs in Rev. 4:6; 21:11; 22:1. It is a stone of the flint order, the most refined kind of quartz. The Greek word here used means also literally "ice." The ancients regarded the crystal as only pure water congealed into extreme hardness by great length of time.

cubit.d: Heb. 'ammah; i.e., "mother of the arm," the fore-arm, is a word derived from the Latin cubitus, the lower arm. It is difficult to determine the exact length of this measure, from the uncertainty whether it included the entire length from the elbow to the tip of the longest finger, or only from the elbow to the root of the hand at the wrist. The probability is that the longer was the original cubit. The common computation as to the length of the cubit makes it 20.24 inches for the ordinary cubit, and 21.888 inches for the sacred one. This is the same as the Egyptian measurements.

cuckoo.d: (Heb. shahaph), from a root meaning "to be lean; slender." This bird is mentioned only in Lev. 11:16 and Deut. 14:15 (R.V., "seamew"). Some have interpreted the Hebrew word by "petrel" or "shearwater" (Puffinus cinereus), which is found on the coast of Syria; others think it denotes the "sea-gull" or "seamew." The common cuckoo (Cuculus canorus) feeds on reptiles and large insects. It is found in Asia and Africa as well as in Europe. It only passes the winter in Palestine. The Arabs suppose it to utter the cry _Yakub_, and hence they call it _tir el-Yakub_; i.e., "Jacob's bird."

cucumbers.d: (Heb. plur. kishshuim; i.e., "hard," "difficult" of digestion, only in Num. 11:5). This vegetable is extensively cultivated in the East at the present day, as it appears to have been in earlier times among the Hebrews. It belongs to the gourd family of plants. In the East its cooling pulp and juice are most refreshing. "We need not altogether wonder that the Israelites, wearily marching through the arid solitudes of the Sinaitic peninsula, thought more of the cucumbers and watermelons of which they had had no lack in Egypt, rather than of the cruel bondage which was the price of these luxuries." Groser's Scripture Natural History.

cummin.d: (Heb. kammon; i.e., a "condiment"), the fruit or seed of an umbelliferous plant, the Cuminum sativum, still extensively cultivated in the East. Its fruit is mentioned in Isa. 28:25, 27. In the New Testament it is mentioned in Matt. 23:23, where our Lord pronounces a "woe" on the scribes and Pharisees, who were zealous in paying tithes of "mint and anise and cummin," while they omitted the weightier matters of the law." "It is used as a spice, both bruised, to mix with bread, and also boiled, in the various messes and stews which compose an Oriental banquet." Tristram, Natural History.

cup.d: a wine-cup (<reflink>Gen. 40:11, 21</reflink>), various forms of which are found on Assyrian and Egyptian monuments. All Solomon's drinking vessels were of gold (<reflink>1 Kings 10: 21</reflink>). The cups mentioned in the New Testament were made after Roman and Greek models, and were sometimes of gold (<reflink>Rev. 17:4</reflink>).

cup-bearer.d: an officer of high rank with Egyptian, Persian, Assyrian, and Jewish monarchs. The cup-bearer of the king of Egypt is mentioned in connection with Joseph's history (<reflink>Gen. 40:1-21; 41:9</reflink>). Rabshakeh (q.v.) was cup-bearer in the Assyrian court (<reflink>2 Kings 18:17</reflink>). Nehemiah filled this office to the king of Persia (<reflink>Neh. 1:11</reflink>). We read also of Solomon's cup-bearers (<reflink>1 Kings 10:5; 2 Chr. 9:4</reflink>).

curious arts.d: (<reflink>Acts 19:19</reflink>), magical arts; jugglery practised by the Ephesian conjurers. Ephesus was noted for its wizard and the "Ephesian spells;" i.e., charms or scraps of parchment written over with certain formula, which were worn as a safeguard against all manner of evils. The more important and powerful of these charms were written out in books which circulated among the exorcists, and were sold at a great price.

curse.d: denounced by God against the serpent (<reflink>Gen. 3:14</reflink>), and against Cain (4:11). These divine maledictions carried their effect with them. Prophetical curses were sometimes pronounced by holy men (<reflink>Gen. 9:25; 49:7; Deut. 27:15; Josh. 6:26</reflink>). Such curses are not the consequence of passion or revenge, they are predictions.

curtain.d: (1.) Ten curtains, each twenty-eight cubits long and four wide, made of fine linen, also eleven made of goat's hair, covered the tabernacle (<reflink>Ex. 26:1-13; 36:8-17</reflink>).

cush.d: black. (1.) A son, probably the eldest, of Ham, and the father of Nimrod (<reflink>Gen. 10:8; 1 Chr. 1:10</reflink>). From him the land of Cush seems to have derived its name. The question of the precise locality of the land of Cush has given rise to not a little controversy. The second river of Paradise surrounded the whole land of Cush (<reflink>Gen. 2:13, R.V.</reflink>). The term Cush is in the Old Testament generally applied to the countries south of the Israelites. It was the southern limit of Egypt (<reflink>Ezek. 29:10, A.V. "Ethiopia," Heb. Cush</reflink>), with which it is generally associated (<reflink>Ps. 68:31; Isa. 18:1; Jer. 46:9, etc.</reflink>). It stands also associated with Elam (<reflink>Isa. 11:11</reflink>), with Persia (<reflink>Ezek. 38:5</reflink>), and with the Sabeans (<reflink>Isa. 45:14</reflink>). From these facts it has been inferred that Cush included Arabia and the country on the west coast of the Red Sea. …

cushan.d: probably a poetic or prolonged name of the land of Cush, the Arabian Cush (<reflink>Hab. 3:7</reflink>). Some have, however, supposed this to be the same as Chushan-rishathaim (<reflink>Judg. 3:8, 10</reflink>), i.e., taking the latter part of the name as a title or local appellation, Chushan "of the two iniquities" (= oppressing Israel, and provoking them to idolatry), a Mesopotamian king, identified by Rawlinson with Asshur-ris-ilim (the father of Tiglathpileser I.); but incorrectly, for the empire of Assyria was not yet founded. He held Israel in bondage for eight years.

cushite.d: (1.) The messenger sent by Joab to David to announce his victory over Absalom (<reflink>2 Sam. 18:32</reflink>).

custom.d: a tax imposed by the Romans. The tax-gatherers were termed publicans (q.v.), who had their stations at the gates of cities, and in the public highways, and at the place set apart for that purpose, called the "receipt of custom" (<reflink>Matt.9: 9; Mark 2:14</reflink>), where they collected the money that was to be paid on certain goods (<reflink>Matt.17:25</reflink>). These publicans were tempted to exact more from the people than was lawful, and were, in consequence of their extortions, objects of great hatred. The Pharisees would have no intercourse with them (<reflink>Matt.5:46, 47; 9:10, 11</reflink>).

cuthah.d: one of the Babylonian cities or districts from which Shalmaneser transplanted certain colonists to Samaria (<reflink>2 Kings 17:24</reflink>). Some have conjectured that the "Cutheans" were identical with the "Cossaeans" who inhabited the hill-country to the north of the river Choaspes. Cuthah is now identified with Tell Ibrahim, 15 miles north-east of Babylon.

cutting.d: the flesh in various ways was an idolatrous practice, a part of idol-worship (<reflink>Deut. 14:1; 1 Kings 18:28</reflink>). The Israelites were commanded not to imitate this practice (<reflink>Lev. 19:28; 21:5; Deut. 14:1</reflink>). The tearing of the flesh from grief and anguish of spirit in mourning for the dead was regarded as a mark of affection (<reflink>Jer. 16:6; 41:5; 48:37</reflink>).

cymbals.d: (Heb. tzeltzelim, from a root meaning to "tinkle"), musical instruments, consisting of two convex pieces of brass one held in each hand, which were clashed together to produce a loud clanging sound; castanets; "loud cymbals." "Highsounding cymbals" consisted of two larger plates, one held also in each hand (<reflink>2 Sam. 6:5; Ps. 150:5; 1 Chr. 13:8; 15:16, 19, 28; 1 Cor. 13:1</reflink>).

cypress.d: (Heb. tirzah, "hardness"), mentioned only in Isa. 44:14 (R.V., "holm tree"). The oldest Latin version translates this word by ilex, i.e., the evergreen oak, which may possibly have been the tree intended; but there is great probability that our Authorized Version is correct in rendering it "cypress." This tree grows abundantly on the mountains of Hermon. Its wood is hard and fragrant, and very durable. Its foliage is dark and gloomy. It is an evergreen (Cupressus sempervirens). "Throughout the East it is used as a funereal tree; and its dark, tall, waving plumes render it peculiarly appropriate among the tombs."

cyprus.d: one of the largest islands of the Mediterranean, about 148 miles long and 40 broad. It is distant about 60 miles from the Syrian coast. It was the "Chittim" of the Old Testament (<reflink>Num. 24:24</reflink>). The Greek colonists gave it the name of Kypros, from the cyprus, i.e., the henna (<see target="x-self">see CAMPHIRE</see>), which grew on this island. It was originally inhabited by Phoenicians. In B.C. 477 it fell under the dominion of the Greeks; and became a Roman province B.C. 58. In ancient times it was a centre of great commercial activity. Corn and wine and oil were produced here in the greatest perfection. It was rich also in timber and in mineral wealth.

cyrene.d: a city (now Tripoli) in Upper Libya, North Africa, founded by a colony of Greeks (B.C. 630). It contained latterly a large number of Jews, who were introduced into the city by Ptolemy, the son of Lagus, because he thought they would contribute to the security of the place. They increased in number and influence; and we are thus prepared for the frequent references to them in connection with the early history of Christianity. Simon, who bore our Lord's cross, was a native of this place (<reflink>Matt. 27:32; Mark 15:21</reflink>). Jews from Cyrene were in Jerusalem at Pentecost (<reflink>Acts 2:10</reflink>); and Cyrenian Jews had a synagogue at Jerusalem (6:9). Converts belonging to Cyrene contributed to the formation of the first Gentile church at Antioch (11:20). Among "the prophets and teachers" who "ministered to the Lord at Antioch" was Lucius of Cyrene (13:1).

cyrenius.d: the Grecized form of Quirinus. His full name was Publius Sulpicius Quirinus. Recent historical investigation has proved that Quirinus was governor of Cilicia, which was annexed to Syria at the time of our Lord's birth. Cilicia, which he ruled, being a province of Syria, he is called the governor, which he was de jure, of Syria. Some ten years afterwards he was appointed governor of Syria for the second time. During his tenure of office, at the time of our Lord's birth (<reflink>Luke 2:2</reflink>), a "taxing" (R.V., "enrolment;" i.e., a registration) of the people was "first made;" i.e., was made for the first time under his government. (<see target="x-self">See TAXING.</see>)

cyrus.d: (Heb. Ko'resh), the celebrated "King of Persia" (Elam) who was conqueror of Babylon, and issued the decree of liberation to the Jews (<reflink>Ezra 1:1, 2</reflink>). He was the son of Cambyses, the prince of Persia, and was born about B.C. 599. In the year B.C. 559 he became king of Persia, the kingdom of Media being added to it partly by conquest. Cyrus was a great military leader, bent on universal conquest. Babylon fell before his army (B.C. 538) on the night of Belshazzar's feast (<reflink>Dan. 5:30</reflink>), and then the ancient dominion of Assyria was also added to his empire (cf., "Go up, O Elam", Isa.21:2).

daberath.d: pasture, a Levitical town of Issachar (<reflink>Josh. 19:12; 21:28</reflink>), near the border of Zebulum. It is the modern small village of Deburich, at the base of Mount Tabor. Tradition has incorrectly made it the scene of the miracle of the cure of the lunatic child (<reflink>Matt. 17:14</reflink>).

daemon.d: the Greek form, rendered "devil" in the Authorized Version of the New Testament. Daemons are spoken of as spiritual beings (<reflink>Matt. 8:16; 10:1; 12:43-45</reflink>) at enmity with God, and as having a certain power over man (<reflink>James 2:19; Rev. 16:14</reflink>). They recognize our Lord as the Son of God (<reflink>Matt. 8:20; Luke 4:41</reflink>). They belong to the number of those angels that "kept not their first estate," "unclean spirits," "fallen angels," the angels of the devil (<reflink>Matt. 25:41; Rev. 12:7-9</reflink>). They are the "principalities and powers" against which we must "wrestle" (<reflink>Eph. 6:12</reflink>).

daemoniac.d: one "possessed with a devil." In the days of our Lord and his apostles, evil spirits, "daemons," were mysteriously permitted by God to exercise an influence both over the souls and bodies of men, inflicting dumbness (<reflink>Matt. 9:32</reflink>), blindness (12:22), epilepsy (<reflink>Mark 9:17-27</reflink>), insanity (<reflink>Matt. 8:28; Mark 5:1-5</reflink>). Daemoniacs are frequently distinguished from those who are afflicted with ordinary bodily maladies (<reflink>Mark 1:32; 16:17, 18; Luke 6:17, 18</reflink>). The daemons speak in their own persons (<reflink>Matt. 8:29; Mark 1:23, 24; 5:7</reflink>). This influence is clearly distinguished from the ordinary power of corruption and of temptation over men. In the daemoniac his personality seems to be destroyed, and his actions, words, and even thoughts to be overborne by the evil spirit (Mark, l.c.; Acts 19:15).

dagon.d: little fish; diminutive from dag = a fish, the fish-god; the national god of the Philistines (<reflink>Judg. 16:23</reflink>). This idol had the body of a fish with the head and hands of a man. It was an Assyrio-Babylonian deity, the worship of which was introduced among the Philistines through Chaldea. The most famous of the temples of Dagon were at Gaza (<reflink>Judg. 16:23-30</reflink>) and Ashdod (<reflink>1 Sam. 5:1-7</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See FISH.</see>)

dagon's house.d: (<reflink>1 Sam. 5:2</reflink>), or Beth-dagon, as elsewhere rendered (<reflink>Josh.15: 41; 19:27</reflink>), was the sanctuary or temple of Dagon.

daily sacrifice.d: (<reflink>Dan. 8:12; 11:31; 12:11</reflink>), a burnt offering of two lambs of a year old, which were daily sacrificed in the name of the whole Israelitish people upon the great altar, the first at dawn of day, and the second at evening (<reflink>Dan. 9:21</reflink>), or more correctly, "between the two evenings." (<see target="x-self">See SACRIFICE.</see>)

dale, the king's.d: the name of a valley, the alternative for "the valley of Shaveh" (q.v.), near the Dead Sea, where the king of Sodom met Abraham (<reflink>Gen. 14:17</reflink>). Some have identified it with the southern part of the valley of Jehoshaphat, where Absalom reared his family monument (<reflink>2 Sam. 18:18</reflink>).

dalmanutha.d: a place on the west of the Sea of Galilee, mentioned only in Mark 8:10. In the parallel passage it is said that Christ came "into the borders of Magdala" (<reflink>Matt. 15:39</reflink>). It is plain, then, that Dalmanutha was near Magdala, which was probably the Greek name of one of the many Migdols (i.e., watch-towers) on the western side of the lake of Gennesaret. It has been identified in the ruins of a village about a mile from Magdala, in the little open valley of 'Ain-el-Barideh, "the cold fountain," called el-Mejdel, possibly the "Migdal-el" of Josh. 19:38.

dalmatia.d: a mountainous country on the eastern shore of the Adriatic, a part of the Roman province of Illyricum. It still bears its ancient name. During Paul's second imprisonment at Rome, Titus left him to visit Dalmatia (<reflink>2 Tim. 4:10</reflink>) for some unknown purpose. Paul had himself formerly preached in that region (<reflink>Rom. 15:19</reflink>).

damaris.d: a heifer, an Athenian woman converted to Christianity under the preaching of Paul (<reflink>Acts 17:34</reflink>). Some have supposed that she may have been the wife of Dionysius the Areopagite.

damascus.d: activity, the most ancient of Oriental cities; the capital of Syria (<reflink>Isa. 7:8; 17:3</reflink>); situated about 133 miles to the north of Jerusalem. Its modern name is Esh-Sham; i.e., "the East."

damnation.d: in Rom. 13:2, means "condemnation," which comes on those who withstand God's ordinance of magistracy. This sentence of condemnation comes not from the magistrate, but from God, whose authority is thus resisted.

dan.d: a judge. (1.) The fifth son of Jacob. His mother was Bilhah, Rachel's maid (<reflink>Gen. 30:6, "God hath judged me", Heb. dananni</reflink>). The blessing pronounced on him by his father was, "Dan shall judge his people" (49:16), probably in allusion to the judgeship of Samson, who was of the tribe of Dan.

dan-jaan.d: woodland Dan, a place probably somewhere in the direction of Dan, near the sources of the Jordan (<reflink>2 Sam. 24:6</reflink>). The LXX. and the Vulgate read "Dan-ja'ar", i.e., "Dan in the forest."

dance.d: found in Judg. 21:21, 23; Ps. 30:11; 149:3; 150:4; Jer. 31:4, 13, etc., as the translation of _hul_, which points to the whirling motion of Oriental sacred dances. It is the rendering of a word (rakad') which means to skip or leap for joy, in Eccl. 3:4; Job 21:11; Isa. 13:21, etc.

daniel.d: God is my judge, or judge of God. (1.) David's second son, "born unto him in Hebron, of Abigail the Carmelitess" (<reflink>1 Chr. 3:1</reflink>). He is called also Chileab (<reflink>2 Sam. 3:3</reflink>).

daniel, book of.d: is ranked by the Jews in that division of their Bible called the Hagiographa (Heb. Khethubim). (<see target="x-self">See </see>) It consists of two distinct parts. The first part, consisting of the first six chapters, is chiefly historical; and the second part, consisting of the remaining six chapters, is chiefly prophetical.

dannah.d: murmuring, a city (<reflink>Josh. 15:49</reflink>) in the mountains of Judah about 8 miles south-west of Hebron.

dimnah.d: dunghill, a city of Zebulun given to the Merarite Levites (<reflink>Josh. 21:35</reflink>). In 1 Chr. 6:77 the name "Rimmon" is substituted.

dinah.d: judged; vindicated, daughter of Jacob by Leah, and sister of Simeon and Levi (<reflink>Gen. 30:21</reflink>). She was seduced by Shechem, the son of Hamor, the Hivite chief, when Jacob's camp was in the neighbourhood of Shechem. This led to the terrible revenge of Simeon and Levi in putting the Shechemites to death (Gen. 34). Jacob makes frequent reference to this deed of blood with abhorrence and regret (<reflink>Gen. 34:30; 49:5-7</reflink>). She is mentioned among the rest of Jacob's family that went down into Egypt (<reflink>Gen. 46:8, 15</reflink>).

dine.d: (<reflink>Gen. 43:16</reflink>). It was the custom in Egypt to dine at noon. But it is probable that the Egyptians took their principal meal in the evening, as was the general custom in the East (<reflink>Luke 14:12</reflink>).

dinhabah.d: robbers' den, an Edomitish city, the capital of king Bela (<reflink>Gen. 36:32</reflink>). It is probably the modern Dibdiba, a little north-east of Petra.

dionysius.d: the Areopagite, one of Paul's converts at Athens (<reflink>Acts 17:34</reflink>).

diotrephes.d: Jove-nourished, rebuked by John for his pride (<reflink>3 John 1:9</reflink>). He was a Judaizer, prating against John and his fellow-labourers "with malicious words" (7).

disciple.d: a scholar, sometimes applied to the followers of John the Baptist (<reflink>Matt. 9:14</reflink>), and of the Pharisees (22:16), but principally to the followers of Christ.
