A disciple of Christ is one who (1) believes his doctrine, (2) rests on his sacrifice, (3) imbibes his spirit, and (4) imitates his example (<reflink>Matt. 10:24; Luke 14:26, 27, 33; John 6:69</reflink>).

dish.d: for eating from (<reflink>2 Kings 21:13</reflink>). Judas dipped his hand with a "sop" or piece of bread in the same dish with our Lord, thereby indicating friendly intimacy (<reflink>Matt. 26:23</reflink>). The "lordly dish" in Judg. 5:25 was probably the shallow drinking cup, usually of brass. In Judg. 6:38 the same Hebrew word is rendered "bowl."

dishan.d: antelope, the youngest son of Seir the Horite, head of one of the tribes of Idumaea (<reflink>Gen. 36:21, 28, 30</reflink>).

dispensation.d: (Gr. oikonomia, "management," "economy"). (1.) The method or scheme according to which God carries out his purposes towards men is called a dispensation. There are usually reckoned three dispensations, the Patriarchal, the Mosaic or Jewish, and the Christian. (<see target="x-self">See COVENANT, Administration of.</see>) These were so many stages in God's unfolding of his purpose of grace toward men. The word is not found with this meaning in Scripture.

dispersion.d: (Gr. diaspora, "scattered," James 1:1; 1 Pet. 1:1) of the Jews. At various times, and from the operation of divers causes, the Jews were separated and scattered into foreign countries "to the outmost parts of heaven" (<reflink>Deut. 30:4</reflink>).

distaff.d: (Heb. pelek, a "circle"), the instrument used for twisting threads by a whirl (<reflink>Prov. 31:19</reflink>).

divination.d: of false prophets (<reflink>Deut. 18:10, 14; Micah 3:6, 7, 11</reflink>), of necromancers (<reflink>1 Sam. 28:8</reflink>), of the Philistine priests and diviners (<reflink>1 Sam. 6:2</reflink>), of Balaam (<reflink>Josh. 13:22</reflink>). Three kinds of divination are mentioned in Ezek. 21:21, by arrows, consulting with images (the teraphim), and by examining the entrails of animals sacrificed. The practice of this art seems to have been encouraged in ancient Egypt. Diviners also abounded among the aborigines of Canaan and the Philistines (<reflink>Isa. 2:6; 1 Sam. 28</reflink>). At a later period multitudes of magicians poured from Chaldea and Arabia into the land of Israel, and pursued their occupations (<reflink>Isa. 8:19; 2 Kings 21:6; 2 Chr. 33:6</reflink>). …

divorce.d: The dissolution of the marriage tie was regulated by the Mosaic law (<reflink>Deut. 24:1-4</reflink>). The Jews, after the Captivity, were reguired to dismiss the foreign women they had married contrary to the law (<reflink>Ezra 10:11-19</reflink>). Christ limited the permission of divorce to the single case of adultery. It seems that it was not uncommon for the Jews at that time to dissolve the union on very slight pretences (<reflink>Matt. 5:31, 32; 19:1-9; Mark 10:2-12; Luke 16:18</reflink>). These precepts given by Christ regulate the law of divorce in the Christian Church.

dizahab.d: region of gold, a place in the desert of Sinai, on the western shore of the Elanitic gulf (<reflink>Deut. 1:1</reflink>). It is now called Dehab.

doctor.d: (<reflink>Luke 2:46; 5:17; Acts 5:34</reflink>), a teacher. The Jewish doctors taught and disputed in synagogues, or wherever they could find an audience. Their disciples were allowed to propose to them questions. They assumed the office without any appointment to it. The doctors of the law were principally of the sect of the Pharisees. Schools were established after the destruction of Jerusalem at Babylon and Tiberias, in which academical degrees were conferred on those who passed a certain examination. Those of the school of Tiberias were called by the title "rabbi," and those of Babylon by that of "master."

dodai.d: loving, one of David's captains (<reflink>1 Chr. 27:4</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See DODO [2].</see>)

dodanim.d: leaders, a race descended from Javan (<reflink>Gen. 10:4</reflink>). They are known in profane history as the Dardani, originally inhabiting Illyricum. They were a semi-Pelasgic race, and in the ethnographical table (Gen. 10) they are grouped with the Chittim (q.v.). In 1 Chr. 1:7, they are called Rodanim. The LXX. and the Samaritan Version also read Rhodii, whence some have concluded that the Rhodians, the inhabitants of the island of Rhodes, are meant.

dodo.d: amatory; loving. (1.) A descendant of Issachar (<reflink>Judg. 10:1</reflink>).

doeg.d: fearful, an Edomite, the chief overseer of Saul's flocks (<reflink>1 Sam. 21:7</reflink>). At the command of Saul he slew the high priest Ahimelech (q.v.) at Nob, together with all the priests to the number of eighty-five persons. (Comp. Ps. 52, title.)

dog.d: frequently mentioned both in the Old and New Testaments. Dogs were used by the Hebrews as a watch for their houses (<reflink>Isa. 56:10</reflink>), and for guarding their flocks (<reflink>Job 30:1</reflink>). There were also then as now troops of semi-wild dogs that wandered about devouring dead bodies and the offal of the streets (<reflink>1 Kings 14:11; 16:4; 21:19, 23; 22:38; Ps. 59:6, 14</reflink>).

doleful creatures.d: (<reflink>occurring only Isa. 13:21. Heb. ochim, i.e., "shrieks;" hence "howling animals"</reflink>), a general name for screech owls (howlets), which occupy the desolate palaces of Babylon. Some render the word "hyaenas."

door-keeper.d: This word is used in Ps. 84:10 (R.V. marg., "stand at the threshold of," etc.), but there it signifies properly "sitting at the threshold in the house of God." The psalmist means that he would rather stand at the door of God's house and merely look in, than dwell in houses where iniquity prevailed.

door-posts.d: The Jews were commanded to write the divine name on the posts (mezuzoth') of their doors (<reflink>Deut. 6:9</reflink>). The Jews, misunderstanding this injunction, adopted the custom of writing on a slip of parchment these verses (<reflink>Deut. 6:4-9, and 11:13-21</reflink>), which they enclosed in a reed or cylinder and fixed on the right-hand door-post of every room in the house.

doors.d: moved on pivots of wood fastened in sockets above and below (<reflink>Prov. 26:14</reflink>). They were fastened by a lock (<reflink>Judg. 3:23, 25; Cant. 5:5</reflink>) or by a bar (<reflink>Judg. 16:3; Job 38:10</reflink>). In the interior of Oriental houses, curtains were frequently used instead of doors.

dophkah.d: knocking, an encampment of the Israelites in the wilderness (<reflink>Num. 33:12</reflink>). It was in the desert of Sin, on the eastern shore of the western arm of the Red Sea, somewhere in the Wady Feiran.

dor.d: dwelling, the Dora of the Romans, an ancient royal city of the Canaanites (<reflink>Josh. 11:1, 2; 12:23</reflink>). It was the most southern settlement of the Phoenicians on the coast of Syria. The original inhabitants seem never to have been expelled, although they were made tributary by David. It was one of Solomon's commissariat districts (<reflink>Judg. 1:27; 1 Kings 4:11</reflink>). It has been identified with Tantura (so named from the supposed resemblance of its tower to a tantur, i.e., "a horn"). This tower fell in 1895, and nothing remains but debris and foundation walls, the remains of an old Crusading fortress. It is about 8 miles north of Caesarea, "a sad and sickly hamlet of wretched huts on a naked sea-beach."

dorcas.d: a female antelope, or gazelle, a pious Christian widow at Joppa whom Peter restored to life (<reflink>Acts 9:36-41</reflink>). She was a Hellenistic Jewess, called Tabitha by the Jews and Dorcas by the Greeks.

dothan.d: two wells, a famous pasture-ground where Joseph found his brethren watching their flocks. Here, at the suggestion of Judah, they sold him to the Ishmaelite merchants (<reflink>Gen. 37:17</reflink>). It is mentioned on monuments in B.C. 1600.

dough.d: (batsek, meaning "swelling," i.e., in fermentation). The dough the Israelites had prepared for baking was carried away by them out of Egypt in their kneading-troughs (<reflink>Ex. 12:34, 39</reflink>). In the process of baking, the dough had to be turned (<reflink>Hos. 7:8</reflink>).

dove.d: In their wild state doves generally build their nests in the clefts of rocks, but when domesticated "dove-cots" are prepared for them (<reflink>Cant. 2:14; Jer. 48:28; Isa. 60:8</reflink>). The dove was placed on the standards of the Assyrians and Babylonians in honour, it is supposed, of Semiramis (<reflink>Jer. 25:38; Vulg., "fierceness of the dove;" comp. Jer. 46:16; 50:16</reflink>). Doves and turtle-doves were the only birds that could be offered in sacrifice, as they were clean according to the Mosaic law (<reflink>Ge. 15:9; Lev. 5:7; 12:6; Luke 2:24</reflink>). The dove was the harbinger of peace to Noah (<reflink>Gen. 8:8, 10</reflink>). It is often mentioned as the emblem of purity (<reflink>Ps. 68:13</reflink>). It is a symbol of the Holy Spirit (<reflink>Gen. 1:2; Matt. 3:16; Mark 1:10; Luke 3:22; John 1:32</reflink>); also of tender and devoted affection (<reflink>Cant. 1:15; 2:14</reflink>). …

dove's dung.d: (<reflink>2 Kings 6:25</reflink>) has been generally understood literally. There are instances in history of the dung of pigeons being actually used as food during a famine. Compare also the language of Rabshakeh to the Jews (<reflink>2 Kings 18:27; Isa. 36:12</reflink>). This name, however, is applied by the Arabs to different vegetable substances, and there is room for the opinion of those who think that some such substance is here referred to, as, e.g., the seeds of a kind of millet, or a very inferior kind of pulse, or the root of the ornithogalum, i.e., bird-milk, the star-of-Bethlehem.

dowry.d: (mohar; i.e., price paid for a wife, Gen. 34:12; Ex. 22:17; 1 Sam. 18:25), a nuptial present; some gift, as a sum of money, which the bridegroom offers to the father of his bride as a satisfaction before he can receive her. Jacob had no dowry to give for his wife, but he gave his services (<reflink>Gen. 29:18; 30:20; 34:12</reflink>).

dragon.d: (1.) Heb. tannim, plural of tan. The name of some unknown creature inhabiting desert places and ruins (<reflink>Job 30:29; Ps. 44:19; Isa. 13:22; 34:13; 43:20; Jer. 10:22; Micah 1:8; Mal. 1:3</reflink>); probably, as translated in the Revised Version, the jackal (q.v.).

dragon well.d: (<reflink>Neh. 2:13</reflink>), supposed by some to be identical with the Pool of Gihon.

dram.d: The Authorized Version understood the word 'adarkonim (<reflink>1 Chr. 29:7; Ezra 8:27</reflink>), and the similar word darkomnim (<reflink>Ezra 2:69; Neh. 7:70</reflink>), as equivalent to the Greek silver coin the drachma. But the Revised Version rightly regards it as the Greek dareikos, a Persian gold coin (the daric) of the value of about 1 pound, 2s., which was first struck by Darius, the son of Hystaspes, and was current in Western Asia long after the fall of the Persian empire. (<see target="x-self">See DARIC.</see>)

draught-house.d: (<reflink>2 Kings 10:27</reflink>). Jehu ordered the temple of Baal to be destroyed, and the place to be converted to the vile use of receiving offal or ordure. (<reflink>Comp. Matt. 15:17.</reflink>)

drawer of water.d: (<reflink>Deut. 29:11; Josh. 9:21, 23</reflink>), a servile employment to which the Gibeonites were condemned.

dream.d: God has frequently made use of dreams in communicating his will to men. The most remarkable instances of this are recorded in the history of Jacob (<reflink>Gen. 28:12; 31:10</reflink>), Laban (31:24), Joseph (37:9-11), Gideon (Judg. 7), and Solomon (<reflink>1 Kings 3:5</reflink>). Other significant dreams are also recorded, such as those of Abimelech (<reflink>Gen. 20:3-7</reflink>), Pharaoh's chief butler and baker (40:5), Pharaoh (41:1-8), the Midianites (<reflink>Judg. 7:13</reflink>), Nebuchadnezzar (<reflink>Dan. 2:1; 4:10, 18</reflink>), the wise men from the east (<reflink>Matt. 2:12</reflink>), and Pilate's wife (27:19).

dregs.d: (<reflink>Ps. 75:8; Isa. 51:17, 22</reflink>), the lees of wine which settle at the bottom of the vessel.

dress.d: (1.) Materials used. The earliest and simplest an apron of fig-leaves sewed together (<reflink>Gen. 3:7</reflink>); then skins of animals (3:21). Elijah's dress was probably the skin of a sheep (<reflink>2 Kings 1:8</reflink>). The Hebrews were early acquainted with the art of weaving hair into cloth (<reflink>Ex. 26:7; 35:6</reflink>), which formed the sackcloth of mourners. This was the material of John the Baptist's robe (<reflink>Matt. 3:4</reflink>). Wool was also woven into garments (<reflink>Lev. 13:47; Deut. 22:11; Ezek. 34:3; Job 31:20; Prov. 27:26</reflink>). The Israelites probably learned the art of weaving linen when they were in Egypt (<reflink>1 Chr. 4:21</reflink>). Fine linen was used in the vestments of the high priest (<reflink>Ex. 28:5</reflink>), as well as by the rich (<reflink>Gen. 41:42; Prov. 31:22; Luke 16:19</reflink>). The use of mixed material, as wool and flax, was forbidden (<reflink>Lev. 19:19; Deut. 22:11</reflink>).

drink.d: The drinks of the Hebrews were water, wine, "strong drink," and vinegar. Their drinking vessels were the cup, goblet or "basin," the "cruse" or pitcher, and the saucer.

drink, strong.d: (Heb. shekar'), an intoxicating liquor (<reflink>Judg. 13:4; Luke 1:15; Isa. 5:11; Micah 2:11</reflink>) distilled from corn, honey, or dates. The effects of the use of strong drink are referred to in Ps. 107:27; Isa. 24:20; 49:26; 51:17-22. Its use prohibited, Prov. 20:1. (<see target="x-self">See WINE.</see>)

drink-offering.d: consisted of wine (<reflink>Num. 15:5; Hos. 9:4</reflink>) poured around the altar (<reflink>Ex. 30:9</reflink>). Joined with meat-offerings (<reflink>Num. 6:15, 17; 2 Kings 16:13; Joel 1:9, 13; 2:14</reflink>), presented daily (<reflink>Ex. 29:40</reflink>), on the Sabbath (<reflink>Num. 28:9</reflink>), and on feast-days (28:14). One-fourth of an hin of wine was required for one lamb, one-third for a ram, and one-half for a bullock (<reflink>Num. 15:5; 28:7, 14</reflink>). "Drink offerings of blood" (<reflink>Ps. 16:4</reflink>) is used in allusion to the heathen practice of mingling the blood of animals sacrificed with wine or water, and pouring out the mixture in the worship of the gods, and the idea conveyed is that the psalmist would not partake of the abominations of the heathen.

dromedary.d: (<reflink>Isa. 60:6</reflink>), an African or Arabian species of camel having only one hump, while the Bactrian camel has two. It is distinguished from the camel only as a trained saddle-horse is distinguished from a cart-horse. It is remarkable for its speed (<reflink>Jer. 2:23</reflink>). Camels are frequently spoken of in partriarchal times (<reflink>Gen. 12:16; 24:10; 30:43; 31:17, etc.</reflink>). They were used for carrying burdens (<reflink>Gen. 37:25; Judg. 6:5</reflink>), and for riding (<reflink>Gen. 24:64</reflink>). The hair of the camel falls off of itself in spring, and is woven into coarse cloths and garments (<reflink>Matt. 3:4</reflink>). (See CAMEL

dropsy.d: mentioned only in Luke 14:2. The man afflicted with it was cured by Christ on the Sabbath.

eth-baal.d: with Baal, a king of Sidon (B.C. 940-908), father of Jezebel, who was the wife of Ahab (<reflink>1 Kings 16:31</reflink>). He is said to have been also a priest of Astarte, whose worship was closely allied to that of Baal, and this may account for his daughter's zeal in promoting idolatry in Israel. This marriage of Ahab was most fatal to both Israel and Judah. Dido, the founder of Carthage, was his granddaughter.

etham.d: perhaps another name for Khetam, or "fortress," on the Shur or great wall of Egypt, which extended from the Mediterranean to the Gulf of Suez. Here the Israelites made their third encampment (<reflink>Ex. 13:20; Num. 33:6</reflink>). The camp was probably a little to the west of the modern town of Ismailia. Here the Israelites were commanded to change their route (<reflink>Ex. 14:2</reflink>), and "turn" towards the south, and encamp before Pi-hahiroth. (<see target="x-self">See EXODUS; PITHOM.</see>)

ethan.d: firm. (1.) "The Ezrahite," distinguished for his wisdom (<reflink>1 Kings 4:31</reflink>). He is named as the author of the 89th Psalm. He was of the tribe of Levi.

ethanim.d: the month of gifts, i.e., of vintage offerings; called Tisri after the Exile; corresponding to part of September and October. It was the first month of the civil year, and the seventh of the sacred year (<reflink>1 Kings 8:2</reflink>).

ethiopia.d: country of burnt faces; the Greek word by which the Hebrew Cush is rendered (<reflink>Gen. 2:13; 2 Kings 19:9; Esther 1:1; Job 28:19; Ps. 68:31; 87:4</reflink>), a country which lay to the south of Egypt, beginning at Syene on the First Cataract (<reflink>Ezek. 29:10; 30:6</reflink>), and extending to beyond the confluence of the White and Blue Nile. It corresponds generally with what is now known as the Soudan (i.e., the land of the blacks). This country was known to the Hebrews, and is described in Isa. 18:1; Zeph. 3:10. They carried on some commercial intercourse with it (<reflink>Isa. 45:14</reflink>).

ethiopian eunuch.d: the chief officer or prime minister of state of Candace (q.v.), queen of Ethiopia. He was converted to Christianity through the instrumentality of Philip (<reflink>Act 8:27</reflink>). The northern portion of Ethiopia formed the kingdom of Meroe, which for a long period was ruled over by queens, and it was probably from this kingdom that the eunuch came.

ethiopian woman.d: the wife of Moses (<reflink>Num. 12:1</reflink>). It is supposed that Zipporah, Moses' first wife (<reflink>Ex. 2:21</reflink>), was now dead. His marriage of this "woman" descended from Ham gave offence to Aaron and Miriam.

eunice.d: happily conquering, the mother of Timothy, a believing Jewess, but married to a Greek (<reflink>Acts 16:1</reflink>). She trained her son from his childhood in the knowledge of the Scriptures (<reflink>2 Tim. 3:15</reflink>). She was distinguished by her "unfeigned faith."

eunuch.d: literally bed-keeper or chamberlain, and not necessarily in all cases one who was mutilated, although the practice of employing such mutilated persons in Oriental courts was common (<reflink>2 Kings 9:32; Esther 2:3</reflink>). The law of Moses excluded them from the congregation (<reflink>Deut. 23:1</reflink>). They were common also among the Greeks and Romans. It is said that even to-day there are some in Rome who are employed in singing soprano in the Sistine Chapel. Three classes of eunuchs are mentioned in Matt. 19:12.

euodias.d: a good journey, a female member of the church at Philippi. She was one who laboured much with Paul in the gospel. He exhorts her to be of one mind with Syntyche (<reflink>Phil. 4:2</reflink>). From this it seems they had been at variance with each other.

euphrates.d: Hebrew, Perath; Assyrian, Purat; Persian cuneiform, Ufratush, whence Greek Euphrates, meaning "sweet water." The Assyrian name means "the stream," or "the great stream." It is generally called in the Bible simply "the river" (<reflink>Ex. 23:31</reflink>), or "the great river" (<reflink>Deut. 1:7</reflink>).

euroclydon.d: south-east billow, the name of the wind which blew in the Adriatic Gulf, and which struck the ship in which Paul was wrecked on the coast of Malta (<reflink>Acts 27:14; R.V., "Euraquilo," i.e., north-east wind</reflink>). It is called a "tempestuous wind," i.e., as literally rendered, a "typhonic wind," or a typhoon. It is the modern Gregalia or Levanter. (<reflink>Comp. Jonah 1:4.</reflink>)

eutychus.d: fortunate, (<reflink>Acts 20:9-12</reflink>), a young man of Troas who fell through drowsiness from the open window of the third floor of the house where Paul was preaching, and was "taken up dead." The lattice-work of the window being open to admit the air, the lad fell out and down to the court below. Paul restored him to life again. (Comp. 1 Kings 17:21; 2 Kings 4:34.)

evangelist.d: a "publisher of glad tidings;" a missionary preacher of the gospel (<reflink>Eph. 4:11</reflink>). This title is applied to Philip (<reflink>Acts 21:8</reflink>), who appears to have gone from city to city preaching the word (8:4, 40). Judging from the case of Philip, evangelists had neither the authority of an apostle, nor the gift of prophecy, nor the responsibility of pastoral supervision over a portion of the flock. They were itinerant preachers, having it as their special function to carry the gospel to places where it was previously unknown. The writers of the four Gospels are known as the Evangelists.

eve.d: life; living, the name given by Adam to his wife (<reflink>Gen. 3:20; 4:1</reflink>). The account of her creation is given in Gen. 2:21, 22. The Creator, by declaring that it was not good for man to be alone, and by creating for him a suitable companion, gave sanction to monogamy. The commentator Matthew Henry says: "This companion was taken from his side to signify that she was to be dear unto him as his own flesh. Not from his head, lest she should rule over him; nor from his feet, lest he should tyrannize over her; but from his side, to denote that species of equality which is to subsist in the marriage state." And again, "That wife that is of God's making by special grace, and of God's bringing by special providence, is likely to prove a helpmeet to her husband." Through the subtle temptation of the serpent she violated the commandment of God by taking of the forbidden fruit, which she gave also unto her husband (<reflink>1 Tim. 2:13-15; 2 Cor. 11:3</reflink>). …

evening.d: the period following sunset with which the Jewish day began (<reflink>Gen. 1:5; Mark 13:35</reflink>). The Hebrews reckoned two evenings of each day, as appears from Ex. 16:12: 30:8; 12:6 (marg.); Lev. 23:5 (marg. R.V., "between the two evenings"). The "first evening" was that period when the sun was verging towards setting, and the "second evening" the moment of actual sunset. The word "evenings" in Jer. 5:6 should be "deserts" (marg. R.V.).

everlasting.d: eternal, applied to God (<reflink>Gen. 21:33; Deut. 33:27; Ps. 41:13; 90:2</reflink>). We also read of the "everlasting hills" (<reflink>Gen. 49:26</reflink>); an "everlasting priesthood" (<reflink>Ex. 40:15; Num. 25:13</reflink>). (See ETERNAL

evil eye.d: (<reflink>Prov. 23:6</reflink>), figuratively, the envious or covetous. (<reflink>Comp. Deut. 15:9; Matt. 20:15.</reflink>)

evil-merodach.d: Merodach's man, the son and successor of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon (<reflink>2 Kings 25:27; Jer. 52:31, 34</reflink>). He seems to have reigned but two years (B.C. 562-560). Influenced probably by Daniel, he showed kindness to Jehoiachin, who had been a prisoner in Babylon for thirty-seven years. He released him, and "spoke kindly to him." He was murdered by Nergal-sharezer=Neriglissar, his brother-in-law, who succeeded him (<reflink>Jer. 39:3, 13</reflink>).

evil-speaking.d: is expressly forbidden (<reflink>Titus 3:2; James 4:11</reflink>), and severe punishments are denounced against it (<reflink>1 Cor. 5:11; 6:10</reflink>). It is spoken of also with abhorrence (<reflink>Ps. 15:3; Prov. 18:6, 7</reflink>), and is foreign to the whole Christian character and the example of Christ.

example.d: of Christ (<reflink>1 Pet. 2:21; John 13:15</reflink>); of pastors to their flocks (<reflink>Phil. 3:17; 2 Thess. 3:9; 1 Tim. 4:12; 1 Pet. 5:3</reflink>); of the Jews as a warning (<reflink>Heb. 4:11</reflink>); of the prophets as suffering affliction (<reflink>James 5:10</reflink>).

executioner.d: (<reflink>Mark 6:27</reflink>). Instead of the Greek word, Mark here uses a Latin word, speculator, which literally means "a scout," "a spy," and at length came to denote one of the armed bodyguard of the emperor. Herod Antipas, in imitation of the emperor, had in attendance on him a company of speculatores. They were sometimes employed as executioners, but this was a mere accident of their office. (<see target="x-self">See MARK, GOSPEL OF.</see>)

exercise, bodily.d: (<reflink>1 Tim. 4:8</reflink>). An ascetic mortification of the flesh and denial of personal gratification (<reflink>comp. Col. 2:23</reflink>) to which some sects of the Jews, especially the Essenes, attached importance.

exile.d: (1.) Of the kingdom of Israel. In the time of Pekah, Tiglath-pileser II. carried away captive into Assyria (<reflink>2 Kings 15:29; comp. Isa. 10:5, 6</reflink>) a part of the inhabitants of Galilee and of Gilead (B.C. 741).

exodus.d: the great deliverance wrought for the children of Isreal when they were brought out of the land of Egypt with "a mighty hand and with an outstretched arm" (<reflink>Ex 12:51; Deut. 26:8; Ps 114; 136</reflink>), about B.C. 1490, and four hundred and eighty years (<reflink>1 Kings 6:1</reflink>) before the building of Solomon's temple.

exodus, book of.d: Exodus is the name given in the LXX. to the second book of the Pentateuch (q.v.). It means "departure" or "outgoing." This name was adopted in the Latin translation, and thence passed into other languages. The Hebrews called it by the first words, according to their custom, Ve-eleh shemoth (i.e., "and these are the names").

exorcist.d: (<reflink>Acts 19:13</reflink>). "In that sceptical and therefore superstitious age professional exorcist abounded. Many of these professional exorcists were disreputable Jews, like Simon in Samaria and Elymas in Cyprus (8:9; 13:6)." Other references to exorcism as practised by the Jews are found in Matt. 12:27; Mark 9:38; Luke 9:49, 50. It would seem that it was an opinion among the Jews that miracles might be wrought by invoking the divine name. Thus also these "vagabond Jews" pretended that they could expel daemons.

expiation.d: Guilt is said to be expiated when it is visited with punishment falling on a substitute. Expiation is made for our sins when they are punished not in ourselves but in another who consents to stand in our room. It is that by which reconciliation is effected. Sin is thus said to be "covered" by vicarious satisfaction.

eye.d: (Heb. 'ain, meaning "flowing"), applied (1) to a fountain, frequently; (2) to colour (<reflink>Num. 11:7; R.V., "appearance," marg. "eye"</reflink>); (3) the face (<reflink>Ex. 10:5, 15; Num. 22:5, 11</reflink>), in Num. 14:14, "face to face" (R.V. marg., "eye to eye"). "Between the eyes", i.e., the forehead (<reflink>Ex. 13:9, 16</reflink>).

ezekiel, book of.d: consists mainly of three groups of prophecies. After an account of his call to the prophetical office (1-3:21), Ezekiel (1) utters words of denunciation against the Jews (3:22-24), warning them of the certain destruction of Jerusalem, in opposition to the words of the false prophets (4:1-3). The symbolical acts, by which the extremities to which Jerusalem would be reduced are described in ch. 4,5, show his intimate acquaintance with the Levitical legislation. (<reflink>See Ex. 22:30; Deut. 14:21; Lev. 5:2; 7:18,24; 17:15; 19:7; 22:8, etc.</reflink>)

ezel.d: a separation, (<reflink>1 Sam. 20:19</reflink>), a stone, or heap of stones, in the neighbourhood of Saul's residence, the scene of the parting of David and Jonathan (42). The margin of the Authorized Version reads, "The stone that sheweth the way," in this rendering following the Targum.

ezer.d: treasure. (1.) One of the sons of Seir, the native princes, "dukes," of Mount Hor (<reflink>Gen. 36:21, 27</reflink>). (2.) 1 Chr. 7:21; (3.) 4:4. (4.) One of the Gadite champions who repaired to David at Ziklag (12:9). (5.) A Levite (<reflink>Neh. 3:19</reflink>). (6.) A priest (12:42).

ezion-geber.d: the giant's backbone (so called from the head of a mountain which runs out into the sea), an ancient city and harbour at the north-east end of the Elanitic branch of the Red Sea, the Gulf of Akabah, near Elath or Eloth (<reflink>Num. 33:35; Deut. 2:8</reflink>). Here Solomon built ships, "Tarshish ships," like those trading from Tyre to Tarshish and the west, which traded with Ophir (<reflink>1 Kings 9:26; 2 Chr. 8:17</reflink>); and here also Jehoshaphat's fleet was shipwrecked (<reflink>1 Kings 22:48; 2 Chr. 20:36</reflink>). It became a populous town, many of the Jews settling in it (<reflink>2 Kings 16:6, "Elath"</reflink>). It is supposed that anciently the north end of the gulf flowed further into the country than now, as far as 'Ain el-Ghudyan, which is 10 miles up the dry bed of the Arabah, and that Ezion-geber may have been there.

ezra.d: help. (1.) A priest among those that returned to Jerusalem under Zerubabel (<reflink>Neh. 12:1</reflink>).

ezra, book of.d: This book is the record of events occurring at the close of the Babylonian exile. It was at one time included in Nehemiah, the Jews regarding them as one volume. The two are still distinguished in the Vulgate version as I. and II. Esdras. It consists of two principal divisions:

ezrahite.d: a title given to Ethan (<reflink>1 Kings 4:31; Ps. 89, title</reflink>) and Heman (Ps. 88, title). They were both sons of Zerah (<reflink>1 Chr. 2:6</reflink>).

ezri.d: help of Jehovah, the son of Chelub. He superintended, under David, those who "did the work of the field for tillage" (<reflink>1 Chr. 27:26</reflink>).

fable.d: applied in the New Testament to the traditions and speculations, "cunningly devised fables", of the Jews on religious questions (<reflink>1 Tim. 1:4; 4:7; 2 Tim. 4:4; Titus 1:14; 2 Pet. 1:16</reflink>). In such passages the word means anything false and unreal. But the word is used as almost equivalent to parable. Thus we have (1) the fable of Jotham, in which the trees are spoken of as choosing a king (<reflink>Judg. 9:8-15</reflink>); and (2) that of the cedars of Lebanon and the thistle as Jehoash's answer to Amaziah (<reflink>2 Kings 14:9</reflink>).

face.d: means simply presence, as when it is recorded that Adam and Eve hid themselves from the "face [R.V., 'presence'] of the Lord God" (<reflink>Gen. 3:8; comp. Ex. 33:14, 15, where the same Hebrew word is rendered "presence"</reflink>). The "light of God's countenance" is his favour (<reflink>Ps. 44:3; Dan. 9:17</reflink>). "Face" signifies also anger, justice, severity (<reflink>Gen. 16:6, 8; Ex. 2:15; Ps. 68:1; Rev. 6:16</reflink>). To "provoke God to his face" (<reflink>Isa. 65:3</reflink>) is to sin against him openly.

fair havens.d: a harbour in the south of Crete, some 5 miles to the east of which was the town of Lasea (<reflink>Acts 27:8</reflink>). Here the ship of Alexandria in which Paul and his companions sailed was detained a considerable time waiting for a favourable wind. Contrary to Paul's advice, the master of the ship determined to prosecute the voyage, as the harbour was deemed incommodious for wintering in (9-12). The result was that, after a stormy voyage, the vessel was finally wrecked on the coast of Malta (27:40-44).

fairs.d: (Heb. 'izabhonim), found seven times in Ezek. 27, and nowhere else. The Authorized Version renders the word thus in all these instances, except in verse 33, where "wares" is used. The Revised Version uniformly renders by "wares," which is the correct rendering of the Hebrew word. It never means "fairs" in the modern sense of the word.

faith.d: Faith is in general the persuasion of the mind that a certain statement is true (<reflink>Phil. 1:27; 2 Thess. 2:13</reflink>). Its primary idea is trust. A thing is true, and therefore worthy of trust. It admits of many degrees up to full assurance of faith, in accordance with the evidence on which it rests.

faithful.d: as a designation of Christians, means full of faith, trustful, and not simply trustworthy (<reflink>Acts 10:45; 16:1; 2 Cor. 6:15; Col. 1:2; 1 Tim. 4:3, 12; 5:16; 6:2; Titus 1:6; Eph. 1:1; 1 Cor. 4:17, etc.</reflink>).

fall of man.d: an expression probably borrowed from the Apocryphal Book of Wisdom, to express the fact of the revolt of our first parents from God, and the consequent sin and misery in which they and all their posterity were involved.

fallow-deer.d: Deut. 14:5 (R.V., "Wild goat"); 1 Kings 4:23 (R.V., "roebucks"). This animal, called in Hebrew _yahmur_, from a word meaning "to be red," is regarded by some as the common fallow-deer, the Cervus dama, which is said to be found very generally over Western and Southern Asia. It is called "fallow" from its pale-red or yellow colour. Some interpreters, however, regard the name as designating the bubale, Antelope bubale, the "wild cow" of North Africa, which is about the size of a stag, like the hartebeest of South Africa. A species of deer has been found at Mount Carmel which is called _yahmur_ by the Arabs. It is said to be similar to the European roebuck.

fallow-ground.d: The expression, "Break up your fallow ground" (<reflink>Hos. 10:12; Jer. 4:3</reflink>) means, "Do not sow your seed among thorns", i.e., break off all your evil habits; clear your hearts of weeds, in order that they may be prepared for the seed of righteousness. Land was allowed to lie fallow that it might become more fruitful; but when in this condition, it soon became overgrown with thorns and weeds. The cultivator of the soil was careful to "break up" his fallow ground, i.e., to clear the field of weeds, before sowing seed in it. So says the prophet, "Break off your evil ways, repent of your sins, cease to do evil, and then the good seed of the word will have room to grow and bear fruit."

familiar spirit.d: Sorcerers or necormancers, who professed to call up the dead to answer questions, were said to have a "familiar spirit" (<reflink>Deut. 18:11; 2 Kings 21:6; 2 Chr. 33:6; Lev. 19:31; 20:6; Isa. 8:19; 29:4</reflink>). Such a person was called by the Hebrews an _'ob_, which properly means a leathern bottle; for sorcerers were regarded as vessels containing the inspiring demon. This Hebrew word was equivalent to the pytho of the Greeks, and was used to denote both the person and the spirit which possessed him (<reflink>Lev. 20:27; 1 Sam. 28:8; comp. Acts 16:16</reflink>). The word "familiar" is from the Latin familiaris, meaning a "household servant," and was intended to express the idea that sorcerers had spirits as their servants ready to obey their commands.

famine.d: The first mentioned in Scripture was so grievous as to compel Abraham to go down to the land of Egypt (<reflink>Gen. 26:1</reflink>). Another is mentioned as having occurred in the days of Isaac, causing him to go to Gerar (<reflink>Gen. 26:1, 17</reflink>). But the most remarkable of all was that which arose in Egypt in the days of Joseph, which lasted for seven years (Gen. 41-45).

fan.d: a winnowing shovel by which grain was thrown up against the wind that it might be cleansed from broken straw and chaff (<reflink>Isa. 30:24; Jer. 15:7; Matt. 3:12</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See AGRICULTURE.</see>)

farm.d: (<reflink>Matt. 22:5</reflink>). Every Hebrew had a certain portion of land assigned to him as a possession (<reflink>Num. 26:33-56</reflink>). In Egypt the lands all belonged to the king, and the husbandmen were obliged to give him a fifth part of the produce; so in Palestine Jehovah was the sole possessor of the soil, and the people held it by direct tenure from him. By the enactment of Moses, the Hebrews paid a tithe of the produce to Jehovah, which was assigned to the priesthood. Military service when required was also to be rendered by every Hebrew at his own expense. The occuptaion of a husbandman was held in high honour (<reflink>1 Sam. 11:5-7; 1 Kings 19:19; 2 Chr. 26:10</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See LAND LAWS (n/a</see>); TITHE.)

farthing.d: (1.) Matt. 10:29; Luke 12:6. Greek assarion, i.e., a small _as_, which was a Roman coin equal to a tenth of a denarius or drachma, nearly equal to a halfpenny of our money.

fast.d: The sole fast required by the law of Moses was that of the great Day of Atonement (q.v.), Lev. 23:26-32. It is called "the fast" (<reflink>Acts 27:9</reflink>).

fat.d: (Heb. heleb) denotes the richest part of the animal, or the fattest of the flock, in the account of Abel's sacrifice (<reflink>Gen. 4:4</reflink>). It sometimes denotes the best of any production (<reflink>Gen. 45:18; Num. 18:12; Ps. 81:16; 147:47</reflink>). The fat of sacrifices was to be burned (<reflink>Lev. 3:9-11; 4:8; 7:3; 8:25; Num. 18:17. Comp. Ex. 29:13-22; Lev. 3:3-5</reflink>).

father.d: a name applied (1) to any ancestor (<reflink>Deut. 1:11; 1 Kings 15:11; Matt. 3:9; 23:30, etc.</reflink>); and (2) as a title of respect to a chief, ruler, or elder, etc. (<reflink>Judg. 17:10; 18:19; 1 Sam. 10:12; 2 Kings 2:12; Matt. 23:9, etc.</reflink>). (3) The author or beginner of anything is also so called; e.g., Jabal and Jubal (<reflink>Gen. 4:20, 21; comp. Job 38:28</reflink>).

fathom.d: (Old A.S. faethm, "bosom," or the outstretched arms), a span of six feet (<reflink>Acts 27:28</reflink>). Gr. orguia (from orego, "I stretch"), the distance between the extremities of both arms fully stretched out.

fatling.d: (1.) A fatted animal for slaughter (<reflink>2 Sam. 6:13; Isa. 11:6; Ezek. 39:18. Comp. Matt. 22:4, where the word used in the original, sitistos, means literally "corn-fed;" i.e., installed, fat</reflink>). (2.) Ps. 66:15 (Heb. meah, meaning "marrowy," "fat," a species of sheep). (3.) 1 Sam. 15:9 (Heb. mishneh, meaning "the second," and hence probably "cattle of a second quality," or lambs of the second birth, i.e., autmnal lambs, and therfore of less value).

fear of the lord the.d: is in the Old Testament used as a designation of true piety (<reflink>Prov. 1:7; Job 28:28; Ps. 19:9</reflink>). It is a fear conjoined with love and hope, and is therefore not a slavish dread, but rather filial reverence. (<reflink>Comp. Deut. 32:6; Hos. 11:1; Isa. 1:2; 63:16; 64:8.</reflink>) God is called "the Fear of Isaac" (<reflink>Gen. 31:42, 53</reflink>), i.e., the God whom Isaac feared.

feast.d: as a mark of hospitality (<reflink>Gen. 19:3; 2 Sam. 3:20; 2 Kings 6:23</reflink>); on occasions of domestic joy (<reflink>Luke 15:23; Gen. 21:8</reflink>); on birthdays (<reflink>Gen. 40:20; Job 1:4; Matt. 14:6</reflink>); and on the occasion of a marriage (<reflink>Judg. 14:10; Gen. 29:22</reflink>).

felix.d: happy, the Roman procurator of Judea before whom Paul "reasoned" (<reflink>Acts 24:25</reflink>). He appears to have expected a bribe from Paul, and therefore had several interviews with him. The "worthy deeds" referred to in 24:2 was his clearing the country of banditti and impostors.

fellowship.d: (1.) With God, consisting in the knowledge of his will (<reflink>Job 22:21; John 17:3</reflink>); agreement with his designs (<reflink>Amos 3:2</reflink>); mutual affection (<reflink>Rom. 8: 38, 39</reflink>); enjoyment of his presence (<reflink>Ps. 4:6</reflink>); conformity to his image (<reflink>1 John 2:6; 1:6</reflink>); and participation of his felicity (<reflink>1 John 1:3, 4; Eph. 3:14-21</reflink>).

fence.d: (Heb. gader), Num. 22:24 (R.V.). Fences were constructions of unmortared stones, to protect gardens, vineyards, sheepfolds, etc. From various causes they were apt to bulge out and fall (<reflink>Ps. 62:3</reflink>). In Ps. 80:12, R.V. (<reflink>see Isa. 5:5</reflink>), the psalmist says, "Why hast thou broken down her fences?" Serpents delight to lurk in the crevices of such fences (<reflink>Eccl. 10:8; comp. Amos 5:19</reflink>).

fenced cities.d: There were in Palestine (1) cities, (2) unwalled villages, and (3) villages with castles or towers (<reflink>1 Chr. 27:25</reflink>). Cities, so called, had walls, and were thus fenced. The fortifications consisted of one or two walls, on which were towers or parapets at regular intervals (<reflink>2 Chr. 32:5; Jer. 31:38</reflink>). Around ancient Jerusalem were three walls, on one of which were ninety towers, on the second fourteen, and on the third sixty. The tower of Hananeel, near the north-east corner of the city wall, is frequently referred to (<reflink>Neh. 3:1; 12:39; Zech. 14:10</reflink>). The gateways of such cities were also fortified (<reflink>Neh. 2:8; 3:3, 6; Judg. 16:2, 3; 1 Sam. 23:7</reflink>).

ferret.d: Lev. 11:30 (R.V., "gecko"), one of the unclean creeping things. It was perhaps the Lacerta gecko which was intended by the Hebrew word (anakah, a cry, "mourning," the creature which groans) here used, i.e., the "fan-footed" lizard, the gecko which makes a mournful wail. The LXX. translate it by a word meaning "shrew-mouse," of which there are three species in Palestine. The Rabbinical writers regard it as the hedgehog. The translation of the Revised Version is to be preferred.

ferry boat.d: (<reflink>2 Sam. 19:18</reflink>), some kind of boat for crossing the river which the men of Judah placed at the service of the king. Floats or rafts for this purpose were in use from remote times (<reflink>Isa. 18:2</reflink>).

festivals, religious.d: There were daily (Lev. 23), weekly, monthly, and yearly festivals, and great stress was laid on the regular observance of them in every particular (<reflink>Num. 28:1-8; Ex. 29:38-42; Lev. 6:8-23; Ex. 30:7-9; 27:20</reflink>).

festus, porcius.d: the successor of Felix (A.D. 60) as procurator of Judea (<reflink>Acts 24:27</reflink>). A few weeks after he had entered on his office the case of Paul, then a prisoner at Caesarea, was reported to him. The "next day," after he had gone down to Caesarea, he heard Paul defend himself in the presence of Herod Agrippa II. and his sister Bernice, and not finding in him anything worthy of death or of bonds, would have set him free had he not appealed unto Caesar (<reflink>Acts 25:11, 12</reflink>). In consequence of this appeal Paul was sent to Rome. Festus, after being in office less than two years, died in Judea. (<see target="x-self">See AGRIPPA.</see>)

fever.d: (<reflink>Deut. 28:22; Matt. 8:14; Mark 1:30; John 4:52; Acts 28:8</reflink>), a burning heat, as the word so rendered denotes, which attends all febrile attacks. In all Eastern countries such diseases are very common. Peter's wife's mother is said to have suffered from a "great fever" (<reflink>Luke 4:38</reflink>), an instance of Luke's professional exactitude in describing disease. He adopts here the technical medical distinction, as in those times fevers were divided into the "great" and the "less."

field.d: (Heb. sadeh), a cultivated field, but unenclosed. It is applied to any cultivated ground or pasture (<reflink>Gen. 29:2; 31:4; 34:7</reflink>), or tillage (<reflink>Gen. 37:7; 47:24</reflink>). It is also applied to woodland (<reflink>Ps. 132:6</reflink>) or mountain top (<reflink>Judg. 9:32, 36; 2 Sam. 1:21</reflink>). It denotes sometimes a cultivated region as opposed to the wilderness (<reflink>Gen. 33:19; 36:35</reflink>). Unwalled villages or scattered houses are spoken of as "in the fields" (<reflink>Deut. 28:3, 16; Lev. 25:31; Mark 6:36, 56</reflink>). The "open field" is a place remote from a house (<reflink>Gen. 4:8; Lev. 14:7, 53; 17:5</reflink>). Cultivated land of any extent was called a field (<reflink>Gen. 23:13, 17; 41:8; Lev. 27:16; Ruth 4:5; Neh. 12:29</reflink>).

fig.d: First mentioned in Gen. 3:7. The fig-tree is mentioned (<reflink>Deut. 8:8</reflink>) as one of the valuable products of Palestine. It was a sign of peace and prosperity (<reflink>1 Kings 4:25; Micah 4:4; Zech. 3:10</reflink>). Figs were used medicinally (<reflink>2 Kings 20:7</reflink>), and pressed together and formed into "cakes" as articles of diet (<reflink>1 Sam. 30:12; Jer. 24:2</reflink>).

dross.d: the impurities of silver separated from the one in the process of melting (<reflink>Prov. 25:4; 26:23; Ps. 119:119</reflink>). It is also used to denote the base metal itself, probably before it is smelted, in Isa. 1:22, 25.

drought.d: From the middle of May to about the middle of August the land of Palestine is dry. It is then the "drought of summer" (<reflink>Gen. 31:40; Ps. 32:4</reflink>), and the land suffers (<reflink>Deut. 28:23: Ps. 102:4</reflink>), vegetation being preserved only by the dews (<reflink>Hag. 1:11</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See DEW.</see>)

drown.d: (<reflink>Ex. 15:4; Amos 8:8; Heb. 11:29</reflink>). Drowning was a mode of capital punishment in use among the Syrians, and was known to the Jews in the time of our Lord. To this he alludes in Matt. 18:6.

drunk.d: The first case of intoxication on record is that of Noah (<reflink>Gen. 9:21</reflink>). The sin of drunkenness is frequently and strongly condemned (<reflink>Rom. 13:13; 1 Cor. 6:9, 10; Eph. 5:18; 1 Thess. 5:7, 8</reflink>). The sin of drinking to excess seems to have been not uncommon among the Israelites.

drusilla.d: third and youngest daughter of Herod Agrippa I. (<reflink>Acts 12:1-4, 20-23</reflink>). Felix, the Roman procurator of Judea, induced her to leave her husband, Azizus, the king of Emesa, and become his wife. She was present with Felix when Paul reasoned of "righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come" (<reflink>Acts 24:24</reflink>). She and her son perished in the eruption of Mount Vesuvius, A.D. 79.

duke.d: derived from the Latin dux, meaning "a leader;" Arabic, "a sheik." This word is used to denote the phylarch or chief of a tribe (<reflink>Gen. 36:15-43; Ex. 15:15; 1 Chr. 1:51-54</reflink>).

dulcimer.d: (Heb. sumphoniah), a musical instrument mentioned in Dan. 3:5, 15, along with other instruments there named, as sounded before the golden image. It was not a Jewish instrument. In the margin of the Revised Version it is styled the "bag-pipe." Luther translated it "lute," and Grotius the "crooked trumpet." It is probable that it was introduced into Babylon by some Greek or Western-Asiatic musician. Some Rabbinical commentators render it by "organ," the well-known instrument composed of a series of pipes, others by "lyre." The most probable interpretation is that it was a bag-pipe similar to the zampagna of Southern Europe.

dumah.d: silence, (<reflink>comp. Ps. 94:17</reflink>), the fourth son of Ishmael; also the tribe descended from him; and hence also the region in Arabia which they inhabited (<reflink>Gen. 25:14; 1 Chr. 1:30</reflink>).

dumb.d: from natural infirmity (<reflink>Ex. 4:11</reflink>); not knowing what to say (<reflink>Prov. 31:8</reflink>); unwillingness to speak (<reflink>Ps. 39:9; Lev. 10:3</reflink>). Christ repeatedly restored the dumb (<reflink>Matt. 9:32, 33; Luke 11:14; Matt. 12:22</reflink>) to the use of speech.

dung.d: (1.) Used as manure (<reflink>Luke 13:8</reflink>); collected outside the city walls (<reflink>Neh. 2:13</reflink>). Of sacrifices, burned outside the camp (<reflink>Ex. 29:14; Lev. 4:11; 8:17; Num. 19:5</reflink>). To be "cast out as dung," a figurative expression (<reflink>1 Kings 14:10; 2 Kings 9:37; Jer. 8:2; Ps. 18:42</reflink>), meaning to be rejected as unprofitable.

dung-gate.d: (<reflink>Neh. 2:13</reflink>), a gate of ancient Jerusalem, on the south-west quarter. "The gate outside of which lay the piles of sweepings and offscourings of the streets," in the valley of Tophet.

dung-hill.d: to sit on a, was a sign of the deepest dejection (<reflink>1 Sam. 2:8; Ps. 113:7; Lam. 4:5</reflink>).

dungeon.d: different from the ordinary prison in being more severe as a place of punishment. Like the Roman inner prison (<reflink>Acts 16:24</reflink>), it consisted of a deep cell or cistern (<reflink>Jer. 38:6</reflink>). To be shut up in, a punishment common in Egypt (<reflink>Gen. 39:20; 40:3; 41:10; 42:19</reflink>). It is not mentioned, however, in the law of Moses as a mode of punishment. Under the later kings imprisonment was frequently used as a punishment (<reflink>2 Chron. 16:10; Jer. 20:2; 32:2; 33:1; 37:15</reflink>), and it was customary after the Exile (<reflink>Matt. 11:2; Luke 3:20; Acts 5:18, 21; Matt. 18:30</reflink>).

dura.d: the circle, the plain near Babylon in which Nebuchadnezzar set up a golden image, mentioned in Dan. 3:1. The place still retains its ancient name. On one of its many mounds the pedestal of what must have been a colossal statue has been found. It has been supposed to be that of the golden image.

dust.d: Storms of sand and dust sometimes overtake Eastern travellers. They are very dreadful, many perishing under them. Jehovah threatens to bring on the land of Israel, as a punishment for forsaking him, a rain of "powder and dust" (<reflink>Deut. 28:24</reflink>).

dwell.d: Tents were in primitive times the common dwellings of men. Houses were afterwards built, the walls of which were frequently of mud (<reflink>Job 24:16; Matt. 6:19, 20</reflink>) or of sun-dried bricks.

dwellings.d: The materials used in buildings were commonly bricks, sometimes also stones (<reflink>Lev. 14:40, 42</reflink>), which were held together by cement (<reflink>Jer. 43:9</reflink>) or bitumen (<reflink>Gen. 11:3</reflink>). The exterior was usually whitewashed (<reflink>Lev. 14:41; Ezek. 13:10; Matt. 23:27</reflink>). The beams were of sycamore (<reflink>Isa. 9:10</reflink>), or olive-wood, or cedar (<reflink>1 Kings 7:2; Isa. 9:10</reflink>).

dye.d: The art of dyeing is one of great antiquity, although no special mention is made of it in the Old Testament. The Hebrews probably learned it from the Egyptians (<reflink>see Ex. 26:1; 28:5-8</reflink>), who brought it to great perfection. In New Testament times Thyatira was famed for its dyers (<reflink>Acts 16:14</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See COLOUR.</see>)

eagle.d: (Herb. nesher; properly the griffon vulture or great vulture, so called from its tearing its prey with its beak), referred to for its swiftness of flight (<reflink>Deut. 28:49; 2 Sam. 1:23</reflink>), its mounting high in the air (<reflink>Job 39:27</reflink>), its strength (<reflink>Ps. 103:5</reflink>), its setting its nest in high places (<reflink>Jer. 49:16</reflink>), and its power of vision (<reflink>Job 39:27-30</reflink>).

ear.d: used frequently in a figurative sense (<reflink>Ps. 34:15</reflink>). To "uncover the ear" is to show respect to a person (<reflink>1 Sam. 20:2 marg.</reflink>). To have the "ear heavy", or to have "uncircumcised ears" (<reflink>Isa. 6:10</reflink>), is to be inattentive and disobedient. To have the ear "bored" through with an awl was a sign of perpetual servitude (<reflink>Ex. 21:6</reflink>).

earing.d: an Old English word (from the Latin aro, I plough), meaning "ploughing." It is used in the Authorized Version in Gen. 45:6; Ex. 34:21; 1 Sam. 8:12; Deut. 21:4; Isa. 30:24; but the Revised Version has rendered the original in these places by the ordinary word to plough or till.

earnest.d: The Spirit is the earnest of the believer's destined inheritance (<reflink>2 Cor. 1:22; 5:5; Eph. 1:14</reflink>). The word thus rendered is the same as that rendered "pledge" in Gen. 38:17-20; "indeed, the Hebrew word has simply passed into the Greek and Latin languages, probably through commercial dealings with the Phoenicians, the great trading people of ancient days. Originally it meant no more than a pledge; but in common usage it came to denote that particular kind of pledge which is a part of the full price of an article paid in advance; and as it is joined with the figure of a seal when applied to the Spirit, it seems to be used by Paul in this specific sense." The Spirit's gracious presence and working in believers is a foretaste to them of the blessedness of heaven. God is graciously pleased to give not only pledges but foretastes of future blessedness.

earrings.d: rings properly for the ear (<reflink>Gen. 35:4; Num. 31:50; Ezek. 16:12</reflink>). In Gen. 24:47 the word means a nose-jewel, and is so rendered in the Revised Version. In Isa. 3:20 the Authorized Version has "ear-rings," and the Revised Version "amulets," which more correctly represents the original word (lehashim), which means incantations; charms, thus remedies against enchantment, worn either suspended from the neck or in the ears of females. Ear-rings were ornaments used by both sexes (<reflink>Ex. 32:2</reflink>).

earth.d: (1.) In the sense of soil or ground, the translation of the word _adamah'_. In Gen. 9:20 "husbandman" is literally "man of the ground or earth." Altars were to be built of earth (<reflink>Ex. 20:24</reflink>). Naaman asked for two mules' burden of earth (<reflink>2 Kings 5:17</reflink>), under the superstitious notion that Jehovah, like the gods of the heathen, could be acceptably worshipped only on his own soil.

earthquake.d: mentioned among the extraordinary phenomena of Palestine (<reflink>Ps. 18:7; comp. Hab. 3:6; Nah. 1:5; Isa. 5:25</reflink>).

east.d: (1.) The orient (mizrah); the rising of the sun. Thus "the east country" is the country lying to the east of Syria, the Elymais (<reflink>Zech. 8:7</reflink>).

east gate.d: (<reflink>Jer. 19:2</reflink>), properly the Potter's gate, the gate which led to the potter's field, in the valley of Hinnom.

east sea.d: (<reflink>Joel 2:20; Ezek. 47:18</reflink>), the Dead Sea, which lay on the east side of the Holy Land. The Mediterranean, which lay on the west, was hence called the "great sea for the west border" (<reflink>Num. 34:6</reflink>).

east wind.d: the wind coming from the east (<reflink>Job 27:21; Isa. 27:8, etc.</reflink>). Blight caused by this wind, "thin ears" (<reflink>Gen. 41:6</reflink>); the withered "gourd" (<reflink>Jonah 4: 8</reflink>). It was the cause and also the emblem of evil (<reflink>Ezek. 17:10; 19:12; Hos. 13:15</reflink>). In Palestine this wind blows from a burning desert, and hence is destitute of moisture necessary for vegetation.

east, children of the.d: the Arabs as a whole, known as the Nabateans or Kedarenes, nomad tribes (<reflink>Judg. 6:3,33; 7:12; 8:10</reflink>).

easter.d: originally a Saxon word (Eostre), denoting a goddess of the Saxons, in honour of whom sacrifices were offered about the time of the Passover. Hence the name came to be given to the festival of the Resurrection of Christ, which occured at the time of the Passover. In the early English versions this word was frequently used as the translation of the Greek pascha (the Passover). When the Authorized Version (1611) was formed, the word "passover" was used in all passages in which this word pascha occurred, except in Act 12:4. In the Revised Version the proper word, "passover," is always used.

eating.d: The ancient Hebrews would not eat with the Egyptians (<reflink>Gen. 43:32</reflink>). In the time of our Lord they would not eat with Samaritans (<reflink>John 4:9</reflink>), and were astonished that he ate with publicans and sinners (<reflink>Matt. 9:11</reflink>). The Hebrews originally sat at table, but afterwards adopted the Persian and Chaldean practice of reclining (<reflink>Luke 7:36-50</reflink>). Their principal meal was at noon (<reflink>Gen. 43:16; 1 Kings 20:16; Ruth 2:14; Luke 14:12</reflink>). The word "eat" is used metaphorically in Jer. 15:16; Ezek. 3:1; Rev. 10:9. In John 6:53-58, "eating and drinking" means believing in Christ. Women were never present as guests at meals (q.v.).

ebal.d: stony. (1.) A mountain 3,076 feet above the level of the sea, and 1,200 feet above the level of the valley, on the north side of which stood the city of Shechem (q.v.). On this mountain six of the tribes (<reflink>Deut. 27:12,13</reflink>) were appointed to take their stand and respond according to a prescribed form to the imprecations uttered in the valley, where the law was read by the Levites (11:29; 29:4, 13). This mountain was also the site of the first great altar erected to Jehovah (<reflink>Deut. 27:5-8; Josh. 8:30-35</reflink>). After this the name of Ebal does not again occur in Jewish history. (<see target="x-self">See GERIZIM.</see>)

ebed.d: slave, the father of Gaal, in whom the men of Shechem "put confidence" in their conspiracy against Abimelech (<reflink>Judg. 9:26, 26, 30, 31</reflink>).

ebed-melech.d: a servant of the king; probably an official title, an Ethiopian, "one of the eunuchs which was in the king's house;" i.e., in the palace of Zedekiah, king of Judah. He interceded with the king in Jeremiah's behalf, and was the means of saving him from death by famine (<reflink>Jer. 38:7-13: comp. 39:15-18</reflink>).

eben-ezer.d: stone of help, the memorial stone set up by Samuel to commemorate the divine assistance to Israel in their great battle against the Philistines, whom they totally routed (<reflink>1 Sam. 7:7-12</reflink>) at Aphek, in the neighbourhood of Mizpeh, in Benjamin, near the western entrance of the pass of Beth-horon. On this very battle-field, twenty years before, the Philistines routed the Israelites, "and slew of the army in the field about four thousand men" (4:1,2; here, and at 5:1, called "Eben-ezer" by anticipation). In this extremity the Israelites fetched the ark out of Shiloh and carried it into their camp. The Philistines a second time immediately attacked them, and smote them with a very great slaughter, "for there fell of Israel thirty thousand footmen. And the ark of God was taken" (<reflink>1 Sam. 4:10</reflink>). And now in the same place the Philistines are vanquished, and the memorial stone is erected by Samuel (q.v.). …

eber.d: beyond. (1.). The third post-duluvian patriach after Shem (<reflink>Gen. 10:24; 11:14</reflink>). He is regarded as the founder of the Hebrew race (10:21; Num. 24:24). In Luke 3:35 he is called Heber.

ebony.d: a black, hard wood, brought by the merchants from India to Tyre (<reflink>Ezek. 27:15</reflink>). It is the heart-wood, brought by Diospyros ebenus, which grows in Ceylon and Southern India.

ebronah.d: passage, one of the stations of the Israelites in their wanderings (<reflink>Num. 33:34, 35</reflink>). It was near Ezion-geber.

ecclesiastes.d: the Greek rendering of the Hebrew _Koheleth_, which means "Preacher." The old and traditional view of the authorship of this book attributes it to Solomon. This view can be satisfactorily maintained, though others date it from the Captivity. The writer represents himself implicitly as Solomon (1:12). It has been appropriately styled The Confession of King Solomon. "The writer is a man who has sinned in giving way to selfishness and sensuality, who has paid the penalty of that sin in satiety and weariness of life, but who has through all this been under the discipline of a divine education, and has learned from it the lesson which God meant to teach him." "The writer concludes by pointing out that the secret of a true life is that a man should consecrate the vigour of his youth to God." The key-note of the book is sounded in ch. 1:2,

eclipse.d: of the sun alluded to in Amos 8:9; Micah 3:6; Zech. 14:6; Joel 2:10. Eclipses were regarded as tokens of God's anger (<reflink>Joel 3:15; Job 9:7</reflink>). The darkness at the crucifixion has been ascribed to an eclipse (<reflink>Matt. 27:45</reflink>); but on the other hand it is argued that the great intensity of darkness caused by an eclipse never lasts for more than six minutes, and this darkness lasted for three hours. Moreover, at the time of the Passover the moon was full, and therefore there could not be an eclipse of the sun, which is caused by an interposition of the moon between the sun and the earth.

ed.d: witness, a word not found in the original Hebrew, nor in the LXX. and Vulgate, but added by the translators in the Authorized Version, also in the Revised Version, of Josh. 22:34. The words are literally rendered: "And the children of Reuben and the children of Gad named the altar. It is a witness between us that Jehovah is God." This great altar stood probably on the east side of the Jordan, in the land of Gilead, "over against the land of Canaan." After the division of the Promised Land, the tribes of Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh, on returning to their own settlements on the east of Jordan (<reflink>Josh. 22:1-6</reflink>), erected a great altar, which they affirmed, in answer to the challenge of the other tribes, was not for sacrifice, but only as a witness ('Ed) or testimony to future generations that they still retained the same interest in the nation as the other tribes.

edar.d: tower of the flock, a tower between Bethlehem and Hebron, near which Jacob first halted after leaving Bethlehem (<reflink>Gen. 35:21</reflink>). In Micah 4:8 the word is rendered "tower of the flock" (marg., "Edar"), and is used as a designation of Bethlehem, which figuratively represents the royal line of David as sprung from Bethlehem.

eden.d: delight. (1.) The garden in which our first parents dewlt (<reflink>Gen. 2:8-17</reflink>). No geographical question has been so much discussed as that bearing on its site. It has been placed in Armenia, in the region west of the Caspian Sea, in Media, near Damascus, in Palestine, in Southern Arabia, and in Babylonia. The site must undoubtedly be sought for somewhere along the course of the great streams the Tigris and the Euphrates of Western Asia, in "the land of Shinar" or Babylonia. The region from about lat. 33 degrees 30' to lat. 31 degrees, which is a very rich and fertile tract, has been by the most competent authorities agreed on as the probable site of Eden. "It is a region where streams abound, where they divide and re-unite, where alone in the Mesopotamian tract can be found the phenomenon of a single river parting into four arms, each of which is or has been a river of consequence."

eder.d: flock. (1.) A city in the south of Judah, on the border of Idumea (<reflink>Josh. 15:21</reflink>).

edom.d: (1.) The name of Esau (q.v.), Gen. 25:30, "Feed me, I pray thee, with that same red pottage [Heb. haadom, haadom, i.e., 'the red pottage, the red pottage'] ...Therefore was his name called Edom", i.e., Red.

edrei.d: mighty; strength. (1.) One of the chief towns of the kingdom of Bashan (<reflink>Josh. 12:4, 5</reflink>). Here Og was defeated by the Israelites, and the strength of the Amorites broken (<reflink>Num. 21:33-35</reflink>). It subsequently belonged to Manasseh, for a short time apparently, and afterwards became the abode of banditti and outlaws (<reflink>Josh. 13:31</reflink>). It has been identified with the modern Edr'a, which stands on a rocky promontory on the south-west edge of the Lejah (the Argob of the Hebrews, and Trachonitis of the Greeks). The ruins of Edr'a are the most extensive in the Hauran. They are 3 miles in circumference. A number of the ancient houses still remain; the walls, roofs, and doors being all of stone. …

effectual prayer.d: occurs in Authorized Version, James 5:16. The Revised Version renders appropriately: "The supplication of a righteous man availeth much in its working", i.e., "it moves the hand of Him who moves the world."

egg.d: (Heb. beytsah, "whiteness"). Eggs deserted (<reflink>Isa. 10:14</reflink>), of a bird (<reflink>Deut. 22:6</reflink>), an ostrich (<reflink>Job 39:14</reflink>), the cockatrice (<reflink>Isa. 59:5</reflink>). In Luke 11:12, an egg is contrasted with a scorpion, which is said to be very like an egg in its appearance, so much so as to be with difficulty at times distinguished from it. In Job 6:6 ("the white of an egg") the word for egg (hallamuth') occurs nowhere else. It has been translated "purslain" (R.V. marg.), and the whole phrase "purslain-broth", i.e., broth made of that herb, proverbial for its insipidity; and hence an insipid discourse. Job applies this expression to the speech of Eliphaz as being insipid and dull. But the common rendering, "the white of an egg", may be satisfactorily maintained.

eglah.d: a heifer, one of David's wives, and mother of Ithream (<reflink>2 Sam. 3:5; 1 Chr. 3:3</reflink>). According to a Jewish tradition she was Michal.

eglaim.d: two ponds, (<reflink>Isa. 15:8</reflink>), probably En-eglaim of Ezek. 47:10.

eglon.d: the bullock; place of heifers. (1.) Chieftain or king of one of the Moabite tribes (<reflink>Judg. 3:12-14</reflink>). Having entered into an alliance with Ammon and Amalek, he overran the trans-Jordanic region, and then crossing the Jordan, seized on Jericho, the "city of palm trees," which had been by this time rebuilt, but not as a fortress. He made this city his capital, and kept Israel in subjection for eighteen years. The people at length "cried unto the Lord" in their distress, and he "raised them up a deliverer" in Ehud (q.v.), the son of Gera, a Benjamite.

egypt.d: the land of the Nile and the pyramids, the oldest kingdom of which we have any record, holds a place of great significance in Scripture.

ehud.d: union. (1.) A descendant of Benjamin (<reflink>1 Chr. 7:10</reflink>), his great-grandson.

ekron.d: firm-rooted, the most northerly of the five towns belonging to the lords of the Philistines, about 11 miles north of Gath. It was assigned to Judah (<reflink>Josh. 13:3</reflink>), and afterwards to Dan (19:43), but came again into the full possession of the Philistines (<reflink>1 Sam. 5:10</reflink>). It was the last place to which the Philistines carried the ark before they sent it back to Israel (<reflink>1 Sam. 5:10; 6:1-8</reflink>). There was here a noted sanctuary of Baal-zebub (<reflink>2 Kings 1: 2, 3, 6, 16</reflink>). Now the small village Akir. It is mentioned on monuments in B.C. 702, when Sennacherib set free its king, imprisoned by Hezekiah in Jerusalem, according to the Assyrian record.

el-bethel.d: God of Bethel, the name of the place where Jacob had the vision of the ladder, and where he erected an altar (<reflink>Gen. 31:13; 35:7</reflink>).

el-elohe-isreal.d: mighty one; God of Israel, the name which Jacob gave to the alter which he erected on the piece of land where he pitched his tent before Shechem, and which he afterwards purchased from the sons of Hamor (<reflink>Gen. 33:20</reflink>).

elah.d: terebinth or oak. (1.) Valley of, where the Israelites were encamped when David killed Goliath (<reflink>1 Sam. 17:2, 19</reflink>). It was near Shochoh of Judah and Azekah (17:1). It is the modern Wady es-Sunt, i.e., "valley of the acacia." "The terebinths from which the valley of Elah takes its name still cling to their ancient soil. On the west side of the valley, near Shochoh, there is a very large and ancient tree of this kind known as the 'terebinth of Wady Sur,' 55 feet in height, its trunk 17 feet in circumference, and the breadth of its shade no less than 75 feet. It marks the upper end of the Elah valley, and forms a noted object, being one of the largest terebinths in Palestine." Geikie's, The Holy Land, etc.

elam.d: highland, the son of Shem (<reflink>Gen. 10:22</reflink>), and the name of the country inhabited by his descendants (14:1, 9; Isa. 11:11; 21:2, etc.) lying to the east of Babylonia, and extending to the shore of the Mediterranean, a distance in a direct line of about 1,000 miles. The name Elam is an Assyrian word meaning "high."

elasah.d: God made. (1.) One of the descendants of Judah, of the family of Hezron (<reflink>1 Chr. 2:39, "Eleasah"</reflink>).

elath.d: grove; trees, (<reflink>Deut. 2:8</reflink>), also in plural form Eloth (<reflink>1 Kings 9:26, etc.</reflink>); called by the Greeks and Romans Elana; a city of Idumea, on the east, i.e., the Elanitic, gulf, or the Gulf of Akabah, of the Red Sea. It is first mentioned in Deut. 2:8. It is also mentioned along with Ezion-geber in 1 Kings 9:26. It was within the limits of Solomon's dominion, but afterwards revolted. It was, however, recovered and held for a time under king Uzziah (<reflink>2 Kings 14:22</reflink>). Now the ruin Aila.

eldad.d: whom God has loved, one of the seventy elders whom Moses appointed (<reflink>Num. 11:26, 27</reflink>) to administer justice among the people. He, with Medad, prophesied in the camp instead of going with the rest to the tabernacle, as Moses had commanded. This incident was announced to Moses by Joshua, who thought their conduct in this respect irregular. Moses replied, "Enviest thou for my sake? would God that all the Lord's people were prophets" (<reflink>Num. 11:24-30; comp. Mark 9:38; Luke 9:49</reflink>).

elder.d: a name frequently used in the Old Testament as denoting a person clothed with authority, and entitled to respect and reverence (<reflink>Gen. 50:7</reflink>). It also denoted a political office (<reflink>Num. 22:7</reflink>). The "elders of Israel" held a rank among the people indicative of authority. Moses opened his commission to them (<reflink>Ex. 3:16</reflink>). They attended Moses on all important occasions. Seventy of them attended on him at the giving of the law (<reflink>Ex. 24:1</reflink>). Seventy also were selected from the whole number to bear with Moses the burden of the people (<reflink>Num. 11:16, 17</reflink>). The "elder" is the keystone of the social and political fabric wherever the patriarchal system exists. At the present day this is the case among the Arabs, where the sheik (i.e., "the old man") is the highest authority in the tribe. …

elealeh.d: God has ascended, a place in the pastoral country east of Jordan, in the tribe of Reuben (<reflink>Num. 32:3, 37</reflink>). It is not again mentioned till the time of Isaiah (15:4; 16:9) and Jeremiah (48:34). It is now an extensive ruin called el-A'al, about one mile north-east of Heshbon.

eleazar.d: God has helped. (1.) The third son of Aaron (<reflink>Ex. 6:23</reflink>). His wife, a daughter of Putiel, bore him Phinehas (<reflink>Ex. 6:25</reflink>). After the death of Nadab and Abihu (<reflink>Lev. 10:12; Num. 3:4</reflink>) he was appointed to the charge of the sanctuary (<reflink>Num. 3:32</reflink>). On Mount Hor he was clothed with the sacred vestments, which Moses took from off his brother Aaron and put upon him as successor to his father in the high priest's office, which he held for more than twenty years (<reflink>Num. 20:25-29</reflink>). He took part with Moses in numbering the people (26:3, 4), and assisted at the inauguration of Joshua. He assisted in the distribution of the land after the conquest (<reflink>Josh. 14:1</reflink>). The high-priesthood remained in his family till the time of Eli, into whose family it passed, till it was restored to the family of Eleazar in the person of Zadok (<reflink>1 Sam. 2:35; comp. 1 Kings 2:27</reflink>). …

elect lady.d: to whom the Second Epistle of John is addressed (<reflink>2 John 1:1</reflink>). Some think that the word rendered "lady" is a proper name, and thus that the expression should be "elect Kyria."

election of grace.d: The Scripture speaks (1) of the election of individuals to office or to honour and privilege, e.g., Abraham, Jacob, Saul, David, Solomon, were all chosen by God for the positions they held; so also were the apostles. (2) There is also an election of nations to special privileges, e.g., the Hebrews (<reflink>Deut. 7:6; Rom. 9:4</reflink>). (3) But in addition there is an election of individuals to eternal life (<reflink>2 Thess. 2:13; Eph. 1:4; 1 Pet. 1:2; John 13:18</reflink>).

elements.d: In its primary sense, as denoting the first principles or constituents of things, it is used in 2 Pet. 3:10: "The elements shall be dissolved." In a secondary sense it denotes the first principles of any art or science. In this sense it is used in Gal. 4:3, 9; Col. 2:8, 20, where the expressions, "elements of the world," "week and beggarly elements," denote that state of religious knowledge existing among the Jews before the coming of Christ, the rudiments of religious teaching. They are "of the world," because they are made up of types which appeal to the senses. They are "weak," because insufficient; and "beggarly," or "poor," because they are dry and barren, not being accompanied by an outpouring of spiritual gifts and graces, as the gospel is.

elephant.d: not found in Scripture except indirectly in the original Greek word (elephantinos) translated "of ivory" in Rev. 18:12, and in the Hebrew word (shenhabim, meaning "elephant's tooth") rendered "ivory" in 1 Kings 10:22 and 2 Chr. 9:21.

elhanan.d: whom God has graciously bestowed. (1.) A warrior of the time of David famed for his exploits. In the Authorized Version (<reflink>2 Sam. 21:19</reflink>) it is recorded that "Elhanan the son of Jaare-oregim, a Bethlehemite, slew the brother of Goliath." The Revised Version here rightly omits the words "the brother of." They were introduced in the Authorized Version to bring this passage into agreement with 1 Chr. 20:5, where it is said that he "slew Lahmi the brother of Goliath." Goliath the Gittite was killed by David (1 Sam. 17). The exploit of Elhanan took place late in David's reign.

eli.d: ascent, the high priest when the ark was at Shiloh (<reflink>1 Sam. 1:3, 9</reflink>). He was the first of the line of Ithamar, Aaron's fourth son (<reflink>1 Chr. 24:3; comp. 2 Sam. 8:17</reflink>), who held that office. The office remained in his family till the time of Abiathar (<reflink>1 Kings 2:26, 27</reflink>), whom Solomon deposed, and appointed Zadok, of the family of Eleazar, in his stead (35). He acted also as a civil judge in Israel after the death of Samson (<reflink>1 Sam. 4:18</reflink>), and judged Israel for forty years.

eliab.d: to whom God is father. (1.) A Reubenite, son of Pallu (<reflink>Num. 16:1, 12; 26:8, 9; Deut. 11:6</reflink>).

eliada.d: whom God cares for. (1.) One of David's sons born after his establishment in Jerusalem (<reflink>2 Sam. 5:16</reflink>).

eliakim.d: whom God will raise up. (1.) The son of Melea (<reflink>Luke 3:30</reflink>), and probably grandson of Nathan.

eliam.d: God's people. (1.) The father of Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah (<reflink>2 Sam. 11:3</reflink>). In 1 Chr. 3:5 his name is Ammiel.

elias.d: the Greek form of Elijah (<reflink>Matt. 11:14; 16:14, etc.</reflink>), which the Revised Version has uniformly adopted in the New Testament. (<see target="x-self">See ELIJAH.</see>)

eliashib.d: whom God will restore. (1.) A priest, head of one of the courses of the priests of the time of David (<reflink>1 Chr. 24:12</reflink>).

eliathah.d: to whom God will come, one of the foureen sons of the Levite Heman, and musician of the temple in the time of David (<reflink>1 Chr. 25:4</reflink>).

elidad.d: whom God has loved, son of Chislon, and chief of the tribe of Benjamin; one of those who were appointed to divide the Promised Land among the tribes (<reflink>Num. 34:21</reflink>).

eliel.d: to whom God is might. (1.) A chief of Manasseh, on the east of Jordan (<reflink>1 Chr. 5:24</reflink>).

eliezer.d: God his help. (1.) "Of Damascus," the "steward" (R.V., "possessor") of Abraham's house (<reflink>Gen. 15:2, 3</reflink>). It was probably he who headed the embassy sent by Abraham to the old home of his family in Padan-aram to seek a wife for his son Isaac. The account of this embassy is given at length in Gen. 24.

elihu.d: whose God is he. (1.) "The son of Barachel, a Buzite" (<reflink>Job 32:2</reflink>), one of Job's friends. When the debate between Job and his friends is brought to a close, Elihu for the first time makes his appearance, and delivers his opinion on the points at issue (Job 32-37).

elijah.d: whose God is Jehovah. (1.) "The Tishbite," the "Elias" of the New Testament, is suddenly introduced to our notice in 1 Kings 17:1 as delivering a message from the Lord to Ahab. There is mention made of a town called Thisbe, south of Kadesh, but it is impossible to say whether this was the place referred to in the name given to the prophet.

elika.d: God is his rejector, one of David's thirty-seven distinguished heros (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:25</reflink>).

elim.d: trees, (<reflink>Ex. 15:27; Num. 33:9</reflink>), the name of the second station where the Israelites encamped after crossing the Red Sea. It had "twelve wells of water and threescore and ten palm trees." It has been identified with the Wady Ghurundel, the most noted of the four wadies which descend from the range of et-Tih towards the sea. Here they probably remained some considerable time. The form of expression in Ex. 16:1 seems to imply that the people proceeded in detachments or companies from Elim, and only for the first time were assembled as a complete host when they reached the wilderness of Sin (q.v.).

elimelech.d: God his king, a man of the tribe of Judah, of the family of the Hezronites, and kinsman of Boaz, who dwelt in Bethlehem in the days of the judges. In consequence of a great dearth he, with his wife Naomi and his two sons, went to dwell in the land of Moab. There he and his sons died (<reflink>Ruth 1:2,3; 2:1,3; 4:3,9</reflink>). Naomi afterwards returned to Palestine with her daughter Ruth.

elioenai.d: toward Jehovah are my eyes, the name of several men mentioned in the Old Testament (<reflink>1 Chr. 7:8; 4:36; Ezra 10:22, 27</reflink>). Among these was the eldest son of Neariah, son of Shemaiah, of the descendants of Zerubbabel. His family are the latest mentioned in the Old Testament (<reflink>1 Chr. 3:23, 24</reflink>).

eliphalet.d: God his deliverance, one of David's sons (<reflink>2 Sam. 5:16</reflink>); called also Eliphelet (<reflink>1 Chr. 3:8</reflink>).

eliphaz.d: God his strength. (1.) One of Job's "three friends" who visited him in his affliction (4:1). He was a "Temanite", i.e., a native of Teman, in Idumea. He first enters into debate with Job. His language is uniformly more delicate and gentle than that of the other two, although he imputes to Job special sins as the cause of his present sufferings. He states with remarkable force of language the infinite purity and majesty of God (4:12-21; 15:12-16).

elipheleh.d: God will distinguish him, one of the porters appointed to play "on the Sheminith" on the occasion of the bringing up of the ark to the city of David (<reflink>1 Chr. 15:18, 21</reflink>).

eliphelet.d: God his deliverance. (1.) One of David's distinguished warriors (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:34</reflink>); called also Eliphal in 1 Chr. 11:35.

elisabeth.d: God her oath, the mother of John the Baptist (<reflink>Luke 1:5</reflink>). She was a descendant of Aaron. She and her husband Zacharias (q.v.) "were both righteous before God" (<reflink>Luke 1:5, 13</reflink>). Mary's visit to Elisabeth is described in 1:39-63.

elisha.d: God his salvation, the son of Shaphat of Abel-meholah, who became the attendant and disciple of Elijah (<reflink>1 Kings 19:16-19</reflink>). His name first occurs in the command given to Elijah to anoint him as his successor (<reflink>1 Kings 19:16</reflink>). This was the only one of the three commands then given to Elijah which he accomplished. On his way from Sinai to Damascus he found Elisha at his native place engaged in the labours of the field, ploughing with twelve yoke of oxen. He went over to him, threw over his shoulders his rough mantle, and at once adopted him as a son, and invested him with the prophetical office (<reflink>comp. Luke 9:61, 62</reflink>). Elisha accepted the call thus given (about four years before the death of Ahab), and for some seven or eight years became the close attendant on Elijah till he was parted from him and taken up into heaven. During all these years we hear nothing of Elisha except in connection with the closing scenes of Elijah's life. …

elishah.d: the oldest of the four sons of Javan (<reflink>Gen. 10:4</reflink>), whose descendants peopled Greece. It has been supposed that Elishah's descendants peopled the Peloponnesus, which was known by the name of Elis. This may be meant by "the isles of Elishah" (<reflink>Ezek. 27:7</reflink>).

elishama.d: whom God hears. (1.) A prince of Benjamin, grandfather of Joshua (<reflink>Num. 1:10; 1 Chr. 7:26</reflink>). (2.) One of David's sons (<reflink>2 Sam. 5:16</reflink>). (3.) Another of David's sons (<reflink>1 Chr. 3:6</reflink>). (4.) A priest sent by Jehoshaphat to teach the people the law (<reflink>2 Chr. 17:8</reflink>).

elishaphat.d: whom God has judged, one of the "captains of hundreds" associated with Jehoiada in the league to overthrow the usurpation of Athaliah (<reflink>2 Chr. 23:1</reflink>).

elisheba.d: God is her oath, the daughter of Amminadab and the wife of Aaron (<reflink>Ex. 6:23</reflink>).
