elishua.d: God his salvation, a son of David, 2 Sam. 5:15 = Elishama, 1 Chr. 3:6.

elkanah.d: God-created. (1.) The second son of Korah (<reflink>Ex. 6:24</reflink>), or, according to 1 Chr. 6:22, 23, more correctly his grandson.

elkosh.d: God my bow, the birth-place of Nahum the prophet (<reflink>Nah. 1:1</reflink>). It was probably situated in Galilee, but nothing definite is known of it.

ellasar.d: the oak or heap of Assyria, a territory in Asia of which Arioch was king (<reflink>Gen. 14:1, 9</reflink>). It is supposed that the old Chaldean town of Larsa was the metropolis of this kingdom, situated nearly half-way between Ur (now Mugheir) and Erech, on the left bank of the Euphrates. This town is represented by the mounds of Senkereh, a little to the east of Erech.

elm.d: Hos. 4:13; rendered "terebinth" in the Revised Version. It is the Pistacia terebinthus of Linn., a tree common in Palestine, long-lived, and therefore often employed for landmarks and in designating places (<reflink>Gen. 35:4; Judg. 6:11, 19. Rendered "oak" in both A.V. and R.V.</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See TEIL TREE.</see>)

elnathan.d: whom God has given. (1.) An inhabitant of Jerusalem, the father of Nehushta, who was the mother of king Jehoiachin (<reflink>2 Kings 24:8</reflink>). Probably the same who tried to prevent Jehoiakim from burning the roll of Jeremiah's prophecies (<reflink>Jer. 26:22; 36:12</reflink>). (2.) Ezra 8:16.

elon.d: oak. (1.) A city of Dan (<reflink>Josh. 19:43</reflink>). (2.) A Hittite, father of Bashemath, Esau's wife (<reflink>Gen. 26:34</reflink>). (3.) One of the sons of Zebulun (<reflink>Gen. 46:14</reflink>). (4.) The eleventh of the Hebrew judges. He held office for ten years (<reflink>Judg. 12:11, 12</reflink>). He is called the Zebulonite.

elparan.d: oak of Paran, a place on the edge of the wilderness bordering the territory of the Horites (<reflink>Gen. 14:6</reflink>). This was the farthest point to which Chedorlaomer's expedition extended. It is identified with the modern desert of et-Tih. (See PARAN

eltekeh.d: God is its fear, a city in the tribe of Dan. It was a city of refuge and a Levitical city (<reflink>Josh. 21:23</reflink>). It has been identified with Beit-Likia, north-east of latrum.

elul.d: (<reflink>Neh. 6:15</reflink>), the name of the sixth month of the ecclesiastical year, and the twelfth of the civil year. It began with the new moon of our August and September, and consisted of twenty-nine days.

elymas.d: magician or sorcerer, the Arabic name of the Jew Bar-jesus, who withstood Paul and Barnabas in Cyprus. He was miraculously struck with blindness (<reflink>Acts 13:11</reflink>).

embalming.d: the process of preserving a body by means of aromatics (<reflink>Gen. 50:2, 3, 26</reflink>). This art was practised by the Egyptians from the earliest times, and there brought to great perfection. This custom probably originated in the belief in the future reunion of the soul with the body. The process became more and more complicated, and to such perfection was it carried that bodies embalmed thousands of years ago are preserved to the present day in the numberless mummies that have been discovered in Egypt.

embroider.d: The art of embroidery was known to the Jews (<reflink>Ex. 26:36; 35:35; 38:23; Judg. 5:30; Ps. 45:14</reflink>). The skill of the women in this art was seen in the preparation of the sacerdotal robes of the high priest (Ex. 28). It seems that the art became hereditary in certain families (<reflink>1 Chr. 4:21</reflink>). The Assyrians were also noted for their embroidered robes (<reflink>Ezek. 27:24</reflink>).

emerald.d: Heb. nophek (<reflink>Ex. 28:18; 39:11</reflink>); i.e., the "glowing stone", probably the carbuncle, a precious stone in the breastplate of the high priest. It is mentioned (<reflink>Rev. 21:19</reflink>) as one of the foundations of the New Jerusalem. The name given to this stone in the New Testament Greek is smaragdos, which means "live coal."

emims.d: terrors, a warlike tribe of giants who were defeated by Chedorlaomer and his allies in the plain of Kiriathaim. In the time of Abraham they occupied the country east of Jordan, afterwards the land of the Moabites (<reflink>Gen. 14:5; Deut. 2:10</reflink>). They were, like the Anakim, reckoned among the Rephaim, and were conquered by the Moabites, who gave them the name of Emims, i.e., "terrible men" (<reflink>Deut. 2:11</reflink>). The Ammonites called them Zamzummims (2:20).

emmanuel.d: God with us, Matt. 1:23). (<see target="x-self">See IMMANUEL.</see>)

emmaus.d: hot baths, a village "three-score furlongs" from jerusalem, where our Lord had an interview with two of his disciples on the day of his resurrection (<reflink>Luke 24:13</reflink>). This has been identified with the modern el-Kubeibeh, lying over 7 miles north-west of Jerusalem. This name, el-Kubeibeh, meaning "little dome," is derived from the remains of the Crusaders' church yet to be found there. Others have identified it with the modern Khurbet Khamasa i.e., "the ruins of Khamasa", about 8 miles south-west of Jerusalem, where there are ruins also of a Crusaders' church. Its site, however has been much disputed.

en-eglaim.d: fountain of two calves, a place mentioned only in Ezek. 47:10. Somewhere near the Dead Sea.

en-gannim.d: fountain of gardens. (1.) A town in the plains of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:34</reflink>), north-west of Jerusalem, between Zanoah and Tappuah. It is the modern Umm Jina.

en-hakkore.d: fountain of the crier, the name of the spring in Lehi which burst forth in answer to Samson's prayer when he was exhausted with the slaughter of the Philistines (<reflink>Judg. 15:19</reflink>). It has been identified with the spring 'Ayun Kara, near Zoreah.

en-rogel.d: fountain of the treaders; i.e., "foot-fountain;" also called the "fullers' fountain," because fullers here trod the clothes in water. It has been identified with the "fountain of the virgin" (q.v.), the modern 'Ain Ummel-Daraj. Others identify it, with perhaps some probability, with the Bir Eyub, to the south of the Pool of Siloam, and below the junction of the valleys of Kidron and Hinnom. (<see target="x-self">See FOUNTAIN.</see>)

en-shemesh.d: fountain of the sun a spring which formed one of the landmarks on the boundary between Judah and Benjamin (<reflink>Josh. 15:7; 18:17</reflink>). It was between the "ascent of Adummim" and the spring of En-rogel, and hence was on the east of Jerusalem and of the Mount of Olives. It is the modern 'Ain-Haud i.e., the "well of the apostles" about a mile east of Bethany, the only spring on the road to Jericho. The sun shines on it the whole day long.

encamp.d: An encampment was the resting-place for a longer or shorter period of an army or company of travellers (<reflink>Ex. 13:20; 14:19; Josh. 10:5; 11:5</reflink>).

enchantments.d: (1.) The rendering of Hebrew _latim_ or _lehatim_, which means "something covered," "muffled up;" secret arts, tricks (<reflink>Ex. 7:11, 22; 8:7, 18</reflink>), by which the Egyptian magicians imposed on the credulity of Pharaoh.

end.d: in Heb. 13:7, is the rendering of the unusual Greek word _ekbasin_, meaning "outcome", i.e., death. It occurs only elsewhere in 1 Cor. 10:13, where it is rendered "escape."

endor.d: fountain of Dor; i.e., "of the age", a place in the territory of Issachar (<reflink>Josh. 17:11</reflink>) near the scene of the great victory which was gained by Deborah and Barak over Sisera and Jabin (<reflink>comp. Ps. 83:9, 10</reflink>). To Endor, Saul resorted to consult one reputed to be a witch on the eve of his last engagement with the Philistines (<reflink>1 Sam. 28:7</reflink>). It is identified with the modern village of Endur, "a dirty hamlet of some twenty houses, or rather huts, most of them falling to ruin," on the northern slope of Little Hermon, about 7 miles from Jezreel.

engedi.d: fountain of the kid, place in the wilderness of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:62</reflink>), on the western shore of the Dead Sea (<reflink>Ezek. 47:10</reflink>), and nearly equidistant from both extremities. To the wilderness near this town David fled for fear of Saul (<reflink>Josh. 15:62; 1 Sam. 23:29</reflink>). It was at first called Hazezon-tamar (<reflink>Gen. 14:7</reflink>), a city of the Amorites.

engines.d: (1.) Heb. hishalon i.e., "invention" (<reflink>as in Eccl. 7:29</reflink>) contrivances indicating ingenuity. In 2 Chr. 26:15 it refers to inventions for the purpose of propelling missiles from the walls of a town, such as stones (the Roman balista) and arrows (the catapulta).

engraver.d: Heb. harash (<reflink>Ex. 35:35; 38:23</reflink>) means properly an artificer in wood, stone, or metal. The chief business of the engraver was cutting names or devices on rings and seals and signets (<reflink>Ex. 28:11, 21, 36; Gen. 38:18</reflink>).

enmity.d: deep-rooted hatred. "I will put enmity between thee and the woman, between thy seed and her seed" (<reflink>Gen. 3:15</reflink>). The friendship of the world is "enmity with God" (<reflink>James 4:4; 1 John 2:15, 16</reflink>). The "carnal mind" is "enmity against God" (<reflink>Rom. 8:7</reflink>). By the abrogation of the Mosaic institutes the "enmity" between Jew and Gentile is removed. They are reconciled, are "made one" (<reflink>Eph. 2:15, 16</reflink>).

enoch.d: initiated. (1.) The eldest son of Cain (<reflink>Gen. 4:17</reflink>), who built a city east of Eden in the land of Nod, and called it "after the name of his son Enoch." This is the first "city" mentioned in Scripture.

enos.d: man the son of Seth, and grandson of Adam (<reflink>Gen. 5:6-11; Luke 3:38</reflink>). He lived nine hundred and five years. In his time "men began to call upon the name of the Lord" (<reflink>Gen. 4:26</reflink>), meaning either (1) then began men to call themselves by the name of the Lord (marg.) i.e., to distinguish themselves thereby from idolaters; or (2) then men in some public and earnest way began to call upon the Lord, indicating a time of spiritual revival.

ensign.d: (1.) Heb. 'oth, a military standard, especially of a single tribe (<reflink>Num. 2:2</reflink>). Each separate tribe had its own "sign" or "ensign."

entertain.d: Entertainments, "feasts," were sometimes connected with a public festival (<reflink>Deut. 16:11, 14</reflink>), and accompanied by offerings (<reflink>1 Sam. 9:13</reflink>), in token of alliances (<reflink>Gen. 26:30</reflink>); sometimes in connection with domestic or social events, as at the weaning of children (<reflink>Gen. 21:8</reflink>), at weddings (<reflink>Gen. 29:22; John 2:1</reflink>), on birth-days (<reflink>Matt. 14:6</reflink>), at the time of sheep-shearing (<reflink>2 Sam. 13:23</reflink>), and of vintage (<reflink>Judg. 9:27</reflink>), and at funerals (<reflink>2 Sam. 3:35; Jer. 16:7</reflink>).

epaenetus.d: commendable, a Christian at Rome to whom Paul sent his salutation (<reflink>Rom. 16:5</reflink>). He is spoken of as "the first fruits of Achaia" (R.V., "of Asia", i.e., of proconsular Asia, which is probably the correct reading). As being the first convert in that region, he was peculiarly dear to the apostle. He calls him his "well beloved."

epaphras.d: lovely, spoken of by Paul (<reflink>Col. 1:7; 4:12</reflink>) as "his dear fellow-servant," and "a faithful minister of Christ." He was thus evidently with him at Rome when he wrote to the Colossians. He was a distinguished disciple, and probably the founder of the Colossian church. He is also mentioned in the Epistle to Philemon (1:23), where he is called by Paul his "fellow-prisoner."

epaphroditus.d: fair, graceful; belonging to Aphrodite or Venus the messenger who came from Phillipi to the apostle when he was a prisoner at Rome (<reflink>Phil. 2:25-30; 4:10-18</reflink>). Paul mentions him in words of esteem and affection. On his return to Philippi he was the bearer of Paul's letter to the church there.

ephah.d: gloom. (1.) One of the five sons of Midian, and grandson of Abraham (<reflink>Gen. 25:4</reflink>). The city of Ephah, to which he gave his name, is mentioned Isa. 60:6, 7. This city, with its surrounding territory, formed part of Midian, on the east shore of the Dead Sea. It abounded in dromedaries and camels (<reflink>Judg. 6:5</reflink>).

epher.d: a calf. (1.) One of the sons of Midian, who was Abraham's son by Keturah (<reflink>Gen. 25:4</reflink>).

ephes-dammim.d: boundary of blood, a place in the tribe of Judah where the Philistines encamped when David fought with Goliath (<reflink>1 Sam. 17:1</reflink>). It was probably so called as having been the scene of frequent sanguinary conflicts between Israel and the Philistines. It is called Pas-dammim (<reflink>1 Chr. 11:13</reflink>). It has been identified with the modern Beit Fased, i.e., "house of bleeding", near Shochoh (q.v.).

ephesians, epistle to.d: was written by Paul at Rome about the same time as that to the Colossians, which in many points it resembles.

ephesus.d: the capital of proconsular Asia, which was the western part of Asia Minor. It was colonized principally from Athens. In the time of the Romans it bore the title of "the first and greatest metropolis of Asia." It was distinguished for the Temple of Diana (q.v.), who there had her chief shrine; and for its theatre, which was the largest in the world, capable of containing 50,000 spectators. It was, like all ancient theatres, open to the sky. Here were exhibited the fights of wild beasts and of men with beasts. (Comp. 1 Cor. 4:9; 9:24, 25; 15:32.)

ephod.d: something girt, a sacred vestment worn originally by the high priest (<reflink>Ex. 28:4</reflink>), afterwards by the ordinary priest (<reflink>1 Sam. 22:18</reflink>), and characteristic of his office (<reflink>1 Sam. 2:18, 28; 14:3</reflink>). It was worn by Samuel, and also by David (<reflink>2 Sam. 6:14</reflink>). It was made of fine linen, and consisted of two pieces, which hung from the neck, and covered both the back and front, above the tunic and outer garment (<reflink>Ex. 28:31</reflink>). That of the high priest was embroidered with divers colours. The two pieces were joined together over the shoulders (hence in Latin called superhumerale) by clasps or buckles of gold or precious stones, and fastened round the waist by a "curious girdle of gold, blue, purple, and fine twined linen" (28:6-12).

ephphatha.d: the Greek form of a Syro-Chaldaic or Aramaic word, meaning "Be opened," uttered by Christ when healing the man who was deaf and dumb (<reflink>Mark 7:34</reflink>). It is one of the characteristics of Mark that he uses the very Aramaic words which fell from our Lord's lips. (<reflink>See 3:17; 5:41; 7:11; 14:36; 15:34.</reflink>)

ephraim.d: double fruitfulness ("for God had made him fruitful in the land of his affliction"). The second son of Joseph, born in Egypt (<reflink>Gen. 41:52; 46:20</reflink>). The first incident recorded regarding him is his being placed, along with his brother Manasseh, before their grandfather, Jacob, that he might bless them (48:10; comp. 27:1). The intention of Joseph was that the right hand of the aged patriarch should be placed on the head of the elder of the two; but Jacob set Ephraim the younger before his brother, "guiding his hands wittingly." Before Joseph's death, Ephraim's family had reached the third generation (<reflink>Gen. 50:23</reflink>).

ephraim in the wilderness.d: (<reflink>John 11: 54</reflink>), a town to which our Lord retired with his disciples after he had raised Lazarus, and when the priests were conspiring against him. It lay in the wild, uncultivated hill-country to the north-east of Jerusalem, betwen the central towns and the Jordan valley.

ephraim, gate of.d: one of the gates of Jerusalem (<reflink>2 Kings 14:13; 2 Chr. 25:23</reflink>), on the side of the city looking toward Ephraim, the north side.

ephraim, mount.d: the central mountainous district of Palestine occupied by the tribe of Ephraim (<reflink>Josh. 17:15; 19:50; 20:7</reflink>), extending from Bethel to the plain of Jezreel. In Joshua's time (<reflink>Josh. 17:18</reflink>) these hills were densely wooded. They were intersected by well-watered, fertile valleys, referred to in Jer. 50:19. Joshua was buried at Timnath-heres among the mountains of Ephraim, on the north side of the hill of Gaash (<reflink>Judg. 2:9</reflink>). This region is also called the "mountains of Israel" (<reflink>Josh. 11:21</reflink>) and the "mountains of Samaria" (<reflink>Jer. 31:5, 6: Amos 3:9</reflink>).

ephraim, the tribe of.d: took precedence over that of Manasseh by virtue of Jacob's blessing (<reflink>Gen. 41:52; 48:1</reflink>). The descendants of Joseph formed two of the tribes of Israel, whereas each of the other sons of Jacob was the founder of only one tribe. Thus there were in reality thirteen tribes; but the number twelve was preserved by excluding that of Levi when Ephraim and Manasseh are mentioned separately (<reflink>Num. 1:32-34; Josh. 17:14, 17; 1 Chr. 7:20</reflink>).

ephraim, wood of.d: a forest in which a fatal battle was fought between the army of David and that of Absalom, who was killed there (<reflink>2 Sam. 18:6, 8</reflink>). It lay on the east of Jordan, not far from Mahanaim, and was some part of the great forest of Gilead.

ephratah.d: fruitful. (1.) The second wife of Caleb, the son of Hezron, mother of Hur, and grandmother of Caleb, who was one of those that were sent to spy the land (<reflink>1 Chr. 2:19, 50</reflink>).

ephrathite.d: a citizen of Ephratah, the old name of Bethlehem (<reflink>Ruth 1:2; 1 Sam. 17:12</reflink>), or Bethlehem-Judah.

ephron.d: fawn-like. (1.) The son of Zohar a Hittite, the owner of the field and cave of Machpelah (q.v.), which Abraham bought for 400 shekels of silver (<reflink>Gen. 23:8-17; 25:9; 49:29, 30</reflink>).

epicureans.d: followers of Epicurus (who died at Athens B.C. 270), or adherents of the Epicurean philosophy (<reflink>Acts 17:18</reflink>). This philosophy was a system of atheism, and taught men to seek as their highest aim a pleasant and smooth life. They have been called the "Sadducees" of Greek paganism. They, with the Stoics, ridiculed the teaching of Paul (<reflink>Acts 17:18</reflink>). They appear to have been greatly esteemed at Athens.

epistles.d: the apostolic letters. The New Testament contains twenty-one in all. They are divided into two classes. (1.) Paul's Epistles, fourteen in number, including Hebrews. These are not arranged in the New Testament in the order of time as to their composition, but rather according to the rank of the cities or places to which they were sent. Who arranged them after this manner is unknown. Paul's letters were, as a rule, dictated to an amanuensis, a fact which accounts for some of their peculiarities. He authenticated them, however, by adding a few words in his own hand at the close. (See GALATIANS, EPISTLE TO

erastus.d: beloved. (1.) The "chamberlain" of the city of Corinth (<reflink>Rom. 16:23</reflink>), and one of Paul's disciples. As treasurer of such a city he was a public officer of great dignity, and his conversion to the gospel was accordingly a proof of the wonderful success of the apostle's labours.

erech.d: (LXX., "Orech"), length, or Moon-town, one of the cities of Nimrod's kingdom in the plain of Shinar (<reflink>Gen. 10:10</reflink>); the Orchoe of the Greeks and Romans. It was probably the city of the Archevites, who were transplanted to Samaria by Asnapper (<reflink>Ezra 4:9</reflink>). It lay on the left bank of the Euphrates, about 120 miles south-east of Babylon, and is now represented by the mounds and ruins of Warka. It appears to have been the necropolis of the Assyrian kings, as the whole region is strewed with bricks and the remains of coffins. "Standing on the summit of the principal edifice, called the Buwarizza, a tower 200 feet square in the centre of the ruins, the beholder is struck with astonishment at the enormous accumulation of mounds and ancient relics at his feet. An irregular circle, nearly 6 miles in circumference, is defined by the traces of an earthen rampart, in some places 40 feet high."

esaias.d: the Greek form for Isaiah, constantly used in the Authorized Version of the New Testament (<reflink>Matt. 3:3; 4:14</reflink>), but in the Revised Version always "Isaiah."

esarhaddon.d: Assur has given a brother, successor of Sennacherib (<reflink>2 Kings 19:37; Isa. 37:38</reflink>). He ascended the throne about B.C. 681. Nothing further is recorded of him in Scripture, except that he settled certain colonists in Samaria (<reflink>Ezra 4:2</reflink>). But from the monuments it appears that he was the most powerful of all the Assyrian monarchs. He built many temples and palaces, the most magnificent of which was the south-west palace at Nimrud, which is said to have been in its general design almost the same as Solomon's palace, only much larger (<reflink>1 Kings 7:1-12</reflink>).

esau.d: hairy, Rebekah's first-born twin son (<reflink>Gen. 25:25</reflink>). The name of Edom, "red", was also given to him from his conduct in connection with the red lentil "pottage" for which he sold his birthright (30, 31). The circumstances connected with his birth foreshadowed the enmity which afterwards subsisted between the twin brothers and the nations they founded (25:22, 23, 26). In process of time Jacob, following his natural bent, became a shepherd; while Esau, a "son of the desert," devoted himself to the perilous and toilsome life of a huntsman. On a certain occasion, on returning from the chase, urged by the cravings of hunger, Esau sold his birthright to his brother, Jacob, who thereby obtained the covenant blessing (<reflink>Gen. 27:28, 29, 36; Heb. 12:16, 17</reflink>). He afterwards tried to regain what he had so recklessly parted with, but was defeated in his attempts through the stealth of his brother (<reflink>Gen. 27:4, 34, 38</reflink>).

eschew.d: from old French eschever, "to flee from" (<reflink>Job 1:1, 8; 2:3; 1 Pet. 3:11</reflink>).

esdraelon.d: the Greek form of the Hebrew "Jezreel," the name of the great plain (called by the natives Merj Ibn Amer; i.e., "the meadow of the son of Amer") which stretches across Central Palestine from the Jordan to the Mediterraanean, separating the mountain ranges of Carmel and Samaria from those of Galilee, extending about 14 miles from north to south, and 9 miles from east to west. It is drained by "that ancient river" the Kishon, which flows westward to the Mediterranean. From the foot of Mount Tabor it branches out into three valleys, that on the north passing between Tabor and Little Hermon (<reflink>Judg. 4:14</reflink>); that on the south between Mount Gilboa and En-gannim (<reflink>2 Kings 9:27</reflink>); while the central portion, the "valley of Jezreel" proper, runs into the Jordan valley (which is about 1,000 feet lower than Esdraelon) by Bethshean. Here Gideon gained his great victory over the Midianites (<reflink>Judg. 7:1-25</reflink>). …

esek.d: quarrel, a well which Isaac's herdsmen dug in the valley of Gerar, and so called because the herdsmen of Gerar quarrelled with them for its possession (<reflink>Gen. 26:20</reflink>).

eshbaal.d: man of Baal, the fourth son of king Saul (<reflink>1 Chr. 8:33; 9:39</reflink>). He is also called Ish-bosheth (q.v.), 2 Sam. 2:8.

eshcol.d: bunch; brave. (1.) A young Amoritish chief who joined Abraham in the recovery of Lot from the hands of Chedorlaomer (<reflink>Gen. 14:13, 24</reflink>).

eshean.d: a place in the mountains of Judah (<reflink>Josh.15:52</reflink>), supposed to be the ruin es-Simia, near Dumah, south of Hebron.

eshtaol.d: narrow pass or recess, a town (<reflink>Josh. 15:33</reflink>) in the low country, the She-phelah of Judah. It was allotted to the tribe of Dan (<reflink>Josh. 19:41</reflink>), and was one of their strongholds. Here Samson spent his boyhood, and first began to show his mighty strength; and here he was buried in the burying-place of Manoah his father (<reflink>Judg. 13:25; 16:31; 18:2, 8, 11, 12</reflink>). It is identified with the modern Yeshua, on a hill 2 miles east of Zorah. Others, however, identify it with Kustul, east of Kirjath-jearim.

eshtemoa.d: obedience, a town in the mountains of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 21:14; 1 Chr. 6:57</reflink>), which was allotted, with the land round it, to the priests. It was frequented by David and his followers during their wanderings; and he sent presents of the spoil of the Amalekites to his friends there (<reflink>1 Sam. 30:28</reflink>). It is identified with es-Semu'a, a village about 3 1/2 miles east of Socoh, and 7 or 8 miles south of Hebron, around which there are ancient remains of the ruined city. It is the centre of the "south country" or Negeb. It is also called "Eshtemoh" (<reflink>Josh. 15:50</reflink>).

espouse.d: (<reflink>2 Sam. 3:14</reflink>), to betroth. The espousal was a ceremony of betrothing, a formal agreement between the parties then coming under obligation for the purpose of marriage. Espousals are in the East frequently contracted years before the marriage is celebrated. It is referred to as figuratively illustrating the relations between God and his people (<reflink>Jer. 2:2; Matt. 1:18; 2 Cor. 11:2</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See BETROTH.</see>)

essenes.d: a Jewish mystical sect somewhat resembling the Pharisees. They affected great purity. They originated about B.C. 100, and disappeared from history after the destruction of Jerusalem. They are not directly mentioned in Scripture, although they may be referred to in Matt. 19:11, 12, Col. 2:8, 18, 23.

esther.d: the queen of Ahasuerus, and heroine of the book that bears her name. She was a Jewess named Hadas'sah (the myrtle), but when she entered the royal harem she received the name by which she henceforth became known (<reflink>Esther 2:7</reflink>). It is a Syro-Arabian modification of the Persian word satarah, which means a star. She was the daughter of Abihail, a Benjamite. Her family did not avail themselves of the permission granted by Cyrus to the exiles to return to Jerusalem; and she resided with her cousin Mordecai, who held some office in the household of the Persian king at "Shushan in the palace." Ahasuerus having divorced Vashti, chose Esther to be his wife. Soon after this he gave Haman the Agagite, his prime minister, power and authority to kill and extirpate all the Jews throughout the Persian empire. By the interposition of Esther this terrible catastrophe was averted. …

esther, book of.d: The authorship of this book is unknown. It must have been obviously written after the death of Ahasuerus (the Xerxes of the Greeks), which took place B.C. 465. The minute and particular account also given of many historical details makes it probable that the writer was contemporary with Mordecai and Esther. Hence we may conclude that the book was written probably about B.C. 444-434, and that the author was one of the Jews of the dispersion.

etam.d: eyrie. (1.) A village of the tribe of Simeon (<reflink>1 Chr. 4:32</reflink>). Into some cleft ("top," A.V.,; R.V., "cleft") of a rock here Samson retired after his slaughter of the Philistines (<reflink>Judg. 15:8, 11</reflink>). It was a natural stronghold. It has been identified with Beit 'Atab, west of Bethlehem, near Zorah and Eshtaol. On the crest of a rocky knoll, under the village, is a long tunnel, which may be the "cleft" in which Samson hid.

eternal death.d: The miserable fate of the wicked in hell (<reflink>Matt. 25:46; Mark 3:29; Heb. 6:2; 2 Thess. 1:9; Matt. 18:8; 25:41; Jude 1:7</reflink>). The Scripture as clearly teaches the unending duration of the penal sufferings of the lost as the "everlasting life," the "eternal life" of the righteous. The same Greek words in the New Testament (aion, aionios, aidios) are used to express (1) the eternal existence of God (<reflink>1 Tim. 1:17; Rom. 1:20; 16:26</reflink>); (2) of Christ (<reflink>Rev. 1:18</reflink>); (3) of the Holy Ghost (<reflink>Heb. 9:14</reflink>); and (4) the eternal duration of the sufferings of the lost (<reflink>Matt. 25:46; Jude 1:6</reflink>).

eternal life.d: This expression occurs in the Old Testament only in Dan. 12:2 (R.V., "everlasting life").

furrow.d: an opening in the ground made by the plough (<reflink>Ps. 65:10; Hos. 10:4, 10</reflink>).

fury.d: as attributed to God, is a figurative expression for dispensing afflictive judgments (<reflink>Lev. 26:28; Job 20:23; Isa. 63:3; Jer. 4:4; Ezek. 5:13; Dan. 9:16; Zech. 8:2</reflink>).

gaal.d: loathing, the son of Ebed, in whom the Shechemites "placed their confidence" when they became discontented with Abimelech. He headed the revolution, and led out the men of Shechem against Abimelech; but was defeated, and fled to his own home (<reflink>Judg. 9:26-46</reflink>). We hear no more of him after this battle.

gaash.d: a shaking, a hill, on the north side of which Joshua was buried (<reflink>Josh. 24:30; Judg. 2:9</reflink>), in the territory of Ephraim. (<see target="x-self">See TIMNATH-SERAH.</see>)

gabbatha.d: Gab Baitha, i.e., "the ridge of the house" = "the temple-mound," on a part of which the fortress of Antonia was built. This "temple-mound" was covered with a tesselated "pavement" (Gr. lithostroton, i.e., "stone-paved"). A judgement-seat (bema) was placed on this "pavement" outside the hall of the "praetorium" (q.v.), the judgment-hall (<reflink>John 18:28; 19:13</reflink>).

gabriel.d: champion of God, used as a proper name to designate the angel who was sent to Daniel (8:16) to explain the vision of the ram and the he-goat, and to communicate the prediction of the seventy weeks (<reflink>Dan. 9:21-27</reflink>).

gad.d: fortune; luck. (1.) Jacob's seventh son, by Zilpah, Leah's handmaid, and the brother of Asher (<reflink>Gen. 30:11-13; 46:16, 18</reflink>). In the Authorized Version of 30:11 the words, "A troop cometh: and she called," etc., should rather be rendered, "In fortune [R.V., 'Fortunate']: and she called," etc., or "Fortune cometh," etc.

gadara.d: the capital of the Roman province of Peraea. It stood on the summit of a mountain about 6 miles south-east of the Sea of Galilee. Mark (5:1) and Luke (8:26-39) describe the miracle of the healing of the demoniac (Matthew [8:28-34] says two demoniacs) as having been wrought "in the country of the Gadarenes," thus describing the scene generally. The miracle could not have been wrought at Gadara itself, for between the lake and this town there is the deep, almost impassable ravine of the Hieromax (Jarmuk). It is identified with the modern village of Um-Keis, which is surrounded by very extensive ruins, all bearing testimony to the splendour of ancient Gadara.

gadarenes.d: the inhabitants of Gadara, in Revised Version "Gerasenes" (<reflink>Mark 5:1; Luke 8:26, 37</reflink>). In Matt. 8:28 they are called Gergesenes, Revised Version "Gadarenes."

gaddi.d: fortunate, the representative of the tribe of Manasseh among the twelve "spies" sent by Moses to spy the land (<reflink>Num. 13:11</reflink>).

gaddiel.d: fortune (i.e., sent) of God, the representative of the tribe of Zebulum among the twelve spies (<reflink>Num. 13:10</reflink>).

gahar.d: lurking-place, one of the chief of the Nethinim, whose descendants returned to Jerusalem under Zerubbabel (<reflink>Ezra 2:47</reflink>).

gaius.d: (1.) A Macedonian, Paul's fellow-traveller, and his host at Corinth when he wrote his Epistle to the Romans (16:23). He with his household were baptized by Paul (<reflink>1 Cor. 1:14</reflink>). During a heathen outbreak against Paul at Ephesus the mob seized Gaius and Aristarchus because they could not find Paul, and rushed with them into the theatre. Some have identified this Gaius with No. (2).

galatia.d: has been called the "Gallia" of the East, Roman writers calling its inhabitants Galli. They were an intermixture of Gauls and Greeks, and hence were called Gallo-Graeci, and the country Gallo-Graecia. The Galatians were in their origin a part of that great Celtic migration which invaded Macedonia about B.C. 280. They were invited by the king of Bithynia to cross over into Asia Minor to assist him in his wars. There they ultimately settled, and being strengthened by fresh accessions of the same clan from Europe, they overran Bithynia, and supported themselves by plundering neighbouring countries. They were great warriors, and hired themselves out as mercenary soldiers, sometimes fighting on both sides in the great battles of the times. They were at length brought under the power of Rome in B.C. 189, and Galatia became a Roman province B.C. 25.

galatians, epistle to.d: The genuineness of this epistle is not called in question. Its Pauline origin is universally acknowledged.

galbanum.d: Heb. helbenah, (<reflink>Ex. 30:34</reflink>), one of the ingredients in the holy incense. It is a gum, probably from the Galbanum officinale.

galeed.d: heap of witness, the name of the pile of stones erected by Jacob and Laban to mark the league of friendship into which they entered with each other (<reflink>Gen. 31:47, 48</reflink>). This was the name given to the "heap" by Jacob. It is Hebrew, while the name Jegar-sahadutha, given to it by Laban, is Aramaic (Chaldee or Syriac). Probably Nahor's family originally spoke Aramaic, and Abraham and his descendants learned Hebrew, a kindred dialect, in the land of Canaan.

galilean.d: an inhabitant or native of Galilee. This word was used as a name of contempt as applied to our Lord's disciples (<reflink>Luke 22:59; Acts 2:7</reflink>). All the apostles, with the exception of Judas Iscariot (<reflink>Acts 1:11</reflink>), were Galileans. Peter was detected by his Galilean accent (<reflink>Matt. 26:69; Mark 14:70</reflink>).

galilee.d: circuit. Solomon rewarded Hiram for certain services rendered him by the gift of an upland plain among the mountains of Naphtali. Hiram was dissatisfied with the gift, and called it "the land of Cabul" (q.v.). The Jews called it Galil. It continued long to be occupied by the original inhabitants, and hence came to be called "Galilee of the Gentiles" (<reflink>Matt. …

galilee, sea of.d: (<reflink>Matt. 4:18; 15:29</reflink>), is mentioned in the Bible under three other names. (1.) In the Old Testament it is called the "sea of Chinnereth" (<reflink>Num. 34:11; Josh. 12:3; 13:27</reflink>), as is supposed from its harp-like shape. (2). The "lake of Gennesareth" once by Luke (5:1), from the flat district lying on its west coast. (3.) John (6:1; 21:1) calls it the "sea of Tiberias" (q.v.). The modern Arabs retain this name, Bahr Tabariyeh.

gall.d: (1) Heb. mererah, meaning "bitterness" (<reflink>Job 16:13</reflink>); i.e., the bile secreted in the liver. This word is also used of the poison of asps (20:14), and of the vitals, the seat of life (25).

gallery.d: (1.) Heb. 'attik (<reflink>Ezek. 41:15, 16</reflink>), a terrace; a projection; ledge.

gallim.d: heaps, (<reflink>1 Sam. 25:44; Isa. 10:30</reflink>). The native place of Phalti, to whom Michal was given by Saul. It was probably in Benjamin, to the north of Jerusalem.

gallio.d: the elder brother of Seneca the philosopher, who was tutor and for some time minister of the emperor Nero. He was "deputy", i.e., proconsul, as in Revised Version, of Achaia, under the emperor Claudius, when Paul visited Corinth (<reflink>Acts 18:12</reflink>). The word used here by Luke in describing the rank of Gallio shows his accuracy. Achaia was a senatorial province under Claudius, and the governor of such a province was called a "proconsul." He is spoken of by his contemporaries as "sweet Gallio," and is described as a most popular and affectionate man. When the Jews brought Paul before his tribunal on the charge of persuading "men to worship God contrary to the law" (18:13), he refused to listen to them, and "drave them from the judgment seat" (18:16).

gallows.d: Heb. 'ets, meaning "a tree" (<reflink>Esther 6:4</reflink>), a post or gibbet. In Gen. 40:19 and Deut. 21:22 the word is rendered "tree."

gamaliel.d: reward of God. (1.) A chief of the tribe of Manasseh at the census at Sinai (<reflink>Num. 1:10; 2:20; 7:54, 59</reflink>).

games.d: (1.) Of children (<reflink>Zech. 8:5; Matt. 11:16</reflink>). The Jewish youth were also apparently instructed in the use of the bow and the sling (<reflink>Judg. 20:16; 1 Chr. 12:2</reflink>).

gammadim.d: (<reflink>Ezek. 27:11</reflink>) brave warriors; R.V. marg., "valorous men;" others interpret this word as meaning "short-swordsmen," or "daring ones", the name of a class of men who were defenders of the towers of Tyre.

gamul.d: weaned the leader of one of the priestly courses (<reflink>1 Chr. 24:17</reflink>).

gap.d: a rent or opening in a wall (<reflink>Ezek. 13:5; comp. Amos 4:3</reflink>). The false prophets did not stand in the gap (<reflink>Ezek. 22: 30</reflink>), i.e., they did nothing to stop the outbreak of wickedness.

gardens.d: mentioned in Scripture, of Eden (<reflink>Gen. 2:8, 9</reflink>); Ahab's garden of herbs (<reflink>1 Kings 21:2</reflink>); the royal garden (<reflink>2 Kings 21:18</reflink>); the royal garden at Susa (<reflink>Esther 1:5</reflink>); the garden of Joseph of Arimathea (<reflink>John 19:41</reflink>); of Gethsemane (<reflink>John 18:1</reflink>).

gareb.d: scabby; itch. (1.) One of David's warriors (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:38</reflink>), an Ithrite.

garlands.d: (<reflink>Acts 14:13</reflink>). In heathen sacrifices the victims were adorned with fillets and garlands made of wool, with leaves and flowers interwoven. The altar and the priests and attendants were also in like manner adorned.

garlic.d: (Heb. shum, from its strong odour), mentioned only once (<reflink>Num. 11:5</reflink>). The garlic common in Eastern countries is the Allium sativum or Allium Ascalonicum, so called from its having been brought into Europe from Ascalon by the Crusaders. It is now known by the name of "shallot" or "eschalot."

garner.d: (1.) Heb. 'otsar, a treasure; a store of goods laid up, and hence also the place where they are deposited (<reflink>Joel 1:17; 2 Chr. 32:27, rendered "treasury"</reflink>).

garnish.d: overlay with stones (<reflink>2 Chr. 3:6</reflink>), adorn (<reflink>Rev. 21:19</reflink>), deck with garlands (<reflink>Matt. 23:29</reflink>), furnish (12:44).

garrison.d: (1.) Heb. matstsab, a station; a place where one stands (<reflink>1 Sam. 14:12</reflink>); a military or fortified post (<reflink>1 Sam. 13:23; 14:1, 4, 6, etc.</reflink>).

gate.d: (1.) Of cities, as of Jerusalem (<reflink>Jer. 37:13; Neh. 1:3; 2:3; 3:3</reflink>), of Sodom (<reflink>Gen. 19:1</reflink>), of Gaza (<reflink>Judg. 16:3</reflink>).

gath.d: a wine-vat, one of the five royal cities of the Philistines (<reflink>Josh. 13:3</reflink>) on which the ark brought calamity (<reflink>1 Sam. 5:8, 9; 6:17</reflink>). It was famous also as being the birthplace or residence of Goliath (<reflink>1 Sam. 17:4</reflink>). David fled from Saul to Achish, king of Gath (<reflink>1 Sam. 21:10; 27:2-4; Ps. 56</reflink>), and his connection with it will account for the words in 2 Sam. 1:20. It was afterwards conquered by David (<reflink>2 Sam. 8:1</reflink>). It occupied a strong position on the borders of Judah and Philistia (<reflink>1 Sam. 21:10; 1 Chr. 18:1</reflink>). Its site has been identified with the hill called Tell esSafieh, the Alba Specula of the Middle Ages, which rises 695 feet above the plain on its east edge. It is noticed on monuments about B.C. 1500. (<see target="x-self">See METHEGAMMAH.</see>)

gath-hepher.d: wine-press of the well, a town of Lower Galilee, about 5 miles from Nazareth; the birthplace of Jonah (<reflink>2 Kings 14:25</reflink>); the same as Gittah-hepher (<reflink>Josh. 19:13</reflink>). It has been identified with the modern el-Meshed, a village on the top of a rocky hill. Here the supposed tomb of Jonah, Neby Yunas, is still pointed out.

gath-rimmon.d: press of the pomegranate. (1.) A Levitical city in the tribe of Dan (<reflink>Josh. 19:45; 21:24; 1 Chr. 6:69</reflink>).

gaulanitis.d: a name derived from "Golan" (q.v.), one of the cities of refuge in the territory of Manasseh (<reflink>Josh. 20:8; 21:27; Deut. 4:43</reflink>). This was one of the provinces ruled by Herod Antipas. It lay to the east of the Lake of Galilee, and included among its towns Bethsaida-Julias (<reflink>Mark 8:22</reflink>) and Seleucia.

gaza.d: called also Azzah, which is its Hebrew name (<reflink>Deut. 2:23; 1 Kings 4:24; Jer. 25:20</reflink>), strong, a city on the Mediterranean shore, remarkable for its early importance as the chief centre of a great commercial traffic with Egypt. It is one of the oldest cities of the world (<reflink>Gen. 10:19; Josh. 15:47</reflink>). Its earliest inhabitants were the Avims, who were conquered and displaced by the Caphtorims (<reflink>Deut. 2:23; Josh. 13:2, 3</reflink>), a Philistine tribe. In the division of the land it fell to the lot of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:47; Judg. 1:18</reflink>). It was the southernmost of the five great Philistine cities which gave each a golden emerod as a trespass-offering unto the Lord (<reflink>1 Sam. 6:17</reflink>). Its gates were carried away by Samson (<reflink>Judg. 16:1-3</reflink>). …

geba.d: the hill, (<reflink>2 Sam. 5:25 [1 Chr. 14:16, "Gibeon"]; 2 Kings 23:8; Neh. 11:31</reflink>), a Levitical city of Benjamin (<reflink>1 Kings 15:22; 1 Sam. 13:16; 14:5, wrongly "Gibeah" in the A.V.</reflink>), on the north border of Judah near Gibeah (<reflink>Isa. 10:29; Josh. 18:24, 28</reflink>). "From Geba to Beersheba" expressed the whole extent of the kingdom of Judah, just as "from Dan to Beersheba" described the whole length of Palestine (<reflink>2 Kings 23:8</reflink>). It has been identified with Gaba (<reflink>Josh. 18:24; Ezra 2:26; Neh. 7:30</reflink>), now Jeb'a, about 5 1/2 miles north of Jerusalem.

gebal.d: a line (or natural boundary, as a mountain range). (1.) A tract in the land of Edom south of the Dead Sea (<reflink>Ps. 83:7</reflink>); now called Djebal.

gebalites.d: (<reflink>1 Kings 5:18 R.V., in A.V. incorrectly rendered, after the Targum, "stone-squarers," but marg. "Giblites"</reflink>), the inhabitants of Gebal (2).

geber.d: a valiant man, (<reflink>1 Kings 4:19</reflink>), one of Solomon's purveyors, having jurisdiction over a part of Gilead, comprising all the kingdom of Sihon and part of the kingdom of Og (Deut. 2; 31).

gebim.d: cisterns, (rendered "pits," Jer. 14:3; "locusts," Isa. 33:4), a small place north of Jerusalem, whose inhabitants fled at the approach of the Assyrian army (<reflink>Isa. 10:31</reflink>). It is probably the modern el-Isawiyeh.

gedaliah.d: made great by Jehovah. (1.) the son of Jeduthum (<reflink>1 Chr. 25:3, 9</reflink>). (2.) The grandfather of the prophet Zephaniah, and the father of Cushi (<reflink>Zeph. 1:1</reflink>). (3.) One of the Jewish nobles who conspired against Jeremiah (<reflink>Jer. 38:1</reflink>). (4.) The son of Ahikam, and grandson of Shaphan, secretary of king Josiah (<reflink>Jer. 26:24</reflink>). After the destruction of Jerusalem (<see target="x-self">see ZEDEKIAH</see>), Nebuchadnezzar left him to govern the country as tributary to him (<reflink>2 Kings 25:22; Jer. 40:5; 52:16</reflink>). Ishmael, however, at the head of a party of the royal family, "Jewish irreconcilables", rose against him, and slew him and "all the Jews that were with him" (<reflink>Jer. 41:2, 3</reflink>) at Mizpah about three months after the destruction of Jerusalem. He and his band also plundered the town of Mizpah, and carried off many captives. He was, however, overtaken by Johanan and routed. …

geder.d: a walled place, (<reflink>Josh. 12:13</reflink>), perhaps the same as Gederah or Gedor (15:58).

gederah.d: the fortress; a fortified place, a town in the plain (shephelah) of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:36</reflink>). This is a very common Canaanite and Phoenician name. It is the feminine form of Geder (12:13); the plural form is Gederoth (15:41). This place has by some been identified with Jedireh, a ruin 9 miles from Lydda, toward Eleutheropolis, and 4 miles north of Sur'ah (Zorah), in the valley of Elah.

gederathite.d: an epithet applied to Josabad, one of David's warriors at Ziklag (<reflink>1 Chr. 12:4</reflink>), a native of Gederah.

fillets.d: Heb. hashukum, plur., joinings (<reflink>Ex. 27:17; 38:17, 28</reflink>), the rods by which the tops of the columns around the tabernacle court were joined together, and from which the curtains were suspended (<reflink>Ex. 27:10, 11; 36:38</reflink>).

finer.d: a worker in silver and gold (<reflink>Prov. 25:4</reflink>). In Judg. 17:4 the word (tsoreph) is rendered "founder," and in Isa. 41:7 "goldsmith."

fir.d: the uniform rendering in the Authorized Version (marg. R.V., "cypress") of _berosh_ (<reflink>2 Sam. 6:5; 1 Kings 5:8, 10; 6:15, 34; 9:11, etc.</reflink>), a lofty tree (<reflink>Isa. 55:13</reflink>) growing on Lebanon (37:24). Its wood was used in making musical instruments and doors of houses, and for ceilings (<reflink>2 Chr. 3:5</reflink>), the decks of ships (<reflink>Ezek. 27:5</reflink>), floorings and spear-shafts (<reflink>Nah. 2:3, R.V.</reflink>). The true fir (abies) is not found in Palestine, but the pine tree, of which there are four species, is common.

fire.d: (1.) For sacred purposes. The sacrifices were consumed by fire (<reflink>Gen. 8:20</reflink>). The ever-burning fire on the altar was first kindled from heaven (<reflink>Lev. 6:9, 13; 9:24</reflink>), and afterwards rekindled at the dedication of Solomon's temple (<reflink>2 Chr. 7:1, 3</reflink>). The expressions "fire from heaven" and "fire of the Lord" generally denote lightning, but sometimes also the fire of the altar was so called (<reflink>Ex. 29:18; Lev. 1:9; 2:3; 3:5, 9</reflink>).

firebrand.d: Isa. 7:4, Amos 4:11, Zech. 3:2, denotes the burnt end of a stick (Heb. 'ud); in Judg. 15:4, a lamp or torch, a flambeau (Heb. lappid); in Prov. 26:18 (<reflink>comp. Eph. 6:16</reflink>), burning darts or arrows (Heb. zikkim).

firepan.d: (<reflink>Ex. 27:3; 38:3</reflink>), one of the vessels of the temple service (rendered "snuff-dish" Ex. 25:38; 37:23; and "censer" Lev. 10:1; 16:12). It was probably a metallic cinder-basin used for the purpose of carrying live coal for burning incense, and of carrying away the snuff in trimming the lamps.

firkin.d: Used only in John 2:6; the Attic amphora, equivalent to the Hebrew bath (q.v.), a measure for liquids containing about 8 7/8 gallons.

firmament.d: from the Vulgate firmamentum, which is used as the translation of the Hebrew _raki'a_. This word means simply "expansion." It denotes the space or expanse like an arch appearing immediately above us. They who rendered _raki'a_ by firmamentum regarded it as a solid body. The language of Scripture is not scientific but popular, and hence we read of the sun rising and setting, and also here the use of this particular word. It is plain that it was used to denote solidity as well as expansion. It formed a division between the waters above and the waters below (<reflink>Gen. 1:7</reflink>). The _raki'a_ supported the upper reservoir (<reflink>Ps. 148:4</reflink>). It was the support also of the heavenly bodies (<reflink>Gen. 1:14</reflink>), and is spoken of as having "windows" and "doors" (<reflink>Gen. 7:11; Isa. 24:18; Mal. 3:10</reflink>) through which the rain and snow might descend.

first-born.d: sons enjoyed certain special privileges (<reflink>Deut. 21:17; Gen. 25:23, 31, 34; 49:3; 1 Chr. 5:1; Heb. 12:16; Ps. 89:27</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See BIRTHRIGHT.</see>)

first-born, redemption of.d: From the beginning the office of the priesthood in each family belonged to the eldest son. But when the extensive plan of sacrificial worship was introduced, requiring a company of men to be exclusively devoted to this ministry, the primitive office of the first-born was superseded by that of the Levites (<reflink>Num. 3:11-13</reflink>), and it was ordained that the first-born of man and of unclean animals should henceforth be redeemed (18:15).

first-born, sanctification of the.d: A peculiar sanctity was attached to the first-born both of man and of cattle. God claimed that the first-born males of man and of animals should be consecrated to him, the one as a priest (<reflink>Ex. 19:22, 24</reflink>), representing the family to which he belonged, and the other to be offered up in sacrifice (<reflink>Gen. 4:4</reflink>).

first-fruits.d: The first-fruits of the ground were offered unto God just as the first-born of man and animals.

fish.d: called _dag_ by the Hebrews, a word denoting great fecundity (<reflink>Gen. 9:2; Num. 11:22; Jonah 2:1, 10</reflink>). No fish is mentioned by name either in the Old or in the New Testament. Fish abounded in the Mediterranean and in the lakes of the Jordan, so that the Hebrews were no doubt acquainted with many species. Two of the villages on the shores of the Sea of Galilee derived their names from their fisheries, Bethsaida (the "house of fish") on the east and on the west. There is probably no other sheet of water in the world of equal dimensions that contains such a variety and profusion of fish. About thirty-seven different kinds have been found. Some of the fishes are of a European type, such as the roach, the barbel, and the blenny; others are markedly African and tropical, such as the eel-like silurus. There was a regular fish-market apparently in Jerusalem (<reflink>2 Chr. 33:14; Neh. 3:3; 12:39; Zeph. …

fish-hooks.d: were used for catching fish (<reflink>Amos 4:2; comp. Isa. 37:29; Jer. 16:16; Ezek. 29:4; Job. 41:1, 2; Matt. 17:27</reflink>).

fish-pools.d: (<reflink>Cant. 7:4</reflink>) should be simply "pools," as in the Revised Version. The reservoirs near Heshbon (q.v.) were probably stocked with fish (<reflink>2 Sam. 2:13; 4:12; Isa. 7:3; 22:9, 11</reflink>).

fisher.d: Besides its literal sense (<reflink>Luke 5:2</reflink>), this word is also applied by our Lord to his disciples in a figurative sense (<reflink>Matt. 4:19; Mark 1:17</reflink>).

fishing, the art of.d: was prosecuted with great industry in the waters of Palestine. It was from the fishing-nets that Jesus called his disciples (<reflink>Mark 1:16-20</reflink>), and it was in a fishing-boat he rebuked the winds and the waves (<reflink>Matt. 8:26</reflink>) and delivered that remarkable series of prophecies recorded in Matt. 13. He twice miraculously fed multitudes with fish and bread (<reflink>Matt. 14:19; 15:36</reflink>). It was in the mouth of a fish that the tribute-money was found (<reflink>Matt. 17:27</reflink>). And he "ate a piece of broiled fish" with his disciples after his resurrection (<reflink>Luke 24:42, 43; comp. Acts 1:3</reflink>). At the Sea of Tiberias (<reflink>John 21:1-14</reflink>), in obedience to his direction, the disciples cast their net "on the right side of the ship," and enclosed so many that "they were not able to draw it for the multitude of fishes."

fitches.d: (<reflink>Isa. 28:25, 27</reflink>), the rendering of the Hebrew _ketsah_, "without doubt the Nigella sativa, a small annual of the order Ranunculacece, which grows wild in the Mediterranean countries, and is cultivated in Egypt and Syria for its seed." It is rendered in margin of the Revised Version "black cummin." The seeds are used as a condiment.

flag.d: (Heb., or rather Egyptian, ahu, Job 8:11), rendered "meadow" in Gen. 41:2, 18; probably the Cyperus esculentus, a species of rush eaten by cattle, the Nile reed. It also grows in Palestine.

flagon.d: Heb. ashishah, (<reflink>2 Sam. 6:19; 1 Chr. 16:3; Cant. 2:5; Hos. 3:1</reflink>), meaning properly "a cake of pressed raisins." "Flagons of wine" of the Authorized Version should be, as in the Revised Version, "cakes of raisins" in all these passages. In Isa. 22:24 it is the rendering of the Hebrew _nebel_, which properly means a bottle or vessel of skin. (Comp. 1 Sam. 1:24; 10:3; 25:18; 2 Sam. 16:1, where the same Hebrew word is used.)

flame of fire.d: is the chosen symbol of the holiness of God (<reflink>Ex. 3:2; Rev. 2:18</reflink>), as indicating "the intense, all-consuming operation of his holiness in relation to sin."

flax.d: (Heb. pishtah, i.e., "peeled", in allusion to the fact that the stalks of flax when dried were first split or peeled before being steeped in water for the purpose of destroying the pulp). This plant was cultivated from earliest times. The flax of Egypt was destroyed by the plague of hail when it "was bolled", i.e., was forming pods for seed (<reflink>Ex. 9:31</reflink>). It was extensively cultivated both in Egypt and Palestine. Reference is made in Josh. 2:6 to the custom of drying flax-stalks by exposing them to the sun on the flat roofs of houses. It was much used in forming articles of clothing such as girdles, also cords and bands (<reflink>Lev. 13:48, 52, 59; Deut. 22:11</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See LINEN.</see>)

flea.d: David at the cave of Adullam thus addressed his persecutor Saul (<reflink>1 Sam. 24:14</reflink>): "After whom is the king of Israel come out? after whom dost thou pursue? after a dead dog, after a flea?" He thus speaks of himself as the poor, contemptible object of the monarch's pursuit, a "worthy object truly for an expedition of the king of Israel with his picked troops!" This insect is in Eastern language the popular emblem of insignificance. In 1 Sam. 26:20 the LXX. read "come out to seek my life" instead of "to seek a flea."

fleece.d: the wool of a sheep, whether shorn off or still attached to the skin (<reflink>Deut. 18:4; Job 31:20</reflink>). The miracle of Gideon's fleece (<reflink>Judg. 6:37-40</reflink>) consisted in the dew having fallen at one time on the fleece without any on the floor, and at another time in the fleece remaining dry while the ground was wet with dew.

flesh.d: in the Old Testament denotes (1) a particular part of the body of man and animals (<reflink>Gen. 2:21; 41:2; Ps. 102:5, marg.</reflink>); (2) the whole body (<reflink>Ps. 16:9</reflink>); (3) all living things having flesh, and particularly humanity as a whole (<reflink>Gen. 6:12, 13</reflink>); (4) mutability and weakness (<reflink>2 Chr. 32:8; comp. Isa. 31:3; Ps. 78:39</reflink>). As suggesting the idea of softness it is used in the expression "heart of flesh" (<reflink>Ezek. 11:19</reflink>). The expression "my flesh and bone" (<reflink>Judg. 9:2; Isa. 58:7</reflink>) denotes relationship.

flesh-hook.d: a many-pronged fork used in the sacrificial services (<reflink>1 Sam. 2:13, 14; Ex. 27:3; 38:3</reflink>) by the priest in drawing away the flesh. The fat of the sacrifice, together with the breast and shoulder (<reflink>Lev. 7:29-34</reflink>), were presented by the worshipper to the priest. The fat was burned on the alter (3:3-5), and the breast and shoulder became the portion of the priests. But Hophni and Phinehas, not content with this, sent a servant to seize with a flesh-hook a further portion.

flint.d: abounds in all the plains and valleys of the wilderness of the forty years' wanderings. In Isa. 50:7 and Ezek. 3:9 the expressions, where the word is used, means that the "Messiah would be firm and resolute amidst all contempt and scorn which he would meet; that he had made up his mind to endure it, and would not shrink from any kind or degree of suffering which would be necessary to accomplish the great work in which he was engaged." (<reflink>Comp. Ezek. 3:8, 9.</reflink>) The words "like a flint" are used with reference to the hoofs of horses (<reflink>Isa. 5:28</reflink>).

flood.d: an event recorded in Gen. 7 and 8. (<see target="x-self">See DELUGE.</see>) In Josh. 24:2, 3, 14, 15, the word "flood" (R.V., "river") means the river Euphrates. In Ps. 66:6, this word refers to the river Jordan.

flour.d: Grain reduced to the form of meal is spoken of in the time of Abraham (<reflink>Gen. 18:6</reflink>). As baking was a daily necessity, grain was also ground daily at the mills (<reflink>Jer. 25:10</reflink>). The flour mingled with water was kneaded in kneading-troughs, and sometimes leaven (<reflink>Ex. 12:34</reflink>) was added and sometimes omitted (<reflink>Gen. 19:3</reflink>). The dough was then formed into thin cakes nine or ten inches in diameter and baked in the oven.

flowers.d: Very few species of flowers are mentioned in the Bible although they abounded in Palestine. It has been calculated that in Western Syria and Palestine from two thousand to two thousand five hundred plants are found, of which about five hundred probably are British wild-flowers. Their beauty is often alluded to (<reflink>Cant. 2:12; Matt. 6:28</reflink>). They are referred to as affording an emblem of the transitory nature of human life (<reflink>Job 14:2; Ps. 103:15; Isa. 28:1; 40:6; James 1:10</reflink>). Gardens containing flowers and fragrant herbs are spoken of (<reflink>Cant. 4:16; 6:2</reflink>).

flute.d: a musical instrument, probably composed of a number of pipes, mentioned Dan. 3:5, 7, 10, 15.

fly.d: Heb. zebub, (<reflink>Eccl. 10:1; Isa. 7:18</reflink>). This fly was so grievous a pest that the Phoenicians invoked against it the aid of their god Baal-zebub (q.v.). The prophet Isaiah (7:18) alludes to some poisonous fly which was believed to be found on the confines of Egypt, and which would be called by the Lord. Poisonous flies exist in many parts of Africa, for instance, the different kinds of tsetse.

foam.d: (<reflink>Hos. 10:7</reflink>), the rendering of _ketseph_, which properly means twigs or splinters (as rendered in the LXX. and marg. R.V.). The expression in Hosea may therefore be read, "as a chip on the face of the water," denoting the helplessness of the piece of wood as compared with the irresistable current.

fodder.d: Heb. belil, (<reflink>Job 6:5</reflink>), meaning properly a mixture or medley (Lat. farrago), "made up of various kinds of grain, as wheat, barley, vetches, and the like, all mixed together, and then sown or given to cattle" (<reflink>Job 24:6, A.V. "corn," R.V. "provender;" Isa. 30:24, provender"</reflink>).

fold.d: an enclosure for flocks to rest together (<reflink>Isa. 13:20</reflink>). Sheep-folds are mentioned Num. 32:16, 24, 36; 2 Sam. 7:8; Zeph. 2:6; John 10:1, etc. It was prophesied of the cities of Ammon (<reflink>Ezek. 25:5</reflink>), Aroer (<reflink>Isa. 17:2</reflink>), and Judaea, that they would be folds or couching-places for flocks. "Among the pots," of the Authorized Version (<reflink>Ps. 68:13</reflink>), is rightly in the Revised Version, "among the sheepfolds."

food.d: Originally the Creator granted the use of the vegetable world for food to man (<reflink>Gen. 1:29</reflink>), with the exception mentioned (2:17). The use of animal food was probably not unknown to the antediluvians. There is, however, a distinct law on the subject given to Noah after the Deluge (<reflink>Gen. 9:2-5</reflink>). Various articles of food used in the patriarchal age are mentioned in Gen. 18:6-8; 25:34; 27:3, 4; 43:11. Regarding the food of the Israelites in Egypt, see Ex. 16:3; Num. 11:5. In the wilderness their ordinary food was miraculously supplied in the manna. They had also quails (<reflink>Ex. 16:11-13; Num. 11:31</reflink>).

footstool.d: connected with a throne (<reflink>2 Chr. 9:18</reflink>). Jehovah symbolically dwelt in the holy place between the cherubim above the ark of the covenant. The ark was his footstool (<reflink>1 Chr. 28:2; Ps. 99:5; 132:7</reflink>). And as heaven is God's throne, so the earth is his footstool (<reflink>Ps. 110:1; Isa. 66:1; Matt. 5:35</reflink>).

forces.d: of the Gentiles (<reflink>Isa. 60:5, 11; R.V., "the wealth of the nations"</reflink>) denotes the wealth of the heathen. The whole passage means that the wealth of the Gentile world should be consecrated to the service of the church.

ford.d: Mention is frequently made of the fords of the Jordan (<reflink>Josh. 2:7; Judg. 3:28; 12:5, 6</reflink>), which must have been very numerous; about fifty perhaps. The most notable was that of Bethabara. Mention is also made of the ford of the Jabbok (<reflink>Gen. 32:22</reflink>), and of the fords of Arnon (<reflink>Isa. 16:2</reflink>) and of the Euphrates (<reflink>Jer. 51:32</reflink>).

forehead.d: The practice common among Oriental nations of colouring the forehead or impressing on it some distinctive mark as a sign of devotion to some deity is alluded to in Rev. 13:16, 17; 14:9; 17:5; 20:4.

foreigner.d: a Gentile. Such as resided among the Hebrews were required by the law to be treated with kindness (<reflink>Ex. 22:21; 23:9; Lev. 19:33, 34; 23:22; Deut. 14:28; 16:10, 11; 24:19</reflink>). They enjoyed in many things equal rights with the native-born residents (<reflink>Ex. 12:49; Lev. 24:22; Num. 15:15; 35:15</reflink>), but were not allowed to do anything which was an abomination according to the Jewish law (<reflink>Ex. 20:10; Lev. 17:15,16; 18:26; 20:2; 24:16, etc.</reflink>).

foreknowledge of god.d: Acts 2:23; Rom. 8:29; 11:2; 1 Pet. 1:2), one of those high attributes essentially appertaining to him the full import of which we cannot comprehend. In the most absolute sense his knowledge is infinite (<reflink>1 Sam. 23:9-13; Jer. 38:17-23; 42:9-22, Matt. 11:21, 23; Acts 15:18</reflink>).

forerunner.d: John the Baptist went before our Lord in this character (<reflink>Mark 1:2, 3</reflink>). Christ so called (<reflink>Heb. 6:20</reflink>) as entering before his people into the holy place as their head and guide.

forest.d: Heb. ya'ar, meaning a dense wood, from its luxuriance. Thus all the great primeval forests of Syria (<reflink>Eccl. 2:6; Isa. 44:14; Jer. 5:6; Micah 5:8</reflink>). The most extensive was the trans-Jordanic forest of Ephraim (<reflink>2 Sam. 18:6, 8; Josh. 17:15, 18</reflink>), which is probably the same as the wood of Ephratah (<reflink>Ps. 132:6</reflink>), some part of the great forest of Gilead. It was in this forest that Absalom was slain by Joab. David withdrew to the forest of Hareth in the mountains of Judah to avoid the fury of Saul (<reflink>1 Sam. 22:5</reflink>). We read also of the forest of Bethel (<reflink>2 Kings 2:23, 24</reflink>), and of that which the Israelites passed in their pursuit of the Philistines (<reflink>1 Sam. 14:25</reflink>), and of the forest of the cedars of Lebanon (<reflink>1 Kings 4:33; 2 Kings 19:23; Hos. 14:5, 6</reflink>).

forgiveness of sin.d: one of the constituent parts of justification. In pardoning sin, God absolves the sinner from the condemnation of the law, and that on account of the work of Christ, i.e., he removes the guilt of sin, or the sinner's actual liability to eternal wrath on account of it. All sins are forgiven freely (<reflink>Acts 5:31; 13:38; 1 John 1:6-9</reflink>). The sinner is by this act of grace for ever freed from the guilt and penalty of his sins. This is the peculiar prerogative of God (<reflink>Ps. 130:4; Mark 2:5</reflink>). It is offered to all in the gospel. (<see target="x-self">See JUSTIFICATION.</see>)

fornication.d: in every form of it was sternly condemned by the Mosaic law (<reflink>Lev. 21:9; 19:29; Deut. 22:20, 21, 23-29; 23:18; Ex. 22:16</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See ADULTERY.</see>)

fortunatus.d: fortunate, a disciple of Corinth who visited Paul at Ephesus, and returned with Stephanas and Achaicus, the bearers of the apostle's first letter to the Corinthians (<reflink>1 Cor. 16:17</reflink>).

fountain.d: (Heb. 'ain; i.e., "eye" of the water desert), a natural source of living water. Palestine was a "land of brooks of water, of fountains, and depths that spring out of valleys and hills" (<reflink>Deut. 8:7; 11:11</reflink>).

fountain of the virgin.d: the perennial source from which the Pool of Siloam (q.v.) is supplied, the waters flowing in a copious stream to it through a tunnel cut through the rock, the actual length of which is 1,750 feet. The spring rises in a cave 20 feet by 7. A serpentine tunnel 67 feet long runs from it toward the left, off which the tunnel to the Pool of Siloam branches. It is the only unfailing fountain in Jerusalem.

fowler.d: the arts of, referred to Ps. 91:3; 124:7; Prov. 6:5; Jer. 5:26; Hos. 9:8; Ezek. 17:20; Eccl. 9:12. Birds of all kinds abound in Palestine, and the capture of these for the table and for other uses formed the employment of many persons. The traps and snares used for this purpose are mentioned Hos. 5:1; Prov. 7:23; 22:5; Amos 3:5; Ps. 69:22; comp. Deut. 22:6, 7.

fox.d: (Heb. shu'al, a name derived from its digging or burrowing under ground), the Vulpes thaleb, or Syrian fox, the only species of this animal indigenous to Palestine. It burrows, is silent and solitary in its habits, is destructive to vineyards, being a plunderer of ripe grapes (<reflink>Cant. 2:15</reflink>). The Vulpes Niloticus, or Egyptian dog-fox, and the Vulpes vulgaris, or common fox, are also found in Palestine.

frankincense.d: (Heb. lebonah; Gr. libanos, i.e., "white"), an odorous resin imported from Arabia (<reflink>Isa. 60:6; Jer. 6:20</reflink>), yet also growing in Palestine (<reflink>Cant. 4:14</reflink>). It was one of the ingredients in the perfume of the sanctuary (<reflink>Ex. 30:34</reflink>), and was used as an accompaniment of the meat-offering (<reflink>Lev. 2:1, 16; 6:15; 24:7</reflink>). When burnt it emitted a fragrant odour, and hence the incense became a symbol of the Divine name (<reflink>Mal. 1:11; Cant. 1:3</reflink>) and an emblem of prayer (<reflink>Ps. 141:2; Luke 1:10; Rev. 5:8; 8:3</reflink>).

free-will offering.d: a spontaneous gift (<reflink>Ex. 35:29</reflink>), a voluntary sacrifice (<reflink>Lev. 22:23; Ezra 3:5</reflink>), as opposed to one in consequence of a vow, or in expiation of some offence.

freedom.d: The law of Moses pointed out the cases in which the servants of the Hebrews were to receive their freedom (<reflink>Ex. 21:2-4, 7, 8; Lev. 25:39-42, 47-55; Deut. 15:12-18</reflink>). Under the Roman law the "freeman" (ingenuus) was one born free; the "freedman" (libertinus) was a manumitted slave, and had not equal rights with the freeman (<reflink>Acts 22:28; comp. Acts 16:37-39; 21:39; 22:25; 25:11, 12</reflink>).

frog.d: (Heb. tsepharde'a, meaning a "marsh-leaper"). This reptile is mentioned in the Old Testament only in connection with one of the plagues which fell on the land of Egypt (<reflink>Ex. 8:2-14; Ps. 78:45; 105:30</reflink>).

frontlets.d: occurs only in Ex. 13:16; Deut. 6:8, and 11:18. The meaning of the injunction to the Israelites, with regard to the statues and precepts given them, that they should "bind them for a sign upon their hand, and have them as frontlets between their eyes," was that they should keep them distinctly in view and carefully attend to them. But soon after their return from Babylon they began to interpret this injunction literally, and had accordingly portions of the law written out and worn about their person. These they called tephillin, i.e., "prayers." The passages so written out on strips of parchment were these, Ex. 12:2-10; 13:11-21; Deut. 6:4-9; 11:18-21. They were then "rolled up in a case of black calfskin, which was attached to a stiffer piece of leather, having a thong one finger broad and one cubit and a half long. …

frost.d: (Heb. kerah, from its smoothness) Job 37:10 (R.V., "ice"); Gen. 31:40; Jer. 36:30; rendered "ice" in Job 6:16, 38:29; and "crystal" in Ezek. 1:22. "At the present day frost is entirely unknown in the lower portions of the valley of the Jordan, but slight frosts are sometimes felt on the sea-coast and near Lebanon." Throughout Western Asia cold frosty nights are frequently succeeded by warm days.

fruit.d: a word as used in Scripture denoting produce in general, whether vegetable or animal. The Hebrews divided the fruits of the land into three classes:,

frying-pan.d: (Heb. marhesheth, a "boiler"), a pot for boiling meat (<reflink>Lev. 2:7; 7:9</reflink>).

fuel.d: Almost every kind of combustible matter was used for fuel, such as the withered stalks of herbs (<reflink>Matt. 6:30</reflink>), thorns (<reflink>Ps. 58:9; Eccl. 7:6</reflink>), animal excrements (<reflink>Ezek. 4:12-15; 15:4, 6; 21:32</reflink>). Wood or charcoal is much used still in all the towns of Syria and Egypt. It is largely brought from the region of Hebron to Jerusalem. (<see target="x-self">See COAL.</see>)

fugitive.d: Gen. 4:12, 14, a rover or wanderer (Heb. n'a); Judg. 12:4, a refugee, one who has escaped (Heb. palit); 2 Kings 25:11, a deserter, one who has fallen away to the enemy (Heb. nophel); Ezek. 17:21, one who has broken away in flight (Heb. mibrah); Isa. 15:5; 43:14, a breaker away, a fugitive (Heb. beriah), one who flees away.

fuller.d: The word "full" is from the Anglo-Saxon fullian, meaning "to whiten." To full is to press or scour cloth in a mill. This art is one of great antiquity. Mention is made of "fuller's soap" (<reflink>Mal. 3:2</reflink>), and of "the fuller's field" (<reflink>2 Kings 18:17</reflink>). At his transfiguration our Lord's rainment is said to have been white "so as no fuller on earth could white them" (<reflink>Mark 9:3</reflink>). En-rogel (q.v.), meaning literally "foot-fountain," has been interpreted as the "fuller's fountain," because there the fullers trod the cloth with their feet.

fuller's field.d: a spot near Jerusalem (<reflink>2 Kings 18:17; Isa. 36:2; 7:3</reflink>), on the side of the highway west of the city, not far distant from the "upper pool" at the head of the valley of Hinnom. Here the fullers pursued their occupation.

fuller's soap.d: (Heb. borith mekabbeshim, i.e., "alkali of those treading cloth"). Mention is made (<reflink>Prov. 25:20; Jer. 2:22</reflink>) of nitre and also (<reflink>Mal. 3:2</reflink>) of soap (Heb. borith) used by the fuller in his operations. Nitre is found in Syria, and vegetable alkali was obtained from the ashes of certain plants. (<see target="x-self">See SOAP.</see>)

fulness.d: (1.) Of time (<reflink>Gal. 4:4</reflink>), the time appointed by God, and foretold by the prophets, when Messiah should appear. (2.) Of Christ (<reflink>John 1:16</reflink>), the superabundance of grace with which he was filled. (3.) Of the Godhead bodily dwelling in Christ (<reflink>Col. 2:9</reflink>), i.e., the whole nature and attributes of God are in Christ. (4.) Eph. 1:23, the church as the fulness of Christ, i.e., the church makes Christ a complete and perfect head.

funeral.d: Burying was among the Jews the only mode of disposing of corpses (<reflink>Gen. 23:19; 25:9; 35:8, 9, etc.</reflink>).

furlong.d: a stadium, a Greek measure of distance equal to 606 feet and 9 inches (<reflink>Luke 24:13; John 6:19; 11:18; Rev. 14:20; 21:16</reflink>).

furnace.d: (1.) Chald. attun, a large furnace with a wide open mouth, at the top of which materials were cast in (<reflink>Dan. 3:22, 23; comp. Jer. 29:22</reflink>). This furnace would be in constant requisition, for the Babylonians disposed of their dead by cremation, as did also the Accadians who invaded Mesopotamia.

gob.d: a pit, a place mentioned in 2 Sam. 21:18, 19; called also Gezer, in 1 Chr. 20:4.

goblet.d: a laver or trough for washing garments. In Cant. 7:2, a bowl or drinking vessel, a bowl for mixing wine; in Ex. 24:6, a sacrificial basin. (<see target="x-self">See CUP.</see>)

god.d: (A.S. and Dutch God; Dan. Gud; Ger. Gott), the name of the Divine Being. It is the rendering (1) of the Hebrew _'El_, from a word meaning to be strong; (2) of _'Eloah_, plural _'Elohim_. The singular form, _Eloah_, is used only in poetry. The plural form is more commonly used in all parts of the Bible, The Hebrew word Jehovah (q.v.), the only other word generally employed to denote the Supreme Being, is uniformly rendered in the Authorized Version by "LORD," printed in small capitals. The existence of God is taken for granted in the  There is nowhere any argument to prove it. He who disbelieves this truth is spoken of as one devoid of understanding (<reflink>Ps. 14:1</reflink>).

godhead.d: (<reflink>Acts 17:29; Rom. 1:20; Col. 2:9</reflink>), the essential being or the nature of God.

godliness.d: the whole of practical piety (<reflink>1 Tim. 4:8; 2 Pet. 1:6</reflink>). "It supposes knowledge, veneration, affection, dependence, submission, gratitude, and obedience." In 1 Tim. 3:16 it denotes the substance of revealed religion.

goel.d: in Hebrew the participle of the verb _gaal_, "to redeem." It is rendered in the Authorized Version "kinsman," Num. 5:8; Ruth 3:12; 4:1,6,8; "redeemer," Job 19:25; "avenger," Num. 35:12; Deut. 19:6, etc. The Jewish law gave the right of redeeming and repurchasing, as well as of avenging blood, to the next relative, who was accordingly called by this name. (See REDEEMER

gog.d: (1.) A Reubenite (<reflink>1 Chr. 5:4</reflink>), the father of Shimei.

golan.d: exile, a city of Bashan (<reflink>Deut. 4:43</reflink>), one of the three cities of refuge east of Jordan, about 12 miles north-east of the Sea of Galilee (<reflink>Josh. 20:8</reflink>). There are no further notices of it in Scripture. It became the head of the province of Gaulanitis, one of the four provinces into which Bashan was divided after the Babylonish captivity, and almost identical with the modern Jaulan, in Western Hauran, about 39 miles in length and 18 in breath.

gold.d: (1.) Heb. zahab, so called from its yellow colour (<reflink>Ex. 25:11; 1 Chr. 28:18; 2 Chr. 3:5</reflink>).

golden calf.d: (<reflink>Ex. 32:4,8; Deut. 9:16; Neh. 9:18</reflink>). This was a molten image of a calf which the idolatrous Israelites formed at Sinai. This symbol was borrowed from the custom of the Egyptians. It was destroyed at the command of Moses (<reflink>Ex. 32:20</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See AARON ; MOSES.</see>)

goldsmith.d: (<reflink>Neh. 3:8,32; Isa. 40:19; 41:7; 46:6</reflink>). The word so rendered means properly a founder or finer.

golgotha.d: the common name of the spot where Jesus was crucified. It is interpreted by the evangelists as meaning "the place of a skull" (<reflink>Matt. 27:33; Mark 15:22; John 19:17</reflink>). This name represents in Greek letters the Aramaic word Gulgaltha, which is the Hebrew Gulgoleth (<reflink>Num. 1:2; 1 Chr. 23:3, 24; 2 Kings 9:35</reflink>), meaning "a skull." It is identical with the word Calvary (q.v.). It was a little knoll rounded like a bare skull. It is obvious from the evangelists that it was some well-known spot outside the gate (<reflink>comp. Heb. 13:12</reflink>), and near the city (<reflink>Luke 23:26</reflink>), containing a "garden" (<reflink>John 19:41</reflink>), and on a thoroughfare leading into the country. Hence it is an untenable idea that it is embraced within the present "Church of the Holy Sepulchre." The hillock above Jeremiah's Grotto, to the north of the city, is in all probability the true site of Calvary. …

goliath.d: great. (1.) A famous giant of Gath, who for forty days openly defied the armies of Israel, but was at length slain by David with a stone from a sling (<reflink>1 Sam. 17:4</reflink>). He was probably descended from the Rephaim who found refuge among the Philistines after they were dispersed by the Ammonites (<reflink>Deut. 2:20, 21</reflink>). His height was "six cubits and a span," which, taking the cubit at 21 inches, is equal to 10 1/2 feet. David cut off his head (<reflink>1 Sam. 17:51</reflink>) and brought it to Jerusalem, while he hung the armour which he took from him in his tent. His sword was preserved at Nob as a religious trophy (21:9). David's victory over Goliath was the turning point in his life. He came into public notice now as the deliverer of Israel and the chief among Saul's men of war (18:5), and the devoted friend of Jonathan.

gomer.d: complete; vanishing. (1.) The daughter of Diblaim, who (probably in vision only) became the wife of Hosea (1:3).

gomorrah.d: submersion, one of the five cities of the plain of Siddim (q.v.) which were destroyed by fire (<reflink>Gen. 10:19; 13:10; 19:24, 28</reflink>). These cities probably stood close together, and were near the northern extremity of what is now the Dead Sea. This city is always mentioned next after Sodom, both of which were types of impiety and wickedness (<reflink>Gen. 18:20; Rom. 9:29</reflink>). Their destruction is mentioned as an "ensample unto those that after should live ungodly" (<reflink>2 Pet. 2:6; Jude 1:4-7</reflink>). Their wickedness became proverbial (<reflink>Deut. 32:32; Isa. 1:9, 10; Jer. 23:14</reflink>). But that wickedness may be exceeded (<reflink>Matt. 10:15; Mark 6:11</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See DEAD SEA</see>).

goodly trees.d: boughs of, were to be carried in festive procession on the first day of the feast of Tabernacles (<reflink>Lev. 23:40</reflink>). This was probably the olive tree (<reflink>Neh. 8:15</reflink>), although no special tree is mentioned.

goodness.d: in man is not a mere passive quality, but the deliberate preference of right to wrong, the firm and persistent resistance of all moral evil, and the choosing and following of all moral good.

goodness of god.d: a perfection of his character which he exercises towards his creatures according to their various circumstances and relations (<reflink>Ps. 145:8, 9; 103:8; 1 John 4:8</reflink>). Viewed generally, it is benevolence; as exercised with respect to the miseries of his creatures it is mercy, pity, compassion, and in the case of impenitent sinners, long-suffering patience; as exercised in communicating favour on the unworthy it is grace. "Goodness and justice are the several aspects of one unchangeable, infinitely wise, and sovereign moral perfection. God is not sometimes merciful and sometimes just, but he is eternally infinitely just and merciful." God is infinitely and unchangeably good (<reflink>Zeph. 3:17</reflink>), and his goodness is incomprehensible by the finite mind (<reflink>Rom. 11: 35, 36</reflink>). "God's goodness appears in two things, giving and forgiving."

gopher.d: a tree from the wood of which Noah was directed to build the ark (<reflink>Gen. 6:14</reflink>). It is mentioned only there. The LXX. render this word by "squared beams," and the Vulgate by "planed wood." Other versions have rendered it "pine" and "cedar;" but the weight of authority is in favour of understanding by it the cypress tree, which grows abundantly in Chaldea and Armenia.

goshen.d: (1.) A district in Egypt where Jacob and his family settled, and in which they remained till the Exodus (<reflink>Gen. 45:10; 46:28, 29, 31, etc.</reflink>). It is called "the land of Goshen" (47:27), and also simply "Goshen" (46:28), and "the land of Rameses" (47:11; Ex. 12:37), for the towns Pithom and Rameses lay within its borders; also Zoan or Tanis (<reflink>Ps. 78:12</reflink>). It lay on the east of the Nile, and apparently not far from the royal residence. It was "the best of the land" (<reflink>Gen. 47:6, 11</reflink>), but is now a desert. It is first mentioned in Joseph's message to his father. It has been identified with the modern Wady Tumilat, lying between the eastern part of the Delta and the west border of Palestine. It was a pastoral district, where some of the king's cattle were kept (<reflink>Gen. 47:6</reflink>). The inhabitants were not exclusively Israelites (<reflink>Ex. 3:22; 11:2; 12:35, 36</reflink>).

gospel.d: a word of Anglo-Saxon origin, and meaning "God's spell", i.e., word of God, or rather, according to others, "good spell", i.e., good news. It is the rendering of the Greek _evangelion_, i.e., "good message." It denotes (1) "the welcome intelligence of salvation to man as preached by our Lord and his followers. (2.) It was afterwards transitively applied to each of the four histories of our Lord's life, published by those who are therefore called 'Evangelists', writers of the history of the gospel (the evangelion). (3.)
