The term is often used to express collectively the gospel doctrines; and 'preaching the gospel' is often used to include not only the proclaiming of the good tidings, but the teaching men how to avail themselves of the offer of salvation, the declaring of all the truths, precepts, promises, and threatenings of Christianity." It is termed "the gospel of the grace of God" (<reflink>Acts 20:24</reflink>), "the gospel of the kingdom" (<reflink>Matt. …

gospels.d: The central fact of Christian preaching was the intelligence that the Saviour had come into the world (<reflink>Matt. 4:23; Rom. 10:15</reflink>); and the first Christian preachers who called their account of the person and mission of Christ by the term _evangelion_ (= good message) were called _evangelistai_ (= evangelists) (<reflink>Eph. 4:11; Acts 21:8</reflink>).

gourd.d: (1.) Jonah's gourd (<reflink>Jonah 4:6-10</reflink>), bearing the Hebrew name _kikayon_ (found only here), was probably the kiki of the Egyptians, the croton. This is the castor-oil plant, a species of ricinus, the palma Christi, so called from the palmate division of its leaves. Others with more probability regard it as the cucurbita the el-keroa of the Arabs, a kind of pumpkin peculiar to the East. "It is grown in great abundance on the alluvial banks of the Tigris and on the plain between the river and the ruins of Nineveh." At the present day it is trained to run over structures of mud and brush to form boots to protect the gardeners from the heat of the noon-day sun. It grows with extraordinary rapidity, and when cut or injured withers away also with great rapidity.

governments.d: (<reflink>1 Cor. 12:28</reflink>), the powers which fit a man for a place of influence in the church; "the steersman's art; the art of guiding aright the vessel of church or state."

governor.d: (1.) Heb. nagid, a prominent, conspicuous person, whatever his capacity: as, chief of the royal palace (<reflink>2 Chr. 28:7; comp. 1 Kings 4:6</reflink>), chief of the temple (<reflink>1 Chr. 9:11; Jer. 20:1</reflink>), the leader of the Aaronites (<reflink>1 Chr. 12:27</reflink>), keeper of the sacred treasury (26:24), captain of the army (13:1), the king (<reflink>1 Sam. 9:16</reflink>), the Messiah (<reflink>Dan. 9:25</reflink>).

gozan.d: a region in Central Asia to which the Israelites were carried away captive (<reflink>2 Kings 17:6; 1 Chr. 5:26; 2 Kings 19:12; Isa. 37:12</reflink>). It was situated in Mesopotamia, on the river Habor (<reflink>2 Kings 17:6; 18:11</reflink>), the Khabur, a tributary of the Euphrates. The "river of Gozan" (<reflink>1 Chr. 5:26</reflink>) is probably the upper part of the river flowing through the province of Gozan, now Kizzel-Ozan.

grace.d: (1.) Of form or person (<reflink>Prov. 1:9; 3:22; Ps. 45:2</reflink>). (2.) Favour, kindness, friendship (<reflink>Gen. 6:8; 18:3; 19:19; 2 Tim. 1:9</reflink>). (3.) God's forgiving mercy (<reflink>Rom. 11:6; Eph. 2:5</reflink>). (4.) The gospel as distinguished from the law (<reflink>John 1:17; Rom. 6:14; 1 Pet. 5:12</reflink>). (5.) Gifts freely bestowed by God; as miracles, prophecy, tongues (<reflink>Rom. 15:15; 1 Cor. 15:10; Eph. 3:8</reflink>). (6.) Christian virtues (<reflink>2 Cor. 8:7; 2 Pet. 3:18</reflink>). (7.) The glory hereafter to be revealed (<reflink>1 Pet. 1:13</reflink>).

grace, means of.d: an expression not used in Scripture, but employed (1) to denote those institutions ordained by God to be the ordinary channels of grace to the souls of men. These are the Word, Sacraments, and Prayer.

graft.d: the process of inoculating fruit-trees (<reflink>Rom. 11:17-24</reflink>). It is peculiarly appropriate to olive-trees. The union thus of branches to a stem is used to illustrate the union of true believers to the true Church.

grain.d: used, in Amos 9:9, of a small stone or kernel; in Matt. 13:31, of an individual seed of mustard; in John 12:24, 1 Cor. 15:37, of wheat. The Hebrews sowed only wheat, barley, and spelt; rye and oats are not mentioned in Scripture.

grape.d: the fruit of the vine, which was extensively cultivated in Palestine. Grapes are spoken of as "tender" (<reflink>Cant. 2:13, 15</reflink>), "unripe" (<reflink>Job 15:33</reflink>), "sour" (<reflink>Isa. 18:5</reflink>), "wild" (<reflink>Isa. 5:2,4</reflink>). (<reflink>See Rev. 14:18; Micah 7:1; Jer. 6:9; Ezek. 18:2, for figurative use of the word.</reflink>) (<see target="x-self">See VINE.</see>)

grass.d: (1.) Heb. hatsir, ripe grass fit for mowing (<reflink>1 Kings 18:5; Job 40:15; Ps. 104:14</reflink>). As the herbage rapidly fades under the scorching sun, it is used as an image of the brevity of human life (<reflink>Isa. 40:6, 7; Ps. 90:5</reflink>). In Num. 11:5 this word is rendered "leeks."

grasshopper.d: belongs to the class of neuropterous insects called Gryllidae. This insect is not unknown in Palestine.

grate.d: a network of brass for the bottom of the great altar of sacrifice (<reflink>Ex. 27:4; 35:16; 38:4, 5, 30</reflink>).

grave.d: Among the ancient Hebrews graves were outside of cities in the open field (<reflink>Luke 7:12; John 11:30</reflink>). Kings (<reflink>1 Kings 2:10</reflink>) and prophets (<reflink>1 Sam. 25:1</reflink>) were generally buried within cities. Graves were generally grottoes or caves, natural or hewn out in rocks (<reflink>Isa. 22:16; Matt. 27:60</reflink>). There were family cemeteries (<reflink>Gen. 47:29; 50:5; 2 Sam. 19:37</reflink>). Public burial-places were assigned to the poor (<reflink>Jer. 26:23; 2 Kings 23:6</reflink>). Graves were usually closed with stones, which were whitewashed, to warn strangers against contact with them (<reflink>Matt. 23:27</reflink>), which caused ceremonial pollution (<reflink>Num. 19:16</reflink>).

graven image.d: Deut. 27:15; Ps. 97:7 (Heb. pesel), refers to the household gods of idolaters. "Every nation and city had its own gods...Yet every family had its separate household or tutelary god."

graving.d: (1.) Heb. hatsabh. Job 19:24, rendered "graven," but generally means hewn stone or wood, in quarry or forest.

greaves.d: only in 1 Sam. 17:6, a piece of defensive armour (q.v.) reaching from the foot to the knee; from French greve, "the shin." They were the Roman cothurni.

grecians.d: Hellenists, Greek-Jews; Jews born in a foreign country, and thus did not speak Hebrew (<reflink>Acts 6:1; 9:29</reflink>), nor join in the Hebrew services of the Jews in Palestine, but had synagogues of their own in Jerusalem. Joel 3:6 =Greeks.

greece.d: orginally consisted of the four provinces of Macedonia, Epirus, Achaia, and Peleponnesus. In Acts 20:2 it designates only the Roman province of Macedonia. Greece was conquered by the Romans B.C. 146. After passing through various changes it was erected into an independent monarchy in 1831.

greek.d: Found only in the New Testament, where a distinction is observed between "Greek" and "Grecian" (q.v.). The former is (1) a Greek by race (<reflink>Acts 16:1-3; 18:17; Rom. 1:14</reflink>), or (2) a Gentile as opposed to a Jew (<reflink>Rom. 2:9, 10</reflink>). The latter, meaning properly "one who speaks Greek," is a foreign Jew opposed to a home Jew who dwelt in Palestine.

greyhound.d: (<reflink>Prov. 30:31</reflink>), the rendering of the Hebrew _zarzir mothnayim_, meaning literally "girded as to the lions." Some (Gesen.; R.V. marg.) render it "war-horse." The LXX. and Vulgate versions render it "cock." It has been by some interpreters rendered also "stag" and "warrior," as being girded about or panoplied, and "wrestler." The greyhound, however, was evidently known in ancient times, as appears from Egyptian monuments.

grind.d: (<reflink>Ex. 32:20; Deut. 9:21; Judg. 16:21</reflink>), to crush small (Heb. tahan); to oppress the poor (<reflink>Isa. 3:5</reflink>). The hand-mill was early used by the Hebrews (<reflink>Num. 11:8</reflink>). It consisted of two stones, the upper (<reflink>Deut. 24:6; 2 Sam. 11:21</reflink>) being movable and slightly concave, the lower being stationary. The grinders mentioned Eccl. 12:3 are the teeth. (<see target="x-self">See MILL.</see>)

grove.d: (1.) Heb. 'asherah, properly a wooden image, or a pillar representing Ashtoreth, a sensual Canaanitish goddess, probably usually set up in a grove (<reflink>2 Kings 21:7; 23:4</reflink>). In the Revised Version the word "Asherah" (q.v.) is introduced as a proper noun, the name of the wooden symbol of a goddess, with the plurals Asherim (<reflink>Ex. 34:13</reflink>) and Asheroth (<reflink>Judg. 3:13</reflink>).

guard.d: (1.) Heb. tabbah (properly a "cook," and in a secondary sense "executioner," because this office fell to the lot of the cook in Eastern countries), the bodyguard of the kings of Egypt (<reflink>Gen. 37:36</reflink>) and Babylon (<reflink>2 Kings 25:8; Jer. 40:1; Dan. 2:14</reflink>).

gedor.d: a wall. (1.) A city in the mountains or hill country of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:58</reflink>), identified with Jedar, between Jerusalem and Hebron.

gehazi.d: valley of vision, Elisha's trusted servant (<reflink>2 Kings 4:31; 5:25; 8:4, 5</reflink>). He appears in connection with the history of the Shunammite (<reflink>2 Kings 4:14, 31</reflink>) and of Naaman the Syrian. On this latter occasion he was guilty of duplicity and dishonesty of conduct, causing Elisha to denounce his crime with righteous sternness, and pass on him the terrible doom that the leprosy of Naaman would cleave to him and his for ever (5:20-27).

gehenna.d: (originally Ge bene Hinnom; i.e., "the valley of the sons of Hinnom"), a deep, narrow glen to the south of Jerusalem, where the idolatrous Jews offered their children in sacrifice to Molech (<reflink>2 Chr. 28:3; 33:6; Jer. 7:31; 19:2-6</reflink>). This valley afterwards became the common receptacle for all the refuse of the city. Here the dead bodies of animals and of criminals, and all kinds of filth, were cast and consumed by fire kept always burning. It thus in process of time became the image of the place of everlasting destruction. In this sense it is used by our Lord in Matt. 5:22, 29, 30; 10:28; 18:9; 23:15, 33; Mark 9:43, 45, 47; Luke 12:5. In these passages, and also in James 3:6, the word is uniformly rendered "hell," the Revised Version placing "Gehenna" in the margin. (See HELL; HINNOM

geliloth.d: circles; regions, a place in the border of Benjamin (<reflink>Josh. 18:17</reflink>); called Gilgal in 15:7.

gemariah.d: Jehovah has made perfect. (1.) The son of Shaphan, and one of the Levites of the temple in the time of Jehoiakim (<reflink>Jer. 36:10; 2 Kings 22:12</reflink>). Baruch read aloud to the people from Gemariah's chamber, and again in the hearing of Gemariah and other scribes, the prophecies of Jeremiah (<reflink>Jer. 36:11-20</reflink>), which filled him with terror. He joined with others in entreating the king not to destroy the roll of the prophecies which Baruch had read (21-25).

generation.d: Gen. 2:4, "These are the generations," means the "history." 5:1, "The book of the generations," means a family register, or history of Adam. 37:2, "The generations of Jacob" = the history of Jacob and his descendants. 7:1, "In this generation" = in this age. Ps. 49:19, "The generation of his fathers" = the dwelling of his fathers, i.e., the grave. Ps. 73:15, "The generation of thy children" = the contemporary race. Isa. 53:8, "Who shall declare his generation?" = His manner of life who shall declare? or rather = His race, posterity, shall be so numerous that no one shall be able to declare it.

genesis.d: The five books of Moses were collectively called the Pentateuch, a word of Greek origin meaning "the five-fold book." The Jews called them the Torah, i.e., "the law." It is probable that the division of the Torah into five books proceeded from the Greek translators of the Old Testament. The names by which these several books are generally known are Greek.

gennesaret.d: a garden of riches. (1.) A town of Naphtali, called Chinnereth (<reflink>Josh. 19:35</reflink>), sometimes in the plural form Chinneroth (11:2). In later times the name was gradually changed to Genezar and Gennesaret (<reflink>Luke 5:1</reflink>). This city stood on the western shore of the lake to which it gave its name. No trace of it remains. The plain of Gennesaret has been called, from its fertility and beauty, "the Paradise of Galilee." It is now called el-Ghuweir.

gentiles.d: (Heb., usually in plural, goyim), meaning in general all nations except the Jews. In course of time, as the Jews began more and more to pride themselves on their peculiar privileges, it acquired unpleasant associations, and was used as a term of contempt.

genubath.d: theft, the son of Hadad, of the Edomitish royal family. He was brought up in Pharaoh's household. His mother was a sister of Tahpenes, the king of Egypt's wife, mentioned in 1 Kings 11:20.

gera.d: grain. (1.) The son of Bela and grandson of Benjamin (<reflink>1 Chr. 8:3, 5,7</reflink>).

gerah.d: a bean, probably of the carob tree, the smallest weight, and also the smallest piece of money, among the Hebrews, equal to the twentieth part of a shekel (<reflink>Ex. 30:13; Lev. 27:25; Num. 3:47</reflink>). This word came into use in the same way as our word "grain," from a grain of wheat.

gerar.d: a region; lodging-place, a very ancient town and district in the south border of Palestine, which was ruled over by a king named Abimelech (<reflink>Gen. 10:19; 20:1, 2</reflink>). Abraham sojourned here, and perhaps Isaac was born in this place. Both of these patriarchs were guilty of the sin of here denying their wives, and both of them entered into a treaty with the king before they departed to Beersheba (21:23-34; 26). It seems to have been a rich pastoral country (<reflink>2 Chr. 14:12-18</reflink>). Isaac here reaped an hundred-fold, and was blessed of God (<reflink>Gen. 26:12</reflink>). The "valley of Gerar" (<reflink>Gen. 26:17</reflink>) was probably the modern Wady el-Jerdr.

gergesa.d: =Gerasa, identified with the modern Khersa, "over against Galilee," close to the lake. This was probably the scene of the miracle, Mark 5:1-20, etc. "From the base of the great plateau of Bashan, 2,000 feet or more overhead, the ground slopes down steeply, in places precipitously, to the shore. And at the foot of the declivity a bold spur runs out to the water's edge. By it the frantic swine would rush on headlong into the lake and perish." Porter's Through Samaria. (<see target="x-self">See GADARA.</see>)

gerizim.d: a mountain of Samaria, about 3,000 feet above the Mediterranean. It was on the left of the valley containing the ancient town of Shechem (q.v.), on the way to Jerusalem. It stood over against Mount Ebal, the summits of these mountains being distant from each other about 2 miles (Deut. 27; Josh. 8:30-35). On the slopes of this mountain the tribes descended from the handmaids of Leah and Rachel, together with the tribe of Reuben, were gathered together, and gave the responses to the blessing pronounced as the reward of obedience, when Joshua in the valley below read the whole law in the hearing of all the people; as those gathered on Ebal responded with a loud Amen to the rehearsal of the curses pronounced on the disobedient. It was probably at this time that the coffin containing the embalmed body of Joseph was laid in the "parcel of ground which Jacob bought of the sons of Hamor" (<reflink>Gen. 33:19; 50:25</reflink>).

gershom.d: expulsion. (1.) The eldest son of Levi (<reflink>1 Chr. 6:16, 17, 20, 43, 62, 71; 15:7</reflink>)=GERSHON (q.v.).

gershon.d: =Ger'shom expulsion, the eldest of Levi's three sons (<reflink>Gen. 46:11; Ex. 6:16</reflink>).

geshem.d: or Gashmu, firmness, probably chief of the Arabs south of Palestine, one of the enemies of the Jews after the return from Babylon (<reflink>Neh. 2:19; 6:1, 2</reflink>). He united with Sanballat and Tobiah in opposing the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem.

geshur.d: bridge, the name of a district or principality of Syria near Gilead, between Mount Hermon and the Lake of Tiberias (<reflink>2 Sam. 15:8; 1 Chr. 2:23</reflink>). The Geshurites probably inhabited the rocky fastness of Argob, the modern Lejah, in the north-east corner of Bashan. In the time of David it was ruled by Talmai, whose daughter he married, and who was the mother of Absalom, who fled to Geshur after the murder of Amnon (<reflink>2 Sam. 13:37</reflink>).

geshurites.d: (1.) The inhabitants of Geshur. They maintained friendly relations with the Israelites on the east of Jordan (<reflink>Josh. 12:5; 13:11, 13</reflink>).

gethsemane.d: oil-press, the name of an olive-yard at the foot of the Mount of Olives, to which Jesus was wont to retire (<reflink>Luke 22:39</reflink>) with his disciples, and which is specially memorable as being the scene of his agony (<reflink>Mark 14:32; John 18:1; Luke 22:44</reflink>). The plot of ground pointed out as Gethsemane is now surrounded by a wall, and is laid out as a modern European flower-garden. It contains eight venerable olive-trees, the age of which cannot, however, be determined. The exact site of Gethsemane is still in question. Dr. Thomson (The Land and the Book) says: "When I first came to Jerusalem, and for many years afterward, this plot of ground was open to all whenever they chose to come and meditate beneath its very old olivetrees. The Latins, however, have within the last few years succeeded in gaining sole possession, and have built a high wall around it...The Greeks have invented another site a little to the north of it...My own impression is that both are wrong.

gezer.d: a precipice, an ancient royal Canaanitish city (<reflink>Josh. 10:33; 12:12</reflink>). It was allotted with its suburbs to the Kohathite Levites (21:21; 1 Chr. 6:67). It stood between the lower Beth-horon and the sea (<reflink>Josh. 16:3; 1 Kings 9:17</reflink>). It was the last point to which David pursued the Philistines (<reflink>2 Sam. 5:25; 1 Chr. 14:16</reflink>) after the battle of Baal-perazim. The Canaanites retained possession of it till the time of Solomon, when the king of Egypt took it and gave it to Solomon as a part of the dowry of the Egyptian princess whom he married (<reflink>1 Kings 9:15-17</reflink>). It is identified with Tell el-Jezer, about 10 miles south-west of Beth-horon. It is mentioned in the Amarna tablets.

ghost.d: an old Saxon word equivalent to soul or spirit. It is the translation of the Hebrew _nephesh_ and the Greek _pneuma_, both meaning "breath," "life," "spirit," the "living principle" (<reflink>Job 11:20; Jer. 15:9; Matt. 27:50; John 19:30</reflink>). The expression "to give up the ghost" means to die (<reflink>Lam. 1:19; Gen. 25:17; 35:29; 49:33; Job 3:11</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See HOLY GHOST.</see>)

giants.d: (1.) Heb. nephilim, meaning "violent" or "causing to fall" (<reflink>Gen. 6:4</reflink>). These were the violent tyrants of those days, those who fell upon others. The word may also be derived from a root signifying "wonder," and hence "monsters" or "prodigies." In Num. 13:33 this name is given to a Canaanitish tribe, a race of large stature, "the sons of Anak." The Revised Version, in these passages, simply transliterates the original, and reads "Nephilim."

gibbethon.d: a height, a city of the Philistines in the territory of Dan, given to the Kohathites (<reflink>Josh. 19:44; 21:23</reflink>). Nadab the king of Israel, while besieging it, was slain under its walls by Baasha, one of his own officers (<reflink>1 Kings 15:27</reflink>). It was in the possession of the Philistines after the secession of the ten tribes (<reflink>2 Chr. 11:13, 14</reflink>).

gibeah.d: a hill or hill-town, "of Benjamin" (<reflink>1 Sam. 13:15</reflink>), better known as "Gibeah of Saul" (11:4; Isa. 10:29). It was here that the terrible outrage was committed on the Levite's concubine which led to the almost utter extirpation of the tribe of Benjamin (Judg. 19; 20), only six hundred men surviving after a succession of disastrous battles. This was the birthplace of Saul, and continued to be his residence after he became king (<reflink>1 Sam. 10:26; 11:4; 15:34</reflink>). It was reckoned among the ancient sanctuaries of Palestine (10:26; 15:34; 23:19; 26:1; 2 Sam. 21:6-10), and hence it is called "Gibeah of God" (<reflink>1 Sam. 10:5, R.V. marg.</reflink>). It has been identified with the modern Tell el-Ful (i.e., "hill of the bean"), about 3 miles north of Jerusalem.

gibeah of judah.d: (<reflink>Josh. 15:57</reflink>), a city in the mountains of Judah, the modern Jeba, on a hill in the Wady Musurr, about 7 1/2 miles west-south-west of Bethlehem.

gibeah of phinehas.d: (<reflink>Josh. 15:57, R.V. marg.</reflink>), a city on Mount Ephraim which had been given to Phinehas (24:33 "hill," A.V.; R.V. marg. and Heb., "Gibeah."). Here Eleazar the son of Aaron was buried. It has been identified with the modern Khurbet Jibia, 5 miles north of Guphna towards Shechem.

gibeah-haaraloth.d: (<reflink>Josh. 5:3, marg.</reflink>), hill of the foreskins, a place at Gilgal where those who had been born in the wilderness were circumcised. All the others, i.e., those who were under twenty years old at the time of the sentence at Kadesh, had already been circumcised.

gibeon.d: hill-city, "one of the royal cities, greater than Ai, and all the men thereof were mighty" (<reflink>Josh. 10:2</reflink>). Its inhabitants were Hivites (11:19). It lay within the territory of Benjamin, and became a priest-city (18:25; 21:17). Here the tabernacle was set up after the destruction of Nob, and here it remained many years till the temple was built by Solomon. It is represented by the modern el-Jib, to the south-west of Ai, and about 5 1/2 miles north-north-west of Jerusalem.

gideon.d: called also Jerubbaal (<reflink>Judg. 6:29, 32</reflink>), was the first of the judges whose history is circumstantially narrated (Judg. 6-8). His calling is the commencement of the second period in the history of the judges. After the victory gained by Deborah and Barak over Jabin, Israel once more sank into idolatry, and the Midianites (q.v.) and Amalekites, with other "children of the east," crossed the Jordan each year for seven successive years for the purpose of plundering and desolating the land. Gideon received a direct call from God to undertake the task of delivering the land from these warlike invaders. He was of the family of Abiezer (<reflink>Josh. 17:2; 1 Chr. 7:18</reflink>), and of the little township of Ophrah (<reflink>Judg. 6:11</reflink>). …

gier eagle.d: Heb. raham = "parental affection," Lev. 11:18; Deut. 14:17; R.V., "vulture"), a species of vulture living entirely on carrion. "It is about the size of a raven; has an almost triangular, bald, and wrinkled head, a strong pointed beak, black at the tip, large eyes and ears, the latter entirely on the outside, and long feet." It is common in Egypt, where it is popularly called "Pharaoh's chicken" (the Neophron percnopterus), and is found in Palestine only during summer. Tristram thinks that the Hebrew name, which is derived from a root meaning "to love," is given to it from the fact that the male and female bird never part company.

gift.d: (1.) An gratuity (<reflink>Prov. 19:6</reflink>) to secure favour (18:16; 21:14), a thank-offering (<reflink>Num. 18:11</reflink>), or a dowry (<reflink>Gen. 34:12</reflink>).

gifts, spiritual.d: (Gr. charismata), gifts supernaturally bestowed on the early Christians, each having his own proper gift or gifts for the edification of the body of Christ. These were the result of the extraordinary operation of the Spirit, as on the day of Pentecost. They were the gifts of speaking with tongues, casting out devils, healing, etc. (<reflink>Mark 16:17, 18</reflink>), usually communicated by the medium of the laying on of the hands of the apostles (<reflink>Acts 8:17; 19:6; 1 Tim. 4:14</reflink>). These charismata were enjoyed only for a time. They could not continue always in the Church. They were suited to its infancy and to the necessities of those times.

gihon.d: a stream. (1.) One of the four rivers of Eden (<reflink>Gen. 2:13</reflink>). It has been identified with the Nile. Others regard it as the Oxus, or the Araxes, or the Ganges. But as, according to the sacred narrative, all these rivers of Eden took their origin from the head-waters of the Euphrates and the Trigris, it is probable that the Gihon is the ancient Araxes, which, under the modern name of the Arras, discharges itself into the Caspian Sea. It was the Asiatic and not the African "Cush" which the Gihon compassed (<reflink>Gen. 10:7-10</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See EDEN.</see>)

gilboa.d: boiling spring, a mountain range, now Jebel Fukua', memorable as the scene of Saul's disastrous defeat by the Philistines. Here also his three sons were slain, and he himself died by his own hand (<reflink>1 Sam. 28:4; 31:1-8; 2 Sam. 1:6-21; 21:12; 1 Chr. 10:1, 8</reflink>). It was a low barren range of mountains bounding the valley of Esdraelon (Jezreel) on the east, between it and the Jordan valley. When the tidings of this defeat were conveyed to David, he gave utterance to those pathetic words in the "Song of the Bow" (<reflink>2 Sam. 1:19-27</reflink>).

gilead.d: hill of testimony, (<reflink>Gen. 31:21</reflink>), a mountainous region east of Jordan. From its mountainous character it is called "the mount of Gilead" (<reflink>Gen. 31:25</reflink>). It is called also "the land of Gilead" (<reflink>Num. 32:1</reflink>), and sometimes simply "Gilead" (<reflink>Ps. 60:7; Gen. 37:25</reflink>). It comprised the possessions of the tribes of Gad and Reuben and the south part of Manasseh (<reflink>Deut. 3:13; Num. 32:40</reflink>). It was bounded on the north by Bashan, and on the south by Moab and Ammon (<reflink>Gen. 31:21; Deut. 3:12-17</reflink>). "Half Gilead" was possessed by Sihon, and the other half, separated from it by the river Jabbok, by Og, king of Bashan. The deep ravine of the river Hieromax (the modern Sheriat el-Mandhur) separated Bashan from Gilead, which was about 60 miles in length and 20 in breadth, extending from near the south end of the Lake of Gennesaret to the north end of the Dead Sea. …

gilead, balm of.d: The region of Gilead abounded in spices and aromatic gums, which were exported to Egypt and Tyre (<reflink>Gen. 37:25; Jer. 8:22; 46:11; Ezek. 27:17</reflink>). The word "balm" is a contracted form of "balsam," a word derived from the Greek _balsamon_, which was adopted as the representative of the Hebrew words _baal shemen_, meaning "lord" or "chief of oils."

gilgal.d: rolling. (1.) From the solemn transaction of the reading of the law in the valley of Shechem between Ebal and Gerizim the Israelites moved forward to Gilgal, and there made a permanent camp (<reflink>Josh. 9:6; 10:6</reflink>). It was "beside the oaks of Moreh," near which Abraham erected his first altar (<reflink>Gen. 12:6, 7</reflink>). This was one of the three towns to which Samuel resorted for the administration of justice (<reflink>1 Sam. 7:16</reflink>), and here also he offered sacrifices when the ark was no longer in the tabernacle at Shiloh (<reflink>1 Sam. 10:8; 13:7-9</reflink>). To this place, as to a central sanctuary, all Israel gathered to renew their allegiance to Saul (11:14). At a later period it became the scene of idolatrous worship (<reflink>Hos. 4:15; 9:15</reflink>). It has been identified with the ruins of Jiljilieh, about 5 miles south-west of Shiloh and about the same distance from Bethel.

giloh.d: exile, a city in the south-west part of the hill-country of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:51</reflink>). It was the native place or residence of the traitor Ahithophel "the Gilonite" (<reflink>Josh. 15:51; 2 Sam. 15:12</reflink>), and where he committed suicide (17:23). It has been identified with Kurbet Jala, about 7 miles north of Hebron.

gimzo.d: a place fertile in sycamores, a city in the plain of Judah, the villages of which were seized by the Philistines (<reflink>2 Chr. 28:18</reflink>). It is now called Jimzu, about 3 miles south-east of Ludd, i.e., Lydda.

gin.d: a trap. (1.) Ps. 140:5, 141:9, Amos 3:5, the Hebrew word used, _mokesh_, means a noose or "snare," as it is elsewhere rendered (<reflink>Ps. 18:5; Prov. 13:14, etc.</reflink>).

girdle.d: (1.) Heb. hagor, a girdle of any kind worn by soldiers (<reflink>1 Sam. 18:4; 2 Sam. 20:8; 1 Kings 2:5; 2 Kings 3:21</reflink>) or women (<reflink>Isa. 3:24</reflink>).

girgashite.d: dwelling in clayey soil, the descendants of the fifth son of Canaan (<reflink>Gen. 10:16</reflink>), one of the original tribes inhabiting the land of Canaan before the time of the Israelites (<reflink>Gen. 15:21; Deut. 7:1</reflink>). They were a branch of the great family of the Hivites. Of their geographical position nothing is certainly known. Probably they lived somewhere in the central part of Western Palestine.

gittaim.d: two wine-presses, (<reflink>2 Sam. 4:3; Neh. 11:33</reflink>), a town probably in Benjamin to which the Beerothites fled.

gittite.d: a native of the Philistine city of Gath (<reflink>Josh. 13:3</reflink>). Obed-edom, in whose house the ark was placed, is so designated (<reflink>2 Sam. 6:10</reflink>). Six hundred Gittites came with David from Gath into Israel (15:18, 19).

gittith.d: a stringed instrument of music. This word is found in the titles of Ps. 8, 81, 84. In these places the LXX. render the word by "on the wine-fats." The Targum explains by "on the harp which David brought from Gath." It is the only stringed instrument named in the titles of the Psalms.

gizonite.d: a name given to Hashem, an inhabitant of Gizoh, a place somewhere in the mountains of Judah (<reflink>1 Chr. 11:34; 2 Sam. 23:32, 34</reflink>).

glass.d: was known to the Egyptians at a very early period of their national history, at least B.C. 1500. Various articles both useful and ornamental were made of it, as bottles, vases, etc. A glass bottle with the name of Sargon on it was found among the ruins of the north-west palace of Nimroud. The Hebrew word _zekukith_ (<reflink>Job 28:17</reflink>), rendered in the Authorized Version "crystal," is rightly rendered in the Revised Version "glass." This is the only allusion to glass found in the Old Testament. It is referred to in the New Testament in Rev. 4:6; 15:2; 21:18, 21. In Job 37:18, the word rendered "looking-glass" is in the Revised Version properly rendered "mirror," formed, i.e., of some metal. (<reflink>Comp. Ex. 38:8: "looking-glasses" are brazen mirrors, R.V.</reflink>). A mirror is referred to also in James 1:23.

glean.d: The corners of fields were not to be reaped, and the sheaf accidentally left behind was not to be fetched away, according to the law of Moses (<reflink>Lev. 19:9; 23:22; Deut. 24:21</reflink>). They were to be left for the poor to glean. Similar laws were given regarding vineyards and oliveyards. (<reflink>Comp. Ruth 2:2.</reflink>)

glede.d: an Old English name for the common kite, mentioned only in Deut. 14:13 (Heb. ra'ah), the Milvus ater or black kite. The Hebrew word does not occur in the parallel passage in Leviticus (11:14, da'ah, rendered "vulture;" in R.V., "kite"). It was an unclean bird. The Hebrew name is from a root meaning "to see," "to look," thus designating a bird with a keen sight. The bird intended is probably the buzzard, of which there are three species found in Palestine. (<see target="x-self">See VULTURE.</see>)

glorify.d: (1.) To make glorious, or cause so to appear (<reflink>John 12:28; 13:31, 32; 17:4,5</reflink>).

glory.d: (Heb. kabhod; Gr. doxa). (1.) Abundance, wealth, treasure, and hence honour (<reflink>Ps. 49:12</reflink>); glory (<reflink>Gen. 31:1; Matt. 4:8; Rev. 21:24, 26</reflink>).

glutton.d: (<reflink>Deut. 21:20</reflink>), Heb. zolel, from a word meaning "to shake out," "to squander;" and hence one who is prodigal, who wastes his means by indulgence. In Prov. 23:21, the word means debauchees or wasters of their own body. In Prov. 28:7, the word (pl.) is rendered Authorized Version "riotous men;" Revised Version, "gluttonous." Matt. 11:19, Luke 7:34, Greek phagos, given to eating, gluttonous.

gnash.d: Heb. harak, meaning "to grate the teeth", (<reflink>Job 16:9; Ps. 112:10; Lam. 2:16</reflink>), denotes rage or sorrow. (<reflink>See also Acts 7:54; Mark 9:18.</reflink>)

gnat.d: only in Matt. 23:24, a small two-winged stinging fly of the genus Culex, which includes mosquitoes. Our Lord alludes here to the gnat in a proverbial expression probably in common use, "who strain out the gnat;" the words in the Authorized Version, "strain at a gnat," being a mere typographical error, which has been corrected in the Revised Version. The custom of filtering wine for this purpose was common among the Jews. It was founded on Lev. 11:23. It is supposed that the "lice," Ex. 8:16 (marg. R.V., "sand-flies"), were a species of gnat.

goad.d: (Heb. malmad, only in Judg. 3: 31), an instrument used by ploughmen for guiding their oxen. Shamgar slew six hundred Philistines with an ox-goad. "The goad is a formidable weapon. It is sometimes ten feet long, and has a sharp point. We could now see that the feat of Shamgar was not so very wonderful as some have been accustomed to think."

goat.d: (1.) Heb. 'ez, the she-goat (<reflink>Gen. 15:9; 30:35; 31:38</reflink>). This Hebrew word is also used for the he-goat (<reflink>Ex. 12:5; Lev. 4:23; Num. 28:15</reflink>), and to denote a kid (<reflink>Gen. 38:17, 20</reflink>). Hence it may be regarded as the generic name of the animal as domesticated. It literally means "strength," and points to the superior strength of the goat as compared with the sheep.

goath.d: a lowing, a place near Jerusalem, mentioned only in Jer. 31:39.

harvest.d: the season for gathering grain or fruit. On the 16th day of Abib (or April) a handful of ripe ears of corn was offered as a first-fruit before the Lord, and immediately after this the harvest commenced (<reflink>Lev. 23:9-14; 2 Sam. 21:9, 10; Ruth 2:23</reflink>). It began with the feast of Passover and ended with Pentecost, thus lasting for seven weeks (<reflink>Ex. 23:16</reflink>). The harvest was a season of joy (<reflink>Ps. 126:1-6; Isa. 9:3</reflink>). This word is used figuratively Matt. 9:37; 13:30; Luke 10:2; John 4:35. (See AGRICULTURE

hasadiah.d: favoured by Jehovah, one of the sons of Pedaiah (<reflink>1 Chr. 3:20</reflink>), of the royal line of David.

hasenuah.d: bristling or hated, a Benjamite (<reflink>1 Chr. 9:7</reflink>).

hashabiah.d: regarded by Jehovah. (1.) Merarite Levite (<reflink>1 Chr. 6:45; 9:14</reflink>). (2.) A son of Jeduthun (25:3, 19). (3.) Son of Kemuel (26:30). (4.) One of the chief Levites (<reflink>2 Chr. 35:9</reflink>). (5.) A Levite (<reflink>Neh. 11:22</reflink>). (6.) One of the chief priests in the time of Ezra (<reflink>Ezra 8:24</reflink>). (7.) A chief of the Levites (<reflink>Neh. 12:24</reflink>). (8.) Ezra 8:19. (9.) Neh. 3:17.

hashabniah.d: (1.) Neh. 3:10. (2.) One of the Levites whom Ezra appointed to interpret the law to the people (<reflink>Neh. 9:5</reflink>).

hashbadana.d: consideration in judging, stood at Ezra's left hand when he read the law (<reflink>Neh. 8:4</reflink>).

hashmonah.d: fatness, the thirtieth halting-place of the Israelites during their wanderings in the wilderness, not far from Mount Hor (<reflink>Num. 33:29, 30</reflink>).

hashub.d: intelligent. (1.) A Levite of the family of Merari (<reflink>Neh. 11:15; 1 Chr. 9:14</reflink>). (2.) Neh. 3:23. 3:11.

hashubah.d: ibid., a descendant of David (<reflink>1 Chr. 3:20</reflink>).

hashum.d: opulent. (1.) Ezra 2:19; Neh. 7:22. (2.) Stood on Ezra's left hand while he read the law (<reflink>Neh. 8:4</reflink>).

hasrah.d: poverty, "keeper of the wardrobe," i.e., of the sacerdotal vestments (<reflink>2 Chr. 34:22</reflink>); called Harhas 2 Kings 22:14. He was husband of the prophetess Huldah.

hasupha.d: uncovered, one of the Nethinim (<reflink>Ezra 2:43; Neh. 7:46</reflink>).

hat.d: Chald. karb'ela, (<reflink>Dan. 3:21</reflink>), properly mantle or pallium. The Revised Version renders it "tunic."

hatach.d: verity, one of the eunuchs or chamberlains in the palace of Ahasuerus (<reflink>Esther 4:5, 6, 9, 10</reflink>).

hatita.d: exploration, one of the temple porters or janitors (<reflink>Ezra 2:42</reflink>). He returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel.

hatred.d: among the works of the flesh (<reflink>Gal. 5:20</reflink>). Altogether different is the meaning of the word in Deut. 21:15; Matt. 6:24; Luke 14:26; Rom. 9:13, where it denotes only a less degree of love.

hattush.d: assembled. (1.) A priest who returned with Zerubbabel (<reflink>Neh. 12:2</reflink>). (2.) Ezra 8:2. (3.) Neh. 3:10. (4.) Neh. 10:4. (5.) 1 Chr. 3:22.

hauran.d: cave-land, mentioned only in Ezek. 47:16, 18. It was one of the ancient divisions of Bashan (q.v.), and lay on the south-east of Gaulanitis or the Jaulan, and on the south of Lejah, extending from the Arnon to the Hieromax. It was the most fertile region in Syria, and to this day abounds in the ruins of towns, many of which have stone doors and massive walls. It retains its ancient name. It was known by the Greeks and Romans as "Auranitis."

haven.d: a harbour (<reflink>Ps. 107:30; Acts 27: 12</reflink>). The most famous on the coast of Palestine was that of Tyre (<reflink>Ezek. 27:3</reflink>). That of Crete, called "Fair Havens," is mentioned Acts 27:8.

havilah.d: the sand region. (1.) A land mentioned in Gen. 2:11 rich in gold and bdellium and onyx stone. The question as to the locality of this region has given rise to a great diversity of opinion. It may perhaps be identified with the sandy tract which skirts Babylonia along the whole of its western border, stretching from the lower Euphrates to the mountains of Edom.

havoth-jair.d: hamlets of the enlightener a district in the east of Jordan. (1.) Jair, the son of Manasseh, took some villages of Gilead and called them by this name (<reflink>Num. 32:41</reflink>).

hawk.d: (Heb. netz, a word expressive of strong and rapid flight, and hence appropriate to the hawk). It is an unclean bird (<reflink>Lev. 11:16; Deut. 14:15</reflink>). It is common in Syria and surrounding countries. The Hebrew word includes various species of Falconidae, with special reference perhaps to the kestrel (Falco tinnunculus), the hobby (Hypotriorchis subbuteo), and the lesser kestrel (Tin, Cenchris). The kestrel remains all the year in Palestine, but some ten or twelve other species are all migrants from the south. Of those summer visitors to Palestine special mention may be made of the Falco sacer and the Falco lanarius. (<see target="x-self">See NIGHT-HAWK.</see>)

hay.d: properly so called, was not in use among the Hebrews; straw was used instead. They cut the grass green as it was needed. The word rendered "hay" in Prov. 27:25 means the first shoots of the grass. In Isa. 15:6 the Revised Version has correctly "grass," where the Authorized Version has "hay."

hazael.d: whom God beholds, an officer of Ben-hadad II., king of Syria, who ultimately came to the throne, according to the word of the Lord to Elijah (<reflink>1 Kings 19:15</reflink>), after he had put the king to death (<reflink>2 Kings 8:15</reflink>). His interview with Elisha is mentioned in 2 Kings 8. The Assyrians soon after his accession to the throne came against him and defeated him with very great loss; and three years afterwards again invaded Syria, but on this occasion Hazael submitted to them. He then turned his arms against Israel, and ravaged "all the land of Gilead," etc. (<reflink>2 Kings 10:33</reflink>), which he held in a degree of subjection to him (13:3-7, 22). He aimed at the subjugation also of the kingdom of Judah, when Joash obtained peace by giving him "all the gold that was found in the treasures of the house of the Lord, and in the king's house" (<reflink>2 Kings 12:18; 2 Chr. 24:24</reflink>). …

hazar-addar.d: village of Addar, a place in the southern boundary of Palestine (<reflink>Num. 34:4</reflink>), in the desert to the west of Kadesh-barnea. It is called Adar in Josh. 15:3.

hazar-enan.d: village of fountains, a place on the north-east frontier of Palestine (<reflink>Num. 34:9, 10</reflink>). Some have identified it with Ayan ed-Dara in the heart of the central chain of Anti-Libanus. More probably, however, it has been identified with Kuryetein, about 60 miles east-north-east of Damascus. (<reflink>Comp. Ezek. 47:17; 48:1.</reflink>)

hazar-gaddah.d: village of fortune, a city on the south border of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:27</reflink>), midway between the Mediterranean and the Dead Sea.

hazar-hatticon.d: village of the midway, a place near Hamath in the confines of Hauran (<reflink>Ezek. 47:16</reflink>), probably on the north brow of Hermon.

hazar-maveth.d: court of death, the third son of Joktan, and a region in Arabia-Felix settled by him (<reflink>Gen. 10:26; 1 Chr. 1:20</reflink>). It is probably the modern province of Hadramaut, situated on the Indian Ocean east of the modern Yemen.

hazar-shual.d: village or enclosure of the jackal, a city on the south border of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:28; Neh. 11:27</reflink>). It has been identified with the ruins of Saweh, half-way between Beersheba and Moladah.

hazar-susah.d: village of the horse, the same as Sansannah, one of Solomon's "chariot cities" (<reflink>Josh. 15:31; 2 Chr. 1:14</reflink>), a depot in the south border of Judah.

hazel.d: Heb. luz, (<reflink>Gen. 30:37</reflink>), a nutbearing tree. The Hebrew word is rendered in the Vulgate by amygdalinus, "the almond-tree," which is probably correct. That tree flourishes in Syria.

hazerim.d: villages, probably the name of the temporary villages in which the nomad Avites resided (<reflink>Deut. 2:23</reflink>).

guest-chamber.d: the spare room on the upper floor of an Eastern dwelling (<reflink>Mark 14:14; Luke 22:11</reflink>). In Luke 2:7 the word is translated "inn" (q.v.).

gur.d: a whelp, a place near Ibleam where Jehu's servants overtook and mortally wounded king Ahaziah (<reflink>2 Kings 9:27</reflink>); an ascent from the plain of Jezreel.

gur-baal.d: sojourn of Baal, a place in Arabia (<reflink>2 Chr. 26:7</reflink>) where there was probably a temple of Baal.

gutter.d: Heb. tsinnor, (<reflink>2 Sam. 5:8</reflink>). This Hebrew word occurs only elsewhere in Ps. 42:7 in the plural, where it is rendered "waterspouts." It denotes some passage through which water passed; a water-course.

habakkuk.d: embrace, the eighth of the twelve minor prophets. Of his personal history we have no reliable information. He was probably a member of the Levitical choir. He was contemporary with Jeremiah and Zephaniah.

habakkuk, prophecies of.d: were probably written about B.C. 650-627, or, as some think, a few years later. This book consists of three chapters, the contents of which are thus comprehensively described: "When the prophet in spirit saw the formidable power of the Chaldeans approaching and menacing his land, and saw the great evils they would cause in Judea, he bore his complaints and doubts before Jehovah, the just and the pure (1:2-17). And on this occasion the future punishment of the Chaldeans was revealed to him (2). In the third chapter a presentiment of the destruction of his country, in the inspired heart of the prophet, contends with his hope that the enemy would be chastised." The third chapter is a sublime song dedicated "to the chief musician," and therefore intended apparently to be used in the worship of God. It is "unequalled in majesty and splendour of language and imagery."

habergeon.d: an Old English word for breastplate. In Job 41:26 (Heb. shiryah) it is properly a "coat of mail;" the Revised Version has "pointed shaft." In Ex. 28:32, 39:23, it denotes a military garment strongly and thickly woven and covered with mail round the neck and breast. Such linen corselets have been found in Egypt. The word used in these verses is _tahra_, which is of Egyptian origin. The Revised Version, however, renders it by "coat of mail." (<see target="x-self">See ARMOUR.</see>)

habitation.d: God is the habitation of his people, who find rest and safety in him (<reflink>Ps. 71:3; 91:9</reflink>). Justice and judgment are the habitation of God's throne (<reflink>Ps. 89:14, Heb. mekhon, "foundation"</reflink>), because all his acts are founded on justice and judgment. (<reflink>See Ps. 132:5, 13; Eph. 2:22, of Canaan, Jerusalem, and the temple as God's habitation.</reflink>) God inhabits eternity (<reflink>Isa. 57:15</reflink>), i.e., dwells not only among men, but in eternity, where time is unknown; and "the praises of Israel" (<reflink>Ps. 22:3</reflink>), i.e., he dwells among those praises and is continually surrounded by them.

habor.d: the united stream, or, according to others, with beautiful banks, the name of a river in Assyria, and also of the district through which it flowed (<reflink>1 Chr. 5:26</reflink>). There is a river called Khabur which rises in the central highlands of Kurdistan, and flows south-west till it falls into the Tigris, about 70 miles above Mosul. This was not, however, the Habor of Scripture.

hachilah.d: the darksome hill, one of the peaks of the long ridge of el-Kolah, running out of the Ziph plateau, "on the south of Jeshimon" (i.e., of the "waste"), the district to which one looks down from the plateau of Ziph (<reflink>1 Sam. 23:19</reflink>). After his reconciliation with Saul at Engedi (24:1-8), David returned to Hachilah, where he had fixed his quarters. The Ziphites treacherously informed Saul of this, and he immediately (26:1-4) renewed his pursuit of David, and "pitched in the hill of Hachilah." David and his nephew Abishai stole at night into the midst of Saul's camp, when they were all asleep, and noiselessly removed the royal spear and the cruse from the side of the king, and then, crossing the intervening valley to the height on the other side, David cried to the people, and thus awoke the sleepers. He then addressed Saul, who recognized his voice, and expostulated with him. …

hadad.d: Adod, brave(?), the name of a Syrian god. (1.) An Edomite king who defeated the Midianites (<reflink>Gen. 36:35; 1 Chr. 1:46</reflink>).

hadad-rimmon.d: (composed of the names of two Syrian idols), the name of a place in the valley of Megiddo. It is alluded to by the prophet Zechariah (12:11) in a proverbial expression derived from the lamentation for Josiah, who was mortally wounded near this place (<reflink>2 Chr. 35:22-25</reflink>). It has been identified with the modern Rummaneh, a village "at the foot of the Megiddo hills, in a notch or valley about an hour and a half south of Tell Metzellim."

hadadezer.d: Hadad is help; called also Hadarezer, Adod is his help, the king of Zobah. Hanun, the king of the Ammonites, hired among others the army of Hadadezer to assist him in his war against David. Joab, who was sent against this confederate host, found them in double battle array, the Ammonities toward their capital of Rabbah, and the Syrian mercenaries near Medeba. In the battle which was fought the Syrians were scattered, and the Ammonites in alarm fled into their capital. After this Hadadezer went north "to recover his border" (<reflink>2 Sam. 8:3, A.V.</reflink>); but rather, as the Revised Version renders, "to recover his dominion", i.e., to recruit his forces. Then followed another battle with the Syrian army thus recruited, which resulted in its being totally routed at Helam (<reflink>2 Sam. 10:17</reflink>). Shobach, the leader of the Syrian army, died on the field of battle. …

hadar.d: Adod, brave(?). (1.) A son of Ishmael (<reflink>Gen. 25:15</reflink>); in 1 Chr. 1:30 written Hadad.

hadarezer.d: Adod is his help, the name given to Hadadezer (<reflink>2 Sam. 8:3-12</reflink>) in 2 Sam. 10.

hadashah.d: new, a city in the valley of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:37</reflink>).

hadassah.d: myrtle, the Jewish name of Esther (q.v.), Esther 2:7.

hadattah.d: new, one of the towns in the extreme south of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:25</reflink>).

hades.d: that which is out of sight, a Greek word used to denote the state or place of the dead. All the dead alike go into this place. To be buried, to go down to the grave, to descend into hades, are equivalent expressions. In the LXX. this word is the usual rendering of the Hebrew sheol, the common receptacle of the departed (<reflink>Gen. 42:38; Ps. 139:8; Hos. 13:14; Isa. 14:9</reflink>). This term is of comparatively rare occurrence in the Greek New Testament. Our Lord speaks of Capernaum as being "brought down to hell" (hades), i.e., simply to the lowest debasement, (<reflink>Matt. 11:23</reflink>). It is contemplated as a kind of kingdom which could never overturn the foundation of Christ's kingdom (16:18), i.e., Christ's church can never die.

hadid.d: pointed, a place in the tribe of Benjamin near Lydda, or Lod, and Ono (<reflink>Ezra 2:33; Neh. 7:37</reflink>). It is identified with the modern el-Haditheh, 3 miles east of Lydda.

hadlai.d: resting, an Ephraimite; the father of Amasa, mentioned in 2 Chr. 28:12.

hadoram.d: is exalted. (1.) The son of Tou, king of Hamath, sent by his father to congratulate David on his victory over Hadarezer, king of Syria (<reflink>1 Chr. 18:10; called Joram 2 Sam. 8:10</reflink>).

hadrach.d: the name of a country (<reflink>Zech. 9:1</reflink>) which cannot be identified. Rawlinson would identify it with Edessa. He mentions that in the Assyrian inscriptions it is recorded that "Shalmanezer III. made two expeditions, the first against Damascus B.C. 773, and the second against Hadrach B.C. 772; and again that Asshurdanin-il II. made expeditions against Hadrach in B.C. 765 and 755."

haemorrhoids.d: or Emerods, bleeding piles known to the ancient Romans as mariscae, but more probably malignant boils of an infectious and fatal character. With this loathsome and infectious disease the men of Ashdod were smitten by the hand of the Lord. This calamity they attributed to the presence of the ark in their midst, and therefore they removed it to Gath (<reflink>1 Sam. 5:6-8</reflink>). But the same consequences followed from its presence in Gath, and therefore they had it removed to Ekron, 11 miles distant. The Ekronites were afflicted with the same dreadful malady, but more severely; and a panic seizing the people, they demanded that the ark should be sent back to the land of Israel (9-12; 6:1-9).

haft.d: a handle as of a dagger (<reflink>Judg. 3:22</reflink>).

hagar.d: flight, or, according to others, stranger, an Egyptian, Sarah's handmaid (<reflink>Gen. 16:1; 21:9, 10</reflink>), whom she gave to Abraham (q.v.) as a secondary wife (16:2). When she was about to become a mother she fled from the cruelty of her mistress, intending apparently to return to her relatives in Egypt, through the desert of Shur, which lay between. Wearied and worn she had reached the place she distinguished by the name of Beer-lahai-roi ("the well of the visible God"), where the angel of the Lord appeared to her. In obedience to the heavenly visitor she returned to the tent of Abraham, where her son Ishmael was born, and where she remained (16) till after the birth of Isaac, the space of fourteen years. Sarah after this began to vent her dissatisfaction both on Hagar and her child. Ishmael's conduct was insulting to Sarah, and she insisted that he and his mother should be dismissed. This was accordingly done, although with reluctance on the part of Abraham (<reflink>Gen. …

hagarene.d: or Hagarite. (1.) One of David's mighty men (<reflink>1 Chr. 11:38</reflink>), the son of a foreigner.

haggai.d: festive, one of the twelve so-called minor prophets. He was the first of the three (Zechariah, his contemporary, and Malachi, who was about one hundred years later, being the other two) whose ministry belonged to the period of Jewish history which began after the return from captivity in Babylon. Scarcely anything is known of his personal history. He may have been one of the captives taken to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar. He began his ministry about sixteen years after the Return. The work of rebuilding the temple had been put a stop to through the intrigues of the Samaritans. After having been suspended for fifteen years, the work was resumed through the efforts of Haggai and Zechariah (<reflink>Ezra 6:14</reflink>), who by their exhortations roused the people from their lethargy, and induced them to take advantage of the favourable opportunity that had arisen in a change in the policy of the Persian government. …

haggai, book of.d: consists of two brief, comprehensive chapters. The object of the prophet was generally to urge the people to proceed with the rebuilding of the temple.

haggith.d: festive; the dancer, a wife of David and the mother of Adonijah (<reflink>2 Sam. 3:4; 1 Kings 1:5, 11; 2:13; 1 Chr. 3:2</reflink>), who, like Absalom, was famed for his beauty.

hagiographa.d: the holy writings, a term which came early into use in the Christian church to denote the third division of the Old Testament scriptures, called by the Jews Kethubim, i.e., "Writings." It consisted of five books, viz., Job, Proverbs, and Psalms, and the two books of Chronicles. The ancient Jews classified their sacred books as the Law, the Prophets, and the Kethubim, or Writings. (<see target="x-self">See </see>)

hail.d: frozen rain-drops; one of the plagues of Egypt (<reflink>Ex. 9:23</reflink>). It is mentioned by Haggai as a divine judgment (<reflink>Hag. 2:17</reflink>). A hail-storm destroyed the army of the Amorites when they fought against Joshua (<reflink>Josh. 10:11</reflink>). Ezekiel represents the wall daubed with untempered mortar as destroyed by great hail-stones (<reflink>Ezek. 13:11</reflink>). (<reflink>See also 38:22; Rev. 8:7; 11:19; 16:21.</reflink>)

hail!.d: a salutation expressive of a wish for the welfare of the person addressed; the translation of the Greek _Chaire_, "Rejoice" (<reflink>Luke 1:8</reflink>). Used in mockery in Matt. 27:29.

hair.d: (1.) The Egyptians let the hair of their head and beard grow only when they were in mourning, shaving it off at other times. "So particular were they on this point that to have neglected it was a subject of reproach and ridicule; and whenever they intended to convey the idea of a man of low condition, or a slovenly person, the artists represented him with a beard." Joseph shaved himself before going in to Pharoah (<reflink>Gen. 41:14</reflink>). The women of Egypt wore their hair long and plaited. Wigs were worn by priests and laymen to cover the shaven skull, and false beards were common. The great masses of hair seen in the portraits and statues of kings and priests are thus altogether artificial.

hakkoz.d: the thorn, the head of one of the courses of the priests (<reflink>1 Chr. 24:10</reflink>).

halah.d: a district of Media to which captive Israelites were transported by the Assyrian kings (<reflink>2 Kings 17:6; 18:11; 1 Chr. 5:26</reflink>). It lay along the banks of the upper Khabur, from its source to its junction with the Jerujer. Probably the district called by Ptolemy Chalcitis.

halak.d: smooth; bald, a hill at the southern extremity of Canaan (<reflink>Josh. 11:17</reflink>). It is referred to as if it were a landmark in that direction, being prominent and conspicuous from a distance. It has by some been identified with the modern Jebel el-Madura, on the south frontier of Judah, between the south end of the Dead Sea and the Wady Gaian.

halhul.d: full of hollows, a town in the highlands of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:58</reflink>). It is now a small village of the same name, and is situated about 5 miles north-east of Hebron on the way to Jerusalem. There is an old Jewish tradition that Gad, David's seer (<reflink>2 Sam. 24:11</reflink>), was buried here.

hall.d: (Gr. aule, Luke 22:55; R.V., "court"), the open court or quadrangle belonging to the high priest's house. In Matt. 26:69 and Mark 14:66 this word is incorrectly rendered "palace" in the Authorized Version, but correctly "court" in the Revised Version. In John 10:1,16 it means a "sheep-fold." In Matt. 27:27 and Mark 15:16 (A.V., "common hall;" R.V., "palace") it refers to the proetorium or residence of the Roman governor at Jerusalem. The "porch" in Matt. 26:71 is the entrance-hall or passage leading into the central court, which is open to the sky.

hallel.d: praise, the name given to the group of Psalms 113-118, which are preeminently psalms of praise. It is called "The Egyptian Hallel," because it was chanted in the temple whilst the Passover lambs were being slain. It was chanted also on other festival occasions, as at Pentecost, the feast of Tabernacles, and the feast of Dedication. The Levites, standing before the altar, chanted it verse by verse, the people responding by repeating the verses or by intoned hallelujahs. It was also chanted in private families at the feast of Passover. This was probably the hymn which our Saviour and his disciples sung at the conclusion of the Passover supper kept by them in the upper room at Jerusalem (<reflink>Matt. 26:30; Mark 14:26</reflink>).

hallelujah.d: praise ye Jehovah, frequently rendered "Praise ye the LORD," stands at the beginning of ten of the psalms (106, 111-113, 135, 146-150), hence called "hallelujah psalms." From its frequent occurrence it grew into a formula of praise. The Greek form of the word (alleluia) is found in Rev. 19:1, 3, 4, 6.

hallow.d: to render sacred, to consecrate (<reflink>Ex. 28:38; 29:1</reflink>). This word is from the Saxon, and properly means "to make holy." The name of God is "hallowed", i.e., is reverenced as holy (<reflink>Matt. 6:9</reflink>).

halt.d: lame on the feet (<reflink>Gen. 32:31; Ps. 38:17</reflink>). To "halt between two opinions" (<reflink>1 Kings 18:21</reflink>) is supposed by some to be an expression used in "allusion to birds, which hop from spray to spray, forwards and backwards." The LXX. render the expression "How long go ye lame on both knees?" The Hebrew verb rendered "halt" is used of the irregular dance ("leaped upon") around the altar (ver. 26). It indicates a lame, uncertain gait, going now in one direction, now in another, in the frenzy of wild leaping.

ham.d: warm, hot, and hence the south; also an Egyptian word meaning "black", the youngest son of Noah (<reflink>Gen. 5:32; comp. 9:22,24</reflink>). The curse pronounced by Noah against Ham, properly against Canaan his fourth son, was accomplished when the Jews subsequently exterminated the Canaanites.

haman.d: (of Persian origin), magnificent, the name of the vizier (i.e., the prime minister) of the Persian king Ahasuerus (<reflink>Esther 3:1, etc.</reflink>). He is called an "Agagite," which seems to denote that he was descended from the royal family of the Amalekites, the bitterest enemies of the Jews, as Agag was one of the titles of the Amalekite kings. He or his parents were brought to Persia as captives taken in war. He was hanged on the gallows which he had erected for Mordecai the Jew (<reflink>Esther 7:10</reflink>). (See ESTHER

hamath.d: fortress, the capital of one of the kingdoms of Upper Syria of the same name, on the Orontes, in the valley of Lebanon, at the northern boundary of Palestine (<reflink>Num. 13:21; 34:8</reflink>), at the foot of Hermon (<reflink>Josh. 13:5</reflink>) towards Damascus (<reflink>Zech. 9:2; Jer. 49:23</reflink>). It is called "Hamath the great" in Amos 6:2, and "Hamath-zobah" in 2 Chr. 8:3.

hamath-zobah.d: fortress of Zobah, (<reflink>2 Chr. 8:3</reflink>) is supposed by some to be a different place from the foregoing; but this is quite uncertain.

hammath.d: warm springs, one of the "fenced cities" of Naphtali (<reflink>Josh. 19:35</reflink>). It is identified with the warm baths (the heat of the water ranging from 136 degrees to 144 degrees) still found on the shore a little to the south of Tiberias under the name of Hummam Tabariyeh ("Bath of Tiberias").

hammedatha.d: father of Haman, designated usually "the Agagite" (<reflink>Esther 3:1, 10; 8:5</reflink>).

hammelech.d: the king's, the father of Jerahmeel, mentioned in Jer. 36:26. Some take this word as a common noun, "the king", and understand that Jerahmeel was Jehoiakim's son. Probably, however, it is to be taken as a proper name.

hammer.d: (1.) Heb. pattish, used by gold-beaters (<reflink>Isa. 41:7</reflink>) and by quarry-men (<reflink>Jer. 23:29</reflink>). Metaphorically of Babylon (<reflink>Jer. 50:23</reflink>) or Nebuchadnezzar.

hammoleketh.d: the queen, the daughter of Machir and sister of Gilead (<reflink>1 Chr. 7:17, 18</reflink>). Abiezer was one of her three children.

hammon.d: warm springs. (1.) A town in the tribe of Asher, near Zidon (<reflink>Josh. 19:28</reflink>), identified with 'Ain Hamul.

hammoth-dor.d: warm springs, a Levitical city of Naphtali (<reflink>Josh. 21:32</reflink>); probably Hammath in 19:35.

hamon-gog.d: multitude of Gog, the name of the valley in which the slaughtered forces of Gog are to be buried (<reflink>Ezek. 39:11,15</reflink>), "the valley of the passengers on the east of the sea."

hamonah.d: multitude, a name figuratively assigned to the place in which the slaughter and burial of the forces of Gog were to take place (<reflink>Ezek. 39:16</reflink>).

hamor.d: he-ass, a Hivite from whom Jacob purchased the plot of ground in which Joseph was afterwards buried (<reflink>Gen. 33:19</reflink>). He is called "Emmor" in Acts 7:16. His son Shechem founded the city of that name which Simeon and Levi destroyed because of his crime in the matter of Dinah, Jacob's daughter (<reflink>Gen. 34:20</reflink>). Hamor and Shechem were also slain (ver. 26).

hamul.d: spared, one of the sons of Pharez, son of Judah (<reflink>1 Chr. 2:5</reflink>). His descendants are called Hamulites (<reflink>Num. 26:21</reflink>).

hamutal.d: kinsman of the dew, the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah, wife of king Josiah, and mother of king Jehoahaz (<reflink>2 Kings 23:31</reflink>), also of king Zedekiah (<reflink>2 Kings 24:18</reflink>).

hanameel.d: whom God has graciously given, the cousin of Jeremiah, to whom he sold the field he possessed in Anathoth, before the siege of Jerusalem (<reflink>Jer. 32:6-12</reflink>).

hanan.d: merciful. (1.) A Benjamite (<reflink>1 Chr. 8:23</reflink>). (2.) One of David's heroes (<reflink>1 Chr. 11:43</reflink>). (3.) Jer. 35:4. (4.) A descendant of Saul (<reflink>1 Chr. 8:38</reflink>). (5.) One of the Nethinim (<reflink>Ezra 2:46</reflink>). (6.) One of the Levites who assisted Ezra (<reflink>Neh. 8:7</reflink>). (7.) One of the chiefs who subscribed the covenant (<reflink>Neh. 10:22</reflink>).

hananeel.d: God has graciously given, a tower in the wall of Jerusalem (<reflink>Neh. 3:1; 12:39</reflink>). It is mentioned also in Jer. 31:38; Zech. 14:10.

hanani.d: God has gratified me, or is gracious. (1.) One of the sons of Heman (<reflink>1 Chr. 25:4, 25</reflink>). (2.) A prophet who was sent to rebuke king Asa for entering into a league with Benhadad I., king of Syria, against Judah (<reflink>2 Chr. 16:1-10</reflink>). He was probably the father of the prophet Jehu (<reflink>1 Kings 16:7</reflink>). (3.) Probably a brother of Nehemiah (<reflink>Neh. 1:2; 7:2</reflink>), who reported to him the melancholy condition of Jerusalem. Nehemiah afterwards appointed him to have charge of the city gates.

hananiah.d: Jehovah has given. (1.) A chief of the tribe of Benjamin (<reflink>1 Chr. 8:24</reflink>). (2.) One of the sons of Heman (<reflink>1 Chr. 25:4,23</reflink>). (3.) One of Uzziah's military officers (<reflink>2 Chr. 26:11</reflink>). (4.) Grandfather of the captain who arrested Jeremiah (<reflink>Jer. 37:13</reflink>). (5.) Jer. 36:12. (6.) Neh. 10:23. (7.) Shadrach, one of the "three Hebrew children" (Dan. 1; 6:7). (8.) Son of Zerubbabel (<reflink>1 Chr. 3:19, 21</reflink>). (9.) Ezra 10:28. (10.) The "ruler of the palace; he was a faithful man, and feared God above many" (<reflink>Neh. 7:2</reflink>). (11.) Neh. 3:8. (12.) Neh. 3:30 (13.) A priest, son of Jeremiah (<reflink>Neh. 12:12</reflink>). (14.) A false prophet contemporary with Jeremiah (28:3, 17).

hand.d: Called by Galen "the instrument of instruments." It is the symbol of human action (<reflink>Ps. 9:16; Job 9:30; Isa. 1:15; 1 Tim. 2:8</reflink>). Washing the hands was a symbol of innocence (<reflink>Ps. 26:6; 73:13; Matt. 27:24</reflink>), also of sanctification (<reflink>1 Cor. 6:11; Isa. 51:16; Ps. 24:3, 4</reflink>). In Ps. 77:2 the correct rendering is, as in the Revised Version, "My hand was stretched out," etc., instead of, as in the Authorized Version, "My sore ran in the night," etc.

handbreadth.d: a measure of four fingers, equal to about four inches (<reflink>Ex. 25:25; 37:12; Ps. 39:5, etc.</reflink>).

handkerchief.d: Only once in Authorized Version (<reflink>Acts 19:12</reflink>). The Greek word (sudarion) so rendered means properly "a sweat-cloth." It is rendered "napkin" in John 11:44; 20:7; Luke 19:20.

handmaid.d: servant (<reflink>Gen. 16:1; Ruth 3:9; Luke 1:48</reflink>). It is probable that Hagar was Sarah's personal attendant while she was in the house of Pharaoh, and was among those maid-servants whom Abram had brought from Egypt.

handwriting.d: (<reflink>Col. 2:14</reflink>). The "blotting out the handwriting" is the removal by the grace of the gospel of the condemnation of the law which we had broken.

hanes.d: a place in Egypt mentioned only in Isa. 30:4 in connection with a reproof given to the Jews for trusting in Egypt. It was considered the same as Tahpanhes, a fortified town on the eastern frontier, but has been also identified as Ahnas-el-Medeeneh, 70 miles from Cairo.

hanging.d: (as a punishment), a mark of infamy inflicted on the dead bodies of criminals (<reflink>Deut. 21:23</reflink>) rather than our modern mode of punishment. Criminals were first strangled and then hanged (<reflink>Nu. 25:4; Deut. 21:22</reflink>). (See 2 Sam. 21:6 for the practice of the Gibeonites.)

hannah.d: favour, grace, one of the wives of Elkanah the Levite, and the mother of Samuel (1 Sam. 1; 2). Her home was at Ramathaim-zophim, whence she was wont every year to go to Shiloh, where the tabernacle had been pitched by Joshua, to attend the offering of sacrifices there according to the law (<reflink>Ex. 23:15; 34:18; Deut. 16:16</reflink>), probably at the feast of the Passover (<reflink>comp. Ex. 13:10</reflink>). On occasion of one of these "yearly" visits, being grieved by reason of Peninnah's conduct toward her, she went forth alone, and kneeling before the Lord at the sanctuary she prayed inaudibly. Eli the high priest, who sat at the entrance to the holy place, observed her, and misunderstanding her character he harshly condemned her conduct (<reflink>1 Sam. 1:14-16</reflink>). After hearing her explanation he retracted his injurious charge and said to her, "Go in peace: and the God of Israel grant thee thy petition." Perhaps the story of the wife of Manoah was not unknown to her.

hanniel.d: grace of God. (1.) A chief of the tribe of Manasseh (<reflink>Num. 34:23</reflink>). (2.) A chief of the tribe of Asher (<reflink>1 Chr. 7:39</reflink>).

hanun.d: graciously given. (1.) The son and successor of Nahash, king of Moab. David's messengers, sent on an embassy of condolence to him to Rabbah Ammon, his capital, were so grossly insulted that he proclaimed war against Hanun. David's army, under the command of Joab, forthwith crossed the Jordan, and gained a complete victory over the Moabites and their allies (<reflink>2 Sam. 10:1-14</reflink>) at Medeba (q.v.).

hara.d: mountainous land, a province of Assyria (<reflink>1 Chr. 5:26</reflink>), between the Tigris and the Euphrates, along the banks of the Khabur, to which some of the Israelite captives were carried. It has not been identified. Some think the word a variation of Haran.

haradah.d: fright; fear, the twenty-fifth station of the Israelites in their wanderings (<reflink>Num. 33:24</reflink>).

haran.d: (1.) Heb. haran; i.e., "mountaineer." The eldest son of Terah, brother of Abraham and Nahor, and father of Lot, Milcah, and Iscah. He died before his father (<reflink>Gen. 11:27</reflink>), in Ur of the Chaldees.

harbona.d: (a Persian word meaning "ass-driver"), one of the seven eunuchs or chamberlains of king Ahasuerus (<reflink>Esther 1:10; 7:9</reflink>).

hare.d: (Heb. 'arnebeth) was prohibited as food according to the Mosaic law (<reflink>Lev. 11:6; Deut. 14:7</reflink>), "because he cheweth the cud, but divideth not the hoof." The habit of this animal is to grind its teeth and move its jaw as if it actually chewed the cud. But, like the cony (q.v.), it is not a ruminant with four stomachs, but a rodent like the squirrel, rat, etc. Moses speaks of it according to appearance. It is interdicted because, though apparently chewing the cud, it did not divide the hoof.

hareth.d: thicket, a wood in the mountains of Judah where David hid when pursued by Saul (<reflink>1 Sam. 22:5</reflink>). It was possibly while he was here that the memorable incident narrated in 2 Sam. 23:14-17, 1 Chr. 11:16-19 occurred. This place has not been identified, but perhaps it may be the modern Kharas, on the borders of the chain of mountains some 3 miles east of Keilah.

harhaiah.d: zeal of Jehovah, (<reflink>Neh. 3:8</reflink>) "of the goldsmiths," one whose son helped to repair the wall of Jerusalem.

harim.d: flat-nosed. (1.) The head of the second course of priests (<reflink>1 Chr. 24:8</reflink>). (2.) Ezra 2:32, 39; Neh. 7:35, 42. (3.) Neh. 3:11. (4.) 12:3. (5.) 10:5

harlot.d: (1.) Heb. zonah (<reflink>Gen. 34:31; 38:15</reflink>). In verses 21, 22 the Hebrew word used in _kedeshah_, i.e., a woman consecrated or devoted to prostitution in connection with the abominable worship of Asherah or Astarte, the Syrian Venus. This word is also used in Deut. 23:17; Hos. 4:14. Thus Tamar sat by the wayside as a consecrated kedeshah.

harnepher.d: a chief of the tribe of Asher (<reflink>1 Chr. 7:36</reflink>).

harness.d: (1.) Heb. 'asar, "to bind;" hence the act of fastening animals to a cart (<reflink>1 Sam. 6:7, 10; Jer. 46:4, etc.</reflink>).

harod.d: palpitation, a fountain near which Gideon and his army encamped on the morning of the day when they encountered and routed the Midianites (Judg. 7). It was south of the hill Moreh. The present 'Ain Jalud ("Goliath's Fountain"), south of Jezreel and nearly opposite Shunem, is probably the fountain here referred to (7:4, 5).

harodite.d: an epithet applied to two of David's heroes (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:25</reflink>). (Comp. 1 Chr. 11:27.)

harosheth of the gentiles.d: (<reflink>Judg. 4:2</reflink>) or nations, a city near Hazor in Galilee of the Gentiles, or Upper Galilee, in the north of Palestine. It was here that Jabin's great army was marshalled before it went forth into the great battlefield of Esdraelon to encounter the army of Israel, by which it was routed and put to flight (Judg. 4). It was situated "at the entrance of the pass to Esdraelon from the plain of Acre" at the base of Carmel. The name in the Hebrew is _Harosheth ha Gojim_, i.e., "the smithy of the nations;" probably, as is supposed, so called because here Jabin's iron war-chariots, armed with scythes, were made. It is identified with el-Harithiyeh.

harp.d: (Heb. kinnor), the national instrument of the Hebrews. It was invented by Jubal (<reflink>Gen. 4:21</reflink>). Some think the word _kinnor_ denotes the whole class of stringed instruments. It was used as an accompaniment to songs of cheerfulness as well as of praise to God (<reflink>Gen. 31:27; 1 Sam. 16:23; 2 Chr. 20:28; Ps. 33:2; 137:2</reflink>).

harrow.d: (Heb. harits), a tribulum or sharp threshing sledge; a frame armed on the under side with rollers or sharp spikes (<reflink>2 Sam. 12:31; 1 Chr. 20:3</reflink>).

harsha.d: worker or enchanter, one of the Nethinim (<reflink>Ezra 2:52; Neh. 7:54</reflink>).

hart.d: (Heb. 'ayal), a stag or male deer. It is ranked among the clean animals (<reflink>Deut. 12:15; 14:5; 15:22</reflink>), and was commonly killed for food (<reflink>1 Kings 4:23</reflink>). The hart is frequently alluded to in the poetical and prophetical books (<reflink>Isa. 35:6; Cant. 2:8, 9; Lam. 1:6; Ps. 42:1</reflink>).

harum.d: elevated, (<reflink>1 Chr. 4:8</reflink>), a descendant of Judah.

haruphite.d: a native of Hariph; an epithet given to Shephatiah, one of those who joined David at Ziklag (<reflink>1 Chr. 12:5</reflink>).

haruz.d: eager, the father of Meshullemeth, the wife of king Manasseh (<reflink>2 Kings 21:19</reflink>) and mother of king Amon.

helkath.d: smoothness, a town of Asher, on the east border (<reflink>Josh. 19:25; 21:31</reflink>); called also Hukok (<reflink>1 Chr. 6:75</reflink>).

helkath-hazzurim.d: plot of the sharp blades, or the field of heroes, (<reflink>2 Sam. 2:16</reflink>). After the battle of Gilboa, so fatal to Saul and his house, David, as divinely directed, took up his residence in Hebron, and was there anointed king over Judah. Among the fugitives from Gilboa was Ish-bosheth, the only surviving son of Saul, whom Abner, Saul's uncle, took across the Jordan to Mahanaim, and there had him proclaimed king. Abner gathered all the forces at his command and marched to Gibeon, with the object of wresting Judah from David. Joab had the command of David's army of trained men, who encamped on the south of the pool, which was on the east of the hill on which the town of Gibeon was built, while Abner's army lay on the north of the pool. Abner proposed that the conflict should be decided by twelve young men engaging in personal combat on either side. …

hell.d: derived from the Saxon helan, to cover; hence the covered or the invisible place. In Scripture there are three words so rendered:

helmet.d: (Heb. kob'a), a cap for the defence of the head (<reflink>1 Sam. 17:5, 38</reflink>). In the New Testament the Greek equivalent is used (<reflink>Eph. 6:17; 1 Thess. 5:8</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See ARMS.</see>)

helon.d: strong, father of Eliab, who was "captain of the children of Zebulun" (<reflink>Num. 1:9; 2:7</reflink>).

help-meet.d: (Heb. 'ezer ke-negdo; i.e., "a help as his counterpart" = a help suitable to him), a wife (<reflink>Gen. 2:18-20</reflink>).

helps.d: (<reflink>1 Cor. 12:28</reflink>) may refer to help (i.e., by interpretation) given to him who speaks with tongues, or more probably simply help which Christians can render to one another, such as caring for the poor and needy, etc.

hem.d: of a garment, the fringe of a garment. The Jews attached much importance to these, because of the regulations in Num. 15:38, 39. These borders or fringes were in process of time enlarged so as to attract special notice (<reflink>Matt. 23:5</reflink>). The hem of Christ's garment touched (9:20; 14:36; Luke 8:44).

heman.d: faithful. (1.) 1 Kings 4:31; 1 Chr. 2:6, a son of Zerah, noted for his wisdom. (2.) Grandson of Samuel (<reflink>1 Chr. 6:33; 15:17</reflink>), to whom the 88th Psalm probably was inscribed. He was one of the "seers" named in 2 Chr. 29:14, 30, and took a leading part in the administration of the sacred services.

hemath.d: a Kenite (<reflink>1 Chr. 2:55</reflink>), the father of the house of Rechab.

hemlock.d: (1.) Heb. rosh (<reflink>Hos. 10:4; rendered "gall" in Deut. 29:18; 32:32; Ps. 69:21; Jer. 9:15; 23:15; "poison," Job 20:16; "venom," Deut. 32:33</reflink>). "Rosh is the name of some poisonous plant which grows quickly and luxuriantly; of a bitter taste, and therefore coupled with wormwood (<reflink>Deut. 29:18; Lam. 3:19</reflink>). Hence it would seem to be not the hemlock cicuta, nor the colocynth or wild gourd, nor lolium darnel, but the poppy so called from its heads" (Gesenius, Lex.).

hen.d: common in later times among the Jews in Palestine (<reflink>Matt. 23:37; Luke 13:34</reflink>). It is noticeable that this familiar bird is only mentioned in these passages in connection with our Lord's lamentation over the impenitence of Jerusalem.

hena.d: one of the cities of Mesopotamia destroyed by sennacherib (<reflink>2 Kings 18:34; 19:13</reflink>). It is identified with the modern Anah, lying on the right bank of the Euphrates, not far from Sepharvaim.

henadad.d: favour of Hadad, the name of a Levite after the Captivity (<reflink>Ezra 3:9</reflink>).

hepher.d: a well or stream. (1.) A royal city of the Canaanites taken by Joshua (12:17).

hephzibah.d: my delight is in her. (1.) The wife of Hezekiah and mother of king Manasseh (<reflink>2 Kings 21:1</reflink>).

herb.d: (1.) Heb. 'eseb, any green plant; herbage (<reflink>Gen. 1:11, 12, 29, 30; 2:5; 3:18, etc.</reflink>); comprehending vegetables and all green herbage (<reflink>Amos 7:1, 2</reflink>).

herdsman.d: In Egypt herdsmen were probably of the lowest caste. Some of Joseph's brethren were made rulers over Pharaoh's cattle (<reflink>Gen. 47:6, 17</reflink>). The Israelites were known in Egypt as "keepers of cattle;" and when they left it they took their flocks and herds with them (<reflink>Ex. 12:38</reflink>). Both David and Saul came from "following the herd" to occupy the throne (1 Sam. 9; 11:5; Ps. 78:70). David's herd-masters were among his chief officers of state. The daughters also of wealthy chiefs were wont to tend the flocks of the family (<reflink>Gen. 29:9; Ex. 2:16</reflink>). The "chief of the herdsmen" was in the time of the monarchy an officer of high rank (<reflink>1 Sam. 21:7; comp. 1 Chr. 27:29</reflink>). The herdsmen lived in tents (<reflink>Isa. 38:12; Jer. 6:3</reflink>); and there were folds for the cattle (<reflink>Num. 32:16</reflink>), and watch-towers for the herdsmen, that he might therefrom observe any coming danger (<reflink>Micah 4:8; Nah. 3:8</reflink>).

heres.d: sun. (1.) "Mount Heres" (<reflink>Judg. 1:35</reflink>), Heb. Har-heres, i.e., "sun-mountain;" probably identical with Irshemesh in Josh. 19:41.

heresy.d: from a Greek word signifying (1) a choice, (2) the opinion chosen, and (3) the sect holding the opinion. In the Acts of the Apostles (5:17; 15:5; 24:5, 14; 26:5) it denotes a sect, without reference to its character. Elsewhere, however, in the New Testament it has a different meaning attached to it. Paul ranks "heresies" with crimes and seditions (<reflink>Gal. 5:20</reflink>). This word also denotes divisions or schisms in the church (<reflink>1 Cor. 11:19</reflink>). In Titus 3:10 a "heretical person" is one who follows his own self-willed "questions," and who is to be avoided. Heresies thus came to signify self-chosen doctrines not emanating from God (<reflink>2 Pet. 2:1</reflink>).

hermas.d: Mercury, a Roman Christian to whom Paul sends greetings (<reflink>Rom. 16: 14</reflink>). Some suppose him to have been the author of the celebrated religious romance called The Shepherd, but it is very probable that that work is the production of a later generation.

hermogenes.d: Mercury-born, at one time Paul's fellow-labourer in Asia Minor, who, however, afterwards abandoned him, along with one Phygellus, probably on account of the perils by which they were beset (<reflink>2 Tim. 1:15</reflink>).

hermon.d: a peak, the eastern prolongation of the Anti-Lebanon range, reaching to the height of about 9,200 feet above the Mediterranean. It marks the north boundary of Palestine (<reflink>Deut. 3:8, 4:48; Josh. 11:3, 17; 13:11; 12:1</reflink>), and is seen from a great distance. It is about 40 miles north of the Sea of Galilee. It is called "the Hermonites" (<reflink>Ps. 42:6</reflink>) because it has more than one summit. The Sidonians called it Sirion, and the Amorites Shenir (<reflink>Deut. 3:9; Cant. 4:8</reflink>). It is also called Baal-hermon (<reflink>Judg. 3:3; 1 Chr. 5:23</reflink>) and Sion (<reflink>Deut. 4:48</reflink>).
