There is every probability that one of its three summits was the scene of the transfiguration (q.v.). The "dew of Hermon" is referred to (<reflink>Ps. 89: 12</reflink>). Its modern name is Jebel-esh-Sheikh, "the chief mountain." It is one of the most conspicuous mountains in Palestine or Syria. …

hermonites, the.d: (<reflink>Ps. 42:6, 7</reflink>) = "the Hermons", i.e., the three peaks or summits of Hermon, which are about a quarter of a mile apart.

herod agrippa i.d: son of Aristobulus and Bernice, and grandson of Herod the Great. He was made tetrarch of the provinces formerly held by Lysanias II., and ultimately possessed the entire kingdom of his grandfather, Herod the Great, with the title of king. He put the apostle James the elder to death, and cast Peter into prison (<reflink>Luke 3:1; Acts 12:1-19</reflink>). On the second day of a festival held in honour of the emperor Claudius, he appeared in the great theatre of Caesarea. "The king came in clothed in magnificent robes, of which silver was the costly brilliant material. It was early in the day, and the sun's rays fell on the king, so that the eyes of the beholders were dazzled with the brightness which surrounded him. Voices here and there from the crowd exclaimed that it was the apparition of something divine. …

herod antipas.d: Herod's son by Malthace (<reflink>Matt. 14:1; Luke 3:1, 19; 9:7; Acts 13:1</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See ANTIPAS.</see>)

herod arippa ii.d: the son of Herod Agrippa I. and Cypros. The emperor Claudius made him tetrarch of the provinces of Philip and Lysanias, with the title of king (<reflink>Acts 25:13; 26:2, 7</reflink>). He enlarged the city of Caesarea Philippi, and called it Neronias, in honour of Nero. It was before him and his sister that Paul made his defence at Caesarea (<reflink>Acts 25:12-27</reflink>). He died at Rome A.D. 100, in the third year of the emperor Trajan.

herod philip i.d: (<reflink>Mark 6:17</reflink>), the son of Herod the Great by Mariamne, the daughter of Simon, the high priest. He is distinguished from another Philip called "the tetrarch." He lived at Rome as a private person with his wife Herodias and his daughter Salome.

herod philip ii.d: the son of Herod the Great and Cleopatra of Jerusalem. He was "tetrarch" of Batanea, Iturea, Trachonitis, and Auranitis. He rebuilt the city of Caesarea Philippi, calling it by his own name to distinguish it from the Caesarea on the sea-coast which was the seat of the Roman government. He married Salome, the daughter of Herodias (<reflink>Matt. 16:13; Mark 8:27; Luke 3:1</reflink>).

herod the great.d: (<reflink>Matt. 2:1-22; Luke 1:5; Acts 23:35</reflink>), the son of Antipater, an Idumaean, and Cypros, an Arabian of noble descent. In the year B.C. 47 Julius Caesar made Antipater, a "wily Idumaean," procurator of Judea, who divided his territories between his four sons, Galilee falling to the lot of Herod, who was afterwards appointed tetrarch of Judea by Mark Antony (B.C. 40), and also king of Judea by the Roman senate.

herodians.d: a Jewish political party who sympathized with (<reflink>Mark 3:6; 12:13; Matt, 22:16; Luke 20:20</reflink>) the Herodian rulers in their general policy of government, and in the social customs which they introduced from Rome. They were at one with the Sadducees in holding the duty of submission to Rome, and of supporting the Herods on the throne. (<reflink>Comp. Mark 8:15; Matt. 16:6.</reflink>)

herodias.d: (<reflink>Matt. 14:3-11; Mark 6:17-28; Luke 3:19</reflink>), the daughter of Aristobulus and Bernice. While residing at Rome with her husband Herod Philip I. and her daughter, Herod Antipas fell in with her during one of his journeys to that city. She consented to leave her husband and become his wife. Some time after, Herod met John the Baptist, who boldly declared the marriage to be unlawful. For this he was "cast into prison," in the castle probably of Machaerus (q.v.), and was there subsequently beheaded.

herodion.d: a Christian at Rome whom Paul salutes and calls his "kinsman" (<reflink>Rom. 16:11</reflink>).

heron.d: (<reflink>Lev. 11:19; Deut. 14:18</reflink>), ranked among the unclean birds. The Hebrew name is _'anaphah_, and indicates that the bird so named is remarkable for its angry disposition. "The herons are wading-birds, peculiarly irritable, remarkable for their voracity, frequenting marshes and oozy rivers, and spread over the regions of the East." The Ardea russeta, or little golden egret, is the commonest species in Asia.

heshbon.d: intelligence, a city ruled over by Sihon, king of the Amorites (<reflink>Josh. 3:10; 13:17</reflink>). It was taken by Moses (<reflink>Num. 21:23-26</reflink>), and became afterwards a Levitical city (<reflink>Josh. 21:39</reflink>) in the tribe of Reuben (<reflink>Num. 32:37</reflink>). After the Exile it was taken possession of by the Moabites (<reflink>Isa. 15:4; Jer. 48:2, 34, 45</reflink>). The ruins of this town are still seen about 20 miles east of Jordan from the north end of the Dead Sea. There are reservoirs in this district, which are probably the "fishpools" referred to in Cant. 7:4.

heshmon.d: fatness, a town in the south of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:27</reflink>).

heth.d: dread, a descendant of Canaan, and the ancestor of the Hittites (<reflink>Gen. 10:18; Deut. 7:1</reflink>), who dwelt in the vicinity of Hebron (<reflink>Gen. 23:3, 7</reflink>). The Hittites were a Hamitic race. They are called "the sons of Heth" (<reflink>Gen. 23:3, 5, 7, 10, 16, 18, 20</reflink>).

hethlon.d: wrapped up, a place on the north border of Palestine. The "way of Hethlon" (<reflink>Ezek. 47:15; 48:1</reflink>) is probably the pass at the end of Lebanon from the Mediterranean to the great plain of Hamath (q.v.), or the "entrance of Hamath."

hezekiah.d: whom Jehovah has strengthened. (1.) Son of Ahaz (<reflink>2 Kings 18:1; 2 Chr. 29:1</reflink>), whom he succeeded on the throne of the kingdom of Judah. He reigned twenty-nine years (B.C. 726-697). The history of this king is contained in 2 Kings 18:20, Isa. 36-39, and 2 Chr. 29-32. He is spoken of as a great and good king. In public life he followed the example of his great-granfather Uzziah. He set himself to abolish idolatry from his kingdom, and among other things which he did for this end, he destroyed the "brazen serpent," which had been removed to Jerusalem, and had become an object of idolatrous worship (<reflink>Num. 21:9</reflink>). A great reformation was wrought in the kingdom of Judah in his day (<reflink>2 Kings 18:4; 2 Chr. 29:3-36</reflink>).

hezion.d: vision, the father of Tabrimon, and grandfather of Ben-hadad, king of Syria (<reflink>1 Kings 15:18</reflink>).

hazeroth.d: fenced enclosures consisting of "a low wall of stones in which thick bundles of thorny acacia are inserted, the tangled branches and long needle-like spikes forming a perfectly impenetrable hedge around the encampment" of tents and cattle which they sheltered. Such like enclosures abound in the wilderness of Paran, which the Israelites entered after leaving Sinai (<reflink>Num. 11:35; 12:16; 33:17, 18</reflink>). This third encampment of the Israelites has been identified with the modern 'Ain el-Hudhera, some 40 miles north-east of Sinai. Here Miriam (q.v.), being displeased that Moses had married a Cushite wife (<reflink>Num. 12:1</reflink>), induced Aaron to join with her in rebelling against Moses. God vindicated the authority of his "servant Moses," and Miriam was smitten with leprosy. Moses interceded for her, and she was healed (<reflink>Num. 12:4-16</reflink>). From this encampment the Israelites marched northward across the plateau of et-Tih, and at length reached KADESH.

hazezon-tamar.d: pruning of the palm, the original name of the place afterwards called ENGEDI (q.v.), Gen. 14:7; called also HAZAZON-TAMAR (<reflink>2 Chr. 20:2</reflink>).

hazo.d: vision, one of the sons of Nahor (<reflink>Gen. 22:22</reflink>).

hazor.d: enclosed; fortified. (1.) A stronghold of the Canaanites in the mountains north of Lake Merom (<reflink>Josh. 11:1-5</reflink>). Jabin the king with his allied tribes here encountered Joshua in a great battle. Joshua gained a signal victory, which virtually completed his conquest of Canaan (11:10-13). This city was, however, afterwards rebuilt by the Canaanites, and was ruled by a king with the same hereditary name of Jabin. His army, under a noted leader of the name of Sisera, swept down upon the south, aiming at the complete subjugation of the country. This powerful army was met by the Israelites under Barak, who went forth by the advice of the prophetess Deborah. The result was one of the most remarkable victories for Israel recorded in the Old Testament (<reflink>Josh. 19:36; Judg. 4:2; 1 Sam. 12:9</reflink>). The city of Hazor was taken and occupied by the Israelites. It was fortified by Solomon to defend the entrance into the kingdom from Syria and Assyria. …

hazor-hadattah.d: New Hazor, a city in the south of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:25</reflink>). It is probably identified with the ruins of el-Hazzarah, near Beit Jebrin.

he-ass.d: Heb. hamor, (<reflink>Gen. 12:16</reflink>), the general designation of the donkey used for carrying burdens (<reflink>Gen. 42:26</reflink>) and for ploughing (<reflink>Isa. 30:24</reflink>). It is described in Gen. 49:14, 2 Sam. 19:26. (See ASS

head-bands.d: (Heb. kishshurim), properly girdles or belts for the waist (<reflink>Isa. 3:20, R.V., "sashes;" Jer. 2:32, rendered "attire", i.e., a girdle round the waist</reflink>).

head-dress.d: Not in common use among the Hebrews. It is first mentioned in Ex. 28:40 (A.V., "bonnets;" R.V., "head-tires"). It was used especially for purposes of ornament (<reflink>Job 29:14; Isa. 3:23; 62:3</reflink>). The Hebrew word here used, _tsaniph_, properly means a turban, folds of linen wound round the head. The Hebrew word _peer_, used in Isa. 61:3, there rendered "beauty" (A.V.) and "garland" (R.V.), is a head-dress or turban worn by females (<reflink>Isa. 3: 20, "bonnets"</reflink>), priests (<reflink>Ex. 39:28</reflink>), a bridegroom (<reflink>Isa. 61:10, "ornament;" R.V., "garland"</reflink>). Ezek. 16:10 and Jonah 2:5 are to be understood of the turban wrapped round the head. The Hebrew _shebisim_ (<reflink>Isa. 3:18</reflink>), in the Authorized Version rendered "cauls," and marg. "networks," denotes probably a kind of netted head-dress. The "horn" (Heb. keren) mentioned in 1 Sam. 2:1 is the head-dress called by the Druses of Mount Lebanon the tantura.

heap.d: When Joshua took the city of Ai (Josh. 8), he burned it and "made it an heap [Heb. tel] for ever" (8:28). The ruins of this city were for a long time sought for in vain. It has been at length, however, identified with the mound which simply bears the name of "Tel." "There are many Tels in modern Palestine, that land of Tels, each Tel with some other name attached to it to mark the former site. But the site of Ai has no other name 'unto this day.' It is simply et-Tel, 'the heap' par excellence."

heart.d: According to the Bible, the heart is the centre not only of spiritual activity, but of all the operations of human life. "Heart" and "soul" are often used interchangeably (<reflink>Deut. 6:5; 26:16; comp. Matt. 22:37; Mark 12:30, 33</reflink>), but this is not generally the case.

hearth.d: Heb. ah (<reflink>Jer. 36:22, 23; R.V., "brazier"</reflink>), meaning a large pot like a brazier, a portable furnace in which fire was kept in the king's winter apartment.

heath.d: Heb. 'arar, (<reflink>Jer. 17:6; 48:6</reflink>), a species of juniper called by the Arabs by the same name ('arar), the Juniperus sabina or savin. "Its gloomy, stunted appearance, with its scale-like leaves pressed close to its gnarled stem, and cropped close by the wild goats, as it clings to the rocks about Petra, gives great force to the contrast suggested by the prophet, between him that trusteth in man, naked and destitute, and the man that trusteth in the Lord, flourishing as a tree planted by the waters" (Tristram, Natural History of the Bible).

heathen.d: (Heb. plural goyum). At first the word _goyim_ denoted generally all the nations of the world (<reflink>Gen. 18:18; comp. Gal. 3:8</reflink>). The Jews afterwards became a people distinguished in a marked manner from the other _goyim_. They were a separate people (<reflink>Lev. 20:23; 26:14-45; Deut. 28</reflink>), and the other nations, the Amorites, Hittites, etc., were the _goyim_, the heathen, with whom the Jews were forbidden to be associated in any way (<reflink>Josh. 23:7; 1 Kings 11:2</reflink>). The practice of idolatry was the characteristic of these nations, and hence the word came to designate idolaters (<reflink>Ps. 106:47; Jer. 46:28; Lam. 1:3; Isa. 36:18</reflink>), the wicked (<reflink>Ps. 9:5, 15, 17</reflink>).

heave offering.d: Heb. terumah, (<reflink>Ex. 29:27</reflink>) means simply an offering, a present, including all the offerings made by the Israelites as a present. This Hebrew word is frequently employed. Some of the rabbis attach to the word the meaning of elevation, and refer it to the heave offering, which consisted in presenting the offering by a motion up and down, distinguished from the wave offering, which consisted in a repeated movement in a horizontal direction, a "wave offering to the Lord as ruler of earth, a heave offering to the Lord as ruler of heaven." The right shoulder, which fell to the priests in presenting thank offerings, was called the heave shoulder (<reflink>Lev. 7:34; Num. 6:20</reflink>). The first fruits offered in harvest-time (<reflink>Num. 15:20, 21</reflink>) were heave offerings.

heaven.d: (1.) Definitions. The phrase "heaven and earth" is used to indicate the whole universe (<reflink>Gen. 1:1; Jer. 23:24; Acts 17:24</reflink>). According to the Jewish notion there were three heavens,

heber.d: passing over. (1.) Son of Beriah and grandson of Asher (<reflink>Gen. 46:17; 1 Chr. 7:31, 32</reflink>).

hebrew.d: a name applied to the Israelites in Scripture only by one who is a foreigner (<reflink>Gen. 39:14, 17; 41:12, etc.</reflink>), or by the Israelites when they speak of themselves to foreigners (40:15; Ex. 1:19), or when spoken of an contrasted with other peoples (<reflink>Gen. 43:32; Ex. 1:3, 7, 15; Deut. 15:12</reflink>). In the New Testament there is the same contrast between Hebrews and foreigners (<reflink>Acts 6:1; Phil. 3:5</reflink>).

hebrew language.d: the language of the Hebrew nation, and that in which the Old Testament is written, with the exception of a few portions in Chaldee. In the Old Testament it is only spoken of as "Jewish" (<reflink>2 Kings 18:26, 28; Isa. 36:11, 13; 2 Chr 32:18</reflink>). This name is first used by the Jews in times subsequent to the close of the Old Testament.

hebrew of the hebrews.d: one whose parents are both Hebrews (<reflink>Phil. 3:5; 2 Cor. 11:22</reflink>); a genuine Hebrew.

hebrews.d: (<reflink>Acts 6:1</reflink>) were the Hebrew-speaking Jews, as distinguished from those who spoke Greek. (<see target="x-self">See GREEKS.</see>)

hebrews, epistle to.d: (1.) Its canonicity. All the results of critical and historical research to which this epistle has been specially subjected abundantly vindicate its right to a place in the New Testament canon among the other inspired books.

hebron.d: a community; alliance. (1.) A city in the south end of the valley of Eshcol, about midway between Jerusalem and Beersheba, from which it is distant about 20 miles in a straight line. It was built "seven years before Zoan in Egypt" (<reflink>Gen. 13:18; Num. 13:22</reflink>). It still exists under the same name, and is one of the most ancient cities in the world. Its earlier name was Kirjath-arba (<reflink>Gen. 23:2; Josh. 14:15; 15:3</reflink>). But "Hebron would appear to have been the original name of the city, and it was not till after Abraham's stay there that it received the name Kirjath-arba, who [i.e., Arba] was not the founder but the conqueror of the city, having led thither the tribe of the Anakim, to which he belonged. It retained this name till it came into the possession of Caleb, when the Israelites restored the original name Hebron" (Keil, Com.). The name of this city does not occur in any of the prophets or in the New Testament. It is found about forty times in the Old.

hegai.d: eunuch, had charge of the harem of Ahasuerus (<reflink>Esther 2:8</reflink>).

heifer.d: Heb. 'eglah, (<reflink>Deut. 21:4, 6; Jer. 46:20</reflink>). Untrained to the yoke (<reflink>Hos. 10:11</reflink>); giving milk (<reflink>Isa. 7:21</reflink>); ploughing (<reflink>Judg. 14:18</reflink>); treading out grain (<reflink>Jer. 50:11</reflink>); unsubdued to the yoke an emblem of Judah (<reflink>Isa. 15:5; Jer. 48:34</reflink>).

heir.d: Under the patriarchs the property of a father was divided among the sons of his legitimate wives (<reflink>Gen. 21:10; 24:36; 25:5</reflink>), the eldest son getting a larger portion than the rest. The Mosaic law made specific regulations regarding the transmission of real property, which are given in detail in Deut. 21:17; Num. 27:8; 36:6; 27:9-11. Succession to property was a matter of right and not of favour. Christ is the "heir of all things" (<reflink>Heb. 1:2; Col. 1:15</reflink>). Believers are heirs of the "promise," "of righteousness," "of the kingdom," "of the world," "of God," "joint heirs" with Christ (<reflink>Gal 3:29; Heb. 6:17; 11:7; James 2:5; Rom. 4:13; 8:17</reflink>).

helah.d: rust, (<reflink>1 Chr. 4:5, 7</reflink>), one of the wives of Ashur.

helam.d: place of abundance, a place on the east of Jordan and west of the Euphrates where David gained a great victory over the Syrian army (<reflink>2 Sam. 10:16</reflink>), which was under the command of Shobach. Some would identify it with Alamatta, near Nicephorium.

helbah.d: fatness, a town of the tribe of Asher (<reflink>Judg. 1:31</reflink>), in the plain of Phoenicia.

helbon.d: fat; i.e., "fertile", (<reflink>Ezek. 27: 18 only</reflink>), a place whence wine was brought to the great market of Tyre. It has been usually identified with the modern Aleppo, called Haleb by the native Arabs, but is more probably to be found in one of the villages in the Wady Helbon, which is celebrated for its grapes, on the east slope of Anti-Lebanon, north of the river Barada (Abana).

heldai.d: wordly. (1.) 1 Chr. 27:15; called also Heleb (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:29</reflink>); one of David's captains.

heleb.d: fatness, one of David's warriors (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:29</reflink>).

heled.d: this world, (<reflink>1 Chr. 11:30</reflink>); called Heleb (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:29</reflink>).

helem.d: a stroke, great-grandson of Asher (<reflink>1 Chr. 7:35</reflink>).

heleph.d: exchange, a city on the north border of Naphtali (<reflink>Josh. 19:33</reflink>).

helez.d: strong, or loin (?) (1.) One of Judah's posterity (<reflink>1 Chr. 2:39</reflink>).

heli.d: elevation, father of Joseph in the line of our Lord's ancestry (<reflink>Luke 3:23</reflink>).

helkai.d: smooth-tongued, one of the chief priests in the time of Joiakim (<reflink>Neh. 12:15</reflink>).

imla.d: replenisher, the father of Micaiah the prophet (<reflink>2 Chr. 18:7,8</reflink>).

immanuel.d: God with us. In the Old Testament it occurs only in Isa. 7:14 and 8:8. Most Christian interpreters have regarded these words as directly and exclusively a prophecy of our Saviour, an interpretation borne out by the words of the evangelist Matthew (1:23).

immer.d: talkative. (1.) The head of the sixteenth priestly order (<reflink>1 Chr. 24:14</reflink>). (2.) Jer. 20:1. (3.) Ezra 2:37; Neh. 7:40. (4.) Ezra 2:59; Neh. 7:61. (5.) The father of Zadok (<reflink>Neh. 3:29</reflink>).

immortality.d: perpetuity of existence. The doctrine of immortality is taught in the Old Testament. It is plainly implied in the writings of Moses (<reflink>Gen. 5:22, 24; 25:8; 37:35; 47:9; 49:29, comp. Heb. 11:13-16; Ex. 3:6, comp. Matt. 22:23</reflink>). It is more clearly and fully taught in the later books (<reflink>Isa. 14:9; Ps. 17:15; 49:15; 73:24</reflink>). It was thus a doctrine obviously well known to the Jews.

imputation.d: is used to designate any action or word or thing as reckoned to a person. Thus in doctrinal language (1) the sin of Adam is imputed to all his descendants, i.e., it is reckoned as theirs, and they are dealt with therefore as guilty; (2) the righteousness of Christ is imputed to them that believe in him, or so attributed to them as to be considered their own; and (3) our sins are imputed to Christ, i.e., he assumed our "law-place," undertook to answer the demands of justice for our sins. In all these cases the nature of imputation is the same (<reflink>Rom. 5:12-19; comp. Philemon 1:18, 19</reflink>).

incarnation.d: that act of grace whereby Christ took our human nature into union with his Divine Person, became man. Christ is both God and man. Human attributes and actions are predicated of him, and he of whom they are predicated is God. A Divine Person was united to a human nature (<reflink>Acts 20:28; Rom. 8:32; 1 Cor. 2:8; Heb. 2:11-14; 1 Tim. 3:16; Gal. 4:4, etc.</reflink>). The union is hypostatical, i.e., is personal; the two natures are not mixed or confounded, and it is perpetual.

incense.d: a fragrant composition prepared by the "art of the apothecary." It consisted of four ingredients "beaten small" (<reflink>Ex. 30:34-36</reflink>). That which was not thus prepared was called "strange incense" (30:9). It was offered along with every meat-offering; and besides was daily offered on the golden altar in the holy place, and on the great day of atonement was burnt by the high priest in the holy of holies (30:7, 8). It was the symbol of prayer (<reflink>Ps. 141:1,2; Rev. 5:8; 8:3, 4</reflink>).

india.d: occurs only in Esther 1:1 and 8:9, where the extent of the dominion of the Persian king is described. The country so designated here is not the peninsula of Hindustan, but the country surrounding the Indus, the Punjab. The people and the products of India were well known to the Jews, who seem to have carried on an active trade with that country (<reflink>Ezek. 27:15, 24</reflink>).

inkhorn.d: The Hebrew word so rendered means simply a round vessel or cup for containing ink, which was generally worn by writers in the girdle (<reflink>Ezek. 9:2, 3,11</reflink>). The word "inkhorn" was used by the translators, because in former times in this country horns were used for containing ink.

inn.d: in the modern sense, unknown in the East. The khans or caravanserais, which correspond to the European inn, are not alluded to in the Old Testament. The "inn" mentioned in Ex. 4:24 was just the halting-place of the caravan. In later times khans were erected for the accommodation of travellers. In Luke 2:7 the word there so rendered denotes a place for loosing the beasts of their burdens. It is rendered "guest-chamber" in Mark 14:14 and Luke 22:11. In Luke 10:34 the word so rendered is different. That inn had an "inn-keeper," who attended to the wants of travellers.

inspiration.d: that extraordinary or supernatural divine influence vouchsafed to those who wrote the Holy Scriptures, rendering their writings infallible. "All scripture is given by inspiration of God" (R.V., "Every scripture inspired of God"), 2 Tim. 3:16. This is true of all the "sacred writings," not in the sense of their being works of genius or of supernatural insight, but as "theopneustic," i.e., "breathed into by God" in such a sense that the writers were supernaturally guided to express exactly what God intended them to express as a revelation of his mind and will. The testimony of the sacred writers themselves abundantly demonstrates this truth; and if they are infallible as teachers of doctrine, then the doctrine of plenary inspiration must be accepted. There are no errors in the Bible as it came from God, none have been proved to exist. Difficulties and phenomena we cannot explain are not errors. All these books of the Old and New Testaments are inspired. …

intercession of christ.d: Christ's priestly office consists of these two parts, (1) the offering up of himself as a sacrifice, and (2) making continual intercession for us.

intercession of the spirit.d: (<reflink>Rom. 8:26, 27; John 14:26</reflink>). "Christ is a royal Priest (<reflink>Zech. 6:13</reflink>). From the same throne, as King, he dispenses his Spirit to all the objects of his care, while as Priest he intercedes for them. The Spirit acts for him, taking only of his things. They both act with one consent, Christ as principal, the Spirit as his agent. Christ intercedes for us, without us, as our advocate in heaven, according to the provisions of the everlasting covenant. The Holy Spirit works upon our minds and hearts, enlightening and quickening, and thus determining our desires 'according to the will of God,' as our advocate within us. The work of the one is complementary to that of the other, and together they form a complete whole.", Hodge's Outlines of Theology.

iphedeiah.d: set free by Jehovah, a chief of the tribe of Benjamin (<reflink>1 Chr. 8:25</reflink>).

ira.d: citizen; wakeful. (1.) A Tekoite, one of David's thirty warriors (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:26</reflink>).

irad.d: runner; wild ass, one of the antediluvian patriarchs, the father of Mehujael (<reflink>Gen. 4:18</reflink>), and grandson of Cain.

iram.d: citizen, chief of an Edomite tribe in Mount Seir (<reflink>Gen. 36:43</reflink>).

irha-heres.d: according to some MSS., meaning "city of destruction." Other MSS. read _'Irhahares_; rendered "city of the sun", Isa. 19:18, where alone the word occurs. This name may probably refer to Heliopolis. The prophecy here points to a time when the Jews would so increase in number there as that the city would fall under their influence. This might be in the time of the Ptolemies. (<see target="x-self">See ON.</see>)

iron.d: Tubal-Cain is the first-mentioned worker in iron (<reflink>Gen. 4:22</reflink>). The Egyptians wrought it at Sinai before the Exodus. David prepared it in great abundance for the temple (<reflink>1 Chr. 22:3: 29:7</reflink>). The merchants of Dan and Javan brought it to the market of Tyre (<reflink>Ezek. 27:19</reflink>). Various instruments are mentioned as made of iron (<reflink>Deut. 27:5; 19:5; Josh. 17:16, 18; 1 Sam. 17:7; 2 Sam. 12:31; 2 Kings 6:5, 6; 1 Chr. 22:3; Isa. 10:34</reflink>).

irrigation.d: As streams were few in Palestine, water was generally stored up in winter in reservoirs, and distributed through gardens in numerous rills, which could easily be turned or diverted by the foot (<reflink>Deut. 11:10</reflink>).

isaac.d: laughter. (1) Israel, or the kingdom of the ten tribes (<reflink>Amos 7:9, 16</reflink>).

isaiah.d: (Heb. Yesh'yahu, i.e., "the salvation of Jehovah"). (1.) The son of Amoz (<reflink>Isa. 1:1; 2:1</reflink>), who was apparently a man of humble rank. His wife was called "the prophetess" (8:3), either because she was endowed with the prophetic gift, like Deborah (<reflink>Judg. 4:4</reflink>) and Huldah (<reflink>2 Kings 22:14-20</reflink>), or simply because she was the wife of "the prophet" (<reflink>Isa. 38:1</reflink>). He had two sons, who bore symbolical names.

isaiah, the book of.d: consists of prophecies delivered (Isa. 1) in the reign of Uzziah (1-5), (2) of Jotham (6), (3) Ahaz (7-14:28), (4) the first half of Hezekiah's reign (14:28-35), (5) the second half of Hezekiah's reign (36-66). Thus, counting from the fourth year before Uzziah's death (B.C. 762) to the last year of Hezekiah (B.C. 698), Isaiah's ministry extended over a period of sixty-four years. He may, however, have survived Hezekiah, and may have perished in the way indicated above.

iscah.d: spy, the daughter of Haran and sister of Milcah and Lot (<reflink>Gen. 11:29, 31</reflink>).

ish-bosheth.d: man of shame or humiliation, the youngest of Saul's four sons, and the only one who survived him (2 Sam. 2-4). His name was originally Eshbaal (<reflink>1 Chr. 8:33; 9:39</reflink>). He was about forty years of age when his father and three brothers fell at the battle of Gilboa. Through the influence of Abner, Saul's cousin, he was acknowledged as successor to the throne of Saul, and ruled over all Israel, except the tribe of Judah (over whom David was king), for two years, having Mahanaim, on the east of Jordan, as his capital (<reflink>2 Sam. 2:9</reflink>). After a troubled and uncertain reign he was murdered by his guard, who stabbed him while he was asleep on his couch at mid-day (<reflink>2 Sam. 4:5-7</reflink>); and having cut off his head, presented it to David, who sternly rebuked them for this cold-blooded murder, and ordered them to be immediately executed (9-12).

ishbak.d: leaving, one of Abraham's sons by Keturah (<reflink>Gen. 25:2</reflink>).

ishbi-benob.d: my seat at Nob, one of the Rephaim, whose spear was three hundred shekels in weight. He was slain by Abishai (<reflink>2 Sam. 21:16, 17</reflink>).

ishi.d: my husband, a symbolical name used in Hos. 2:16 (See BAALI

ishmael.d: God hears. (1.) Abraham's eldest son, by Hagar the concubine (<reflink>Gen. 16:15; 17:23</reflink>). He was born at Mamre, when Abraham was eighty-six years of age, eleven years after his arrival in Canaan (16:3; 21:5). At the age of thirteen he was circumcised (17:25). He grew up a true child of the desert, wild and wayward. On the occasion of the weaning of Isaac his rude and wayward spirit broke out in expressions of insult and mockery (21:9, 10); and Sarah, discovering this, said to Abraham, "Expel this slave and her son." Influenced by a divine admonition, Abraham dismissed Hagar and her son with no more than a skin of water and some bread. The narrative describing this act is one of the most beautiful and touching incidents of patriarchal life (<reflink>Gen. 21:14-16</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See HAGAR.</see>)

ishmaiah.d: heard by Jehovah. (1.) A Gibeonite who joined David at Ziklag, "a hero among the thirty and over the thirty" (<reflink>1 Chr. 12:4</reflink>).

ishmeelites.d: (<reflink>Gen. 37:28; 39:1, A.V.</reflink>) should be "Ishmaelites," as in the Revised Version.

ishtob.d: man of Tob, one of the small Syrian kingdoms which together constituted Aram (<reflink>2 Sam. 10:6,8</reflink>).

island.d: (Heb. 'i, "dry land," as opposed to water) occurs in its usual signification (<reflink>Isa. 42:4, 10, 12, 15, comp. Jer. 47:4</reflink>), but more frequently simply denotes a maritime region or sea-coast (<reflink>Isa. 20:6, R.V.," coastland;" 23:2, 6; Jer. 2:10; Ezek. 27:6, 7</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See CHITTIM.</see>) The shores of the Mediterranean are called the "islands of the sea" (<reflink>Isa. 11:11</reflink>), or the "isles of the Gentiles" (<reflink>Gen. 10:5</reflink>), and sometimes simply "isles" (<reflink>Ps. 72:10</reflink>); Ezek. 26:15, 18; 27:3, 35; Dan. 11:18).

israel.d: the name conferred on Jacob after the great prayer-struggle at Peniel (<reflink>Gen. 32:28</reflink>), because "as a prince he had power with God and prevailed." (<see target="x-self">See JACOB.</see>) This is the common name given to Jacob's descendants. The whole people of the twelve tribes are called "Israelites," the "children of Israel" (<reflink>Josh. 3:17; 7:25; Judg. 8:27; Jer. 3:21</reflink>), and the "house of Israel" (<reflink>Ex. 16:31; 40:38</reflink>).

israel, kingdom of.d: (B.C. 975-B.C. 722). Soon after the death of Solomon, Ahijah's prophecy (<reflink>1 Kings 11:31-35</reflink>) was fulfilled, and the kingdom was rent in twain. Rehoboam, the son and successor of Solomon, was scarcely seated on his throne when the old jealousies between Judah and the other tribes broke out anew, and Jeroboam was sent for from Egypt by the malcontents (12:2,3). Rehoboam insolently refused to lighten the burdensome taxation and services which his father had imposed on his subjects (12:4), and the rebellion became complete. Ephraim and all Israel raised the old cry, "Every man to his tents, O Israel" (<reflink>2 Sam. 20:1</reflink>). Rehoboam fled to Jerusalem (<reflink>1 Kings 12:1-18; 2 Chr. 10</reflink>), and Jeroboam was proclaimed king over all Israel at Shechem, Judah and Benjamin remaining faithful to Solomon's son. …

issachar.d: hired (<reflink>Gen. 30:18</reflink>). "God hath given me," said Leah, "my hire (Heb. sekhari)...and she called his name Issachar." He was Jacob's ninth son, and was born in Padan-aram (<reflink>comp. 28:2</reflink>). He had four sons at the going down into Egypt (46:13; Num. 26:23, 25).

italian band.d: the name of the Roman cohort to which Cornelius belonged (<reflink>Acts 10:1</reflink>), so called probably because it consisted of men recruited in Italy.

italy.d: Acts 18:2; 27:1, 6; Heb. 13:24), like most geographical names, was differently used at different periods of history. As the power of Rome advanced, nations were successively conquered and added to it till it came to designate the whole country to the south of the Alps. There was constant intercourse between Palestine and Italy in the time of the Romans.

ithamar.d: palm isle, the fourth and youngest son of Aaron (<reflink>1 Chr. 6:3</reflink>). He was consecrated to the priesthood along with his brothers (<reflink>Ex. 6:23</reflink>); and after the death of Nadab and Abihu, he and Eleazar alone discharged the functions of that office (<reflink>Lev. 10:6, 12; Num. 3:4</reflink>). He and his family occupied the position of common priest till the high priesthood passed into his family in the person of Eli (<reflink>1 Kings 2:27</reflink>), the reasons for which are not recorded. (<see target="x-self">See ZADOK.</see>)

ithrite.d: two of David's warriors so designated (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:38; 1 Chr. 11:40</reflink>).

ittai.d: near; timely; or, with the Lord. (1.) A Benjamite, one of David's thirty heroes (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:29</reflink>).

hezir.d: swine or strong. (1.) The head of the seventeenth course of the priests (<reflink>1 Chr. 24:15</reflink>). (2.) Neh. 10:20, one who sealed Nehemiah's covenant.

hezro.d: a Carmelite, one of David's warriors (<reflink>1 Chr. 11:37</reflink>).

hezron.d: enclosed. (1.) One of the sons of Reuben (<reflink>Gen. 46:9; Ex. 6:14</reflink>). (2.) The older of the two sons of Pharez (<reflink>Gen. 46:12</reflink>). (3.) A plain in the south of Judah, west of Kadesh-barnea (<reflink>Josh. 15:3</reflink>).

hiddai.d: rejoicing of Jehovah, one of David's thirty-seven guards (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:30</reflink>).

hiddekel.d: called by the Accadians id Idikla; i.e., "the river of Idikla", the third of the four rivers of Paradise (<reflink>Gen. 2:14</reflink>). Gesenius interprets the word as meaning "the rapid Tigris." The Tigris rises in the mountains of Armenia, 15 miles south of the source of the Euphrates, which, after pursuing a south-east course, it joins at Kurnah, about 50 miles above Bassorah. Its whole length is about 1,150 miles.

hiel.d: life of (i.e., from) God, a native of Bethel, who built (i.e., fortified) Jericho some seven hundred years after its destruction by the Israelites. There fell on him for such an act the imprecation of Joshua (6:26). He laid the foundation in his first-born, and set up the gates in his youngest son (<reflink>1 Kings 16:34</reflink>), i.e., during the progress of the work all his children died.

hierapolis.d: sacred city, a city of Phrygia, where was a Christian church under the care of Epaphras (<reflink>Col. 4:12, 13</reflink>). This church was founded at the same time as that of Colosse. It now bears the name of Pambuk-Kalek, i.e., "Cotton Castle", from the white appearance of the cliffs at the base of which the ruins are found.

higgaion.d: in Ps. 92:3 means the murmuring tone of the harp. In Ps. 9:16 it is a musical sign, denoting probably a pause in the instrumental interlude. In Ps. 19:14 the word is rendered "meditation;" and in Lam. 3:62, "device" (R.V., "imagination").

high place.d: an eminence, natural or artificial, where worship by sacrifice or offerings was made (<reflink>1 Kings 13:32; 2 Kings 17:29</reflink>). The first altar after the Flood was built on a mountain (<reflink>Gen. 8:20</reflink>). Abraham also built an altar on a mountain (12:7, 8). It was on a mountain in Gilead that Laban and Jacob offered sacrifices (31:54). After the Israelites entered the Promised Land they were strictly enjoined to overthrow the high places of the Canaanites (<reflink>Ex. 34:13; Deut. 7:5; 12:2, 3</reflink>), and they were forbidden to worship the Lord on high places (<reflink>Deut. 12:11-14</reflink>), and were enjoined to use but one altar for sacrifices (<reflink>Lev. 17:3, 4; Deut. 12; 16:21</reflink>). The injunction against high places was, however, very imperfectly obeyed, and we find again and again mention made of them (<reflink>2 Kings 14:4; 15:4, 35:2 Chr. 15:17, etc.</reflink>).

high priest.d: Aaron was the first who was solemnly set apart to this office (<reflink>Ex. 29:7; 30:23; Lev. 8:12</reflink>). He wore a peculiar dress, which on his death passed to his successor in office (<reflink>Ex. 29:29, 30</reflink>). Besides those garments which he wore in common with all priests, there were four that were peculiar to himself as high priest:

highway.d: a raised road for public use. Such roads were not found in Palestine; hence the force of the language used to describe the return of the captives and the advent of the Messiah (<reflink>Isa. 11:16; 35:8; 40:3; 62:10</reflink>) under the figure of the preparation of a grand thoroughfare for their march.

hilkiah.d: portion of Jehovah. (1.) 1 Chr. 6:54. (2.) 1 Chr. 26:11. (3.) The father of Eliakim (<reflink>2 Kings 18:18, 26, 37</reflink>). (4.) The father of Gemariah (<reflink>Jer. 29:3</reflink>). (5.) The father of the prophet Jeremiah (1:1).

hill.d: (1.) Heb. gib'eah, a curved or rounded hill, such as are common to Palestine (<reflink>Ps. 65:12; 72:3; 114:4, 6</reflink>).

hill of evil counsel.d: on the south of the Valley of Hinnom. It is so called from a tradition that the house of the high priest Caiaphas, when the rulers of the Jews resolved to put Christ to death, stood here.

hillel.d: praising, a Pirathonite, father of the judge Abdon (<reflink>Judg. 12:13, 15</reflink>).

hind.d: Heb. 'ayalah (<reflink>2 Sam. 22:34; Ps. 18:33, etc.</reflink>) and 'ayeleth (Ps. 22, title), the female of the hart or stag. It is referred to as an emblem of activity (<reflink>Gen. 49:21</reflink>), gentleness (<reflink>Prov. 5:19</reflink>), feminine modesty (<reflink>Cant. 2:7; 3:5</reflink>), earnest longing (<reflink>Ps. 42:1</reflink>), timidity (<reflink>Ps. 29:9</reflink>). In the title of Ps. 22, the word probably refers to some tune bearing that name.

hinge.d: (Heb. tsir), that on which a door revolves. "Doors in the East turn rather on pivots than on what we term hinges. In Syria, and especially in the Hauran, there are many ancient doors, consisting of stone slabs with pivots carved out of the same piece inserted in sockets above and below, and fixed during the building of the house" (<reflink>Prov. 26:14</reflink>).

hinnom.d: a deep, narrow ravine separating Mount Zion from the so-called "Hill of Evil Counsel." It took its name from "some ancient hero, the son of Hinnom." It is first mentioned in Josh. 15:8. It had been the place where the idolatrous Jews burned their children alive to Moloch and Baal. A particular part of the valley was called Tophet, or the "fire-stove," where the children were burned. After the Exile, in order to show their abhorrence of the locality, the Jews made this valley the receptacle of the offal of the city, for the destruction of which a fire was, as is supposed, kept constantly burning there.

hiram.d: high-born. (1.) Generally "Huram," one of the sons of Bela (<reflink>1 Chr. 8:5</reflink>).

hireling.d: a labourer employed on hire for a limited time (<reflink>Job 7:1; 14:6; Mark 1:20</reflink>). His wages were paid as soon as his work was over (<reflink>Lev. 19:13</reflink>). In the time of our Lord a day's wage was a "penny" (q.v.) i.e., a Roman denarius (<reflink>Matt. 20:1-14</reflink>).

hiss.d: to express contempt (<reflink>Job 27:23</reflink>). The destruction of the temple is thus spoken of (<reflink>1 Kings 9:8</reflink>). Zechariah (10:8) speaks of the Lord gathering the house of Judah as it were with a hiss: "I will hiss for them." This expression may be "derived from the noise made to attract bees in hiving, or from the sound naturally made to attract a person's attention."

hittites.d: Palestine and Syria appear to have been originally inhabited by three different tribes. (1.) The Semites, living on the east of the isthmus of Suez. They were nomadic and pastoral tribes. (2.) The Phoenicians, who were merchants and traders; and (3.) the Hittites, who were the warlike element of this confederation of tribes. They inhabited the whole region between the Euphrates and Damascus, their chief cities being Carchemish on the Euphrates, and Kadesh, now Tell Neby Mendeh, in the Orontes valley, about six miles south of the Lake of Homs. These Hittites seem to have risen to great power as a nation, as for a long time they were formidable rivals of the Egyptian and Assyrian empires. In the book of Joshua they always appear as the dominant race to the north of Galilee.

hivites.d: one of the original tribes scattered over Palestine, from Hermon to Gibeon in the south. The name is interpreted as "midlanders" or "villagers" (<reflink>Gen. 10:17; 1 Chr. 1:15</reflink>). They were probably a branch of the Hittites. At the time of Jacob's return to Canaan, Hamor the Hivite was the "prince of the land" (<reflink>Gen. 24:2-28</reflink>).

hizkiah.d: an ancestor of the prophet Zephaniah (1:1).

hobab.d: beloved, the Kenite, has been usually identified with Jethro (q.v.), Ex. 18:5, 27; comp. Num. 10:29, 30. In Judg. 4:11, the word rendered "father-in-law" means properly any male relative by marriage (<reflink>comp. Gen. 19:14, "son-in-law," A.V.</reflink>), and should be rendered "brother-in-law," as in the R.V. His descendants followed Israel to Canaan (<reflink>Num. 10:29</reflink>), and at first pitched their tents near Jericho, but afterwards settled in the south in the borders of Arad (<reflink>Judg. 1:8-11, 16</reflink>).

hobah.d: hiding-place, a place to the north of Damascus, to which Abraham pursued Chedorlaomer and his confederates (<reflink>Gen. 14:15</reflink>).

hodijah.d: majesty of Jehovah. (1.) One of the Levites who assisted Ezra in expounding the law (<reflink>Neh. 8:7; 9:5</reflink>). (2.) Neh. 10:18, a Levite who sealed the covenant.

hoglah.d: partridge, one of the daughters of Zelophehad the Gileadite, to whom portions were assigned by Moses (<reflink>Num. 26:33; 27:1; 36:11</reflink>).

hoham.d: Jehovah impels, the king of Hebron who joined the league against Gibeon. He and his allies were defeated (<reflink>Josh. 10:3, 5, 16-27</reflink>).

hold.d: a fortress, the name given to David's lurking-places (<reflink>1 Sam. 22:4, 5; 24:22</reflink>).

holiness.d: in the highest sense belongs to God (<reflink>Isa. 6:3; Rev. 15:4</reflink>), and to Christians as consecrated to God's service, and in so far as they are conformed in all things to the will of God (<reflink>Rom. 6:19, 22; Eph. 1:4; Titus 1:8; 1 Pet. 1:15</reflink>). Personal holiness is a work of gradual development. It is carried on under many hindrances, hence the frequent admonitions to watchfulness, prayer, and perseverance (<reflink>1 Cor. 1:30; 2 Cor. 7:1; Eph. 4:23, 24</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See SANCTIFICATION.</see>)

holy ghost.d: the third Person of the adorable Trinity.

holy of holies.d: the second or interior portion of the tabernacle. It was left in total darkness. No one was permitted to enter it except the high priest, and that only once a year. It contained the ark of the covenant only (<reflink>Ex. 25:10-16</reflink>). It was in the form of a perfect cube of 20 cubits. (<see target="x-self">See TABERNACLE.</see>)

holy place.d: one of the two portions into which the tabernacle was divided (<reflink>Ex. 26:31; 37:17-25; Heb. 9:2</reflink>). It was 20 cubits long and 10 in height and breadth. It was illuminated by the golden candlestick, as it had no opening to admit the light. It contained the table of showbread (<reflink>Ex. 25:23-29</reflink>) and the golden altar of incense (30:1-11). It was divided from the holy of holies by a veil of the most costly materials and the brightest colours.

homer.d: heap, the largest of dry measures, containing about 8 bushels or 1 quarter English = 10 ephahs (<reflink>Lev. 27:16; Num. 11:32</reflink>) = a COR. (<see target="x-self">See OMER.</see>)

honey.d: (1.) Heb. ya'ar, occurs only 1 Sam. 14:25, 27, 29; Cant. 5:1, where it denotes the honey of bees. Properly the word signifies a forest or copse, and refers to honey found in woods.

hood.d: (Heb. tsaniph) a tiara round the head (<reflink>Isa. 3:23; R.V., pl., "turbans"</reflink>). Rendered "diadem," Job 29:14; high priest's "mitre," Zech. 3:5; "royal diadem," Isa. 62:3.

hoof.d: a cleft hoof as of neat cattle (<reflink>Ex. 10:26; Ezek. 32:13</reflink>); hence also of the horse, though not cloven (<reflink>Isa. 5:28</reflink>). The "parting of the hoof" is one of the distinctions between clean and unclean animals (<reflink>Lev. 11:3; Deut. 14:7</reflink>).

hook.d: (1.) Heb. hah, a "ring" inserted in the nostrils of animals to which a cord was fastened for the purpose of restraining them (<reflink>2 Kings 19:28; Isa. 37:28, 29; Ezek. 29:4; 38:4</reflink>). "The Orientals make use of this contrivance for curbing their work-beasts...When a beast becomes unruly they have only to draw the cord on one side, which, by stopping his breath, punishes him so effectually that after a few repetitions he fails not to become quite tractable whenever he begins to feel it" (Michaelis). So God's agents are never beyond his control.

hope.d: one of the three main elements of Christian character (<reflink>1 Cor. 13:13</reflink>). It is joined to faith and love, and is opposed to seeing or possessing (<reflink>Rom. 8:24; 1 John 3:2</reflink>). "Hope is an essential and fundamental element of Christian life, so essential indeed, that, like faith and love, it can itself designate the essence of Christianity (<reflink>1 Pet. 3:15; Heb. 10:23</reflink>). In it the whole glory of the Christian vocation is centred (<reflink>Eph. 1:18; 4:4</reflink>)." Unbelievers are without this hope (<reflink>Eph. 2:12; 1 Thess. 4:13</reflink>). Christ is the actual object of the believer's hope, because it is in his second coming that the hope of glory will be fulfilled (<reflink>1 Tim. 1:1; Col. 1:27; Titus 2:13</reflink>). It is spoken of as "lively", i.e., a living, hope, a hope not frail and perishable, but having a perennial life (<reflink>1 Pet. 1:3</reflink>). In Rom. …

hophni.d: pugilist or client, one of the two sons of Eli, the high priest (<reflink>1 Sam. 1:3; 2:34</reflink>), who, because he was "very old," resigned to them the active duties of his office. By their scandalous conduct they brought down a curse on their father's house (2:22, 12-27, 27-36; 3:11-14). For their wickedness they were called "sons of Belial," i.e., worthless men (2:12). They both perished in the disastrous battle with the Philistines at Aphek (4:11). (<see target="x-self">See PHINEHAS.</see>)

hophra.d: i.e., PHARAOH-HOPHRA (called Apries by the Greek historian Herodotus) king of Egypt (B.C. 591-572) in the time of Zedekiah, king of Judah (<reflink>Jer. 37:5 44:30; Ezek. 29:6, 7</reflink>).

hor.d: mountain. (1.) One of the mountains of the chain of Seir or Edom, on the confines of Idumea (<reflink>Num. 20:22-29; 33:37</reflink>). It was one of the stations of the Israelites in the wilderness (33:37), which they reached in the circuitous route they were obliged to take because the Edomites refused them a passage through their territory. It was during the encampment here that Aaron died (<reflink>Num. 33:37-41</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See AARON.</see>) The Israelites passed this mountain several times in their wanderings. It bears the modern name of Jebel Harun, and is the highest and most conspicious of the whole range. It stands about midway between the Dead Sea and the Elanitic gulf. It has two summits, in the hallow between which it is supposed that Aaron died. Others, however, suppose that this mountain is the modern Jebel Madurah, on the opposite, i.e., the western, side of the Arabah.

horeb.d: desert or mountain of the dried-up ground, a general name for the whole mountain range of which Sinai was one of the summits (<reflink>Ex. 3:1; 17:6; 33:6; Ps. 106:19, etc.</reflink>). The modern name of the whole range is Jebel Musa. It is a huge mountain block, about 2 miles long by about 1 in breadth, with a very spacious plain at its north-east end, called the Er Rahah, in which the Israelites encamped for nearly a whole year. (<see target="x-self">See SINAI.</see>)

horem.d: consecrated, one of the fenced cities of Naphtali (<reflink>Josh. 19:38</reflink>).

horites.d: cave-men, a race of Troglodytes who dwelt in the limestone caves which abounded in Edom. Their ancestor was "Seir," who probably gave his name to the district where he lived. They were a branch of the Hivites (<reflink>Gen. 14:6; 36:20-30; 1 Chr. 1:38, 39</reflink>). They were dispossessed by the descendants of Esau, and as a people gradually became extinct (<reflink>Deut. 2:12-22</reflink>).

hormah.d: banning; i.e., placing under a "ban," or devoting to utter destruction. After the manifestation of God's anger against the Israelites, on account of their rebellion and their murmurings when the spies returned to the camp at Kadesh, in the wilderness of Paran, with an evil report of the land, they quickly repented of their conduct, and presumed to go up "to the head of the mountain," seeking to enter the Promised Land, but without the presence of the Lord, without the ark of the convenant, and without Moses. The Amalekites and the Canaanites came down and "smote and discomfited them even unto Hormah" (<reflink>Num. 14:45</reflink>). This place, or perhaps the watch-tower commanding it, was originally called Zephath (<reflink>Judg. 1:17</reflink>), the modern Sebaiteh. Afterwards (<reflink>Num. …

horn.d: Trumpets were at first horns perforated at the tip, used for various purposes (<reflink>Josh. 6:4,5</reflink>).

hornet.d: Heb. tsir'ah, "stinging", (<reflink>Ex. 23:28; Deut. 7:20; Josh. 24:12</reflink>). The word is used in these passages as referring to some means by which the Canaanites were to be driven out from before the Israelites. Some have supposed that the word is used in a metaphorical sense as the symbol of some panic which would seize the people as a "terror of God" (<reflink>Gen. 35:5</reflink>), the consternation with which God would inspire the Canaanites. In Palestine there are four species of hornets, differing from our hornets, being larger in size, and they are very abundant. They "attack human beings in a very furious manner." "The furious attack of a swarm of hornets drives cattle and horses to madness, and has even caused the death of the animals."

horonaim.d: two caverns, a city of Moab to the south of the Arnon, built, apparently, upon an eminence, and a place of some importance (<reflink>Isa. 15:5; Jer. 48:3, 5, 34</reflink>).

horonite.d: the designation of Sanballat (<reflink>Neh. 2:10, 19</reflink>), a native of Horonaim, or of one of the two Beth-horons, the "upper" or the "nether," mentioned in Josh. 16:3,5.

horse.d: always referred to in the Bible in connection with warlike operations, except Isa. 28:28. The war-horse is described Job 39:19-25. For a long period after their settlement in Canaan the Israelites made no use of horses, according to the prohibition, Deut. 17:16. David was the first to form a force of cavalry (<reflink>2 Sam. 8:4</reflink>). But Solomon, from his connection with Egypt, greatly multiplied their number (<reflink>1 Kings 4:26; 10:26, 29</reflink>). After this, horses were freely used in Israel (<reflink>1 Kings 22:4; 2 Kings 3:7; 9:21, 33; 11:16</reflink>). The furniture of the horse consisted simply of a bridle (<reflink>Isa. 30:28</reflink>) and a curb (<reflink>Ps. 32:9</reflink>).

horse-gate.d: a gate in the wall of Jerusalem, at the west end of the bridge, leading from Zion to the temple (<reflink>Neh. 3:28; Jer. 31:40</reflink>).

horse-leech.d: occurs only in Prov. 30:15 (Heb. 'alukah); the generic name for any blood-sucking annelid. There are various species in the marshes and pools of Palestine. That here referred to, the Hoemopis, is remarkable for the coarseness of its bite, and is therefore not used for medical purposes. They are spoken of in the East with feelings of aversion and horror, because of their propensity to fasten on the tongue and nostrils of horses when they come to drink out of the pools. The medicinal leech (Hirudo medicinalis), besides other species of leeches, are common in the waters of Syria.

horseman.d: Heb. ba'al parash, "master of a horse." The "horsemen" mentioned Ex. 14:9 were "mounted men", i.e., men who rode in chariots. The army of Pharaoh consisted of a chariot and infantry force. We find that at a later period, however, the Egyptians had cavalry (<reflink>2 Chr. 12:3</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See HORSE.</see>)

hosah.d: refuge. (1.) A place on the border of the tribe of Asher (<reflink>Josh. 19:29</reflink>), a little to the south of Zidon.

hosanna.d: Save now! or Save, we beseech, (<reflink>Matt. 21:9</reflink>). This was a customary form of acclamation at the feast of Tabernacles. (<reflink>Comp. Ps. 118:25.</reflink>)

hosea.d: salvation, the son of Beeri, and author of the book of prophecies bearing his name. He belonged to the kingdom of Israel. "His Israelitish origin is attested by the peculiar, rough, Aramaizing diction, pointing to the northern part of Palestine; by the intimate acquaintance he evinces with the localities of Ephraim (5:1; 6:8, 9; 12:12; 14:6, etc.); by passages like 1:2, where the kingdom is styled 'the land', and 7:5, where the Israelitish king is designated as 'our' king." The period of his ministry (extending to some sixty years) is indicated in the superscription (<reflink>Hos. 1:1, 2</reflink>). He is the only prophet of Israel who has left any written prophecy.

hosea, prophecies of.d: This book stands first in order among the "Minor Prophets." "The probable cause of the location of Hosea may be the thoroughly national character of his oracles, their length, their earnest tone, and vivid representations." This was the longest of the prophetic books written before the Captivity. Hosea prophesied in a dark and melancholy period of Israel's history, the period of Israel's decline and fall. Their sins had brought upon them great national disasters. "Their homicides and fornication, their perjury and theft, their idolatry and impiety, are censured and satirized with a faithful severity." He was a contemporary of Isaiah. The book may be divided into two parts, the first containing chapters 1-3, and symbolically representing the idolatry of Israel under imagery borrowed from the matrimonial relation. The figures of marriage and adultery are common in the Old Testament writings to represent the spiritual relations between Jehovah and the people of Israel. …

hoshea.d: salvation. (1.) The original name of the son of Nun, afterwards called Joshua (<reflink>Num. 13:8, 16; Deut. 32:44</reflink>).

host.d: an entertainer (<reflink>Rom. 16:23</reflink>); a tavern-keeper, the keeper of a caravansary (<reflink>Luke 10:35</reflink>).

host of heaven.d: The sun, moon, and stars are so designated (<reflink>Gen. 2:1</reflink>). When the Jews fell into idolatry they worshipped these (<reflink>Deut. 4:19; 2 Kings 17:16; 21:3,5; 23:5; Jer. 19:13; Zeph. 1:5; Acts 7:42</reflink>).

hostage.d: a person delivered into the hands of another as a security for the performance of some promise, etc. (<reflink>2 Kings 14:14; 2 Chr. 25:24</reflink>).

hough.d: to hamstring, i.e., sever the "tendon of Achilles" of the hinder legs of captured horses (<reflink>Josh. 11:6; 2 Sam. 8:4; 1 Chr. 18:4</reflink>), so as to render them useless.

hour.d: First found in Dan. 3:6; 4:19, 33;5:5. It is the rendering of the Chaldee shaah, meaning a "moment," a "look." It is used in the New Testament frequently to denote some determinate season (<reflink>Matt. 8:13; Luke 12:39</reflink>).

house.d: Till their sojourn in Egypt the Hebrews dwelt in tents. They then for the first time inhabited cities (<reflink>Gen. 47:3; Ex. 12:7; Heb. 11:9</reflink>). From the earliest times the Assyrians and the Canaanites were builders of cities. The Hebrews after the Conquest took possession of the captured cities, and seem to have followed the methods of building that had been pursued by the Canaanites. Reference is made to the stone (<reflink>1 Kings 7:9; Isa. 9:10</reflink>) and marble (<reflink>1 Chr. 29:2</reflink>) used in building, and to the internal wood-work of the houses (<reflink>1 Kings 6:15; 7:2; 10:11, 12; 2 Chr. 3:5; Jer. 22:14</reflink>). "Ceiled houses" were such as had beams inlaid in the walls to which wainscotting was fastened (<reflink>Ezra 6:4; Jer. 22:14; Hag. 1:4</reflink>). "Ivory houses" had the upper parts of the walls adorned with figures in stucco with gold and ivory (<reflink>1 Kings 22:39; 2 Chr. 3:6; Ps. 45:8</reflink>).

hukkok.d: decreed, a town near Zebulun, not far from Jordan, on the border of Naphtali (<reflink>Josh. 19:34</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See HELKATH.</see>)

hul.d: circle, the second son of Aram (<reflink>Gen. 10:23</reflink>), and grandson of Shem.

huldah.d: weasel, a prophetess; the wife of Shallum. She was consulted regarding the "book of the law" discovered by the high priest Hilkiah (<reflink>2 Kings 22:14-20; 2 Chr. 34:22-28</reflink>). She resided in that part of Jerusalem called the Mishneh (A.V., "the college;" R.V., "the second quarter"), supposed by some to be the suburb between the inner and the outer wall, the second or lower city, Akra. Miriam (<reflink>Ex. 15:20</reflink>) and Deborah (<reflink>Judg. 4:4</reflink>) are the only others who bear the title of "prophetess," for the word in Isa. 8:3 means only the prophet's wife.

humiliation of christ.d: (<reflink>Phil. 2:8</reflink>), seen in (1) his birth (<reflink>Gal. 4:4; Luke 2:7; John 1:46; Heb. 2:9</reflink>), (2) his circumstances, (3) his reputation (Isa. 53; Matt. 26:59, 67; Ps. 22:6; Matt. 26:68), (4) his soul (<reflink>Ps. 22:1; Matt. 4:1-11; Luke 22:44; Heb. 2:17, 18; 4:15</reflink>), (5) his death (Luke 23; John 19; Mark 15:24, 25), (6) and his burial (<reflink>Isa. 53:9; Matt. 27:57, 58, 60</reflink>).

humility.d: a prominent Christian grace (<reflink>Rom. 12:3; 15:17, 18; 1 Cor. 3:5-7; 2 Cor. 3:5; Phil. 4:11-13</reflink>). It is a state of mind well pleasing to God (<reflink>1 Pet. 3:4</reflink>); it preserves the soul in tranquillity (<reflink>Ps. 69:32, 33</reflink>), and makes us patient under trials (<reflink>Job 1:22</reflink>).

hunting.d: mentioned first in Gen. 10:9 in connection with Nimrod. Esau was "a cunning hunter" (<reflink>Gen. 25:27</reflink>). Hunting was practised by the Hebrews after their settlement in the "Land of Promise" (<reflink>Lev. 17:15; Prov. 12:27</reflink>). The lion and other ravenous beasts were found in Palestine (<reflink>1 Sam. 17:34; 2 Sam. 23:20; 1 Kings 13:24; Ezek. 19:3-8</reflink>), and it must have been necessary to hunt and destroy them. Various snares and gins were used in hunting (<reflink>Ps. 91:3; Amos 3:5; 2 Sam. 23:20</reflink>).

hur.d: a hole, as of a viper, etc. (1.) A son of Caleb (<reflink>1 Chr. 2:19, 50; 4:1, 4; comp. 2 Chr. 1:5</reflink>).

hurai.d: linen-worker, one of David's heroes, a native of the valley of Mount Gaash (<reflink>1 Chr. 11:32</reflink>).

husband.d: i.e., the "house-band," connecting and keeping together the whole family. A man when betrothed was esteemed from that time a husband (<reflink>Matt. 1:16, 20; Luke 2:5</reflink>). A recently married man was exempt from going to war for "one year" (<reflink>Deut. 20:7; 24:5</reflink>).

husbandman.d: one whose business it is to cultivate the ground. It was one of the first occupations, and was esteemed most honourable (<reflink>Gen. 9:20; 26:12, 14; 37:7, etc.</reflink>). All the Hebrews, except those engaged in religious services, were husbandmen. (See AGRICULTURE

hushai.d: quick, "the Archite," "the king's friend" (<reflink>1 Chr. 27:33</reflink>). When David fled from Jerusalem, on account of the rebellion of Absalom, and had reached the summit of Olivet, he there met Hushai, whom he sent back to Jerusalem for the purpose of counteracting the influence of Ahithophel, who had joined the ranks of Absalom (<reflink>2 Sam. 15:32, 37; 16:16-18</reflink>). It was by his advice that Absalom refrained from immediately pursuing after David. By this delay the cause of Absalom was ruined, for it gave David time to muster his forces.

husk.d: In Num. 6:4 (Heb. zag) it means the "skin" of a grape. In 2 Kings 4:42 (Heb. tsiqlon) it means a "sack" for grain, as rendered in the Revised Version. In Luke 15:16, in the parable of the Prodigal Son, it designates the beans of the carob tree, or Ceratonia siliqua. From the supposition, mistaken, however, that it was on the husks of this tree that John the Baptist fed, it is called "St. John's bread" and "locust tree." This tree is in "February covered with innumerable purple-red pendent blossoms, which ripen in April and May into large crops of pods from 6 to 10 inches long, flat, brown, narrow, and bent like a horn (whence the Greek name keratia, meaning 'little horns'), with a sweetish taste when still unripe. …

hymn.d: occurs only Eph. 5:19 and Col. 3:16. The verb to "sing an hymn" occurs Matt. 26:30 and Mark 14:26. The same Greek word is rendered to "sing praises" Acts 16:25 (R.V., "sing hymns") and Heb. 2:12. The "hymn" which our Lord sang with his disciples at the last Supper is generally supposed to have been the latter part of the Hallel, comprehending Ps. 113-118. It was thus a name given to a number of psalms taken together and forming a devotional exercise.

hypocrite.d: one who puts on a mask and feigns himself to be what he is not; a dissembler in religion. Our Lord severely rebuked the scribes and Pharisees for their hypocrisy (<reflink>Matt. 6:2, 5, 16</reflink>). "The hypocrite's hope shall perish" (<reflink>Job 8:13</reflink>). The Hebrew word here rendered "hypocrite" rather means the "godless" or "profane," as it is rendered in Jer. 23:11, i.e., polluted with crimes.

hyssop.d: (Heb. 'ezob; LXX. hyssopos), first mentioned in Ex. 12:22 in connection with the institution of the Passover. We find it afterwards mentioned in Lev. 14:4, 6, 52; Num. 19:6, 18; Heb. 9:19. It is spoken of as a plant "springing out of the wall" (<reflink>1 Kings 4:33</reflink>). Many conjectures have been formed as to what this plant really was. Some contend that it was a species of marjoram (origanum), six species of which are found in Palestine. Others with more probability think that it was the caper plant, the Capparis spinosa of Linnaeus. This plant grew in Egypt, in the desert of Sinai, and in Palestine. It was capable of producing a stem three or four feet in length (<reflink>Matt. 27:48; Mark 15:36. Comp. John 19:29</reflink>).

ibhar.d: chosen, one of David's sons (<reflink>1 Chr. 3:6; 2 Sam. 5:15</reflink>).

ibleam.d: people-waster, a city assigned to Manasseh (<reflink>Josh. 17:11</reflink>), from which the Israelites, however, could not expel the Canaanites (<reflink>Judg. 1:27</reflink>). It is also called Bileam (<reflink>1 Chr. 6:70</reflink>). It was probably the modern Jelamah, a village 2 1/2 miles north of Jenin.

ibzan.d: illustrious, the tenth judge of Israel (<reflink>Judg. 12:8-10</reflink>). He ruled seven years.

ice.d: frequently mentioned (<reflink>Job 6:16; 38:29; Ps. 147:17, etc.</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See CRYSTAL.</see>)

ichabod.d: When the tidings of the disastrous defeat of the Israelites in the battle against the Philistines near to Mizpeh were carried to Shiloh, the wife of Phinehas "was near to be delivered. And when she heard the tidings that the ark of God was taken, and that her father-in-law and her husband were dead, she bowed herself and travailed" (<reflink>1 Sam. 4:19-22</reflink>). In her great distress she regarded not "the women that stood by her," but named the child that was born "Ichabod" i.e., no glory, saying, "The glory is departed from Isreal;" and with that word on her lips she expired.

iconium.d: the capital of ancient Lycaonia. It was first visited by Paul and Barnabas from Antioch-in-Pisidia during the apostle's first missionary journey (<reflink>Acts 13:50, 51</reflink>). Here they were persecuted by the Jews, and being driven from the city, they fled to Lystra. They afterwards returned to Iconium, and encouraged the church which had been founded there (14:21,22). It was probably again visited by Paul during his third missionary journey along with Silas (18:23). It is the modern Konieh, at the foot of Mount Taurus, about 120 miles inland from the Mediterranean.

idalah.d: snares(?), a city near the west border of Zebulun (<reflink>Josh. 19:15</reflink>). It has been identified with the modern Jeida, in the valley of Kishon.

idol.d: (1.) Heb. aven, "nothingness;" "vanity" (<reflink>Isa. 66:3; 41:29; Deut. 32:21; 1 Kings 16:13; Ps. 31:6; Jer. 8:19, etc.</reflink>).

idolatry.d: image-worship or divine honour paid to any created object. Paul describes the origin of idolatry in Rom. 1:21-25: men forsook God, and sank into ignorance and moral corruption (1:28).

idumaea.d: the Greek form of Edom (<reflink>Isa. 34:5, 6; Ezek. 35:15; 36:5, but in R.V. "Edom"</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See EDOM</see>).

igal.d: avengers. (1.) Num. 13:7, one of the spies of the tribe of Issachar. (2.) Son of Nathan of Zobah, and one of David's warriors (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:36</reflink>). (3.) 1 Chr. 3:22.

iim.d: ruins. (1.) A city in the south of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:29</reflink>).

ije-abarim.d: ruins of Abarim, the forty-seventh station of the Israelites in the wilderness, "in the border of Moab" (<reflink>Num. 33:44</reflink>).

ijon.d: a ruin, a city of Naphtali, captured by Ben-hadad of Syria at the instance of Asa (<reflink>1 Kings 15:20</reflink>), and afterwards by Tiglath-pileser of Assyria (<reflink>2 Kings 15:29</reflink>) in the reign of Pekah; now el-Khiam.

ilai.d: an Ahohite, one of David's chief warriors (<reflink>1 Chr. 11:29</reflink>); called also Zalmon (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:28</reflink>).

illyricum.d: a country to the north-west of Macedonia, on the eastern shores of the Adriatic, now almost wholly comprehended in Dalmatia, a name formerly given to the southern part of Illyricum (<reflink>2 Tim. 4:10</reflink>). It was traversed by Paul in his third missionary journey (<reflink>Rom. 15:19</reflink>). It was the farthest district he had reached in preaching the gospel of Christ. This reference to Illyricum is in harmony with Acts 20:2, inasmuch as the apostle's journey over the parts of Macedonia would bring him to the borders of Illyricum.

imagery.d: only in the phrase "chambers of his imagery" (<reflink>Ezek. 8:12</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See CHAMBER.</see>)

jachin and boaz.d: the names of two brazen columns set up in Solomon's temple (<reflink>1 Kings 7:15-22</reflink>). Each was eighteen cubits high and twelve in circumference (<reflink>Jer. 52:21, 23; 1 Kings 7:17-21</reflink>). They had doubtless a symbolical import.

jacinth.d: properly a flower of a reddish blue or deep purple (hyacinth), and hence a precious stone of that colour (<reflink>Rev. 21:20</reflink>). It has been supposed to designate the same stone as the ligure (Heb. leshem) mentioned in Ex. 28:19 as the first stone of the third row in the high priest's breast-plate. In Rev. 9:17 the word is simply descriptive of colour.

jacob.d: one who follows on another's heels; supplanter, (<reflink>Gen. 25:26; 27:36; Hos. 12:2-4</reflink>), the second born of the twin sons of Isaac by Rebekah. He was born probably at Lahai-roi, when his father was fifty-nine and Abraham one hundred and fifty-nine years old. Like his father, he was of a quiet and gentle disposition, and when he grew up followed the life of a shepherd, while his brother Esau became an enterprising hunter. His dealing with Esau, however, showed much mean selfishness and cunning (<reflink>Gen. 25:29-34</reflink>).

jacob's well.d: (<reflink>John 4:5, 6</reflink>). This is one of the few sites in Palestine about which there is no dispute. It was dug by Jacob, and hence its name, in the "parcel of ground" which he purchased from the sons of Hamor (<reflink>Gen. 33:19</reflink>). It still exists, but although after copious rains it contains a little water, it is now usually quite dry. It is at the entrance to the valley between Ebal and Gerizim, about 2 miles south-east of Shechem. It is about 9 feet in diameter and about 75 feet in depth, though in ancient times it was no doubt much deeper, probably twice as deep. The digging of such a well must have been a very laborious and costly undertaking.

jaddua.d: known. (1.) One of the chiefs who subscribed the covenant (<reflink>Neh. 10:21</reflink>).

jadon.d: judge, a Meronothite who assisted in rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem (<reflink>Neh. 3:7</reflink>).

jael.d: mountain-goat, the wife of Heber the Kenite (<reflink>Judg. 4:17-22</reflink>). When the Canaanites were defeated by Barak, Sisera, the captain of Jabin's army, fled and sought refuge with the friendly tribe of Heber, beneath the oaks of Zaanaim. As he drew near, Jael invited him to enter her tent. He did so, and as he lay wearied on the floor he fell into a deep sleep. She then took in her left hand one of the great wooden pins ("nail") which fastened down the cords of the tent, and in her right hand the mallet, or "hammer," used for driving it into the ground, and stealthily approaching her sleeping guest, with one well-directed blow drove the nail through his temples into the earth (<reflink>Judg. 5:27</reflink>). She then led Barak, who was in pursuit, into her tent, and boastfully showed him what she had done. (<see target="x-self">See SISERA; DEBORAH.</see>)

jagur.d: place of sojourn, a city on the southern border of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:21</reflink>).

jahath.d: union. (1.) A son of Shimei, and grandson of Gershom (<reflink>1 Chr. 23:10</reflink>).

jahaz.d: trodden down (called also Jahaza, Josh. 13:18; Jahazah, 21:36; Jahzah, 1 Chr. 6:78), a town where Sihon was defeated, in the borders of Moab and in the land of the Ammonites beyond Jordan, and north of the river Arnon (<reflink>Num. 21:23; Deut. 2:32</reflink>). It was situated in the tribe of Reuben, and was assigned to the Merarite Levites (<reflink>Josh. 13:18; 21:36</reflink>). Here was fought the decisive battle in which Sihon (q.v.) was completely routed, and his territory (the modern Belka) came into the possession of Israel. This town is mentioned in the denunciations of the prophets against Moab (<reflink>Isa. 15:4; Jer. 48:34</reflink>).

jahaziel.d: beheld by God. (1.) The third son of Hebron (<reflink>1 Chr. 23:19</reflink>).

jahdai.d: grasper, a descendant of Caleb, of the family of Hezron (<reflink>1 Chr. 2:47</reflink>).

jahzeel.d: allotted by God, the first of the sons of Naphtali (<reflink>Gen. 46:24</reflink>).

jahzerah.d: returner, the son of Meshullam, and father of Adiel (<reflink>1 Chr. 9:12</reflink>).

jailer.d: (of Philippi), Acts 16:23. The conversion of the Roman jailer, a man belonging to a class "insensible as a rule and hardened by habit, and also disposed to despise the Jews, who were the bearers of the message of the gospel," is one of those cases which illustrate its universality and power.

jair.d: enlightener. (1.) The son of Segub. He was brought up with his mother in Gilead, where he had possessions (<reflink>1 Chr. 2:22</reflink>). He distinguished himself in an expedition against Bashan, and settled in the part of Argob on the borders of Gilead. The small towns taken by him there are called Havoth-jair, i.e., "Jair's villages" (<reflink>Num. 32:41; Deut. 3:14; Josh. 13:30</reflink>).

jairus.d: a ruler of the synagogue at Capernaum, whose only daughter Jesus restored to life (<reflink>Mark 5:22; Luke 8:41</reflink>). Entering into the chamber of death, accompanied by Peter and James and John and the father and mother of the maiden, he went forward to the bed whereon the corpse lay, and said, Talitha cumi, i.e., "Maid, arise," and immediately the spirit of the maiden came to her again, and she arose straightway; and "at once to strengthen that life which had come back to her, and to prove that she was indeed no ghost, but had returned to the realities of a mortal existence, he commanded to give her something to eat" (<reflink>Mark 5:43</reflink>).

jakeh.d: pious, the father of Agur (<reflink>Prov. 30:1</reflink>). Nothing is known of him.

jakim.d: establisher. (1.) Chief of the twelfth priestly order (<reflink>1 Chr. 24:12</reflink>).

jalon.d: lodger, the last of the four sons of Ezra, of the tribe of Judah (<reflink>1 Chr. 4:17</reflink>).

jambres.d: one of those who opposed Moses in Egypt (<reflink>2 Tim. 3:8</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See JANNES.</see>)

james.d: (1.) The son of Zebedee and Salome; an elder brother of John the apostle. He was one of the twelve. He was by trade a fisherman, in partnership with Peter (<reflink>Matt. 20:20; 27:56</reflink>). With John and Peter he was present at the transfiguration (<reflink>Matt. 17:1; Mark 9:2</reflink>), at the raising of Jairus's daughter (<reflink>Mark 5:37-43</reflink>), and in the garden with our Lord (14:33). Because, probably, of their boldness and energy, he and John were called Boanerges, i.e., "sons of thunder." He was the first martyr among the apostles, having been beheaded by King Herod Agrippa (<reflink>Acts 12:1, 2</reflink>), A.D. 44. (<reflink>Comp. Matt. 4:21; 20:20-23</reflink>).

james, epistle of.d: (1.) Author of, was James the Less, the Lord's brother, one of the twelve apostles. He was one of the three pillars of the Church (<reflink>Gal. 2:9</reflink>).

jannes.d: one of the Egyptians who "withstood Moses" (<reflink>2 Tim. 3:8</reflink>).

janoah.d: or Jano'hah, rest. (1.) A town on the north-eastern border of Ephraim, in the Jordan valley (<reflink>Josh. 16:6, 7</reflink>). Identified with the modern Yanun, 8 miles south-east of Nablus.

janum.d: slumber, a town in the mountains of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:53</reflink>).

japheth.d: wide spreading: "God shall enlarge Japheth" (Heb. Yaphat Elohim le-Yephet, Gen. 9:27. Some, however, derive the name from _yaphah_, "to be beautiful;" hence white), one of the sons of Noah, mentioned last in order (<reflink>Gen. 5:32; 6:10; 7:13</reflink>), perhaps first by birth (10:21; comp. 9:24). He and his wife were two of the eight saved in the ark (<reflink>1 Pet. 3:20</reflink>). He was the progenitor of many tribes inhabiting the east of Europe and the north of Asia (<reflink>Gen. 10:2-5</reflink>). An act of filial piety (9:20-27) was the occasion of Noah's prophecy of the extension of his posterity.

japhia.d: splendid. (1.) The king of Lachish, who joined in the confederacy against Joshua (<reflink>Josh. 10:3</reflink>), and was defeated and slain. In one of the Amarna tablets he speaks of himself as king of Gezer. Called also Horam (<reflink>Josh. 10:33</reflink>).

japho.d: beauty, a sea-port in Dan (<reflink>Josh. 19:46</reflink>); called Joppa (q.v.) in 2 Chr. 2:16; Ezra 3:7; Jonah 1:3; and in New Testament.

jared.d: descent. (1.) The fourth antediluvian patriarch in descent from Seth (<reflink>Gen. 5:15-20; Luke 3:37</reflink>), the father of Enoch; called Jered in 1 Chr. 1:2.

jarib.d: an adversary. (1.) A son of Simeon (<reflink>1 Chr. 4:24</reflink>).

ituraea.d: a district in the north-east of Palestine, forming, along with the adjacent territory of Trachonitis, the tetrarchy of Philip (<reflink>Luke 3:1</reflink>). The present Jedur comprehends the chief part of Ituraea. It is bounded on the east by Trachonitis, on the south by Gaulanitis, on the west by Hermon, and on the north by the plain of Damascus.

ivah.d: overturning, a city of the Assyrians, whence colonists were brought to Samaria (<reflink>2 Kings 18:34; 19:13</reflink>). It lay on the Euphrates, between Sepharvaim and Henah, and is supposed by some to have been the Ahava of Ezra (8:15).

ivory.d: (Heb. pl. shenhabbim, the "tusks of elephants") was early used in decorations by the Egyptians, and a great trade in it was carried on by the Assyrians (<reflink>Ezek. 27:6; Rev. 18:12</reflink>). It was used by the Phoenicians to ornament the box-wood rowing-benches of their galleys, and Hiram's skilled workmen made Solomon's throne of ivory (<reflink>1 Kings 10:18</reflink>). It was brought by the caravans of Dedan (<reflink>Isa. 21:13</reflink>), and from the East Indies by the navy of Tarshish (<reflink>1 Kings 10:22</reflink>). Many specimens of ancient Egyptian and Assyrian ivory-work have been preserved. The word _habbim_ is derived from the Sanscrit _ibhas_, meaning "elephant," preceded by the Hebrew article (ha); and hence it is argued that Ophir, from which it and the other articles mentioned in 1 Kings 10:22 were brought, was in India.

izhar.d: oil, one of the sons of Kohath, and grandson of Levi (<reflink>Ex. 6:18, 21; Num. 16:1</reflink>).

izrahite.d: the designation of one of David's officers (<reflink>1 Chr. 27:8</reflink>).

jaakan.d: he twists, one of the sons of Ezer, the son of Seir the Horite (<reflink>1 Chr. 1:42</reflink>).

jaakobah.d: heel-catcher, a form of the name Jacob, one of the descendants of Simeon (<reflink>1 Chr. 4:36</reflink>).

jaala.d: a wild she-goat, one of the Nethinim, whose descendants returned from the Captivity (<reflink>Neh. 7:58</reflink>).

jaalam.d: concealer, the second of Esau's three sons by Aholibamah (<reflink>Gen. 36:5, 14</reflink>).

jaanai.d: mourner, one of the chief Gadites (<reflink>1 Chr. 5:12</reflink>).

jaare-oregim.d: forests of the weavers, a Bethlehemite (<reflink>2 Sam. 21:19</reflink>), and the father of Elhanan, who slew Goliath. In 1 Chr. 20:5 called JAIR.

jaasau.d: fabricator, an Israelite who renounced his Gentile wife after the Return (<reflink>Ezra 10:37</reflink>).

jaasiel.d: made by God, one of David's body-guard, the son of Abner (<reflink>1 Chr. 27:21</reflink>), called Jasiel in 1 Chr. 11:47.

jaaz-aniah.d: heard by Jehovah. (1.) The son of Jeremiah, and one of the chief Rechabites (<reflink>Jer. 35:3</reflink>).

jaazer.d: he (God) helps, a city of the Amorites on the east of Jordan, and assigned, with neighbouring places in Gilead, to Gad (<reflink>Num. 32:1, 35; Josh. 13:25</reflink>). It was allotted to the Merarite Levites (21:39). In David's time it was occupied by the Hebronites, i.e., the descendants of Kohath (<reflink>1 Chr. 26:31</reflink>). It is mentioned in the "burdens" proclaimed over Moab (<reflink>Isa. 16:8, 9; Jer. 48:32</reflink>). Its site is marked by the modern ruin called Sar or Seir, about 10 miles west of Amman, and 12 from Heshbon. "The vineyards that once covered the hill-sides are gone; and the wild Bedawin from the eastern desert make cultivation of any kind impossible."

jaaziah.d: comforted by Jehovah, a descendant of Merari the Levite (<reflink>1 Chr. 24:26,27</reflink>).

jaaziel.d: comforted by God, a Levitical musician (<reflink>1 Chr. 15:18</reflink>).
