They become stupidly secure (<reflink>comp. Ps. 55:19; Amos 6:1</reflink>). To drink the lees (<reflink>Ps. 75:8</reflink>) denotes severe suffering.

left hand.d: among the Hebrews, denoted the north (<reflink>Job 23:9; Gen. 14:15</reflink>), the face of the person being supposed to be toward the east.

left-handed.d: (<reflink>Judg. 3:15; 20:16</reflink>), one unable to use the right hand skilfully, and who therefore uses the left; and also one who uses the left as well as the right, ambidexter. Such a condition of the hands is due to physical causes. This quality was common apparently in the tribe of Benjamin.

legion.d: a regiment of the Roman army, the number of men composing which differed at different times. It originally consisted of three thousand men, but in the time of Christ consisted of six thousand, exclusive of horsemen, who were in number a tenth of the foot-men. The word is used (<reflink>Matt. 26:53; Mark 5:9</reflink>) to express simply a great multitude.

lehi.d: a jawbone, a place in the tribe of Judah where Samson achieved a victory over the Philistines (<reflink>Judg. 15:9, 14, 16</reflink>), slaying a thousand of them with the jawbone of an ass. The words in 15:19, "a hollow place that was in the jaw" (A.V.), should be, as in Revised Version, "the hollow place that is in Lehi."

lemuel.d: dedicated to God, a king whom his mother instructed (<reflink>Prov. 31:1-9</reflink>). Nothing is certainly known concerning him. The rabbis identified him with Solomon.

lentiles.d: (Heb. 'adashim), a species of vetch (<reflink>Gen. 25:34; 2 Sam. 23:11</reflink>), common in Syria under the name addas. The red pottage made by Jacob was of lentils (<reflink>Gen. 25:29-34</reflink>). They were among the provisions brought to David when he fled from Absalom (<reflink>2 Sam. 17:28</reflink>). It is the Ervum lens of Linnaeus, a leguminous plant which produces a fruit resembling a bean.

leopard.d: (Heb. namer, so called because spotted, Cant. 4:8), was that great spotted feline which anciently infested the mountains of Syria, more appropriately called a panther (Felis pardus). Its fierceness (<reflink>Isa. 11:6</reflink>), its watching for its prey (<reflink>Jer. 5:6</reflink>), its swiftness (<reflink>Hab. 1:8</reflink>), and the spots of its skin (<reflink>Jer. 13:23</reflink>), are noticed. This word is used symbolically (<reflink>Dan. 7:6; Rev. 13:2</reflink>).

leprosy.d: (Heb. tsara'ath, a "smiting," a "stroke," because the disease was regarded as a direct providential infliction). This name is from the Greek lepra, by which the Greek physicians designated the disease from its scaliness. We have the description of the disease, as well as the regulations connected with it, in Lev. 13; 14; Num. 12:10-15, etc. There were reckoned six different circumstances under which it might develop itself, (1) without any apparent cause (<reflink>Lev. 13:2-8</reflink>); (2) its reappearance (9-17); (3) from an inflammation (18-28); (4) on the head or chin (29-37); (5) in white polished spots (38, 39); (6) at the back or in the front of the head (40-44).

letter.d: in Rom. 2:27, 29 means the outward form. The "oldness of the letter" (7:6) is a phrase which denotes the old way of literal outward obedience to the law as a system of mere external rules of conduct. In 2 Cor. 3:6, "the letter" means the Mosaic law as a written law. (<see target="x-self">See WRITING.</see>)

leummim.d: peoples; nations, the last mentioned of the three sons of Dedan, and head of an Arabian tribe (<reflink>Gen. 25:3</reflink>).

levi.d: adhesion. (1.) The third son of Jacob by Leah. The origin of the name is found in Leah's words (<reflink>Gen. 29:34</reflink>), "This time will my husband be joined [Heb. yillaveh] unto me." He is mentioned as taking a prominent part in avenging his sister Dinah (<reflink>Gen. 34:25-31</reflink>). He and his three sons went down with Jacob (46:11) into Egypt, where he died at the age of one hundred and thirty-seven years (<reflink>Ex. 6:16</reflink>).

leviathan.d: a transliterated Hebrew word (livyathan), meaning "twisted," "coiled." In Job 3:8, Revised Version, and marg. of Authorized Version, it denotes the dragon which, according to Eastern tradition, is an enemy of light; in 41:1 the crocodile is meant; in Ps. 104:26 it "denotes any large animal that moves by writhing or wriggling the body, the whale, the monsters of the deep." This word is also used figuratively for a cruel enemy, as some think "the Egyptian host, crushed by the divine power, and cast on the shores of the Red Sea" (<reflink>Ps. 74:14</reflink>). As used in Isa. 27:1, "leviathan the piercing [R.V. 'swift'] serpent, even leviathan that crooked [R.V. marg. 'winding'] serpent," the word may probably denote the two empires, the Assyrian and the Babylonian.

levirate law.d: from Latin levir, "a husband's brother," the name of an ancient custom ordained by Moses, by which, when an Israelite died without issue, his surviving brother was required to marry the widow, so as to continue his brother's family through the son that might be born of that marriage (<reflink>Gen. 38:8; Deut. 25:5-10; comp. Ruth 3; 4:10</reflink>). Its object was "to raise up seed to the departed brother."

levite.d: a descendant of the tribe of Levi (<reflink>Ex. 6:25; Lev. 25:32; Num. 35:2; Josh. 21:3, 41</reflink>). This name is, however, generally used as the title of that portion of the tribe which was set apart for the subordinate offices of the sanctuary service (<reflink>1 Kings 8:4; Ezra 2:70</reflink>), as assistants to the priests.

leviticus.d: the third book of the Pentateuch; so called in the Vulgate, after the LXX., because it treats chiefly of the Levitical service.

levy.d: (<reflink>1 Kings 4:6, R.V.; 5:13</reflink>), forced service. The service of tributaries was often thus exacted by kings. Solomon raised a "great levy" of 30,000 men, about two per cent. of the population, to work for him by courses on Lebanon. Adoram (12:18) presided over this forced labour service (Ger. Frohndienst; Fr. corvee).

lewdness.d: (<reflink>Acts 18:14</reflink>), villany or wickedness, not lewdness in the modern sense of the word. The word "lewd" is from the Saxon, and means properly "ignorant," "unlearned," and hence low, vicious (<reflink>Acts 17:5</reflink>).

libertine.d: found only Acts 6:9, one who once had been a slave, but who had been set at liberty, or the child of such a person. In this case the name probably denotes those descendants of Jews who had been carried captives to Rome as prisoners of war by Pompey and other Roman generals in the Syrian wars, and had afterwards been liberated. In A.D. 19 these manumitted Jews were banished from Rome. Many of them found their way to Jerusalem, and there established a synagogue.

libnah.d: transparency; whiteness. (1.) One of the stations of the Israelites in the wilderness (<reflink>Num. 33:20, 21</reflink>).

libni.d: white, one of the two sons of Gershon, the son of Levi (<reflink>Ex. 6:17; Num. 3:18, 21</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See LAADAN (n/a</see>).)

libya.d: the country of the Ludim (<reflink>Gen. 10:13</reflink>), Northern Africa, a large tract lying along the Mediterranean, to the west of Egypt (<reflink>Acts 2:10</reflink>). Cyrene was one of its five cities.

lice.d: (Heb. kinnim), the creatures employed in the third plague sent upon Egypt (<reflink>Ex. 8:16-18</reflink>). They were miraculously produced from the dust of the land. "The entomologists Kirby and Spence place these minute but disgusting insects in the very front rank of those which inflict injury upon man. A terrible list of examples they have collected of the ravages of this and closely allied parasitic pests." The plague of lice is referred to in Ps. 105:31.

lie.d: an intentional violation of the truth. Lies are emphatically condemned in Scripture (<reflink>John 8:44; 1 Tim. 1:9, 10; Rev. 21:27; 22:15</reflink>). Mention is made of the lies told by good men, as by Abraham (<reflink>Gen. 12:12, 13; 20:2</reflink>), Isaac (26:7), and Jacob (27:24); also by the Hebrew midwives (<reflink>Ex. 1:15-19</reflink>), by Michal (<reflink>1 Sam. 19:14</reflink>), and by David (<reflink>1 Sam. 20:6</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See ANANIAS.</see>)

kenath.d: possession, a city of Gilead. It was captured by Nobah, who called it by his own name (<reflink>Num. 32:42</reflink>). It has been identified with Kunawat, on the slopes of Jebel Hauran (Mount Bashan), 60 miles east from the south end of the Sea of Galilee.

kenaz.d: hunter. (1.) One of the sons of Eliphaz, the son of Esau. He became the chief of an Edomitish tribe (<reflink>Gen. 36:11, 15, 42</reflink>).

kenites.d: smiths, the name of a tribe inhabiting the desert lying between southern Palestine and the mountains of Sinai. Jethro was of this tribe (<reflink>Judg. 1:16</reflink>). He is called a "Midianite" (<reflink>Num. 10:29</reflink>), and hence it is concluded that the Midianites and the Kenites were the same tribe. They were wandering smiths, "the gipsies and travelling tinkers of the old Oriental world. They formed an important guild in an age when the art of metallurgy was confined to a few" (Sayce's Races, etc.). They showed kindness to Israel in their journey through the wilderness. They accompanied them in their march as far as Jericho (<reflink>Judg. 1:16</reflink>), and then returned to their old haunts among the Amalekites, in the desert to the south of Judah. They sustained afterwards friendly relations with the Israelites when settled in Canaan (<reflink>Judg. 4:11, 17-21; 1 Sam. 27:10; 30:29</reflink>). The Rechabites belonged to this tribe (<reflink>1 Chr. …

kenizzite.d: (1.) The name of a tribe referred to in the covenant God made with Abraham (<reflink>Gen. 15:19</reflink>). They are not mentioned among the original inhabitants of Canaan (<reflink>Ex. 3:8; Josh. 3:10</reflink>), and probably they inhabited some part of Arabia, in the confines of Syria.

kerchief.d: mentioned only Ezek. 13:18, 21, as an article of apparel or ornament applied to the head of the idolatrous women of Israel. The precise meaning of the word is uncertain. It appears to have been a long loose shawl, such as Oriental women wrap themselves in (<reflink>Ruth 3:15; Isa. 3:22</reflink>). Some think that it was a long veil or head-dress, denoting by its form the position of those who wore it.

keren-happuch.d: horn of the face-paint = cosmetic-box, the name of Job's third daughter (<reflink>Job. 42:14</reflink>), born after prosperity had returned to him.

kerioth.d: cities. (1.) A town in the south of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:25</reflink>). Judas the traitor was probably a native of this place, and hence his name Iscariot. It has been identified with the ruins of el-Kureitein, about 10 miles south of Hebron. (<see target="x-self">See HAZOR [4]</see>).

kesitah.d: (<reflink>Gen. 33:19, R.V., marg., a Hebrew word, rendered, A.V., pl. "pieces of money," marg., "lambs;" Josh. 24:32, "pieces of silver;" Job 42:11, "piece of money"</reflink>). The kesitah was probably a piece of money of a particular weight, cast in the form of a lamb. The monuments of Egypt show that such weights were used. (<see target="x-self">See PIECES.</see>)

kettle.d: a large pot for cooking. The same Hebrew word (dud, "boiling") is rendered also "pot" (<reflink>Ps. 81:6</reflink>), "caldron" (<reflink>2 Chr. 35:13</reflink>), "basket" (<reflink>Jer. 24:2</reflink>). It was used for preparing the peace-offerings (<reflink>1 Sam. 2:13, 14</reflink>).

keturah.d: incense, the wife of Abraham, whom he married probably after Sarah's death (<reflink>Gen. 25:1-6</reflink>), by whom he had six sons, whom he sent away into the east country. Her nationality is unknown. She is styled "Abraham's concubine" (<reflink>1 Chr. 1:32</reflink>). Through the offshoots of the Keturah line Abraham became the "father of many nations."

key.d: frequently mentioned in Scripture. It is called in Hebrew _maphteah_, i.e., the opener (<reflink>Judg. 3:25</reflink>); and in the Greek New Testament _kleis_, from its use in shutting (<reflink>Matt. 16:19; Luke 11:52; Rev. 1:18, etc.</reflink>). Figures of ancient Egyptian keys are frequently found on the monuments, also of Assyrian locks and keys of wood, and of a large size (<reflink>comp. Isa. 22:22</reflink>).

kezia.d: cassia, the name of Job's second daughter (42:14), born after prosperity had returned to him.

keziz.d: abrupt; cut off, a city of the tribe of Benjamin (<reflink>Josh. 18:21</reflink>).

kibroth-hattaavah.d: the graves of the longing or of lust, one of the stations of the Israelites in the wilderness. It was probably in the Wady Murrah, and has been identified with the Erweis el-Ebeirig, where the remains of an ancient encampment have been found, about 30 miles north-east of Sinai, and exactly a day's journey from 'Ain Hudherah.

kibzaim.d: two heaps, a city of Ephraim, assigned to the Kohathite Levites, and appointed as a city of refuge (<reflink>Josh. 21: 22</reflink>). It is also called Jokmeam (<reflink>1 Chr. 6:68</reflink>).

kid.d: the young of the goat. It was much used for food (<reflink>Gen. 27:9; 38:17; Judg. 6:19; 14:6</reflink>). The Mosaic law forbade to dress a kid in the milk of its dam, a law which is thrice repeated (<reflink>Ex. 23:19; 34:26; Deut. 14:21</reflink>). Among the various reasons assigned for this law, that appears to be the most satisfactory which regards it as "a protest against cruelty and outraging the order of nature." A kid cooked in its mother's milk is "a gross, unwholesome dish, and calculated to kindle animal and ferocious passions, and on this account Moses may have forbidden it. Besides, it is even yet associated with immoderate feasting; and originally, I suspect," says Dr. Thomson (Land and the Book), "was connected with idolatrous sacrifices."

kidron.d: = Kedron = Cedron, turbid, the winter torrent which flows through the Valley of Jehoshaphat, on the eastern side of Jerusalem, between the city and the Mount of Olives. This valley is known in Scripture only by the name "the brook Kidron." David crossed this brook bare-foot and weeping, when fleeing from Absalom (<reflink>2 Sam. 15:23, 30</reflink>), and it was frequently crossed by our Lord in his journeyings to and fro (<reflink>John 18:1</reflink>). Here Asa burned the obscene idols of his mother (<reflink>1 Kings 15:13</reflink>), and here Athaliah was executed (<reflink>2 Kings 11:16</reflink>). It afterwards became the receptacle for all manner of impurities (<reflink>2 Chr. 29:16; 30:14</reflink>); and in the time of Josiah this valley was the common cemetery of the city (<reflink>2 Kings 23:6; comp. Jer. 26:23</reflink>).

kinah.d: an elegy, a city in the extreme south of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:22</reflink>). It was probably not far from the Dead Sea, in the Wady Fikreh.

kine.d: (Heb. sing. parah, i.e., "fruitful"), mentioned in Pharaoh's dream (<reflink>Gen. 41: 18</reflink>). Here the word denotes "buffaloes," which fed on the reeds and sedge by the river's brink.

king.d: is in Scripture very generally used to denote one invested with authority, whether extensive or limited. There were thirty-one kings in Canaan (<reflink>Josh. 12:9, 24</reflink>), whom Joshua subdued. Adonibezek subdued seventy kings (<reflink>Judg. 1:7</reflink>). In the New Testament the Roman emperor is spoken of as a king (<reflink>1 Pet. 2:13, 17</reflink>); and Herod Antipas, who was only a tetrarch, is also called a king (<reflink>Matt. 14:9; Mark 6:22</reflink>).

king's dale.d: mentioned only in Gen. 14:17; 2 Sam. 18:18, the name given to "the valley of Shaveh," where the king of Sodom met Abram.

kingdom of god.d: (<reflink>Matt. 6:33; Mark 1:14, 15; Luke 4:43</reflink>) = "kingdom of Christ" (<reflink>Matt. 13:41; 20:21</reflink>) = "kingdom of Christ and of God" (<reflink>Eph. 5:5</reflink>) = "kingdom of David" (<reflink>Mark 11:10</reflink>) = "the kingdom" (<reflink>Matt. 8:12; 13:19</reflink>) = "kingdom of heaven" (<reflink>Matt. 3:2; 4:17; 13:41</reflink>), all denote the same thing under different aspects, viz.: (1) Christ's mediatorial authority, or his rule on the earth; (2) the blessings and advantages of all kinds that flow from this rule; (3) the subjects of this kingdom taken collectively, or the Church.

kingly office of christ.d: one of the three special relations in which Christ stands to his people. Christ's office as mediator comprehends three different functions, viz., those of a prophet, priest, and king. These are not three distinct offices, but three functions of the one office of mediator.

kings, the books of.d: The two books of Kings formed originally but one book in the Hebrew Scriptures. The present division into two books was first made by the LXX., which now, with the Vulgate, numbers them as the third and fourth books of Kings, the two books of Samuel being the first and second books of Kings.

kinsman.d: Heb. goel, from root meaning to redeem. The goel among the Hebrews was the nearest male blood relation alive. Certain important obligations devolved upon him toward his next of kin. (1.) If any one from poverty was unable to redeem his inheritance, it was the duty of the kinsman to redeem it (<reflink>Lev. 25:25,28; Ruth 3:9, 12</reflink>). He was also required to redeem his relation who had sold himself into slavery (<reflink>Lev. 25:48, 49</reflink>).

kir.d: a wall or fortress, a place to which Tiglath-pileser carried the Syrians captive after he had taken the city of Damascus (<reflink>2 Kings 16:9; Amos 1:5; 9:7</reflink>). Isaiah (22:6), who also was contemporary with these events, mentions it along with Elam. Some have supposed that Kir is a variant of Cush (Susiana), on the south of Elam.

kir of moab.d: Isa. 15:1. The two strongholds of Moab were Ar and Kir, which latter is probably the Kir-haraseth (16:7) following.

kir-haraseth.d: built fortress, a city and fortress of Moab, the modern Kerak, a small town on the brow of a steep hill about 6 miles from Rabbath-Moab and 10 miles from the Dead Sea; called also Kir-haresh, Kir-hareseth, Kir-heres (<reflink>Isa. 16:7, 11; Jer. 48:31, 36</reflink>). After the death of Ahab, Mesha, king of Moab (<see target="x-self">see MOABITE STONE</see>), threw off allegiance to the king of Israel, and fought successfully for the independence of his kingdom. After this Jehoram, king of Israel, in seeking to regain his supremacy over Moab, entered into an alliance with Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, and with the king of Edom. The three kings led their armies against Mesha, who was driven back to seek refuge in Kir-haraseth. The Moabites were driven to despair. Mesha then took his eldest son, who would have reigned in his stead, and offered him as a burnt-offering on the wall of the fortress in the sight of the allied armies. …

kirjath.d: city, a city belonging to Benjamin (<reflink>Josh. 18:28</reflink>), the modern Kuriet el-'Enab, i.e., "city of grapes", about 7 1/2 miles west-north-west of Jerusalem.

kirjath-arba.d: city of Arba, the original name of Hebron (q.v.), so called from the name of its founder, one of the Anakim (<reflink>Gen. 23:2; 35:27; Josh. 15:13</reflink>). It was given to Caleb by Joshua as his portion. The Jews interpret the name as meaning "the city of the four", i.e., of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Adam, who were all, as they allege, buried there.

kirjath-huzoth.d: city of streets, Num. 22:39, a Moabite city, which some identify with Kirjathaim. Balak here received and entertained Balaam, whom he had invited from Pethor, among the "mountains of the east," beyond the Euphrates, to lay his ban upon the Israelites, whose progress he had no hope otherwise of arresting. It was probably from the summit of Attarus, the high place near the city, that the soothsayer first saw the encampments of Israel.

kirjath-jearim.d: city of jaars; i.e., of woods or forests, a Gibeonite town (<reflink>Josh. 9:17</reflink>) on the border of Benjamin, to which tribe it was assigned (18:15, 28). The ark was brought to this place (<reflink>1 Sam. 7:1, 2</reflink>) from Beth-shemesh and put in charge of Abinadab, a Levite. Here it remained till it was removed by David to Jerusalem (<reflink>2 Sam. 6:2, 3, 12; 1 Chr. 15:1-29; comp. Ps. 132</reflink>). It was also called Baalah (<reflink>Josh. 15:9</reflink>) and Kirjath-baal (60). It has been usually identified with Kuriet el-'Enab (i.e., "city of grapes"), among the hills, about 8 miles north-east of 'Ain Shems (i.e., Beth-shemesh). The opinion, however, that it is to be identified with 'Erma, 4 miles east of 'Ain Shems, on the edge of the valley of Sorek, seems to be better supported. (<see target="x-self">See KIRJATH.</see>)

kirjath-sannah.d: city of the sannah; i.e., of the palm(?), Josh. 15:49; the same as Kirjath-sepher (15:16; Judg. 1:11) and Debir (q.v.), a Canaanitish royal city included in Judah (<reflink>Josh. 10:38; 15:49</reflink>), and probably the chief seat of learning among the Hittites. It was about 12 miles to the south-west of Hebron.

kirjath-sepher.d: city of books, Josh. 15:15; same as Kirjath-sannah (q.v.), now represented by the valley of ed-Dhaberiyeh, south-west of Hebron. The name of this town is an evidence that the Canaanites were acquainted with writing and books. "The town probably contained a noted school, or was the site of an oracle and the residence of some learned priest." The "books" were probably engraved stones or bricks.

kirjathaim.d: two cities; a double city. (1.) A city of refuge in Naphtali (<reflink>1 Chr. 6:76</reflink>).

kish.d: a bow. (1.) A Levite of the family of Merari (<reflink>1 Chr. 23:21; 24:29</reflink>).

kishion.d: hardness, a city of Issachar assigned to the Gershonite Levites (<reflink>Josh. 19:20</reflink>), the same as Kishon (21:28).

kishon.d: winding, a winter torrent of Central Palestine, which rises about the roots of Tabor and Gilboa, and passing in a northerly direction through the plains of Esdraelon and Acre, falls into the Mediterranean at the north-eastern corner of the bay of Acre, at the foot of Carmel. It is the drain by which the waters of the plain of Esdraelon and of the mountains that surround it find their way to the sea. It bears the modern name of Nahr el-Mokattah, i.e., "the river of slaughter" (comp. 1 Kings 18:40). In the triumphal song of Deborah (<reflink>Judg. 5:21</reflink>) it is spoken of as "that ancient river," either (1) because it had flowed on for ages, or (2), according to the Targum, because it was "the torrent in which were shown signs and wonders to Israel of old;" or (3) probably the reference is to the exploits in that region among the ancient Canaanites, for the adjoining plain of Esdraelon was the great battle-field of Palestine.

kiss.d: of affection (<reflink>Gen. 27:26, 27; 29:13; Luke 7:38, 45</reflink>); reconciliation (<reflink>Gen. 33:4; 2 Sam. 14:33</reflink>); leave-taking (<reflink>Gen. 31:28,55; Ruth 1:14; 2 Sam. 19:39</reflink>); homage (<reflink>Ps. 2:12; 1 Sam. 10:1</reflink>); spoken of as between parents and children (<reflink>Gen. 27:26; 31:28, 55; 48:10; 50:1; Ex. 18:7; Ruth 1:9, 14</reflink>); between male relatives (<reflink>Gen. 29:13; 33:4; 45:15</reflink>). It accompanied social worship as a symbol of brotherly love (<reflink>Rom. 16:16; 1 Cor. 16:20; 2 Cor. 13:12; 1 Thess. 5:26; 1 Pet. 5:14</reflink>). The worship of idols was by kissing the image or the hand toward the image (<reflink>1 Kings 19:18; Hos. 13:2</reflink>).

kite.d: an unclean and keen-sighted bird of prey (<reflink>Lev. 11:14; Deut. 14:13</reflink>). The Hebrew word used, _'ayet_, is rendered "vulture" in Job 28:7 in Authorized Version, "falcon" in Revised Version. It is probably the red kite (Milvus regalis), a bird of piercing sight and of soaring habits found all over Palestine.

kithlish.d: a man's wall, a town in the plain of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:40</reflink>). It has been identified with Jelameh.

kitron.d: knotty, a city of Zebulun (<reflink>Judg. 1:30</reflink>), called also Kattath (<reflink>Josh. 19:15</reflink>); supposed to be "Cana of Galilee."

knead.d: to prepare dough in the process of baking (<reflink>Gen. 18:6; 1 Sam. 28:24; Hos. 7:4</reflink>).

kneading-trough.d: the vessel in which the dough, after being mixed and leavened, was left to swell or ferment (<reflink>Ex. 8:3; 12:34; Deut. 28:5, 7</reflink>). The dough in the vessels at the time of the Exodus was still unleavened, because the people were compelled to withdraw in haste.

knife.d: (1.) Heb. hereb, "the waster," a sharp instrument for circumcision (<reflink>Josh. 5:2, 3, lit. "knives of flint;" comp. Ex. 4:25</reflink>); a razor (<reflink>Ezek. 5:1</reflink>); a graving tool (<reflink>Ex. 20:25</reflink>); an axe (<reflink>Ezek. 26:9</reflink>).

knock.d: "Though Orientals are very jealous of their privacy, they never knock when about to enter your room, but walk in without warning or ceremony. It is nearly impossible to teach an Arab servant to knock at your door. They give warning at the outer gate either by calling or knocking. To stand and call is a very common and respectful mode. Thus Moses commanded the holder of a pledge to stand without and call to the owner to come forth (<reflink>Deut. 24:10</reflink>). This was to avoid the violent intrusion of cruel creditors. Peter stood knocking at the outer door (<reflink>Acts 12:13, 16</reflink>), and the three men sent to Joppa by Cornelius made inquiry and 'stood before the gate' (10:17, 18). The idea is that the guard over your privacy is to be placed at the entrance."

knop.d: some architectural ornament. (1.) Heb. kaphtor (<reflink>Ex. 25:31-36</reflink>), occurring in the description of the candlestick. It was an ornamental swell beneath the cups of the candlestick, probably an imitation of the fruit of the almond.

koa.d: he-camel, occurs only in Ezek. 23:23, some province or place in the Babylonian empire, used in this passage along with Shoa (q.v.).

kohath.d: assembly, the second son of Levi, and father of Amram (<reflink>Gen. 46:11</reflink>). He came down to Egypt with Jacob, and lived to the age of one hundred and thirty-three years (<reflink>Ex. 6:18</reflink>).

kohathites.d: the descendants of Kohath. They formed the first of the three divisions of the Levites (<reflink>Ex. 6:16, 18; Num. 3:17</reflink>). In the journeyings of the Israelites they had the charge of the most holy portion of the vessels of the tabernacle, including the ark (Num. 4). Their place in the marching and encampment was south of the tabernacle (<reflink>Num. 3:29, 31</reflink>). Their numbers at different times are specified (3:28; 4:36; 26:57, 62). Samuel was of this division.

korah.d: ice, hail. (1.) The third son of Esau, by Aholibamah (<reflink>Gen. 36:14; 1 Chr. 1:35</reflink>).

maath.d: small, a person named in our Lord's ancestry (<reflink>Luke 3:26</reflink>).

maaziah.d: strength or consolation of Jehovah. (1.) The head of the twenty-fourth priestly course (<reflink>1 Chr. 24:18</reflink>) in David's reign.

maccabees.d: This word does not occur in Scripture. It was the name given to the leaders of the national party among the Jews who suffered in the persecution under Antiochus Epiphanes, who succeeded to the Syrian throne B.C. 175. It is supposed to have been derived from the Hebrew word (makkabah) meaning "hammer," as suggestive of the heroism and power of this Jewish family, who are, however, more properly called Asmoneans or Hasmonaeans, the origin of which is much disputed.

maccabees, books of the.d: There were originally five books of the Maccabees. The first contains a history of the war of independence, commencing (B.C. 175) in a series of patriotic struggles against the tyranny of Antiochus Epiphanes, and terminating B.C. 135. It became part of the Vulgate Version of the Bible, and was thus retained among the Apocrypha.

macedonia.d: in New Testament times, was a Roman province lying north of Greece. It was governed by a propraetor with the title of proconsul. Paul was summoned by the vision of the "man of Macedonia" to preach the gospel there (<reflink>Acts 16:9</reflink>). Frequent allusion is made to this event (18:5; 19:21; Rom. 15:26; 2 Cor. 1:16; 11:9; Phil. 4:15). The history of Paul's first journey through Macedonia is given in detail in Acts 16:10-17:15. At the close of this journey he returned from Corinth to Syria. He again passed through this country (20:1-6), although the details of the route are not given. After many years he probably visited it for a third time (<reflink>Phil. 2:24; 1 Tim. 1:3</reflink>). The first convert made by Paul in Europe was (<reflink>Acts 16:13-15</reflink>) Lydia (q.v.), a "seller of purple," residing in Philippi, the chief city of the eastern division of Macedonia.

machaerus.d: the Black Fortress, was built by Herod the Great in the gorge of Callirhoe, one of the wadies 9 miles east of the Dead Sea, as a frontier rampart against Arab marauders. John the Baptist was probably cast into the prison connected with this castle by Herod Antipas, whom he had reproved for his adulterous marriage with Herodias. Here Herod "made a supper" on his birthday. He was at this time marching against Aretas, king of Perea, to whose daughter he had been married. During the revelry of the banquet held in the border fortress, to please Salome, who danced before him, he sent an executioner, who beheaded John, and "brought his head in a charger, and gave it to the damsel" (<reflink>Mark 6:14-29</reflink>). This castle stood "starkly bold and clear" 3,860 feet above the Dead Sea, and 2,546 above the Mediterranean. Its ruins, now called M'khaur, are still visible on the northern end of Jebel Attarus.

machbanai.d: clad with a mantle, or bond of the Lord, one of the Gadite heroes who joined David in the wilderness (<reflink>1 Chr. 12:13</reflink>).

machir.d: sold. (1.) Manasseh's oldest son (<reflink>Josh. 17:1</reflink>), or probably his only son (see 1 Chr. 7:14, 15; comp. Num. 26:29-33; Josh. 13:31). His descendants are referred to under the name of Machirites, being the offspring of Gilead (<reflink>Num. 26:29</reflink>). They settled in land taken from the Amorites (<reflink>Num. 32:39, 40; Deut. 3:15</reflink>) by a special enactment (<reflink>Num. 36:1-3; Josh. 17:3, 4</reflink>). He is once mentioned as the representative of the tribe of Manasseh east of Jordan (<reflink>Judg. 5:14</reflink>).

machpelah.d: portion; double cave, the cave which Abraham bought, together with the field in which it stood, from Ephron the Hittite, for a family burying-place (Gen. 23). It is one of those Bible localities about the identification of which there can be no doubt. It was on the slope of a hill on the east of Hebron, "before Mamre." Here were laid the bodies of Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, Jacob and Leah (<reflink>Gen. 23:19; 25:9; 49:31; 50:13</reflink>). Over the cave an ancient Christian church was erected, probably in the time of Justinian, the Roman emperor. This church has been converted into a Mohammedan mosque. The whole is surrounded by the el-Haram i.e., "the sacred enclosure," about 200 feet long, 115 broad, and of an average height of about 50. This building, from the immense size of some of its stones, and the manner in which they are fitted together, is supposed by some to have been erected in the days of David or of Solomon, while others ascribe it to the time of Herod. …

madai.d: middle land, the third "son" of Japheth (<reflink>Gen. 10:2</reflink>), the name by which the Medes are known on the Assyrian monuments.

madmannah.d: dunghill, the modern el-Minyay, 15 miles south-south-west of Gaza (<reflink>Josh. 15:31; 1 Chr. 2:49</reflink>), in the south of Judah. The Pal. Mem., however, suggest Umm Deimneh, 12 miles north-east of Beersheba, as the site.

madmen.d: ibid., a Moabite town threatened with the sword of the Babylonians (<reflink>Jer. 48:2</reflink>).

madmenah.d: ibid., a town in Benjamin, not far from Jerusalem, towards the north (<reflink>Isa. 10:31</reflink>). The same Hebrew word occurs in Isa. 25:10, where it is rendered "dunghill." This verse has, however, been interpreted as meaning "that Moab will be trodden down by Jehovah as teben [broken straw] is trodden to fragments on the threshing-floors of Madmenah."

madness.d: This word is used in its proper sense in Deut. 28:34, John 10:20, 1 Cor. 14:23. It also denotes a reckless state of mind arising from various causes, as over-study (<reflink>Eccl. 1:17; 2:12</reflink>), blind rage (<reflink>Luke 6:11</reflink>), or a depraved temper (<reflink>Eccl. 7:25; 9:3; 2 Pet. 2:16</reflink>). David feigned madness (<reflink>1 Sam. 21:13</reflink>) at Gath because he "was sore afraid of Achish."

madon.d: strife, a Canaanitish city in the north of Palestine (<reflink>Josh. 11:1; 12:19</reflink>), whose king was slain by Joshua; perhaps the ruin Madin, near Hattin, some 5 miles west of Tiberias.

magdala.d: a tower, a town in Galilee, mentioned only in Matt. 15:39. In the parallel passage in Mark 8:10 this place is called Dalmanutha. It was the birthplace of Mary called the Magdalen, or Mary Magdalene. It was on the west shore of the Lake of Tiberias, and is now probably the small obscure village called el-Mejdel, about 3 miles north-west of Tiberias. In the Talmud this city is called "the city of colour," and a particular district of it was called "the tower of dyers." The indigo plant was much cultivated here.

magdalene.d: a surname derived from Magdala, the place of her nativity, given to one of the Marys of the Gospels to distinguish her from the other Marys (<reflink>Matt. 27:56, 61; 28:1, etc.</reflink>). A mistaken notion has prevailed that this Mary was a woman of bad character, that she was the woman who is emphatically called "a sinner" (<reflink>Luke 7:36-50</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See MARY.</see>)

magic.d: The Jews seem early to have consulted the teraphim (q.v.) for oracular answers (<reflink>Judg. 18:5, 6; Zech. 10:2</reflink>). There is a remarkable illustration of this divining by teraphim in Ezek. 21:19-22. We read also of the divining cup of Joseph (<reflink>Gen. 44:5</reflink>). The magicians of Egypt are frequently referred to in the history of the Exodus. Magic was an inherent part of the ancient Egyptian religion, and entered largely into their daily life.

magicians.d: Heb. hartumim, (<reflink>dan. 1:20</reflink>) were sacred scribes who acted as interpreters of omens, or "revealers of secret things."

magistrate.d: a public civil officer invested with authority. The Hebrew shophetim, or judges, were magistrates having authority in the land (<reflink>Deut. 1:16, 17</reflink>). In Judg. 18:7 the word "magistrate" (A.V.) is rendered in the Revised Version "possessing authority", i.e., having power to do them harm by invasion. In the time of Ezra (9:2) and Nehemiah (2:16; 4:14; 13:11) the Jewish magistrates were called _seganim_, properly meaning "nobles." In the New Testament the Greek word _archon_, rendered "magistrate" (<reflink>Luke 12:58; Titus 3:1</reflink>), means one first in power, and hence a prince, as in Matt. 20:25, 1 Cor. 2:6, 8. This term is used of the Messiah, "Prince of the kings of the earth" (<reflink>Rev. 1:5</reflink>). In Acts 16:20, 22, 35, 36, 38, the Greek term _strategos_, rendered "magistrate," properly signifies the leader of an army, a general, one having military authority. …

magog.d: region of Gog, the second of the "sons" of Japheth (<reflink>Gen. 10:2; 1 Chr. 1:5</reflink>). In Ezekiel (38:2; 39:6) it is the name of a nation, probably some Scythian or Tartar tribe descended from Japheth. They are described as skilled horsemen, and expert in the use of the bow. The Latin father Jerome says that this word denotes "Scythian nations, fierce and innumerable, who live beyond the Caucasus and the Lake Maeotis, and near the Caspian Sea, and spread out even onward to India." Perhaps the name "represents the Assyrian Mat Gugi, or 'country of Gugu,' the Gyges of the Greeks" (Sayce's Races, etc.).

magor-missabib.d: fear on every side, (<reflink>Jer. 20:3</reflink>), a symbolical name given to the priest Pashur, expressive of the fate announced by the prophet as about to come upon him. Pashur was to be carried to Babylon, and there die.

mahalaleel.d: praise of God. (1.) The son of Cainan, of the line of Seth (<reflink>Gen. 5:12-17</reflink>); called Maleleel (<reflink>Luke 3:37</reflink>).

mahalath.d: a lute; lyre. (1.) The daughter of Ishmael, and third wife of Esau (<reflink>Gen. 28:9</reflink>); called also Bashemath (<reflink>Gen. 36:3</reflink>).

mahalath leannoth maschil.d: This word leannoth seems to point to some kind of instrument unknown (Ps. 88, title). The whole phrase has by others been rendered, "On the sickness of affliction: a lesson;" or, "Concerning afflictive sickness: a didactic psalm."

mahalath maschil.d: in the title of Ps. 53, denoting that this was a didactic psalm, to be sung to the accompaniment of the lute or guitar. Others regard this word "mahalath" as the name simply of an old air to which the psalm was to be sung. Others, again, take the word as meaning "sickness," and regard it as alluding to the contents of the psalm.

mahanaim.d: two camps, a place near the Jabbok, beyond Jordan, where Jacob was met by the "angels of God," and where he divided his retinue into "two hosts" on his return from Padan-aram (<reflink>Gen. 32:2</reflink>). This name was afterwards given to the town which was built at that place. It was the southern boundary of Bashan (<reflink>Josh. 13:26, 30</reflink>), and became a city of the Levites (21:38). Here Saul's son Ishbosheth reigned (<reflink>2 Sam. 2:8, 12</reflink>), while David reigned at Hebron. Here also, after a troubled reign, Ishbosheth was murdered by two of his own bodyguard (<reflink>2 Sam. 4:5-7</reflink>), who brought his head to David at Hebron, but were, instead of being rewarded, put to death by him for their cold-blooded murder. …

mahaneh-dan.d: Judg. 18:12 = "camp of Dan" 13:25 (R.V., "Mahaneh-dan"), a place behind (i.e., west of) Kirjath-jearim, where the six hundred Danites from Zorah and Eshtaol encamped on their way to capture the city of Laish, which they rebuilt and called "Dan, after the name of their father" (18:11-31). The Palestine Explorers point to a ruin called 'Erma, situated about 3 miles from the great corn valley on the east of Samson's home.

mahath.d: grasping. (1.) A Kohathite Levite, father of Elkanah (<reflink>1 Chr. 6:35</reflink>).

mahazioth.d: visions, a Kohathite Levite, chief of the twenty-third course of musicians (<reflink>1 Chr. 25:4, 30</reflink>).

maher-shalal-hash-baz.d: plunder speedeth; spoil hasteth, (<reflink>Isa. 8:1-3; comp. Zeph. 1:14</reflink>), a name Isaiah was commanded first to write in large characters on a tablet, and afterwards to give as a symbolical name to a son that was to be born to him (<reflink>Isa. 8:1, 3</reflink>), as denoting the sudden attack on Damascus and Syria by the Assyrian army.

mahlah.d: disease, one of the five daughters of Zelophehad (<reflink>Num. 27:1-11</reflink>) who had their father's inheritance, the law of inheritance having been altered in their favour.

mahlon.d: sickly, the elder of Elimelech the Bethlehemite's two sons by Naomi. He married Ruth and died childless (<reflink>Ruth 1:2, 5; 4:9, 10</reflink>), in the land of Moab.

mahol.d: dance, the father of four sons (<reflink>1 Kings 4:31</reflink>) who were inferior in wisdom only to Solomon.

mail, coat of.d: "a corselet of scales," a cuirass formed of pieces of metal overlapping each other, like fish-scales (<reflink>1 Sam. 17:5</reflink>); also (38) a corselet or garment thus encased.

main-sail.d: (Gr. artemon), answering to the modern "mizzen-sail," as some suppose. Others understand the "jib," near the prow, or the "fore-sail," as likely to be most useful in bringing a ship's head to the wind in the circumstances described (<reflink>Acts 27:40</reflink>).

makheloth.d: assemblies, a station of the Israelites in the desert (<reflink>Num. 33:25, 26</reflink>).

makkedah.d: herdsman's place, one of the royal cities of the Canaanites (<reflink>Josh. 12:16</reflink>), near which was a cave where the five kings who had confederated against Israel sought refuge (10:10-29). They were put to death by Joshua, who afterwards suspended their bodies upon five trees. It has been identified with the modern village called Sumeil, standing on a low hill about 7 miles to the north-west of Eleutheropolis (Beit Jibrin), where are ancient remains and a great cave. The Palestine Exploration surveyors have, however, identified it with el-Mughar, or "the caves," 3 miles from Jabneh and 2 1/2 southwest of Ekron, because, they say, "at this site only of all possible sites for Makkedah in the Palestine plain do caves still exist." (<see target="x-self">See ADONI-ZEDEC.</see>)

maktesh.d: mortar, a place in or near Jerusalem inhabited by silver merchants (<reflink>Zeph. 1:11</reflink>). It has been conjectured that it was the "Phoenician quarter" of the city, where the traders of that nation resided, after the Oriental custom.

malachi.d: messenger or angel, the last of the minor prophets, and the writer of the last book of the Old Testament canon (<reflink>Mal. 4:4, 5, 6</reflink>). Nothing is known of him beyond what is contained in his book of prophecies. Some have supposed that the name is simply a title descriptive of his character as a messenger of Jehovah, and not a proper name. There is reason, however, to conclude that Malachi was the ordinary name of the prophet.

malachi, prophecies of.d: The contents of the book are comprised in four chapters. In the Hebrew text the third and fourth chapters (of the A.V.) form but one. The whole consists of three sections, preceded by an introduction (<reflink>Mal. 1:1-5</reflink>), in which the prophet reminds Israel of Jehovah's love to them. The first section (1:6-2:9) contains a stern rebuke addressed to the priests who had despised the name of Jehovah, and been leaders in a departure from his worship and from the covenant, and for their partiality in administering the law. In the second (2:9-16) the people are rebuked for their intermarriages with idolatrous heathen. In the third (2:17-4:6) he addresses the people as a whole, and warns them of the coming of the God of judgment, preceded by the advent of the Messiah.

malcam.d: (<reflink>2 Sam. 12:30, Heb., R.V., "their king;" Jer. 49:1, 3, R.V.; Zeph. 1:5</reflink>), the national idol of the Ammonites. When Rabbah was taken by David, the crown of this idol was among the spoils. The weight is said to have been "a talent of gold" (above 100 lbs.). The expression probably denotes its value rather than its weight. It was adorned with precious stones.

malchi-shua.d: king of help, one of the four sons of Saul (<reflink>1 Chr. 8:33</reflink>). He perished along with his father in the battle of Gilboa (<reflink>1 Sam. 31:2</reflink>).

malchiah.d: Jehovah's king. (1.) The head of the fifth division of the priests in the time of David (<reflink>1 Chr. 24:9</reflink>).

malchus.d: reigning, the personal servant or slave of the high priest Caiaphas. He is mentioned only by John. Peter cut off his right ear in the garden of Gethsemane (<reflink>John 18:10</reflink>). But our Lord cured it with a touch (<reflink>Matt. 26:51; Mark 14:47; Luke 22:51</reflink>). This was the last miracle of bodily cure wrought by our Lord. It is not mentioned by John.

mallothi.d: my fulness, a Kohathite Levite, one of the sons of Heman the Levite (<reflink>1 Chr. 25:4</reflink>), and chief of the nineteenth division of the temple musicians (26).

mallows.d: occurs only in Job 30:4 (R.V., "saltwort"). The word so rendered (malluah, from melah, "salt") most probably denotes the Atriplex halimus of Linnaeus, a species of sea purslane found on the shores of the Dead Sea, as also of the Mediterranean, and in salt marshes. It is a tall shrubby orach, growing to the height sometimes of 10 feet. Its buds and leaves, with those of other saline plants, are eaten by the poor in Palestine.

malluch.d: reigned over, or reigning. (1.) A Levite of the family of Merari (<reflink>1 Chr. 6:44</reflink>).

mammon.d: a Chaldee or Syriac word meaning "wealth" or "riches" (<reflink>Luke 16:9-11</reflink>); also, by personification, the god of riches (<reflink>Matt. 6:24; Luke 16:9-11</reflink>).

mamre.d: manliness. (1.) An Amoritish chief in alliance with Abraham (<reflink>Gen. 14:13, 24</reflink>).

lieutenant.d: (<reflink>only in A.V. Esther 3:12; 8:9; 9:3; Ezra 8:36</reflink>), a governor or viceroy of a Persian province having both military and civil power. Correctly rendered in the Revised Version "satrap."

life.d: generally of physical life (<reflink>Gen. 2:7; Luke 16:25, etc.</reflink>); also used figuratively (1) for immortality (<reflink>Heb. 7:16</reflink>); (2) conduct or manner of life (<reflink>Rom. 6:4</reflink>); (3) spiritual life or salvation (<reflink>John 3:16, 17, 18, 36</reflink>); (4) eternal life (<reflink>Matt. 19:16, 17; John 3:15</reflink>); of God and Christ as the absolute source and cause of all life (<reflink>John 1:4; 5:26, 39; 11:25; 12:50</reflink>).

light.d: the offspring of the divine command (<reflink>Gen. 1:3</reflink>). "All the more joyous emotions of the mind, all the pleasing sensations of the frame, all the happy hours of domestic intercourse were habitually described among the Hebrews under imagery derived from light" (<reflink>1 Kings 11:36; Isa. 58:8; Esther 8:16; Ps. 97:11</reflink>). Light came also naturally to typify true religion and the felicity it imparts (<reflink>Ps. 119:105; Isa. 8:20; Matt. 4:16, etc.</reflink>), and the glorious inheritance of the redeemed (<reflink>Col. 1:12; Rev. 21:23-25</reflink>). God is said to dwell in light inaccessible (<reflink>1 Tim. 6:16</reflink>). It frequently signifies instruction (<reflink>Matt. 5:16; John 5:35</reflink>). In its highest sense it is applied to Christ as the "Sun of righteousness" (<reflink>Mal. 4:2; Luke 2:32; John 1:7-9</reflink>). God is styled "the Father of lights" (<reflink>James 1:17</reflink>). It is used of angels (<reflink>2 Cor. …

lightning.d: frequently referred to by the sacred writers (<reflink>Nah. 1:3-6</reflink>). Thunder and lightning are spoken of as tokens of God's wrath (<reflink>2 Sam. 22:15; Job 28:26; 37:4; Ps. 135:7; 144:6; Zech. 9:14</reflink>). They represent God's glorious and awful majesty (<reflink>Rev. 4:5</reflink>), or some judgment of God on the world (20:9).

lign-aloes.d: (only in pl., Heb. 'ahalim), a perfume derived from some Oriental tree (<reflink>Num. 24:6</reflink>), probably the agallochum or aloe-wood. (<see target="x-self">See ALOES</see>).

ligure.d: (Heb. leshem) occurs only in Ex. 28:19 and 39:12, as the name of a stone in the third row on the high priest's breastplate. Some have supposed that this stone was the same as the jacinth (q.v.), others that it was the opal. There is now no mineral bearing this name. The "ligurite" is so named from Liguria in Italy, where it was found.

lily.d: The Hebrew name shushan or shoshan, i.e., "whiteness", was used as the general name of several plants common to Syria, such as the tulip, iris, anemone, gladiolus, ranunculus, etc. Some interpret it, with much probability, as denoting in the Old Testament the water-lily (Nymphoea lotus of Linn.), or lotus (<reflink>Cant. 2:1, 2; 2:16; 4:5; 5:13; 6:2, 3; 7:2</reflink>). "Its flowers are large, and they are of a white colour, with streaks of pink. They supplied models for the ornaments of the pillars and the molten sea" (<reflink>1 Kings 7:19, 22, 26; 2 Chr. 4:5</reflink>). In the Canticles its beauty and fragrance shadow forth the preciousness of Christ to the Church. Groser, however (Scrip. Nat. Hist.), strongly argues that the word, both in the Old and New Testaments, denotes liliaceous plants in general, or if one genus is to be selected, that it must be the genus Iris, which is "large, vigorous, elegant in form, and gorgeous in colouring."

lime.d: The Hebrew word so rendered means "boiling" or "effervescing." From Isa. 33:12 it appears that lime was made in a kiln lighted by thorn-bushes. In Amos 2:1 it is recorded that the king of Moab "burned the bones of the king of Edom into lime." The same Hebrew word is used in Deut. 27:2-4, and is there rendered "plaster." Limestone is the chief constituent of the mountains of Syria.

linen.d: (1.) Heb., pishet, pishtah, denotes "flax," of which linen is made (<reflink>Isa. 19:9</reflink>); wrought flax, i.e., "linen cloth", Lev. 13:47, 48, 52, 59; Deut. 22:11.

lines.d: were used for measuring and dividing land; and hence the word came to denote a portion or inheritance measured out; a possession (<reflink>Ps. 16:6</reflink>).

lintel.d: (1.) Heb. mashkoph, a projecting cover (<reflink>Ex. 12:22, 23; ver. 7, "upper door post," but R.V. "lintel"</reflink>); the head-piece of a door, which the Israelites were commanded to mark with the blood of the paschal lamb.

lions.d: the most powerful of all carnivorous animals. Although not now found in Palestine, they must have been in ancient times very numerous there. They had their lairs in the forests (<reflink>Jer. 5:6; 12:8; Amos 3:4</reflink>), in the caves of the mountains (<reflink>Cant. 4:8; Nah. 2:12</reflink>), and in the canebrakes on the banks of the Jordan (<reflink>Jer. 49:19; 50:44; Zech. 11:3</reflink>).

lip.d: besides its literal sense (<reflink>Isa. 37:29, etc.</reflink>), is used in the original (saphah) metaphorically for an edge or border, as of a cup (<reflink>1 Kings 7:26</reflink>), a garment (<reflink>Ex. 28:32</reflink>), a curtain (26:4), the sea (<reflink>Gen. 22:17</reflink>), the Jordan (<reflink>2 Kings 2:13</reflink>). To "open the lips" is to begin to speak (<reflink>Job 11:5</reflink>); to "refrain the lips" is to keep silence (<reflink>Ps. 40:9; 1 Pet. 3:10</reflink>). The "fruit of the lips" (<reflink>Heb. 13:15</reflink>) is praise, and the "calves of the lips" thank-offerings (<reflink>Hos. 14:2</reflink>). To "shoot out the lip" is to manifest scorn and defiance (<reflink>Ps. 22:7</reflink>). Many similar forms of expression are found in Scripture.

litter.d: (Heb. tsab, as being lightly and gently borne), a sedan or palanquin for the conveyance of persons of rank (<reflink>Isa. 66:20</reflink>). In Num. 7:3, the words "covered wagons" are more literally "carts of the litter kind." There they denote large and commodious vehicles drawn by oxen, and fitted for transporting the furniture of the temple.

liver.d: (Heb. kabhed, "heavy;" hence the liver, as being the heaviest of the viscera, Ex. 29:13, 22; Lev. 3:4, 1, 10, 15) was burnt upon the altar, and not used as sacrificial food. In Ezek. 21:21 there is allusion, in the statement that the king of Babylon "looked upon the liver," to one of the most ancient of all modes of divination. The first recorded instance of divination (q.v.) is that of the teraphim of Laban. By the teraphim the LXX. and Josephus understood "the liver of goats." By the "caul above the liver," in Lev. 4:9; 7:4, etc., some understand the great lobe of the liver itself.

living creatures.d: as represented by Ezekiel (1-10) and John (Rev. 4, etc.), are the cherubim. They are distinguished from angels (<reflink>Rev. 15:7</reflink>); they join the elders in the "new song" (5:8, 9); they warn of danger from divine justice (<reflink>Isa. 6:3-5</reflink>), and deliver the commission to those who execute it (<reflink>Ezek. 10:2, 7</reflink>); they associate with the elders in their sympathy with the hundred and forty-four thousand who sing the new song (<reflink>Rev. 14:3</reflink>), and with the Church in the overthrow of her enemies (19:4).

lizard.d: Only in Lev. 11:30, as rendering of Hebrew _letaah_, so called from its "hiding." Supposed to be the Lacerta gecko or fan-foot lizard, from the toes of which poison exudes. (See CHAMELEON

lo-ammi.d: not my people, a symbolical name given by God's command to Hosea's second son in token of Jehovah's rejection of his people (<reflink>Hos. 1:9, 10</reflink>), his treatment of them as a foreign people. This Hebrew word is rendered by "not my people" in ver. 10; 2:23.

lo-debar.d: no pasture, (<reflink>2 Sam. 17:27</reflink>), a town in Gilead not far from Mahanaim, north of the Jabbok (9:4, 5). It is probably identical with Debir (<reflink>Josh. 13:26</reflink>).

lo-ruhamah.d: not pitied, the name of the prophet Hosea's first daughter, a type of Jehovah's temporary rejection of his people (<reflink>Hos. 1:6; 2:23</reflink>).

loan.d: The Mosaic law required that when an Israelite needed to borrow, what he asked was to be freely lent to him, and no interest was to be charged, although interest might be taken of a foreigner (<reflink>Ex. 22:25; Deut. 23:19, 20; Lev. 25:35-38</reflink>). At the end of seven years all debts were remitted. Of a foreigner the loan might, however, be exacted. At a later period of the Hebrew commonwealth, when commerce increased, the practice of exacting usury or interest on loans, and of suretiship in the commercial sense, grew up. Yet the exaction of it from a Hebrew was regarded as discreditable (<reflink>Ps. 15:5; Prov. 6:1, 4; 11:15; 17:18; 20:16; 27:13; Jer. 15:10</reflink>).

lock.d: The Hebrews usually secured their doors by bars of wood or iron (<reflink>Isa. 45:2; 1 Kings 4:3</reflink>). These were the locks originally used, and were opened and shut by large keys applied through an opening in the outside (<reflink>Judg. 3:24</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See KEY.</see>)

locust.d: There are ten Hebrew words used in Scripture to signify locust. In the New Testament locusts are mentioned as forming part of the food of John the Baptist (<reflink>Matt. 3:4; Mark 1:6</reflink>). By the Mosaic law they were reckoned "clean," so that he could lawfully eat them. The name also occurs in Rev. 9:3, 7, in allusion to this Oriental devastating insect.

lodge.d: a shed for a watchman in a garden (<reflink>Isa. 1:8</reflink>). The Hebrew name _melunah_ is rendered "cottage" (q.v.) in Isa. 24:20. It also denotes a hammock or hanging-bed.

log.d: the smallest measure for liquids used by the Hebrews (<reflink>Lev. 14:10, 12, 15, 21, 24</reflink>), called in the Vulgate sextarius. It is the Hebrew unit of measure of capacity, and is equal to the contents of six ordinary hen's eggs=the twelfth part of a him, or nearly a pint.

lois.d: the maternal grandmother of Timothy. She is commended by Paul for her faith (<reflink>2 Tim. 1:5</reflink>).

loop.d: a knotted "eye" of cord, corresponding to the "taches" or knobs in the edges of the curtains of the tabernacle, for joining them into a continuous circuit, fifty to a curtain (<reflink>Ex. 26:4, 5, 10, 11</reflink>).

lord.d: There are various Hebrew and Greek words so rendered.

lord's day.d: only once, in Rev. 1:10, was in the early Christian ages used to denote the first day of the week, which commemorated the Lord's resurrection. There is every reason to conclude that John thus used the name. (<see target="x-self">See SABBATH.</see>)

lord's prayer.d: the name given to the only form of prayer Christ taught his disciples (<reflink>Matt. 6:9-13</reflink>). The closing doxology of the prayer is omitted by Luke (11:2-4), also in the R.V. of Matt. 6:13. This prayer contains no allusion to the atonement of Christ, nor to the offices of the Holy Spirit. "All Christian prayer is based on the Lord's Prayer, but its spirit is also guided by that of His prayer in Gethsemane and of the prayer recorded John 17. The Lord's Prayer is the comprehensive type of the simplest and most universal prayer."

lord's supper.d: (<reflink>1 Cor. 11:20</reflink>), called also "the Lord's table" (10:21), "communion," "cup of blessing" (10:16), and "breaking of bread" (<reflink>Acts 2:42</reflink>).

lot.d: (Heb. goral, a "pebble"), a small stone used in casting lots (<reflink>Num. 33:54; Jonah 1:7</reflink>). The lot was always resorted to by the Hebrews with strictest reference to the interposition of God, and as a method of ascertaining the divine will (<reflink>Prov. 16:33</reflink>), and in serious cases of doubt (<reflink>Esther 3:7</reflink>). Thus the lot was used at the division of the land of Canaan among the serveral tribes (<reflink>Num. 26:55; 34:13</reflink>), at the detection of Achan (<reflink>Josh. 7:14, 18</reflink>), the election of Saul to be king (<reflink>1 Sam. 10:20, 21</reflink>), the distribution of the priestly offices of the temple service (<reflink>1 Chr. 24:3, 5, 19; Luke 1:9</reflink>), and over the two goats at the feast of Atonement (<reflink>Lev. 16:8</reflink>). Matthias, who was "numbered with the eleven" (<reflink>Acts 1:24-26</reflink>), was chosen by lot.

lotan.d: coverer, one of the sons of Seir, the Horite (<reflink>Gen. 36:20, 29</reflink>).

love.d: This word seems to require explanation only in the case of its use by our Lord in his interview with "Simon, the son of Jonas," after his resurrection (<reflink>John 21:16, 17</reflink>). When our Lord says, "Lovest thou me?" he uses the Greek word _agapas_; and when Simon answers, he uses the Greek word _philo_, i.e., "I love." This is the usage in the first and second questions put by our Lord; but in the third our Lord uses Simon's word. The distinction between these two Greek words is thus fitly described by Trench:, "_Agapan_ has more of judgment and deliberate choice; _philein_ has more of attachment and peculiar personal affection. Thus the 'Lovest thou' (Gr. agapas) on the lips of the Lord seems to Peter at this moment too cold a word, as though his Lord were keeping him at a distance, or at least not inviting him to draw near, as in the passionate yearning of his heart he desired now to do. Therefore he puts by the word and substitutes his own stronger 'I love' (Gr. …

lubims.d: the inhabitants of a thirsty or scorched land; the Lybians, an African nation under tribute to Egypt (<reflink>2 Chr. 12:3; 16:8</reflink>). Their territory was apparently near Egypt. They were probably the Mizraite Lehabim.

lucas.d: a friend and companion of Paul during his imprisonment at Rome; Luke (q.v.), the beloved physician (<reflink>Philemon 1:24; Col. 4:14</reflink>).

lucifer.d: brilliant star, a title given to the king of Babylon (<reflink>Isa. 14:12</reflink>) to denote his glory.

lucius.d: of Cyrene, a Christian teacher at Antioch (<reflink>Acts 13:1</reflink>), and Paul's kinsman (<reflink>Rom. 16:21</reflink>). His name is Latin, but his birthplace seems to indicate that he was one of the Jews of Cyrene, in North Africa.

lucre.d: from the Lat. lucrum, "gain." 1 Tim. 3:3, "not given to filthy lucre." Some MSS. have not the word so rendered, and the expression has been omitted in the Revised Version.

lud.d: (1.) The fourth son of Shem (<reflink>Gen. 10:22; 1 Chr. 1:17</reflink>), ancestor of the Lydians probably.

ludim.d: probably the same as Lud (2) (<reflink>comp. Gen. 10:13; 1 Chr. 1:11</reflink>). They are associated (<reflink>Jer. 46:9</reflink>) with African nations as mercenaries of the king of Egypt.

luhith.d: made of boards, a Moabitish place between Zoar and Horonaim (<reflink>Isa. 15:5; Jer. 48:5</reflink>).

luke.d: the evangelist, was a Gentile. The date and circumstances of his conversion are unknown. According to his own statement (<reflink>Luke 1:2</reflink>), he was not an "eye-witness and minister of the word from the beginning." It is probable that he was a physician in Troas, and was there converted by Paul, to whom he attached himself. He accompanied him to Philippi, but did not there share his imprisonment, nor did he accompany him further after his release in his missionary journey at this time (<reflink>Acts 17:1</reflink>). On Paul's third visit to Philippi (20:5, 6) we again meet with Luke, who probably had spent all the intervening time in that city, a period of seven or eight years. From this time Luke was Paul's constant companion during his journey to Jerusalem (20:6-21:18). …

luke, gospel according to.d: was written by Luke. He does not claim to have been an eye-witness of our Lord's ministry, but to have gone to the best sources of information within his reach, and to have written an orderly narrative of the facts (<reflink>Luke 1:1-4</reflink>). The authors of the first three Gospels, the synoptics, wrote independently of each other. Each wrote his independent narrative under the guidance of the Holy Spirit.

lunatic.d: probably the same as epileptic, the symptoms of which disease were supposed to be more aggravated as the moon increased. In Matt. 4:24 "lunatics" are distinguished from demoniacs. In 17:15 the name "lunatic" is applied to one who is declared to have been possessed. (<see target="x-self">See DAEMONIAC.</see>)

lust.d: sinful longing; the inward sin which leads to the falling away from God (<reflink>Rom. 1:21</reflink>). "Lust, the origin of sin, has its place in the heart, not of necessity, but because it is the centre of all moral forces and impulses and of spiritual activity." In Mark 4:19 "lusts" are objects of desire.

luz.d: a nut-bearing tree, the almond. (1.) The ancient name of a royal Canaanitish city near the site of Bethel (<reflink>Gen. 28:19; 35:6</reflink>), on the border of Benjamin (<reflink>Josh. 18:13</reflink>). Here Jacob halted, and had a prophetic vision. (<see target="x-self">See BETHEL.</see>)

lycaonia.d: an inland province of Asia Minor, on the west of Cappadocia and the south of Galatia. It was a Roman province, and its chief towns were Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe. The "speech of Lycaonia" (<reflink>Acts 14:11</reflink>) was probably the ancient Assyrian language, or perhaps, as others think, a corrupt Greek intermingled with Syriac words. Paul preached in this region, and revisited it (<reflink>Acts 16:1-6; 18:23; 19:1</reflink>).

lycia.d: a wolf, a province in the south-west of Asia Minor, opposite the island of Rhodes. It forms part of the region now called Tekeh. It was a province of the Roman empire when visited by Paul (<reflink>Acts 21:1; 27:5</reflink>). Two of its towns are mentioned, Patara (21:1, 2) and Myra (27:5).

lydda.d: a town in the tribe of Ephraim, mentioned only in the New Testament (<reflink>Acts 9:32, 35, 38</reflink>) as the scene of Peter's miracle in healing the paralytic AEneas. It lay about 9 miles east of Joppa, on the road from the sea-port to Jerusalem. In the Old Testament (<reflink>1 Chr. 8:12</reflink>) it is called Lod. It was burned by the Romans, but was afterwards rebuilt, and was known by the name of Diospolis. Its modern name is Ludd. The so-called patron saint of England, St. George, is said to have been born here.

lydia.d: (1.) Ezek. 30:5 (Heb. Lud), a province in the west of Asia Minor, which derived its name from the fourth son of Shem (<reflink>Gen. 10:22</reflink>). It was bounded on the east by the greater Phrygia, and on the west by Ionia and the AEgean Sea.

lysanias.d: tetrarch of Abilene (<reflink>Luke 3:1</reflink>), on the eastern slope of Anti-Lebanon, near the city of Damascus.

lysias, claudius.d: the chief captain (chiliarch) who commanded the Roman troops in Jerusalem, and sent Paul under guard to the procurator Felix at Caesarea (<reflink>Acts 21:31-38; 22:24-30</reflink>). His letter to his superior officer is an interesting specimen of Roman military correspondence (23:26-30). He obtained his Roman citizenship by purchase, and was therefore probably a Greek. (See CLAUDIUS

lystra.d: a town of Lycaonia, in Asia Minor, in a wild district and among a rude population. Here Paul preached the gospel after he had been driven by persecution from Iconium (<reflink>Acts 14:2-7</reflink>). Here also he healed a lame man (8), and thus so impressed the ignorant and superstitious people that they took him for Mercury, because he was the "chief speaker," and his companion Barnabas for Jupiter, probably in consequence of his stately, venerable appearance; and were proceeding to offer sacrifices to them (13), when Paul earnestly addressed them and turned their attention to the true source of all blessings. But soon after, through the influence of the Jews from Antioch in Pisidia and Iconium, they stoned Paul and left him for dead (14:19). On recovering, Paul left for Derbe; but soon returned again, through Lystra, encouraging the disciples there to steadfastness. He in all likelihood visited this city again on his third missionary tour (<reflink>Acts 18:23</reflink>). …

maachah.d: oppression, a small Syrian kingdom near Geshur, east of the Hauran, the district of Batanea (<reflink>Josh. 13:13; 2 Sam. 10:6,8; 1 Chr. 19:7</reflink>).

maaleh-acrabbim.d: ascent of the scorpions; i.e., "scorpion-hill", a pass on the south-eastern border of Palestine (<reflink>Num. 34:4; Josh. 15:3</reflink>). It is identified with the pass of Sufah, entering Palestine from the great Wady el-Fikreh, south of the Dead Sea. (See AKRABBIM

maarath.d: desolation, a place in the mountains of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:59</reflink>), probably the modern village Beit Ummar, 6 miles north of Hebron.

maaseiah.d: the work of Jehovah. (1.) One of the Levites whom David appointed as porter for the ark (<reflink>1 Chr. 15:18, 20</reflink>).

maasiai.d: work of Jehovah, one of the priests resident at Jerusalem at the Captivity (<reflink>1 Chr. 9:12</reflink>).

man.d: (1.) Heb. 'Adam, used as the proper name of the first man. The name is derived from a word meaning "to be red," and thus the first man was called Adam because he was formed from the red earth. It is also the generic name of the human race (<reflink>Gen. 1:26, 27; 5:2; 8:21; Deut. 8:3</reflink>). Its equivalents are the Latin homo and the Greek anthropos (<reflink>Matt. 5:13, 16</reflink>). It denotes also man in opposition to woman (<reflink>Gen. 3:12; Matt. 19:10</reflink>).

man of sin.d: a designation of Antichrist given in 2 Thess. 2:3-10, usually regarded as descriptive of the Papal power; but "in whomsoever these distinctive features are found, whoever wields temporal and spiritual power in any degree similar to that in which the man of sin is here described as wielding it, he, be he pope or potentate, is beyond all doubt a distinct type of Antichrist."

manaen.d: consoler, a Christian teacher at Antioch. Nothing else is known of him beyond what is stated in Acts 13:1, where he is spoken of as having been brought up with (Gr. syntrophos; rendered in R.V. "foster brother" of) Herod, i.e., Herod Antipas, the tetrach, who, with his brother Archelaus, was educated at Rome.

manasseh.d: who makes to forget. "God hath made me forget" (Heb. nashshani), Gen. 41:51. (1.) The elder of the two sons of Joseph. He and his brother Ephraim were afterwards adopted by Jacob as his own sons (48:1). There is an account of his marriage to a Syrian (<reflink>1 Chr. 7:14</reflink>); and the only thing afterwards recorded of him is, that his grandchildren were "brought up upon Joseph's knees" (<reflink>Gen. 50:23; R.V., "born upon Joseph's knees"</reflink>) i.e., were from their birth adopted by Joseph as his own children.

mandrakes.d: Hebrew dudaim; i.e., "love-plants", occurs only in Gen. 30:14-16 and Cant. 7:13. Many interpretations have been given of this word _dudaim_. It has been rendered "violets," "Lilies," "jasmines," "truffles or mushrooms," "flowers," the "citron," etc. The weight of authority is in favour of its being regarded as the Mandragora officinalis of botanists, "a near relative of the night-shades, the 'apple of Sodom' and the potato plant." It possesses stimulating and narcotic properties (<reflink>Gen. 30:14-16</reflink>). The fruit of this plant resembles the potato-apple in size, and is of a pale orange colour. It has been called the "love-apple." The Arabs call it "Satan's apple." It still grows near Jerusalem, and in other parts of Palestine.

maneh.d: portion (<reflink>Ezek. 45:12</reflink>), rendered "pound" (<reflink>1 Kings 10:17; Ezra 2:69; Neh. 7:71, 72</reflink>), a weight variously estimated, probably about 2 1/2 or 3 lbs. A maneh of gold consisted of a hundred common shekels (q.v.). (Comp. 1 Kings 10:17, and 2 Chr. 9:16).

manger.d: (<reflink>Luke 2:7, 12, 16</reflink>), the name (Gr. phatne, rendered "stall" in Luke 13:15) given to the place where the infant Redeemer was laid. It seems to have been a stall or crib for feeding cattle. Stables and mangers in our modern sense were in ancient times unknown in the East. The word here properly denotes "the ledge or projection in the end of the room used as a stall on which the hay or other food of the animals of travellers was placed." (<see target="x-self">See INN.</see>)

manna.d: Heb. man-hu, "What is that?" the name given by the Israelites to the food miraculously supplied to them during their wanderings in the wilderness (<reflink>Ex. 16:15-35</reflink>). The name is commonly taken as derived from _man_, an expression of surprise, "What is it?" but more probably it is derived from _manan_, meaning "to allot," and hence denoting an "allotment" or a "gift." This "gift" from God is described as "a small round thing," like the "hoar-frost on the ground," and "like coriander seed," "of the colour of bdellium," and in taste "like wafers made with honey." It was capable of being baked and boiled, ground in mills, or beaten in a mortar (<reflink>Ex. 16:23; Num. 11:7</reflink>). If any was kept over till the following morning, it became corrupt with worms; but as on the Sabbath none fell, on the preceding day a double portion was given, and that could be kept over to supply the wants of the Sabbath without becoming corrupt. …

manoah.d: rest, a Danite, the father of Samson (<reflink>Judg. 13:1-22, and 14:2-4</reflink>).

manslayer.d: one who was guilty of accidental homicide, and was entitled to flee to a city of refuge (<reflink>Num. 35:6, 12, 22, 23</reflink>), his compulsory residence in which terminated with the death of the high priest. (<see target="x-self">See CITY OF REFUGE.</see>)

mantle.d: (1.) Heb. 'addereth, a large over-garment. This word is used of Elijah's mantle (<reflink>1 Kings 19:13, 19; 2 Kings 2:8, 13, etc.</reflink>), which was probably a sheepskin. It appears to have been his only garment, a strip of skin or leather binding it to his loins. _'Addereth_ twice occurs with the epithet "hairy" (<reflink>Gen. 25:25; Zech. 13:4, R.V.</reflink>). It is the word denoting the "goodly Babylonish garment" which Achan coveted (<reflink>Josh. 7:21</reflink>).

maoch.d: compressed, the father of Achish, king of Gath (<reflink>1 Sam. 27:2</reflink>). Called also Maachah (<reflink>1 Kings 2:39</reflink>).

maon.d: habitation, a town in the tribe of Judah, about 7 miles south of Hebron, which gave its name to the wilderness, the district round the conical hill on which the town stood. Here David hid from Saul, and here Nabal had his possessions and his home (<reflink>1 Sam. 23:24, 25; 25:2</reflink>). "Only some small foundations of hewn stone, a square enclosure, and several cisterns are now to be seen at Maon. Are they the remains of Nabal's great establishment?" The hill is now called Tell M'ain.

mara.d: bitter; sad, a symbolical name which Naomi gave to herself because of her misfortunes (<reflink>Ruth 1:20</reflink>).

marah.d: bitterness, a fountain at the sixth station of the Israelites (<reflink>Ex. 15:23, 24; Num. 33:8</reflink>) whose waters were so bitter that they could not drink them. On this account they murmured against Moses, who, under divine direction, cast into the fountain "a certain tree" which took away its bitterness, so that the people drank of it. This was probably the 'Ain Hawarah, where there are still several springs of water that are very "bitter," distant some 47 miles from 'Ayun Mousa.

maralah.d: trembling, a place on the southern boundary of Zebulun (<reflink>Josh. 19:11</reflink>). It has been identified with the modern M'alul, about 4 miles south-west of Nazareth.

maranatha.d: (<reflink>1 Cor. 16:22</reflink>) consists of two Aramean words, Maran'athah, meaning, "our Lord comes," or is "coming." If the latter interpretation is adopted, the meaning of the phrase is, "Our Lord is coming, and he will judge those who have set him at nought." (<reflink>Comp. Phil. 4:5; James 5:8, 9.</reflink>)

marble.d: as a mineral, consists of carbonate of lime, its texture varying from the highly crystalline to the compact. In Esther 1:6 there are four Hebrew words which are rendered marble:, (1.) Shesh, "pillars of marble." But this word probably designates dark-blue limestone rather than marble. (2.) Dar, some regard as Parian marble. It is here rendered "white marble." But nothing is certainly known of it. (3.) Bahat, "red marble," probably the verd-antique or half-porphyry of Egypt. (4.) Sohareth, "black marble," probably some spotted variety of marble. "The marble pillars and tesserae of various colours of the palace at Susa came doubtless from Persia itself, where marble of various colours is found, especially in the province of Hamadan Susiana." The marble of Solomon's architectural works may have been limestone from near Jerusalem, or from Lebanon, or possibly white marble from Arabia. …

marcheshvan.d: the post-biblical name of the month which was the eighth of the sacred and the second of the civil year of the Jews. It began with the new moon of our November. It is once called Bul (<reflink>1 Kings 6:38</reflink>). Assyrian, Arah Samna, "eighth month,"

mareshah.d: possession, a city in the plain of Judah (<reflink>John. 15:44</reflink>). Here Asa defeated Zerah the Ethiopian (<reflink>2 Chr. 14:9, 10</reflink>). It is identified with the ruin el-Mer'ash, about 1 1/2 mile south of Beit Jibrin.

mark.d: the evangelist; "John whose surname was Mark" (<reflink>Acts 12:12, 25</reflink>). Mark (Marcus, Col. 4:10, etc.) was his Roman name, which gradually came to supersede his Jewish name John. He is called John in Acts 13:5, 13, and Mark in 15:39, 2 Tim. 4:11, etc.

mark, gospel according to.d: It is the current and apparently well-founded tradition that Mark derived his information mainly from the discourses of Peter. In his mother's house he would have abundant opportunities of obtaining information from the other apostles and their coadjutors, yet he was "the disciple and interpreter of Peter" specially.

market-place.d: any place of public resort, and hence a public place or broad street (<reflink>Matt. 11:16; 20:3</reflink>), as well as a forum or market-place proper, where goods were exposed for sale, and where public assemblies and trials were held (<reflink>Acts 16:19; 17:17</reflink>). This word occurs in the Old Testament only in Ezek. 27:13.

maroth.d: bitterness; i.e., "perfect grief", a place not far from Jerusalem; mentioned in connection with the invasion of the Assyrian army (<reflink>Micah 1:12</reflink>).

marriage.d: was instituted in Paradise when man was in innocence (<reflink>Gen. 2:18-24</reflink>). Here we have its original charter, which was confirmed by our Lord, as the basis on which all regulations are to be framed (<reflink>Matt. 19:4, 5</reflink>). It is evident that monogamy was the original law of marriage (<reflink>Matt. 19:5; 1 Cor. 6:16</reflink>). This law was violated in after times, when corrupt usages began to be introduced (<reflink>Gen. 4:19; 6:2</reflink>). We meet with the prevalence of polygamy and concubinage in the patriarchal age (<reflink>Gen. 16:1-4; 22:21-24; 28:8, 9; 29:23-30, etc.</reflink>). Polygamy was acknowledged in the Mosaic law and made the basis of legislation, and continued to be practised all down through the period of Jewish histroy to the Captivity, after which there is no instance of it on record.

marriage-feasts.d: (<reflink>John 2:1-11</reflink>) "lasted usually for a whole week; but the cost of such prolonged rejoicing is very small in the East. The guests sit round the great bowl or bowls on the floor, the meal usually consisting of a lamb or kid stewed in rice or barley. The most honoured guests sit nearest, others behind; and all in eating dip their hand into the one smoking mound, pieces of the thin bread, bent together, serving for spoons when necessary. After the first circle have satisfied themselves, those lower in honour sit down to the rest, the whole company being men, for women are never seen at a feast. …

mars hill.d: the Areopagus or rocky hill in Athens, north-west of the Acropolis, where the Athenian supreme tribunal and court of morals was held. From some part of this hill Paul delivered the address recorded in Acts 17:22-31. (<see target="x-self">See AREOPAGUS.</see>)

martha.d: bitterness, the sister of Lazarus and Mary, and probably the eldest of the family, who all resided at Bethany (<reflink>Luke 10:38, 40, 41; John 11:1-39</reflink>). From the residence being called "her house," some have supposed that she was a widow, and that her brother and sister lodged with her. She seems to have been of an anxious, bustling spirit, anxious to be helpful in providing the best things for the Master's use, in contrast to the quiet earnestness of Mary, who was more concerned to avail herself of the opportunity of sitting at his feet and learning of him. Afterwards at a supper given to Christ and his disciples in her house "Martha served." Nothing further is known of her.

martyr.d: one who bears witness of the truth, and suffers death in the cause of Christ (<reflink>Acts 22:20; Rev. 2:13; 17:6</reflink>). In this sense Stephen was the first martyr. The Greek word so rendered in all other cases is translated "witness." (1.) In a court of justice (<reflink>Matt. 18:16; 26:65; Acts 6:13; 7:58; Heb. 10:28; 1 Tim. 5:19</reflink>). (2.) As of one bearing testimony to the truth of what he has seen or known (<reflink>Luke 24:48; Acts 1:8, 22; Rom. 1:9; 1 Thess. 2:5, 10; 1 John 1:2</reflink>).

mary.d: Hebrew Miriam. (1.) The wife of Joseph, the mother of Jesus, called the "Virgin Mary," though never so designated in Scripture (<reflink>Matt. 2:11; Acts 1:14</reflink>). Little is known of her personal history. Her genealogy is given in Luke 3. She was of the tribe of Judah and the lineage of David (<reflink>Ps. 132:11; Luke 1:32</reflink>). She was connected by marriage with Elisabeth, who was of the lineage of Aaron (<reflink>Luke 1:36</reflink>).

maschil.d: instructing, occurs in the title of thirteen Psalms (32, 42, 44, etc.). It denotes a song enforcing some lesson of wisdom or piety, a didactic song. In Ps. 47:7 it is rendered, Authorized Version, "with understanding;" Revised Version, marg., "in a skilful psalm."

mash.d: (= Meshech 1 Chr. 1:17), one of the four sons of Aram, and the name of a tribe descended from him (<reflink>Gen. 10:23</reflink>) inhabiting some part probably of Mesopotamia. Some have supposed that they were the inhabitants of Mount Masius, the present Karja Baghlar, which forms part of the chain of Taurus.

mashal.d: entreaty, a levitical town in the tribe of Asher (<reflink>1 Chr. 6:74</reflink>); called Mishal (<reflink>Josh. 21:30</reflink>).

mason.d: an artificer in stone. The Tyrians seem to have been specially skilled in architecture (<reflink>1 Kings 5:17, 18; 2 Sam. 5:11</reflink>). This art the Hebrews no doubt learned in Egypt (<reflink>Ex. 1:11, 14</reflink>), where ruins of temples and palaces fill the traveller with wonder at the present day.

masrekah.d: vineyard of noble vines, a place in Idumea, the native place of Samlah, one of the Edomitish kings (<reflink>Gen. 36:36; 1 Chr. 1:47</reflink>).

massa.d: a lifting up, gift, one of the sons of Ishmael, the founder of an Arabian tribe (<reflink>Gen. 25:14</reflink>); a nomad tribe inhabiting the Arabian desert toward Babylonia.
