massah.d: trial, temptation, a name given to the place where the Israelites, by their murmuring for want of water, provoked Jehovah to anger against them. It is also called Meribah (<reflink>Ex. 17:7; Deut. 6:16; Ps. 95:8, 9; Heb. 3:8</reflink>).

mattan.d: gift. (1.) A priest of Baal, slain before his altar during the reformation under Jehoiada (<reflink>2 Kings 11:18</reflink>).

mattanah.d: a gift, a station of the Israelites (<reflink>Num. 21:18, 19</reflink>) between the desert and the borders of Moab, in the Wady Waleh.

mattaniah.d: gift of Jehovah. (1.) A Levite, son of Heman, the chief of the ninth class of temple singers (<reflink>1 Chr. 25:4, 16</reflink>).

mattathias.d: ibid. (1.) The son of Amos, in the genealogy of our Lord (<reflink>Luke 3:25</reflink>).

matthan.d: gift, one of our Lord's ancestry (<reflink>Matt. 1:15</reflink>).

matthat.d: gift of God. (1.) The son of Levi, and father of Heli (<reflink>Luke 3:24</reflink>).

matthew.d: gift of God, a common Jewish name after the Exile. He was the son of Alphaeus, and was a publican or tax-gatherer at Capernaum. On one occasion Jesus, coming up from the side of the lake, passed the custom-house where Matthew was seated, and said to him, "Follow me." Matthew arose and followed him, and became his disciple (<reflink>Matt. 9:9</reflink>). Formerly the name by which he was known was Levi (<reflink>Mark 2:14; Luke 5:27</reflink>); he now changed it, possibly in grateful memory of his call, to Matthew. The same day on which Jesus called him he made a "great feast" (<reflink>Luke 5:29</reflink>), a farewell feast, to which he invited Jesus and his disciples, and probably also many of old associates. He was afterwards selected as one of the twelve (6:15). His name does not occur again in the Gospel history except in the lists of the apostles. The last notice of him is in Acts 1:13. The time and manner of his death are unknown.

matthew, gospel according to.d: The author of this book was beyond a doubt the Matthew, an apostle of our Lord, whose name it bears. He wrote the Gospel of Christ according to his own plans and aims, and from his own point of view, as did also the other "evangelists."

mattithiah.d: gift of Jehovah. (1.) One of the sons of Jeduthun (<reflink>1 Chr. 25:3, 21</reflink>).

mattock.d: (1.) Heb. ma'eder, an instrument for dressing or pruning a vineyard (<reflink>Isa. 7:25</reflink>); a weeding-hoe.

maul.d: an old name for a mallet, the rendering of the Hebrew mephits (<reflink>Prov. 25:18</reflink>), properly a war-club.

mazzaroth.d: prognostications, found only Job 38:32, probably meaning "the twelve signs" (of the zodiac), as in the margin (comp. 2 Kings 23:5).

me-jarkon.d: waters of yellowness, or clear waters, a river in the tribe of Dan (<reflink>Josh. 19:46</reflink>). It has been identified with the river 'Aujeh, which rises at Antipatris.

meadow.d: (1.) Heb. ha'ahu (<reflink>Gen. 41:2, 18</reflink>), probably an Egyptain word transferred to the Hebrew; some kind of reed or water-plant. In the Revised Version it is rendered "reed-grass", i.e., the sedge or rank grass by the river side.

meah.d: an hundred, a tower in Jersalem on the east wall (<reflink>Neh. 3:1</reflink>) in the time of Nehemiah.

meals.d: are at the present day "eaten from a round table little higher than a stool, guests sitting cross-legged on mats or small carpets in a circle, and dipping their fingers into one large dish heaped with a mixture of boiled rice and other grain and meat. But in the time of our Lord, and perhaps even from the days of Amos (6:4, 7), the foreign custom had been largely introduced of having broad couches, forming three sides of a small square, the guests reclining at ease on their elbows during meals, with their faces to the space within, up and down which servants passed offering various dishes, or in the absence of servants, helping themselves from dishes laid on a table set between the couches." Geikie's Life of Christ. (<reflink>Comp. Luke 7:36-50.</reflink>) (<see target="x-self">See ABRAHAM'S BOSOM; BANQUET; FEAST.</see>)

mearah.d: a cave, a place in the northern boundary of Palestine (<reflink>Josh. 13:4</reflink>). This may be the cave of Jezzin in Lebanon, 10 miles east of Sidon, on the Damascus road; or probably, as others think, Mogheirizeh, north-east of Sidon.

measure.d: Several words are so rendered in the Authorized Version. (1.) Those which are indefinite. (a) Hok, Isa. 5:14, elsewhere "statute." (b) Mad, Job 11:9; Jer. 13:25, elsewhere "garment." (c) Middah, the word most frequently thus translated, Ex. 26:2, 8, etc. (d) Mesurah, Lev. 19:35; 1 Chr. 23:29. (e) Mishpat, Jer. 30:11, elsewhere "judgment." (f) Mithkoneth and token, Ezek. 45:11. (g) In New Testament metron, the usual Greek word thus rendered (<reflink>Matt. 7:2; 23:32; Mark 4:24</reflink>).

meat-offering.d: (Heb. minhah), originally a gift of any kind. This Hebrew word came latterly to denote an "unbloody" sacrifice, as opposed to a "bloody" sacrifice. A "drink-offering" generally accompanied it. The law regarding it is given in Lev. 2, and 6:14-23. It was a recognition of the sovereignty of God and of his bounty in giving all earthly blessings (<reflink>1 Chr. 29:10-14; Deut. 26:5-11</reflink>). It was an offering which took for granted and was based on the offering for sin. It followed the sacrifice of blood. It was presented every day with the burnt-offering (<reflink>Ex. 29:40, 41</reflink>), and consisted of flour or of cakes prepared in a special way with oil and frankincense.

mebunnai.d: construction, building of Jehovah, one of David's bodyguard (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:27; comp. 21:18</reflink>); called Sibbechai and Sibbecai (<reflink>1 Chr. 11:29; 27:11</reflink>).

medad.d: love, one of the elders nominated to assist Moses in the government of the people. He and Eldad "prophesied in the camp" (<reflink>Num. 11:24-29</reflink>).

medan.d: contention, the third son of Abraham by Keturah (<reflink>Gen. 25:2</reflink>).

mede.d: (Heb. Madai), a Median or inhabitant of Media (<reflink>Dan. 11:1</reflink>). In Gen. 10:2 the Hebrew word occurs in the list of the sons of Japheth. But probably this is an ethnic and not a personal name, and denotes simply the Medes as descended from Japheth.

medeba.d: waters of quiet, an ancient Moabite town (<reflink>Num. 21:30</reflink>). It was assigned to the tribe of Reuben (<reflink>Josh. 13:16</reflink>). Here was fought the great battle in which Joab defeated the Ammonites and their allies (<reflink>1 Chr. 19:7-15; comp. 2 Sam. 10:6-14</reflink>). In the time of Isaiah (15:2) the Moabites regained possession of it from the Ammonites. (<see target="x-self">See HANUN.</see>)

media.d: Heb. Madai, which is rendered in the Authorized Version (1) "Madai," Gen. 10:2; (2) "Medes," 2 Kings 17:6; 18:11; (3) "Media," Esther 1:3; 10:2; Isa. 21:2; Dan. 8:20; (4) "Mede," only in Dan. 11:1.

mediator.d: one who intervenes between two persons who are at variance, with a view to reconcile them. This word is not found in the Old Testament; but the idea it expresses is found in Job 9:33, in the word "daysman" (q.v.), marg., "umpire."

meekness.d: a calm temper of mind, not easily provoked (<reflink>James 3:13</reflink>). Peculiar promises are made to the meek (<reflink>Matt. 5:5; Isa. 66:2</reflink>). The cultivation of this spirit is enjoined (<reflink>Col. 3:12; 1 Tim. 6:11; Zeph. 2:3</reflink>), and is exemplified in Christ (<reflink>Matt. 11:29</reflink>), Abraham (Gen. 13; 16:5, 6) Moses (<reflink>Num. 12:3</reflink>), David (<reflink>Zech. 12:8; 2 Sam. 16:10, 12</reflink>), and Paul (<reflink>1 Cor. 9:19</reflink>).

megiddo.d: place of troops, originally one of the royal cities of the Canaanites (<reflink>Josh. 12:21</reflink>), belonged to the tribe of Manasseh (<reflink>Judg. 1:27</reflink>), but does not seem to have been fully occupied by the Israelites till the time of Solomon (<reflink>1 Kings 4:12; 9:15</reflink>).

mehetabeel.d: whose benefactor is God, the father of Delaiah, and grandfather of Shemaiah, who joined Sanballat against Nehemiah (<reflink>Neh. 6:10</reflink>).

mehetabel.d: wife of Hadad, one of the kings of Edom (<reflink>Gen. 36:39</reflink>).

mehujael.d: smitten by God, the son of Irad, and father of Methusael (<reflink>Gen. 4:18</reflink>).

mehuman.d: faithful, one of the eunchs whom Ahasuerus (Xerxes) commanded to bring in Vashti (<reflink>Esther 1:10</reflink>).

mehunims.d: habitations, (<reflink>2 Chr. 26:7; R.V. "Meunim," Vulg. Ammonitae</reflink>), a people against whom Uzziah waged a successful war. This word is in Hebrew the plural of Ma'on, and thus denotes the Maonites who inhabited the country on the eastern side of the Wady el-Arabah. They are again mentioned in 1 Chr. 4:41 (R.V.), in the reign of King Hezekiah, as a Hamite people, settled in the eastern end of the valley of Gedor, in the wilderness south of Palestine. In this passage the Authorized Version has "habitation," erroneously following the translation of Luther.

mekonah.d: a base or foundation, a town in the south of Judah (<reflink>Neh. 11:28</reflink>), near Ziklag.

melchi.d: my king. (1.) The son of Addi, and father of Neri (<reflink>Luke 3:28</reflink>). (2.) Luke 3:24.

melchizedek.d: king of righteousness, the king of Salem (q.v.). All we know of him is recorded in Gen. 14:18-20. He is subsequently mentioned only once in the Old Testament, in Ps. 110:4. The typical significance of his history is set forth in detail in the Epistle to the Hebrews, ch. 7. The apostle there points out the superiority of his priesthood to that of Aaron in these several respects, (1) Even Abraham paid him tithes; (2) he blessed Abraham; (3) he is the type of a Priest who lives for ever; (4) Levi, yet unborn, paid him tithes in the person of Abraham; (5) the permanence of his priesthood in Christ implied the abrogation of the Levitical system; (6) he was made priest not without an oath; and (7) his priesthood can neither be transmitted nor interrupted by death: "this man, because he continueth ever, hath an unchangeable priesthood."

melea.d: fulness, the son of Menan and father of Eliakim, in the genealogy of our Lord (<reflink>Luke 3:31</reflink>).

melech.d: king, the second of Micah's four sons (<reflink>1 Chr. 8:35</reflink>), and thus grandson of Mephibosheth.

melita.d: (<reflink>Acts 27:28</reflink>), an island in the Mediterranean, the modern Malta. Here the ship in which Paul was being conveyed a prisoner to Rome was wrecked. The bay in which it was wrecked now bears the name of "St. Paul's Bay", "a certain creek with a shore." It is about 2 miles deep and 1 broad, and the whole physical condition of the scene answers the description of the shipwreck given in Acts 28. It was originally colonized by Phoenicians ("barbarians," 28:2). It came into the possession of the Greeks (B.C. 736), from whom it was taken by the Carthaginians (B.C. 528). In B.C. 242 it was conquered by the Romans, and was governed by a Roman propraetor at the time of the shipwreck (<reflink>Acts 28:7</reflink>). Since 1800, when the French garrison surrendered to the English force, it has been a British dependency. The island is about 17 miles long and 9 wide, and about 60 in circumference. …

melons.d: only in Num. 11:5, the translation of the Hebrew abattihim, the LXX. and Vulgate pepones, Arabic britikh. Of this plant there are various kinds, the Egyptian melon, the Cucumus chate, which has been called "the queen of cucumbers;" the water melon, the Cucurbita citrullus; and the common or flesh melon, the Cucumus melo. "A traveller in the East who recollects the intense gratitude which a gift of a slice of melon inspired while journeying over the hot and dry plains, will readily comprehend the regret with which the Hebrews in the Arabian desert looked back upon the melons of Egypt" (Kitto).

melzar.d: probably a Persian word meaning master of wine, i.e., chief butler; the title of an officer at the Babylonian court (<reflink>Dan. 1:11, 16</reflink>) who had charge of the diet of the Hebrew youths.

memphis.d: only in Hos. 9:6, Hebrew Moph. In Isa. 19:13; Jer. 2:16; 46:14, 19; Ezek. 30:13, 16, it is mentioned under the name Noph. It was the capital of Lower, i.e., of Northern Egypt. From certain remains found half buried in the sand, the site of this ancient city has been discovered near the modern village of Minyet Rahinch, or Mitraheny, about 16 miles above the ancient head of the Delta, and 9 miles south of Cairo, on the west bank of the Nile. It is said to have been founded by Menes, the first king of Egypt, and to have been in circumference about 19 miles. "There are few remains above ground," says Manning (The Land of the Pharaohs), "of the splendour of ancient Memphis. The city has utterly disappeared. If any traces yet exist, they are buried beneath the vast mounds of crumbling bricks and broken pottery which meet the eye in every direction. Near the village of Mitraheny is a colossal statue of Rameses the Great. …

memucan.d: dignified, one of the royal counsellors at the court of Ahasuerus, by whose suggestion Vashti was divorced (<reflink>Esther 1:14, 16, 21</reflink>).

menahem.d: conforting, the son of Gadi, and successor of Shallum, king of Israel, whom he slew. After a reign of about ten years (B.C. 771-760) he died, leaving the throne to his son Pekahiah. His reign was one of cruelty and oppression (<reflink>2 Kings 15:14-22</reflink>). During his reign, Pul (q.v.), king of Assyria, came with a powerful force against Israel, but was induced to retire by a gift from Menahem of 1,000 talents of silver.

mene.d: (<reflink>Dan. 5:25, 26</reflink>), numbered, one of the words of the mysterious inscription written "upon the plaister of the wall" in Belshazzar's palace at Babylon. The writing was explained by Daniel. (<see target="x-self">See BELSHAZZAR.</see>)

meni.d: Isa. 65:11, marg. (A.V., "that number;" R.V., "destiny"), probably an idol which the captive Israelites worshipped after the example of the Babylonians. It may have been a symbol of destiny. LXX., tuche.

meonenim.d: (<reflink>Judg. 9:37; A.V., "the plain of Meonenim;" R.V., "the oak of Meonenim"</reflink>) means properly "soothsayers" or "sorcerers," "wizards" (<reflink>Deut. 18:10, 14; 2 Kings 21:6; Micah 5:12</reflink>). This may be the oak at Shechem under which Abram pitched his tent (<see target="x-self">see SHECHEM</see>), the "enchanter's oak," so called, perhaps, from Jacob's hiding the "strange gods" under it (<reflink>Gen. 35:4</reflink>).

mephaath.d: splendour, a Levitical city (<reflink>Josh. 21:37</reflink>) of the tribe of Reuben (13:18).

mephibosheth.d: exterminator of shame; i.e., of idols. (1.) The name of Saul's son by the concubine Rizpah (q.v.), the daughter of Aiah. He and his brother Armoni were with five others "hanged on a hill before the Lord" by the Gibeonites, and their bodies exposed in the sun for five months (<reflink>2 Sam. 21:8-10</reflink>). (2.) The son of Jonathan, and grandson of Saul (<reflink>2 Sam. 4:4</reflink>). He was but five years old when his father and grandfather fell on Mount Gilboa. The child's nurse hearing of this calamity, fled with him from Gibeah, the royal residence, and stumbling in her haste, the child was thrown to the ground and maimed in both his feet, and ever after was unable to walk (19:26). He was carried to the land of Gilead, where he found a refuge in the house of Machir, the son of Ammiel, at Lo-debar, by whom he was brought up.

merab.d: increase, the eldest of Saul's two daughters (<reflink>1 Sam. 14:49</reflink>). She was betrothed to David after his victory over Goliath, but does not seem to have entered heartily into this arrangement (18:2, 17, 19). She was at length, however, married to Adriel of Abel-Meholah, a town in the Jordan valley, about 10 miles south of Bethshean, with whom the house of Saul maintained alliance. She had five sons, who were all put to death by the Gibeonites on the hill of Gibeah (<reflink>2 Sam. 21:8</reflink>).

meraiah.d: resistance, a chief priest, a contemporary of the high priest Joiakim (<reflink>Neh. 12:12</reflink>).

meraioth.d: rebellions. (1.) Father of Amariah, a high priest of the line of Eleazar (<reflink>1 Chr. 6:6, 7, 52</reflink>).

merari.d: sad; bitter, the youngest son of Levi, born before the descent of Jacob into Egypt, and one of the seventy who accompanied him thither (<reflink>Gen. 46:11; Ex. 6:16</reflink>). He became the head of one of the great divisions of the Levites (<reflink>Ex. 6:19</reflink>). (See MERARITES

merarites.d: the descendants of Merari (<reflink>Num. 26:57</reflink>). They with the Gershonites and the Kohathites had charge of the tabernacle, which they had to carry from place to place (<reflink>Num. 3:20, 33-37; 4:29-33</reflink>). In the distribution of the oxen and waggons offered by the princes (Num. 7), Moses gave twice as many to the Merarites (four waggons and eight oxen) as he gave to the Gershonites, because the latter had to carry only the lighter furniture of the tabernacle, such as the curtains, hangings, etc., while the former had to carry the heavier portion, as the boards, bars, sockets, pillars, etc., and consequently needed a greater supply of oxen and waggons. This is a coincidence illustrative of the truth of the narrative. Their place in marching and in the camp was on the north of the tabernacle. The Merarites afterwards took part with the other Levitical families in the various functions of their office (<reflink>1 Chr. 23:6, 21-23; 2 Chr. 29:12, 13</reflink>). …

merathaim.d: double rebellion, probably a symbolical name given to Babylon (<reflink>Jer. 50:21</reflink>), denoting rebellion exceeding that of other nations.

midianite.d: an Arabian tribe descended from Midian. They inhabited principally the desert north of the peninsula of Arabia. The peninsula of Sinai was the pasture-ground for their flocks. They were virtually the rulers of Arabia, being the dominant tribe. Like all Arabians, they were a nomad people. They early engaged in commercial pursuits. It was to one of their caravans that Joseph was sold (<reflink>Gen. 37:28, 36</reflink>). The next notice of them is in connection with Moses' flight from Egypt (<reflink>Ex. 2:15-21</reflink>). Here in Midian Moses became the servant and afterwards the son-in-law of Reuel or Jethro, the priest. After the Exodus, the Midianites were friendly to the Israelites so long as they traversed only their outlying pasture-ground on the west of the Arabah; but when, having passed the southern end of Edom, they entered into the land of Midian proper, they joined with Balak, the king of Moab, in a conspiracy against them (<reflink>Num. 22:4-7</reflink>). …

midwife.d: The two midwives mentioned in Ex. 1:15 were probably the superintendents of the whole class.

migdal-edar.d: tower of the flock, a place 2 miles south of Jerusalem, near the Bethlehem road (<reflink>Gen. 35:21</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See EDAR.</see>)

migdal-el.d: tower of God, a fortified city of Naphtali (<reflink>Josh. 19:38</reflink>), supposed by some to be identical with Magdala (q.v.).

migdal-gad.d: tower of fortune, a town in the plains of Judah, probably the modern el-Mejdel, a little to the north-east of Ascalon (<reflink>Josh. 15:37</reflink>).

migdol.d: tower. (1.) A strongly-fortified place 12 miles from Pelusium, in the north of Egypt (<reflink>Jer. 44:1; 46:14</reflink>). This word is rendered "tower" in Ezek. 29:10, but the margin correctly retains the name Migdol, "from Migdol to Syene;" i.e., from Migdol in the north to Syene in the south, in other words, the whole of Egypt.

migron.d: precipice or landslip, a place between Aiath and Michmash (<reflink>Isa. 10:28</reflink>). The town of the same name mentioned in 1 Sam. 14:2 was to the south of this.

mikloth.d: staves. (1.) An officer under Dodai, in the time of David and Solomon (<reflink>1 Chr. 27:4</reflink>).

milaiai.d: eloquent, a Levitical musician (<reflink>Neh. 12:36</reflink>) who took part in the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem.

mildew.d: (the rendering of a Hebrew word meaning "to be yellow," yellowness), the result of cutting east winds blighting and thus rendering the grain unproductive (<reflink>Deut. 28:22; 1 Kings 8:37; 2 Chr. 6:28</reflink>).

mile.d: (from Lat. mille, "a thousand;" Matt. 5:41), a Roman measure of 1,000 paces of 5 feet each. Thus the Roman mile has 1618 yards, being 142 yards shorter than the English mile.

miletus.d: (Miletum, 2 Tim. 4:20), a seaport town and the ancient capital of Ionia, about 36 miles south of Ephesus. On his voyage from Greece to Syria, Paul touched at this port, and delivered that noble and pathetic address to the elders ("presbyters," ver. 28) of Ephesus recorded in Acts 20:15-35. The site of Miletus is now some 10 miles from the coast. (See EPHESIANS, EPISTLE TO

milk.d: (1.) Hebrew halabh, "new milk", milk in its fresh state (<reflink>Judg. 4:19</reflink>). It is frequently mentioned in connection with honey (<reflink>Ex. 3:8; 13:5; Josh. 5:6; Isa. 7:15, 22; Jer. 11:5</reflink>). Sheep (<reflink>Deut. 32:14</reflink>) and goats (<reflink>Prov. 27:27</reflink>) and camels (<reflink>Gen. 32:15</reflink>), as well as cows, are made to give their milk for the use of man. Milk is used figuratively as a sign of abundance (<reflink>Gen. 49:12; Ezek. 25:4; Joel 3:18</reflink>). It is also a symbol of the rudiments of doctrine (<reflink>1 Cor. 3:2; Heb. 5:12, 13</reflink>), and of the unadulterated word of God (<reflink>1 Pet. 2:2</reflink>).

mill.d: for grinding corn, mentioned as used in the time of Abraham (<reflink>Gen. 18:6</reflink>). That used by the Hebrews consisted of two circular stones, each 2 feet in diameter and half a foot thick, the lower of which was called the "nether millstone" (<reflink>Job 41:24</reflink>) and the upper the "rider." The upper stone was turned round by a stick fixed in it as a handle. There were then no public mills, and thus each family required to be provided with a hand-mill. The corn was ground daily, generally by the women of the house (<reflink>Isa. 47:1, 2; Matt. 24:41</reflink>). It was with the upper stone of a hand-mill that "a certain woman" at Thebez broke Abimelech's skull (<reflink>Judg. 9:53, "a piece of a millstone;" literally, "a millstone rider", i.e., the "runner," the stone which revolves. Comp. 2 Sam. 11:21</reflink>). Millstones could not be pledged (<reflink>Deut. 24:6</reflink>), as they were necessary in every family.

millennium.d: a thousand years; the name given to the era mentioned in Rev. 20:1-7. Some maintain that Christ will personally appear on earth for the purpose of establishing his kingdom at the beginning of this millennium. Those holding this view are usually called "millenarians." On the other hand, it is maintained, more in accordance with the teaching of Scripture, we think, that Christ's second advent will not be premillennial, and that the right conception of the prospects and destiny of his kingdom is that which is taught, e.g., in the parables of the leaven and the mustard-seed. The triumph of the gospel, it is held, must be looked for by the wider and more efficient operation of the very forces that are now at work in extending the gospel; and that Christ will only come again at the close of this dispensation to judge the world at the "last day." The millennium will thus precede his coming.

millet.d: (Heb. dohan; only in Ezek. 4:9), a small grain, the produce of the Panicum miliaceum of botanists. It is universally cultivated in the East as one of the smaller corn-grasses. This seed is the cenchros of the Greeks. It is called in India warree, and by the Arabs dukhan, and is extensively used for food, being often mixed with other grain. In this country it is only used for feeding birds.

millo.d: (Heb. always with the article, "the" Millo). (1.) Probably the Canaanite name of some fortification, consisting of walls filled in with earth and stones, which protected Jerusalem on the north as its outermost defence. It is always rendered Akra i.e., "the citadel", in the LXX. It was already existing when David conquered Jerusalem (<reflink>2 Sam. 5:9</reflink>). He extended it to the right and left, thus completing the defence of the city. It was rebuilt by Solomon (<reflink>1 Kings 9:15, 24; 11:27</reflink>) and repaired by Hezekiah (<reflink>2 Chr. 32:5</reflink>).

mincing.d: (Heb. taphoph, Isa. 3:16), taking affectedly short and quick steps. Luther renders the word by "wag" or "waggle," thus representing "the affected gait of coquettish females."

mine.d: The process of mining is described in Job 28:1-11. Moses speaks of the mineral wealth of Palestine (<reflink>Deut. 8:9</reflink>). Job 28:4 is rightly thus rendered in the Revised Version, "He breaketh open a shaft away from where men sojourn; they are forgotten of the foot [that passeth by]; they hang afar from men, they swing to and fro." These words illustrate ancient mining operations.

minister.d: one who serves, as distinguished from the master. (1.) Heb. meshereth, applied to an attendant on one of superior rank, as to Joshua, the servant of Moses (<reflink>Ex. 33:11</reflink>), and to the servant of Elisha (<reflink>2 Kings 4:43</reflink>). This name is also given to attendants at court (<reflink>2 Chr. 22:8</reflink>), and to the priests and Levites (<reflink>Jer. 33:21; Ezek. 44:11</reflink>).

minni.d: only in Jer. 51:27, as the name of a province in Armenia, which was at this time under the Median kings. Armenia is regarded by some as = Har-minni i.e., the mountainous country of Minni. (<see target="x-self">See ARMENIA.</see>)

minnith.d: distribution, an Ammonitish town (<reflink>Judg. 11:33</reflink>) from which wheat was exported to Tyre (<reflink>Ezek. 27:17</reflink>). It was probably somewhere in the Mishor or table-land on the east of Jordan. There is a gentle valley running for about 4 miles east of Dhiban called Kurm Dhiban, "the vineyards of Dibon." Tristram supposes that this may be the "vineyards" mentioned in Judg. (l.c.).

minstrel.d: (<reflink>Matt. 9:23</reflink>), a flute-player. Such music was a usual accompaniment of funerals. In 2 Kings 3:15 it denotes a player on a stringed instrument.

mint.d: (Gr. heduosmon, i.e., "having a sweet smell"), one of the garden herbs of which the Pharisees paid tithes (<reflink>Matt. 23:23; Luke 11:42</reflink>). It belongs to the labiate family of plants. The species most common in Syria is the Mentha sylvestris, the wild mint, which grows much larger than the garden mint (M. sativa). It was much used in domestic economy as a condiment, and also as a medicine. The paying of tithes of mint was in accordance with the Mosiac law (<reflink>Deut. 14:22</reflink>), but the error of the Pharisees lay in their being more careful about this little matter of the mint than about weightier matters.

miracle.d: an event in the external world brought about by the immediate agency or the simple volition of God, operating without the use of means capable of being discerned by the senses, and designed to authenticate the divine commission of a religious teacher and the truth of his message (<reflink>John 2:18; Matt. 12:38</reflink>). It is an occurrence at once above nature and above man. It shows the intervention of a power that is not limited by the laws either of matter or of mind, a power interrupting the fixed laws which govern their movements, a supernatural power.

miriam.d: their rebellion. (1.) The sister of Moses and Aaron (<reflink>Ex. 2:4-10; 1 Chr. 6:3</reflink>). Her name is prominent in the history of the Exodus. She is called "the prophetess" (<reflink>Ex. 15:20</reflink>). She took the lead in the song of triumph after the passage of the Red Sea. She died at Kadesh during the second encampment at that place, toward the close of the wanderings in the wilderness, and was buried there (<reflink>Num. 20:1</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See AARON; MOSES.</see>)

misdeem.d: (<reflink>Deut. 32:27, R.V.</reflink>). The Authorized Version reads, "should behave themselves strangely;" i.e., not recognize the truth, misunderstand or mistake the cause of Israel's ruin, which was due to the fact that God had forsaken them on account of their apostasy.

misgab.d: height, a town of Moab, or simply, the height=the citadel, some fortress so called; or perhaps a general name for the highlands of Moab, as some think (<reflink>Jer. 48:1</reflink>). In Isa. 25:12, the word is rendered "high fort."

mishael.d: who is like God! (1.) A Levite; the eldest of the three sons of Uzziel (<reflink>Ex. 6:22</reflink>).

mishal.d: a city of the tribe of Asher (<reflink>Josh. 21:30; 1 Chr. 6:74</reflink>). It is probably the modern Misalli, on the shore near Carmel.

misham.d: their cleansing or their beholding, a Benjamite, one of the sons of Elpaal (<reflink>1 Chr. 8:12</reflink>).

misheal.d: (<reflink>Josh. 19:26</reflink>), a town of Asher, probably the same as Mishal.

mishma.d: hearing. (1.) One of the sons of Ishmael (<reflink>Gen. 25:14</reflink>), and founder of an Arab tribe.

mishmannah.d: fatness, one of the Gadite heroes who gathered to David at Ziklag (<reflink>1 Chr. 12:10</reflink>).

misrephoth-maim.d: burning of waters, supposed to be salt-pans, or lime-kilns, or glass-factories, a place to which Joshua pursued a party of Canaanites after the defeat of Jabin (<reflink>Josh. 11:8</reflink>). It is identified with the ruin Musheirifeh, at the promontory of en-Nakhurah, some 11 miles north of Acre.

mite.d: contraction of minute, from the Latin minutum, the translation of the Greek word lepton, the very smallest bronze of copper coin (<reflink>Luke 12:59; 21:2</reflink>). Two mites made one quadrans, i.e., the fourth part of a Roman as, which was in value nearly a halfpenny. (<see target="x-self">See FARTHING.</see>)

mithcah.d: sweetness, one of the stations of the Israelites in the wilderness (<reflink>Num. 33:28, 29</reflink>).

mithredath.d: given by Mithra, or dedicated to Mithra, i.e., the sun, the Hebrew form of the Greek name Mithridates. (1.) The "treasurer" of King Cyrus (<reflink>Ezra 1:8</reflink>).

mitre.d: (Heb. mitsnepheth), something rolled round the head; the turban or head-dress of the high priest (<reflink>Ex. 28:4, 37, 39; 29:6, etc.</reflink>). In the Authorized Version of Ezek. 21:26, this Hebrew word is rendered "diadem," but in the Revised Version, "mitre." It was a twisted band of fine linen, 8 yards in length, coiled into the form of a cap, and worn on official occasions (<reflink>Lev. 8:9; 16:4; Zech. 3:5</reflink>). On the front of it was a golden plate with the inscription, "Holiness to the Lord." The mitsnepheth differed from the mitre or head-dress (migba'ah) of the common priest. (<see target="x-self">See BONNET.</see>)

mitylene.d: the chief city of the island of Lesbos, on its east coast, in the AEgean Sea. Paul, during his third missionary journey, touched at this place on his way from Corinth to Judea (<reflink>Acts 20:14</reflink>), and here tarried for a night. It lies between Assos and Chios. It is now under the Turkish rule, and bears the name of Metelin.

mixed multitude.d: (<reflink>Ex. 12:38</reflink>), a class who accompanied the Israelites as they journeyed from Rameses to Succoth, the first stage of the Exodus. These were probably miscellaneous hangers-on to the Hebrews, whether Egyptians of the lower orders, or the remains of the Hyksos (<see target="x-self">see EGYPT; MOSES</see>), as some think. The same thing happened on the return of the Jews from Babylon (<reflink>Neh. 13:3</reflink>), a "mixed multitude" accompanied them so far.

mizar.d: smallness, a summit on the eastern ridge of Lebanon, near which David lay after escaping from Absalom (<reflink>Ps. 42:6</reflink>). It may, perhaps, be the present Jebel Ajlun, thus named, "the little", in contrast with the greater elevation of Lebanon and Hermon.

mizpah.d: or Miz'peh, watch-tower; the look-out. (1.) A place in Gilead, so named by Laban, who overtook Jacob at this spot (<reflink>Gen. 31:49</reflink>) on his return to Palestine from Padan-aram. Here Jacob and Laban set up their memorial cairn of stones. It is the same as Ramath-mizpeh (<reflink>Josh. 13:26</reflink>).

mizpar.d: number, one of the Jews who accompanied Zerubbabel from Babylon (<reflink>Ezra 2:2</reflink>); called also Mispereth (<reflink>Neh. 7:7</reflink>).

mizraim.d: the dual form of matzor, meaning a "mound" or "fortress," the name of a people descended from Ham (<reflink>Gen. 10:6, 13; 1 Chr. 1:8, 11</reflink>). It was the name generally given by the Hebrews to the land of Egypt (q.v.), and may denote the two Egypts, the Upper and the Lower. The modern Arabic name for Egypt is Muzr.

mizzah.d: despair, one of the four sons of Reuel, the son of Esau (<reflink>Gen. 36:13, 17</reflink>).

merchant.d: The Hebrew word so rendered is from a root meaning "to travel about," "to migrate," and hence "a traveller." In the East, in ancient times, merchants travelled about with their merchandise from place to place (<reflink>Gen. 37:25; Job 6:18</reflink>), and carried on their trade mainly by bartering (<reflink>Gen. 37:28; 39:1</reflink>). After the Hebrews became settled in Palestine they began to engage in commercial pursuits, which gradually expanded (49:13; Deut. 33:18; Judg. 5:17), till in the time of Solomon they are found in the chief marts of the world (<reflink>1 Kings 9:26; 10:11, 26, 28; 22:48; 2 Chr. 1:16; 9:10, 21</reflink>). After Solomon's time their trade with foreign nations began to decline. After the Exile it again expanded into wider foreign relations, because now the Jews were scattered in many lands.

mercurius.d: the Hermes (i.e., "the speaker") of the Greeks (<reflink>Acts 14:12</reflink>), a heathen God represented as the constant attendant of Jupiter, and the god of eloquence. The inhabitants of Lystra took Paul for this god because he was the "chief speaker."

mercy.d: compassion for the miserable. Its object is misery. By the atoning sacrifice of Christ a way is open for the exercise of mercy towards the sons of men, in harmony with the demands of truth and righteousness (<reflink>Gen. 19:19; Ex. 20:6; 34:6, 7; Ps. 85:10; 86:15, 16</reflink>). In Christ mercy and truth meet together. Mercy is also a Christian grace (<reflink>Matt. 5:7; 18:33-35</reflink>).

mercy-seat.d: (Heb. kapporeth, a "covering;" LXX. and N.T., hilasterion; Vulg., propitiatorium), the covering or lid of the ark of the covenant (q.v.). It was of acacia wood, overlaid with gold, or perhaps rather a plate of solid gold, 2 1/2 cubits long and 1 1/2 broad (<reflink>Ex. 25:17; 30:6; 31:7</reflink>). It is compared to the throne of grace (<reflink>Heb. 9:5; Eph. 2:6</reflink>). The holy of holies is called the "place of the mercy-seat" (<reflink>1 Chr. 28:11: Lev. 16:2</reflink>).

mered.d: rebellion, one of the sons of Ezra, of the tribe of Judah (<reflink>1 Chr. 4:17</reflink>).

meremoth.d: exaltations, heights, a priest who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel (<reflink>Neh. 12:3</reflink>), to whom were sent the sacred vessels (<reflink>Ezra 8:33</reflink>) belonging to the temple. He took part in rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem (<reflink>Neh. 3:4</reflink>).

merib-baal.d: contender with Baal, (<reflink>1 Chr. 8:34; 9:40</reflink>), elsewhere called Mephibosheth (<reflink>2 Sam. 4:4</reflink>), the son of Jonathan.

meribah.d: quarrel or strife. (1.) One of the names given by Moses to the fountain in the desert of Sin, near Rephidim, which issued from the rock in Horeb, which he smote by the divine command, "because of the chiding of the children of Israel" (<reflink>Ex. 17:1-7</reflink>). It was also called Massah (q.v.). It was probably in Wady Feiran, near Mount Serbal.

merodach.d: death; slaughter, the name of a Babylonian god, probably the planet Mars (<reflink>Jer. 50:2</reflink>), or it may be another name of Bel, the guardian divinity of Babylon. This name frequently occurs as a surname to the kings of Assyria and Babylon.

merodach-baladan.d: Merodach has given a son, (<reflink>Isa. 39:1</reflink>), "the hereditary chief of the Chaldeans, a small tribe at that time settled in the marshes at the mouth of the Euphrates, but in consequence of his conquest of Babylon afterwards, they became the dominant caste in Babylonia itself." One bearing this name sent ambassadors to Hezekiah (B.C. 721). He is also called Berodach-baladan (<reflink>2 Kings 20:12; 2 Chr. 20:31</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See HEZEKIAH.</see>)

merom.d: height, a lake in Northern Palestine through which the Jordan flows. It was the scene of the third and last great victory gained by Joshua over the Canaanites (<reflink>Josh. 11:5-7</reflink>). It is not again mentioned in Scripture. Its modern name is Bakrat el-Huleh. "The Ard el-Huleh, the centre of which the lake occupies, is a nearly level plain of 16 miles in length from north to south, and its breadth from east to west is from 7 to 8 miles. On the west it is walled in by the steep and lofty range of the hills of Kedesh-Naphtali; on the east it is bounded by the lower and more gradually ascending slopes of Bashan; on the north it is shut in by a line of hills hummocky and irregular in shape and of no great height, and stretching across from the mountains of Naphtali to the roots of Mount Hermon, which towers up at the north-eastern angle of the plain to a height of 10,000 feet. …

meronothite.d: a name given to Jehdeiah, the herdsman of the royal asses in the time of David and Solomon (<reflink>1 Chr. 27:30</reflink>), probably as one being a native of some unknown town called Meronoth.

meroz.d: a plain in the north of Palestine, the inhabitants of which were severely condemned because they came not to help Barak against Sisera (<reflink>Judg. 5:23: comp. 21:8-10; 1 Sam. 11:7</reflink>). It has been identified with Marassus, on a knoll to the north of Wady Jalud, but nothing certainly is known of it. Like Chorazin, it is only mentioned in Scripture in connection with the curse pronounced upon it.

mesha.d: middle district, Vulgate, Messa. (1.) A plain in that part of the boundaries of Arabia inhabited by the descendants of Joktan (<reflink>Gen. 10:30</reflink>).

meshach.d: the title given to Mishael, one of the three Hebrew youths who were under training at the Babylonian court for the rank of Magi (<reflink>Dan. 1:7; 2:49; 3:12-30</reflink>). This was probably the name of some Chaldean god.

meshech.d: drawing out, the sixth son of Japheth (<reflink>Gen. 10:2</reflink>), the founder of a tribe (<reflink>1 Chr. 1:5; Ezek. 27:13; 38:2,3</reflink>). They were in all probability the Moschi, a people inhabiting the Moschian Mountains, between the Black and the Caspian Seas. In Ps. 120:5 the name occurs as simply a synonym for foreigners or barbarians. "During the ascendency of the Babylonians and Persians in Western Asia, the Moschi were subdued; but it seems probable that a large number of them crossed the Caucasus range and spread over the northern steppes, mingling with the Scythians. There they became known as Muscovs, and gave that name to the Russian nation and its ancient capital by which they are still generally known throughout the East"

meshelemiah.d: friendship of Jehovah, a Levite of the family of the Korhites, called also Shelemiah (<reflink>1 Chr. 9:21; 26:1, 2, 9, 14</reflink>). He was a temple gate-keeper in the time of David.

meshillemoth.d: requitals. (1.) The father of Berechiah (<reflink>2 Chr. 28:12</reflink>).

meshullam.d: befriended. (1.) One of the chief Gadites in Bashan in the time of Jotham (<reflink>1 Chr. 5:13</reflink>).

meshullemeth.d: friend, the wife of Manasseh, and the mother of Amon (<reflink>2 Kings 21:19</reflink>), Kings of Judah.

mesopotamia.d: the country between the two rivers (Heb. Aram-naharaim; i.e., "Syria of the two rivers"), the name given by the Greeks and Romans to the region between the Euphrates and the Tigris (<reflink>Gen. 24:10; Deut. 23:4; Judg. 3:8, 10</reflink>). In the Old Testament it is mentioned also under the name "Padan-aram;" i.e., the plain of Aram, or Syria (<reflink>Gen. 25:20</reflink>). The northern portion of this fertile plateau was the original home of the ancestors of the Hebrews (Gen. 11; Acts 7:2). From this region Isaac obtained his wife Rebecca (<reflink>Gen. 24:10, 15</reflink>), and here also Jacob sojourned (28:2-7) and obtained his wives, and here most of his sons were born (35:26; 46:15). The petty, independent tribes of this region, each under its own prince, were warlike, and used chariots in battle. They maintained their independence till after the time of David, when they fell under the dominion of Assyria, and were absorbed into the empire (<reflink>2 Kings 19:13</reflink>).

mess.d: a portion of food given to a guest (<reflink>Gen. 43:34; 2 Sam. 11:8</reflink>).

messenger.d: (Heb. mal'ak, Gr. angelos), an angel, a messenger who runs on foot, the bearer of despatches (<reflink>Job 1:14; 1 Sam. 11:7; 2 Chr. 36:22</reflink>); swift of foot (<reflink>2 Kings 9:18</reflink>).

messiah.d: (Heb. mashiah), in all the thirty-nine instances of its occurring in the Old Testament, is rendered by the LXX. "Christos." It means anointed. Thus priests (<reflink>Ex. 28:41; 40:15; Num. 3:3</reflink>), prophets (<reflink>1 Kings 19:16</reflink>), and kings (<reflink>1 Sam. 9:16; 16:3; 2 Sam. 12:7</reflink>) were anointed with oil, and so consecrated to their respective offices. The great Messiah is anointed "above his fellows" (<reflink>Ps. 45:7</reflink>); i.e., he embraces in himself all the three offices. The Greek form "Messias" is only twice used in the New Testament, in John 1:41 and 4:25 (R.V., "Messiah"), and in the Old Testament the word Messiah, as the rendering of the Hebrew, occurs only twice (<reflink>Dan 9:25, 26; R.V., "the anointed one"</reflink>).

metheg-ammah.d: bridle of the mother, a figurative name for a chief city, as in 2 Sam. 8:1, "David took Metheg-ammah out of the hand of the Philistines" (R.V., "took the bridle of the mother-city"); i.e., subdued their capital or strongest city, viz., Gath (<reflink>1 Chr. 18:1</reflink>).

methusael.d: champion of El; man of God, a descendant of Cain (<reflink>Gen. 4:18</reflink>), so called, perhaps, to denote that even among the descendants of Cain God had not left himself without a witness.

methuselah.d: man of the dart, the son of Enoch, and grandfather of Noah. He was the oldest man of whom we have any record, dying at the age of nine hundred and sixty-nine years, in the year of the Flood (<reflink>Gen. 5:21-27; 1 Chr. 1:3</reflink>).

mezahab.d: water of gold, the father of Matred (<reflink>Gen. 36:39; 1 Chr. 1:50</reflink>), and grandfather of Mehetabel, wife of Hadar, the last king of Edom.

miamin.d: =Mijamin, from the right hand. (1.) The head of one of the divisions of the priests (<reflink>1 Chr. 24:9</reflink>).

mibhar.d: choice, a Hagarene, one of David's warriors (<reflink>1 Chr. 11:38</reflink>); called also Bani the Gadite (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:36</reflink>).

mibsam.d: fragrance. (1.) One of Ishmael's twelve sons, and head of an Arab tribe (<reflink>Gen. 25:13</reflink>).

mibzar.d: fortress, one of the Edomitish "dukes" descended from Esau (<reflink>Gen. 36:42; 1 Chr. 1:53</reflink>).

micah.d: a shortened form of Micaiah, who is like Jehovah? (1.) A man of Mount Ephraim, whose history so far is introduced in Judg. 17, apparently for the purpose of leading to an account of the settlement of the tribe of Dan in Northern Palestine, and for the purpose also of illustrating the lawlessness of the times in which he lived (Judg. 18; 19:1-29; 21:25).

micah, book of.d: the sixth in order of the so-called minor prophets. The superscription to this book states that the prophet exercised his office in the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. If we reckon from the beginning of Jotham's reign to the end of Hezekiah's (B.C. 759-698), then he ministered for about fifty-nine years; but if we reckon from the death of Jotham to the accession of Hezekiah (B.C. 743-726), his ministry lasted only sixteen years. It has been noticed as remarkable that this book commences with the last words of another prophet, "Micaiah the son of Imlah" (<reflink>1 Kings 22:28</reflink>): "Hearken, O people, every one of you."

micaiah.d: who is like Jehovah?, the son of Imlah, a faithful prophet of Samaria (<reflink>1 Kings 22:8-28</reflink>). Three years after the great battle with Ben-hadad (20:29-34), Ahab proposed to Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, that they should go up against Ramoth-Gilead to do battle again with Ben-hadad. Jehoshaphat agreed, but suggested that inquiry should be first made "at the word of Jehovah." Ahab's prophets approved of the expedition; but Jehoshaphat, still dissatisfied, asked if there was no other prophet besides the four hundred that had appeared, and was informed of this Micaiah. He was sent for from prison, where he had been confined, probably on account of some prediction disagreeable to Ahab; and he condemned the expedition, and prophesied that it would end, as it did, in disaster. We hear nothing further of this prophet. Some have supposed that he was the unnamed prophet referred to in 1 Kings 20:35-42.

michael.d: who is like God? (1.) The title given to one of the chief angels (<reflink>Dan. 10:13, 21; 12:1</reflink>). He had special charge of Israel as a nation. He disputed with Satan (<reflink>Jude 1:9</reflink>) about the body of Moses. He is also represented as warning against "that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world" (<reflink>Rev. 12:7-9</reflink>).

michaiah.d: (1.) The queen-mother of King Abijah (<reflink>2 Chr. 13:2</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See MAACAH [4]</see>).

michal.d: rivulet, or who as God?, the younger of Saul's two daughters by his wife Ahinoam (<reflink>1 Sam. 14:49, 50</reflink>). "Attracted by the graces of his person and the gallantry of his conduct, she fell in love with David and became his wife" (18:20-28). She showed her affection for him by promoting his escape to Naioth when Saul sought his life (<reflink>1 Sam. 19:12-17. Comp. Ps. 59. See TERAPHIM</reflink>). After this she did not see David for many years. Meanwhile she was given in marriage to another man, Phalti or Phaltiel of Gallim (<reflink>1 Sam. 25:44</reflink>), but David afterwards formally reclaimed her as his lawful wife (<reflink>2 Sam. 3:13-16</reflink>). The relation between her and David soon after this was altered. They became alienated from each other. This happened on that memorable day when the ark was brought up in great triumph from its temporary resting-place to the Holy City. …

michmash.d: something hidden, a town of Benjamin (<reflink>Ezra 2:27</reflink>), east of Bethel and south of Migron, on the road to Jerusalem (<reflink>Isa. 10:28</reflink>). It lay on the line of march of an invading army from the north, on the north side of the steep and precipitous Wady es-Suweinit ("valley of the little thorn-tree" or "the acacia"), and now bears the name of Mukhmas. This wady is called "the passage of Michmash" (<reflink>1 Sam. 13:23</reflink>). Immediately facing Mukhmas, on the opposite side of the ravine, is the modern representative of Geba, and behind this again are Ramah and Gibeah.

michmethah.d: hiding-place, a town in the northern border of Ephraim and Manasseh, and not far west of Jordan (<reflink>Josh. 16:6; 17:7</reflink>).

michri.d: prize of Jehovah, a Benjamite, the father of Uzzi (<reflink>1 Chr. 9:8</reflink>).

michtam.d: writing; i.e., a poem or song found in the titles of Ps. 16; 56-60. Some translate the word "golden", i.e., precious. It is rendered in the LXX. by a word meaning "tablet inscription" or a "stelograph." The root of the word means to stamp or grave, and hence it is regarded as denoting a composition so precious as to be worthy to be engraven on a durable tablet for preservation; or, as others render, "a psalm precious as stamped gold," from the word _kethem_, "fine or stamped gold."

middin.d: measures, one of the six cities "in the wilderness," on the west of the Dead Sea, mentioned along with En-gedi (<reflink>Josh. 15:61</reflink>).

midian.d: strife, the fourth son of Abraham by Keturah, the father of the Midianites (<reflink>Gen. 25:2; 1 Chr. 1:32</reflink>).

olympas.d: a Roman Christian whom Paul salutes (<reflink>Rom. 16:15</reflink>).

omar.d: eloquent, the son of Eliphaz, who was Esau's eldest son (<reflink>Gen. 36:11-15</reflink>).

omega.d: (<reflink>Rev. 1:8</reflink>), the last letter in the Greek alphabet. (See A

omer.d: a handful, one-tenth of an ephah=half a gallon dry measure (<reflink>Ex. 16:22, 32, 33, 36</reflink>)="tenth deal."

omri.d: servant of Jehovah. When Elah was murdered by Zimri at Tirzah (<reflink>1 Kings 16:15-27</reflink>), Omri, his captain, was made king (B.C. 931). For four years there was continued opposition to his reign, Tibni, another claimant to the throne, leading the opposing party; but at the close of that period all his rivals were defeated, and he became king of Israel, "Tibni died and Omri reigned" (B.C. 927). By his vigour and power he gained great eminence and consolidated the kingdom. He fixed his dynasty on the throne so firmly that it continued during four succeeding reigns. Tirza was for six years the seat of his government. He then removed the capital to Samaria (q.v.), where he died, and was succeeded by his son Ahab. "He wrought evil in the eyes of the Lord, and did worse than all that were before him."

on.d: light; the sun, (<reflink>Gen. 41:45, 50</reflink>), the great seat of sun-worship, called also Bethshemesh (<reflink>Jer. 43:13</reflink>) and Aven (<reflink>Ezek. 30:17</reflink>), stood on the east bank of the Nile, a few miles north of Memphis, and near Cairo, in the north-east. The Vulgate and the LXX. Versions have "Heliopolis" ("city of the sun") instead of On in Genesis and of Aven in Ezekiel. The "city of destruction" Isaiah speaks of (19:18, marg. "of Heres;" Heb. 'Ir-ha-heres, which some MSS. read Ir-ha-heres, i.e., "city of the sun") may be the name given to On, the prophecy being that the time will come when that city which was known as the "city of the sun-god" shall become the "city of destruction" of the sun-god, i.e., when idolatry shall cease, and the worship of the true God be established.

onan.d: strong, the second son of Judah (<reflink>Gen. 38:4-10; comp. Deut. 25:5; Matt. 22:24</reflink>). He died before the going down of Jacob and his family into Egypt.

onesimus.d: useful, a slave who, after robbing his master Philemon (q.v.) at Colosse, fled to Rome, where he was converted by the apostle Paul, who sent him back to his master with the epistle which bears his name. In it he beseeches Philemon to receive his slave as a "faithful and beloved brother." Paul offers to pay to Philemon anything his slave had taken, and to bear the wrong he had done him. He was accompanied on his return by Tychicus, the bearer of the Epistle to the Colossians (<reflink>Philemon 1:16, 18</reflink>).

onesiphorus.d: bringing profit, an Ephesian Christian who showed great kindness to Paul at Rome. He served him in many things, and had oft refreshed him. Paul expresses a warm interest in him and his household (<reflink>2 Tim. 1:16-18; 4:19</reflink>).

onion.d: The Israelites in the wilderness longed for the "onions and garlick of Egypt" (<reflink>Num. 11:5</reflink>). This was the _betsel_ of the Hebrews, the Allium cepe of botanists, of which it is said that there are some thirty or forty species now growing in Palestine. The onion is "the 'undivided' leek, _unio_, _unus_, one."

ono.d: a town of Benjamin, in the "plain of Ono" (<reflink>1 Chr. 8:12; Ezra 2:33</reflink>); now Kefr 'Ana, 5 miles north of Lydda, and about 30 miles north-west of Jerusalem. Not succeeding in their attempts to deter Nehemiah from rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem, Sanballat and Tobiah resorted to strategem, and pretending to wish a conference with him, they invited him to meet them at Ono. Four times they made the request, and every time Nehemiah refused to come. Their object was to take him prisoner.

onycha.d: a nail; claw; hoof, (Heb. sheheleth; Ex. 30:34), a Latin word applied to the operculum, i.e., the claw or nail of the strombus or wing-shell, a univalve common in the Red Sea. The opercula of these shell-fish when burned emit a strong odour "like castoreum." This was an ingredient in the sacred incense.

onyx.d: a hail; claw; hoof, (Heb. shoham), a precious stone adorning the breast-plate of the high priest and the shoulders of the ephod (<reflink>Ex. 28:9-12, 20; 35:27; Job 28:16; Ezek. 28:13</reflink>). It was found in the land of Havilah (<reflink>Gen. 2:12</reflink>). The LXX. translates the Hebrew word by smaragdos, an emerald. Some think that the sardonyx is meant. But the onyx differs from the sardonyx in this, that while the latter has two layers (black and white) the former has three (black, white, and red).

open place.d: Gen. 38:14, 21, mar. Enaim; the same probably as Enam (<reflink>Josh. 15:34</reflink>), a city in the lowland or Shephelah.

ophel.d: hill; mound, the long, narrow, rounded promontory on the southern slope of the temple hill, between the Tyropoeon and the Kedron valley (<reflink>2 Chr. 27:3; 33:14; Neh. 3:26, 27</reflink>). It was surrounded by a separate wall, and was occupied by the Nethinim after the Captivity. This wall has been discovered by the engineers of the Palestine Exploration Fund at the south-eastern angle of the temple area. It is 4 feet below the present surface. In 2 Kings 5:24 this word is translated "tower" (R.V., "hill"), denoting probably some eminence near Elisha's house.

ophir.d: (1.) One of the sons of Joktan (<reflink>Gen. 10:29</reflink>).

ophrah.d: a fawn. 1 Chr. 4:14. (1.) A city of Benjamin (<reflink>Josh. 18:23</reflink>); probably identical with Ephron (<reflink>2 Chr. 13:19</reflink>) and Ephraim (<reflink>John 11:54</reflink>).

oracle.d: In the Old Testament used in every case, except 2 Sam. 16:23, to denote the most holy place in the temple (<reflink>1 Kings 6:5, 19-23; 8:6</reflink>). In 2 Sam. 16:23 it means the Word of God. A man inquired "at the oracle of God" by means of the Urim and Thummim in the breastplate on the high priest's ephod. In the New Testament it is used only in the plural, and always denotes the Word of God (<reflink>Rom. 3:2; Heb. 5:12, etc.</reflink>). The Scriptures are called "living oracles" (<reflink>comp. Heb. 4:12</reflink>) because of their quickening power (<reflink>Acts 7:38</reflink>).

oreb.d: raven, a prince of Midian, who, being defeated by Gideon and put to straits, was slain along with Zeeb (<reflink>Judg. 7:20-25</reflink>). Many of the Midianites perished along with him (<reflink>Ps. 83:9; Isa. 10:26</reflink>).

oreb, the rock of.d: the place where Gideon slew Oreb after the defeat of the Midianites (<reflink>Judg. 7:25; Isa. 10:26</reflink>). It was probably the place now called Orbo, on the east of Jordan, near Bethshean.

oren.d: ash or pine, the son of Jerahmeel (<reflink>1 Chr. 2:25</reflink>).

organ.d: some kind of wind instrument, probably a kind of Pan's pipes (<reflink>Gen. 4:21; Job 21:12; Ps. 150:4</reflink>), which consisted of seven or eight reeds of unequal length.

orion.d: Heb. Kesil; i.e., "the fool", the name of a constellation (<reflink>Job 9:9; 38:31; Amos 5:8</reflink>) consisting of about eighty stars. The Vulgate renders thus, but the LXX. renders by Hesperus, i.e., "the evening-star," Venus. The Orientals "appear to have conceived of this constellation under the figure of an impious giant bound upon the sky." This giant was, according to tradition, Nimrod, the type of the folly that contends against God. In Isa. 13:10 the plural form of the Hebrew word is rendered "constellations."

orpah.d: forelock or fawn, a Moabitess, the wife of Chilion (<reflink>Ruth 1:4; 4:10</reflink>). On the death of her husband she accompanied Naomi, her mother-in-law, part of the way to Bethlehem, and then returned to Moab.

orphans.d: (<reflink>Lam. 5:3</reflink>), i.e., desolate and without protectors. The word occurs only here. In John 14:18 the word there rendered "comfortless" (R.V., "desolate;" marg., "orphans") properly means "orphans." The same Greek word is rendered "fatherless" in James 1:27.

osprey.d: Heb. 'ozniyyah, an unclean bird according to the Mosaic law (<reflink>Lev. 11:13; Deut. 14:12</reflink>); the fish-eating eagle (Pandion haliaetus); one of the lesser eagles. But the Hebrew word may be taken to denote the short-toed eagle (Circaetus gallicus of Southern Europe), one of the most abundant of the eagle tribe found in Palestine.

ossifrage.d: Heb. peres = to "break" or "crush", the lammer-geier, or bearded vulture, the largest of the whole vulture tribe. It was an unclean bird (<reflink>Lev. 11:13; Deut. 14:12</reflink>). It is not a gregarious bird, and is found but rarely in Palestine. "When the other vultures have picked the flesh off any animal, he comes in at the end of the feast, and swallows the bones, or breaks them, and swallows the pieces if he cannot otherwise extract the marrow. The bones he cracks [hence the appropriateness of the name ossifrage, i.e., "bone-breaker"] by letting them fall on a rock from a great height. He does not, however, confine himself to these delicacies, but whenever he has an opportunity will devour lambs, kids, or hares. These he generally obtains by pushing them over cliffs, when he has watched his opportunity; and he has been known to attack men while climbing rocks, and dash them against the bottom. …

ostrich.d: (<reflink>Lam. 4:3</reflink>), the rendering of Hebrew pl. enim; so called from its greediness and gluttony. The allusion here is to the habit of the ostrich with reference to its eggs, which is thus described: "The outer layer of eggs is generally so ill covered that they are destroyed in quantities by jackals, wild-cats, etc., and that the natives carry them away, only taking care not to leave the marks of their footsteps, since, when the ostrich comes and finds that her nest is discovered, she crushes the whole brood, and builds a nest elsewhere." In Job 39:13 this word in the Authorized Version is the rendering of a Hebrew word (notsah) which means "feathers," as in the Revised Version. In the same verse the word "peacocks" of the Authorized Version is the rendering of the Hebrew pl. renanim, properly meaning "ostriches," as in the Revised Version. (<see target="x-self">See OWL [1].</see>)

othni.d: a lion of Jehovah, a son of Shemaiah, and one of the temple porters in the time of David (<reflink>1 Chr. 26:7</reflink>). He was a "mighty man of valour."

othniel.d: lion of God, the first of the judges. His wife Achsah was the daughter of Caleb (<reflink>Josh. 15:16, 17; Judg. 1:13</reflink>). He gained her hand as a reward for his bravery in leading a successful expedition against Debir (q.v.). Some thirty years after the death of Joshua, the Israelites fell under the subjection of Chushan-rishathaim (q.v.), the king of Mesopotamia. He oppressed them for full eight years, when they "cried" unto Jehovah, and Othniel was raised up to be their deliverer. He was the younger brother of Caleb (<reflink>Judg. 3:8, 9-11</reflink>). He is the only judge mentioned connected with the tribe of Judah. Under him the land had rest forty years.

ouches.d: an Old English word denoting cavities or sockets in which gems were set (<reflink>Ex. 28:11</reflink>).

oven.d: Heb. tannur, (<reflink>Hos. 7:4</reflink>). In towns there appear to have been public ovens. There was a street in Jerusalem (<reflink>Jer. 37:21</reflink>) called "bakers' street" (the only case in which the name of a street in Jerusalem is preserved). The words "tower of the furnaces" (<reflink>Neh. 3:11; 12:38</reflink>) is more properly "tower of the ovens" (Heb. tannurim). These resemble the ovens in use among ourselves.

owl.d: (1.) Heb. bath-haya'anah, "daughter of greediness" or of "shouting." In the list of unclean birds (<reflink>Lev. 11:16; Deut. 14:15</reflink>); also mentioned in Job 30:29; Isa. 13:21; 34:13; 43:20; Jer. 50:39; Micah 1:8. In all these passages the Revised Version translates "ostrich" (q.v.), which is the correct rendering.

ox.d: Heb. bakar, "cattle;" "neat cattle", (<reflink>Gen. 12:16; 34:28; Job 1:3, 14; 42:12, etc.</reflink>); not to be muzzled when treading the corn (<reflink>Deut. 25:4</reflink>). Referred to by our Lord in his reproof to the Pharisees (<reflink>Luke 13:15; 14:5</reflink>).

ox goad.d: mentioned only in Judg. 3:31, the weapon with which Shamgar (q.v.) slew six hundred Philistines. "The ploughman still carries his goad, a weapon apparently more fitted for the hand of the soldier than the peaceful husbandman. The one I saw was of the 'oak of Bashan,' and measured upwards of ten feet in length. At one end was an iron spear, and at the other a piece of the same metal flattened. One can well understand how a warrior might use such a weapon with effect in the battle-field" (Porter's Syria, etc.). (<see target="x-self">See GOAD.</see>)

ozem.d: strong. (1.) One of David's brothers; the sixth son of Jesse (<reflink>1 Chr. 2:15</reflink>).

ozias.d: son of Joram (<reflink>Matt. 1:8</reflink>); called also Uzziah (<reflink>2 Kings 15:32, 34</reflink>).

ozni.d: hearing, one of the sons of Gad; also called Ezbon (<reflink>Gen. 46:16; Num. 26:16</reflink>).

paarai.d: opening of the Lord, "the Arbite," one of David's heroes (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:35</reflink>); called also Naarai, 1 Chr. 11:37.

padan.d: a plain, occurring only in Gen. 48:7, where it designates Padan-aram.

mnason.d: reminding, or remembrancer, a Christian of Jerusalem with whom Paul lodged (<reflink>Acts 21:16</reflink>). He was apparently a native of Cyprus, like Barnabas (11:19, 20), and was well known to the Christians of Caesarea (4:36). He was an "old disciple" (R.V., "early disciple"), i.e., he had become a Christian in the beginning of the formation of the Church in Jerusalem.

moab.d: the seed of the father, or, according to others, the desirable land, the eldest son of Lot (<reflink>Gen. 19:37</reflink>), of incestuous birth.

moabite.d: the designation of a tribe descended from Moab, the son of Lot (<reflink>Gen. 19:37</reflink>). From Zoar, the cradle of this tribe, on the south-eastern border of the Dead Sea, they gradually spread over the region on the east of Jordan. Rameses II., the Pharaoh of the Oppression, enumerates Moab (Muab) among his conquests. Shortly before the Exodus, the warlike Amorites crossed the Jordan under Sihon their king and drove the Moabites (<reflink>Num. 21:26-30</reflink>) out of the region between the Arnon and the Jabbok, and occupied it, making Heshbon their capital. They were then confined to the territory to the south of the Arnon.

moabite stone.d: a basalt stone, bearing an inscription by King Mesha, which was discovered at Dibon by Klein, a German missionary at Jerusalem, in 1868. It was 3 1/2 feet high and 2 in breadth and in thickness, rounded at the top. It consisted of thirty-four lines, written in Hebrew-Phoenician characters. It was set up by Mesha as a record and memorial of his victories. It records (1) Mesha's wars with Omri, (2) his public buildings, and (3) his wars against Horonaim. This inscription in a remarkable degree supplements and corroborates the history of King Mesha recorded in 2 Kings 3:4-27.

moladah.d: birth, a city in the south of Judah which fell to Simeon (<reflink>Josh. 15:21-26; 19:2</reflink>). It has been identified with the modern el-Milh, 10 miles east of Beersheba.

mole.d: Heb. tinshameth (<reflink>Lev. 11:30</reflink>), probably signifies some species of lizard (rendered in R.V., "chameleon"). In Lev. 11:18, Deut. 14:16, it is rendered, in Authorized Version, "swan" (R.V., "horned owl").

moloch.d: king, the name of the national god of the Ammonites, to whom children were sacrificed by fire. He was the consuming and destroying and also at the same time the purifying fire. In Amos 5:26, "your Moloch" of the Authorized Version is "your king" in the Revised Version (<reflink>comp. Acts 7:43</reflink>). Solomon (<reflink>1 Kings 11:7</reflink>) erected a high place for this idol on the Mount of Olives, and from that time till the days of Josiah his worship continued (<reflink>2 Kings 23:10, 13</reflink>). In the days of Jehoahaz it was partially restored, but after the Captivity wholly disappeared. He is also called Molech (<reflink>Lev. 18:21; 20:2-5, etc.</reflink>), Milcom (<reflink>1 Kings 11:5, 33, etc.</reflink>), and Malcham (<reflink>Zeph. 1:5</reflink>). This god became Chemosh among the Moabites.

money.d: Of uncoined money the first notice we have is in the history of Abraham (<reflink>Gen. 13:2; 20:16; 24:35</reflink>). Next, this word is used in connection with the purchase of the cave of Machpelah (23:16), and again in connection with Jacob's purchase of a field at Shalem (<reflink>Gen. 33:18, 19</reflink>) for "an hundred pieces of money"=an hundred Hebrew kesitahs (q.v.), i.e., probably pieces of money, as is supposed, bearing the figure of a lamb.

money-changer.d: (<reflink>Matt. 21:12; Mark 11:15; John 2:15</reflink>). Every Israelite from twenty years and upwards had to pay (<reflink>Ex. 30:13-15</reflink>) into the sacred treasury half a shekel every year as an offering to Jehovah, and that in the exact Hebrew half-shekel piece. There was a class of men, who frequented the temple courts, who exchanged at a certain premium foreign moneys for these half-shekels to the Jews who came up to Jerusalem from all parts of the world. (<see target="x-self">See PASSOVER.</see>) When our Lord drove the traffickers out of the temple, these money-changers fared worst. Their tables were overturned and they themselves were expelled.

month.d: Among the Egyptians the month of thirty days each was in use long before the time of the Exodus, and formed the basis of their calculations. From the time of the institution of the Mosaic law the month among the Jews was lunar. The cycle of religious feasts depended on the moon. The commencement of a month was determined by the observation of the new moon. The number of months in the year was usually twelve (<reflink>1 Kings 4:7; 1 Chr. 27:1-15</reflink>); but every third year an additional month (ve-Adar) was inserted, so as to make the months coincide with the seasons.

moon.d: heb. yareah, from its paleness (<reflink>Ezra 6:15</reflink>), and lebanah, the "white" (<reflink>Cant. 6:10; Isa. 24:23</reflink>), was appointed by the Creator to be with the sun "for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and years" (<reflink>Gen. 1:14-16</reflink>). A lunation was among the Jews the period of a month, and several of their festivals were held on the day of the new moon. It is frequently referred to along with the sun (<reflink>Josh. 10:12; Ps. 72:5, 7, 17; 89:36, 37; Eccl. 12:2; Isa. 24:23, etc.</reflink>), and also by itself (<reflink>Ps. 8:3; 121:6</reflink>).

mordecai.d: the son of Jair, of the tribe of Benjamin. It has been alleged that he was carried into captivity with Jeconiah, and hence that he must have been at least one hundred and twenty-nine years old in the twelfth year of Ahasuerus (Xerxes). But the words of Esther do not necessarily lead to this conclusion. It was probably Kish of whom it is said (ver. 6) that he "had been carried away with the captivity."

moreh.d: an archer, teacher; fruitful. (1.) A Canaanite probably who inhabited the district south of Shechem, between Mounts Ebal and Gerizim, and gave his name to the "plain" there (<reflink>Gen. 12:6</reflink>). Here at this "plain," or rather (R.V.) "oak," of Moreh, Abraham built his first altar in the land of Palestine; and here the Lord appeared unto him. He afterwards left this plain and moved southward, and pitched his tent between Bethel on the west and Hai on the east (<reflink>Gen. 12:7, 8</reflink>).

moreh, the hill of.d: probably identical with "little Hermon," the modern Jebel ed-Duhy, or perhaps one of the lower spurs of this mountain. It is a gray ridge parallel to Gilboa on the north; and between the two lay the battle-field, the plain of Jezreel (q.v.), where Gideon overthrew the Midianites (<reflink>Judg. 7:1-12</reflink>).

moresheth-gath.d: possession of the wine-press, the birthplace of the prophet Micah (1:14), who is called the "Morasthite" (<reflink>Jer. 26:18</reflink>). This place was probably a suburb of Gath.

moriah.d: the chosen of Jehovah. Some contend that Mount Gerizim is meant, but most probably we are to regard this as one of the hills of Jerusalem. Here Solomon's temple was built, on the spot that had been the threshing-floor of Ornan the Jebusite (<reflink>2 Sam. 24:24, 25; 2 Chr. 3:1</reflink>). It is usually included in Zion, to the north-east of which it lay, and from which it was separated by the Tyropoean valley. This was "the land of Moriah" to which Abraham went to offer up his son Isaac (<reflink>Gen. 22:2</reflink>). It has been supposed that the highest point of the temple hill, which is now covered by the Mohammedan Kubbetes-Sakhrah, or "Dome of the Rock," is the actual site of Araunah's threshing-floor. Here also, one thousand years after Abraham, David built an altar and offered sacrifices to God. (<see target="x-self">See JERUSALEM; NUMBERING THE PEOPLE.</see>)

mortar.d: (Heb. homer), cement of lime and sand (<reflink>Gen. 11:3; Ex. 1:14</reflink>); also potter's clay (<reflink>Isa. 41:25; Nah. 3:14</reflink>). Also Heb. 'aphar, usually rendered "dust," clay or mud used for cement in building (<reflink>Lev. 14:42, 45</reflink>).

mosera.d: a bond, one of the stations of the Israelites in the wilderness (<reflink>Deut. 10:6</reflink>), at the foot of Mount Hor. (<reflink>Comp. Num. 33:37, 38</reflink>). It has been identified with el-Tayibeh, a small fountain at the bottom of the pass leading to the ascent of Mount Hor.

moseroth.d: bonds, one of the stations in the wilderness (<reflink>Num. 33:30, 31</reflink>), probably the same as Mosera.

moses.d: drawn (or Egypt. mesu, "son;" hence Rameses, royal son). On the invitation of Pharaoh (<reflink>Gen. 45:17-25</reflink>), Jacob and his sons went down into Egypt. This immigration took place probably about 350 years before the birth of Moses. Some centuries before Joseph, Egypt had been conquered by a pastoral Semitic race from Asia, the Hyksos, who brought into cruel subjection the native Egyptians, who were an African race. Jacob and his retinue were accustomed to a shepherd's life, and on their arrival in Egypt were received with favour by the king, who assigned them the "best of the land", the land of Goshen, to dwell in. The Hyksos or "shepherd" king who thus showed favour to Joseph and his family was in all probability the Pharaoh Apopi (or Apopis).

mote.d: (Gr. karphos, something dry, hence a particle of wood or chaff, etc.). A slight moral defect is likened to a mote (<reflink>Matt. 7:3-5; Luke 6:41, 42</reflink>).

moth.d: Heb. 'ash, from a root meaning "to fall away," as moth-eaten garments fall to pieces (<reflink>Job 4:19; 13:28; Isa. 50:9; 51:8; Hos. 5:12</reflink>).

mouldy.d: Of the Gibeonites it is said that "all the bread of their provision was dry and mouldy" (<reflink>Josh. 9:5, 12</reflink>). The Hebrew word here rendered "mouldy" (nikuddim) is rendered "cracknels" in 1 Kings 14:3, and denotes a kind of crisp cake. The meaning is that the bread of the Gibeonites had become dry and hard, hard as biscuits, and thus was an evidence of the length of the journey they had travelled.

mount.d: Palestine is a hilly country (<reflink>Deut. 3:25; 11:11; Ezek. 34:13</reflink>). West of Jordan the mountains stretch from Lebanon far down into Galilee, terminating in Carmel. The isolated peak of Tabor rises from the elevated plain of Esdraelon, which, in the south, is shut in by hills spreading over the greater part of Samaria. The mountains of Western and Middle Palestine do not extend to the sea, but gently slope into plains, and toward the Jordan fall down into the Ghor.

mount of corruption.d: (<reflink>2 Kings 23:13; Vulg., "mount of offence"</reflink>), the name given to a part of the Mount of Olives, so called because idol temples were there erected in the time of Solomon, temples to the Zidonian Ashtoreth and to the "abominations" of Moab and Ammon.

mount of the amalekites.d: a place near Pirathon (q.v.), in the tribe of Ephraim (<reflink>Judg. 12:15</reflink>).

mount of the amorites.d: the range of hills which rises abruptly in the wilderness of et-Tih ("the wandering"), mentioned Deut. 1:19, 20, "that great and terrible wilderness."

mount of the congregation.d: only in Isa. 14:13, a mythic mountain of the Babylonians, regarded by them as the seat of the gods. It was situated in the far north, and in Babylonian inscriptions is described as a mountain called Im-Kharasak, "the mighty mountain of Bel, whose head reaches heaven, whose root is the holy deep." In their geography they are said to have identified it with mount El-wend, near Ecbatana.

mount of the valley.d: (<reflink>Josh. 13:19</reflink>), a district in the east of Jordan, in the territory of Reuben. The "valley" here was probably the Ghor or valley of the Jordan, and hence the "mount" would be the hilly region in the north end of the Dead Sea. (See ZARETH-SHAHAR

mourn.d: Frequent references are found in Scripture to, (1.) Mourning for the dead. Abraham mourned for Sarah (<reflink>Gen. 23:2</reflink>); Jacob for Joseph (37:34, 35); the Egyptians for Jacob (50:3-10); Israel for Aaron (<reflink>Num. 20:29</reflink>), for Moses (<reflink>Deut. 34:8</reflink>), and for Samuel (<reflink>1 Sam. 25:1</reflink>); David for Abner (<reflink>2 Sam. 3:31, 35</reflink>); Mary and Martha for Lazarus (John 11); devout men for Stephen (<reflink>Acts 8:2</reflink>), etc.

mouse.d: Heb. 'akhbar, "swift digger"), properly the dormouse, the field-mouse (<reflink>1 Sam. 6:4</reflink>). In Lev. 11:29, Isa. 66:17 this word is used generically, and includes the jerboa (Mus jaculus), rat, hamster (Cricetus), which, though declared to be unclean animals, were eaten by the Arabs, and are still eaten by the Bedouins. It is said that no fewer than twenty-three species of this group ('akhbar=Arab. ferah) of animals inhabit Palestine. God "laid waste" the people of Ashdod by the terrible visitation of field-mice, which are like locusts in their destructive effects (<reflink>1 Sam. 6:4, 11, 18</reflink>). Herodotus, the Greek historian, accounts for the destruction of the army of Sennacherib (<reflink>2 Kings 19:35</reflink>) by saying that in the night thousands of mice invaded the camp and gnawed through the bow-strings, quivers, and shields, and thus left the Assyrians helpless. (See SENNACHERIB

mowing.d: (Heb. gez), rendered in Ps. 72:6 "mown grass." The expression "king's mowings" (<reflink>Amos 7:1</reflink>) refers to some royal right of early pasturage, the first crop of grass for the cavalry (comp. 1 Kings 18:5).

moza.d: a going forth. (1.) One of the sons of Caleb (<reflink>1 Chr. 2:46</reflink>).

mozah.d: an issuing of water, a city of Benjamin (<reflink>Josh. 18:26</reflink>).

mufflers.d: (<reflink>Isa. 3:19</reflink>), veils, light and tremulous. Margin, "spangled ornaments."

mulberry.d: Heb. bakah, "to weep;" rendered "Baca" (R.V., "weeping") in Ps. 84:6. The plural form of the Hebrew bekaim is rendered "mulberry trees" in 2 Sam. 5:23, 24 and 1 Chr. 14:14, 15. The tree here alluded to was probably the aspen or trembling poplar. "We know with certainty that the black poplar, the aspen, and the Lombardy poplar grew in Palestine. The aspen, whose long leaf-stalks cause the leaves to tremble with every breath of wind, unites with the willow and the oak to overshadow the watercourses of the Lebanon, and with the oleander and the acacia to adorn the ravines of Southern Palestine" (Kitto). By "the sound of a going in the tops of the mulberry trees" we are to understand a rustling among the trees like the marching of an army. This was the signal that the Lord himself would lead forth David's army to victory. (<see target="x-self">See SYCAMINE.</see>)

mule.d: (Heb. pered), so called from the quick step of the animal or its power of carrying loads. It is not probable that the Hebrews bred mules, as this was strictly forbidden in the law (<reflink>Lev. 19:19</reflink>), although their use was not forbidden. We find them in common use even by kings and nobles (<reflink>2 Sam. 18:9; 1 Kings 1:33; 2 Kings 5:17; Ps. 32:9</reflink>). They are not mentioned, however, till the time of David, for the word rendered "mules" (R.V. correctly, "hot springs") in Gen. 36:24 (yemim) properly denotes the warm springs of Callirhoe, on the eastern shore of the Dead Sea. In David's reign they became very common (<reflink>2 Sam. 13:29; 1 Kings 10:25</reflink>).

murder.d: Wilful murder was distinguished from accidental homicide, and was invariably visited with capital punishment (<reflink>Num. 35:16, 18, 21, 31; Lev. 24:17</reflink>). This law in its principle is founded on the fact of man's having been made in the likeness of God (<reflink>Gen. 9:5, 6; John 8:44; 1 John 3:12, 15</reflink>). The Mosiac law prohibited any compensation for murder or the reprieve of the murderer (<reflink>Ex. 21:12, 14; Deut. 19:11, 13; 2 Sam. 17:25; 20:10</reflink>). Two witnesses were required in any capital case (<reflink>Num. 35:19-30; Deut. 17:6-12</reflink>). If the murderer could not be discovered, the city nearest the scene of the murder was required to make expiation for the crime committed (<reflink>Deut. 21:1-9</reflink>). These offences also were to be punished with death, (1) striking a parent; (2) cursing a parent; (3) kidnapping (<reflink>Ex. 21:15-17; Deut. 27:16</reflink>).

murmuring.d: of the Hebrews in the wilderness, called forth the displeasure of God, which was only averted by the earnest prayer of Moses (<reflink>Num. 11:33, 34; 12; 14:27, 30, 31; 16:3; 21:4-6; Ps. 106:25</reflink>). Forbidden by Paul (<reflink>1 Cor. 10:10</reflink>).

murrain.d: Heb. deber, "destruction," a "great mortality", the fifth plague that fell upon the Egyptians (<reflink>Ex. 9:3</reflink>). It was some distemper that resulted in the sudden and widespread death of the cattle. It was confined to the cattle of the Egyptians that were in the field (9:6).

mushi.d: receding, the second of the two sons of Merari (<reflink>Ex. 6:19; Num. 3:20</reflink>). His sons were called Mushites (<reflink>Num. 3:33; 26:58</reflink>).

music.d: Jubal was the inventor of musical instruments (<reflink>Gen. 4:21</reflink>). The Hebrews were much given to the cultivation of music. Their whole history and literature afford abundant evidence of this. After the Deluge, the first mention of music is in the account of Laban's interview with Jacob (<reflink>Gen. 31:27</reflink>). After their triumphal passage of the Red Sea, Moses and the children of Israel sang their song of deliverance (Ex. 15).

music, instrumental.d: Among instruments of music used by the Hebrews a principal place is given to stringed instruments. These were, (1.) The kinnor, the "harp." (2.) The nebel, "a skin bottle," rendered "psaltery." (3.) The sabbeka, or "sackbut," a lute or lyre. (4.) The gittith, occurring in the title of Ps. 8; 8; 84. (5.) Minnim (<reflink>Ps. 150:4</reflink>), rendered "stringed instruments;" in Ps. 45:8, in the form _minni_, probably the apocopated (i.e., shortened) plural, rendered, Authorized Version, "whereby," and in the Revised Version "stringed instruments." (6.) Machalath, in the titles of Ps. 53 and 88; supposed to be a kind of lute or guitar.
