musician, chief.d: (Heb. menatstseah), the precentor of the Levitical choir or orchestra in the temple, mentioned in the titles of fifty-five psalms, and in Hab. 3:19, Revised Version. The first who held this office was Jeduthun (<reflink>1 Chr. 16:41</reflink>), and the office appears to have been hereditary. Heman and Asaph were his two colleagues (<reflink>2 Chr. 35:15</reflink>).

mustard.d: a plant of the genus sinapis, a pod-bearing, shrub-like plant, growing wild, and also cultivated in gardens. The little round seeds were an emblem of any small insignificant object. It is not mentioned in the Old Testament; and in each of the three instances of its occurrence in the New Testament (<reflink>Matt. 13:31, 32; Mark 4:31, 32; Luke 13:18, 19</reflink>) it is spoken of only with reference to the smallness of its seed. The common mustard of Palestine is the Sinapis nigra. This garden herb sometimes grows to a considerable height, so as to be spoken of as "a tree" as compared with garden herbs.

muth-labben.d: occurring only in the title of Psalm 9. Some interpret the words as meaning "on the death of Labben," some unknown person. Others render the word, "on the death of the son;" i.e., of Absalom (<reflink>2 Sam. 18:33</reflink>). Others again have taken the word as the name of a musical instrument, or as the name of an air to which the psalm was sung.

muzzle.d: Grain in the East is usually thrashed by the sheaves being spread out on a floor, over which oxen and cattle are driven to and fro, till the grain is trodden out. Moses ordained that the ox was not to be muzzled while thrashing. It was to be allowed to eat both the grain and the straw (<reflink>Deut. 25:4</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See AGRICULTURE.</see>)

myra.d: one of the chief towns of Lycia, in Asia Minor, about 2 1/2 miles from the coast (<reflink>Acts 27:5</reflink>). Here Paul removed from the Adramyttian ship in which he had sailed from Caesarea, and entered into the Alexandrian ship, which was afterwards wrecked at Melita (27:39-44).

myrrh.d: Heb. mor. (1.) First mentioned as a principal ingredient in the holy anointing oil (<reflink>Ex. 30:23</reflink>). It formed part of the gifts brought by the wise men from the east, who came to worship the infant Jesus (<reflink>Matt. 2:11</reflink>). It was used in embalming (<reflink>John 19:39</reflink>), also as a perfume (<reflink>Esther 2:12; Ps. 45:8; Prov. 7:17</reflink>). It was a custom of the Jews to give those who were condemned to death by crucifixion "wine mingled with myrrh" to produce insensibility. This drugged wine was probably partaken of by the two malefactors, but when the Roman soldiers pressed it upon Jesus "he received it not" (<reflink>Mark 15:23</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See GALL.</see>)

myrtle.d: (<reflink>Isa. 41:19; Neh. 8:15; Zech. 1:8</reflink>), Hebrew hadas, known in the East by the name _as_, the Myrtus communis of the botanist. "Although no myrtles are now found on the mount (of Olives), excepting in the gardens, yet they still exist in many of the glens about Jerusalem, where we have often seen its dark shining leaves and white flowers. There are many near Bethlehem and about Hebron, especially near Dewir Dan, the ancient Debir. It also sheds its fragrance on the sides of Carmel and of Tabor, and fringes the clefts of the Leontes in its course through Galilee. We meet with it all through Central Palestine" (Tristram).

mysia.d: a province in the north-west of Asia Minor. On his first voyage to Europe (<reflink>Acts 16:7, 8</reflink>) Paul passed through this province and embarked at its chief port Troas.

mystery.d: the calling of the Gentiles into the Christian Church, so designated (<reflink>Eph. 1:9, 10; 3:8-11; Col. 1:25-27</reflink>); a truth undiscoverable except by revelation, long hid, now made manifest. The resurrection of the dead (<reflink>1 Cor. 15:51</reflink>), and other doctrines which need to be explained but which cannot be fully understood by finite intelligence (<reflink>Matt. 13:11; Rom. 11:25; 1 Cor. 13:2</reflink>); the union between Christ and his people symbolized by the marriage union (<reflink>Eph. 5:31, 32; comp. 6:19</reflink>); the seven stars and the seven candlesticks (<reflink>Rev. 1:20</reflink>); and the woman clothed in scarlet (17:7), are also in this sense mysteries. The anti-Christian power working in his day is called by the apostle (<reflink>2 Thess. 2:7</reflink>) the "mystery of iniquity."

naam.d: pleasantness, one of the three sons of Caleb, the son of Jephunneh (<reflink>1 Chr. 4:15</reflink>).

naamah.d: the beautiful. (1.) The daughter of Lamech and Zillah (<reflink>Gen. 4: 22</reflink>).

naaman.d: pleasantness, a Syrian, the commander of the armies of Benhadad II. in the time of Joram, king of Israel. He was afflicted with leprosy; and when the little Hebrew slave-girl that waited on his wife told her of a prophet in Samaria who could cure her master, he obtained a letter from Benhadad and proceeded with it to Joram. The king of Israel suspected in this some evil design against him, and rent his clothes. Elisha the prophet hearing of this, sent for Naaman, and the strange interview which took place is recorded in 2 Kings 5. The narrative contains all that is known of the Syrian commander. He was cured of his leprosy by dipping himself seven times in the Jordan, according to the word of Elisha. His cure is alluded to by our Lord (<reflink>Luke 4:27</reflink>).

naamathite.d: the designation of Zophar, one of Job's three friends (<reflink>Job 2:11; 11:1</reflink>), so called from some place in Arabia, called Naamah probably.

naarah.d: a girl, the second of Ashur's two wives, of the tribe of Judah (<reflink>1 Chr. 4:5, 6</reflink>).

naarai.d: youthful, a military chief in David's army (<reflink>1 Chr. 11:37</reflink>), called also Paarai (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:35</reflink>).

naaran.d: boyish, juvenile, a town in Ephraim between Bethel and Jericho (<reflink>1 Chr. 7:28</reflink>).

naarath.d: girl, a town on the boundary between Ephraim and Benjamin (<reflink>Josh. 16:7</reflink>), not far probably from Jericho, to the north (<reflink>1 Chr. 7:28</reflink>).

nabal.d: foolish, a descendant of Caleb who dwelt at Maon (1 Sam. 25), the modern Main, 7 miles south-east of Hebron. He was "very great, and he had 3,000 sheep and 1,000 goats...but the man was churlish and evil in his doings." During his wanderings David came into that district, and hearing that Nabal was about to shear his sheep, he sent ten of his young men to ask "whatsoever cometh unto thy hand for thy servants." Nabal insultingly resented the demand, saying, "Who is David, and who is the son of Jesse?" (<reflink>1 Sam. 25:10, 11</reflink>). One of the shepherds that stood by and saw the reception David's messengers had met with, informed Abigail, Nabal's wife, who at once realized the danger that threatened her household. She forthwith proceeded to the camp of David, bringing with her ample stores of provisions (25:18). …

naboth.d: fruits, "the Jezreelite," was the owner of a portion of ground on the eastern slope of the hill of Jezreel (<reflink>2 Kings 9:25, 26</reflink>). This small "plat of ground" seems to have been all he possessed. It was a vineyard, and lay "hard by the palace of Ahab" (<reflink>1 Kings 21:1, 2</reflink>), who greatly coveted it. Naboth, however, refused on any terms to part with it to the king. He had inherited it from his fathers, and no Israelite could lawfully sell his property (<reflink>Lev. 25:23</reflink>). Jezebel, Ahab's wife, was grievously offended at Naboth's refusal to part with his vineyard. By a crafty and cruel plot she compassed his death. His sons also shared his fate (<reflink>2 Kings 9:26; 1 Kings 21:19</reflink>). …

nachon.d: prepared, the owner of a thrashing-floor near which Uzzah was slain (<reflink>2 Sam. 6:6</reflink>); called also Chidon (<reflink>1 Chr. 13:9</reflink>).

nadab.d: liberal, generous. (1.) The eldest of Aaron's four sons (<reflink>Ex. 6:23; Num. 3:2</reflink>). He with his brothers and their father were consecrated as priests of Jehovah (<reflink>Ex. 28:1</reflink>). He afterwards perished with Abihu for the sin of offering strange fire on the altar of burnt-offering (<reflink>Lev. 10:1,2; Num. 3:4; 26:60</reflink>).

nagge.d: illuminating, one of the ancestors of Christ in the maternal line (<reflink>Luke 3:25</reflink>).

nahaliel.d: possession, or valley of God, one of the encampments of the Israelites in the wilderness (<reflink>Num. 21:19</reflink>), on the confines of Moab. This is identified with the ravine of the Zerka M'ain, the ancient Callirhoe, the hot springs on the east of the Jordan, not far from the Dead Sea.

nahallal.d: pasture, a city in Zebulun on the border of Issachar (<reflink>Josh. 19:15</reflink>), the same as Nahalol (<reflink>Judg. 1:30</reflink>). It was given to the Levites. It has been by some identified with Malul in the plain of Esdraelon, 4 miles from Nazareth.

naharai.d: snorer, a Berothite, one of David's heroes, and armour-bearer of Joab (<reflink>1 Chr. 11:39</reflink>).

nahash.d: serpent. (1.) King of the Ammonites in the time of Saul. The inhabitants of Jabesh-Gilead having been exposed to great danger from Nahash, sent messengers to Gibeah to inform Saul of their extremity. He promptly responded to the call, and gathering together an army he marched against Nahash. "And it came to pass that they which remained were scattered, so that two of them [the Ammonites] were not left together" (<reflink>1 Sam. 11:1-11</reflink>).

nahath.d: rest. (1.) One of the four sons of Reuel, the son of Esau (<reflink>Gen. 36:13, 17</reflink>). (2.) A Kohathite Levite (<reflink>1 Chr. 6:26</reflink>). (3.) A Levite, one of the overseers of the sacred offerings of the temple (<reflink>2 Chr. 31:13</reflink>).

nahbi.d: hidden, one of the twelve spies sent out to explore the land of Canaan (<reflink>Num. 13:14</reflink>).

nahor.d: snorting. (1.) The father of Terah, who was the father of Abraham (<reflink>Gen. 11:22-25; Luke 3:34</reflink>).

nahshon.d: sorcerer, the son of Aminadab, and prince of the children of Judah at the time of the first numbering of the tribes in the wilderness (<reflink>Ex. 6:23</reflink>). His sister Elisheba was the wife of Aaron. He died in the wilderness (<reflink>Num. 26:64, 65</reflink>). His name occurs in the Greek form Naasson in the genealogy of Christ (Matt, 1:4; Luke 3:32).

nahum.d: consolation, the seventh of the so-called minor prophets, an Elkoshite. All we know of him is recorded in the book of his prophecies. He was probably a native of Galilee, and after the deportation of the ten tribes took up his residence in Jerusalem. Others think that Elkosh was the name of a place on the east bank of the Tigris, and that Nahum dwelt there.

nahum, book of.d: Nahum prophesied, according to some, in the beginning of the reign of Ahaz (B.C. 743). Others, however, think that his prophecies are to be referred to the latter half of the reign of Hezekiah (about B.C. 709). This is the more probable opinion, internal evidences leading to that conclusion. Probably the book was written in Jerusalem (soon after B.C. 709), where he witnessed the invasion of Sennacherib and the destruction of his host (<reflink>2 Kings 19:35</reflink>).

nail.d: for fastening. (1.) Hebrew yathed, "piercing," a peg or nail of any material (<reflink>Ezek. 15:3</reflink>), more especially a tent-peg (<reflink>Ex. 27:19; 35:18; 38:20</reflink>), with one of which Jael (q.v.) pierced the temples of Sisera (<reflink>Judg. 4:21, 22</reflink>). This word is also used metaphorically (<reflink>Zech. 10:4</reflink>) for a prince or counsellor, just as "the battle-bow" represents a warrior.

nain.d: (from Heb. nain, "green pastures," "lovely"), the name of a town near the gate of which Jesus raised to life a widow's son (<reflink>Luke 7:11-17</reflink>). It is identified with the village called Nein, standing on the north-western slope of Jebel ed-Duhy (=the "hill Moreh" = "Little hermon"), about 4 miles from Tabor and 25 southwest of Capernaum. At the foot of the slope on which it stands is the great plain of Esdraelon.

naioth.d: dwellings, the name given to the prophetical college established by Samuel near Ramah. It consisted of a cluster of separate dwellings, and hence its name. David took refuge here when he fled from Saul (<reflink>1 Sam. 19:18, 19, 22, 23</reflink>), and here he passed a few weeks in peace (comp. Ps. 11). It was probably the common residence of the "sons of the prophets."

naked.d: This word denotes (1) absolute nakedness (<reflink>Gen. 2:25; Job 1:21; Eccl. 5:15; Micah 1:8; Amos 2:16</reflink>); (2) being poorly clad (<reflink>Isa. 58:7; James 2:15</reflink>). It denotes also (3) the state of one who has laid aside his loose outer garment (Lat. nudus), and appears clothed only in a long tunic or under robe worn next the skin (<reflink>1 Sam. 19:24; Isa. 47:3; comp. Mark 14:52; John 21:7</reflink>). It is used figuratively, meaning "being discovered" or "made manifest" (<reflink>Job 26:6; Heb. 4:13</reflink>). In Ex. 32:25 the expression "the people were naked" (A.V.) is more correctly rendered in the Revised Version "the people were broken loose", i.e., had fallen into a state of lawlessness and insubordination. In 2 Chr. 28:19 the words "he made Judah naked" (A.V.), but Revised Version "he had dealt wantonly in Judah," mean "he had permitted Judah to break loose from all the restraints of religion."

naomi.d: the lovable; my delight, the wife of Elimelech, and mother of Mahlon and Chilion, and mother-in-law of Ruth (1:2, 20, 21; 2:1). Elimelech and his wife left the district of Bethlehem-Judah, and found a new home in the uplands of Moab. In course of time he died, as also his two sons Mahlon and Chilion, who had married women of Moab, and three widows were left mourning the loss of their husbands. Naomi longs to return now to her own land, to Bethlehem. One of her widowed daughters-in-law, Ruth, accompanies her, and is at length married to Boaz (q.v.).

naphish.d: refresher, one of the sons of Ishmael (<reflink>Gen. 25:15; 1 Chr. 1:31</reflink>). He was the father of an Arab tribe.

naphtali.d: my wrestling, the fifth son of Jacob. His mother was Bilhah, Rachel's handmaid (<reflink>Gen. 30:8</reflink>). When Jacob went down into Egypt, Naphtali had four sons (<reflink>Gen. 46:24</reflink>). Little is known of him as an individual.

naphtali, tribe of.d: On this tribe Jacob pronounced the patriarchal blessing, "Naphtali is a hind let loose: he giveth goodly words" (<reflink>Gen. 49:21</reflink>). It was intended thus to set forth under poetic imagery the future character and history of the tribe.

naphtuhim.d: a Hamitic tribe descended from Mizraim (<reflink>Gen. 10:13</reflink>). Others identify this word with Napata, the name of the city and territory on the southern frontier of Mizraim, the modern Meroe, at the great bend of the Nile at Soudan. This city was the royal residence, it is said, of Queen Candace (<reflink>Acts 8:27</reflink>). Here there are extensive and splendid ruins.

napkin.d: (Gr. soudarion, John 11:44; 20:7; Lat. sudarium, a "sweat-cloth"), a cloth for wiping the sweat from the face. But the word is used of a wrapper to fold money in (<reflink>Luke 19:20</reflink>), and as an article of dress, a "handkerchief" worn on the head (<reflink>Acts 19:12</reflink>).

narcissus.d: daffodil, a Roman whom Paul salutes (<reflink>Rom. 16:11</reflink>). He is supposed to have been the private secretary of the emperor Claudius. This is, however, quite uncertain.

nathan.d: given. (1.) A prophet in the reigns of David and Solomon (<reflink>2 Chr. 9:29</reflink>). He is first spoken of in connection with the arrangements David made for the building of the temple (<reflink>2 Sam. 7:2, 3, 17</reflink>), and next appears as the reprover of David on account of his sin with Bathsheba (12:1-14). He was charged with the education of Solomon (12:25), at whose inauguration to the throne he took a prominent part (<reflink>1 Kings 1:8, 10, 11, 22-45</reflink>). His two sons, Zabad (<reflink>1 Chr. 2:36</reflink>) and Azariah (<reflink>1 Kings 4:5</reflink>) occupied places of honour at the king's court. He last appears in assisting David in reorganizing the public worship (<reflink>2 Chr. 29:25</reflink>). He seems to have written a life of David, and also a life of Solomon (<reflink>1 Chr. 29:29; 2 Chr. 9:29</reflink>).

nathanael.d: given or gift of God, one of our Lord's disciples, "of Cana in Galilee" (<reflink>John 21:2</reflink>). He was "an Israelite indeed, in whom was no guile" (1:47, 48). His name occurs only in the Gospel of John, who in his list of the disciples never mentions Bartholomew, with whom he has consequently been identified. He was one of those to whom the Lord showed himself alive after his resurrection, at the Sea of Tiberias.

nativity of christ.d: The birth of our Lord took place at the time and place predicted by the prophets (<reflink>Gen. 49:10; Isa. 7:14; Jer. 31:15; Micah 5:2; Hag. 2:6-9; Dan. 9:24, 25</reflink>). Joseph and Mary were providentially led to go up to Bethlehem at this period, and there Christ was born (<reflink>Matt. 2:1, 6; Luke 2:1, 7</reflink>). The exact year or month or day of his birth cannot, however, now be exactly ascertained. We know, however, that it took place in the "fulness of the time" (<reflink>Gal. 4:4</reflink>), i.e., at the fittest time in the world's history. Chronologists are now generally agreed that the year 4 before the Christian era was the year of Christ's nativity, and consequently that he was about four years old in the year 1 A.D.

naughty figs.d: (<reflink>Jer. 24:2</reflink>). "The bad figs may have been such either from having decayed, and thus been reduced to a rotten condition, or as being the fruit of the sycamore, which contains a bitter juice" (Tristram, Nat. Hist.). The inferiority of the fruit is here referred to as an emblem of the rejected Zedekiah and his people.

nazarene.d: This epithet (Gr. Nazaraios) is applied to Christ only once (<reflink>Matt. 2:23</reflink>). In all other cases the word is rendered "of Nazareth" (<reflink>Mark 1:24; 10:47; 14:67, etc.</reflink>). When this Greek designation was at first applied to our Lord, it was meant simply to denote the place of his residence. In course of time the word became a term of reproach. Thus the word "Nazarene" carries with it an allusion to those prophecies which speak of Christ as "despised of men" (<reflink>Isa. 53:3</reflink>). Some, however, think that in this name there is an allusion to the Hebrew _netser_, which signifies a branch or sprout. It is so applied to the Messiah (<reflink>Isa. 11:1</reflink>), i.e., he whom the prophets called the _Netse_, the "Branch."

nazareth.d: separated, generally supposed to be the Greek form of the Hebrew _netser_, a "shoot" or "sprout." Some, however, think that the name of the city must be connected with the name of the hill behind it, from which one of the finest prospects in Palestine is obtained, and accordingly they derive it from the Hebrew _notserah_, i.e., one guarding or watching, thus designating the hill which overlooks and thus guards an extensive region.

nazarite.d: (Heb. form Nazirite), the name of such Israelites as took on them the vow prescribed in Num. 6:2-21. The word denotes generally one who is separated from others and consecrated to God. Although there is no mention of any Nazarite before Samson, yet it is evident that they existed before the time of Moses. The vow of a Nazarite involved these three things, (1) abstinence from wine and strong drink, (2) refraining from cutting the hair off the head during the whole period of the continuance of the vow, and (3) the avoidance of contact with the dead.

neah.d: shaking, or settlement, or descent, a town on the east side of Zebulun, not far from Rimmon (<reflink>Josh. 19:13</reflink>).

neapolis.d: new city, a town in Thrace at which Paul first landed in Europe (<reflink>Acts 16:11</reflink>). It was the sea-port of the inland town of Philippi, which was distant about 10 miles. From this port Paul embarked on his last journey to Jerusalem (<reflink>Acts 20:6</reflink>). It is identified with the modern Turco-Grecian Kavalla.

nebaioth.d: height. (1.) Ishmael's eldest son (<reflink>Gen. 25:13</reflink>), and the prince of an Israelitish tribe (16). He had a sister, Mahalath, who was one of Esau's wives (<reflink>Gen. 28:9; 36:3</reflink>).

neballat.d: wickedness in secret, (<reflink>Neh. 11:34</reflink>), probably the village of Beit Nebala, about 4 miles north of Lydda.

nebat.d: sight; aspect, the father of Jeroboam, the king of Israel (<reflink>1 Kings 11:26, etc.</reflink>).

nebo.d: proclaimer; prophet. (1.) A Chaldean god whose worship was introduced into Assyria by Pul (<reflink>Isa. 46:1; Jer. 48:1</reflink>). To this idol was dedicated the great temple whose ruins are still seen at Birs Nimrud. A statue of Nebo found at Calah, where it was set up by Pul, king of Assyria, is now in the British Museum.

nebuchadnezzar.d: in the Babylonian orthography Nabu-kudur-uzur, which means "Nebo, protect the crown!" or the "frontiers." In an inscription he styles himself "Nebo's favourite." He was the son and successor of Nabopolassar, who delivered Babylon from its dependence on Assyria and laid Nineveh in ruins. He was the greatest and most powerful of all the Babylonian kings. He married the daughter of Cyaxares, and thus the Median and Babylonian dynasties were united.

nebuchadrezzar.d: =Nebuchadnezzar (<reflink>Jer. 21:2, 7; 22:25; 24:1, etc.</reflink>), a nearer approach to the correct spelling of the word.

nebushasban.d: adorer of Nebo, or Nebo saves me, the "Rabsaris," or chief chamberlain, of the court of Babylon. He was one of those whom the king sent to release Jeremiah from prison in Jerusalem (<reflink>Jer. 39:13</reflink>).

nebuzaradan.d: "the captain of the guard," in rank next to the king, who appears prominent in directing affairs at the capture of Jerusalem (<reflink>2 Kings 25:8-20; Jer. 39:11; 40:2-5</reflink>). He showed kindness toward Jeremiah, as commanded by Nebuchadnezzar (40:1). Five years after this he again came to Jerusalem and carried captive seven hundred and forty-five more Jews.

necho ii.d: an Egyptian king, the son and successor of Psammetichus (B.C. 610-594), the contemporary of Josiah, king of Judah. For some reason he proclaimed war against the king of Assyria. He led forth a powerful army and marched northward, but was met by the king of Judah at Megiddo, who refused him a passage through his territory. Here a fierce battle was fought and Josiah was slain (<reflink>2 Chr. 35:20-24</reflink>). Possibly, as some suppose, Necho may have brought his army by sea to some port to the north of Dor (<reflink>comp. Josh. 11:2; 12:23</reflink>), a Phoenician town at no great distance from Megiddo. After this battle Necho marched on to Carchemish (q.v.), where he met and conquered the Assyrian army, and thus all the Syrian provinces, including Palestine, came under his dominion.

neck.d: used sometimes figuratively. To "lay down the neck" (<reflink>Rom. 16:4</reflink>) is to hazard one's life. Threatenings of coming judgments are represented by the prophets by their laying bands upon the people's necks (<reflink>Deut. 28:48; Isa. 10:27; Jer. 27:2</reflink>). Conquerors put their feet on the necks of their enemies as a sign of their subjection (<reflink>Josh. 10:24; 2 Sam. 22:41</reflink>).

necromancer.d: (<reflink>Deut. 15:11</reflink>), i.e., "one who interrogates the dead," as the word literally means, with the view of discovering the secrets of futurity (comp. 1 Sam. 28:7). (<see target="x-self">See DIVINATION.</see>)

nedabiah.d: moved of Jehovah, one of the sons of Jeconiah (<reflink>1 Chr. 3:18</reflink>).

needle.d: used only in the proverb, "to pass through a needle's eye" (<reflink>Matt. 19:24; Mark 10:25; Luke 18:25</reflink>). Some interpret the expression as referring to the side gate, close to the principal gate, usually called the "eye of a needle" in the East; but it is rather to be taken literally. The Hebrew females were skilled in the use of the needle (<reflink>Ex. 28:39; 26:36; Judg. 5:30</reflink>).

neginah.d: in the title of Ps. 61, denotes the music of stringed instruments (<reflink>1 Sam. 16:16; Isa. 38:20</reflink>). It is the singular form of Neginoth.

neginoth.d: i.e., songs with instrumental accompaniment, found in the titles of Ps. 4; 6; 54; 55; 67; 76; rendered "stringed instruments," Hab. 3:19, A.V. It denotes all kinds of stringed instruments, as the "harp," "psaltery," "viol," etc. The "chief musician on Neginoth" is the leader of that part of the temple choir which played on stringed instruments.

nehelamite.d: the name given to a false prophet Shemaiah, who went with the captives to Babylon (<reflink>Jer. 29:24, 31, 32</reflink>). The origin of the name is unknown. It is rendered in the marg, "dreamer."

nehemiah.d: comforted by Jehovah. (1.) Ezra 2:2; Neh. 7:7. (2.) Neh. 3:16.

nehemiah, book of.d: The author of this book was no doubt Nehemiah himself. There are portions of the book written in the first person (ch. 1-7; 12:27-47, and 13). But there are also portions of it in which Nehemiah is spoken of in the third person (ch. 8; 9; 10). It is supposed that these portions may have been written by Ezra; of this, however, there is no distinct evidence. These portions had their place assigned them in the book, there can be no doubt, by Nehemiah. He was the responsible author of the whole book, with the exception of ch. 12:11, 22, 23.

nehiloth.d: only in the title of Ps. 5. It is probably derived from a root meaning "to bore," "perforate," and hence denotes perforated wind instruments of all kinds. The psalm may be thus regarded as addressed to the conductor of the temple choir which played on flutes and such-like instruments.

nehushta.d: copper, the daughter of Elnathan of Jerusalem, and the wife of Jehoiakin (<reflink>2 Kings 24:8</reflink>), king of Judah.

nehushtan.d: of copper; a brazen thing a name of contempt given to the serpent Moses had made in the wilderness (<reflink>Num. 21:8</reflink>), and which Hezekiah destroyed because the children of Israel began to regard it as an idol and "burn incense to it." The lapse of nearly one thousand years had invested the "brazen serpent" with a mysterious sanctity; and in order to deliver the people from their infatuation, and impress them with the idea of its worthlessness, Hezekiah called it, in contempt, "Nehushtan," a brazen thing, a mere piece of brass (<reflink>2 Kings 18:4</reflink>).

neiel.d: dwelling-place of God, a town in the territory of Asher, near its southern border (<reflink>Josh. 19:27</reflink>). It has been identified with the ruin Y'anin, near the outlet of the Wady esh Sha-ghur, less than 2 miles north of Kabul, and 16 miles east of Caesarea.

nekeb.d: cavern, a town on the boundary of Naphtali (<reflink>Josh. 19:33</reflink>). It has with probability, been identified with Seiyadeh, nearly 2 miles east of Bessum, a ruin half way between Tiberias and Mount Tabor.

nemuel.d: day of God. (1.) One of Simeon's five sons (<reflink>1 Chr. 4:24</reflink>), called also Jemuel (<reflink>Gen. 46:10</reflink>). (2.) A Reubenite, a son of Eliab, and brother of Dathan and Abiram (<reflink>Num. 26:9</reflink>).

nephilim.d: (<reflink>Gen. 6:4; Num. 13:33, R.V.</reflink>), giants, the Hebrew word left untranslated by the Revisers, the name of one of the Canaanitish tribes. The Revisers have, however, translated the Hebrew gibborim, in Gen. 6:4, "mighty men."

nephtoah.d: opened, a fountain and a stream issuing from it on the border between Judah and Benjamin (<reflink>Josh. 15:8, 9; 18:15</reflink>). It has been identified with 'Ain Lifta, a spring about 2 1/2 miles north-west of Jerusalem. Others, however, have identified it with 'Ain' Atan, on the south-west of Bethlehem, whence water is conveyed through "Pilate's aqueduct" to the Haram area at Jerusalem.

ner.d: light, the father of Kish (<reflink>1 Chr. 8:33</reflink>). 1 Sam. 14:51 should be read, "Kish, the father of Saul, and Ner, the father of Abner, were the sons of Abiel." And hence this Kish and Ner were brothers, and Saul and Abner were first cousins (comp. 1 Chr. 9:36).

nereus.d: a Christian at Rome to whom Paul sent his salutation (<reflink>Rom. 16:15</reflink>).

nergal.d: the great dog; that is, lion, one of the chief gods of the Assyrians and Babylonians (<reflink>2 Kings 17:30</reflink>), the god of war and hunting. He is connected with Cutha as its tutelary deity.

nergal-sharezer.d: Nergal, protect the king! (1.) One of the "princes of the king of Babylon who accompanied him in his last expedition against Jerusalem" (<reflink>Jer. 39:3, 13</reflink>).

nero.d: occurs only in the superscription (which is probably spurious, and is altogether omitted in the R.V.) to the Second Epistle to Timothy. He became emperor of Rome when he was about seventeen years of age (A.D. 54), and soon began to exhibit the character of a cruel tyrant and heathen debauchee. In May A.D. 64, a terrible conflagration broke out in Rome, which raged for six days and seven nights, and totally destroyed a great part of the city. The guilt of this fire was attached to him at the time, and the general verdict of history accuses him of the crime. "Hence, to suppress the rumour," says Tacitus (Annals, xv. 44), "he falsely charged with the guilt, and punished with the most exquisite tortures, the persons commonly called Christians, who are hated for their enormities. …

net.d: in use among the Hebrews for fishing, hunting, and fowling. The fishing-net was probably constructed after the form of that used by the Egyptians (<reflink>Isa. 19:8</reflink>). There were three kinds of nets. (1.) The drag-net or hauling-net (Gr. sagene), of great size, and requiring many men to work it. It was usually let down from the fishing-boat, and then drawn to the shore or into the boat, as circumstances might require (<reflink>Matt. 13:47, 48</reflink>). (2.) The hand-net or casting-net (Gr. amphiblestron), which was thrown from a rock or a boat at any fish that might be seen (<reflink>Matt. 4:18; Mark 1:16</reflink>). It was called by the Latins funda. It was of circular form, "like the top of a tent." (3.) The bag-net (Gr. diktyon), used for enclosing fish in deep water (<reflink>Luke 5:4-9</reflink>).

nethaneel.d: given of God. (1.) The son of Zuar, chief of the tribe of Issachar at the Exodus (<reflink>Num. 1:8; 2:5</reflink>).

nethaniah.d: given of Jehovah. (1.) One of Asaph's sons, appointed by David to minister in the temple (<reflink>1 Chr. 25:2, 12</reflink>).

nethinim.d: the name given to the hereditary temple servants in all the post-Exilian books of Scripture. The word means given, i.e., "those set apart", viz., to the menial work of the sanctuary for the Levites. The name occurs seventeen times, and in each case in the Authorized Version incorrectly terminates in "s", "Nethinims;" in the Revised Version, correctly without the "s" (<reflink>Ezra 2:70; 7:7, 24; 8:20, etc.</reflink>). The tradition is that the Gibeonites (<reflink>Josh. 9:27</reflink>) were the original caste, afterwards called Nethinim. Their numbers were added to afterwards from captives taken in battle; and they were formally given by David to the Levites (<reflink>Ezra 8:20</reflink>), and so were called Nethinim, i.e., the given ones, given to the Levites to be their servants. Only 612 Nethinim returned from Babylon (<reflink>Ezra 2:58; 8:20</reflink>). They were under the control of a chief from among themselves (2:43; Neh. 7:46). …

netophah.d: distillation; dropping, a town in Judah, in the neighbourhood, probably, of Bethlehem (<reflink>Neh. 7:26; 1 Chr. 2:54</reflink>). Two of David's guards were Netophathites (<reflink>1 Chr. 27:13, 15</reflink>). It has been identified with the ruins of Metoba, or Um Toba, to the north-east of Bethlehem.

nettle.d: (1.) Heb. haral, "pricking" or "burning," Prov. 24:30, 31 (R.V. marg., "wild vetches"); Job 30:7; Zeph. 2:9. Many have supposed that some thorny or prickly plant is intended by this word, such as the bramble, the thistle, the wild plum, the cactus or prickly pear, etc. It may probably be a species of mustard, the Sinapis arvensis, which is a pernicious weed abounding in corn-fields. Tristram thinks that this word "designates the prickly acanthus (Acanthus spinosus), a very common and troublesome weed in the plains of Palestine."

new moon, feast of.d: Special services were appointed for the commencement of a month (<reflink>Num. 28:11-15; 10:10</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See FESTIVALS.</see>)

new testament.d: (<reflink>Luke 22:20</reflink>), rather "New Covenant," in contrast to the old covenant of works, which is superseded. "The covenant of grace is called new; it succeeds to the old broken covenant of works. It is ever fresh, flourishing, and excellent; and under the gospel it is dispensed in a more clear, spiritual, extensive, and powerful manner than of old" (Brown of Haddington). Hence is derived the name given to the latter portion of the  (<see target="x-self">See TESTAMENT.</see>)

nezib.d: a town in the "plain" of Judah. It has been identified with Beit Nuzib, about 14 miles south-west of Jerusalem, in the Wady Sur (<reflink>Josh. 15:43</reflink>).

nibhaz.d: barker, the name of an idol, supposed to be an evil demon of the Zabians. It was set up in Samaria by the Avites (<reflink>2 Kings 17:31</reflink>), probably in the form of a dog.

nibshan.d: fertile; light soil, a city somewhere "in the wilderness" of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:62</reflink>), probably near Engedi.

nicanor.d: conqueror, one of the seven deacons appointed in the apostolic Church (<reflink>Acts 6:1-6</reflink>). Nothing further is known of him.

nicodemus.d: the people is victor, a Pharisee and a member of the Sanhedrin. He is first noticed as visiting Jesus by night (<reflink>John 3:1-21</reflink>) for the purpose of learning more of his doctrines, which our Lord then unfolded to him, giving prominence to the necessity of being "born again." He is next met with in the Sanhedrin (7:50-52), where he protested against the course they were taking in plotting against Christ. Once more he is mentioned as taking part in the preparation for the anointing and burial of the body of Christ (<reflink>John 19:39</reflink>). We hear nothing more of him. There can be little doubt that he became a true disciple.

nicolaitanes.d: The church at Ephesus (<reflink>Rev. 2:6</reflink>) is commended for hating the "deeds" of the Nicolaitanes, and the church of Pergamos is blamed for having them who hold their "doctrines" (15). They were seemingly a class of professing Christians, who sought to introduce into the church a false freedom or licentiousness, thus abusing Paul's doctrine of grace (comp. 2 Pet. 2:15, 16, 19), and were probably identical with those who held the doctrine of Baalam (q.v.), Rev. 2:14.

nicolas.d: the victory of the people, a proselyte of Antioch, one of the seven deacons (<reflink>Acts 6:5</reflink>).

nicopolis.d: city of victory, where Paul intended to winter (<reflink>Titus 3:12</reflink>). There were several cities of this name. The one here referred to was most probably that in Epirus, which was built by Augustus Caesar to commemorate his victory at the battle of Actium (B.C. 31). It is the modern Paleoprevesa, i.e., "Old Prevesa." The subscription to the epistle to Titus calls it "Nicopolis of Macedonia", i.e., of Thrace. This is, however, probably incorrect.

niger.d: black, a surname of Simeon (<reflink>Acts 13:1</reflink>). He was probably so called from his dark complexion.

night-hawk.d: (Heb. tahmas) occurs only in the list of unclean birds (<reflink>Lev. 11:16; Deut. 14:15</reflink>). This was supposed to be the night-jar (Caprimulgus), allied to the swifts. The Hebrew word is derived from a root meaning "to scratch or tear the face," and may be best rendered, in accordance with the ancient versions, "an owl" (Strix flammea). The Revised Version renders "night-hawk."

nile.d: dark; blue, not found in Scripture, but frequently referred to in the Old Testament under the name of Sihor, i.e., "the black stream" (<reflink>Isa. 23:3; Jer. 2:18</reflink>) or simply "the river" (<reflink>Gen. 41:1; Ex. 1:22, etc.</reflink>) and the "flood of Egypt" (<reflink>Amos 8:8</reflink>). It consists of two rivers, the White Nile, which takes its rise in the Victoria Nyanza, and the Blue Nile, which rises in the Abyssinian Mountains. These unite at the town of Khartoum, whence it pursues its course for 1,800 miles, and falls into the Mediterranean through its two branches, into which it is divided a few miles north of Cairo, the Rosetta and the Damietta branch. (<see target="x-self">See EGYPT.</see>)

nimrah.d: pure, a city on the east of Jordan (<reflink>Num. 32:3</reflink>); probably the same as Beth-nimrah (<reflink>Josh. 13:27</reflink>). It has been identified with the Nahr Nimrin, at one of the fords of Jordan, not far from Jericho.

nimrim, waters of.d: the stream of the leopards, a stream in Moab (<reflink>Isa. 15:6; Jer. 48:34</reflink>); probably the modern Wady en-Nemeirah, a rich, verdant spot at the south-eastern end of the Dead Sea.

nimrod.d: firm, a descendant of Cush, the son of Ham. He was the first who claimed to be a "mighty one in the earth." Babel was the beginning of his kingdom, which he gradually enlarged (<reflink>Gen. 10:8-10</reflink>). The "land of Nimrod" (<reflink>Micah 5:6</reflink>) is a designation of Assyria or of Shinar, which is a part of it.

nimshi.d: saved. Jehu was "the son of Jehoshaphat, the son of Nimshi" (<reflink>2 Kings 9:2; comp. 1 Kings 19:16</reflink>).

nineveh.d: First mentioned in Gen. 10:11, which is rendered in the Revised Version, "He [i.e., Nimrod] went forth into Assyria and builded Nineveh." It is not again noticed till the days of Jonah, when it is described (<reflink>Jonah 3:3; 4:11</reflink>) as a great and populous city, the flourishing capital of the Assyrian empire (<reflink>2 Kings 19:36; Isa. 37:37</reflink>). The book of the prophet Nahum is almost exclusively taken up with prophetic denunciations against this city. Its ruin and utter desolation are foretold (<reflink>Nah.1:14; 3:19, etc.</reflink>). Zephaniah also (2:13-15) predicts its destruction along with the fall of the empire of which it was the capital. From this time there is no mention of it in Scripture till it is named in gospel history (<reflink>Matt. 12:41; Luke 11:32</reflink>).

nisan.d: month of flowers, (<reflink>Neh. 2:1</reflink>) the first month of the Jewish sacred year. (<see target="x-self">See ABIB.</see>) Assyrian nisannu, "beginning."

nisroch.d: probably connected with the Hebrew word _nesher_, an eagle. An Assyrian god, supposed to be that represented with the head of an eagle. Sennacherib was killed in the temple of this idol (<reflink>2 Kings 19:37; Isa. 37:38</reflink>).

nitre.d: (<reflink>Prov. 25:20; R.V. marg., "soda"</reflink>), properly "natron," a substance so called because, rising from the bottom of the Lake Natron in Egypt, it becomes dry and hard in the sun, and is the soda which effervesces when vinegar is poured on it. It is a carbonate of soda, not saltpetre, which the word generally denotes (<reflink>Jer. 2:22; R.V. "lye"</reflink>).

no.d: or No-A'mon, the home of Amon, the name of Thebes, the ancient capital of what is called the Middle Empire, in Upper or Southern Egypt. "The multitude of No" (<reflink>Jer. 46:25</reflink>) is more correctly rendered, as in the Revised Version, "Amon of No", i.e., No, where Jupiter Amon had his temple. In Ezek. 30:14, 16 it is simply called "No;" but in ver. 15 the name has the Hebrew Hamon prefixed to it, "Hamon No." This prefix is probably the name simply of the god usually styled Amon or Ammon. In Nah. 3:8 the "populous No" of the Authorized Version is in the Revised Version correctly rendered "No-Amon."

noadiah.d: meeting with the Lord. (1.) A Levite who returned from Babylon (<reflink>Ezra 8:33</reflink>).

noah.d: rest, (Heb. Noah) the grandson of Methuselah (<reflink>Gen. 5:25-29</reflink>), who was for two hundred and fifty years contemporary with Adam, and the son of Lamech, who was about fifty years old at the time of Adam's death. This patriarch is rightly regarded as the connecting link between the old and the new world. He is the second great progenitor of the human family.

nob.d: high place, a city of the priests, first mentioned in the history of David's wanderings (<reflink>1 Sam. 21:1</reflink>). Here the tabernacle was then standing, and here Ahimelech the priest resided. (<see target="x-self">See AHIMELECH.</see>) From Isa. 10:28-32 it seems to have been near Jerusalem. It has been identified by some with el-Isawiyeh, one mile and a half to the north-east of Jerusalem. But according to Isa. 10:28-32 it was on the south of Geba, on the road to Jerusalem, and within sight of the city. This identification does not meet these conditions, and hence others (as Dean Stanley) think that it was the northern summit of Mount Olivet, the place where David "worshipped God" when fleeing from Absalom (<reflink>2 Sam. 15:32</reflink>), or more probably (Conder) that it was the same as Mizpeh (q.v.), Judg. 20:1; Josh. 18:26; 1 Sam. 7:16, at Nebi Samwil, about 5 miles north-west of Jerusalem.

nobleman.d: (Gr. basilikos, i.e., "king's man"), an officer of state (<reflink>John 4:49</reflink>) in the service of Herod Antipas. He is supposed to have been the Chuza, Herod's steward, whose wife was one of those women who "ministered unto the Lord of their substance" (<reflink>Luke 8:3</reflink>). This officer came to Jesus at Cana and besought him to go down to Capernaum and heal his son, who lay there at the point of death. Our Lord sent him away with the joyful assurance that his son was alive.

nod.d: exile; wandering; unrest, a name given to the country to which Cain fled (<reflink>Gen.4:16</reflink>). It lay on the east of Eden.

nodab.d: noble, probably a tribe descended from one of the sons of Ishmael, with whom the trans-Jordanic tribes made war (<reflink>1 Chr.5:19</reflink>).

nogah.d: splendour, one of David's sons, born at Jerusalem (<reflink>1 Chr. 3:7</reflink>).

noph.d: the Hebrew name of an Egyptian city (<reflink>Isa. 19:13; Jer.2:16; 44:1; 46:14, 19; Ezek. 30:13, 16</reflink>). In Hos. 9:6 the Hebrew name is Moph, and is translated "Memphis," which is its Greek and Latin form. It was one of the most ancient and important cities of Egypt, and stood a little to the south of the modern Cairo, on the western bank of the Nile. It was the capital of Lower Egypt. Among the ruins found at this place is a colossal statue of Rameses the Great. (<see target="x-self">See MEMPHIS.</see>)

nophah.d: blast, a city of Moab which was occupied by the Amorites (<reflink>Num. 21:30</reflink>).

north country.d: a general name for the countries that lay north of Palestine. Most of the invading armies entered Palestine from the north (<reflink>Isa. 41:25; Jer. 1:14,15; 50:3,9,41; 51:48; Ezek. 26:7</reflink>).

northward.d: (Heb. tsaphon), a "hidden" or "dark place," as opposed to the sunny south (<reflink>Deut. 3:27</reflink>). A Hebrew in speaking of the points of the compass was considered as always having his face to the east, and hence "the left hand" (<reflink>Gen. 14:15; Job 23:9</reflink>) denotes the north. The "kingdoms of the north" are Chaldea, Assyria, Media, etc.

nose-jewels.d: Only mentioned in Isa. 3:21, although refered to in Gen. 24:47, Prov. 11:22, Hos. 2:13. They were among the most valued of ancient female ornaments. They "were made of ivory or metal, and occasionally jewelled. They were more than an inch in diameter, and hung upon the mouth. Eliezer gave one to Rebekah which was of gold and weighed half a shekel...At the present day the women in the country and in the desert wear these ornaments in one of the sides of the nostrils, which droop like the ears in consequence."

numbering of the people.d: Besides the numbering of the tribes mentioned in the history of the wanderings in the wilderness, we have an account of a general census of the whole nation from Dan to Beersheba, which David gave directions to Joab to make (<reflink>1 Chr. 21:1</reflink>). Joab very reluctantly began to carry out the king's command.

numbers, book of.d: the fourth of the books of the Pentateuch, called in the Hebrew be-midbar, i.e., "in the wilderness." In the LXX. version it is called "Numbers," and this name is now the usual title of the book. It is so called because it contains a record of the numbering of the people in the wilderness of Sinai (1-4), and of their numbering afterwards on the plain of Moab (26).

nun.d: Beyond the fact that he was the father of Joshua nothing more is known of him (<reflink>Ex. 33:11</reflink>).

nuts.d: were among the presents Jacob sent into Egypt for the purpose of conciliating Joseph (<reflink>Gen. 43:11</reflink>). This was the fruit of the pistachio tree, which resembles the sumac. It is of the size of an olive. In Cant. 6:11 a different Hebrew word ('egoz), which means "walnuts," is used.

nymphas.d: nymph, saluted by Paul in his Epistle to the Colossians as a member of the church of Laodicea (<reflink>Col. 4:15</reflink>).

oak.d: There are six Hebrew words rendered "oak."

oath.d: a solemn appeal to God, permitted on fitting occasions (<reflink>Deut. 6:13; Jer. 4:2</reflink>), in various forms (<reflink>Gen. 16:5; 2 Sam. 12:5; Ruth 1:17; Hos. 4:15; Rom. 1:9</reflink>), and taken in different ways (<reflink>Gen. 14:22; 24:2; 2 Chr. 6:22</reflink>). God is represented as taking an oath (<reflink>Heb. 6:16-18</reflink>), so also Christ (<reflink>Matt. 26:64</reflink>), and Paul (<reflink>Rom. 9:1; Gal. 1:20; Phil. 1:8</reflink>). The precept, "Swear not at all," refers probably to ordinary conversation between man and man (<reflink>Matt. 5:34,37</reflink>). But if the words are taken as referring to oaths, then their intention may have been to show "that the proper state of Christians is to require no oaths; that when evil is expelled from among them every yea and nay will be as decisive as an oath, every promise as binding as a vow."

obadiah.d: servant of the Lord. (1.) An Israelite who was chief in the household of King Ahab (<reflink>1 Kings 18:3</reflink>). Amid great spiritual degeneracy he maintained his fidelity to God, and interposed to protect The Lord's prophets, an hundred of whom he hid at great personal risk in a cave (4, 13). Ahab seems to have held Obadiah in great honour, although he had no sympathy with his piety (5, 6, 7). The last notice of him is his bringing back tidings to Ahab that Elijah, whom he had so long sought for, was at hand (9-16). "Go," said Elijah to him, when he met him in the way, "go tell thy lord, Behold, Elijah is here."

obadiah, book of.d: consists of one chapter, "concerning Edom," its impending doom (1:1-16), and the restoration of Israel (1:17-21). This is the shortest book of the Old Testament.

obal.d: stripped, the eight son of Joktan (<reflink>Gen. 10:28</reflink>); called also Ebal (<reflink>1 Chr. 1:22</reflink>).

obed.d: serving; worshipping. (1.) A son of Boaz and Ruth (<reflink>Ruth 4:21, 22</reflink>), and the grandfather of David (<reflink>Matt. 1:5</reflink>).

obed-edom.d: servant of Edom. (1.) "The Gittite" (probably so called because he was a native of Gath-rimmon), a Levite of the family of the Korhites (<reflink>1 Chr. 26:1, 4-8</reflink>), to whom was specially intrusted the custody of the ark (<reflink>1 Chr. 15:18</reflink>). When David was bringing up the ark "from the house of Abinadab, that was in Gibeah" (probably some hill or eminence near Kirjath-jearim), and had reached Nachon's threshing-floor, he became afraid because of the "breach upon Uzzah," and carried it aside into the house of Obededom (<reflink>2 Sam. 6:1-12</reflink>). There it remained for six months, and was to him and his house the occasion of great blessing. David then removed it with great rejoicing to Jerusalem, and set it in the midst of the tabernacle he had pitched for it.

obeisance.d: homage or reverence to any one (<reflink>Gen. 37:7; 43:28</reflink>).

obil.d: a keeper of camels, an Ishmaelite who was "over the camels" in the time of David (<reflink>1 Chr. 27:30</reflink>).

oboth.d: bottles, an encampment of the Israelites during the wanderings in the wilderness (<reflink>Num. 33:43</reflink>), the first after the setting up of the brazen serpent.

oded.d: restoring, or setting up. (1.) Father of the prophet Azariah (<reflink>2 Chr. 15:1, 8</reflink>).

offence.d: (1.) An injury or wrong done to one (<reflink>1 Sam. 25:31; Rom. 5:15</reflink>).

offering.d: an oblation, dedicated to God. Thus Cain consecrated to God of the first-fruits of the earth, and Abel of the firstlings of the flock (<reflink>Gen. 4:3, 4</reflink>). Under the Levitical system different kinds of offerings are specified, and laws laid down as to their presentation. These are described under their distinctive names.

og.d: gigantic, the king of Bashan, who was defeated by Moses in a pitched battle at Edrei, and was slain along with his sons (<reflink>Deut. 1:4</reflink>), and whose kingdom was given to the tribes of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh (<reflink>Num. 21:32-35; Deut. 3:1-13</reflink>). His bedstead (or rather sarcophagus) was of iron (or ironstone), 9 cubits in length and 4 cubits in breadth. His overthrow was afterwards celebrated in song (<reflink>Ps. 135:11; 136:20</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See SIHON.</see>)

ohad.d: united, or power, the third son of Simeon (<reflink>Gen. 46:10</reflink>).

ohel.d: a house; tent, the fourth son of Zerubbabel (<reflink>1 Chr. 3:20</reflink>).

oil.d: Only olive oil seems to have been used among the Hebrews. It was used for many purposes: for anointing the body or the hair (<reflink>Ex. 29:7; 2 Sam. 14:2; Ps. 23:5; 92:10; 104:15; Luke 7:46</reflink>); in some of the offerings (<reflink>Ex. 29:40; Lev. 7:12; Num. 6:15; 15:4</reflink>), but was excluded from the sin-offering (<reflink>Lev. 5:11</reflink>) and the jealousy-offering (<reflink>Num. 5:15</reflink>); for burning in lamps (<reflink>Ex. 25:6; 27:20; Matt. 25:3</reflink>); for medicinal purposes (<reflink>Isa. 1:6; Luke 10:34; James 5:14</reflink>); and for anointing the dead (<reflink>Matt. 26:12; Luke 23:56</reflink>).

oil-tree.d: (<reflink>Isa. 41:19; R.V. marg., "oleaster"</reflink>), Heb. 'etz shemen, rendered "olive tree" in 1 Kings 6:23, 31, 32, 33 (R.V., "olive wood") and "pine branches" in Neh. 8:15 (R.V., "branches of wild olive"), was some tree distinct from the olive. It was probably the oleaster (Eleagnus angustifolius), which grows abundantly in almost all parts of Palestine, especially about Hebron and Samaria. "It has a fine hard wood," says Tristram, "and yields an inferior oil, but it has no relationship to the olive, which, however, it resembles in general appearance."

ointment.d: Various fragrant preparations, also compounds for medical purposes, are so called (<reflink>Ex. 30:25; Ps. 133:2; Isa. 1:6; Amos 6:6; John 12:3; Rev. 18:13</reflink>).

old gate.d: one of the gates in the north wall of Jerusalem, so called because built by the Jebusites (<reflink>Neh. 3:6; 12:39</reflink>).

olive.d: the fruit of the olive-tree. This tree yielded oil which was highly valued. The best oil was from olives that were plucked before being fully ripe, and then beaten or squeezed (<reflink>Deut. 24:20; Isa. 17:6; 24:13</reflink>). It was called "beaten," or "fresh oil" (<reflink>Ex. 27:20</reflink>). There were also oil-presses, in which the oil was trodden out by the feet (<reflink>Micah 6:15</reflink>). James (3:12) calls the fruit "olive berries." The phrase "vineyards and olives" (<reflink>Judg. 15:5, A.V.</reflink>) should be simply "olive-yard," or "olive-garden," as in the Revised Version. (<see target="x-self">See OIL.</see>)

olive-tree.d: is frequently mentioned in Scripture. The dove from the ark brought an olive-branch to Noah (<reflink>Gen. 8:11</reflink>). It is mentioned among the most notable trees of Palestine, where it was cultivated long before the time of the Hebrews (<reflink>Deut. 6:11; 8:8</reflink>). It is mentioned in the first Old Testament parable, that of Jotham (<reflink>Judg. 9:9</reflink>), and is named among the blessings of the "good land," and is at the present day the one characteristic tree of Palestine. The oldest olive-trees in the country are those which are enclosed in the Garden of Gethsemane. It is referred to as an emblem of prosperity and beauty and religious privilege (<reflink>Ps. 52:8; Jer. 11:16; Hos. 14:6</reflink>). The two "witnesses" mentioned in Rev. 11:4 are spoken of as "two olive trees standing before the God of the earth." (<reflink>Comp. Zech. 4:3, 11-14.</reflink>)

olves, mount of.d: so called from the olive trees with which its sides are clothed, is a mountain ridge on the east of Jerusalem (<reflink>1 Kings 11:7; Ezek. 11:23; Zech. 14:4</reflink>), from which it is separated by the valley of Kidron. It is first mentioned in connection with David's flight from Jerusalem through the rebellion of Absalom (<reflink>2 Sam. 15:30</reflink>), and is only once again mentioned in the Old Testament, in Zech. 14:4. It is, however, frequently alluded to (<reflink>1 Kings 11:7; 2 Kings 23:13; Neh. 8:15; Ezek. 11:23</reflink>).

peulthai.d: wages of the Lord, one of the sons of Obed-edom, a Levite porter (<reflink>1 Chr. 26:5</reflink>).

phallu.d: separated, the second son of Reuben (<reflink>Gen. 46:9</reflink>).

phalti.d: deliverance of the Lord, the son of Laish of Gallim (<reflink>1 Sam. 25:44</reflink>)= Phaltiel (<reflink>2 Sam. 3:15</reflink>). Michal, David's wife, was given to him.

phanuel.d: face of God, father of the prophetess Anna (q.v.), Luke 2:36.

pharaoh.d: the official title borne by the Egyptian kings down to the time when that country was conquered by the Greeks. (See EGYPT

pharaoh's daughters.d: Three princesses are thus mentioned in Scripture: (1.) The princess who adopted the infant Moses (q.v.), Ex. 2:10. She is twice mentioned in the New Testament (<reflink>Acts 7:21: Heb. 11:24</reflink>). It would seem that she was alive and in some position of influence about the court when Moses was compelled to flee from Egypt, and thus for forty years he had in some way been under her influence. She was in all probability the sister of Rameses, and the daughter of Seti I. Josephus calls her Thermuthis. It is supposed by some that she was Nefert-ari, the wife as well as sister of Rameses. The mummy of this queen was among the treasures found at Deir-el-Bahari.

pharez.d: breach, the elder of the twin sons of Judah (<reflink>Gen. 38:29</reflink>). From him the royal line of David sprang (<reflink>Ruth 4:18-22</reflink>). "The chief of all the captains of the host" was of the children of Perez (<reflink>1 Chr. 27:3; Matt. 1:3</reflink>).

pharisees.d: separatists (Heb. persahin, from parash, "to separate"). They were probably the successors of the Assideans (i.e., the "pious"), a party that originated in the time of Antiochus Epiphanes in revolt against his heathenizing policy. The first mention of them is in a description by Josephus of the three sects or schools into which the Jews were divided (B.C. 145). The other two sects were the Essenes and the Sadducees. In the time of our Lord they were the popular party (<reflink>John 7:48</reflink>). They were extremely accurate and minute in all matters appertaining to the law of Moses (<reflink>Matt. 9:14; 23:15; Luke 11:39; 18:12</reflink>). Paul, when brought before the council of Jerusalem, professed himself a Pharisee (<reflink>Acts 23:6-8; 26:4, 5</reflink>).

pharpar.d: swift, one of the rivers of Damascus (<reflink>2 Kings 5:12</reflink>). It has been identified with the 'Awaj, "a small lively river." The whole of the district watered by the 'Awaj is called the Wady el-'Ajam, i.e., "the valley of the Persians", so called for some unknown reason. This river empties itself into the lake or marsh Bahret Hijaneh, on the east of Damascus. One of its branches bears the modern name of Wady Barbar, which is probably a corruption of Pharpar.

phebe.d: a "deaconess of the church at Cenchrea," the port of Corinth. She was probably the bearer of Paul's epistle to the Romans. Paul commended her to the Christians at Rome; "for she hath been," says he, "a succourer of many, and of myself also" (<reflink>Rom. 16:1, 2</reflink>).

phenice.d: properly Phoenix a palm-tree (as in the R.V.), a town with a harbour on the southern side of Crete (<reflink>Acts 27:12</reflink>), west of the Fair Havens. It is now called Lutro.

phenicia.d: (<reflink>Acts 21:2</reflink>) = Phenice (11:19; 15:3; R.V., Phoenicia), Gr. phoinix, "a palm", the land of palm-trees; a strip of land of an average breadth of about 20 miles along the shores of the Mediterranean, from the river Eleutherus in the north to the promotory of Carmel in the south, about 120 miles in length. This name is not found in the Old Testament, and in the New Testament it is mentioned only in the passages above referred to.

phicol.d: great, the chief captain of the army of Abimelech, the Philistine king of Gerar. He entered into an alliance with Abraham with reference to a certain well which, from this circumstance, was called Beersheba (q.v.), "the well of the oath" (<reflink>Gen. 21:22, 32; 26:26</reflink>).

philadelphia.d: brotherly love, a city of Lydia in Asia Minor, about 25 miles south-east of Sardis. It was the seat of one of the "seven churches" (<reflink>Rev. 3:7-12</reflink>). It came into the possession of the Turks in A.D. 1392. It has several times been nearly destroyed by earthquakes. It is still a town of considerable size, called Allahshehr, "the city of God."

philemon.d: an inhabitant of Colosse, and apparently a person of some note among the citizens (<reflink>Col. 4:9; Philemon 1:2</reflink>). He was brought to a knowledge of the gospel through the instrumentality of Paul (19), and held a prominent place in the Christian community for his piety and beneficence (4-7). He is called in the epistle a "fellow-labourer," and therefore probably held some office in the church at Colosse; at all events, the title denotes that he took part in the work of spreading a knowledge of the gospel.

philemon, epistle to.d: was written from Rome at the same time as the epistles to the Colossians and Ephesians, and was sent also by Onesimus. It was addressed to Philemon and the members of his family.

philetus.d: amiable, with Hymenaeus, at Ephesus, said that the "resurrection was past already" (<reflink>2 Tim. 2:17, 18</reflink>). This was a Gnostic heresy held by the Nicolaitanes. (<see target="x-self">See ALEXANDER [4].</see>)

philip.d: lover of horses. (1.) One of the twelve apostles; a native of Bethsaida, "the city of Andrew and Peter" (<reflink>John 1:44</reflink>). He readily responded to the call of Jesus when first addressed to him (43), and forthwith brought Nathanael also to Jesus (45,46). He seems to have held a prominent place among the apostles (<reflink>Matt. 10:3; Mark 3:18; John 6:5-7; 12:21, 22; 14:8, 9; Acts 1:13</reflink>). Of his later life nothing is certainly known. He is said to have preached in Phrygia, and to have met his death at Hierapolis.

philippi.d: (1.) Formerly Crenides, "the fountain," the capital of the province of Macedonia. It stood near the head of the Sea, about 8 miles north-west of Kavalla. It is now a ruined village, called Philibedjik. Philip of Macedonia fortified the old Thracian town of Crenides, and called it after his own name Philippi (B.C. 359-336). In the time of the Emperor Augustus this city became a Roman colony, i.e., a military settlement of Roman soldiers, there planted for the purpose of controlling the district recently conquered. It was a "miniature Rome," under the municipal law of Rome, and governed by military officers, called duumviri, who were appointed directly from Rome. Having been providentially guided thither, here Paul and his companion Silas preached the gospel and formed the first church in Europe. (<see target="x-self">See LYDIA.</see>) This success stirred up the enmity of the people, and they were "shamefully entreated" (<reflink>Acts 16:9-40; 1 Thess. 2:2</reflink>). …

philippians, epistle to.d: was written by Paul during the two years when he was "in bonds" in Rome (<reflink>Phil. 1:7-13</reflink>), probably early in the year A.D. 62 or in the end of 61.

philistia.d: =Palestine (q.v.), "the land of the Philistines" (<reflink>Ps. 60:8; 87:4; 108:9</reflink>). The word is supposed to mean "the land of wanderers" or "of strangers."

philistines.d: (<reflink>Gen. 10:14, R.V.; but in A.V., "Philistim"</reflink>), a tribe allied to the Phoenicians. They were a branch of the primitive race which spread over the whole district of the Lebanon and the valley of the Jordan, and Crete and other Mediterranean islands. Some suppose them to have been a branch of the Rephaim (<reflink>2 Sam. 21:16-22</reflink>). In the time of Abraham they inhabited the south-west of Judea, Abimelech of Gerar being their king (<reflink>Gen. 21:32, 34; 26:1</reflink>). They are, however, not noticed among the Canaanitish tribes mentioned in the Pentateuch. They are spoken of by Amos (9:7) and Jeremiah (47:4) as from Caphtor, i.e., probably Crete, or, as some think, the Delta of Egypt. In the whole record from Exodus to Samuel they are represented as inhabiting the tract of country which lay between Judea and Egypt (<reflink>Ex. 13:17; 15:14, 15; Josh. 13:3; 1 Sam. 4</reflink>).

phinehas.d: mouth of brass, or from old Egypt, the negro. (1.) Son of Eleazar, the high priest (<reflink>Ex. 6:25</reflink>). While yet a youth he distinguished himself at Shittim by his zeal against the immorality into which the Moabites had tempted the people (<reflink>Num. 25:1-9</reflink>), and thus "stayed the plague" that had broken out among the people, and by which twenty-four thousand of them perished. For his faithfulness on that occasion he received the divine approbation (10-13). He afterwards commanded the army that went out against the Midianites (31:6-8). When representatives of the people were sent to expostulate with the two and a half tribes who, just after crossing Jordan, built an altar and departed without giving any explanation, Phinehas was their leader, and addressed them in the words recorded in Josh. 22:16-20. Their explanation follows. This great altar was intended to be all ages only a witness that they still formed a part of Israel. …

phlegon.d: burning, a Roman Christian to whom Paul sent salutations (<reflink>Rom. 16:14</reflink>).

phrygia.d: dry, an irregular and ill-defined district in Asia Minor. It was divided into two parts, the Greater Phrygia on the south, and the Lesser Phrygia on the west. It is the Greater Phrygia that is spoken of in the New Testament. The towns of Antioch in Pisidia (<reflink>Acts 13:14</reflink>), Colosse, Hierapolis, Iconium, and Laodicea were situated in it.

phut.d: Phut is placed between Egypt and Canaan in Gen. 10:6, and elsewhere we find the people of Phut described as mercenaries in the armies of Egypt and Tyre (<reflink>Jer. 46:9; Ezek. 30:5; 27:10</reflink>). In a fragment of the annuals of Nebuchadrezzar which records his invasion of Egypt, reference is made to "Phut of the Ionians."

phygellus.d: fugitive, a Christian of Asia, who "turned away" from Paul during his second imprisonment at Rome (<reflink>2 Tim. 1:15</reflink>). Nothing more is known of him.

phylacteries.d: (Gr. phulakteria; i.e., "defences" or "protections"), called by modern Jews tephillin (i.e., "prayers") are mentioned only in Matt. 23:5. They consisted of strips of parchment on which were inscribed these four texts: (1.) Ex. 13:1-10; (2.) 11-16; (3.) Deut. 6:4-9; (4.) 11:18-21, and which were enclosed in a square leather case, on one side of which was inscribed the Hebrew letter shin, to which the rabbis attached some significance. This case was fastened by certain straps to the forehead just between the eyes. The "making broad the phylacteries" refers to the enlarging of the case so as to make it conspicuous. (<see target="x-self">See FRONTLETS.</see>)

physician.d: Asa, afflicted with some bodily malady, "sought not to the Lord but to the physicians" (<reflink>2 Chr. 16:12</reflink>). The "physicians" were those who "practised heathen arts of magic, disavowing recognized methods of cure, and dissociating the healing art from dependence on the God of Israel. The sin of Asa was not, therefore, in seeking medical advice, as we understand the phrase, but in forgetting Jehovah."

pi-beseth.d: (<reflink>Ezek. 30:17</reflink>), supposed to mean. "a cat," or a deity in the form of a cat, worshipped by the Egyptians. It was called by the Greeks Bubastis. The hieroglyphic name is "Pe-bast", i.e., the house of Bast, the Artemis of the Egyptians. The town of Bubasts was situated on the Pelusian branch, i.e., the easternmost branch, of the Delta. It was the seat of one of the chief annual festivals of the Egyptians. Its ruins bear the modern name of Tel-Basta.

pi-hahiroth.d: place where the reeds grow (LXX. and Copt. read "farmstead"), the name of a place in Egypt where the children of Israel encamped (<reflink>Ex. 14:2, 9</reflink>), how long is uncertain. Some have identified it with Ajrud, a fortress between Etham and Suez. The condition of the Isthmus of Suez at the time of the Exodus is not exactly known, and hence this, with the other places mentioned as encampments of Israel in Egypt, cannot be definitely ascertained. The isthmus has been formed by the Nile deposits. This increase of deposit still goes on, and so rapidly that within the last fifty years the mouth of the Nile has advanced northward about four geographical miles. In the maps of Ptolemy (of the second and third centuries A.D.) the mouths of the Nile are forty miles further south than at present. (<see target="x-self">See EXODUS.</see>)

pieces.d: (1) of silver. In Ps. 68:30 denotes "fragments," and not properly money. In 1 Sam. 2:36 (Heb. agorah), properly a "small sum" as wages, weighed rather than coined. Josh. 24:32 (Heb. kesitah, q.v.), supposed by some to have been a piece of money bearing the figure of a lamb, but rather simply a certain amount. (<reflink>Comp. Gen. 33:19</reflink>).

piety.d: Lat. pietas, properly honour and respect toward parents (<reflink>1 Tim. 5:4</reflink>). In Acts 17:23 the Greek verb is rendered "ye worship," as applicable to God.

pigeon.d: Pigeons are mentioned as among the offerings which, by divine appointment, Abram presented unto the Lord (<reflink>Gen. 15:9</reflink>). They were afterwards enumerated among the sin-offerings (<reflink>Lev. 1:14; 12:6</reflink>), and the law provided that those who could not offer a lamb might offer two young pigeons (5:7; comp. Luke 2:24). (<see target="x-self">See DOVE.</see>)

pilate, pontius.d: probably connected with the Roman family of the Pontii, and called "Pilate" from the Latin pileatus, i.e., "wearing the pileus", which was the "cap or badge of a manumitted slave," as indicating that he was a "freedman," or the descendant of one. He was the sixth in the order of the Roman procurators of Judea (A.D. 26-36). His headquarters were at Caesarea, but he frequently went up to Jerusalem. His reign extended over the period of the ministry of John the Baptist and of Jesus Christ, in connection with whose trial his name comes into prominent notice. Pilate was a "typical Roman, not of the antique, simple stamp, but of the imperial period, a man not without some remains of the ancient Roman justice in his soul, yet pleasure-loving, imperious, and corrupt. He hated the Jews whom he ruled, and in times of irritation freely shed their blood. They returned his hatred with cordiality, and accused him of every crime, maladministration, cruelty, and robbery. …

pillar.d: used to support a building (<reflink>Judg. 16:26, 29</reflink>); as a trophy or memorial (<reflink>Gen. 28:18; 35:20; Ex. 24:4; 1 Sam. 15:12, A.V., "place," more correctly "monument," or "trophy of victory," as in 2 Sam. 18:18</reflink>); of fire, by which the Divine Presence was manifested (<reflink>Ex. 13:2</reflink>). The "plain of the pillar" in Judg. 9:6 ought to be, as in the Revised Version, the "oak of the pillar", i.e., of the monument or stone set up by Joshua (24:26).

pine tree.d: Heb. tidhar, mentioned along with the fir-tree in Isa. 41:19; 60:13. This is probably the cypress; or it may be the stone-pine, which is common on the northern slopes of Lebanon. Some suppose that the elm, others that the oak, or holm, or ilex, is meant by the Hebrew word. In Neh. 8:15 the Revised Version has "wild olive" instead of "pine." (<see target="x-self">See FIR.</see>)

pinnacle.d: a little wing, (<reflink>Matt. 4:5; Luke 4:9</reflink>). On the southern side of the temple court was a range of porches or cloisters forming three arcades. At the south-eastern corner the roof of this cloister was some 300 feet above the Kidron valley. The pinnacle, some parapet or wing-like projection, was above this roof, and hence at a great height, probably 350 feet or more above the valley.

pipe.d: (<reflink>1 Sam. 10:5; 1 Kings 1:40; Isa. 5:12; 30:29</reflink>). The Hebrew word halil, so rendered, means "bored through," and is the name given to various kinds of wind instruments, as the fife, flute, Pan-pipes, etc. In Amos 6:5 this word is rendered "instrument of music." This instrument is mentioned also in the New Testament (<reflink>Matt. 11:17; 1 Cor. 14:7</reflink>). It is still used in Palestine, and is, as in ancient times, made of different materials, as reed, copper, bronze, etc.

piram.d: like a wild ass, a king of Jarmuth, a royal city of the Canaanites, who was conquered and put to death by Joshua (10:3, 23, 26).

pirathon.d: prince, or summit, a place "in the land of Ephraim" (<reflink>Judg. 12:15</reflink>), now Fer'on, some 10 miles south-west of Shechem. This was the home of Abdon the judge.

pirathonite.d: (1.) Abdon, the son of Hillel, so called, Judg. 12:13, 15.

pisgah.d: a part, a mountain summit in the land of Moab, in the territory of Reuben, where Balak offered up sacrifices (<reflink>Num. 21:20; 23:14</reflink>), and from which Moses viewed the promised land (<reflink>Deut. 3:27</reflink>). It is probably the modern Jebel Siaghah. (See NEBO

pisidia.d: a district in Asia Minor, to the north of Pamphylia. The Taurus range of mountains extends through it. Antioch, one of its chief cities, was twice visited by Paul (<reflink>Acts 13:14; 14:21-24</reflink>).

pison.d: Babylonian, the current, broad-flowing, one of the "four heads" into which the river which watered the garden of Eden was divided (<reflink>Gen. 2:11</reflink>). Some identify it with the modern Phasis, others with the Halys, others the Jorak or Acampis, others the Jaab, the Indus, the Ganges, etc.

pit.d: a hole in the ground (<reflink>Ex. 21:33, 34</reflink>), a cistern for water (<reflink>Gen. 37:24; Jer. 14:3</reflink>), a vault (41:9), a grave (<reflink>Ps. 30:3</reflink>). It is used as a figure for mischief (<reflink>Ps. 9:15</reflink>), and is the name given to the unseen place of woe (<reflink>Rev. 20:1, 3</reflink>). The slime-pits in the vale of Siddim were wells which yielded asphalt (<reflink>Gen. 14:10</reflink>).

pitch.d: (<reflink>Gen. 6:14</reflink>), asphalt or bitumen in its soft state, called "slime" (<reflink>Gen. 11:3; 14:10; Ex. 2:3</reflink>), found in pits near the Dead Sea (q.v.). It was used for various purposes, as the coating of the outside of vessels and in building. Allusion is made in Isa. 34:9 to its inflammable character. (<see target="x-self">See SLIME.</see>)

pitcher.d: a vessel for containing liquids. In the East pitchers were usually carried on the head or shoulders (<reflink>Gen. 24:15-20; Judg. 7:16, 19; Mark 14:13</reflink>).

pithom.d: Egyptian, Pa-Tum, "house of Tum," the sun-god, one of the "treasure" cities built for Pharaoh Rameses II. by the Israelites (<reflink>Ex. 1:11</reflink>). It was probably the Patumos of the Greek historian Herodotus. It has now been satisfactorily identified with Tell-el-Maskhuta, about 12 miles west of Ismailia, and 20 east of Tel-el-Kebir, on the southern bank of the present Suez Canal. Here have recently (1883) been discovered the ruins of supposed grain-chambers, and other evidences to show that this was a great "store city." Its immense ruin-heaps show that it was built of bricks, and partly also of bricks without straw. Succoth (<reflink>Ex. 12:37</reflink>) is supposed by some to be the secular name of this city, Pithom being its sacred name. This was the first halting-place of the Israelites in their exodus. It has been argued (Dr. …

plague.d: a "stroke" of affliction, or disease. Sent as a divine chastisement (<reflink>Num. 11:33; 14:37; 16:46-49; 2 Sam. 24:21</reflink>). Painful afflictions or diseases, (<reflink>Lev. 13:3, 5, 30; 1 Kings 8:37</reflink>), or severe calamity (<reflink>Mark 5:29; Luke 7:21</reflink>), or the judgment of God, so called (<reflink>Ex. 9:14</reflink>). Plagues of Egypt were ten in number.

plain.d: (1.) Heb. 'abel (<reflink>Judg. 11:33</reflink>), a "grassy plain" or "meadow." Instead of "plains of the vineyards," as in the Authorized Version, the Revised Version has "Abel-cheramim" (q.v.), comp. Judg. 11:22; 2 Chr. 16:4.

plain of mamre.d: (<reflink>Gen. 13:18; 14:13; R.V., "oaks of Mamre;" marg., "terebinths"</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See MAMRE; TEIL-TREE.</see>)

plane tree.d: Heb. 'armon (<reflink>Gen. 30:37; Ezek. 31:8</reflink>), rendered "chesnut" in the Authorized Version, but correctly "plane tree" in the Revised Version and the LXX. This tree is frequently found in Palestine, both on the coast and in the north. It usually sheds its outer bark, and hence its Hebrew name, which means "naked." (<see target="x-self">See CHESTNUT.</see>)

pleiades.d: Heb. kimah, "a cluster" (<reflink>Job 9:9; 38:31; Amos 5:8, A.V., "seven stars;" R.V., "Pleiades"</reflink>), a name given to the cluster of stars seen in the shoulder of the constellation Taurus.

plough.d: first referred to in Gen. 45:6, where the Authorized Version has "earing," but the Revised Version "ploughing;" next in Ex. 34:21 and Deut. 21:4. The plough was originally drawn by oxen, but sometimes also by asses and by men. (<see target="x-self">See AGRICULTURE.</see>)

poetry.d: has been well defined as "the measured language of emotion." Hebrew poetry deals almost exclusively with the great question of man's relation to God. "Guilt, condemnation, punishment, pardon, redemption, repentance are the awful themes of this heaven-born poetry."

padan-aram.d: the plain of Aram, or the plain of the highlands, (<reflink>Gen. 25:20; 28:2, 5-7; 31:18, etc.</reflink>), commonly regarded as the district of Mesopotamia (q.v.) lying around Haran.

pagiel.d: God allots, a prince of the tribe of Asher (<reflink>Num. 1:13</reflink>), in the wilderness.

pahath-moab.d: governor of Moab, a person whose descendants returned from the Captivity and assisted in rebuilding Jerusalem (<reflink>Ezra 2:6; 8:4; 10:30</reflink>).

paint.d: Jezebel "painted her face" (<reflink>2 Kings 9:30</reflink>); and the practice of painting the face and the eyes seems to have been common (<reflink>Jer. 4:30; Ezek. 23:40</reflink>). An allusion to this practice is found in the name of Job's daughter (42:14) Kerenhappuch (q.v.). Paintings in the modern sense of the word were unknown to the ancient Jews.

palace.d: Used now only of royal dwellings, although originally meaning simply (as the Latin word palatium, from which it is derived, shows) a building surrounded by a fence or a paling. In the Authorized Version there are many different words so rendered, presenting different ideas, such as that of citadel or lofty fortress or royal residence (<reflink>Neh. 1:1; Dan. 8:2</reflink>). It is the name given to the temple fortress (<reflink>Neh. 2:8</reflink>) and to the temple itself (<reflink>1 Chr. 29:1</reflink>). It denotes also a spacious building or a great house (<reflink>Dan. 1:4; 4:4, 29: Esther 1:5; 7:7</reflink>), and a fortified place or an enclosure (<reflink>Ezek. 25:4</reflink>). Solomon's palace is described in 1 Kings 7:1-12 as a series of buildings rather than a single great structure. Thirteen years were spent in their erection. This palace stood on the eastern hill, adjoining the temple on the south.

palestine.d: originally denoted only the sea-coast of the land of Canaan inhabited by the Philistines (<reflink>Ex. 15:14; Isa. 14:29, 31; Joel 3:4</reflink>), and in this sense exclusively the Hebrew name Pelesheth (rendered "Philistia" in Ps. 60:8; 83:7; 87:4; 108:9) occurs in the Old Testament.

pallu.d: separated, the second son of Reuben (<reflink>1 Chr. 5:3</reflink>); called Phallu, Gen. 46:9. He was the father of the Phalluites (<reflink>Ex. 6:14; Num. 26:5, 8</reflink>).

palm tree.d: (Heb. tamar), the date-palm characteristic of Palestine. It is described as "flourishing" (<reflink>Ps. 92:12</reflink>), tall (<reflink>Cant. 7:7</reflink>), "upright" (<reflink>Jer. 10:5</reflink>). Its branches are a symbol of victory (<reflink>Rev. 7:9</reflink>). "Rising with slender stem 40 or 50, at times even 80, feet aloft, its only branches, the feathery, snow-like, pale-green fronds from 6 to 12 feet long, bending from its top, the palm attracts the eye wherever it is seen." The whole land of Palestine was called by the Greeks and Romans Phoenicia, i.e., "the land of palms." Tadmor in the desert was called by the Greeks and Romans Palmyra, i.e., "the city of palms." The finest specimens of this tree grew at Jericho (<reflink>Deut. 34:3</reflink>) and Engedi and along the banks of the Jordan. Branches of the palm tree were carried at the feast of Tabernacles (<reflink>Lev. 23:40</reflink>). …

palm trees, the city of.d: the name given to Jericho (q.v.), Deut. 34:3; Judg. 1:16; 3:13.

palmer-worm.d: (Heb. gazam). The English word may denote either a caterpillar (as rendered by the LXX.), which wanders like a palmer or pilgrim, or which travels like pilgrims in bands (<reflink>Joel 1:4; 2:25</reflink>), the wingless locusts, or the migratory locust in its larva state.

palsy.d: a shorter form of "paralysis." Many persons thus afflicted were cured by our Lord (<reflink>Matt. 4:24; 8:5-13; 9:2-7; Mark 2:3-11; Luke 7:2-10; John 5:5-7</reflink>) and the apostles (<reflink>Acts 8:7; 9:33, 34</reflink>).

palti.d: deliverance from the Lord, one of the spies representing the tribe of Benjamin (<reflink>Num. 13:9</reflink>).

paltiel.d: deliverance of God, the prince of Issachar who assisted "to divide the land by inheritance" (<reflink>Num. 34:26</reflink>).

paltite.d: the designation of one of David's heroes (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:26</reflink>); called also the Pelonite (<reflink>1 Chr. 11:27</reflink>).

pamphylia.d: Paul and his company, loosing from Paphos, sailed north-west and came to Perga, the capital of Pamphylia (<reflink>Acts 13:13, 14</reflink>), a province about the middle of the southern sea-board of Asia Minor. It lay between Lycia on the west and Cilicia on the east. There were strangers from Pamphylia at Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost (2:10).

pan.d: a vessel of metal or earthenware used in culinary operations; a cooking-pan or frying-pan frequently referred to in the Old Testament (<reflink>Lev. 2:5; 6:21; Num. 11:8; 1 Sam. 2:14, etc.</reflink>).
