Hostilities between the two kingdoms still continued; but during Rehoboam's reign there was not again the intervention of a third party.

shittah-tree.d: (<reflink>Isa. 41:19; R.V., "acacia tree"</reflink>). Shittah wood was employed in making the various parts of the tabernacle in the wilderness, and must therefore have been indigenous in the desert in which the Israelites wandered. It was the acacia or mimosa (Acacia Nilotica and A. seyal). "The wild acacia (Mimosa Nilotica), under the name of _sunt_, everywhere represents the seneh, or senna, of the burning bush. A slightly different form of the tree, equally common under the name of _seyal_, is the ancient 'shittah,' or, as more usually expressed in the plural form, the 'shittim,' of which the tabernacle was made." Stanley's Sinai, etc. (<reflink>Ex. 25:10, 13, 23, 28</reflink>).

shittim.d: acacias, also called "Abel-shittim" (<reflink>Num. 33:49</reflink>), a plain or valley in the land of Moab where the Israelites were encamped after their two victories over Sihon and Og, at the close of their desert wanderings, and from which Joshua sent forth two spies (q.v.) "secretly" to "view" the land and Jericho (<reflink>Josh. 2:1</reflink>).

shoa.d: opulent, the mountain district lying to the north-east of Babylonia, anciently the land of the Guti, or Kuti, the modern Kurdistan. The plain lying between these mountains and the Tigris was called su-Edina, i.e., "the border of the plain." This name was sometimes shortened into Suti and Su, and has been regarded as = Shoa (<reflink>Ezek. 23:23</reflink>). Some think it denotes a place in Babylon. (<see target="x-self">See PEKOD.</see>)

shobab.d: apostate. (1.) One of David's sons by Bathseheba (<reflink>2 Sam. 5:14</reflink>).

shechinah.d: a Chaldee word meaning resting-place, not found in Scripture, but used by the later Jews to designate the visible symbol of God's presence in the tabernacle, and afterwards in Solomon's temple. When the Lord led Israel out of Egypt, he went before them "in a pillar of a cloud." This was the symbol of his presence with his people. For references made to it during the wilderness wanderings, see Ex. 14:20; 40:34-38; Lev. 9:23, 24; Num. 14:10; 16:19, 42.

sheep.d: are of different varieties. Probably the flocks of Abraham and Isaac were of the wild species found still in the mountain regions of Persia and Kurdistan. After the Exodus, and as a result of intercourse with surrounding nations, other species were no doubt introduced into the herds of the people of Israel. They are frequently mentioned in Scripture. The care of a shepherd over his flock is referred to as illustrating God's care over his people (<reflink>Ps. 23:1, 2; 74:1; 77:20; Isa. 40:11; 53:6; John 10:1-5, 7-16</reflink>).

sheep-fold.d: a strong fenced enclosure for the protection of the sheep gathered within it (<reflink>Num. 32:24; 1 Chr. 17:7; Ps. 50:9; 78:70</reflink>). In John 10:16 the Authorized Version renders by "fold" two distinct Greek words, aule and poimne, the latter of which properly means a "flock," and is so rendered in the Revised Version. (<reflink>See also Matt. 26:31; Luke 2:8; 1 Cor. 9:7.</reflink>) (See FOLD

sheep-gate.d: one of the gates of Jerusalem mentioned by Nehemiah (3:1, 32; 12:39). It was in the eastern wall of the city.

sheep-market.d: occurs only in John 5:2 (marg., also R.V., "sheep-gate"). The word so rendered is an adjective, and it is uncertain whether the noun to be supplied should be "gate" or, following the Vulgate Version, "pool."

shekel.d: weight, the common standard both of weight and value among the Hebrews. It is estimated at 220 English grains, or a little more than half an ounce avoirdupois. The "shekel of the sanctuary" (<reflink>Ex. 30:13; Num. 3:47</reflink>) was equal to twenty gerahs (<reflink>Ezek. 45:12</reflink>). There were shekels of gold (<reflink>1 Chr. 21:25</reflink>), of silver (<reflink>1 Sam. 9:8</reflink>), of brass (17:5), and of iron (7). When it became a coined piece of money, the shekel of gold was equivalent to about 2 pound of our money. Six gold shekels, according to the later Jewish system, were equal in value to fifty silver ones.

shem.d: a name; renown, the first mentioned of the sons of Noah (<reflink>Gen. 5:32; 6:10</reflink>). He was probably the eldest of Noah's sons. The words "brother of Japheth the elder" in Gen. 10:21 are more correctly rendered "the elder brother of Japheth," as in the Revised Version. Shem's name is generally mentioned first in the list of Noah's sons. He and his wife were saved in the ark (7:13). Noah foretold his preeminence over Canaan (9:23-27). He died at the age of six hundred years, having been for many years contemporary with Abraham, according to the usual chronology. The Israelitish nation sprang from him (<reflink>Gen. 11:10-26; 1 Chr. 1:24-27</reflink>).

shemaah.d: rumour, a Benjamite whose sons "came to David to Ziklag" (<reflink>1 Chr. 12:3</reflink>).

shemaiah.d: whom Jehovah heard. (1.) A prophet in the reign of Rehoboam (<reflink>1 Kings 12:22-24</reflink>).

shemariah.d: whom Jehovah guards. (1.) One who joined David at Ziklag (<reflink>1 Chr. 12:5</reflink>).

shemeber.d: soaring on high, the king of Zeboiim, who joined with the other kings in casting off the yoke of Chedorlaomer. After having been reconquered by him, he was rescued by Abraham (<reflink>Gen. 14:2</reflink>).

sheminith.d: eight; octave, a musical term, supposed to denote the lowest note sung by men's voices (<reflink>1 Chr. 15:21; Ps. 6; 12, title</reflink>).

shemiramoth.d: most high name. (1.) A Levite in the reign of Jehoshaphat (<reflink>2 Chr. 17:8</reflink>).

shemuel.d: heard of God. (1.) The son of Ammihud. He represented Simeon in the division of the land (<reflink>Num. 34:20</reflink>).

shen.d: a tooth, probably some conspicuous tooth-shaped rock or crag (<reflink>1 Sam. 7:12</reflink>), a place between which and Mizpeh Samuel set up his "Ebenezer." In the Hebrew the word has the article prefixed, "the Shen." The site is unknown.

shenir.d: =Senir, (<reflink>Deut. 3:9; Cant. 4:8</reflink>), the name given to Mount Hermon (q.v.) by the Sidonians.

sheol.d: (Heb., "the all-demanding world" = Gr. Hades, "the unknown region"), the invisible world of departed souls. (See HELL

shepham.d: a treeless place, Num. 34:10, 11: "The coast shall go down from Shepham to Riblah."

shephatiah.d: judged of the Lord. (1.) A son of David by Abital (<reflink>2 Sam. 3:4</reflink>).

shepherd.d: a word naturally of frequent occurence in Scripture. Sometimes the word "pastor" is used instead (<reflink>Jer. 2:8; 3:15; 10:21; 12:10; 17:16</reflink>). This word is used figuratively to represent the relation of rulers to their subjects and of God to his people (<reflink>Ps. 23:1; 80:1; Isa. 40:11; 44:28; Jer. 25:34, 35; Nahum 3:18; John 10:11, 14; Heb. 13:20; 1 Pet. 2:25; 5:4</reflink>).

sherebiah.d: flame of the Lord, a priest whose name is prominent in connection with the work carried on by Ezra and Nehemiah at Jerusalem (<reflink>Ezra 8:17, 18, 24-30; Neh. 8:7; 9:4, 5; 10:12</reflink>).

sheresh.d: root, a descendant of Manasseh (<reflink>1 Chr. 7:16</reflink>).

sherezer.d: one of the messengers whom the children of the Captivity sent to Jerusalem "to pray for them before the Lord" (<reflink>Zech. 7:2</reflink>).

sheshach.d: (<reflink>Jer. 25:26</reflink>), supposed to be equivalent to Babel (Babylon), according to a secret (cabalistic) mode of writing among the Jews of unknown antiquity, which consisted in substituting the last letter of the Hebrew alphabet for the first, the last but one for the second, and so on. Thus the letters sh, sh, ch become b, b, l, i.e., Babel. This is supposed to be confirmed by a reference to Jer. 51:41, where Sheshach and Babylon are in parallel clauses. There seems to be no reason to doubt that Babylon is here intended by this name. (<see target="x-self">See Streane's Jeremiah, l.c.</see>)

sheshai.d: whitish, one of the sons of Anak (<reflink>Num. 13:22</reflink>). When the Israelites obtained possession of the country the sons of Anak were expelled and slain (<reflink>Josh. 15:14; Judg. 1:10</reflink>).

sheshbazzar.d: O sun-god, defend the lord! (<reflink>Ezra 1:8, 11</reflink>), probably another name for Zerubbabel (q.v.), Ezra 2:2; Hag. 1:12, 14; Zech. 4:6, 10.

sheth.d: tumult. (1.) "The children of Sheth" (<reflink>Num. 24:17</reflink>); R.V., "the sons of tumult," which is probably the correct rendering, as there is no evidence that this is a proper name here.

shethar.d: a star, a prince at the court of Ahasuerus (<reflink>Esther 1:14</reflink>).

shethar-boznai.d: star of splendour, a Persian officer who vainly attempted to hinder the rebuilding of the temple (<reflink>Ezra 5:3, 6; 6:6, 13</reflink>).

sion.d: elevated. (1.) Denotes Mount Hermon in Deut. 4:48; called Sirion by the Sidonians, and by the Amorites Shenir (<reflink>Deut. 3:9</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See HERMON.</see>)

siphmoth.d: fruitful places, some unknown place in the south, where David found friends when he fled from Saul (<reflink>1 Sam. 30:28</reflink>).

sirah.d: retiring, a well from which Joab's messenger brought back Abner (<reflink>2 Sam. 3:26</reflink>). It is now called 'Ain Sarah, and is situated about a mile from Hebron, on the road to the north.

sirion.d: a breastplate, the Sidonian name of Hermon (q.v.), Deut. 3:9; Ps. 29:6.

sisera.d: (Egypt. Ses-Ra, "servant of Ra"). (1.) The captain of Jabin's army (<reflink>Judg. 4:2</reflink>), which was routed and destroyed by the army of Barak on the plain of Esdraelon. After all was lost he fled to the settlement of Heber the Kenite in the plain of Zaanaim. Jael, Heber's wife, received him into her tent with apparent hospitality, and "gave him butter" (i.e., lebben, or curdled milk) "in a lordly dish." Having drunk the refreshing beverage, he lay down, and soon sank into the sleep of the weary. While he lay asleep Jael crept stealthily up to him, and taking in her hand one of the tent pegs, with a mallet she drove it with such force through his temples that it entered into the ground where he lay, and "at her feet he bowed, he fell; where he bowed, there he fell down dead." The part of Deborah's song (<reflink>Judg. …

sitnah.d: strife, the second of the two wells dug by Isaac, whose servants here contended with the Philistines (<reflink>Gen. 26:21</reflink>). It has been identified with the modern Shutneh, in the valley of Gerar, to the west of Rehoboth, about 20 miles south of Beersheba.

sitting.d: the attitude generally assumed in Palestine by those who were engaged in any kind of work. "The carpenter saws, planes, and hews with his hand-adze, sitting on the ground or upon the plank he is planning. The washerwoman sits by the tub; and, in a word, no one stands when it is possible to sit. Shopkeepers always sit, and Levi sitting at the receipt of custom (<reflink>Matt. 9:9</reflink>) is the exact way to state the case.", Thomson, Land and Book.

sivan.d: a Persian word (Assyr, sivanu, "bricks"), used after the Captivity as the name of the third month of the Jewish year, extending from the new moon in June to the new moon in July (<reflink>Esther 8:9</reflink>).

skin, coats made of.d: (<reflink>Gen. 3:21</reflink>). Skins of rams and badgers were used as a covering for the tabernacle (<reflink>Ex. 25:5; Num. 4:8-14</reflink>).

slave.d: Jer. 2:14 (A.V.), but not there found in the original. In Rev. 18:13 the word "slaves" is the rendering of a Greek word meaning "bodies." The Hebrew and Greek words for slave are usually rendered simply "servant," "bondman," or "bondservant." Slavery as it existed under the Mosaic law has no modern parallel. That law did not originate but only regulated the already existing custom of slavery (<reflink>Ex. 21:20, 21, 26, 27; Lev. 25:44-46; Josh. 9:6-27</reflink>). The gospel in its spirit and genius is hostile to slavery in every form, which under its influence is gradually disappearing from among men.

slime.d: (<reflink>Gen. 11:3; LXX., "asphalt;" R.V. marg., "bitumen"</reflink>). The vale of Siddim was full of slime pits (14:10). Jochebed daubed the "ark of bulrushes" with slime (<reflink>Ex. 2:3</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See PITCH.</see>)

sling.d: With a sling and a stone David smote the Philistine giant (<reflink>1 Sam. 17:40, 49</reflink>). There were 700 Benjamites who were so skilled in its use that with the left hand they "could sling stones at a hair breadth, and not miss" (<reflink>Judg. 20:16; 1 Chr. 12:2</reflink>). It was used by the Israelites in war (<reflink>2 Kings 3:25</reflink>). (See ARMS

smith.d: The Hebrews were not permitted by the Philistines in the days of Samuel to have a smith amongst them, lest they should make them swords and spears (<reflink>1 Sam. 13:19</reflink>). Thus the Philistines sought to make their conquest permanent (comp. 2 Kings 24:16).

smyrna.d: myrrh, an ancient city of Ionia, on the western coast of Asia Minor, about 40 miles to the north of Ephesus. It is now the chief city of Anatolia, having a mixed population of about 200,000, of whom about one-third are professed Christians. The church founded here was one of the seven addressed by our Lord (<reflink>Rev. 2:8-11</reflink>). The celebrated Polycarp, a pupil of the apostle John, was in the second century a prominent leader in the church of Smyrna. Here he suffered martyrdom, A.D. 155.

snail.d: (1.) Heb. homit, among the unclean creeping things (<reflink>Lev. 11:30</reflink>). This was probably the sand-lizard, of which there are many species in the wilderness of Judea and the Sinai peninsula.

snare.d: The expression (<reflink>Amos 3:5</reflink>), "Shall one take up a snare from the earth?" etc. (Authorized Version), ought to be, as in the Revised Version, "Shall a snare spring up from the ground?" etc. (<see target="x-self">See GIN.</see>)

snow.d: Common in Palestine in winter (<reflink>Ps. 147:16</reflink>). The snow on the tops of the Lebanon range is almost always within view throughout the whole year. The word is frequently used figuratively by the sacred writers (<reflink>Job 24:19; Ps. 51:7; 68:14; Isa. 1:18</reflink>). It is mentioned only once in the historical books (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:20</reflink>). It was "carried to Tyre, Sidon, and Damascus as a luxury, and labourers sweltering in the hot harvest-fields used it for the purpose of cooling the water which they drank (<reflink>Prov. 25:13; Jer. 18:14</reflink>). No doubt Herod Antipas, at his feasts in Tiberias, enjoyed also from this very source the modern luxury of ice-water."

so.d: (Nubian, Sabako), an Ethiopian king who brought Egypt under his sway. He was bribed by Hoshea to help him against the Assyrian monarch Shalmaneser (<reflink>2 Kings 17:4</reflink>). This was a return to the policy that had been successful in the reign of Jeroboam I.

soap.d: (<reflink>Jer. 2:22; Mal. 3:2; Heb. borith</reflink>), properly a vegetable alkali, obtained from the ashes of certain plants, particularly the salsola kali (saltwort), which abounds on the shores of the Dead Sea and of the Mediterranean. It does not appear that the Hebrews were acquainted with what is now called "soap," which is a compound of alkaline carbonates with oleaginous matter. The word "purely" in Isa. 1:25 (R.V., "throughly;" marg., "as with lye") is lit. "as with _bor_." This word means "clearness," and hence also that which makes clear, or pure, alkali. "The ancients made use of alkali mingled with oil, instead of soap (<reflink>Job 9:30</reflink>), and also in smelting metals, to make them melt and flow more readily and purely" (Gesenius).

socho.d: a fence; hedge, (<reflink>1 Chr. 4:18; R.V., Soco</reflink>)=So'choh (<reflink>1 Kings 4:10; R.V., Socoh</reflink>), Sho'choh (<reflink>1 Sam. 17:1; R.V., Socoh</reflink>), Sho'co (<reflink>2 Chr. 11:7; R.V., Soco</reflink>), Sho'cho (<reflink>2 Chr. 28:18; R.V., Soco</reflink>), a city in the plain or lowland of Judah, where the Philistines encamped when they invaded Judah after their defeat at Michmash. It lay on the northern side of the valley of Elah (Wady es-Sunt). It has been identified with the modern Khurbet Shuweikeh, about 14 miles south-west of Jerusalem. In this campaign Goliath was slain, and the Philistines were completely routed.

sodom.d: burning; the walled, a city in the vale of Siddim (<reflink>Gen. 13:10; 14:1-16</reflink>). The wickedness of its inhabitants brought down upon it fire from heaven, by which it was destroyed (18:16-33; 19:1-29; Deut. 23:17). This city and its awful destruction are frequently alluded to in Scripture (<reflink>Deut. 29:23; 32:32; Isa. 1:9, 10; 3:9; 13:19; Jer. 23:14; Ezek. 16:46-56; Zeph. 2:9; Matt. 10:15; Rom. 9:29; 2 Pet. 2:6, etc.</reflink>). No trace of it or of the other cities of the plain has been discovered, so complete was their destruction. Just opposite the site of Zoar, on the south-west coast of the Dead Sea, is a range of low hills, forming a mass of mineral salt called Jebel Usdum, "the hill of Sodom." It has been concluded, from this and from other considerations, that the cities of the plain stood at the southern end of the Dead Sea. Others, however, with much greater probability, contend that they stood at the northern end of the sea. [in 1897].

sodoma.d: (<reflink>Rom. 9:29; R.V., "Sodom"</reflink>), the Greek form for Sodom.

sodomites.d: those who imitated the licentious wickedness of Sodom (<reflink>Deut. 23:17; 1 Kings 14:24; Rom. 1:26, 27</reflink>). Asa destroyed them "out of the land" (<reflink>1 Kings 15:12</reflink>), as did also his son Jehoshaphat (22:46).

solemn meeting.d: (<reflink>Isa. 1:13</reflink>), the convocation on the eighth day of the Feast of Tabernacles (<reflink>Lev. 23:36; Num. 29:35, R.V., "solemn assembly;" marg., "closing festival"</reflink>).  It is the name given also to the convocation held on the seventh day of the Passover (<reflink>Deut. 16:8</reflink>).

solomon.d: peaceful, (Heb. Shelomoh), David's second son by Bathsheba, i.e., the first after their legal marriage (2 Sam. 12). He was probably born about B.C. 1035 (<reflink>1 Chr. 22:5; 29:1</reflink>). He succeeded his father on the throne in early manhood, probably about sixteen or eighteen years of age. Nathan, to whom his education was intrusted, called him Jedidiah, i.e., "beloved of the Lord" (<reflink>2 Sam. 12:24, 25</reflink>). He was the first king of Israel "born in the purple." His father chose him as his successor, passing over the claims of his elder sons: "Assuredly Solomon my son shall reign after me." His history is recorded in 1 Kings 1-11 and 2 Chr. 1-9. His elevation to the throne took place before his father's death, and was hastened on mainly by Nathan and Bathsheba, in consequence of the rebellion of Adonijah (<reflink>1 Kings 1:5-40</reflink>). During his long reign of forty years the Hebrew monarchy gained its highest splendour. …

solomon's porch.d: (<reflink>John 10:23; Acts 3:11; 5:12</reflink>), a colonnade, or cloister probably, on the eastern side of the temple. It is not mentioned in connection with the first temple, but Josephus mentions a porch, so called, in Herod's temple (q.v.).

solomon, song of.d: called also, after the Vulgate, the "Canticles." It is the "song of songs" (1:1), as being the finest and most precious of its kind; the noblest song, "das Hohelied," as Luther calls it. The Solomonic authorship of this book has been called in question, but evidences, both internal and external, fairly establish the traditional view that it is the product of Solomon's pen. It is an allegorical poem setting forth the mutual love of Christ and the Church, under the emblem of the bridegroom and the bride. (<reflink>Compare Matt. 9:15; John 3:29; Eph. 5:23, 27, 29; Rev. 19:7-9; 21:2, 9; 22:17. Compare also Ps. 45; Isa. 54:4-6; 62:4, 5; Jer. 2:2; 3:1, 20; Ezek. 16; Hos. 2:16, 19, 20.</reflink>)

son of god.d: The plural, "sons of God," is used (<reflink>Gen. 6:2, 4</reflink>) to denote the pious descendants of Seth. In Job 1:6; 38:7 this name is applied to the angels. Hosea uses the phrase (1:10) to designate the gracious relation in which men stand to God.

son of man.d: (1.) Denotes mankind generally, with special reference to their weakness and frailty (<reflink>Job 25:6; Ps. 8:4; 144:3; 146:3; Isa. 51:12, etc.</reflink>).

songs.d: of Moses (Ex. 15; Num. 21:17; Deut. 32; Rev. 15:3), Deborah (Judg. 5), Hannah (1 Sam. 2), David (2 Sam. 22, and Psalms), Mary (<reflink>Luke 1:46-55</reflink>), Zacharias (<reflink>Luke 1:68-79</reflink>), the angels (<reflink>Luke 2:13</reflink>), Simeon (<reflink>Luke 2:29</reflink>), the redeemed (<reflink>Rev. 5:9; 19</reflink>), Solomon (<see target="x-self">see SOLOMON, SONGS OF</see>).

soothsayer.d: one who pretends to prognosticate future events. Baalam is so called (<reflink>Josh. 13:22; Heb. kosem, a "diviner," as rendered 1 Sam. 6:2; rendered "prudent," Isa. 3:2</reflink>). In Isa. 2:6 and Micah 5:12 (Heb. yonenim, i.e., "diviners of the clouds") the word is used of the Chaldean diviners who studied the clouds. In Dan. 2:27; 5:7 the word is the rendering of the Chaldee gazrin, i.e., "deciders" or "determiners", here applied to Chaldean astrologers, "who, by casting nativities from the place of the stars at one's birth, and by various arts of computing and divining, foretold the fortunes and destinies of individuals.", Gesenius, Lex. Heb. (<see target="x-self">See SORCERER.</see>)

sop.d: a morsel of bread (<reflink>John 13:26; comp. Ruth 2:14</reflink>). Our Lord took a piece of unleavened bread, and dipping it into the broth of bitter herbs at the Paschal meal, gave it to Judas. (<reflink>Comp. Ruth 2:14.</reflink>)

sopater.d: the father who saves, probably the same as Sosipater, a kinsman of Paul (<reflink>Rom. 16:21</reflink>), a Christian of the city of Berea who accompanied Paul into Asia (<reflink>Acts 20:4-6</reflink>).

sorcerer.d: from the Latin sortiarius, one who casts lots, or one who tells the lot of others. (<see target="x-self">See DIVINATION.</see>)

sorek.d: choice vine, the name of a valley, i.e., a torrent-bed, now the Wady Surar, "valley of the fertile spot," which drains the western Judean hills, and flowing by Makkedah and Jabneel, falls into the sea some eight miles south of Joppa. This was the home of Deliah, whom Samson loved (<reflink>Judg. 16:4</reflink>).

sosthenes.d: safe in strength, the chief ruler of the synagogue at Corinth, who was seized and beaten by the mob in the presence of Gallio, the Roman governor, when he refused to proceed against Paul at the instigation of the Jews (<reflink>Acts 18:12-17</reflink>). The motives of this assault against Sosthenes are not recorded, nor is it mentioned whether it was made by Greeks or Romans. Some identify him, but without sufficient grounds, with one whom Paul calls "Sosthenes our brother," a convert to the faith (<reflink>1 Cor. 1:1</reflink>).

south.d: Heb. Negeb, that arid district to the south of Palestine through which lay the caravan route from Central Palestine to Egypt (<reflink>Gen. 12:9; 13:1, 3; 46:1-6</reflink>). "The Negeb comprised a considerable but irregularly-shaped tract of country, its main portion stretching from the mountains and lowlands of Judah in the north to the mountains of Azazemeh in the south, and from the Dead Sea and southern Ghoron the east to the Mediterranean on the west." In Ezek. 20:46 (21:1 in Heb.) three different Hebrew words are all rendered "south." (1) "Set thy face toward the south" (Teman, the region on the right, 1 Sam. 33:24); (2) "Drop thy word toward the south" (Negeb, the region of dryness, Josh. 15:4); (3) "Prophesy against the forest of the south field" (Darom, the region of brightness, Deut. 33:23). In Job 37:9 the word "south" is literally "chamber," used here in the sense of treasury (<reflink>comp. 38:22; Ps. 135:7</reflink>). …

sovereignty.d: of God, his absolute right to do all things according to his own good pleasure (<reflink>Dan. 4:25, 35; Rom. 9:15-23; 1 Tim. 6:15; Rev. 4:11</reflink>).

spain.d: Paul expresses his intention (<reflink>Rom. 15:24, 28</reflink>) to visit Spain. There is, however, no evidence that he ever carried it into effect, although some think that he probably did so between his first and second imprisonment. (<see target="x-self">See TARSHISH.</see>)

sparrow.d: Mentioned among the offerings made by the very poor. Two sparrows were sold for a farthing (<reflink>Matt. 10:29</reflink>), and five for two farthings (<reflink>Luke 12:6</reflink>). The Hebrew word thus rendered is _tsippor_, which properly denotes the whole family of small birds which feed on grain (<reflink>Lev. 14:4; Ps. 84:3; 102:7</reflink>). The Greek word of the New Testament is _strouthion_ (<reflink>Matt. 10:29-31</reflink>), which is thus correctly rendered.

spicery.d: Heb. nechoth, identified with the Arabic naka'at, the gum tragacanth, obtained from the astralagus, of which there are about twenty species found in Palestine. The tragacanth of commerce is obtained from the A. tragacantha. "The gum exudes plentifully under the heat of the sun on the leaves, thorns, and exteremity of the twigs."

spices.d: aromatic substances, of which several are named in Ex. 30. They were used in the sacred anointing oil (<reflink>Ex. 25:6; 35:8; 1 Chr. 9:29</reflink>), and in embalming the dead (<reflink>2 Chr. 16:14; Luke 23:56; 24:1; John 19:39, 40</reflink>). Spices were stored by Hezekiah in his treasure-house (<reflink>2 Kings 20:13; Isa. 39:2</reflink>).

spider.d: The trust of the hypocrite is compared to the spider's web or house (<reflink>Job 8:14</reflink>). It is said of the wicked by Isaiah that they "weave the spider's web" (59:5), i.e., their works and designs are, like the spider's web, vain and useless. The Hebrew word here used is _'akkabish_, "a swift weaver."

spies.d: When the Israelites reached Kadesh for the first time, and were encamped there, Moses selected twelve spies from among the chiefs of the divisions of the tribes, and sent them forth to spy the land of Canaan (Num. 13), and to bring back to him a report of its actual condition. They at once proceeded on their important errand, and went through the land as far north as the district round Lake Merom. After about six weeks' absence they returned. Their report was very discouraging, and the people were greatly alarmed, and in a rebellious spirit proposed to elect a new leader and return to Egypt. Only two of the spies, Caleb and Joshua, showed themselves on this occasion stout-hearted and faithful. All their appeals and remonstrances were in vain. Moses announced that as a punishment for their rebellion they must now wander in the wilderness till a new generation should arise which would go up and posses the land. …

spikenard.d: (Heb. nerd), a much-valued perfume (<reflink>Cant. 1:12; 4:13, 14</reflink>). It was "very precious", i.e., very costly (<reflink>Mark 14:3; John 12:3,5</reflink>). It is the root of an Indian plant, the Nardostachys jatamansi, of the family of Valeriance, growing on the Himalaya mountains. It is distinguished by its having many hairy spikes shooting out from one root. It is called by the Arabs sunbul Hindi, "the Indian spike." In the New Testament this word is the rendering of the Greek nardos pistike. The margin of the Revised Version in these passages has "pistic nard," pistic being perhaps a local name. Some take it to mean genuine, and others liquid. The most probable opinion is that the word pistike designates the nard as genuine or faithfully prepared.

spirit.d: (Heb. ruah; Gr. pneuma), properly wind or breath. In 2 Thess. 2:8 it means "breath," and in Eccl. 8:8 the vital principle in man. It also denotes the rational, immortal soul by which man is distinguished (<reflink>Acts 7:59; 1 Cor. 5:5; 6:20; 7:34</reflink>), and the soul in its separate state (<reflink>Heb. 12:23</reflink>), and hence also an apparition (<reflink>Job 4:15; Luke 24:37, 39</reflink>), an angel (<reflink>Heb. 1:14</reflink>), and a demon (<reflink>Luke 4:36; 10:20</reflink>). This word is used also metaphorically as denoting a tendency (<reflink>Zech. 12:10; Luke 13:11</reflink>).

sponge.d: occurs only in the narrative of the crucifixion (<reflink>Matt. 27:48; Mark 15:36; John 19:29</reflink>). It is ranked as a zoophyte. It is found attached to rocks at the bottom of the sea.

spouse.d: (<reflink>Cant. 4:8-12; Hos. 4:13, 14</reflink>) may denote either husband or wife, but in the Scriptures it denotes only the latter.

spring.d: (Heb. 'ain, "the bright open source, the eye of the landscape"). To be carefully distinguished from "well" (q.v.). "Springs" mentioned in Josh. 10:40 (Heb. 'ashdoth) should rather be "declivities" or "slopes" (R.V.), i.e., the undulating ground lying between the lowlands (the shephelah) and the central range of hills.

stachys.d: spike; an ear of corn, a convert at Rome whom Paul salutes (<reflink>Rom. 16:9</reflink>).

stacte.d: (Heb. nataph), one of the components of the perfume which was offered on the golden altar (<reflink>Ex. 30:34; R.V. marg., "opobalsamum"</reflink>). The Hebrew word is from a root meaning "to distil," and it has been by some interpreted as distilled myrrh. Others regard it as the gum of the storax tree, or rather shrub, the Styrax officinale. "The Syrians value this gum highly, and use it medicinally as an emulcent in pectoral complaints, and also in perfumery."

star, morning.d: a name figuratively given to Christ (<reflink>Rev. 22:16; comp. 2 Pet. 1:19</reflink>). When Christ promises that he will give the "morning star" to his faithful ones, he "promises that he will give to them himself, that he will give to them himself, that he will impart to them his own glory and a share in his own royal dominion; for the star is evermore the symbol of royalty (<reflink>Matt. 2:2</reflink>), being therefore linked with the sceptre (<reflink>Num. 24:17</reflink>). All the glory of the world shall end in being the glory of the Church." Trench's Comm.

stargazers.d: (<reflink>Isa. 47:13</reflink>), those who pretend to tell what will occur by looking upon the stars. The Chaldean astrologers "divined by the rising and setting, the motions, aspects, colour, degree of light, etc., of the stars."

stars.d: The eleven stars (<reflink>Gen. 37:9</reflink>); the seven (<reflink>Amos 5:8</reflink>); wandering (<reflink>Jude 1:13</reflink>); seen in the east at the birth of Christ, probably some luminous meteors miraculously formed for this specific purpose (<reflink>Matt. 2:2-10</reflink>); stars worshipped (<reflink>Deut. 4:19; 2 Kings 17:16; 21:3; Jer. 19:13</reflink>); spoken of symbolically (<reflink>Num. 24:17; Rev. 1:16, 20; 12:1</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See ASTROLOGERS.</see>)

stater.d: Greek word rendered "piece of money" (<reflink>Matt. 17:27, A.V.; and "shekel" in R.V.</reflink>). It was equal to two didrachmas ("tribute money," 17:24), or four drachmas, and to about 2s. 6d. of our money. (<see target="x-self">See SHEKEL.</see>)

steel.d: The "bow of steel" in (A.V.) 2 Sam. 22:35; Job 20:24; Ps. 18:34 is in the Revised Version "bow of brass" (Heb. kesheth-nehushah). In Jer. 15:12 the same word is used, and is also rendered in the Revised Version "brass." But more correctly it is copper (q.v.), as brass in the ordinary sense of the word (an alloy of copper and zinc) was not known to the ancients.

stephanas.d: crown, a member of the church at Corinth, whose family were among those the apostle had baptized (<reflink>1 Cor. 1:16; 16:15, 17</reflink>). He has been supposed by some to have been the "jailer of Philippi" (<reflink>comp. Acts 16:33</reflink>). The First Epistle to the Corinthians was written from Philippi some six years after the jailer's conversion, and he was with the apostle there at that time.

stephen.d: one of the seven deacons, who became a preacher of the gospel. He was the first Christian martyr. His personal character and history are recorded in Acts 6. "He fell asleep" with a prayer for his persecutors on his lips (7:60). Devout men carried him to his grave (8:2).

stoics.d: a sect of Greek philosophers at Athens, so called from the Greek word stoa i.e., a "porch" or "portico," where they have been called "the Pharisees of Greek paganism." The founder of the Stoics was Zeno, who flourished about B.C. 300. He taught his disciples that a man's happiness consisted in bringing himself into harmony with the course of the universe. They were trained to bear evils with indifference, and so to be independent of externals. Materialism, pantheism, fatalism, and pride were the leading features of this philosophy.

stomacher.d: (<reflink>Isa. 3:24</reflink>), an article of female attire, probably some sort of girdle around the breast.

stone.d: Stones were commonly used for buildings, also as memorials of important events (<reflink>Gen. 28:18; Josh. 24:26, 27; 1 Sam. 7:12, etc.</reflink>). They were gathered out of cultivated fields (<reflink>Isa. 5:2; comp. 2 Kings 3:19</reflink>). This word is also used figuratively of believers (<reflink>1 Pet. 2:4, 5</reflink>), and of the Messiah (<reflink>Ps. 118:22; Isa. 28:16; Matt. 21:42; Acts 4:11, etc.</reflink>). In Dan. 2:45 it refers also to the Messiah. He is there described as "cut out of the mountain." (<see target="x-self">See ROCK.</see>)

stones, precious.d: Frequently referred to (<reflink>1 Kings 10:2; 2 Chr. 3:6; 9:10; Rev. 18:16; 21:19</reflink>). There are about twenty different names of such stones in the  They are figuratively introduced to denote value, beauty, durability (<reflink>Cant. 5:14; Isa 54:11, 12; Lam. 4:7</reflink>).

stoning.d: a form of punishment (<reflink>Lev. 20:2; 24:14; Deut. 13:10; 17:5; 22:21</reflink>) prescribed for certain offences. Of Achan (<reflink>Josh. 7:25</reflink>), Naboth (1 Kings 21), Stephen (<reflink>Acts 7:59</reflink>), Paul (<reflink>Acts 14:19; 2 Cor. 11:25</reflink>).

stork.d: Heb. hasidah, meaning "kindness," indicating thus the character of the bird, which is noted for its affection for its young. It is in the list of birds forbidden to be eaten by the Levitical law (<reflink>Lev. 11:19; Deut. 14:18</reflink>). It is like the crane, but larger in size. Two species are found in Palestine, the white, which are dispersed in pairs over the whole country; and the black, which live in marshy places and in great flocks. They migrate to Palestine periodically (about the 22nd of March). Jeremiah alludes to this (<reflink>Jer. 8:7</reflink>). At the appointed time they return with unerring sagacity to their old haunts, and re-occupy their old nests. "There is a well-authenticated account of the devotion of a stork which, at the burning of the town of Delft, after repeated and unsuccessful attempts to carry off her young, chose rather to remain and perish with them than leave them to their fate. Well might the Romans call it the pia avis!"

shobach.d: poured out, the "captain of the host of Hadarezer" when he mustered his vassals and tributaries from beyond "the river Euphrates" (<reflink>2 Sam. 10:15-18</reflink>); called also Shophach (<reflink>1 Chr. 19:16</reflink>).

shobal.d: pilgrim. (1.) The second son of Seir the Horite; one of the Horite "dukes" (<reflink>Gen. 36:20</reflink>).

shobi.d: captor, son of Nahash of Rabbah, the Ammonite. He showed kindness to David when he fled from Jerusalem to Mahanaim (<reflink>2 Sam. 17:27</reflink>).

shocho.d: (<reflink>2 Chr. 28:18</reflink>) = Shochoh (<reflink>1 Sam. 17:1</reflink>) = Shoco (<reflink>2 Chr. 11:7</reflink>). See SOCOH.

shoe.d: Of various forms, from the mere sandal (q.v.) to the complete covering of the foot. The word so rendered (A.V.) in Deut. 33:25, _min'al_, "a bar," is derived from a root meaning "to bolt" or "shut fast," and hence a fastness or fortress. The verse has accordingly been rendered "iron and brass shall be thy fortress," or, as in the Revised Version, "thy bars [marg., "shoes"] shall be iron and brass."

shomer.d: watchman. (1.) The mother of Jehozabad, who murdered Joash (<reflink>2 Kings 12:21</reflink>); called also Shimrith, a Moabitess (<reflink>2 Chr. 24:26</reflink>).

shophan.d: hidden, or hollow, a town east of Jordan (<reflink>Num. 32:35</reflink>), built by the children of Gad. This word should probably be joined with the word preceding it in this passage, Atroth-Shophan, as in the Revised Version.

shoshannim.d: lilies, the name of some musical instrument, probably like a lily in shape (Ps. 45; 69, title). Some think that an instrument of six strings is meant.

shoshannim-eduth.d: in title of Ps. 80 (R.V. marg., "lilies, a testimony"), probably the name of the melody to which the psalm was to be sung.

shrines, silver.d: little models and medallions of the temple and image of Diana of Ephesus (<reflink>Acts 19:24</reflink>). The manufacture of these was a very large and profitable business.

shua.d: wealth. (1.) A Canaanite whose daughter was married to Judah (<reflink>1 Chr. 2:3</reflink>).

shuah.d: prostration; a pit. (1.) One of Abraham's sons by Keturah (<reflink>Gen. 25:2; Chr. 1:32</reflink>). (2.) 1 Chr. 4:11.

shual, the land of.d: land of the fox, a district in the tribe of Benjamin (<reflink>1 Sam. 13:17</reflink>); possibly the same as Shalim (9:4), in the neighbourhood of Shaalabbin (<reflink>Josh. 19:42</reflink>).

shuhite.d: a designation of Bildad (<reflink>Job 2:11</reflink>), probably because he was a descendant of Shuah.

shulamite.d: the same, as some think, with "Shunammite," from "Shunem:" otherwise, the import of the word is uncertain (<reflink>Cant. 6:13; R.V., "Shulammite"</reflink>).

shunammite.d: a person of Shunem (<reflink>1 Kings 1:3; 2 Kings 4:12</reflink>). The Syr. and Arab. read "Sulamite."

shunem.d: two resting-places, a little village in the tribe of Issachar, to the north of Jezreel and south of Mount Gilboa (<reflink>Josh. 19:18</reflink>), where the Philistines encamped when they came against Saul (<reflink>1 Sam. 28:4</reflink>), and where Elisha was hospitably entertained by a rich woman of the place. On the sudden death of this woman's son she hastened to Carmel, 20 miles distant across the plain, to tell Elisha, and to bring him with her to Shunem. There, in the "prophet's chamber," the dead child lay; and Elisha entering it, shut the door and prayed earnestly: and the boy was restored to life (<reflink>2 Kings 4:8-37</reflink>). This woman afterwards retired during the famine to the low land of the Philistines; and on returning a few years afterwards, found her house and fields in the possession of a stranger. She appealed to the king at Samaria, and had them in a somewhat remarkable manner restored to her (comp. 2 Kings 8:1-6).

shur.d: an enclosure; a wall, a part, probably, of the Arabian desert, on the north-eastern border of Egypt, giving its name to a wilderness extending from Egypt toward Philistia (<reflink>Gen. 16:7; 20:1; 25:18; Ex.15:22</reflink>). The name was probably given to it from the wall (or shur) which the Egyptians built to defend their frontier on the north-east from the desert tribes. This wall or line of fortifications extended from Pelusium to Heliopolis.

shushan.d: a lily, the Susa of Greek and Roman writers, once the capital of Elam. It lay in the uplands of Susiana, on the east of the Tigris, about 150 miles to the north of the head of the Persian Gulf. It is the modern Shush, on the northwest of Shuster. Once a magnificent city, it is now an immense mass of ruins. Here Daniel saw one of his visions (Dan. 8); and here also Nehemiah (Neh. 1) began his public life. Most of the events recorded in the Book of Esther took place here. Modern explorers have brought to light numerous relics, and the ground-plan of the splendid palace of Shushan, one of the residences of the great king, together with numerous specimens of ancient art, which illustrate the statements of Scripture regarding it (<reflink>Dan. 8:2</reflink>). The great hall of this palace (Esther 1) "consisted of several magnificent groups of columns, together with a frontage of 343 feet 9 inches, and a depth of 244 feet. …

shushan-eduth.d: lily of the testimony, the title of Ps. 60. (See SHOSHANNIM

sibbecai.d: the Lord sustains, one of David's heroes (<reflink>1 Chr. 11:29</reflink>), general of the eighth division of the army (27:11). He slew the giant Saph in the battle of Gob (<reflink>2 Sam. 21:18; R.V., "Sibbechai"</reflink>). Called also Mebunnai (23:27).

sibmah.d: coolness; fragrance, a town in Reuben, in the territory of Moab, on the east of Jordan (<reflink>Josh. 13:19</reflink>); called also Shebam and Shibmah (<reflink>Num. 32:3, 38</reflink>). It was famous for its vines (<reflink>Isa. 16:9; Jer. 48:32</reflink>). It has been identified with the ruin of Sumieh, where there are rock-cut wine-presses. This fact explains the words of the prophets referred to above. It was about 5 miles east of Heshbon.

sickle.d: of the Egyptians resembled that in modern use. The ears of corn were cut with it near the top of the straw. There was also a sickle used for warlike purposes, more correctly, however, called a pruning-hook (<reflink>Deut. 16:9; Jer. 50:16, marg., "scythe;" Joel 3:13; Mark 4:29</reflink>).

siddim, vale of.d: valley of the broad plains, "which is the salt sea" (<reflink>Gen. 14:3, 8, 10</reflink>), between Engedi and the cities of the plain, at the south end of the Dead Sea. It was "full of slime-pits" (R.V., "bitumen pits"). Here Chedorlaomer and the confederate kings overthrew the kings of Sodom and the cities of the plain. God afterwards, on account of their wickedness, "overthrew those cities, and all the plain, and all the inhabitants of the cities;" and the smoke of their destruction "went up as the smoke of a furnace" (19:24-28), and was visible from Mamre, where Abraham dwelt.

sidon.d: fishing; fishery, Gen. 10:15, 19 (A.V. marg., Tzidon; R.V., Zidon); Matt. 11:21, 22; Luke 6:17. (<see target="x-self">See ZIDON.</see>)

signet.d: a seal used to attest documents (<reflink>Dan. 6:8-10, 12</reflink>). In 6:17, this word properly denotes a ring. The impression of a signet ring on fine clay has recently been discovered among the ruins at Nineveh. It bears the name and title of an Egyptian king. Two actual signet rings of ancient Egyptian monarchs (Cheops and Horus) have also been discovered.

sihon.d: striking down. The whole country on the east of Jordan, from the Arnon to the Jabbok, was possessed by the Amorites, whose king, Sihon, refused to permit the Israelites to pass through his territory, and put his army in array against them. The Israelites went forth against him to battle, and gained a complete victory. The Amorites were defeated; Sihon, his sons, and all his people were smitten with the sword, his walled towns were captured, and the entire country of the Amorites was taken possession of by the Israelites (<reflink>Num. 21:21-30; Deut. 2:24-37</reflink>).

sihor.d: (correctly Shi'hor) black; dark the name given to the river Nile in Isa. 23:3; Jer. 2:18. In Josh. 13:3 it is probably "the river of Egypt", i.e., the Wady el-Arish (<reflink>1 Chr. 13:5</reflink>), which flows "before Egypt", i.e., in a north-easterly direction from Egypt, and enters the sea about 50 miles south-west of Gaza.

silas.d: wood, a prominent member of the church at Jerusalem; also called Silvanus. He and Judas, surnamed Barsabas, were chosen by the church there to accompany Paul and Barnabas on their return to Antioch from the council of the apostles and elders (<reflink>Acts 15:22</reflink>), as bearers of the decree adopted by the council. He assisted Paul there in his evangelistic labours, and was also chosen by him to be his companion on his second missionary tour (<reflink>Acts 16:19-24</reflink>). He is referred to in the epistles under the name of Silvanus (<reflink>2 Cor. 1:19; 1 Thess. 1:1; 2 Thess. 1:1; 1 Pet. 5:12</reflink>). There is no record of the time or place of his death.

silk.d: Heb. demeshek, "damask," silk cloth manufactured at Damascus, Amos 3:12. A.V., "in the corner of a bed, and in Damascus in a couch;" R.V., "in the corner of a couch, and on the silken cushions of a bed" (marg., "in Damascus on a bed").

silla.d: a highway; a twig, only in 2 Kings 12:20. If taken as a proper name (as in the LXX. and other versions), the locality is unknown.

siloah, the pool of.d: Heb. shelah; i.e., "the dart", Neh. 3:15; with the art. _shiloah_, "sending," Isa. 8:6 (<reflink>comp. 7:3</reflink>)=Siloam (q.v.)

siloam, pool of.d: sent or sending. Here a notable miracle was wrought by our Lord in giving sight to the blind (<reflink>John 9:7-11</reflink>). It has been identified with the Birket Silwan in the lower Tyropoeon valley, to the south-east of the hill of Zion.

siloam, tower of.d: mentioned only Luke 13:4. The place here spoken of is the village now called Silwan, or Kefr Silwan, on the east of the valley of Kidron, and to the north-east of the pool. It stands on the west slope of the Mount of Olives.

silver.d: used for a great variety of purposes, as may be judged from the frequent references to it in Scripture. It first appears in commerce in Gen. 13:2; 23:15, 16. It was largely employed for making vessels for the sanctuary in the wilderness (<reflink>Ex. 26:19; 27:17; Num. 7:13, 19; 10:2</reflink>). There is no record of its having been found in Syria or Palestine. It was brought in large quantities by foreign merchants from abroad, from Spain and India and other countries probably.

silverling.d: (<reflink>Isa. 7:23</reflink>). Literally the words are "at a thousand of silver", i.e., "pieces of silver," or shekels.

simeon.d: hearing. (1.) The second son of Jacob by Leah (<reflink>Gen. 29:33</reflink>). He was associated with Levi in the terrible act of vengeance against Hamor and the Shechemites (34:25, 26). He was detained by Joseph in Egypt as a hostage (42:24). His father, when dying, pronounced a malediction against him (49:5-7). The words in the Authorized Version (49:6), "they digged down a wall," ought to be, as correctly rendered in the Revised Version, "they houghed an ox."

simeon, the tribe of.d: was "divided and scattered" according to the prediction in Gen. 49:5-7. They gradually dwindled in number, and sank into a position of insignificance among the other tribes. They decreased in the wilderness by about two-thirds (<reflink>comp. Num. 1:23; 26:14</reflink>). Moses pronounces no blessing on this tribe. It is passed by in silence (Deut. 33).

simon.d: the abbreviated form of Simeon. (1.) One of the twelve apostles, called the Canaanite (<reflink>Matt. 10:4; Mark 3:18</reflink>). This word "Canaanite" does not mean a native of Canaan, but is derived from the Syriac word Kanean or Kaneniah, which was the name of a Jewish sect. The Revised Version has "Cananaean;" marg., "or Zealot" He is also called "Zelotes" (<reflink>Luke 6:15; Acts 1:13; R.V., "the Zealot"</reflink>), because previous to his call to the apostleship he had been a member of the fanatical sect of the Zealots. There is no record regarding him.

simri.d: watchman, a Levite of the family of Merari (<reflink>1 Chr. 26:10</reflink>).

sin.d: is "any want of conformity unto or transgression of the law of God" (<reflink>1 John 3:4; Rom. 4:15</reflink>), in the inward state and habit of the soul, as well as in the outward conduct of the life, whether by omission or commission (<reflink>Rom. 6:12-17; 7:5-24</reflink>). It is "not a mere violation of the law of our constitution, nor of the system of things, but an offence against a personal lawgiver and moral governor who vindicates his law with penalties. The soul that sins is always conscious that his sin is (1) intrinsically vile and polluting, and (2) that it justly deserves punishment, and calls down the righteous wrath of God. Hence sin carries with it two inalienable characters, (1) ill-desert, guilt (reatus); and (2) pollution (macula).", Hodge's Outlines.

sin-offering.d: (Heb. hattath), the law of, is given in detail in Lev. 4-6:13; 9:7-11, 22-24; 12:6-8; 15:2, 14, 25-30; 14:19, 31; Num. 6:10-14. On the day of Atonement it was made with special solemnity (<reflink>Lev. 16:5, 11, 15</reflink>). The blood was then carried into the holy of holies and sprinkled on the mercy-seat. Sin-offerings were also presented at the five annual festivals (Num. 28, 29), and on the occasion of the consecration of the priests (<reflink>Ex. 29:10-14, 36</reflink>). As each individual, even the most private member of the congregation, as well as the congregation at large, and the high priest, was obliged, on being convicted by his conscience of any particular sin, to come with a sin-offering, we see thus impressively disclosed the need in which every sinner stands of the salvation of Christ, and the necessity of making application to it as often as the guilt of sin renews itself upon his conscience. …

sinai.d: of Sin (the moon god), called also Horeb, the name of the mountain district which was reached by the Hebrews in the third month after the Exodus. Here they remained encamped for about a whole year. Their journey from the Red Sea to this encampment, including all the windings of the route, was about 150 miles. The last twenty-two chapters of Exodus, together with the whole of Leviticus and Num. ch. 1-11, contain a record of all the transactions which occurred while they were here. From Rephidim (<reflink>Ex. 17:8-13</reflink>) the Israelites journeyed forward through the Wady Solaf and Wady esh-Sheikh into the plain of er-Rahah, "the desert of Sinai," about 2 miles long and half a mile broad, and encamped there "before the mountain." The part of the mountain range, a protruding lower bluff, known as the Ras Sasafeh (Sufsafeh), rises almost perpendicularly from this plain, and is in all probability the Sinai of history. …

sinaiticus codex.d: usually designated by the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, is one of the most valuable of ancient MSS. of the Greek New Testament. On the occasion of a third visit to the convent of St. Catherine, on Mount Sinai, in 1859, it was discovered by Dr. Tischendorf. He had on a previous visit in 1844 obtained forty-three parchment leaves of the LXX., which he deposited in the university library of Leipsic, under the title of the Codex Frederico-Augustanus, after his royal patron the king of Saxony. In the year referred to (1859) the emperor of Russia sent him to prosecute his search for MSS., which he was convinced were still to be found in the Sinai convent. The story of his finding the manuscript of the New Testament has all the interest of a romance. He reached the convent on 31st January; but his inquiries appeared to be fruitless. On the 4th February he had resolved to return home without having gained his object. …

sinim, the land of.d: (<reflink>Isa. 49:12</reflink>), supposed by some to mean China, but more probably Phoenicia (<reflink>Gen. 10:17</reflink>) is intended.

sinite.d: an inhabitant of Sin, near Arka (<reflink>Gen. 10:17; 1 Chr. 1:15</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See ARKITE.</see>)

stranger.d: This word generally denotes a person from a foreign land residing in Palestine. Such persons enjoyed many privileges in common with the Jews, but still were separate from them. The relation of the Jews to strangers was regulated by special laws (<reflink>Deut. 23:3; 24:14-21; 25:5; 26:10-13</reflink>). A special signification is also sometimes attached to this word. In Gen. 23:4 it denotes one resident in a foreign land; Ex. 23:9, one who is not a Jew; Num. 3:10, one who is not of the family of Aaron; Ps. 69:8, an alien or an unknown person. The Jews were allowed to purchase strangers as slaves (<reflink>Lev. 25:44, 45</reflink>), and to take usury from them (<reflink>Deut. 23:20</reflink>).

straw.d: Used in brick-making (<reflink>Ex. 5:7-18</reflink>). Used figuratively in Job 41:27; Isa. 11:7; 25:10; 65:25.

stream of egypt.d: (<reflink>Isa. 27:12</reflink>), the Wady el-'Arish, called also "the river of Egypt," R.V., "brook of Egypt" (<reflink>Num. 34:5; Josh. 15:4; 2 Kings 24:7</reflink>). It is the natural boundary of Egypt. Occasionally in winter, when heavy rains have fallen among the mountains inland, it becomes a turbulent rushing torrent. The present boundary between Egypt and Palestine is about midway between el-'Arish and Gaza.

street.d: The street called "Straight" at Damascus (<reflink>Acts 9:11</reflink>) is "a long broad street, running from east to west, about a mile in length, and forming the principal thoroughfare in the city." In Oriental towns streets are usually narrow and irregular and filthy (<reflink>Ps. 18:42; Isa. 10:6</reflink>). "It is remarkable," says Porter, "that all the important cities of Palestine and Syria Samaria, Caesarea, Gerasa, Bozrah, Damascus, Palmyra, had their 'straight streets' running through the centre of the city, and lined with stately rows of columns. The most perfect now remaining are those of Palmyra and Gerasa, where long ranges of the columns still stand.", Through Samaria, etc.

stripes.d: as a punishment were not to exceed forty (<reflink>Deut. 25:1-3</reflink>), and hence arose the custom of limiting them to thirty-nine (<reflink>2 Cor. 11:24</reflink>). Paul claimed the privilege of a Roman citizen in regard to the infliction of stripes (<reflink>Acts 16:37, 38; 22:25-29</reflink>). Our Lord was beaten with stripes (<reflink>Matt. 27:26</reflink>).

subscriptions.d: The subscriptions to Paul's epistles are no part of the original. In their present form they are ascribed to Euthalius, a bishop of the fifth century. Some of them are obviously incorrect.

suburbs.d: the immediate vicinity of a city or town (<reflink>Num. 35:3, 7; Ezek. 45:2</reflink>). In 2 Kings 23:11 the Hebrew word there used (parvarim) occurs nowhere else. The Revised Version renders it "precincts." The singular form of this Hebrew word (parvar) is supposed by some to be the same as Parbar (q.v.), which occurs twice in 1 Chr. 26:18.

succoth.d: booths. (1.) The first encampment of the Israelites after leaving Ramesses (<reflink>Ex. 12:37</reflink>); the civil name of Pithom (q.v.).

succoth-benoth.d: tents of daughters, supposed to be the name of a Babylonian deity, the goddess Zir-banit, the wife of Merodach, worshipped by the colonists in Samaria (<reflink>2 Kings 17:30</reflink>).

sukkiims.d: dwellers in tents, (Vulg. and LXX., "troglodites;" i.e., cave-dwellers in the hills along the Red Sea). Shiskak's army, with which he marched against Jerusalem, was composed partly of this tribe (<reflink>2 Chr. 12:3</reflink>).

sun.d: (Heb. shemesh), first mentioned along with the moon as the two great luminaries of heaven (<reflink>Gen. 1:14-18</reflink>). By their motions and influence they were intended to mark and divide times and seasons. The worship of the sun was one of the oldest forms of false religion (<reflink>Job 31:26,27</reflink>), and was common among the Egyptians and Chaldeans and other pagan nations. The Jews were warned against this form of idolatry (<reflink>Deut. 4:19; 17:3; comp. 2 Kings 23:11; Jer. 19:13</reflink>).

suph.d: (<reflink>Deut. 1:1, R.V.; marg., "some ancient versions have the Red Sea," as in the A.V.</reflink>). Some identify it with Suphah (<reflink>Num. 21:14, marg., A.V.</reflink>) as probably the name of a place. Others identify it with es-Sufah = Maaleh-acrabbim (<reflink>Josh. 15:3</reflink>), and others again with Zuph (<reflink>1 Sam. 9:5</reflink>). It is most probable, however, that, in accordance with the ancient versions, this word is to be regarded as simply an abbreviation of Yam-suph, i.e., the "Red Sea."

suphah.d: (<reflink>Num. 21:14, marg.; also R.V.</reflink>), a place at the south-eastern corner of the Dead Sea, the Ghor es-Safieh. This name is found in an ode quoted from the "Book of the Wars of the Lord," probably a collection of odes commemorating the triumphs of God's people (<reflink>comp. 21:14, 17, 18, 27-30</reflink>).

supper.d: the principal meal of the day among the Jews. It was partaken of in the early part of the evening (<reflink>Mark 6:21; John 12:2; 1 Cor. 11:21</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See LORD'S SUPPER.</see>)

surety.d: one who becomes responsible for another. Christ is the surety of the better covenant (<reflink>Heb. 7:22</reflink>). In him we have the assurance that all its provisions will be fully and faithfully carried out. Solomon warns against incautiously becoming security for another (<reflink>Prov. 6:1-5; 11:15; 17:18; 20:16</reflink>).

susanchites.d: the inhabitants of Shushan, who joined the other adversaries of the Jews in the attempt to prevent the rebuilding of the temple (<reflink>Ezra 4:9</reflink>).

susanna.d: lily, with other pious women, ministered to Jesus (<reflink>Luke 8:3</reflink>).

susi.d: the father of Gaddi, who was one of the twelve spies (<reflink>Num. 13:11</reflink>).

swallow.d: (1.) Heb. sis (<reflink>Isa. 38:14; Jer. 8:7</reflink>), the Arabic for the swift, which "is a regular migrant, returning in myriads every spring, and so suddenly that while one day not a swift can be seen in the country, on the next they have overspread the whole land, and fill the air with their shrill cry." The swift (cypselus) is ordinarily classed with the swallow, which it resembles in its flight, habits, and migration.

swan.d: mentioned in the list of unclean birds (<reflink>Lev. 11:18; Deut. 14:16</reflink>), is sometimes met with in the Jordan and the Sea of Galilee.

swelling.d: of Jordan (<reflink>Jer. 12:5</reflink>), literally the "pride" of Jordan (as in R.V.), i.e., the luxuriant thickets of tamarisks, poplars, reeds, etc., which were the lair of lions and other beasts of prey. The reference is not to the overflowing of the river banks. (<reflink>Comp. 49:19; 50:44; Zech. 11:3</reflink>).

swine.d: (Heb. hazir), regarded as the most unclean and the most abhorred of all animals (<reflink>Lev. 11:7; Isa. 65:4; 66:3, 17; Luke 15:15, 16</reflink>). A herd of swine were drowned in the Sea of Galilee (<reflink>Luke 8:32, 33</reflink>). Spoken of figuratively in Matt. 7:6 (<reflink>see Prov. 11:22</reflink>). It is frequently mentioned as a wild animal, and is evidently the wild boar (Arab. khanzir), which is common among the marshes of the Jordan valley (<reflink>Ps. 80:13</reflink>).

sword.d: of the Hebrew was pointed, sometimes two-edged, was worn in a sheath, and suspended from the girdle (<reflink>Ex. 32:27; 1 Sam. 31:4; 1 Chr. 21:27; Ps. 149:6: Prov. 5:4; Ezek. 16:40; 21:3-5</reflink>).

sycamine tree.d: mentioned only in Luke 17:6. It is rendered by Luther "mulberry tree" (q.v.), which is most probably the correct rendering. It is found of two species, the black mulberry (Morus nigra) and the white mulberry (Mourea), which are common in Palestine. The silk-worm feeds on their leaves. The rearing of them is one of the chief industries of the peasantry of Lebanon and of other parts of the land. It is of the order of the fig-tree. Some contend, however, that this name denotes the sycamore-fig of Luke 19:4.

sycamore.d: more properly sycomore (Heb. shikmoth and shikmim, Gr. sycomoros), a tree which in its general character resembles the fig-tree, while its leaves resemble those of the mulberry; hence it is called the fig-mulberry (Ficus sycomorus). At Jericho, Zacchaeus climbed a sycomore-tree to see Jesus as he passed by (<reflink>Luke 19:4</reflink>). This tree was easily destroyed by frost (<reflink>Ps. 78:47</reflink>), and therefore it is found mostly in the "vale" (<reflink>1 Kings 10:27; 2 Chr. 1:15: in both passages the R.V. has properly "lowland"</reflink>), i.e., the "low country," the shephelah, where the climate is mild. Amos (7:14) refers to its fruit, which is of an inferior character; so also probably Jeremiah (24:2). It is to be distinguished from our sycamore (the Acer pseudo-platanus), which is a species of maple often called a plane-tree.

sychar.d: liar or drunkard (<reflink>see Isa. 28:1, 7</reflink>), has been from the time of the Crusaders usually identified with Sychem or Shechem (<reflink>John 4:5</reflink>). It has now, however, as the result of recent explorations, been identified with 'Askar, a small Samaritan town on the southern base of Ebal, about a mile to the north of Jacob's well.

syene.d: opening (<reflink>Ezek. 29:10; 30:6</reflink>), a town of Egypt, on the borders of Ethiopia, now called Assouan, on the right bank of the Nile, notable for its quarries of beautiful red granite called "syenite." It was the frontier town of Egypt in the south, as Migdol was in the north-east.

synagogue.d: (Gr. sunagoge, i.e., "an assembly"), found only once in the Authorized Version of Ps. 74:8, where the margin of Revised Version has "places of assembly," which is probably correct; for while the origin of synagogues is unknown, it may well be supposed that buildings or tents for the accommodation of worshippers may have existed in the land from an early time, and thus the system of synagogues would be gradually developed.

syntyche.d: fortunate; affable, a female member of the church at Philippi, whom Paul beseeches to be of one mind with Euodias (<reflink>Phil. 4:2,3</reflink>).

syracuse.d: a city on the south-east coast of Sicily, where Paul landed and remained three days when on his way to Rome (<reflink>Acts 28:12</reflink>). It was distinguished for its magnitude and splendour. It is now a small town of some 13,000 inhabitants.

syria.d: (Heb. Aram), the name in the Old Testament given to the whole country which lay to the north-east of Phoenicia, extending to beyond the Euphrates and the Tigris. Mesopotamia is called (<reflink>Gen. 24:10; Deut. 23:4</reflink>) Aram-naharain (=Syria of the two rivers), also Padan-aram (<reflink>Gen. 25:20</reflink>). Other portions of Syria were also known by separate names, as Aram-maahah (<reflink>1 Chr. 19:6</reflink>), Aram-beth-rehob (<reflink>2 Sam. 10:6</reflink>), Aram-zobah (<reflink>2 Sam. 10:6, 8</reflink>). All these separate little kingdoms afterwards became subject to Damascus. In the time of the Romans, Syria included also a part of Palestine and Asia Minor.

syriac.d: (<reflink>2 Kings 18:26; Ezra 4:7; Dan. 2:4</reflink>), more correctly rendered "Aramaic," including both the Syriac and the Chaldee languages. In the New Testament there are several Syriac words, such as "Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani?" (<reflink>Mark 15:34; Matt. 27:46 gives the Heb. form, "Eli, Eli"</reflink>), "Raca" (<reflink>Matt. 5:22</reflink>), "Ephphatha" (<reflink>Mark 7:34</reflink>), "Maran-atha" (<reflink>1 Cor. 16:22</reflink>).

syrophenician.d: "a Greek, a Syrophenician by nation" (<reflink>Mark 7:26</reflink>), i.e., a Gentile born in the Phoenician part of Syria. (See PHENICIA

taanach.d: a sandy place, an ancient royal city of the Canaanites, on the south-western border of the plain of Esdraelon, 4 miles south of Megiddo. Its king was conquered by Joshua (12:21). It was assigned to the Levites of the family of Kohath (17:11-18; 21:25). It is mentioned in the song of Deborah (<reflink>Judg. 5:19</reflink>). It is identified with the small modern village of Ta'annuk.

taanath-shiloh.d: approach to Shiloh, a place on the border of Ephraim (<reflink>Josh. 16:6</reflink>), probably the modern T'ana, a ruin 7 miles south-east of Shechem, on the ridge east of the Mukhnah plain.

tabbaoth.d: impressions; rings, "the children of," returned from the Captivity (<reflink>Ezra 2:43</reflink>).

tabbath.d: famous, a town in the tribe of Ephraim (<reflink>Judg. 7:22</reflink>), to the south of Bethshean, near the Jordan.

tabeal.d: goodness of God, the father of one whom the kings of Syria and Samaria in vain attempted to place on the throne of Ahaz (<reflink>Isa. 7:6</reflink>).

tabeel.d: a Persian governor of Samaria, who joined others in the attempt to prevent the rebuilding of Jerusalem (<reflink>Ezra 4:7</reflink>).

taberah.d: burning, a place in the wilderness of Paran, where the "fire of the Lord" consumed the murmuring Israelites (<reflink>Num. 11:3; Deut. 9:22</reflink>). It was also called Kibroth-hattaavah (q.v.).

tabering.d: playing on a small drum or tabret. In Nahum 2:7, where alone it occurs, it means beating on the breast, as players beat on the tabret.

tabernacles, feast of.d: the third of the great annual festivals of the Jews (<reflink>Lev. 23:33-43</reflink>). It is also called the "feast of ingathering" (<reflink>Ex. 23:16; Deut. 16:13</reflink>). It was celebrated immediately after the harvest, in the month Tisri, and the celebration lasted for eight days (<reflink>Lev. 23:33-43</reflink>). During that period the people left their homes and lived in booths formed of the branches of trees. The sacrifices offered at this time are mentioned in Num. 29:13-38. It was at the time of this feast that Solomon's temple was dedicated (<reflink>1 Kings 8:2</reflink>). Mention is made of it after the return from the Captivity. This feast was designed (1) to be a memorial of the wilderness wanderings, when the people dwelt in booths (<reflink>Lev. 23:43</reflink>), and (2) to be a harvest thanksgiving (<reflink>Neh. 8:9-18</reflink>). …

tabitha.d: (in Greek called Dorcas), gazelle, a disciple at Joppa. She was distinguished for her alms-deeds and good works. Peter, who was sent for from Lydda on the occasion of her death, prayed over the dead body, and said, "Tabitha, arise." And she opened her eyes and sat up; and Peter "gave her his hand, and raised her up; and calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive" (<reflink>Acts 9:36-43</reflink>).

tables.d: (<reflink>Mark 7:4</reflink>) means banqueting-couches or benches, on which the Jews reclined when at meals. This custom, along with the use of raised tables like ours, was introduced among the Jews after the Captivity. Before this they had, properly speaking, no table. That which served the purpose was a skin or piece of leather spread out on the carpeted floor. Sometimes a stool was placed in the middle of this skin. (<see target="x-self">See ABRAHAM'S BOSOM; BANQUET; MEALS.</see>)

tablet.d: probably a string of beads worn round the neck (<reflink>Ex. 35:22; Num. 31:50</reflink>). In Isa. 3:20 the Hebrew word means a perfume-box, as it is rendered in the Revised Version.

tabor.d: a height. (1.) Now Jebel et-Tur, a cone-like prominent mountain, 11 miles west of the Sea of Galilee. It is about 1,843 feet high. The view from the summit of it is said to be singularly extensive and grand. This is alluded to in Ps. 89:12; Jer. 46:18. It was here that Barak encamped before the battle with Sisera (q.v.) Judg. 4:6-14. There is an old tradition, which, however, is unfounded, that it was the scene of the transfiguration of our Lord. (<see target="x-self">See HERMON.</see>) "The prominence and isolation of Tabor, standing, as it does, on the border-land between the northern and southern tribes, between the mountains and the central plain, made it a place of note in all ages, and evidently led the psalmist to associate it with Hermon, the one emblematic of the south, the other of the north." There are some who still hold that this was the scene of the transfiguration (q.v.).

tabret.d: (Heb. toph), a timbrel (q.v.) or tambourine, generally played by women (<reflink>Gen. 31:27; 1 Sam. 10:5; 18:6</reflink>). In Job 17:6 the word (Heb. topheth) "tabret" should be, as in the Revised Version, "an open abhorring" (marg., "one in whose face they spit;" lit., "a spitting in the face").

tabrimon.d: good is Rimmon, the father of Benhadad, king of Syria (<reflink>1 Kings 15:18</reflink>).

taches.d: hooks or clasps by which the tabernacle curtains were connected (<reflink>Ex. 26:6, 11, 33; 35:11</reflink>).

tachmonite.d: =Hach'monite, a name given to Jashobeam (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:8; comp. 1 Chr. 11:11</reflink>).

tackling.d: (<reflink>Isa. 33:23</reflink>), the ropes attached to the mast of a ship. In Acts 27:19 this word means generally the furniture of the ship or the "gear" (27:17), all that could be removed from the ship.

tadmor.d: palm, a city built by Solomon "in the wilderness" (<reflink>2 Chr. 8:4</reflink>). In 1 Kings 9:18, where the word occurs in the Authorized Version, the Hebrew text and the Revised Version read "Tamar," which is properly a city on the southern border of Palestine and toward the wilderness (<reflink>comp. Ezek. 47:19; 48:28</reflink>). In 2 Chr. 8:14 Tadmor is mentioned in connection with Hamath-zobah. It is called Palmyra by the Greeks and Romans. It stood in the great Syrian wilderness, 176 miles from Damascus and 130 from the Mediterranean and was the centre of a vast commercial traffic with Western Asia. It was also an important military station. …

tahapanes.d: =Tahpanhes=Tehaphnehes, (called "Daphne" by the Greeks, now Tell Defenneh), an ancient Egyptian city, on the Tanitic branch of the Nile, about 16 miles from Pelusium. The Jews from Jerusalem fled to this place after the death of Gedaliah (q.v.), and settled there for a time (<reflink>Jer. 2:16; 43:7; 44:1; 46:14</reflink>). A platform of brick-work, which there is every reason to believe was the pavement at the entry of Pharaoh's palace, has been discovered at this place. "Here," says the discoverer, Mr. Petrie, "the ceremony described by Jeremiah [43:8-10; "brick-kiln", i.e., pavement of brick] took place before the chiefs of the fugitives assembled on the platform, and here Nebuchadnezzar spread his royal pavilion" (R.V., "brickwork").

tahpenes.d: the wife of Pharaoh, who gave her sister in marriage to Hadad the Edomite (<reflink>1 Kings 11:19, 20</reflink>).

tahtim-hodshi.d: the land of the newly inhabited, (<reflink>2 Sam. 24:6</reflink>). It is conjectured that, instead of this word, the reading should be, "the Hittites of Kadesh," the Hittite capital, on the Orontes. It was apparently some region east of the Jordan and north of Gilead.

tale.d: (1.) Heb. tokhen, "a task," as weighed and measured out = tally, i.e., the number told off; the full number (<reflink>Ex. 5:18; see 1 Sam. 18:27; 1 Chr. 9:28</reflink>). In Ezek. 45:11 rendered "measure."

talent.d: of silver contained 3,000 shekels (<reflink>Ex. 38:25, 26</reflink>), and was equal to 94 3/7 lbs. avoirdupois. The Greek talent, however, as in the LXX., was only 82 1/4 lbs. It was in the form of a circular mass, as the Hebrew name _kikkar_ denotes. A talent of gold was double the weight of a talent of silver (<reflink>2 Sam. 12:30</reflink>). Parable of the talents (<reflink>Matt. 18:24; 25:15</reflink>).

talitha cumi.d: (<reflink>Mark 5:41</reflink>), a Syriac or Aramaic expression, meaning, "Little maid, arise." Peter, who was present when the miracle was wrought, recalled the actual words used by our Lord, and told them to Mark.

talmai.d: abounding in furrows. (1.) One of the Anakim of Hebron, who were slain by the men of Judah under Caleb (<reflink>Num. 13:22; Josh. 15:14; Judg. 1:10</reflink>).

talmon.d: oppressed. (1.) A Levite porter (<reflink>1 Chr. 9:17; Neh. 11:19</reflink>).

tamar.d: palm. (1.) A place mentioned by Ezekiel (47:19; 48:28), on the southeastern border of Palestine. Some suppose this was "Tadmor" (q.v.).

tamarisk.d: Heb. 'eshel (<reflink>Gen. 21:33; 1 Sam. 22:6; 31:13, in the R.V.; but in A.V., "grove," "tree"</reflink>); Arab. asal. Seven species of this tree are found in Palestine. It is a "very graceful tree, with long feathery branches and tufts closely clad with the minutest of leaves, and surmounted in spring with spikes of beautiful pink blosoms, which seem to envelop the whole tree in one gauzy sheet of colour" (Tristram's Nat. Hist.).

tammuz.d: a corruption of Dumuzi, the Accadian sun-god (the Adonis of the Greeks), the husband of the goddess Ishtar. In the Chaldean calendar there was a month set apart in honour of this god, the month of June to July, the beginning of the summer solstice. At this festival, which lasted six days, the worshippers, with loud lamentations, bewailed the funeral of the god, they sat "weeping for Tammuz" (<reflink>Ezek. 8:14</reflink>).

tanhumeth.d: consolation, a Netophathite; one of the captains who supported Gedaliah (<reflink>2 Kings 25:23; Jer. 40:8</reflink>).

tappuah.d: apple-region. (1.) A town in the valley or lowland of Judah; formerly a royal city of the Canaanites (<reflink>Josh. 12:17; 15:34</reflink>). It is now called Tuffuh, about 12 miles west of Jerusalem.

tarah.d: stopping; station, an encampment of the Hebrews in the wilderness (<reflink>Num. 33:27, 28</reflink>).

tares.d: the bearded darnel, mentioned only in Matt. 13:25-30. It is the Lolium temulentum, a species of rye-grass, the seeds of which are a strong soporific poison. It bears the closest resemblance to wheat till the ear appears, and only then the difference is discovered. It grows plentifully in Syria and Palestine.

target.d: (<reflink>1 Sam. 17:6, A.V., after the LXX. and Vulg.</reflink>), a kind of small shield. The margin has "gorget," a piece of armour for the throat. The Revised Version more correctly renders the Hebrew word (kidon) by "javelin." The same Hebrew word is used in Josh. 8:18 (A.V., "spear;" R.V., "javelin"); Job 39:23 (A.V., "shield;" R.V., "javelin"); 41:29 (A.V., "spear;" R.V., "javelin").

tarshish.d: a Sanscrit or Aryan word, meaning "the sea coast." (1.) One of the "sons" of Javan (<reflink>Gen. 10:4; 1 Chr. 1:7</reflink>).

tarsus.d: the chief city of Cilicia. It was distinguished for its wealth and for its schools of learning, in which it rivalled, nay, excelled even Athens and Alexandria, and hence was spoken of as "no mean city." It was the native place of the Apostle Paul (<reflink>Acts 21:39</reflink>). It stood on the banks of the river Cydnus, about 12 miles north of the Mediterranean. It is said to have been founded by Sardanapalus, king of Assyria. It is now a filthy, ruinous Turkish town, called Tersous. (<see target="x-self">See PAUL.</see>)

tartak.d: prince of darkness, one of the gods of the Arvites, who colonized part of Samaria after the deportation of Israel by Shalmaneser (<reflink>2 Kings 17:31</reflink>).

tartan.d: an Assyrian word, meaning "the commander-in-chief." (1.) One of Sennacherib's messengers to Hezekiah (<reflink>2 Kings 18:17</reflink>). (2.) One of Sargon's generals (<reflink>Isa. 20:1</reflink>).

tatnai.d: gift, a Persian governor (Heb. pehah, i.e., "satrap;" modern "pasha") "on this side the river", i.e., of the whole tract on the west of the Euphrates. This Hebrew title _pehah_ is given to governors of provinces generally. It is given to Nehemiah (5:14) and to Zerubbabel (<reflink>Hag. 1:1</reflink>). It is sometimes translated "captain" (<reflink>1 Kings 20:24; Dan. 3:2, 3</reflink>), sometimes also "deputy" (<reflink>Esther 8:9; 9:3</reflink>). With others, Tatnai opposed the rebuilding of the temple (<reflink>Ezra 5:6</reflink>); but at the command of Darius, he assisted the Jews (6:1-13).

taverns, the three.d: a place on the great "Appian Way," about 11 miles from Rome, designed for the reception of travellers, as the name indicates. Here Paul, on his way to Rome, was met by a band of Roman Christians (<reflink>Acts 28:15</reflink>). The "Tres Tabernae was the first mansio or mutatio, that is, halting-place for relays, from Rome, or the last on the way to the city. At this point three roads run into the Via Appia, that from Tusculum, that from Alba Longa, and that from Antium; so necessarily here would be a halting-place, which took its name from the three shops there, the general store, the blacksmith's, and the refreshment-house...Tres Tabernae is translated as Three Taverns, but it more correctly means three shops" (Forbes's Footsteps of St. Paul, p.20).

taxes.d: first mentioned in the command (<reflink>Ex. 30:11-16</reflink>) that every Jew from twenty years and upward should pay an annual tax of "half a shekel for an offering to the Lord." This enactment was faithfully observed for many generations (<reflink>2 Chr. 24:6; Matt. 17:24</reflink>).

taxing.d: (<reflink>Luke 2:2; R.V., "enrolment"</reflink>), "when Cyrenius was governor of Syria," is simply a census of the people, or an enrolment of them with a view to their taxation. The decree for the enrolment was the occasion of Joseph and Mary's going up to Bethlehem. It has been argued by some that Cyrenius (q.v.) was governor of Cilicia and Syria both at the time of our Lord's birth and some years afterwards. This decree for the taxing referred to the whole Roman world, and not to Judea alone. (See CENSUS

tebeth.d: (<reflink>Esther 2:16</reflink>), a word probably of Persian origin, denoting the cold time of the year; used by the later Jews as denoting the tenth month of the year. Assyrian tebituv, "rain."

teil tree.d: (an old name for the lime-tree, the tilia), Isa. 6:13, the terebinth, or turpentine-tree, the Pistacia terebinthus of botanists. The Hebrew word here used (elah) is rendered oak (q.v.) in Gen. 35:4; Judg. 6:11, 19; Isa. 1:29, etc. In Isa. 61:3 it is rendered in the plural "trees;" Hos. 4:13, "elm" (R.V., "terebinth"). Hos. 4:13, "elm" (R.V., "terebinth"). In 1 Sam. 17:2, 19 it is taken as a proper name, "Elah" (R.V. marg., "terebinth").

tekoa, tekoah.d: pitching of tents; fastening down, a town of Judah, about 12 miles south of Jerusalem, and visible from the city. From this place Joab procured a "wise woman," who pretended to be in great affliction, and skilfully made her case known to David. Her address to the king was in the form of an apologue, similar to that of Nathan (<reflink>2 Sam. 12:1-6</reflink>). The object of Joab was, by the intervention of this woman, to induce David to bring back Absalom to Jerusalem (<reflink>2 Sam. 14:2, 4, 9</reflink>).

tel-abib.d: hill of corn, a place on the river Chebar, the residence of Ezekiel (<reflink>Ezek. 3:15</reflink>). The site is unknown.

tel-haresha.d: hill of the wood, a place in Babylon from which some captive Jews returned to Jerusalem (<reflink>Ezra 2:59; Neh. 7:61</reflink>).

tel-melah.d: hill of salt, a place in Babylon from which the Jews returned (id.).

telaim.d: young lambs, a place at which Saul gathered his army to fight against Amalek (<reflink>1 Sam. 15:4</reflink>); probably the same as Telem (2).

telassar.d: or Thelasar, (<reflink>Isa. 37:12; 2 Kings 19:12</reflink>), a province in the south-east of Assyria, probably in Babylonia. Some have identified it with Tel Afer, a place in Mesopotamia, some 30 miles from Sinjar.

telem.d: oppression. (1.) A porter of the temple in the time of Ezra (10:24).

tema.d: south; desert, one of the sons of Ishmael, and father of a tribe so called (<reflink>Gen. 25:15; 1 Chr. 1:30; Job 6:19; Isa. 21:14; Jer. 25:23</reflink>) which settled at a place to which he gave his name, some 250 miles south-east of Edom, on the route between Damascus and Mecca, in the northern part of the Arabian peninsula, toward the Syrian desert; the modern Teyma'.

teman.d: id. (1.) A grandson of Esau, one of the "dukes of Edom" (<reflink>Gen. 36:11, 15, 42</reflink>).

temanite.d: a man of Teman, the designation of Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends (<reflink>Job 2:11; 22:1</reflink>).

temeni.d: one of the sons of Ashur, the father of Tekoa (<reflink>1 Chr. 4:6</reflink>).

temple.d: first used of the tabernacle, which is called "the temple of the Lord" (<reflink>1 Sam. 1:9</reflink>). In the New Testament the word is used figuratively of Christ's human body (<reflink>John 2:19, 21</reflink>). Believers are called "the temple of God" (<reflink>1 Cor. 3:16, 17</reflink>). The Church is designated "an holy temple in the Lord" (<reflink>Eph. 2:21</reflink>). Heaven is also called a temple (<reflink>Rev. 7:5</reflink>). We read also of the heathen "temple of the great goddess Diana" (<reflink>Acts 19:27</reflink>).
