temple, herod's.d: The temple erected by the exiles on their return from Babylon had stood for about five hundred years, when Herod the Great became king of Judea. The building had suffered considerably from natural decay as well as from the assaults of hostile armies, and Herod, desirous of gaining the favour of the Jews, proposed to rebuild it. This offer was accepted, and the work was begun (B.C. 18), and carried out at great labour and expense, and on a scale of surpassing splendour. The main part of the building was completed in ten years, but the erection of the outer courts and the embellishment of the whole were carried on during the entire period of our Lord's life on earth (<reflink>John 2:16, 19-21</reflink>), and the temple was completed only A.D. 65. But it was not long permitted to exist. Within forty years after our Lord's crucifixion, his prediction of its overthrow was accomplished (<reflink>Luke 19: 41-44</reflink>). …

temple, solomon's.d: Before his death David had "with all his might" provided materials in great abundance for the building of the temple on the summit of Mount Moriah (<reflink>1 Chr. 22:14; 29:4; 2 Chr. 3:1</reflink>), on the east of the city, on the spot where Abraham had offered up Isaac (<reflink>Gen. 22:1-14</reflink>). In the beginning of his reign Solomon set about giving effect to the desire that had been so earnestly cherished by his father, and prepared additional materials for the building. From subterranean quarries at Jerusalem he obtained huge blocks of stone for the foundations and walls of the temple. These stones were prepared for their places in the building under the eye of Tyrian master-builders. He also entered into a compact with Hiram II., king of Tyre, for the supply of whatever else was needed for the work, particularly timber from the forests of Lebanon, which was brought in great rafts by the sea to Joppa, whence it was dragged to Jerusalem (1 Kings 5). …

temple, the second.d: After the return from captivity, under Zerubbabel (q.v.) and the high priest Jeshua, arrangements were almost immediately made to reorganize the long-desolated kingdom. The body of pilgrims, forming a band of 42,360, including children, having completed the long and dreary journey of some four months, from the banks of the Euphrates to Jerusalem, were animated in all their proceeding by a strong religious impulse, and therefore one of their first cares was to restore their ancient worship by rebuilding the temple. On the invitation of Zerubbabel, the governor, who showed them a remarkable example of liberality by contributing personally 1,000 golden darics (probably about $6,000), besides other gifts, the people with great enthusiasm poured their gifts into the sacred treasury (Ezra 2). …

ziddim.d: sides, a town of Naphtali (<reflink>Josh. 19:35</reflink>), has been identified with Kefr-Hattin, the "village of the Hittites," about 5 miles west of Tiberias.

zidkijah.d: the Lord is righteous, one who sealed the covenant with Nehemiah (<reflink>Neh. 10:1</reflink>).

zidon.d: a fishery, a town on the Mediterranean coast, about 25 miles north of Tyre. It received its name from the "first-born" of Canaan, the grandson of Noah (<reflink>Gen. 10:15, 19</reflink>). It was the first home of the Phoenicians on the coast of Palestine, and from its extensive commercial relations became a "great" city (<reflink>Josh. 11:8; 19:28</reflink>). It was the mother city of Tyre. It lay within the lot of the tribe of Asher, but was never subdued (<reflink>Judg. 1:31</reflink>). The Zidonians long oppressed Israel (<reflink>Judg. 10:12</reflink>). From the time of David its glory began to wane, and Tyre, its "virgin daughter" (<reflink>Isa. 23:12</reflink>), rose to its place of pre-eminence. Solomon entered into a matrimonial alliance with the Zidonians, and thus their form of idolatrous worship found a place in the land of Israel (<reflink>1 Kings 11:1, 33</reflink>). …

zif.d: brightness; splendour; i.e., "the flower month," mentioned only in 1 Kings 6:1, 37, as the "second month." It was called Iyar by the later Jews. (<see target="x-self">See MONTH.</see>)

ziha.d: drought. (1.) The name of a family of Nethinim (<reflink>Ezra 2:43; Neh. 7:46</reflink>). (2.) A ruler among the Nethinim (<reflink>Neh. 11:21</reflink>).

ziklag.d: a town in the Negeb, or south country of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:31</reflink>), in the possession of the Philistines when David fled to Gath from Ziph with all his followers. Achish, the king, assigned him Ziklag as his place of residence. There he dwelt for over a year and four months. From this time it pertained to the kings of Judah (<reflink>1 Sam. 27:6</reflink>). During his absence with his army to join the Philistine expedition against the Israelites (29:11), it was destroyed by the Amalekites (30:1, 2), whom David, however, pursued and utterly routed, returning all the captives (<reflink>1 Sam. 30:26-31</reflink>). Two days after his return from this expedition, David received tidings of the disastrous battle of Gilboa and of the death of Saul (<reflink>2 Sam. 1:1-16</reflink>). He now left Ziklag and returned to Hebron, along with his two wives, Ahinoam and Abigail, and his band of 600 men. It has been identified with 'Asluj, a heap of ruins south of Beersheba. …

zillah.d: shadow, one of the wives of Lamech, of the line of Cain, and mother of Tubal-cain (<reflink>Gen. 4:19, 22</reflink>).

zilpah.d: drooping, Leah's handmaid, and the mother of Gad and Asher (<reflink>Gen. 30:9-13</reflink>).

zilthai.d: shadow (i.e., protection) of Jehovah. (1.) A Benjamite (<reflink>1 Chr. 8:20</reflink>). (2.) One of the captains of the tribe of Manasseh who joined David at Ziklag (<reflink>1 Chr. 12:20</reflink>).

zimran.d: vine-dressers; celebrated, one of the sons of Abraham by Keturah (<reflink>Gen. 25:2</reflink>).

zimri.d: praise-worthy. (1.) A son of Salu, slain by Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, because of his wickedness in bringing a Midianitish woman into his tent (<reflink>Num. 25:6-15</reflink>).

zin.d: a low palm-tree, the south-eastern corner of the desert et-Tih, the wilderness of Paran, between the Gulf of Akabah and the head of the Wady Guraiyeh (<reflink>Num. 13:21</reflink>). To be distinguished from the wilderness of Sin (q.v.).

zina.d: ornament, one of the sons of Shimei (<reflink>1 Chr. 23:10</reflink>).

zion.d: sunny; height, one of the eminences on which Jerusalem was built. It was surrounded on all sides, except the north, by deep valleys, that of the Tyropoeon (q.v.) separating it from Moriah (q.v.), which it surpasses in height by 105 feet. It was the south-eastern hill of Jerusalem.

zior.d: littleness, a city in the mountains of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:54</reflink>); the modern Si'air, 4 1/2 miles north-north-east of Hebron.

ziph.d: flowing. (1.) A son of Jehaleleel (<reflink>1 Chr. 4:16</reflink>).

ziphron.d: sweet odour, a city on the northern border of Palestine (<reflink>Num. 34:9</reflink>), south-east of Hamath.

zippor.d: a little bird, the father of Balak, king of Moab (<reflink>Num. 22:2, 4</reflink>).

zipporah.d: a female bird. Reuel's daughter, who became the wife of Moses (<reflink>Ex. 2:21</reflink>). In consequence of the event recorded in Ex. 4:24-26, she and her two sons, Gershom and Eliezer, when so far on the way with Moses toward Egypt, were sent back by him to her own kinsfolk, the Midianites, with whom they sojourned till Moses afterwards joined them (18:2-6).

zithri.d: the Lord protects, a Levite, son of Uzziel (<reflink>Ex. 6:22</reflink>).

ziz.d: projecting; a flower, a cleft or pass, probably that near En-gedi, which leads up from the Dead Sea (<reflink>2 Chr. 20:16</reflink>) in the direction of Tekoa; now Tell Hasasah.

ziza.d: splendour; abundance. (1.) A Simeonite prince (<reflink>1 Chr. 4:37-43</reflink>).

zoan.d: (Old Egypt. Sant= "stronghold," the modern San). A city on the Tanitic branch of the Nile, called by the Greeks Tanis. It was built seven years after Hebron in Palestine (<reflink>Num. 13:22</reflink>). This great and important city was the capital of the Hyksos, or Shepherd kings, who ruled Egypt for more than 500 years. It was the frontier town of Goshen. Here Pharaoh was holding his court at the time of his various interviews with Moses and Aaron. "No trace of Zoan exists; Tanis was built over it, and city after city has been built over the ruins of that" (Harper, Bible and Modern Discovery). Extensive mounds of ruins, the wreck of the ancient city, now mark its site (<reflink>Isa. 19:11, 13; 30:4; Ezek. 30:14</reflink>). "The whole constitutes one of the grandest and oldest ruins in the world."

zoar.d: small, a town on the east or south-east of the Dead Sea, to which Lot and his daughters fled from Sodom (<reflink>Gen. 19:22, 23</reflink>). It was originally called Bela (14:2, 8). It is referred to by the prophets Isaiah (15:5) and Jeremiah (48:34). Its ruins are still seen at the opening of the ravine of Kerak, the Kir-Moab referred to in 2 Kings 3, the modern Tell esh-Shaghur.

zobah.d: =Aram-Zobah, (Ps. 60, title), a Syrian province or kingdom to the south of Coele-Syria, and extending from the eastern slopes of Lebanon north and east toward the Euphrates. Saul and David had war with the kings of Zobah (<reflink>1 Sam. 14:47; 2 Sam. 8:3; 10:6</reflink>).

zohar.d: brightness. (1.) The father of Ephron the Hittite (<reflink>Gen. 23:8</reflink>).

zoheleth.d: the serpent-stone, a rocky plateau near the centre of the village of Siloam, and near the fountain of En-rogel, to which the women of the village resort for water (<reflink>1 Kings 1:5-9</reflink>). Here Adonijah (q.v.) feasted all the royal princess except Solomon and the men who took part with him in his effort to succeed to the throne. While they were assembled here Solomon was proclaimed king, through the intervention of Nathan. On hearing this, adonijah fled and took refuge in the sanctuary (<reflink>1 Kings 1:49-53</reflink>). He was afterwards pardoned.

zoheth.d: snatching (?), one of the sons of Ishi (<reflink>1 Chr. 4:20</reflink>).

zophah.d: spreading out, a son of Helem (<reflink>1 Chr. 7:35</reflink>), a chief of Asher.

zophar.d: chirping, one of Job's friends who came to condole with him in his distress (<reflink>Job 2:11. The LXX. render here "king of the Mineans" = Ma'in, Maonites, Judg. 10:12, in Southern Arabia</reflink>). He is called a Naamathite, or an inhabitant of some unknown place called Naamah.

zophim, field of.d: field of watchers, a place in Moab on the range of Pisgah (<reflink>Num. 23:14</reflink>). To this place Balak brought Balaam, that he might from thence curse the children of Israel. Balaam could only speak the word of the Lord, and that was blessing. It is the modern Tal'at-es-Safa. (<see target="x-self">See PISGAH.</see>)

zorah.d: place of wasps, a town in the low country of Judah, afterwards given to Dan (<reflink>Josh. 19:41; Judg. 18:2</reflink>), probably the same as Zoreah (<reflink>Josh. 15:33</reflink>). This was Samson's birthplace (<reflink>Judg. 13:2, 25</reflink>), and near it he found a grave (16:31). It was situated on the crest of a hill overlooking the valley of Sorek, and was fortified by Rehoboam (<reflink>2 Chr. 11:10</reflink>). It has been identified with Sur'ah, in the Wady Surar, 8 miles west of Jerusalem. It is noticed on monuments in the fifteenth century B.C. as attacked by the Abiri or Hebrews.

temptation.d: (1.) Trial; a being put to the test. Thus God "tempted [Gen. 22: 1; R.V., 'did prove'] Abraham;" and afflictions are said to tempt, i.e., to try, men (<reflink>James 1:2, 12; comp. Deut. 8:2</reflink>), putting their faith and patience to the test. (2.) Ordinarily, however, the word means solicitation to that which is evil, and hence Satan is called "the tempter" (<reflink>Matt. 4:3</reflink>). Our Lord was in this way tempted in the wilderness. That temptation was not internal, but by a real, active, subtle being. It was not self-sought. It was submitted to as an act of obedience on his part. "Christ was led, driven. An unseen personal force bore him a certain violence is implied in the words" (<reflink>Matt. 4:1-11</reflink>).

tent.d: (1.) Heb. 'ohel (<reflink>Gen. 9:21, 27</reflink>). This word is used also of a dwelling or habitation (<reflink>1 Kings 8:66; Isa. 16:5; Jer. 4:20</reflink>), and of the temple (<reflink>Ezek. 41:1</reflink>). When used of the tabernacle, as in 1 Kings 1:39, it denotes the covering of goat's hair which was placed over the mishcan.

tenth deal.d: i.e., the tenth part of an ephah (as in the R.V.), equal to an omer or six pints. The recovered leper, to complete his purification, was required to bring a trespass, a sin, and a burnt offering, and to present a meal offering, a tenth deal or an omer of flour for each, with oil to make it into bread or cakes (<reflink>Lev. 14:10, 21; comp. Ex. 16:36; 29:40</reflink>).

terah.d: the wanderer; loiterer, for some unknown reason emigrated with his family from his native mountains in the north to the plains of Mesopotamia. He had three sons, Haran, Nahor, and Abraham, and one daughter, Sarah. He settled in "Ur of the Chaldees," where his son Haran died, leaving behind him his son Lot. Nahor settled at Haran, a place on the way to Ur. Terah afterwards migrated with Abraham (probably his youngest son) and Lot (his grandson), together with their families, from Ur, intending to go with them to Canaan; but he tarried at Haran, where he spent the remainder of his days, and died at the age of two hundred and five years (<reflink>Gen. 11:24-32; Josh. 24:2</reflink>). What a wonderful part the descendants of this Chaldean shepherd have played in the history of the world!

teraphim.d: givers of prosperity, idols in human shape, large or small, analogous to the images of ancestors which were revered by the Romans. In order to deceive the guards sent by Saul to seize David, Michal his wife prepared one of the household teraphim, putting on it the goat's-hair cap worn by sleepers and invalids, and laid it in a bed, covering it with a mantle. She pointed it out to the soldiers, and alleged that David was confined to his bed by a sudden illness (<reflink>1 Sam. 19:13-16</reflink>). Thus she gained time for David's escape. It seems strange to read of teraphim, images of ancestors, preserved for superstitious purposes, being in the house of David. Probably they had been stealthily brought by Michal from her father's house. "Perhaps," says Bishop Wordsworth, "Saul, forsaken by God and possessed by the evil spirit, had resorted to teraphim (as he afterwards resorted to witchcraft); and God overruled evil for good, and made his very teraphim (by the hand of his own daughter)

terebinth.d: (<reflink>R.V. marg. of Deut. 11:30, etc.</reflink>), the Pistacia terebinthus of botanists; a tree very common in the south and east of Palestine. (<see target="x-self">See OAK.</see>)

teresh.d: severe, a eunuch or chamberlain in the palace of Ahasuerus, who conspired with another to murder him. The plot was detected by Mordecai, and the conspirators were put to death (<reflink>Esther 2:21; 6:2</reflink>).

tertius.d: the third, a Roman Christian whom Paul employed as his amanuensis in writing his epistle to the Romans (16:22).

tertullus.d: a modification of "Tertius;" a Roman advocate, whom the Jews employed to state their case against Paul in the presence of Felix (<reflink>Acts 24:1-9</reflink>). The charges he adduced against the apostle were, "First, that he created disturbances among the Romans throughout the empire, an offence against the Roman government (crimen majestatis). Secondly, that he was a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes; disturbed the Jews in the exercise of their religion, guaranteed by the state; introduced new gods, a thing prohibited by the Romans. And thirdly, that he attempted to profane the temple, a crime which the Jews were permitted to punish."

testament.d: occurs twelve times in the New Testament (<reflink>Heb. 9:15, etc.</reflink>) as the rendering of the Gr. diatheke, which is twenty times rendered "covenant" in the Authorized Version, and always so in the Revised Version. The Vulgate translates incorrectly by testamentum, whence the names "Old" and "New Testament," by which we now designate the two sections into which the Bible is divided. (<see target="x-self">See </see>)

testimony, tabernacle of.d: the tabernacle, the great glory of which was that it contained "the testimony", i.e., the "two tables" (<reflink>Ex. 38:21</reflink>). The ark in which these tables were deposited was called the "ark of the testimony" (40:3), and also simply the "testimony" (27:21; 30:6).

tetrarch.d: strictly the ruler over the fourth part of a province; but the word denotes a ruler of a province generally (<reflink>Matt. 14:1; Luke 3:1, 19; 9:7; Acts 13:1</reflink>). Herod and Phasael, the sons of Antipater, were the first tetrarchs in Palestine. Herod the tetrarch had the title of king (<reflink>Matt. 14:9</reflink>).

thaddaeus.d: breast, the name of one of the apostles (<reflink>Mark 3:18</reflink>), called "Lebbaeus" in Matt. 10:3, and in Luke 6:16, "Judas the brother of James;" while John (14:22), probably referring to the same person, speaks of "Judas, not Iscariot." These different names all designate the same person, viz., Jude or Judas, the author of the epistle.

thahash.d: a badger, a son of Nahor, Abraham's brother (<reflink>Gen. 22:24</reflink>).

theatre.d: only mentioned in Acts 19:29, 31. The ruins of this theatre at Ephesus still exist, and they show that it was a magnificent structure, capable of accommodating some 56,700 persons. It was the largest structure of the kind that ever existed. Theatres, as places of amusement, were unknown to the Jews.

thebez.d: brightness, a place some 11 miles north-east of Shechem, on the road to Scythopolis, the modern Tabas. Abimelech led his army against this place, because of its participation in the conspiracy of the men of Shechem; but as he drew near to the strong tower to which its inhabitants had fled for safety, and was about to set fire to it, a woman cast a fragment of millstone at him, and "all to brake his skull" i.e., "altogether brake," etc. His armourbearer thereupon "thrust him through, and he died" (<reflink>Judg. 9:50-55</reflink>).

theft.d: Punished by restitution, the proportions of which are noted in 2 Sam. 12:6. If the thief could not pay the fine, he was to be sold to a Hebrew master till he could pay (<reflink>Ex. 22:1-4</reflink>). A night-thief might be smitten till he died, and there would be no blood-guiltiness for him (22:2). A man-stealer was to be put to death (21:16). All theft is forbidden (<reflink>Ex. 20:15; 21:16; Lev. 19:11; Deut. 5:19; 24:7; Ps. 50:18; Zech. 5:3; Matt. 19:18; Rom. 13:9; Eph. 4:28; 1 Pet. 4:15</reflink>).

theocracy.d: a word first used by Josephus to denote that the Jews were under the direct government of God himself. The nation was in all things subject to the will of their invisible King. All the people were the servants of Jehovah, who ruled over their public and private affairs, communicating to them his will through the medium of the prophets. They were the subjects of a heavenly, not of an earthly, king. They were Jehovah's own subjects, ruled directly by him (comp. 1 Sam. 8:6-9).

theophilus.d: lover of God, a Christian, probably a Roman, to whom Luke dedicated both his Gospel (<reflink>Luke 1:3</reflink>) and the Acts of the Apostles (1:1). Nothing beyond this is known of him. From the fact that Luke applies to him the title "most excellent", the same title Paul uses in addressing Felix (<reflink>Acts 23:26; 24:3</reflink>) and Festus (26:25), it has been concluded that Theophilus was a person of rank, perhaps a Roman officer.

thessalonians, epistles to the.d: The first epistle to the Thessalonians was the first of all Paul's epistles. It was in all probability written from Corinth, where he abode a "long time" (<reflink>Acts 18:11, 18</reflink>), early in the period of his residence there, about the end of A.D. 52.

thessalonica.d: a large and populous city on the Thermaic bay. It was the capital of one of the four Roman districts of Macedonia, and was ruled by a praetor. It was named after Thessalonica, the wife of Cassander, who built the city. She was so called by her father, Philip, because he first heard of her birth on the day of his gaining a victory over the Thessalians. On his second missionary journey, Paul preached in the synagogue here, the chief synagogue of the Jews in that part of Macedonia, and laid the foundations of a church (<reflink>Acts 17:1-4; 1 Thes. 1:9</reflink>). The violence of the Jews drove him from the city, when he fled to Berea (<reflink>Acts 17:5-10</reflink>). The "rulers of the city" before whom the Jews "drew Jason," with whom Paul and Silas lodged, are in the original called politarchai, an unusual word, which was found, however, inscribed on an arch in Thessalonica. This discovery confirms the accuracy of the historian. …

theudas.d: thanksgiving, referred to by Gamaliel in his speech before the council at Jerusalem (<reflink>Acts 5:36</reflink>). He headed an insurrection against the Roman authority. Beyond this nothing is known of him.

thick clay.d: (<reflink>Hab. 2:6</reflink>) is correctly rendered in the Revised Version "pledges." The Chaldean power is here represented as a rapacious usurer, accumulating the wealth that belonged to others.

thieves, the two.d: (<reflink>Luke 23:32, 39-43</reflink>), robbers, rather brigands, probably followers of Barabbas. Our Lord's cross was placed between those of the "malefactors," to add to the ignominy of his position. According to tradition, Demas or Dismas was the name of the penitent thief hanging on the right, and Gestas of the impenitent on the left.

thistle.d: (1.) Heb. hoah (<reflink>2 Kings 14:9; Job 31:40</reflink>). In Job 41:2 the Hebrew word is rendered "thorn," but in the Revised Version "hook." It is also rendered "thorn" in 2 Chr. 33:11; Prov. 26:9; Cant. 2:2; "brambles" in Isa. 34:13. It is supposed to be a variety of the wild plum-tree, but by some it is regarded as the common thistle, of which there are many varieties in Palestine.

thomas.d: twin, one of the twelve (<reflink>Matt. 10:3; Mark 3:18, etc.</reflink>). He was also called Didymus (<reflink>John 11:16; 20:24</reflink>), which is the Greek equivalent of the Hebrew name. All we know regarding him is recorded in the fourth Gospel (<reflink>John 11:15, 16; 14:4, 5; 20:24, 25, 26-29</reflink>). From the circumstance that in the lists of the apostles he is always mentioned along with Matthew, who was the son of Alphaeus (<reflink>Mark 3:18</reflink>), and that these two are always followed by James, who was also the son of Alphaeus, it has been supposed that these three, Matthew, Thomas, and James, were brothers.

thorn.d: (1.) Heb. hedek (<reflink>Prov. 15:19</reflink>), rendered "brier" in Micah 7:4. Some thorny plant, of the Solanum family, suitable for hedges. This is probably the so-called "apple of Sodom," which grows very abundantly in the Jordan valley. "It is a shrubby plant, from 3 to 5 feet high, with very branching stems, thickly clad with spines, like those of the English brier, with leaves very large and woolly on the under side, and thorny on the midriff."

thorn in the flesh.d: (<reflink>2 Cor. 12:7-10</reflink>). Many interpretations have been given of this passage. (1.) Roman Catholic writers think that it denotes suggestions to impiety.

thousands.d: (<reflink>Micah 5:2</reflink>), another name for "families" or "clans" (<reflink>see Num. 1:16; 10:4; Josh. 22:14, 21</reflink>). Several "thousands" or "families" made up a "tribe."

threshold.d: (1.) Heb. miphtan, probably a projecting beam at a higher point than the threshold proper (<reflink>1 Sam. 5:4,5; Ezek. 9:3; 10:4,18; 46:2; 47:1</reflink>); also rendered "door" and "door-post."

throne.d: (Heb. kiss'e), a royal chair or seat of dignity (<reflink>Deut. 17:18; 2 Sam. 7:13; Ps. 45:6</reflink>); an elevated seat with a canopy and hangings, which cover it. It denotes the seat of the high priest in 1 Sam. 1:9; 4:13, and of a provincial governor in Neh. 3:7 and Ps. 122:5. The throne of Solomon is described at length in 1 Kings 10:18-20.

thummim.d: perfection (LXX., "truth;" Vulg., "veritas"), Ex. 28:30; Deut. 33:8; Judg. 1:1; 20:18; 1 Sam. 14:3,18; 23:9; 2 Sam. 21:1. What the "Urim and Thummim" were cannot be determined with any certainty. All we certainly know is that they were a certain divinely-given means by which God imparted, through the high priest, direction and counsel to Israel when these were needed. The method by which this was done can be only a matter of mere conjecture. They were apparently material objects, quite distinct from the breastplate, but something added to it after all the stones had been set in it, something in addition to the breastplate and its jewels. They may have been, as some suppose, two small images, like the teraphim (<reflink>comp. Judg. 17:5; 18:14, 17, 20; Hos. 3:4</reflink>), which were kept in the bag of the breastplate, by which, in some unknown way, the high priest could give forth his divinely imparted decision when consulted. …

thunder.d: often referred to in Scripture (<reflink>Job 40:9; Ps. 77:18; 104:7</reflink>). James and John were called by our Lord "sons of thunder" (<reflink>Mark 3:17</reflink>). In Job 39:19, instead of "thunder," as in the Authorized Version, the Revised Version translates (ra'amah) by "quivering main" (marg., "shaking"). Thunder accompanied the giving of the law at Sinai (<reflink>Ex. 19:16</reflink>). It was regarded as the voice of God (<reflink>Job 37:2; Ps. 18:13; 81:7; comp. John 12:29</reflink>). In answer to Samuel's prayer (<reflink>1 Sam. 12:17, 18</reflink>), God sent thunder, and "all the people greatly feared," for at such a season (the wheat-harvest) thunder and rain were almost unknown in Palestine.

thyatira.d: a city of Asia Minor, on the borders of Lydia and Mysia. Its modern name is Ak-hissar, i.e., "white castle." Here was one of the seven churches (<reflink>Rev. 1:11; 2:18-28</reflink>). Lydia, the seller of purple, or rather of cloth dyed with this colour, was from this city (<reflink>Acts 16:14</reflink>). It was and still is famous for its dyeing. Among the ruins, inscriptions have been found relating to the guild of dyers in that city in ancient times.

thyine wood.d: mentioned only in Rev. 18:12 among the articles which would cease to be purchased when Babylon fell. It was called citrus, citron wood, by the Romans. It was the Callitris quadrivalvis of botanists, of the cone-bearing order of trees, and of the cypress tribe of this order. The name of this wood is derived from the Greek word _thuein_, "to sacrifice," and it was so called because it was burnt in sacrifices, on account of its fragrance. The wood of this tree was reckoned very valuable, and was used for making articles of furniture by the Greeks and Romans. Like the cedars of Lebanon, it is disappearing from the forests of Palestine.

tiberias.d: a city, the modern Tubarich, on the western shore of the Sea of Tiberias. It is said to have been founded by Herod Antipas (A.D. 16), on the site of the ruins of an older city called Rakkath, and to have been thus named by him after the Emperor Tiberius. It is mentioned only three times in the history of our Lord (<reflink>John 6:1,23; 21:1</reflink>).

tiberias, sea of.d: called also the Sea of Galilee (q.v.) and of Gennesaret. In the Old Testament it is called the Sea of Chinnereth or Chinneroth. John (21:1) is the only evangelist who so designates this lake. His doing so incidentally confirms the opinion that he wrote after the other evangelists, and at a period subsequent to the taking of Jerusalem (A.D. 70). Tiberias had by this time become an important city, having been spared by the Romans, and made the capital of the province when Jerusalem was destroyed. It thus naturally gave its name to the lake.

tiberius caesar.d: i.e., as known in Roman history, Tiberius Claudius Nero, only mentioned in Luke 3:1. He was the stepson of Augustus, whom he succeeded on the throne, A.D. 14. He was noted for his vicious and infamous life. In the fifteenth year of his reign John the Baptist entered on his public ministry, and under him also our Lord taught and suffered. He died A.D. 37. He is frequently referred to simply as "Caesar" (<reflink>Matt. 22:17, 21; Mark 12:14, 16, 17; Luke 20:22, 24, 25; 23:2; John 19:12, 15</reflink>).

tibni.d: building of Jehovah, the son of Ginath, a man of some position, whom a considerable number of the people chose as monarch. For the period of four years he contended for the throne with Omri (<reflink>1 Kings 16:21, 22</reflink>), who at length gained the mastery, and became sole monarch of Israel.

tidal.d: (in the LXX. called "Thorgal"), styled the "king of nations" (<reflink>Gen.14:1-9</reflink>). Mentioned as Tudkhula on Arioch's brick (<see target="x-self">see facing page 139</see>). _Goyyim_, translated "nations," is the country called Gutium, east of Tigris and north of Elam.

tiglath-pileser i.d: (not mentioned in Scripture) was the most famous of the monarchs of the first Assyrian empire (about B.C. 1110). After his death, for two hundred years the empire fell into decay. The history of David and Solomon falls within this period. He was succeeded by his son, Shalmaneser II.

tiglath-pileser iii.d: or Tilgath-Pil-neser, the Assyrian throne-name of Pul (q.v.). He appears in the Assyrian records as gaining, in the fifth year of his reign (about B.C. 741), a victory over Azariah (= Uzziah in 2 Chr.26:1), king of Judah, whose achievements are described in 2 Chr. 26:6-15. He is first mentioned in Scripture, however, as gaining a victory over Pekah, king of Israel, and Rezin of Damascus, who were confederates. He put Rezin to death, and punished Pekah by taking a considerable portion of his kingdom, and carrying off (B.C. 734) a vast number of its inhabitants into captivity (<reflink>2 Kings 15:29; 16:5-9; 1 Chr. 5:6, 26</reflink>), the Reubenites, the Gadites, and half the tribe of Manasseh whom he settled in Gozan. In the Assyrian annals it is further related that, before he returned from Syria, he held a court at Damascus, and received submission and tribute from the neighbouring kings, among whom were Pekah of Samaria and "Yahu-khazi [i.e., Ahaz], king of Judah" (comp. …

timaeus.d: defiled, the father of blind Bartimaeus (<reflink>Mark 10:46</reflink>).

timbrel.d: (Heb. toph), a small drum or tambourine; a tabret (q.v.). The antiquity of this musical instrument appears from the scriptural allusions to it (<reflink>Gen. 31:27; Ex. 15:20; Judg. 11:34, etc.</reflink>) (<see target="x-self">See MUSIC.</see>)

timnah.d: a portion. (1.) A town of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:10</reflink>). The Philistines took possession of it in the days of Ahaz (<reflink>2 Chr. 28:18</reflink>). It was about 20 miles west of Jerusalem. It has been identified with Timnatha of Dan (<reflink>Josh. 19:43</reflink>), and also with Timnath (<reflink>Judg. 14:1,5</reflink>).

timnath.d: Gen. 38:12,14. (1.) Heb. Timnathah, which is appropriately rendered in the Revised Version, Timnah, a town in Judah.

timnath-heres.d: portion of the sun, where Joshua was buried (<reflink>Judg. 2:9</reflink>). It was "in the mount of Ephraim, in the north side of the hill Gaash," 10 miles south-west of Shechem. The same as the following.

timnath-serah.d: remaining portion, the city of Joshua in the hill country of Ephraim, the same as Timnath-heres (<reflink>Josh. 19:50; 24:30</reflink>). "Of all sites I have seen," says Lieut. Col. Conder, "none is so striking as that of Joshua's home, surrounded as it is with deep valleys and wild, rugged hills." Opposite the town is a hill, on the northern side of which there are many excavated sepulchres. Among these is the supposed tomb of Joshua, which is said to be "the most striking monument in the country." It is a "square chamber with five excavations in three of its sides, the central one forming a passage leading into a second chamber beyond. A great number of lamp-niches cover the walls of the porch, upwards of two hundred, arranged in vertical rows. A single cavity with a niche for a lamp has been thought to be the resting-place of the warrior-chief of Israel." The modern Kefr Haris, 10 miles south-west of Shechem.

timnite.d: a man of Timnah. Samson's father-in-law is so styled (<reflink>Judg. 15:6</reflink>).

timon.d: honouring, one of the seven deacons at Jerusalem (<reflink>Acts 6:5</reflink>). Nothing further is known of him.

timotheus.d: the Greek form of the name of Timothy (<reflink>Acts 16:1, etc.; the R.V. always "Timothy"</reflink>).

timothy.d: honouring God, a young disciple who was Paul's companion in many of his journeyings. His mother, Eunice, and his grandmother, Lois, are mentioned as eminent for their piety (<reflink>2 Tim. 1:5</reflink>). We know nothing of his father but that he was a Greek (<reflink>Acts 16:1</reflink>). He is first brought into notice at the time of Paul's second visit to Lystra (16:2), where he probably resided, and where it seems he was converted during Paul's first visit to that place (<reflink>1 Tim. 1:2; 2 Tim. 3:11</reflink>). The apostle having formed a high opinion of his "own son in the faith," arranged that he should become his companion (<reflink>Acts 16:3</reflink>), and took and circumcised him, so that he might conciliate the Jews. He was designated to the office of an evangelist (<reflink>1 Tim. 4:14</reflink>), and went with Paul in his journey through Phrygia, Galatia, and Mysia; also to Troas and Philippi and Berea (<reflink>Acts 17:14</reflink>). …

timothy, first epistle to.d: Paul in this epistle speaks of himself as having left Ephesus for Macedonia (1:3), and hence not Laodicea, as mentioned in the subscription; but probably Philippi, or some other city in that region, was the place where this epistle was written. During the interval between his first and second imprisonments he probably visited the scenes of his former labours in Greece and Asia, and then found his way into Macedonia, whence he wrote this letter to Timothy, whom he had left behind in Ephesus.

timothy, second epistle to.d: was probably written a year or so after the first, and from Rome, where Paul was for a second time a prisoner, and was sent to Timothy by the hands of Tychicus. In it he entreats Timothy to come to him before winter, and to bring Mark with him (<reflink>comp. Phil. 2:22</reflink>). He was anticipating that "the time of his departure was at hand" (<reflink>2 Tim. 4:6</reflink>), and he exhorts his "son Timothy" to all diligence and steadfastness, and to patience under persecution (1:6-15), and to a faithful discharge of all the duties of his office (4:1-5), with all the solemnity of one who was about to appear before the Judge of quick and dead.

tin.d: Heb. bedil (<reflink>Num. 31:22; Ezek. 22:18, 20</reflink>), a metal well known in ancient times. It is the general opinion that the Phoenicians of Tyre and Sidon obtained their supplies of tin from the British Isles. In Ezek. 27:12 it is said to have been brought from Tarshish, which was probably a commercial emporium supplied with commodities from other places. In Isa. 1:25 the word so rendered is generally understood of lead, the alloy with which the silver had become mixed (ver. 22). The fire of the Babylonish Captivity would be the means of purging out the idolatrous alloy that had corrupted the people.

tinkling ornaments.d: (<reflink>Isa. 3:18</reflink>), anklets of silver or gold, etc., such as are still used by women in Syria and the East.

tiphsah.d: passing over; ford, one of the boundaries of Solomon's dominions (<reflink>1 Kings 4:24</reflink>), probably "Thapsacus, a great and wealthy town on the western bank of the Euphrates," about 100 miles north-east of Tadmor. All the land traffic between the east and the west passed through it. Menahem undertook an expedition against this city, and "smote Tiphsah and all that were therein" (<reflink>2 Kings 15:16</reflink>). This expedition implied a march of some 300 miles from Tirzah if by way of Tadmor, and about 400 if by way of Aleppo; and its success showed the strength of the Israelite kingdom, for it was practically a defiance to Assyria. Conder, however, identifies this place with Khurbet Tafsah, some 6 miles west of Shechem.

tiras.d: the youngest of the sons of Japheth (<reflink>Gen. 10:2; 1 Chr. 1:5</reflink>).

tires.d: "To tire" the head is to adorn it (<reflink>2 Kings 9:30</reflink>). As a noun the word is derived from "tiara," and is the rendering of the Heb. p'er, a "turban" or an ornament for the head (<reflink>Ezek. 24:17; R.V., "headtire;" 24:23</reflink>). In Isa. 3:18 the word _saharonim_ is rendered "round tires like the moon," and in Judg. 8:21, 26 "ornaments," but in both cases "crescents" in the Revised Version.

tirhakah.d: the last king of Egypt of the Ethiopian (the fifteenth) dynasty. He was the brother-in-law of So (q.v.). He probably ascended the throne about B.C. 692, having been previously king of Ethiopia (<reflink>2 Kings 19:9; Isa. 37:9</reflink>), which with Egypt now formed one nation. He was a great warrior, and but little is known of him. The Assyrian armies under Esarhaddon, and again under Assur-bani-pal, invaded Egypt and defeated Tirhakah, who afterwards retired into Ethiopia, where he died, after reigning twenty-six years.

tirshatha.d: a word probably of Persian origin, meaning "severity," denoting a high civil dignity. The Persian governor of Judea is so called (<reflink>Ezra 2:63; Neh. 7:65, 70</reflink>). Nehemiah is called by this name in Neh. 8:9; 10:1, and the "governor" (pehah) in 5:18. Probably, therefore, tirshatha=pehah=the modern pasha.

tirza.d: pleasantness. (1.) An old royal city of the Canaanites, which was destroyed by Joshua (<reflink>Josh. 12:24</reflink>). Jeroboam chose it for his residence, and he removed to it from Shechem, which at first he made the capital of his kingdom. It remained the chief residence of the kings of Israel till Omri took Samaria (<reflink>1 Kings 14:17; 15:21; 16:6, 8, etc.</reflink>). Here Zimri perished amid the flames of the palace to which in his despair he had set fire (<reflink>1 Kings 16:18</reflink>), and here Menahem smote Shallum (<reflink>2 Kings 15:14, 16</reflink>). Solomon refers to its beauty (<reflink>Cant. 6:4</reflink>). It has been identified with the modern mud hamlet Teiasir, 11 miles north of Shechem. Others, however, would identify it with Telluza, a village about 6 miles east of Samaria.

tishbite.d: Elijah the prophet was thus named (<reflink>1 Kings 17:1; 21:17, 28, etc.</reflink>). In 1 Kings 17:1 the word rendered "inhabitants" is in the original the same as that rendered "Tishbite," hence that verse may be read as in the LXX., "Elijah the Tishbite of Tishbi in Gilead." Some interpret this word as meaning "stranger," and read the verse, "Elijah the stranger from among the strangers in Gilead." This designation is probably given to the prophet as denoting that his birthplace was Tishbi, a place in Upper Galilee (mentioned in the apocryphal book of Tobit), from which for some reason he migrated into Gilead. Josephus, the Jewish historian (<reflink>Ant. 8:13, 2</reflink>), however, supposes that Tishbi was some place in the land of Gilead. It has been identified by some with el-Ishtib, a some place 22 miles due south of the Sea of Galilee, among the mountains of Gilead.

tisri.d: the first month of the civil year, and the seventh of the ecclesiastical year. See ETHANIM (<reflink>1 Kings 8:2</reflink>). Called in the Assyrian inscriptions Tasaritu, i.e. "beginning."

tithe.d: a tenth of the produce of the earth consecrated and set apart for special purposes. The dedication of a tenth to God was recognized as a duty before the time of Moses. Abraham paid tithes to Melchizedek (<reflink>Gen. 14:20; Heb. 7:6</reflink>); and Jacob vowed unto the Lord and said, "Of all that thou shalt give me I will surely give the tenth unto thee."

tittle.d: a point, (<reflink>Matt. 5:18; Luke 16:17</reflink>), the minute point or stroke added to some letters of the Hebrew alphabet to distinguish them from others which they resemble; hence, the very least point.

titus.d: honourable, was with Paul and Barnabas at Antioch, and accompanied them to the council at Jerusalem (<reflink>Gal. 2:1-3; Acts 15:2</reflink>), although his name nowhere occurs in the Acts of the Apostles. He appears to have been a Gentile, and to have been chiefly engaged in ministering to Gentiles; for Paul sternly refused to have him circumcised, inasmuch as in his case the cause of gospel liberty was at stake. We find him, at a later period, with Paul and Timothy at Ephesus, whence he was sent by Paul to Corinth for the purpose of getting the contributions of the church there in behalf of the poor saints at Jerusalem sent forward (<reflink>2 Cor. 8:6; 12:18</reflink>). He rejoined the apostle when he was in Macedonia, and cheered him with the tidings he brought from Corinth (7:6-15). …

titus, epistle to.d: was probably written about the same time as the first epistle to Timothy, with which it has many affinities. "Both letters were addressed to persons left by the writer to preside in their respective churches during his absence. Both letters are principally occupied in describing the qualifications to be sought for in those whom they should appoint to offices in the church; and the ingredients of this description are in both letters nearly the same. Timothy and Titus are likewise cautioned against the same prevailing corruptions, and in particular against the same misdirection of their cares and studies. This affinity obtains not only in the subject of the letters, which from the similarity of situation in the persons to whom they were addressed might be expected to be somewhat alike, but extends in a great variety of instances to the phrases and expressions. …

tob, the land of.d: a district on the east of Jodan, about 13 miles south-east of the Sea of Galilee, to which Jephthah fled from his brethren (<reflink>Judg. 11:3, 5</reflink>). It was on the northern boundary of Perea, between Syria and the land of Ammon (<reflink>2 Sam. 10:6, 8</reflink>). Its modern name is Taiyibeh.

tob-adonijah.d: good is Jehovah, my Lord, a Levite sent out by Jehoshaphat to instruct the people of Judah in the law (<reflink>2 Chr. 17:8</reflink>).

tobiah.d: pleasing to Jehovah, the "servant," the "Ammonite," who joined with those who opposed the rebuilding of Jerusalem after the Exile (<reflink>Neh. 2:10</reflink>). He was a man of great influence, which he exerted in opposition to the Jews, and "sent letters" to Nehemiah "to put him in fear" (<reflink>Neh. 6:17-19</reflink>). "Eliashib the priest" prepared for him during Nehemiah's absence "a chamber in the courts of the house of God," which on his return grieved Nehemiah sore, and therefore he "cast forth all the household stuff of Tobiah out of the chamber" (13:7, 8).

tobijah.d: id., a Levite sent out through Judah by Jehoshaphat to teach the people (<reflink>2 Chr. 17:8</reflink>).

tochen.d: measured, a town of Simeon (<reflink>1 Chr. 4:32</reflink>).

togarmah.d: (1.) A son of Gomer, and grandson of Japheth (<reflink>Gen. 10:3</reflink>).

toi.d: a king of Hamath, who sent "Joram his son unto King David to salute him," when he "heard that David had smitten all the host of Hadadezer" (<reflink>2 Sam. 8:9, 10</reflink>). Called Tou (<reflink>1 Chr. 18:9, 10</reflink>).

tola.d: a scarlet worm. (1.) Eldest son of Issachar (<reflink>Gen. 46:13</reflink>).

tolad.d: productive, a town of Simeon, in the south of Judah (<reflink>1 Chr. 4:29</reflink>).

toll.d: one of the branches of the king of Persia's revenues (<reflink>Ezra 4:13; 7:24</reflink>), probably a tax levied from those who used the bridges and fords and highways.

tombs.d: of the Hebrews were generally excavated in the solid rock, or were natural caves. Mention is made of such tombs in Judg. 8:32; 2 Sam. 2:32; 2 Kings 9:28; 23:30. They were sometimes made in gardens (<reflink>2 Kings 21:26; 23:16; Matt. 27:60</reflink>). They are found in great numbers in and around Jerusalem and all over the land. They were sometimes whitewashed (<reflink>Matt. 23:27, 29</reflink>). The body of Jesus was laid in Joseph's new rock-hewn tomb, in a garden near to Calvary. All evidence is in favour of the opinion that this tomb was somewhere near the Damascus gate, and outside the city, and cannot be identified with the so-called "holy sepulchre." The mouth of such rocky tombs was usually closed by a large stone (Heb. golal), which could only be removed by the united efforts of several men (<reflink>Matt. 28:2; comp. John 11:39</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See GOLGOTHA.</see>)

tongues, confusion of.d: at Babel, the cause of the early separation of mankind and their division into nations. The descendants of Noah built a tower to prevent their dispersion; but God "confounded their language" (<reflink>Gen. 11:1-8</reflink>), and they were scattered over the whole earth. Till this time "the whole earth was of one language and of one speech." (<see target="x-self">See SHINAR.</see>)

tongues, gift of.d: granted on the day of Pentecost (<reflink>Acts 2:4</reflink>), in fulfilment of a promise Christ had made to his disciples (<reflink>Mark 16:17</reflink>). What this gift actually was has been a subject of much discussion. Some have argued that it was merely an outward sign of the presence of the Holy Spirit among the disciples, typifying his manifold gifts, and showing that salvation was to be extended to all nations. But the words of Luke (<reflink>Acts 2:9</reflink>) clearly show that the various peoples in Jerusalem at the time of Pentecost did really hear themselves addressed in their own special language with which they were naturally acquainted (<reflink>comp. Joel 2:28, 29</reflink>).

tooth.d: one of the particulars regarding which retaliatory punishment was to be inflicted (<reflink>Ex. 21:24; Lev. 24:20; Deut. 19:21</reflink>). "Gnashing of teeth" =rage, despair (<reflink>Matt. 8:12; Acts 7:54</reflink>); "cleanness of teeth" =famine (<reflink>Amos 4:6</reflink>); "children's teeth set on edge" =children suffering for the sins of their fathers (<reflink>Ezek. 18:2</reflink>).

topaz.d: Heb. pitdah (<reflink>Ezek. 28:13; Rev. 21:20</reflink>), a golden yellow or "green" stone brought from Cush or Ethiopia (<reflink>Job 28:19</reflink>). It was the second stone in the first row in the breastplate of the high priest, and had the name of Simeon inscribed on it (<reflink>Ex. 28:17</reflink>). It is probably the chrysolite of the moderns.

tophel.d: lime, a place in the wilderness of Sinai (<reflink>Deut. 1:1</reflink>), now identified with Tafyleh or Tufileh, on the west side of the Edomitish mountains.

tophet.d: =Topheth, from Heb. toph "a drum," because the cries of children here sacrificed by the priests of Moloch were drowned by the noise of such an instrument; or from taph or toph, meaning "to burn," and hence a place of burning, the name of a particular part in the valley of Hinnom. "Fire being the most destructive of all elements, is chosen by the sacred writers to symbolize the agency by which God punishes or destroys the wicked. We are not to assume from prophetical figures that material fire is the precise agent to be used. It was not the agency employed in the destruction of Sennacherib, mentioned in Isa. 30:33...Tophet properly begins where the Vale of Hinnom bends round to the east, having the cliffs of Zion on the north, and the Hill of Evil Counsel on the south. It terminates at Beer 'Ayub, where it joins the Valley of Jehoshaphat. The cliffs on the southern side especially abound in ancient tombs. …

torches.d: On the night of his betrayal, when our Lord was in the garden of Gethsemane, Judas, "having received a band of men and officers from the chief priests and Pharisees, cometh thither with lanterns and torches and weapons" (<reflink>John 18:1-3</reflink>). Although it was the time of full moon, yet in the valley of the Kidron "there fell great, deep shadows from the declivity of the mountain and projecting rocks; there were there caverns and grottos, into which a fugitive might retreat; finally, there were probably a garden-house and tower, into whose gloom it might be necessary for a searcher to throw light around." Lange's Commentary. (<reflink>Nahum 2:3, "torches," Revised Version, "steel," probably should be "scythes" for war-chariots.</reflink>)

torment.d: Gr. basanos (<reflink>Matt. 4:24</reflink>), the "touch-stone" of justice; hence inquisition by torture, and then any disease which racks and tortures the limbs.

tortoise.d: (Heb. tsabh). Ranked among the unclean animals (<reflink>Lev. 11:29</reflink>). Land tortoises are common in Syria. The LXX. renders the word by "land crocodile." The word, however, more probably denotes a lizard, called by the modern Arabs _dhabb_.

tower of the furnaces.d: (<reflink>Neh. 3:11; 12:38</reflink>), a tower at the north-western angle of the second wall of Jerusalem. It was probably so named from its contiguity to the "bakers' street" (<reflink>Jer. 37:21</reflink>).

towers.d: of Babel (<reflink>Gen. 11:4</reflink>), Edar (<reflink>Gen. 35:21</reflink>), Penuel (<reflink>Judg. 8:9, 17</reflink>), Shechem (9:46), David (<reflink>Cant. 4:4</reflink>), Lebanon (7:4), Syene (<reflink>Ezek. 29:10</reflink>), Hananeel (<reflink>Zech. 14:10</reflink>), Siloam (<reflink>Luke 13:4</reflink>). There were several towers in Jerusalem (<reflink>2 Chr. 26:9; Ps. 48:12</reflink>). They were erected for various purposes, as watch-towers in vineyard (<reflink>Isa. 5:2; Matt. 21:33</reflink>) and towers for defence.

trachonitis.d: a rugged region, corresponds to the Heb. Argob (q.v.), the Greek name of a region on the east of Jordan (<reflink>Luke 3:1</reflink>); one of the five Roman provinces into which that district was divided. It was in the tetrarchy of Philip, and is now called the Lejah.

tradition.d: any kind of teaching, written or spoken, handed down from generation to generation. In Mark 7:3, 9, 13, Col. 2:8, this word refers to the arbitrary interpretations of the Jews. In 2 Thess. 2:15; 3:6, it is used in a good sense. Peter (<reflink>1 Pet. 1:18</reflink>) uses this word with reference to the degenerate Judaism of the "strangers scattered" whom he addresses (<reflink>comp. Acts 15:10; Matt. 15:2-6; Gal. 1:14</reflink>).

trance.d: (Gr. ekstasis, from which the word "ecstasy" is derived) denotes the state of one who is "out of himself." Such were the trances of Peter and Paul, Acts 10:10; 11:5; 22:17, ecstasies, "a preternatural, absorbed state of mind preparing for the reception of the vision", (comp. 2 Cor. 12:1-4). In Mark 5:42 and Luke 5:26 the Greek word is rendered "astonishment," "amazement" (<reflink>comp. Mark 16:8; Acts 3:10</reflink>).

transfiguration, the.d: of our Lord on a "high mountain apart," is described by each of the three evangelists (<reflink>Matt. 17:1-8; Mark 9:2-8; Luke 9:28-36</reflink>). The fullest account is given by Luke, who, no doubt, was informed by Peter, who was present on the occasion. What these evangelists record was an absolute historical reality, and not a mere vision. The concurrence between them in all the circumstances of the incident is exact. John seems to allude to it also (<reflink>John 1:14</reflink>). Forty years after the event Peter distinctly makes mention of it (<reflink>2 Pet. 1:16-18</reflink>). In describing the sanctification of believers, Paul also seems to allude to this majestic and glorious appearance of our Lord on the "holy mount" (<reflink>Rom. 12:2; 2 Cor. 3:18</reflink>).

treasure cities.d: store cities which the Israelites built for the Egyptians (<reflink>Ex. 1:11</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See PITHOM.</see>) Towns in which the treasures of the kings of Judah were kept were so designated (<reflink>1 Chr. 27:25</reflink>).

treasure houses.d: the houses or magazines built for the safe keeping of treasure and valuable articles of any kind (<reflink>Ezra 5:17; 7:20; Neh. 10:38; Dan. 1:2</reflink>).

treasury.d: (<reflink>Matt. 27:6; Mark 12:41; John 8:20</reflink>). It does not appear that there was a separate building so called. The name was given to the thirteen brazen chests, called "trumpets," from the form of the opening into which the offerings of the temple worshippers were put. These stood in the outer "court of the women." "Nine chests were for the appointed money-tribute and for the sacrifice-tribute, i.e., money-gifts instead of the sacrifices; four chests for freewill-offerings for wood, incense, temple decoration, and burnt-offerings" (Lightfoot's Hor. Heb.).

tree of life.d: stood also in the midst of the garden of Eden (<reflink>Gen. 2:9; 3:22</reflink>). Some writers have advanced the opinion that this tree had some secret virtue, which was fitted to preserve life. Probably the lesson conveyed was that life was to be sought by man, not in himself or in his own power, but from without, from Him who is emphatically the Life (<reflink>John 1:4; 14:6</reflink>). Wisdom is compared to the tree of life (<reflink>Prov. 3:18</reflink>). The "tree of life" spoken of in the Book of Revelation (<reflink>Rev. 2:7; 22:2, 14</reflink>) is an emblem of the joys of the celestial paradise.

tree of the knowledge of good and evil.w: Tree of the knowledge of good and evil
tree of the knowledge of good and evil.d: stood in the midst of the garden of Eden, beside the tree of life (Gen. 2, 3). Adam and Eve were forbidden to take of the fruit which grew upon it. But they disobeyed the divine injunction, and so sin and death by sin entered our world and became the heritage of Adam's posterity. (<see target="x-self">See ADAM.</see>)

trespass offering.d: (Heb. 'asham, "debt"), the law concerning, given in Lev. 5:14-6:7; also in Num. 5:5-8. The idea of sin as a "debt" pervades this legislation. The _asham_, which was always a ram, was offered in cases where sins were more private. (See OFFERING

tribe.d: a collection of families descending from one ancestor. The "twelve tribes" of the Hebrews were the twelve collections of families which sprang from the sons of Jacob. In Matt. 24:30 the word has a wider significance. The tribes of Israel are referred to as types of the spiritual family of God (Rev. 7). (<see target="x-self">See ISRAEL, KINGDOM OF; JUDAH, KINGDOM OF.</see>)

tribulation.d: trouble or affiction of any kind (<reflink>Deut. 4:30; Matt. 13:21; 2 Cor. 7:4</reflink>). In Rom. 2:9 "tribulation and anguish" are the penal sufferings that shall overtake the wicked. In Matt. 24:21, 29, the word denotes the calamities that were to attend the destruction of Jerusalem.

tribute.d: a tax imposed by a king on his subjects (<reflink>2 Sam. 20:24; 1 Kings 4:6; Rom. 13:6</reflink>). In Matt. 17:24-27 the word denotes the temple rate (the "didrachma," the "half-shekel," as rendered by the R.V.) which was required to be paid for the support of the temple by every Jew above twenty years of age (<reflink>Ex. 30:12; 2 Kings 12:4; 2 Chr. 24:6, 9</reflink>). It was not a civil but a religious tax.

trinity.d: a word not found in Scripture, but used to express the doctrine of the unity of God as subsisting in three distinct Persons. This word is derived from the Gr. trias, first used by Theophilus (A.D. 168-183), or from the Lat. trinitas, first used by Tertullian (A.D. 220), to express this doctrine. The propositions involved in the doctrine are these: 1. That God is one, and that there is but one God (<reflink>Deut. 6:4; 1 Kings 8:60; Isa. 44:6; Mark 12:29, 32; John 10:30</reflink>). 2. That the Father is a distinct divine Person (hypostasis, subsistentia, persona, suppositum intellectuale), distinct from the Son and the Holy Spirit. 3. That Jesus Christ was truly God, and yet was a Person distinct from the Father and the Holy Spirit. 4. That the Holy Spirit is also a distinct divine Person.

troas.d: a city on the coast of Mysia, in the north-west of Asia Minor, named after ancient Troy, which was at some little distance from it (about 4 miles) to the north. Here Paul, on his second missionary journey, saw the vision of a "man of Macedonia," who appeared to him, saying, "Come over, and help us" (<reflink>Acts 16:8-11</reflink>). He visited this place also on other occasions, and on one of these visits he left his cloak and some books there (<reflink>2 Cor. 2:12; 2 Tim. 4:13</reflink>). The ruins of Troas extend over many miles, the site being now mostly covered with a forest of oak trees. The modern name of the ruins is Eski Stamboul i.e., Old Constantinople.

trogyllium.d: a town on the western coast of Asia Minor, where Paul "tarried" when on his way from Assos to Miletus, on his third missionary journey (<reflink>Acts 20:15</reflink>).

trophimus.d: a foster-child, an Ephesian who accompanied Paul during a part of his third missionary journey (<reflink>Acts 20:4; 21:29</reflink>). He was with Paul in Jerusalem, and the Jews, supposing that the apostle had brought him with him into the temple, raised a tumult which resulted in Paul's imprisonment. (See TEMPLE, HEROD'S

trumpets.d: were of a great variety of forms, and were made of divers materials. Some were made of silver (<reflink>Num. 10:2</reflink>), and were used only by the priests in announcing the approach of festivals and in giving signals of war. Some were also made of rams' horns (<reflink>Josh. 6:8</reflink>). They were blown at special festivals, and to herald the arrival of special seasons (<reflink>Lev. 23:24; 25:9; 1 Chr. 15:24; 2 Chr. 29:27; Ps. 81:3; 98:6</reflink>).

trumpets, feast of.d: was celebrated at the beginning of the month Tisri, the first month of the civil year. It received its name from the circumstances that the trumpets usually blown at the commencement of each month were on that occasion blown with unusual solemnity (<reflink>Lev. 23:23-25; Num. 10:10; 29:1-6</reflink>). It was one of the seven days of holy convocation. The special design of this feast, which is described in these verses, is not known.

truth.d: Used in various senses in Scripture. In Prov. 12:17, 19, it denotes that which is opposed to falsehood. In Isa. 59:14, 15, Jer. 7:28, it means fidelity or truthfulness. The doctrine of Christ is called "the truth of the gospel" (<reflink>Gal. 2:5</reflink>), "the truth" (<reflink>2 Tim. 3:7; 4:4</reflink>). Our Lord says of himself, "I am the way, and the truth" (<reflink>John 14:6</reflink>).

tryphena and tryphosa.d: two female Christians, active workers, whom Paul salutes in his epistle to the Romans (16:12).

tubal-cain.d: the son of Lamech and Zillah, "an instructor of every artificer in brass and iron" (<reflink>Gen. 4:22; R.V., "the forger of every cutting instrument of brass and iron"</reflink>).

turtle, turtle-dove.d: Its peculiar peaceful and gentle habit its often referred to in Scripture. A pair was offered in sacrifice by Mary at her purification (<reflink>Luke 2:24</reflink>). The pigeon and the turtle-dove were the only birds permitted to be offered in sacrifice (<reflink>Lev. 1:14; 5:7; 14:22; 15:14, 29, etc.</reflink>). The Latin name of this bird, _turtur_, is derived from its note, and is a repetition of the Hebrew name _tor_. Three species are found in Palestine, (1) the turtle-dove (Turtur auritus), (2) the collared turtle (T. risorius), and (3) the palm turtle (T. Senegalensis). But it is to the first of these species which the various passages of Scripture refer. It is a migratory bird (<reflink>Jer. 8:7; Cant. 2:11, 12</reflink>). "Search the glades and valleys, even by sultry Jordan, at the end of March, and not a turtle-dove is to be seen. Return in the second week of April, and clouds of doves are feeding on the clovers of the plain. …

tychicus.d: chance, an Asiatic Christian, a "faithful minister in the Lord" (<reflink>Eph. 6:21, 22</reflink>), who, with Trophimus, accompanied Paul on a part of his journey from Macedonia to Jerusalem (<reflink>Acts 20:4</reflink>). He is alluded to also in Col. 4:7, Titus 3:12, and 2 Tim. 4:12 as having been with Paul at Rome, whence he sent him to Ephesus, probably for the purpose of building up and encouraging the church there.

type.d: occurs only once in Scripture (<reflink>1 Cor. 10:11, A.V. marg.</reflink>). The Greek word _tupos_ is rendered "print" (<reflink>John 20:25</reflink>), "figure" (<reflink>Acts 7:43; Rom. 5:14</reflink>), "fashion" (<reflink>Acts 7:44</reflink>), "manner" (<reflink>Acts 23:25</reflink>), "form" (<reflink>Rom. 6:17</reflink>), "example" or "ensample" (<reflink>1 Cor. 10:6, 11; Phil. 3:17; 1 Thess. 1:7; 2 Thess. 3:9; 1 Tim. 4:12</reflink>). It properly means a "model" or "pattern" or "mould" into which clay or wax was pressed, that it might take the figure or exact shape of the mould. The word "type" is generally used to denote a resemblance between something present and something future, which is called the "antitype."

tyrannus.d: prince, a Greek rhetorician, in whose "school" at Ephesus Paul disputed daily for the space of two years with those who came to him (<reflink>Acts 19:9</reflink>). Some have supposed that he was a Jew, and that his "school" was a private synagogue.

tyre.d: a rock, now es-Sur; an ancient Phoenician city, about 23 miles, in a direct line, north of Acre, and 20 south of Sidon. Sidon was the oldest Phoenician city, but Tyre had a longer and more illustrious history. The commerce of the whole world was gathered into the warehouses of Tyre. "Tyrian merchants were the first who ventured to navigate the Mediterranean waters; and they founded their colonies on the coasts and neighbouring islands of the AEgean Sea, in Greece, on the northern coast of Africa, at Carthage and other places, in Sicily and Corsica, in Spain at Tartessus, and even beyond the pillars of Hercules at Gadeira (Cadiz)" (Driver's Isaiah). In the time of David a friendly alliance was entered into between the Hebrews and the Tyrians, who were long ruled over by their native kings (<reflink>2 Sam. 5:11; 1 Kings 5:1; 2 Chr. 2:3</reflink>).

tyropoeon valley.d: (i.e., "Valley of the Cheesemongers"), the name given by Josephus the historian to the valley or rugged ravine which in ancient times separated Mount Moriah from Mount Zion. This valley, now filled up with a vast accumulation of rubbish, and almost a plain, was spanned by bridges, the most noted of which was Zion Bridge, which was probably the ordinary means of communication between the royal palace on Zion and the temple. A fragment of the arch (q.v.) of this bridge (called "Robinson's Arch"), where it projects from the sanctuary wall, was discovered by Robinson in 1839. This arch was destroyed by the Romans when Jerusalem was taken.

ucal.d: the name of a person to whom Agur's words are addressed (<reflink>Prov. 30:1</reflink>).

ulai.d: the Eulaus of the Greeks; a river of Susiana. It was probably the eastern branch of the Choasper (Kerkhan), which divided into two branches some 20 miles above the city of Susa. Hence Daniel (8:2,16) speaks of standing "between the banks of Ulai", i.e., between the two streams of the divided river.

unction.d: (<reflink>1 John 2:20,27; R.V., "anointing"</reflink>). Kings, prophets, and priests were anointed, in token of receiving divine grace. All believers are, in a secondary sense, what Christ was in a primary sense, "the Lord's anointed."

unicorn.d: described as an animal of great ferocity and strength (<reflink>Num. 23:22, R.V., "wild ox," marg., "ox-antelope;" 24:8; Isa. 34:7, R.V., "wild oxen"</reflink>), and untamable (<reflink>Job 39:9</reflink>). It was in reality a two-horned animal; but the exact reference of the word so rendered (reem) is doubtful. Some have supposed it to be the buffalo; others, the white antelope, called by the Arabs rim. Most probably, however, the word denotes the Bos primigenius ("primitive ox"), which is now extinct all over the world. This was the auerochs of the Germans, and the urus described by Caesar (Gal. Bel., vi.28) as inhabiting the Hercynian forest. The word thus rendered has been found in an Assyrian inscription written over the wild ox or bison, which some also suppose to be the animal intended (<reflink>comp. Deut. 33:17; Ps. 22:21; 29:6; 92:10</reflink>).

unni.d: afficted. (1.) A Levite whom David appointed to take part in bringing the ark up to Jerusalem from the house of Obed-edom by playing the psaltery on that occasion (<reflink>1 Chr. 15:18, 20</reflink>).

upharsin.d: and they divide, one of the words written by the mysterious hand on the wall of Belshazzar's palace (<reflink>Dan. 5:25</reflink>). It is a pure Chaldean word. "Peres" is only a simple form of the same word.

uphaz.d: probably another name for Ophir (<reflink>Jer. 10:9</reflink>). Some, however, regard it as the name of an Indian colony in Yemen, southern Arabia; others as a place on or near the river Hyphasis (now the Ghana), the south-eastern limit of the Punjaub.

ur.d: light, or the moon city, a city "of the Chaldees," the birthplace of Haran (<reflink>Gen. 11:28,31</reflink>), the largest city of Shinar or northern Chaldea, and the principal commercial centre of the country as well as the centre of political power. It stood near the mouth of the Euphrates, on its western bank, and is represented by the mounds (of bricks cemented by bitumen) of el-Mugheir, i.e., "the bitumined," or "the town of bitumen," now 150 miles from the sea and some 6 miles from the Euphrates, a little above the point where it receives the Shat el-Hie, an affluent from the Tigris. It was formerly a maritime city, as the waters of the Persian Gulf reached thus far inland. Ur was the port of Babylonia, whence trade was carried on with the dwellers on the gulf, and with the distant countries of India, Ethiopia, and Egypt. It was abandoned about B.C. 500, but long continued, like Erech, to be a great sacred cemetery city, as is evident from the number of tombs found there. …

uriah.d: the Lord is my light. (1.) A Hittite, the husband of Bathsheba, whom David first seduced, and then after Uriah's death married. He was one of the band of David's "mighty men." The sad story of the curel wrongs inflicted upon him by David and of his mournful death are simply told in the sacred record (<reflink>2 Sam. 11:2-12:26</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See BATHSHEBA; DAVID.</see>)

uriel.d: God is my light. (1.) A Levite of the family of Kohath (<reflink>1 Chr. 6:24</reflink>).

urijah.d: the lord is my light. (1.) A high priest in the time of Ahaz (<reflink>2 Kings 16:10-16</reflink>), at whose bidding he constructed an idolatrous altar like one the king had seen at Damascus, to be set up instead of the brazen altar.

usury.d: the sum paid for the use of money, hence interest; not, as in the modern sense, exorbitant interest. The Jews were forbidden to exact usury (<reflink>Lev. 25:36, 37</reflink>), only, however, in their dealings with each other (<reflink>Deut. 23:19, 20</reflink>). The violation of this law was viewed as a great crime (<reflink>Ps. 15:5; Prov. 28:8; Jer. 15:10</reflink>). After the Return, and later, this law was much neglected (<reflink>Neh. 5:7, 10</reflink>).

uz.d: fertile land. (1.) The son of Aram, and grandson of Shem (<reflink>Gen. 10:23; 1 Chr. 1:17</reflink>).

uz, the land of.d: where Job lived (1:1; Jer. 25:20; Lam. 4:21), probably somewhere to the east or south-east of Palestine and north of Edom. It is mentioned in Scripture only in these three passages.

uzal.d: a wanderer, a descendant of Joktan (<reflink>Gen. 10:27; 1 Chr. 1:21</reflink>), the founder apparently of one of the Arab tribes; the name also probably of the province they occupied and of their chief city.

uzza.d: strengh, a garden in which Manasseh and Amon were buried (<reflink>2 Kings 21:18, 26</reflink>). It was probably near the king's palace in Jerusalem, or may have formed part of the palace grounds. Manasseh may probably have acquired it from some one of this name.

uzzah.d: strength, a son of Abinadab, in whose house the men of Kirjath-jearim placed the ark when it was brought back from the land of the Philistines (<reflink>1 Sam. 7:1</reflink>). He with his brother Ahio drove the cart on which the ark was placed when David sought to bring it up to Jerusalem. When the oxen stumbled, Uzzah, in direct violation of the divine law (<reflink>Num. 4:15</reflink>), put forth his hand to steady the ark, and was immediately smitten unto death. The place where this occurred was henceforth called Perez-uzzah (<reflink>1 Chr. 13:11</reflink>). David on this feared to proceed further, and placed the ark in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite (<reflink>2 Sam. 6:2-11; 1 Chr. 13:6-13</reflink>).

uzzen-sherah.d: a town probably near Beth-horon. It derived its name from the daughter of Ephraim (<reflink>1 Chr. 7:24</reflink>).

uzzi.d: the Lord is my strength. (1.) The son of Bukki, and a descendant of Aaron (<reflink>1 Chr. 6:5, 51; Ezra 7:4</reflink>).

uzziah.d: a contracted form of Azari'ah the Lord is my strength. (1.) One of Amaziah's sons, whom the people made king of Judah in his father's stead (<reflink>2 Kings 14:21; 2 Chr. 26:1</reflink>). His long reign of about fifty-two years was "the most prosperous excepting that of Jehosaphat since the time of Solomon." He was a vigorous and able ruler, and "his name spread abroad, even to the entering in of Egypt" (<reflink>2 Chr. 26:8, 14</reflink>). In the earlier part of his reign, under the influence of Zechariah, he was faithful to Jehovah, and "did that which was right in the sight of the Lord" (<reflink>2 Kings 15:3; 2 Chr. 26:4, 5</reflink>); but toward the close of his long life "his heart was lifted up to his destruction," and he wantonly invaded the priest's office (<reflink>2 Chr. 26:16</reflink>), and entering the sanctuary proceeded to offer incense on the golden altar. …

uzziel.d: strength of God. (1.) One of the sons of Kohath, and uncle of Aaron (<reflink>Ex. 6:18; Lev. 10:4</reflink>).

vagabond.d: from Lat. vagabundus, "a wanderer," "a fugitive;" not used opprobriously (<reflink>Gen. 4:12, R.V., "wanderer;" Ps. 109:10; Acts 19:13, R.V., "strolling"</reflink>).

vajezatha.d: purity; worthy of honour, one of Haman's sons, whom the Jews slew in the palace of Shushan (<reflink>Esther 9:9</reflink>).

valley.d: (1.) Heb. bik'ah, a "cleft" of the mountains (<reflink>Deut. 8:7; 11:11; Ps. 104:8; Isa. 41:18</reflink>); also a low plain bounded by mountains, as the plain of Lebanon at the foot of Hermon around the sources of the Jordan (<reflink>Josh. 11:17; 12:7</reflink>), and the valley of Megiddo (<reflink>2 Chr. 35:22</reflink>).

vashti.d: beautiful, the queen of Ahasuerus, who was deposed from her royal dignity because she refused to obey the king when he desired her to appear in the banqueting hall of Shushan the palace (<reflink>Esther 1:10-12</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See ESTHER.</see>)

vaticanus, codex.d: is said to be the oldest extant vellum manuscript. It and the Codex Sinaiticus are the two oldest uncial manuscripts. They were probably written in the fourth century. The Vaticanus was placed in the Vatican Library at Rome by Pope Nicolas V. in 1448, its previous history being unknown. It originally consisted in all probability of a complete copy of the Septuagint and of the New Testament. It is now imperfect, and consists of 759 thin, delicate leaves, of which the New Testament fills 142. Like the Sinaiticus, it is of the greatest value to Biblical scholars in aiding in the formation of a correct text of the New Testament. It is referred to by critics as Codex B.

veil, vail.d: (1.) Heb. mitpahath (<reflink>Ruth 3:15; marg., "sheet" or "apron;" R.V., "mantle"</reflink>). In Isa. 3:22 this word is plural, rendered "wimples;" R.V., "shawls" i.e., wraps.

version.d: a translation of the holy Scriptures. This word is not found in the Bible, nevertheless, as frequent references are made in this work to various ancient as well as modern versions, it is fitting that some brief account should be given of the most important of these. These versions are important helps to the right interpretation of the Word. (See SAMARITAN PENTATEUCH

villages.d: (<reflink>Judg. 5:7, 11</reflink>). The Hebrew word thus rendered (perazon) means habitations in the open country, unwalled villages (<reflink>Deut. 3:5; 1 Sam. 6:18</reflink>). Others, however, following the LXX. and the Vulgate versions, render the word "rulers."

vine.d: one of the most important products of Palestine. The first mention of it is in the history of Noah (<reflink>Gen. 9:20</reflink>). It is afterwards frequently noticed both in the Old and New Testaments, and in the ruins of terraced vineyards there are evidences that it was extensively cultivated by the Jews. It was cultivated in Palestine before the Israelites took possession of it. The men sent out by Moses brought with them from the Valley of Eshcol a cluster of grapes so large that "they bare it between two upon a staff" (<reflink>Num. 13: 23</reflink>). The vineyards of En-gedi (<reflink>Cant. 1:14</reflink>), Heshbon, Sibmah, Jazer, Elealeh (<reflink>Isa. 16:8-10; Jer. 48:32, 34</reflink>), and Helbon (<reflink>Ezek. 27:18</reflink>), as well as of Eshcol, were celebrated.

vine of sodom.d: referred to only in Deut. 32:32. Among the many conjectures as to this tree, the most probable is that it is the 'osher of the Arabs, which abounds in the region of the Dead Sea. Its fruit are the so-called "apples of Sodom," which, though beautiful to the eye, are exceedingly bitter to the taste. (See EN-GEDI

vinegar.d: Heb. hometz, Gr. oxos, Fr. vin aigre; i.e., "sour wine." The Hebrew word is rendered vinegar in Ps. 69:21, a prophecy fulfilled in the history of the crucifixion (<reflink>Matt. 27:34</reflink>). This was the common sour wine (posea) daily made use of by the Roman soldiers. They gave it to Christ, not in derision, but from compassion, to assuage his thirst. Prov. 10:26 shows that there was also a stronger vinegar, which was not fit for drinking. The comparison, "vinegar upon nitre," probably means "vinegar upon soda" (as in the marg. of the R.V.), which then effervesces.

viol.d: Heb. nebel (<reflink>Isa. 5:12, R.V., "lute;" 14:11</reflink>), a musical instrument, usually rendered "psaltery" (q.v.)

viper.d: In Job 20:16, Isa. 30:6; 59:5, the Heb. word eph'eh is thus rendered. The Hebrew word, however, probably denotes a species of poisonous serpents known by the Arabic name of 'el ephah. Tristram has identified it with the sand viper, a species of small size common in sandy regions, and frequently found under stones by the shores of the Dead Sea. It is rapid in its movements, and highly poisonous. In the New Testament _echidne_ is used (<reflink>Matt. 3:7; 12:34; 23:33</reflink>) for any poisonous snake. The viper mentioned in Acts 28:3 was probably the vipera aspis, or the Mediterranean viper. (<see target="x-self">See ADDER.</see>)

virgin.d: In a prophecy concerning our Lord, Isaiah (7:14) says, "A virgin [R.V. marg., 'the virgin'] shall conceive, and bear a son" (<reflink>comp. Luke 1:31-35</reflink>). The people of the land of Zidon are thus referred to by Isaiah (23:12), "O thou oppressed virgin, daughter of Zidon;" and of the people of Israel, Jeremiah (18:13) says, "The virgin of Israel hath done a very horrible thing."

vision.d: (<reflink>Luke 1:22</reflink>), a vivid apparition, not a dream (<reflink>comp. Luke 24:23; Acts 26:19; 2 Cor. 12:1</reflink>).

vows.d: voluntary promises which, when once made, were to be kept if the thing vowed was right. They were made under a great variety of circumstances (<reflink>Gen. 28: 18-22; Lev. 7:16; Num. 30:2-13; Deut. 23:18; Judg. 11:30, 39; 1 Sam. 1:11; Jonah 1:16; Acts 18:18; 21:23</reflink>).

vulture.d: (1.) Heb. da'ah (<reflink>Lev. 11:14</reflink>). In the parallel passage (<reflink>Deut. 14:13</reflink>) the Hebrew word used is _ra'ah_, rendered "glede;" LXX., "gups;" Vulg., "milvus." A species of ravenous bird, distinguished for its rapid flight. "When used without the epithet 'red,' the name is commonly confined to the black kite. The habits of the bird bear out the allusion in Isa. 34:15, for it is, excepting during the winter three months, so numerous everywhere in Palestine as to be almost gregarious." (See EAGLE

wafers.d: thin cakes (<reflink>Ex. 16:31; 29:2, 23; Lev. 2:4; 7:12; 8:26; Num. 6:15, 19</reflink>) used in various offerings.

wages.d: Rate of (<reflink>mention only in Matt. 20:2</reflink>); to be punctually paid (<reflink>Lev. 19:13; Deut. 24:14, 15</reflink>); judgements threatened against the withholding of (<reflink>Jer. 22:13; Mal. 3:5; comp. James 5:4</reflink>); paid in money (<reflink>Matt. 20:1-14</reflink>); to Jacob in kind (<reflink>Gen. 29:15, 20; 30:28; 31:7, 8, 41</reflink>).

wagon.d: Heb. aghalah; so rendered in Gen. 45:19, 21, 27; 46:5; Num. 7:3, 7,8, but elsewhere rendered "cart" (<reflink>1 Sam. 6:7, etc.</reflink>). This vehicle was used for peaceful purposes. In Ezek. 23:24, however, it is the rendering of a different Hebrew word, and denotes a war-chariot.

wailing-place, jews'.d: a section of the western wall of the temple area, where the Jews assemble every Friday afternoon to bewail their desolate condition (<reflink>Ps. 79:1, 4, 5</reflink>). The stones in this part of the wall are of great size, and were placed, as is generally believed, in the position in which they are now found in the time of Solomon. "The congregation at the wailing-place is one of the most solemn gatherings left to the Jewish Church, and as the writer gazed at the motley concourse he experienced a feeling of sorrow that the remnants of the chosen race should be heartlessly thrust outside the sacred enclosure of their fathers' holy temple by men of an alien race and an alien creed. Many of the elders, seated on the ground, with their backs against the wall, on the west side of the area, and with their faces turned toward the eternal house, read out of their well-thumbed Hebrew books passages from the prophetic writings, such as Isa. 64:9-12" (King's Recent Discoveries, etc.). …

wall.d: Cities were surrounded by walls, as distinguished from "unwalled villages" (<reflink>Ezek. 38:11; Lev. 25:29-34</reflink>). They were made thick and strong (<reflink>Num. 13:28; Deut. 3:5</reflink>). Among the Jews walls were built of stone, some of those in the temple being of great size (<reflink>1 Kings 6:7; 7:9-12; 20:30; Mark 13:1, 2</reflink>). The term is used metaphorically of security and safety (<reflink>Isa. 26:1; 60:18; Rev. 21:12-20</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See FENCE.</see>)

wandering.d: of the Israelites in the wilderness in consequence of their rebellious fears to enter the Promised Land (<reflink>Num. 14:26-35</reflink>). They wandered for forty years before they were permitted to cross the Jordan (<reflink>Josh. 4:19; 5:6</reflink>).

war.d: The Israelites had to take possession of the Promised Land by conquest. They had to engage in a long and bloody war before the Canaanitish tribes were finally subdued. Except in the case of Jericho and Ai, the war did not become aggressive till after the death of Joshua. Till then the attack was always first made by the Canaanites. Now the measure of the iniquity of the Canaanites was full, and Israel was employed by God to sweep them away from off the face of the earth. In entering on this new stage of the war, the tribe of Judah, according to divine direction, took the lead.
