ward.d: a prison (<reflink>Gen. 40:3, 4</reflink>); a watch-station (<reflink>Isa. 21:8</reflink>); a guard (<reflink>Neh. 13:30</reflink>).

wars of the lord, the book of the.w: Wars of the Lord, The Book of the
wars of the lord, the book of the.d: (<reflink>Num. 21:14, 15</reflink>), some unknown book so called (<reflink>comp. Gen. 14:14-16; Ex. 17:8-16; Num. 14:40-45; 21:1-3, 21-25, 33-35; 31. The wars here recorded might be thus designated</reflink>).

washing.d: (<reflink>Mark 7:1-9</reflink>). The Jews, like other Orientals, used their fingers when taking food, and therefore washed their hands before doing so, for the sake of cleanliness. Here the reference is to the ablutions prescribed by tradition, according to which "the disciples ought to have gone down to the side of the lake, washed their hands thoroughly, 'rubbing the fist of one hand in the hollow of the other, then placed the ten finger-tips together, holding the hands up, so that any surplus water might flow down to the elbow, and thence to the ground.'" To neglect to do this had come to be regarded as a great sin, a sin equal to the breach of any of the ten commandments. Moses had commanded washings oft, but always for some definite cause; but the Jews multiplied the legal observance till they formed a large body of precepts. To such precepts about ceremonial washing Mark here refers. (<see target="x-self">See ABLUTION.</see>)

watches.d: the periods into which the time between sunset and sunrise was divided. They are so called because watchmen relieved each other at each of these periods. There are frequent references in Scripture to the duties of watchmen who were appointed to give notice of the approach of an enemy (<reflink>2 Sam. 18:24-27; 2 Kings 9:17-20; Isa. 21:5-9</reflink>). They were sometimes placed for this purpose on watch-towers (<reflink>2 Kings 17:9; 18:8</reflink>). Ministers or teachers are also spoken of under this title (<reflink>Jer. 6:17; Ezek. 33:2-9; Heb. 13:17</reflink>).

watchings.d: (<reflink>2 Cor. 6:5</reflink>), lit. "sleeplessnesses," the result of "manual labour, teaching, travelling, meditating, praying, cares, and the like" (Meyer's Com.).

water of jealousy.d: a phrase employed (not, however, in Scripture) to denote the water used in the solemn ordeal prescribed by the law of Moses (<reflink>Num. 5:11-31</reflink>) in cases of "jealousy."

water of purification.d: used in cases of ceremonial cleansings at the consecration of the Levites (<reflink>Num. 8:7</reflink>). It signified, figuratively, that purifying of the heart which must characterize the servants of God.

water of separation.d: used along with the ashes of a red heifer for the ceremonial cleansing of persons defiled by contact with a dead body (Num. 19).

waterspouts.d: (<reflink>Ps. 42:7; marg. R.V., "cataracts"</reflink>). If we regard this psalm as descriptive of David's feelings when banished from Jerusalem by the revolt of Absalom, this word may denote "waterfalls," inasmuch as Mahanaim, where he abode, was near the Jabbok, and the region abounded with rapids and falls.

wave offerings.d: parts of peace-offerings were so called, because they were waved by the priests (<reflink>Ex. 29:24, 26, 27; Lev. 7:20-34; 8:27; 9:21; 10:14, 15, etc.</reflink>), in token of a solemn special presentation to God. They then became the property of the priests. The first-fruits, a sheaf of barley, offered at the feast of Pentecost (<reflink>Lev. 23:17-20</reflink>), and wheat-bread, the first-fruits of the second harvest, offered at the Passover (10-14), were wave-offerings.

wax.d: Made by melting the combs of bees. Mentioned (<reflink>Ps. 22:14; 68:2; 97:5; Micah 1:4</reflink>) in illustration.

wean.d: Among the Hebrews children (whom it was customary for the mothers to nurse, Ex. 2:7-9; 1 Sam. 1:23; Cant. 8:1) were not generally weaned till they were three or four years old.

weasel.d: (Heb. holedh), enumerated among unclean animals (<reflink>Lev. 11:29</reflink>). Some think that this Hebrew word rather denotes the mole (Spalax typhlus) common in Palestine. There is no sufficient reason, however, to depart from the usual translation. The weasel tribe are common also in Palestine.

weaving, weavers.d: Weaving was an art practised in very early times (<reflink>Ex. 35:35</reflink>). The Egyptians were specially skilled in it (<reflink>Isa. 19:9; Ezek. 27:7</reflink>), and some have regarded them as its inventors.

week.d: From the beginning, time was divided into weeks, each consisting of six days of working and one of rest (<reflink>Gen. 2:2, 3; 7:10; 8:10, 12; 29:28</reflink>). The references to this division of days becomes afterwards more frequent (<reflink>Ex. 34:22; Lev. 12:5; Num. 28:26; Deut. 16:16; 2 Chr. 8:13; Jer. 5:24; Dan. 9:24-27; 10:2, 3</reflink>). It has been found to exist among almost all nations.

weights.d: Reduced to English troy-weight, the Hebrew weights were: (1.) The gerah (<reflink>Lev. 27:25; Num. 3:47</reflink>), a Hebrew word, meaning a grain or kernel, and hence a small weight. It was the twentieth part of a shekel, and equal to 12 grains.

well.d: (Heb. beer), to be distinguished from a fountain (Heb. 'ain). A "beer" was a deep shaft, bored far under the rocky surface by the art of man, which contained water which percolated through the strata in its sides. Such wells were those of Jacob and Beersheba, etc. (<reflink>see Gen. 21:19, 25, 30, 31; 24:11; 26:15, 18-25, 32, etc.</reflink>). In the Pentateuch this word beer, so rendered, occurs twenty-five times.

whale.d: The Hebrew word _tan_ (plural, tannin) is so rendered in Job 7:12 (A.V.; but R.V., "sea-monster"). It is rendered by "dragons" in Deut. 32:33; Ps. 91:13; Jer. 51:34; Ps. 74:13 (marg., "whales;" and marg. of R.V., "sea-monsters"); Isa. 27:1; and "serpent" in Ex. 7:9 (R.V. marg., "any large reptile," and so in ver. 10, 12). The words of Job (7:12), uttered in bitter irony, where he asks, "Am I a sea or a whale?" simply mean, "Have I a wild, untamable nature, like the waves of the sea, which must be confined and held within bounds, that they cannot pass?" "The serpent of the sea, which was but the wild, stormy sea itself, wound itself around the land, and threatened to swallow it up...Job inquires if he must be watched and plagued like this monster, lest he throw the world into disorder" (Davidson's Job).

wheat.d: one of the earliest cultivated grains. It bore the Hebrew name _hittah_, and was extensively cultivated in Palestine. There are various species of wheat. That which Pharaoh saw in his dream was the Triticum compositum, which bears several ears upon one stalk (<reflink>Gen. 41:5</reflink>). The "fat of the kidneys of wheat" (<reflink>Deut. 32:14</reflink>), and the "finest of the wheat" (<reflink>Ps. 81:16; 147:14</reflink>), denote the best of the kind. It was exported from Palestine in great quantities (<reflink>1 Kings 5:11; Ezek. 27:17; Acts 12:20</reflink>).

wheel.d: (Heb. galgal; rendered "wheel" in Ps. 83:13, and "a rolling thing" in Isa. 17:13; R.V. in both, "whirling dust"). This word has been supposed to mean the wild artichoke, which assumes the form of a globe, and in autumn breaks away from its roots, and is rolled about by the wind in some places in great numbers.

white.d: a symbol of purity (<reflink>2 Chr. 5:12; Ps. 51:7; Isa. 1:18; Rev. 3:18; 7:14</reflink>). Our Lord, at his transfiguration, appeared in raiment "white as the light" (<reflink>Matt. 17:2, etc.</reflink>).

widows.d: to be treated with kindness (<reflink>Ex. 22:22; Deut. 14:29; 16:11, 14; 24:17, 19-21; 26:12; 27:19, etc.</reflink>). In the New Testament the same tender regard for them is inculcated (<reflink>Acts 6:1-6; 1 Tim. 5:3-16</reflink>) and exhibited.

wife.d: The ordinance of marriage was sanctioned in Paradise (<reflink>Gen. 2:24; Matt. 19:4-6</reflink>). Monogamy was the original law under which man lived, but polygamy early commenced (<reflink>Gen. 4:19</reflink>), and continued to prevail all down through Jewish history. The law of Moses regulated but did not prohibit polygamy. A man might have a plurality of wives, but a wife could have only one husband. A wife's legal rights (<reflink>Ex. 21:10</reflink>) and her duties (<reflink>Prov. 31:10-31; 1 Tim. 5:14</reflink>) are specified. She could be divorced in special cases (<reflink>Deut. 22:13-21</reflink>), but could not divorce her husband. Divorce was restricted by our Lord to the single case of adultery (<reflink>Matt. 19:3-9</reflink>). The duties of husbands and wives in their relations to each other are distinctly set forth in the New Testament (<reflink>1 Cor. 7:2-5; Eph. 5:22-33; Col. 3:18, 19; 1 Pet. 3:1-7</reflink>).

wilderness.d: (1.) Heb. midhbar, denoting not a barren desert but a district or region suitable for pasturing sheep and cattle (<reflink>Ps. 65:12; Isa. 42:11; Jer. 23:10; Joel 1:19; 2:22</reflink>); an uncultivated place. This word is used of the wilderness of Beersheba (<reflink>Gen. 21:14</reflink>), on the southern border of Palestine; the wilderness of the Red Sea (<reflink>Ex. 13:18</reflink>); of Shur (15:22), a portion of the Sinaitic peninsula; of Sin (17:1), Sinai (<reflink>Lev. 7:38</reflink>), Moab (<reflink>Deut. 2:8</reflink>), Judah (<reflink>Judg. 1:16</reflink>), Ziph, Maon, En-gedi (<reflink>1 Sam. 23:14, 24; 24:1</reflink>), Jeruel and Tekoa (<reflink>2 Chr. 20:16, 20</reflink>), Kadesh (<reflink>Ps. 29:8</reflink>).

willows.d: (1.) Heb. 'arabim (<reflink>Lev. 23:40; Job 40:22; Isa. 15:7; 44:3, 4; Ps. 137:1, 2</reflink>). This was supposed to be the weeping willow, called by Linnaeus Salix Babylonica, from the reference in Ps. 137. This tree is frequently found "on the coast, overhanging wells and pools. There is a conspicuous tree of this species over a pond in the plain of Acre, and others on the Phoenician plain." There are several species of the salix in Palestine, but it is not indigenous to Babylonia, nor was it cultivated there. Some are of opinion that the tree intended is the tamarisk or poplar.

wimple.d: Isa. 3:22, (R.V., "shawls"), a wrap or veil. The same Hebrew word is rendered "vail" (R.V., "mantle") in Ruth 3:15.

window.d: properly only an opening in a house for the admission of light and air, covered with lattice-work, which might be opened or closed (<reflink>2 Kings 1:2; Acts 20:9</reflink>). The spies in Jericho and Paul at Damascus were let down from the windows of houses abutting on the town wall (<reflink>Josh. 2:15; 2 Cor. 11:33</reflink>). The clouds are metaphorically called the "windows of heaven" (<reflink>Gen. 7:11; Mal. 3:10</reflink>). The word thus rendered in Isa. 54:12 ought rather to be rendered "battlements" (LXX., "bulwarks;" R.V., "pinnacles"), or as Gesenius renders it, "notched battlements, i.e., suns or rays of the sun"= having a radiated appearance like the sun.

winds.d: blowing from the four quarters of heaven (<reflink>Jer. 49:36; Ezek. 37:9; Dan. 8:8; Zech. 2:6</reflink>). The east wind was parching (<reflink>Ezek. 17:10; 19:12</reflink>), and is sometimes mentioned as simply denoting a strong wind (<reflink>Job 27:21; Isa. 27:8</reflink>). This wind prevails in Palestine from February to June, as the west wind (<reflink>Luke 12:54</reflink>) does from November to February. The south was a hot wind (<reflink>Job 37:17; Luke 12:55</reflink>). It swept over the Arabian peninsula. The rush of invaders is figuratively spoken of as a whirlwind (<reflink>Isa. 21:1</reflink>); a commotion among the nations of the world as a striving of the four winds (<reflink>Dan. 7:2</reflink>). The winds are subject to the divine power (<reflink>Ps. 18:10; 135:7</reflink>).

wine.d: The common Hebrew word for wine is _yayin_, from a root meaning "to boil up," "to be in a ferment." Others derive it from a root meaning "to tread out," and hence the juice of the grape trodden out. The Greek word for wine is _oinos_, and the Latin _vinun_. But besides this common Hebrew word, there are several others which are thus rendered.

wine-press.d: Consisted of two vats or receptacles, (1) a trough (Heb. gath, Gr. lenos) into which the grapes were thrown and where they were trodden upon and bruised (<reflink>Isa. 16:10; Lam. 1:15; Joel 3:13</reflink>); and (2) a trough or vat (Heb. yekebh, Gr. hypolenion) into which the juice ran from the trough above, the gath (<reflink>Neh. 13:15; Job 24:11; Isa. 63:2, 3; Hag. 2:16; Joel 2:24</reflink>). Wine-presses are found in almost every part of Palestine. They are "the only sure relics we have of the old days of Israel before the Captivity. Between Hebron and Beersheba they are found on all the hill slopes; they abound in southern Judea; they are no less common in the many valleys of Carmel; and they are numerous in Galilee." The "treading of the wine-press" is emblematic of divine judgment (<reflink>Isa. 63:2; Lam. 1:15; Rev. 14:19, 20</reflink>).

winefat.d: (<reflink>Mark 12:1</reflink>). The original word (hypolenion) so rendered occurs only here in the New Testament. It properly denotes the trough or lake (lacus), as it was called by the Romans, into which the juice of the grapes ran from the trough above it. It is here used, however, of the whole apparatus. In the parallel passage in Matt. 21:33 the Greek word _lenos_ is used. This properly denotes the upper one of the two vats. (See WINE-PRESS

winnow.d: Corn was winnowed, (1.) By being thrown up by a shovel against the wind. As a rule this was done in the evening or during the night, when the west wind from the sea was blowing, which was a moderate breeze and fitted for the purpose. The north wind was too strong, and the east wind came in gusts. (2.) By the use of a fan or van, by which the chaff was blown away (<reflink>Ruth 3:2; Isa. 30:24; Jer. 4:11, 12; Matt. 3:12</reflink>).

wise men.d: mentioned in Dan. 2:12 included three classes, (1) astrologers, (2) Chaldeans, and (3) soothsayers. The word in the original (hakamim) probably means "medicine men. In Chaldea medicine was only a branch of magic. The "wise men" of Matt. 2:7, who came from the East to Jerusalem, were magi from Persia or Arabia.

wise, wisdom.d: a moral rather than an intellectual quality. To be "foolish" is to be godless (<reflink>Ps. 14:1; comp. Judg. 19:23; 2 Sam. 13:13</reflink>). True wisdom is a gift from God to those who ask it (<reflink>Job 28:12-28; Prov. 3:13-18; Rom. 1:22; 16:27; 1 Cor. 1:17-21; 2:6-8; James 1:5</reflink>). "Wisdom" in Prov. 1:20; 8:1; 9:1-5 may be regarded not as a mere personification of the attribute of wisdom, but as a divine person, "Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God" (<reflink>1 Cor. 1:24</reflink>). In Matt. 11:19 it is the personified principle of wisdom that is meant.

witch.d: Occurs only in Ex. 22:18, as the rendering of _mekhashshepheh_, the feminine form of the word, meaning "enchantress" (R.V., "sorceress"), and in Deut. 18:10, as the rendering of _mekhashshepheth_, the masculine form of the word, meaning "enchanter."

witchcraft.d: (<reflink>1 Sam. 15:23; 2 Kings 9:22; 2 Chr. 33:6; Micah 5:12; Nahum 3:4; Gal. 5:20</reflink>). In the popular sense of the word no mention is made either of witches or of witchcraft in Scripture.

witness.d: More than one witness was required in criminal cases (<reflink>Deut. 17:6; 19:15</reflink>). They were the first to execute the sentence on the condemned (<reflink>Deut. 13:9; 17:7; 1 Kings 21:13; Matt. 27:1; Acts 7:57, 58</reflink>). False witnesses were liable to punishment (<reflink>Deut. 19:16-21</reflink>). It was also an offence to refuse to bear witness (<reflink>Lev. 5:1</reflink>).

witness of the spirit.d: (<reflink>Rom. 8:16</reflink>), the consciousness of the gracious operation of the Spirit on the mind, "a certitude of the Spirit's presence and work continually asserted within us", manifested "in his comforting us, his stirring us up to prayer, his reproof of our sins, his drawing us to works of love, to bear testimony before the world," etc.

wizard.d: a pretender to supernatural knowledge and power, "a knowing one," as the original Hebrew word signifies. Such an one was forbidden on pain of death to practise his deceptions (<reflink>Lev. 19:31; 20:6, 27; 1 Sam. 28:3; Isa. 8:19; 19:3</reflink>).

wolf.d: Heb. zeeb, frequently referred to in Scripture as an emblem of treachery and cruelty. Jacob's prophecy, "Benjamin shall ravin as a wolf" (<reflink>Gen. 49:27</reflink>), represents the warlike character of that tribe (<see target="x-self">see Judg. 19-21</see>). Isaiah represents the peace of Messiah's kingdom by the words, "The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb" (<reflink>Isa. 11:6</reflink>). The habits of the wolf are described in Jer. 5:6; Hab. 1:8; Zeph. 3:3; Ezek. 22:27; Matt. 7:15; 10:16; Acts 20:29. Wolves are still sometimes found in Palestine, and are the dread of shepherds, as of old.

woman.d: was "taken out of man" (<reflink>Gen. 2:23</reflink>), and therefore the man has the preeminence. "The head of the woman is the man;" but yet honour is to be shown to the wife, "as unto the weaker vessel" (<reflink>1 Cor. 11:3, 8, 9; 1 Pet. 3:7</reflink>). Several women are mentioned in Scripture as having been endowed with prophetic gifts, as Miriam (<reflink>Ex. 15:20</reflink>), Deborah (<reflink>Judg. 4:4, 5</reflink>), Huldah (<reflink>2 Kings 22:14</reflink>), Noadiah (<reflink>Neh. 6:14</reflink>), Anna (<reflink>Luke 2:36, 37</reflink>), and the daughters of Philip the evangelist (<reflink>Acts 21:8, 9</reflink>). Women are forbidden to teach publicly (<reflink>1 Cor. 14:34, 35; 1 Tim. 2:11, 12</reflink>). Among the Hebrews it devolved upon women to prepare the meals for the household (<reflink>Gen. 18:6; 2 Sam. 13:8</reflink>), to attend to the work of spinning (<reflink>Ex. 35:26; Prov. 31:19</reflink>), and making clothes (<reflink>1 Sam. 2:19; Prov. …

wood-offering.d: (<reflink>Neh. 10:34; 13:31</reflink>). It would seem that in the time of Nehemiah arrangements were made, probably on account of the comparative scarcity of wood, by which certain districts were required, as chosen by lot, to furnish wood to keep the altar fire perpetually burning (<reflink>Lev. 6:13</reflink>).

wool.d: one of the first material used for making woven cloth (<reflink>Lev. 13:47, 48, 52, 59; 19:19</reflink>). The first-fruit of wool was to be offered to the priests (<reflink>Deut. 18:4</reflink>). The law prohibiting the wearing of a garment "of divers sorts, as of woollen and linen together" (<reflink>Deut. 22:11</reflink>) may, like some other laws of a similar character, have been intended to express symbolically the separateness and simplicity of God's covenant people. The wool of Damascus, famous for its whiteness, was of great repute in the Tyrian market (<reflink>Ezek. 27:18</reflink>).

word of god.d: (<reflink>Heb. 4:12, etc.</reflink>). The Bible so called because the writers of its several books were God's organs in communicating his will to men. It is his "word," because he speaks to us in its sacred pages. Whatever the inspired writers here declare to be true and binding upon us, God declares to be true and binding. This word is infallible, because written under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, and therefore free from all error of fact or doctrine or precept. (<see target="x-self">See INSPIRATION; </see>) All saving knowledge is obtained from the word of God. In the case of adults it is an indispensable means of salvation, and is efficacious thereunto by the gracious influence of the Holy Spirit (<reflink>John 17:17; 2 Tim. 3:15, 16; 1 Pet. 1:23</reflink>).

word, the.d: (Gr. Logos), one of the titles of our Lord, found only in the writings of John (<reflink>John 1:1-14; 1 John 1:1; Rev. 19:13</reflink>). As such, Christ is the revealer of God. His office is to make God known. "No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him" (<reflink>John 1:18</reflink>). This title designates the divine nature of Christ. As the Word, he "was in the beginning" and "became flesh." "The Word was with God " and "was God," and was the Creator of all things (<reflink>comp. Ps.33: 6; 107:20; 119:89; 147:18; Isa. 40:8</reflink>).

works, covenant of.d: entered into by God with Adam as the representative of the human race (<reflink>comp. Gen. 9:11, 12; 17:1-21</reflink>), so styled because perfect obedience was its condition, thus distinguishing it from the covenant of grace. (<see target="x-self">See COVENANT OF WORKS.</see>)

works, good.d: The old objection against the doctrine of salvation by grace, that it does away with the necessity of good works, and lowers the sense of their importance (Rom. 6), although it has been answered a thousand times, is still alleged by many. They say if men are not saved by works, then works are not necessary. If the most moral of men are saved in the same way as the very chief of sinners, then good works are of no moment. And more than this, if the grace of God is most clearly displayed in the salvation of the vilest of men, then the worse men are the better.

worm.d: (1.) Heb. sas (<reflink>Isa. 51:8</reflink>), denotes the caterpillar of the clothes-moth.

wormwood.d: Heb. la'anah, the Artemisia absinthium of botanists. It is noted for its intense bitterness (<reflink>Deut. 29:18; Prov. 5:4; Jer. 9:15; Amos 5:7</reflink>). It is a type of bitterness, affliction, remorse, punitive suffering. In Amos 6:12 this Hebrew word is rendered "hemlock" (R.V., "wormwood"). In the symbolical language of the Apocalypse (<reflink>Rev. 8:10, 11</reflink>) a star is represented as falling on the waters of the earth, causing the third part of the water to turn wormwood.

worship.d: homage rendered to God which it is sinful (idolatry) to render to any created being (<reflink>Ex. 34:14; Isa. 2:8</reflink>). Such worship was refused by Peter (<reflink>Acts 10:25,26</reflink>) and by an angel (<reflink>Rev. 22:8,9</reflink>).

worshipper.d: (Gr. neocoros = temple-sweeper (<reflink>Acts 19:35</reflink>) of the great goddess Diana). This name neocoros appears on most of the extant Ephesian coins

writing.d: The art of writing must have been known in the time of the early Pharaohs. Moses is commanded "to write for a memorial in a book" (<reflink>Ex. 17:14</reflink>) a record of the attack of Amalek. Frequent mention is afterwards made of writing (28:11, 21, 29, 36; 31:18; 32:15, 16; 34:1, 28; 39:6, 14, 30). The origin of this art is unknown, but there is reason to conclude that in the age of Moses it was well known. The inspired books of Moses are the most ancient extant writings, although there are written monuments as old as about B.C. 2000. The words expressive of "writing," "book," and "ink," are common to all the branches or dialects of the Semitic language, and hence it has been concluded that this art must have been known to the earliest Semites before they separated into their various tribes, and nations, and families.

yarn.d: Found only in 1 Kings 10:28, 2 Chr. 1:16. The Heb. word mikveh, i.e., "a stringing together," so rendered, rather signifies a host, or company, or a string of horses. The Authorized Version has: "And Solomon had horses brought out of Egypt, and linen yarn: the king's merchants received the linen yarn at a price;" but the Revised Version correctly renders: "And the horses which Solomon had were brought out of Egypt; the king's merchants received them in droves, each drove at a price."

year.d: Heb. shanah, meaning "repetition" or "revolution" (<reflink>Gen. 1:14; 5:3</reflink>). Among the ancient Egyptians the year consisted of twelve months of thirty days each, with five days added to make it a complete revolution of the earth round the sun. The Jews reckoned the year in two ways, (1) according to a sacred calendar, in which the year began about the time of the vernal equinox, with the month Abib; and (2) according to a civil calendar, in which the year began about the time of the autumnal equinox, with the month Nisan. The month Tisri is now the beginning of the Jewish year.

yeshebi.d: the Hebrew word rendered "inhabitants" in Josh. 17:7, but probably rather the name of the village Yeshepheh, probably Yassuf, 8 miles south of Shechem.

yoke.d: (1.) Fitted on the neck of oxen for the purpose of binding to them the traces by which they might draw the plough, etc. (<reflink>Num. 19:2; Deut. 21:3</reflink>). It was a curved piece of wood called _'ol_.

yoke-fellow.d: (<reflink>Phil. 4:3</reflink>), one of the apostle's fellow-labourers. Some have conjectured that Epaphroditus is meant. Wyckliffe renders the phrase "the german felowe", i.e., "thee, germane [=genuine] comrade."

zaanaim.d: wanderings; the unloading of tents, so called probably from the fact of nomads in tents encamping amid the cities and villages of that region, a place in the north-west of Lake Merom, near Kedesh, in Naphtali. Here Sisera was slain by Jael, "the wife of Heber the Kenite," who had pitched his tent in the "plain [R.V., 'as far as the oak'] of Zaanaim" (<reflink>Judg. 4:11</reflink>).

zaanan.d: place of flocks, mentioned only in Micah 1:11. It may be identified with Zenan, in the plain country of Judah (<reflink>Josh. 15:37</reflink>).

zaavan.d: terror, one of the "dukes of Edom" (<reflink>Gen. 36:27</reflink>); called also Zavan (<reflink>1 Chr. 1:42</reflink>).

zabad.d: gift. (1.) One of David's valiant men (<reflink>1 Chr. 11:41</reflink>), the descendant of Ahlai, of the "children of Sheshan" (2:31).

zabdi.d: gift of Jehovah. (1.) An ancestor of Achan (<reflink>Josh. 7:1, 17, 18</reflink>). He is probably the "Zimri" of 1 Chr. 2:6.

zabdiel.d: gift of God. (1.) The father of Jashobeam, who was one of David's officers (<reflink>1 Chr. 27:2</reflink>).

zabud.d: gift, the son of Nathan, who was "king's friend" in the court of Solomon (<reflink>1 Kings 4:5</reflink>).

zaccai.d: pure, one whose "sons" returned with Zerubbabel to Jerusalem (<reflink>Ezra 2:9; Neh. 7:14</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See ZABBAI.</see>)

zacchaeus.d: pure, a superintendant of customs; a chief tax-gather (publicanus) at Jericho (<reflink>Luke 19:1-10</reflink>). "The collection of customs at Jericho, which at this time produced and exported a considerable quantity of balsam, was undoubtedly an important post, and would account for Zacchaeus being a rich man." Being short of stature, he hastened on before the multitude who were thronging about Christ as he passed through Jericho on his way to Jerusalem, and climbed up a sycamore tree that he might be able to see him. When our Lord reached the spot he looked up to the publican among the branches, and addressing him by name, told him to make haste and come down, as he intended that day to abide at his house. This led to the remarkable interview recorded by the evangelist, and to the striking parable of the ten pounds (<reflink>Luke 19:12-27</reflink>). At Er-riha (Jericho) there is a large, venerable looking square tower, which goes by the traditional name of the House of Zacchaeus.

zaccur.d: mindful. (1.) Father of Shammua, who was one of the spies sent out by Moses (<reflink>Num. 13:4</reflink>).

zachariah.d: remembered by the Lord. (1.) Son of Jeroboam II., king of Israel. On the death of his father there was an interregnum of ten years, at the end of which he succeeded to the throne, which he occupied only six months, having been put to death by Shallum, who usurped the throne. "He did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord, as his fathers had done" (<reflink>2 Kings 14:29; 15:8-12</reflink>). In him the dynasty of Jehu came to an end.

zacharias.d: (1.) A priest of the course of Abia, the eighth of the twenty-four courses into which the priests had been originally divided by David (<reflink>1 Chr. 23:1-19</reflink>). Only four of these courses or "families" of the priests returned from the Exile (<reflink>Ezra 2:36-39</reflink>); but they were then re-distributed under the old designations. The priests served at the temple twice each year, and only for a week each time. Zacharias's time had come for this service. During this period his home would be one of the chambers set apart for the priests on the sides of the temple ground. The offering of incense was one of the most solemn parts of the daily worship of the temple, and lots were drawn each day to determine who should have this great honour, an honour which no priest could enjoy more than once during his lifetime.

zacher.d: memorial, a son of Jehiel (<reflink>1 Chr. 8:31; 9:35</reflink>); called Zechariah (9:37).

zadok.d: righteous. (1.) A son of Ahitub, of the line of Eleazer (<reflink>2 Sam. 8:17; 1 Chr. 24:3</reflink>), high priest in the time of David (<reflink>2 Sam. 20:25</reflink>) and Solomon (<reflink>1 Kings 4:4</reflink>). He is first mentioned as coming to take part with David at Hebron (<reflink>1 Chr. 12:27, 28</reflink>). He was probably on this account made ruler over the Aaronites (27:17). Zadok and Abiathar acted as high priests on several important occasions (<reflink>1 Chr. 15:11; 2 Sam. 15:24-29, 35, 36</reflink>); but when Adonijah endeavoured to secure the throne, Abiathar went with him, and therefore Solomon "thrust him out from being high priest," and Zadok, remaining faithful to David, became high priest alone (<reflink>1 Kings 2:27, 35; 1 Chr. 29:22</reflink>). In him the line of Phinehas resumed the dignity, and held it till the fall of Jerusalem. He was succeeded in his sacred office by his son Azariah (<reflink>1 Kings 4:2; comp. 1 Chr. 6:3-9</reflink>).

zair.d: little, a place probably east of the Dead Sea, where Joram discomfited the host of Edom who had revolted from him (<reflink>2 Kings 8:21</reflink>).

zalmon.d: shady. (1.) One of David's warriors, called the Ahohite (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:28</reflink>); called also Ilai (<reflink>1 Chr. 11:29</reflink>).

zalmonah.d: shady, one of the stations of the Israelites in the wilderness (<reflink>Num. 33:41, 42</reflink>).

zalmunna.d: one of the two kings of Midian whom the "Lord delivered" into the hands of Gideon. He was slain afterwards with Zebah (<reflink>Judg. 8:5-21</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See ZEBAH.</see>)

zamzummims.d: a race of giants; "a people great, and many, and tall, as the Anakims" (<reflink>Deut. 2:20, 21</reflink>). They were overcome by the Ammonites, "who called them Zamzummims." They belonged to the Rephaim, and inhabited the country afterwards occupied by the Ammonites. It has been conjectured that they might be Ham-zuzims, i.e., Zuzims dwelling in Ham, a place apparently to the south of Ashteroth (<reflink>Gen. 14:5</reflink>), the ancient Rabbath-ammon.

zanoah.d: marsh. (1.) A town in the low country or shephelah of Judah, near Zorah (<reflink>Josh. 15:34</reflink>). It was re-occupied after the return from the Captivity (<reflink>Neh. 11:30</reflink>). Zanu'ah in Wady Ismail, 10 miles west of Jerusalem, occupies probably the same site.

zaphnath-paaneah.d: the name which Pharaoh gave to Joseph when he raised him to the rank of prime minister or grand vizier of the kingdom (<reflink>Gen. 41:45</reflink>). This is a pure Egyptian word, and has been variously explained. Some think it means "creator," or "preserver of life." Brugsch interprets it as "governor of the district of the place of life", i.e., of Goshen, the chief city of which was Pithom, "the place of life." Others explain it as meaning "a revealer of secrets," or "the man to whom secrets are revealed."

zarephath.d: smelting-shop, "a workshop for the refining and smelting of metals", a small Phoenician town, now Surafend, about a mile from the coast, almost midway on the road between Tyre and Sidon. Here Elijah sojourned with a poor widow during the "great famine," when the "heaven was shut up three years and six months" (<reflink>Luke 4:26; 1 Kings 17:10</reflink>). It is called Sarepta in the New Testament (<reflink>Luke 4:26</reflink>).

zaretan.d: When the Hebrews crossed the Jordan, as soon as the feet of the priests were dipped in the water, the flow of the stream was arrested. The point of arrest was the "city of Adam beside Zaretan," probably near Succoth, at the mouth of the Jabbok, some 30 miles up the river from where the people were encamped. There the water "stood and rose upon an heap." Thus the whole space of 30 miles of the river-bed was dry, that the tribes might pass over (<reflink>Josh. 3:16, 17; comp. Ps. 104:3</reflink>).

zareth-shahar.d: the splendour of the dawn, a city "in the mount of the valley" (<reflink>Josh. 13:19</reflink>). It is identified with the ruins of Zara, near the mouth of the Wady Zerka Main, on the eastern shore of the Dead Sea, some 3 miles south of the Callirrhoe. Of this town but little remains. "A few broken basaltic columns and pieces of wall about 200 yards back from the shore, and a ruined fort rather nearer the sea, about the middle of the coast line of the plain, are all that are left" (Tristram's Land of Moab).

zarthan.d: a place near Succoth, in the plain of the Jordan, "in the clay ground," near which Hiram cast the brazen utensils for the temple (<reflink>1 Kings 7:46</reflink>); probably the same as Zartan. It is also called Zeredathah (<reflink>2 Chr. 4:17</reflink>). (<see target="x-self">See ZEREDA.</see>)

zattu.d: id., one whose descendants returned from the Captivity with Zerubbabel (<reflink>Ezra 2:8; Neh. 7:13</reflink>); probably the same as Zatthu.

zaza.d: plenty, a descendant of Judah (<reflink>1 Chr. 2:33</reflink>).

zeal.d: an earnest temper; may be enlightened (<reflink>Num. 25:11-13; 2 Cor. 7:11; 9:2</reflink>), or ignorant and misdirected (<reflink>Rom. 10:2; Phil. 3:6</reflink>). As a Christian grace, it must be grounded on right principles and directed to right ends (<reflink>Gal. 4:18</reflink>). It is sometimes ascribed to God (<reflink>2 Kings 19:31; Isa. 9:7; 37:32; Ezek. 5:13</reflink>).

zealots.d: a sect of Jews which originated with Judas the Gaulonite (<reflink>Acts 5:37</reflink>). They refused to pay tribute to the Romans, on the ground that this was a violation of the principle that God was the only king of Israel. They rebelled against the Romans, but were soon scattered, and became a lawless band of mere brigands. They were afterwards called Sicarii, from their use of the sica, i.e., the Roman dagger.

zebadiah.d: gift of Jehovah. (1.) A son of Asahel, Joab's brother (<reflink>1 Chr. 27:7</reflink>).

zebah.d: man-killer, or sacrifice, one of the two kings who led the vast host of the Midianites who invaded the land of Israel, and over whom Gideon gained a great and decisive victory (Judg. 8). Zebah and Zalmunna had succeeded in escaping across the Jordan with a remnant of the Midianite host, but were overtaken at Karkor, probably in the Hauran, and routed by Gideon. The kings were taken alive and brought back across the Jordan; and confessing that they had personally taken part in the slaughter of Gideon's brothers, they were put to death (comp. 1 Sam. 12:11; Isa. 10:26; Ps. 83:11).

zebaim.d: (<reflink>Ezra 2:57; Neh. 7:59</reflink>). "Pochereth of Zebaim" should be read as in the Revised Version, "Pochereth-hazzebaim" ("snaring the antelopes"), probably the name of some hunter.

zebedee.d: a Galilean fisherman, the husband of Salome (q.v.), and the father of James and John, two of our Lord's disciples (<reflink>Matt. 4:21; 27:56; Mark 15:40</reflink>). He seems to have been a man of some position in Capernaum, for he had two boats (<reflink>Luke 5:4</reflink>) and "hired servants" (<reflink>Mark 1:20</reflink>) of his own. No mention is made of him after the call of his two sons by Jesus.

zeboim.d: gazelles or roes. (1.) One of the "five cities of the plain" of Sodom, generally coupled with Admah (<reflink>Gen. 10:19; 14:2; Deut. 29:23; Hos. 11:8</reflink>). It had a king of its own (Shemeber), and was therefore a place of some importance. It was destroyed along with the other cities of the plain.

zebudah.d: given, the wife of Josiah and mother of Jehoiakim (<reflink>2 Kings 23:36</reflink>).

zebul.d: habitation, the governor of Shechem under Abimelech (<reflink>Judg. 9:28, 30, 36</reflink>). He informed his master of the intention of the people of Shechem to transfer their allegiance to the Hivite tribe of Hamor. This led to Abimelech's destroying the city, when he put its entire population to the sword, and sowed the ruins with salt (<reflink>Judg. 9:28-45</reflink>).

zebulonite.d: the designation of Elon, the judge who belonged to the tribe of Zebulun (<reflink>Judg. 12:11, 12</reflink>).

zebulun.d: dwelling, the sixth and youngest son of Jacob and Leah (<reflink>Gen. 30:20</reflink>). Little is known of his personal history. He had three sons (46:14).

zebulun, lot of.d: in Galilee, to the north of Issachar and south of Asher and Naphtali (<reflink>Josh. 19:10-16</reflink>), and between the Sea of Galilee and the Mediterranean. According to ancient prophecy this part of Galilee enjoyed a large share of our Lord's public ministry (<reflink>Isa. 9:1, 2; Matt. 4:12-16</reflink>).

zebulun, tribe of.d: numbered at Sinai (<reflink>Num. 1:31</reflink>) and before entering Canaan (26:27). It was one of the tribes which did not drive out the Canaanites, but only made them tributary (<reflink>Judg. 1:30</reflink>). It took little interest in public affairs. It responded, however, readily to the summons of Gideon (6:35), and afterwards assisted in enthroning David at Hebron (<reflink>1 Chr. 12:33, 40</reflink>). Along with the other northern tribes, Zebulun was carried away into the land of Assyria by Tiglath-pileser (<reflink>2 Kings 15:29</reflink>).

zechariah.d: Jehovah is renowned or remembered. (1.) A prophet of Judah, the eleventh of the twelve minor prophets. Like Ezekiel, he was of priestly extraction. He describes himself (1:1) as "the son of Berechiah." In Ezra 5:1 and 6:14 he is called "the son of Iddo," who was properly his grandfather. His prophetical career began in the second year of Darius (B.C. 520), about sixteen years after the return of the first company from exile. He was contemporary with Haggai (<reflink>Ezra 5:1</reflink>).

zedad.d: side; sloping place, a town in the north of Palestine, near Hamath (<reflink>Num. 34:8; Ezek. 47:15</reflink>). It has been identified with the ruins of Sudud, between Emesa (Hums) and Baalbec, but that is uncertain.

zedekiah.d: righteousness of Jehovah. (1.) The last king of Judah. He was the third son of Josiah, and his mother's name was Hamutal, the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah, and hence he was the brother of Jehoahaz (<reflink>2 Kings 23:31; 24:17, 18</reflink>). His original name was Mattaniah; but when Nebuchadnezzar placed him on the throne as the successor to Jehoiachin he changed his name to Zedekiah. The prophet Jeremiah was his counsellor, yet "he did evil in the sight of the Lord" (<reflink>2 Kings 24:19, 20; Jer. 52:2, 3</reflink>). He ascended the throne at the age of twenty-one years. The kingdom was at that time tributary to Nebuchadnezzar; but, despite the strong remonstrances of Jeremiah and others, as well as the example of Jehoiachin, he threw off the yoke of Babylon, and entered into an alliance with Hophra, king of Egypt. This brought up Nebuchadnezzar, "with all his host" (<reflink>2 King 25:1</reflink>), against Jerusalem. …

zeeb.d: the wolf, one of the two leaders of the great Midianite host which invaded Israel and was utterly routed by Gideon. The division of that host, which attempted to escape across the Jordan, under Oreb and Zeeb, was overtaken by the Ephraimites, who, in a great battle, completely vanquished them, their leaders being taken and slain (<reflink>Judg. 7:25; Ps. 83:11; Isa. 10:26</reflink>).

zelah.d: slope; side, a town in Benjamin, where Saul and his son Jonathan were buried (<reflink>2 Sam. 21:14</reflink>). It was probably Saul's birthplace.

zelek.d: cleft, an Ammonite; one of David's valiant men (<reflink>2 Sam. 23:37</reflink>).

zelophehad.d: first-born, of the tribe of Manasseh, and of the family of Gilead; died in the wilderness. Having left no sons, his daughters, concerned lest their father's name should be "done away from among his family," made an appeal to Moses, who, by divine direction, appointed it as "a statute of judgment" in Israel that daughters should inherit their father's portion when no sons were left (<reflink>Num. 27:1-11</reflink>). But that the possession of Zelophehad might not pass away in the year of jubilee from the tribe to which he belonged, it was ordained by Moses that his daughters should not marry any one out of their father's tribe; and this afterwards became a general law (Num. 36).

zemaraim.d: (1.) A town of Benjamin (<reflink>Josh. 18:22</reflink>); now the ruin, rather two ruins, es-Sumrah, 4 miles north of Jericho.

zemarite.d: the designation of one of the Phoenician tribes (<reflink>Gen. 10:18</reflink>) who inhabited the town of Sumra, at the western base of the Lebanon range. In the Amarna tablets (B.C. 1400) Zemar, or Zumur, was one of the most important of the Phoenician cities, but it afterwards almost disappears from history.

zemira.d: vine-dresser, a Benjamite; one of the sons of Becher (<reflink>1 Chr. 7:8</reflink>).

zenas.d: a disciple called "the lawyer," whom Paul wished Titus to bring with him (<reflink>Titus 3:13</reflink>). Nothing more is known of him.

zephaniah.d: Jehovah has concealed, or Jehovah of darkness. (1.) The son of Cushi, and great-grandson of Hezekiah, and the ninth in the order of the minor prophets. He prophesied in the days of Josiah, king of Judah (B.C. 641-610), and was contemporary with Jeremiah, with whom he had much in common. The book of his prophecies consists of:

zephath.d: beacon; watch-tower, a Canaanite town; called also Hormah (q.v.), Judg. 1:17. It has been identified with the pass of es-Sufah, but with greater probability with S'beita.

zephathah.d: a valley in the west of Judah, near Mareshah; the scene of Asa's conflict with Zerah the Ethiopian (<reflink>2 Chr. 14:9-13</reflink>). Identified with the Wady Safieh.

zerah.d: sunrise. (1.) An "Ethiopian," probably Osorkon II., the successor of Shishak on the throne of Egypt. With an enormous army, the largest we read of in Scripture, he invaded the kingdom of Judah in the days of Asa (<reflink>2 Chr. 14:9-15</reflink>). He reached Zephathah, and there encountered the army of Asa. This is the only instance "in all the annals of Judah of a victorious encounter in the field with a first-class heathen power in full force." The Egyptian host was utterly routed, and the Hebrews gathered "exceeding much spoil." Three hundred years elapsed before another Egyptian army, that of Necho (B.C. 609), came up against Jerusalem.

zered.d: =Zared, luxuriance; willow bush, a brook or valley communicating with the Dead Sea near its southern extremity (<reflink>Num. 21:12; Deut. 2:14</reflink>). It is called the "brook of the willows" (<reflink>Isa. 15:7</reflink>) and the "river of the wilderness" (<reflink>Amos 6:14</reflink>). It has been identified with the Wady el-Aksy.

zereda.d: the fortress, a city on the north of Mount Ephraim; the birthplace of Jeroboam (<reflink>1 Kings 11:26</reflink>). It is probably the same as Zaretan (<reflink>Josh. 3:16</reflink>), Zererath (<reflink>Judg. 7:22</reflink>), Zartanah (<reflink>1 Kings 4:12</reflink>), or the following.

zeredathah.d: a place in the plain of Jordan; the same as Zarthan (<reflink>2 Chr. 4:17; 1 Kings 7:46</reflink>). Here Solomon erected the foundries in which Hiram made the great castings of bronze for the temple.

zererath.d: (<reflink>Judg. 7:22</reflink>), perhaps identical with Zereda or Zeredathah. Some identify it with Zahrah, a place about 3 miles west of Beth-shean.

zeresh.d: star of Venus, the wife of Haman, whom she instigated to prepare a gallows for Mordecai (<reflink>Esther 5:10</reflink>).

zeruah.d: stricken, mother of Jeroboam, the first king of the ten tribes (<reflink>1 Kings 11:26</reflink>).

zerubbabel.d: the seed of Babylon, the son of Salathiel or Shealtiel (<reflink>Hag. 1:1; Zorobabel, Matt. 1:12</reflink>); called also the son of Pedaiah (<reflink>1 Chr. 3:17-19</reflink>), i.e., according to a frequent usage of the word "son;" the grandson or the nephew of Salathiel. He is also known by the Persian name of Sheshbazzar (<reflink>Ezra 1:8, 11</reflink>). In the first year of Cyrus, king of Persia, he led the first band of Jews, numbering 42,360 (<reflink>Ezra 2:64</reflink>), exclusive of a large number of servants, who returned from captivity at the close of the seventy years. In the second year after the Return, he erected an altar and laid the foundation of the temple on the ruins of that which had been destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar (3:8-13; ch. 4-6). All through the work he occupied a prominent place, inasmuch as he was a descendant of the royal line of David.

zeruiah.d: stricken of the Lord, David's sister, and the mother of Abishai, Joab, and Asahel (<reflink>1 Chr. 2:16</reflink>), who were the three leading heroes of David's army, and being his nephews, they were admitted to the closest companionship with him.

ziba.d: post; statue, "a servant of the house of Saul" (<reflink>2 Sam. 9:2</reflink>), who informed David that Mephibosheth, a son of Jonathan, was alive. He afterwards dealt treacherously toward Mephibosheth, whom he slanderously misrepresented to David.

zibiah.d: the mother of King Joash (<reflink>2 Kings 12:1; 2 Chr. 24:1</reflink>).

zichri.d: remembered; illustrious. (1.) A Benjamite chief (<reflink>1 Chr. 8:19</reflink>).

zuph.d: honeycomb, a Kohathite Levite, ancestor of Elkanah and Samuel (<reflink>1 Sam. 1:1</reflink>); called also Zophai (<reflink>1 Chr. 6:26</reflink>).

zuph, land of.d: (<reflink>1 Sam. 9:5, 6</reflink>), a district in which lay Samuel's city, Ramah. It was probably so named after Elkanah's son, Zuph (<reflink>1 Chr. 6:26, marg.</reflink>).

zur.d: rock. (1.) One of the five Midianite kings whom the Israelites defeated and put to death (<reflink>Num. 31:8</reflink>).

zuriel.d: rock of God, chief of the family of the Merarites (<reflink>Num. 3:35</reflink>) at the time of the Exodus.

zurishaddai.d: rock of the Almighty, the father of Shelumiel, who was chief of the tribe of Simeon when Israel was encamped at Sinai (<reflink>Num. 1:6; 2:12</reflink>).

zuzims.d: restless; sprouting, were smitten "in Ham" by Chedorlaomer and his allies (<reflink>Gen. 14:5</reflink>). Some have identified this tribe with the Zamzummims (q.v.).
